The seven parables in this chapter outline the course of the kingdom in its mystery form during the present age while the King is absent, revealing truths that have historically puzzled those who attempt to spiritualize the literal, earthly Messianic kingdom within the structure of the present-day Church.
[3-9, 18-23] The parable of the sower establishes the inescapable hermeneutical rule that every detail in Christ's parables possesses precise doctrinal significance. The sower is the Son of Man, and the seed is the word of the kingdom. The birds of the air typify the unclean spirits or demons sent by Satan (Revelation 18:2). The four types of soil represent the hearts of the hearers: along the path are those who are lost and whose seed is immediately snatched away; on rocky ground are those who receive the word with joy but, lacking inner root, are offended and stumble when tribulation or persecution arises because of the word; among thorns are those choked by a trinity of temptations: worry, the deceitfulness of riches, and the pleasures of this life; and the good soil represents those who understand, retain the word, and bear fruit thirty, sixty, and a hundredfold.
[10-17] The purpose of teaching by parables is not to simplify the message for the masses, but to deliberately conceal the truth from those who have hardened their hearts and rejected the previous light (Isaiah 6:9-10). By rejecting the Messiah, the nation of Israel experiences a judicial blindness imparted by God Himself; revelation is veiled so that seeing they do not see and hearing they do not understand. Spiritual truth is reserved exclusively for the disciples, who in this historical context represent the Jewish remnant that believes despite the nation's apostasy.
[24-30, 36-43] The parable of the weeds and the wheat exposes the work of Satan infiltrating counterfeits within the ranks. The field is explicitly and directly identified as the world, not the church. The good seed are the children of the kingdom, and the weeds are the children of the evil one, sown by the devil while the servants slept. The fiery furnace mentioned is not metaphorical, but the literal fire of hell, indicating the final destiny of the wicked. The prophetic order of the harvest at the end of the world is highlighted: first the weeds are gathered and tied in bundles to be burned, and later the angels gather the wheat into the barn, an event that points eschatologically to the premillennial judgments and the physical separation on earth.
[31-32] The mustard seed does not represent the progressive and global triumph of the gospel, as opposed to postmillennialist positions. Since mustard is naturally a herb, its growth into an immense tree denotes an abnormal mutation and monstrous growth. The birds nesting in its branches are the same demons mentioned in verse 4. This indicates that the religious system developed during this era, which harbors and shelters unclean spirits, corresponds to the Babylonian system of apostate Christianity.
[33] The parable of the yeast maintains the consistent biblical typology where yeast always represents sin or false doctrine, specifically that of the Pharisees and scribes (Matthew 16:6-12; 1 Corinthians 5:6-8). The woman never represents the true church in Scripture, but rather the great harlot (Revelation 17:4-5), who surreptitiously introduces corrupt doctrines within the three measures of flour, which typify the children of the kingdom. This prophesies the total doctrinal corruption of professing Christendom.
[44] The treasure hidden in the field is the nation of Israel, consistently identified as God's peculiar treasure in the Old Testament (Exodus 19:5; Psalm 135:4). The man is Jesus Christ, who purchases the entire field (the world) by shedding his own blood. Upon finding Israel, he does not hide the treasure, but, in the original language, temporarily hides himself from the nation because of their rejection (Deuteronomy 31:17).
[45-46] The pearl of great price illustrates the true Church, the organic body of Christ. Unlike inorganic minerals, the pearl is a living organism that forms in the depths of the sea due to irritation or injury, covering the affliction with a secretion, which typifies the formation of the Church through suffering. The merchant (Jesus Christ) goes and sells all he has, making himself poor to enrich others (2 Corinthians 8:9), and buys it back with the infinite price of his blood.
[47-50] The sweeping net cast into the sea corresponds to the gathering of the nations and the final judgment at the end of the age. Angels will function as reapers who will physically separate the wicked from the righteous to throw them into the fiery furnace where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. This event does not describe a peaceful conversion of the world, but a violent and literal eschatological judgment of separation.
[51-52] The scribe learned in the kingdom of heaven is compared to a householder who brings out of his storeroom new things as well as old. This establishes the theological principle for the correct interpretation of progressive revelation. It demonstrates that true biblical understanding requires extracting and harmoniously balancing the truths of the Old Testament illuminated by the New, and the doctrines of the New Testament grounded in the Old.

[1-2] The narrative begins with Herod the tetrarch hearing of Jesus' fame and concluding that John the Baptist has risen from the dead. Herod's statement reveals a guilty conscience regarding John's murder and an underlying knowledge of Old Testament prophecies about the resurrection and return of Elijah before the Lord's coming (Malachi 4:5).
[3-12] The retrospective narrative of John the Baptist's imprisonment and death illustrates the attitude and morality of a sinner who rejects God. Herod fears the crowd, ridicule, his own conscience, and breaking his oath—in other words, he fears everything he should not fear and lacks the fear he should have before God (Matthew 10:27-28). Prophetically, John's beheading has direct doctrinal significance: as a precursor and type of Elijah, John suffers death by beheading, foreshadowing the exact manner in which Elijah and the martyrs will die during the Great Tribulation (Revelation 11:3-10; Revelation 20:3-6).
[13-14] Upon hearing the news of John's death, Jesus withdraws to a deserted place. Seeing the large crowd following him, he is moved with compassion and heals their sick. The original term for compassion alludes to the bowels, indicating that the emotional pain over the condition of the multitudes physically affects the Lord, demonstrating His perfect humanity and His absolute capacity to sympathize with human weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).
[15-19] The miraculous feeding occurs at dusk in a deserted place that, contrary to a sandy wasteland, has abundant green grass (John 6:10). Doctrinally and prophetically, this supernatural provision of bread in the desert foreshadows the feeding of the faithful remnant of Israel during the Great Tribulation, when they flee to the desert escaping the persecution of the Antichrist and God miraculously sustains them with manna from heaven (Revelation 12:6, 14; Micah 7:14-15; Jeremiah 50:19-20). Taking the loaves, Jesus blesses and breaks them; Spiritually, the word of God must be broken to be distributed, and the individual himself must be broken by God to be a blessing to others (2 Corinthians 12:1-8).
[20-21] The crowd eats until they are satisfied, and twelve baskets full of leftover pieces are collected. The total number fed easily exceeds ten or fifteen thousand individuals, when counting "five thousand men, besides women and children." The event constitutes a genuine miracle of creation from five loaves and two fish, refuting any attempt at rationalization that suggests the crowd simply shared food they had hidden.
[22-25] Jesus dismisses the crowd and goes up the mountain to pray alone, while the disciples face a storm on the sea. In the "fourth watch of the night" (between three and six in the morning), Jesus walks on the sea toward them. Typologically, this event illustrates the Church Age: the Lord is on high interceding for His own (Romans 8:34), the disciples are going through storms and contrary winds in the world (Ephesians 4:14), and the Lord will physically return for them in the fourth watch, which corresponds to the morning watch in Scripture, pointing to His Second Coming (Malachi 4:2; 2 Peter 1:19).
[26-29] The disciples are troubled, thinking they see a spirit, and cry out in fear. The Lord immediately comforts them. Peter asks to come to Him on the water, demonstrating an initial faith that leads him to get out of the boat. Peter walks on water, which reaffirms the supernatural nature of the event, invalidating critical positions that attempt to explain the miracle as if Christ were walking on ice or shallow sandbanks.
[30-33] Seeing the strength of the wind, Peter is afraid and begins to sink, crying out for salvation. Immediately Jesus reaches out his hand, rescues him, and rebukes his lack of faith. As they both get into the boat, the wind miraculously ceases. Those in the boat then worship him, saying, "Truly you are the Son of God." Jesus accepts this worship without objection. If he were not God manifested in the flesh, accepting such worship would make him a blasphemous imposter; his acceptance of human veneration fully validates his absolute Deity.
[34-36] After crossing the sea, they arrive at the land of Gennesaret. The men of the place recognize Jesus and bring all the sick so that they may touch only the edge of his cloak. All who manage to touch him are completely healed, demonstrating once again his undeniable authority over all illness and physical affliction among the people.

[1-2] The scribes and Pharisees from Jerusalem approach, questioning why the disciples break the "tradition of the elders" by not washing their hands before eating. This encounter highlights the biblical pattern in which religious opposition invariably accompanies the work of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 12:14, Matthew 14:2). The religious leaders are meticulously concerned with outward purification and cleanliness, but they harbor hearts full of impurity and hypocrisy (Matthew 23:25). This tradition did not come from the Law but was a human invention, classified as doctrines and commandments of men (Colossians 2:8).
[3-6] The Lord does not directly answer their question but rebukes them, pointing out that they have invalidated God's commandment through their tradition. He cites the commandments to honor one's father and mother, and the death penalty for anyone who cursed their parents (Exodus 20:12; Exodus 21:17). The Pharisees evaded the responsibility of supporting their parents in their old age by using "Corban," which consisted of dedicating their possessions to the temple as a gift to God. Under this legal subterfuge, the son would give a portion to the priests, keep another portion for himself, and leave his parents destitute, thus remaining free from guilt according to rabbinic tradition (Leviticus 27).
[7-9] Jesus Christ condemns them as hypocrites, declaring that the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled in them, for they honor God with their lips, but their hearts are far from him. This demonstrates that the greatest damage to Scripture does not always come from secular enemies, but from scholars and religious leaders who place their human traditions above the word of God, rendering it ineffective. True worship demands adoration in spirit and in truth (John 4:24), so the observance of purely human rites makes worship a vain act.
[10-14] Addressing the crowd, the Lord clarifies that what goes into the mouth does not defile a person, but what comes out of the mouth. Upon being informed that the Pharisees were offended, he declares, “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be pulled up by the roots.” This “plant” refers not only to reprobate individuals but encompasses the entire Pharisaic religious system, with its doctrines and traditions. Christ then describes them as “blind guides of the blind.” Those religious leaders lacked spiritual regeneration and were headed for destruction, leading their followers into the same pit (Proverbs 23:27; Revelation 17).
[15-20] At Peter's request, Jesus explains that what enters the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled. This infallible statement destroys pagan sacramental doctrines that maintain that the ingestion of physical elements (as in the Mass) bestows saving grace or mystical properties upon the soul (1 Corinthians 11:29). True defilement comes from the heart of the natural man, which produces "evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies." This list describes the human condition and serves as a direct prophecy of the crimes those same Pharisees would later perpetrate by conspiring, bearing false witness, and murdering the Messiah (Matthew 22:15; John 12:10).
[21-24] Jesus Christ withdraws to the coasts of Tyre and Sidon, where he is approached by a Canaanite (Syrophoenician) woman. Despite her Gentile and Hamitic origin, she cries out for mercy for her demon-possessed daughter, using the messianic title "Son of David." Initially, the Lord does not answer her a word, testing her faith. When the disciples ask Him to send her away, He responds, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,” establishing His earthly and historical jurisdiction as the minister of the circumcised (Romans 15:8).
[25-28] The woman falls down before Him in worship (Matthew 15:25), thus acknowledging His divinity. The Lord tests her again with apparent rudeness, saying, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” In biblical language, dogs typify lost and unclean Gentiles (Psalm 22:16; Philippians 3:2; Revelation 22:15). Instead of taking offense and reacting with pride, she assumes a position of humility and responds, “Yes, Lord; but even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.” By demonstrating such importunity and faith, Christ breaks His immediate dispensational limits, commends her faith, and heals the daughter at that very hour. God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (1 Peter 5:5).
[29-31] The Lord returns to the vicinity of the Sea of ​​Galilee. Great multitudes come, bringing the lame, the blind, the mute, and the crippled, throwing them at His feet to be healed. The multitudes are amazed at the complete physical healings and glorify the God of Israel. Historically, corrupt copyists attempted to omit the phrase "the crippled healed" from manuscripts such as the Sinaiticus, in an attempt to diminish the glory of the God of Israel by mutilating the sacred text.
[32-39] The feeding of four thousand men is recounted, not counting women and children, which indicates a crowd of eight to twelve thousand people. The Lord is moved with compassion when he sees that they have been with Him for three days without food, fearing they might faint on the way. The disciples, displaying remarkable hardness of heart and lack of understanding after having witnessed a similar miracle, question where they will get bread in the desert. Upon learning that they have seven loaves and a few small fish, Christ tells the crowd to sit down, gives thanks, breaks the bread, and distributes it. They gather seven baskets full of the leftovers. Prophetically, this miracle of creating bread in the desert foreshadows how God will miraculously feed and sustain the remnant of Israel who will flee from the Antichrist to the mountains during the Great Tribulation, giving them food from heaven (Revelation 12:6, 14; Micah 7:14-15).

[1-3] The Pharisees and Sadducees join together to ask for a sign from heaven. The Lord rebukes them for their ability to discern the physical weather while being blind to the spiritual signs of the times. The sign from heaven points eschatologically to the Second Coming of Jesus Christ (Matthew 24:30), when the Lord will literally descend from heaven. Modern and Catholic texts frequently omit verse 3 due to their postmillennial theology, which resents the prophetic implications of predicting the future.
[6-12] Jesus Christ warns his disciples to beware of the "leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees." In Scripture, leaven never represents the gospel but always typifies corruption, sin, or false doctrine (1 Corinthians 5:6-8; Galatians 5:9). The disciples initially misinterpret the warning literally, thinking of physical bread. The doctrine of the Pharisees includes calling religious leaders Father (Matthew 23:9), wearing long robes, offering lengthy prayers for the dead, and elevating human tradition above the word of God, while the Sadducees deny the literal resurrection and the existence of angels (Acts 23:8).
[16-18] This passage establishes a fundamental distinction in the original languages ​​and in the English text between Peter and the Rock. Simon confesses that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. In response, the Lord uses a contrasting term: Peter ("petros" or "petrus") means a small stone, while the Rock ("petra" or "petram") upon which the church is built refers to an immense rock, that is, Jesus Christ himself. The Old and New Testaments unanimously affirm that the only Rock is God and Jesus Christ (Deuteronomy 32:31; 1 Corinthians 10:4; 1 Peter 2:4-8). Building a church on Simon Peter is equivalent to building on Satan, as Christ Himself calls Peter five verses later (Matthew 16:23). Furthermore, the gates of hell are not spiritual powers, as modern translations claim, but literal gates with bars and keys (Jonah 2:6; Revelation 1:18). The church mentioned here in this transitional context was to come out of hell (Abraham's bosom) after Christ took the keys and led captivity captive in His resurrection (Ephesians 4:8).
[19] The keys given to Peter are not the keys to heaven to let people in, but the keys to the "kingdom of heaven," which is the physical, literal, and earthly kingdom. Biblically, a door represents an opportunity to preach the gospel (1 Corinthians 16:9), and Peter used these keys to open the door of faith to the Jews (Acts 2) and later to the Gentiles (Acts 10). The power to bind and loose on earth was not exclusive to Peter but was delegated to all twelve apostles (Matthew 18:18) and to ordinary believers for the retention or remission of sins through the preaching of the gospel (John 20:23).
[21-23] Jesus Christ predicts with astonishing accuracy ten specific details of His future death and resurrection, which demonstrates His deity. Peter, motivated by human affection but ignorant of the atoning purpose, rebukes his Lord. Christ's stern response reveals that Satan can use even a believer's good intentions to oppose God's will. This definitively proves that Peter was not infallible and that the Roman church, by claiming him as its foundation, is founded on someone whom Christ called Satan.
[24-26] The Lord establishes the rigorous conditions of discipleship, which transcend the Gospel era and apply to the life of the believer in the New Testament. Denying oneself and taking up the cross involves a daily crucifixion of the flesh and its desires (1 Corinthians 15:31; Colossians 3:5; Romans 6:11). This verse illustrates the divine principle that life is found by losing it for Christ's sake. Trying to gain the whole world results in the loss of one's soul, indicating the eternal value of the individual in contrast to material and temporal achievements.
[27-28] Jesus Christ promises that the Son of Man will come in the glory of His Father with His angels to reward each one. Immediately afterward, he declares that some of those present will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom. This does not refer to the spiritual coming at Pentecost or the destruction of Jerusalem, but is fulfilled literally and exactly six days later on the Mount of Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1-5). Peter, James, and John beheld the glory of Christ accompanied by Moses and Elijah, which is the exact prefiguration of the Lord's physical and visible Second Coming, as Peter himself confirms under divine inspiration (2 Peter 1:16-18).

[1-5] The Transfiguration is a literal and visible prophetic representation of the Second Coming, when the Son of Man will come in his kingdom (Matthew 16:28; 2 Peter 1:16-18). The glorious appearance of Moses and Elijah accurately foreshadows their future return to earth before the great and terrible day of the Lord (Malachi 4:4-5; Revelation 11:3-6). Likewise, Peter's proposal to build three tabernacles (Matthew 17:4) is directly linked to the Feast of Tabernacles, which has a profound eschatological and messianic character. This passage establishes that certain Old Testament prophecies have literal and physical applications for the end times, and their fulfillment will be physically revealed to believers before the judgments upon the nations.
[9-13] Upon descending from the mountain, the disciples question Jesus about the scribes' teaching that Elijah must come first (Matthew 17:10). The Lord confirms the truth of this prophecy, declaring, "Elijah does indeed come first, and he will restore all things" (Matthew 17:11). This passage is fundamental in establishing the theological nature of John the Baptist's ministry. John was not literally Elijah, but he operated in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17). Doctrinally, John the Baptist would have fulfilled the prophecies concerning Elijah if the nation of Israel had accepted their King at that historical moment (Matthew 11:14). Due to the national rejection of Jesus Christ, the literal coming of Elijah is postponed to a future fulfillment before the Second Coming.
[14-16] The account of the demon-possessed boy whom the disciples could not heal has a strict typological application. While a select remnant witnesses a foretaste of the glory of the Second Coming on the mountaintop, the nation of Israel according to the flesh is at the foot of the mountain engaged in direct combat with demonic forces over which it is unable to prevail on its own. This foreshadows the spiritual condition and extreme oppression that the nation will suffer during the Tribulation period at the hands of unclean spirits.
[21] The sacred text declares regarding the demon: "But this kind of demon does not go out except by prayer and fasting." The systematic omission of this verse in various critical texts and modern translations (which attempt to justify the removal of passages by relying on Alexandrian manuscripts) demonstrates a harmful alteration of the text. The preservation of this verse in the traditional text demonstrates its superiority, as it establishes an indispensable doctrine: there are specific hierarchies and lineages of unclean spirits that require a higher level of spiritual consecration, prayer, and fasting to be expelled.
[24-25] The incident of the tax collection practically illustrates the temporary poverty that the Lord voluntarily experienced during his earthly ministry (Matthew 17:24). When Peter enters the house, the text indicates that Jesus spoke to him first. This particular act demonstrates the Lord's absolute omniscience in knowing Peter's exact situation and thoughts, and in addressing him before he could utter a word.

[1-3] The disciples' question about who is the greatest in the "kingdom of heaven" frames the entire passage within a context that addresses a literal, physical, visible, messianic, and Davidic kingdom promised to Israel, and not the present dispensation of grace for the church. The stipulation that it is necessary to be "converted" and become like children shows the requirements for entering this millennial earthly kingdom. To be converted, in its root and application, implies turning or turning in a particular direction, which in this context means submitting to the authority of the King of the Jews.
[4-5] The directive to humble oneself and receive little children in the name of Christ establishes a direct prophetic and doctrinal parallel with the treatment that will be given to believers during the Great Tribulation, described later in Matthew 25:30-46. The passage reiterates that the kingdom of heaven points to the Second Coming of Jesus Christ to reign over the house of Jacob, so attempting to insert these doctrinal conditions into the New Testament church alters the biblical dispensation.
[7-9] The warnings about offenses and the command to amputate the hand or foot that causes stumbling operate historically in the Old Testament economy before the crucifixion, and prophetically apply to the time of Tribulation, where works play a role in individual salvation. Spiritually, the teaching conclusively demonstrates that it is preferable to enter life lame than to be cast into eternal fire. This directly refutes theological systems that teach that hell is merely the grave, since all people descend into the grave equally, whether healthy or crippled.
[10-11] It is revealed that little children have angels in heaven who behold the face of the Father. Doctrinally, angels in Scripture are not asexual beings, but always appear in the form of thirty-three-year-old men (Philippians 3:20-21; 1 John 3:1-3; Matthew 22:30). In practical terms, this passage establishes the complete spiritual security of children without the need for rites or sacraments administered by fallen men. Although children inherit a corrupt nature (Ephesians 2:1-3; Romans 5:12-18), sin is not legally imputed to them until they reach the maturity to distinguish between good and evil and consciously understand the transgression of God's law (Deuteronomy 1:39; Romans 4:15, 7:7-9). On the other hand, the phrase "Son of Man" in verse 11 is a strictly messianic designation that identifies Christ in His direct ministry to the nation of Israel.
[12-14] The parable of the lost sheep retains its original context focused on the nation of Israel, systematically identified in the Gospels as the "lost sheep" (Matthew 10:6, Matthew 15:24). Inspirationally and devotionally, one can trace the application of Jesus Christ as the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for every person, whether Jew or Gentile, but the primary doctrinal interpretation should not be forced outside of its original intended audience.
[15-18] In establishing guidelines for rebuke among brothers, the Lord concludes by declaring: "Truly I tell you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven." This text is of immense importance because it refutes the ecclesiastical dogma of a supposed exclusive apostolic succession. Here, the authority to bind and loose is granted equally to all the apostles present, which also included Judas Iscariot, demonstrating that no particular individual (like Simon Peter in Matthew 16:19) possessed monarchical primacy or the power to establish religious myths as infallible.
[23-35] The parable of the king settling accounts with his servants outlines a system of forgiveness conditioned on works. The servant, who had been forgiven an unpayable debt, is later handed over to the executioners for refusing to show compassion to his fellow servant. Doctrinally, this passage predates the cross and falls under the principles of Jewish law (Matthew 6:14-15), also finding future fulfillment in the judgments for works during the Tribulation (Matthew 25:30-44). It cannot be extrapolated to the current dispensation of grace, where the believer's forgiveness is based absolutely and eternally on the atoning blood. Historically, the papal hierarchy has misinterpreted this text to forge the doctrine of purgatory, arguing that sins are purged after death. This interpretation lacks textual support: the parable's setting is not the afterlife, the "executioners" described are literal entities or jailers, not a state of "torment," and unlike the parables of the kingdom that explicitly mention hell (Matthew 13:42, Matthew 13:50), there is no presence of fire or purifying flames here.

[3-9] The Pharisees question Jesus Christ about whether it is lawful to divorce one's wife "for any reason," referring to the concession given in Deuteronomy 24:1-4. The Lord's response appeals to original creation to establish that marriage consists of flesh joining with flesh ("and the two shall become one flesh"), constituting a physical bond and not a mere ceremonial rite (Genesis 2:24; Ephesians 5:31; 1 Corinthians 6:16). Moses' concession was dictated by the "hardness of your hearts," illustrating a theological distinction between God's permissive will and his directive will. Jesus Christ establishes "fornication" (which includes adultery and any sexual sin) as the only legitimate cause for divorce. In such a scenario, the marriage bond is considered broken because the offender united his body with another, and therefore the innocent spouse is free to divorce and remarry without committing adultery (1 Corinthians 7:27-28).
[10-12] In response to the disciples' assertion that "it is not advisable to marry," the Lord replies that "Not everyone can accept this saying," referring to the capacity or gift to remain celibate. The text presents three kinds of eunuchs, which refers strictly to the physical inability to procreate, whether due to a birth defect, mutilation, or voluntary self-control. Doctrinally, this passage refutes the Roman tradition of mandatory clerical celibacy, since Jesus Christ does not impose this condition as a general law and the New Testament permits the marriage of spiritual leaders (1 Timothy 3:2; 1 Corinthians 9:5).
[13-15] In rebuking his disciples for preventing the children from approaching, the Lord declares, "The kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these." Doctrinally, entry into the kingdom of God requires that an individual receive the new birth and enter as a newborn child. Furthermore, the text states that young children inherit the kingdom without the need for sacraments administered by man, such as water baptism, since they have not yet reached the age to know good and evil (Deuteronomy 1:39; Romans 4:15, Romans 5:13).
[16-17] A rich young man approaches, asking, “Good Teacher, what good deed must I do to have eternal life?” The Lord’s response (“Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone”) forces the young man to confront the implications of his own statement: if Jesus Christ is not God manifested in the flesh, then he cannot be called “good,” since in the natural state of man there is no one good (Romans 3:12). Modern critical texts corrupt this doctrine by altering the question to "Why do you ask me about what is good?", adopting a variant originating in the pagan philosophy promoted by Origen in Alexandria. Likewise, the instruction "keep the commandments" demonstrates that, before Christ's crucifixion, eternal life was tied to a system of works and faith under the law, a system that will again be operative during the Great Tribulation (Revelation 12:17, Revelation 14:12, Revelation 22:14).
[18-22] When questioned about "which" commandments to keep, Jesus Christ lists six precepts related to one's neighbor, but deliberately omits the first four, which deal with man's duty to God, as well as the tenth commandment against covetousness. This exegetical omission exposes the idolatry in the young man's heart: the love of money (1 Timothy 6:10). The final command, “Sell what you have and give it to the poor… and come, follow me,” demands total material bankruptcy and exposes the young man’s religion as a facade to hide what he truly loved. By leaving saddened by his “many possessions,” he illustrates the reality that greed stifles submission to God and drowns the individual in perdition.
[23-26] The immense difficulty of a rich person entering the kingdom is illustrated by the image of a camel passing through the eye of a needle. Material wealth hinders salvation because it obscures the need to exercise faith, destroys humility, and magnifies worldliness. The disciples were “greatly astonished” because in the Old Testament covenant, material wealth was frequently a reward for serving Jehovah (Job 1:1-3; 1 Kings 3:11-13; Psalm 112:1-3). However, the statement "but with God all things are possible" assures us that salvation depends on divine power that surpasses human reasoning, allowing for the occasional redemption of wealthy men like Zacchaeus, Joseph of Arimathea, and Nicodemus.
[27-30] Peter asks what reward they will receive after leaving everything to follow him. The Lord's promise is fulfilled "in regeneration." This word appears only twice in the New Testament: once to describe the believer's new birth (Titus 3:5), and here to denote the literal and physical renewal of the earth during Christ's Second Coming (Romans 8:18-22; Isaiah 11). "The throne of his glory" refers absolutely and without exception to the literal, earthly, visible, and Davidic throne in the city of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 14:21; Luke 1:30-33; Matthew 25:31), not to a spiritual throne in heaven. The twelve apostles will rule over the twelve literal tribes of Israel. Obtaining the inheritance and "eternal life" in this passage functions as a strict reward, based on works, service, and suffering for the name of Christ (Colossians 3:24; 2 Timothy 2:12), in contrast to the free gift received by faith in the church age (Ephesians 2:8-9).

[1-16] The parable of the workers in the vineyard illustrates the principles and mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. The "landowner" represents God the Father, who manifests himself in the flesh as the Lord Jesus Christ himself (Zechariah 12:10; John 1:1-14). The temporal context of the parable, along with the verses that follow, has prophetic implications that point to the time of Christ's Second Coming and his return to Jerusalem to establish the literal kingdom (Matthew 20:17, 21). Additionally, the owner's right to pay according to his will, "Am I not allowed to do what I want with my own things?", establishes an exegetical principle that recognizes and defends private property, as well as the legitimate authority of the employer or master, directly refuting contemporary economic systems that oppose these rights, such as socialism or Marxism.
[17-19] By setting the twelve disciples apart on the road to Jerusalem, the Lord prophetically details his future trial, his handing over to the Gentiles, the scourging, the crucifixion, and his resurrection on the third day. The strict and literal fulfillment of the promise "on the third day he will rise again" requires an exact chronological timeframe that places the crucifixion on Wednesday at nine in the morning and the resurrection at the end of Saturday, approximately at six in the evening, which agrees mathematically with the sign of the prophet Jonah (Matthew 12:40).
[20-21] The request of the mother of Zebedee's sons to sit at Christ's right and left in his kingdom demonstrates a legitimate expectation for earthly and political rule. Although the twelve apostles are promised to rule over the twelve tribes of Israel seated on twelve thrones (Matthew 19:28), the two most prominent places at the King's right and left are prepared exclusively by the Father. Typologically, within the structure of that coming kingdom, the right hand is reserved for Moses, who represents the law, and the left hand for Elijah, who represents the prophets (Matthew 17:3).
[23] The statement about drinking from the cup and being baptized with the baptism with which Christ is baptized demonstrates theologically that not all baptisms mentioned in Scripture correspond to the rite of water baptism. Both Jesus Christ and the disciples to whom he directly addresses himself had already been baptized in water long before this event. This passage refutes the dogmas of sacramental systems that attempt to limit baptism solely to the element of water, showing that there is a baptism deeply connected with physical suffering and death.
[28] The verse declares that the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for "many." This portion is often used in isolation by proponents of unconditional election and limited atonement to argue that Christ's death did not encompass all of humanity. However, basing a doctrine on an incomplete statement and ignoring its full counterpart violates the primary rules of biblical interpretation. The parallel and conclusive passage in the Pauline epistles states that He "gave himself as a ransom for all" (1 Timothy 2:6), which universally defines the scope of the atonement through His blood.

[1-5] The sending of two disciples to bring a donkey and its colt establishes a recurring typological pattern in Scripture, where the number two testifies to or prepares the way in anticipation of an event of conquest or redemption (Joshua 2:1; Revelation 11:3). The colt ridden by the Lord, upon which no one had ever sat, represents the unrepentant sinner in his natural state, described in Scripture as being born “like a wild colt” (Job 11:12). To be useful to the Master, this colt needs to be untied from its bonds (Romans 8:2), brought to Jesus Christ, and submitted to His Lordship to be tamed and guided. The phrase "and a colt, the foal of a donkey" (Matthew 21:5) employs the rhetorical figure of hendiadys, indicating that Christ rode on a single animal that was the offspring of another, thus refuting textual criticisms that absurdly claim the text states he rode two animals simultaneously.
[8-11] The crowd spreading their cloaks and branches on the road, proclaiming "Hosanna to the Son of David," makes a public acknowledgment of the literal, physical, Davidic Messianic King entering Jerusalem (Zechariah 9:9; Genesis 49:11). The use of palm branches, historically associated with the cursed city of Jericho (a symbol of Gentile dominion), along with the olive branches lining the road from Bethphage, foreshadows the Messiah's victory and dominion over both the Gentile world and Israel (Revelation 7:9). In this event, the First and Second Comings prophetically overlap, since the acclamation of the multitudes temporarily fulfills the prophecy, but the absolute consummation will occur when Christ returns in glory on a white horse, with His garments washed in the blood of His enemies (Revelation 19:11-16; Isaiah 63:1-6).
[12-13] The second cleansing of the temple illustrates divine severity toward religious greed and the mercantile system established by the priestly caste. By citing Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11, the text establishes that the religious leaders had prioritized economic gain (money changers and sellers of doves for sacrifices) over spiritual worship, turning "my house" into a "den of thieves." Doctrinally, this act of purification anticipates the future eschatological purification at the Second Coming, when the Lord will purify the sons of Levi to offer sacrifices of righteousness in the millennial temple (Malachi 3:2-4).
[18-20] The cursing of the fig tree contains profound doctrinal significance. Throughout biblical revelation, the fig tree, from the making of leaf aprons in Eden (Genesis 3:7), typifies self-righteousness and lifeless, external religion. The nation of Israel is represented as a fig tree (Jeremiah 24:2-8) that, at the time of its King's visit, possessed abundant leaves of religious profession but lacked genuine spiritual fruit (Romans 10:3). By cursing it, the fig tree withers from its roots, foreshadowing the national destruction and spiritual withering of Israel that culminated in 70 CE. Under Titus. Chronologically, this miracle destroys the Roman tradition of "Good Friday," since the text states that the fig tree was cursed on a Monday morning and the disciples noticed its withering on Tuesday morning, establishing a sequence of days that requires the crucifixion to have occurred on Wednesday (Matthew 12:40).
[23-27] Upon entering the temple, the chief priests and elders question the authority of Jesus Christ. The central question, "By what authority are you doing this?", encapsulates the universal conflict and rebellion of the creature against its Creator from Isaiah 14 and Genesis 3, in which fallen humanity constantly disputes God's right to rule. Faced with this attack, the Lord conditions His response on the recognition of the ministry of John the Baptist. The leaders' evasiveness, their response of "We do not know," demonstrates that religious agnosticism almost always masks a hypocritical lie motivated by wickedness, fear of public opinion (Proverbs 29:25), and the protection of their own status and prestige.
[28-32] The parable of the two sons exposes the Pharisees to judgment through their own reasoning. It demonstrates that the Father's will is not fulfilled through a vain profession of obedience, but through genuine repentance that leads to corresponding works. In the dispensational context of Israel, the tax collectors and prostitutes, who initially lived in rebellion but later believed John the Baptist's message of righteousness, enter the kingdom of God, preceding the religious hierarchy, which outwardly displayed devotion but possessed a hardened and unrepentant heart.
[33-41] The parable of the vineyard is a masterful synthesis of Israel's theocratic history. The "head of the household" is God the Father, the "vineyard" is the land of Palestine, the "tenants" are the religious leaders charged with upholding the law, and the "servants" are the Old Testament prophets, whom Israel persecuted, stoned, and murdered throughout the centuries (Matthew 23:37). The sending of the "son" points to the First Coming of Jesus Christ. The act of casting Him out of the vineyard and killing Him accurately foreshadows His crucifixion outside the gates of Jerusalem (Hebrews 13:12). The judgment pronounced, to miserably destroy the tenants, was historically fulfilled by the Roman siege of Jerusalem.
[42-44] Jesus Christ identifies Himself as "the stone the builders rejected." Architecturally, a "cornerstone" or chief cornerstone that crowns a building can only be applied to the apex of a pyramid (Ephesians 3:18). As a direct consequence of this official rejection, the kingdom of God is temporarily withdrawn from Israel and transferred to "a nation that will produce its fruit," which, doctrinally, points to the Church, later defined as a "holy nation" (1 Peter 2:9). Verse 44 reveals humanity's inescapable destiny before Christ in two prophetic times: during the present age, whoever stumbles and falls on the stone in unbelief is broken and offended (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:8); however, at the Second Coming, when this Stone descends from heaven upon the statue of Gentile dominion (Daniel 2:34-35), it will crush and reduce to dust all its enemies.

[1-10] The parable of the wedding feast illustrates the call to the kingdom and the dispensational transition that occurs in the first century. The king prepares a wedding banquet for his son, but the original invited guests, who typify the nation of Israel, reject the invitation with various worldly excuses. In response to their rejection and the mistreatment of his servants, the king sends his armies to destroy the city of the murderers (Matthew 22:7), which is an exact and direct prophecy of the destruction of Jerusalem by the Roman general Titus in 70 AD. Afterward, the servants are sent out into the world to gather all they find, both good and bad. These “guests” (Matthew 22:10) represent the Gentiles, who take their place at the wedding feast after Israel’s national rejection.
[11-14] The appearance of a man without a wedding garment exposes the inescapable judgment on false profession and self-justification. The wedding garment represents the perfect and imputed righteousness of the Son of God; to lack it is to appear before the Supreme Judge clothed in filthy rags (Isaiah 64:6). When questioned by the king, the man is silenced, demonstrating the legal and theological principle that before the majesty of God, every mouth will be silenced and the whole world found guilty (Romans 3:19). This individual is bound and cast out into the outer darkness, indicating that access to the kingdom and the supper requires divinely provided garments, and those who attempt to enter on their own merits will face condemnation.
[15-22] The Pharisees join with the Herodians to try to ensnare the Lord with his words. This coalition is remarkable, since both groups were politically opposed, yet they manage to unite in their mutual hatred of Jesus Christ and the truth. The question of whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar is designed as an inescapable trap: if the Lord approves of paying taxes, the Pharisees would accuse him before the people of violating Mosaic Law, which forbade submission to a foreign king (Deuteronomy 17:14-15); if he rejects it, the Herodians would hand him over to the Romans for sedition. By asking for the coin and pointing to Caesar's image and inscription, the Lord masterfully establishes the jurisdiction of human authorities in civil matters, while subtly rebuking the Pharisees for not giving to God what is due to Him, neglecting judgment, mercy, and faith (Matthew 23:23).
[23-33] The Sadducees, a religious sect that denied the existence of angels, spirits, and the physical resurrection (Acts 23:8), present a hypothetical case about a woman and seven brothers based on the law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5). Their aim is to make the resurrection seem absurd. The Lord completely destroys their heresy by pointing out their ignorance of Scripture and the power of God. Two absolute doctrinal realities are established: first, "in the resurrection... they are like the angels of God in heaven" (Matthew 22:30). This dogmatically refutes the notion of heavenly marriages, demonstrating that the angels who did not sin are male beings without any procreative design or purpose. Second, by quoting Exodus 3:6, it is affirmed that "God is not the God of the dead, but of the living" (Matthew 22:32), demonstrating that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob continue to exist consciously and await the physical bodily resurrection, thus validating life after death and the literal resurrection.
[34-40] A lawyer, attempting to test him again, asks which is the greatest commandment in the law. The Lord's answer consolidates and summarizes the entirety of the Mosaic covenant in two fundamental precepts: to love God with all your being and to love your neighbor as yourself. By stating that all the Law and the Prophets depend on these two commandments, it is shown that the ethical and moral requirement of the Old Testament is essentially fulfilled in the love of God and man (Romans 13:9).
[41-46] The chapter concludes when Jesus Christ takes the offensive and confronts the Pharisees with a question about the Messiah's identity and lineage: “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” When they answer that he is the son of David, the Lord quotes Psalm 110:1, explaining that David, speaking by the Holy Spirit, called the Messiah his “Lord.” This exegesis irrefutably establishes the deity of Jesus Christ. If the Messiah were merely a human descendant, David would never have submitted to him by calling him Lord. The Pharisees' utter inability to respond (Matthew 22:46) seals their public defeat, demonstrating that their rejection of the truth was not based on a lack of scriptural evidence, but on the hardness and unbelief of their own hearts.

[4] The accusation against the Pharisees of tying up “heavy and cumbersome burdens” points to the imposition of human traditions and commandments over the word of God (Mark 7:7–13). The religious leaders demand meticulous legalistic compliance that they themselves do not lift a finger to alter, demonstrating that human religion based on works breeds spiritual oppression and masks a lack of true inner righteousness.
[8–9] The explicit command, “And call no one on earth ‘your Father,’ for you have one Father, and he is in heaven,” absolutely forbids the use of divine titles for religious leaders. Assuming such a title usurps a place of authority reserved exclusively for God the Father (John 17:11). The context condemns the false teachers who walk around in long robes and demand positions of honor (Luke 20:46), establishing a doctrinal rebuke against any ecclesiastical hierarchy or priesthood that exalts man to a position of paternal mediator.
[13-15] The scribes and Pharisees are condemned for shutting “the kingdom of heaven in people’s faces.” Their institutional religion not only prevents them from entering it themselves, but also makes their followers children of hell (“children of Gehenna”). Doctrinally, a “child of hell” in this context is defined as someone who actively opposes the truth of God and hinders sinners from entering the kingdom (Matthew 23:13).
[14] The condemnation for devouring widows’ houses and “making long prayers” exposes religious greed. This warning historically foreshadows those religious systems that extort widows by charging for rituals, masses, or endless prayers under the false promise of rescuing their deceased husbands from places of torment (Luke 20:46-47).
[23-24] The Lord rebukes the hypocrisy of meticulously tithing mint, dill, and cumin while neglecting "the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faith." This illustrates the blindness of religious leaders who "strain out a gnat but swallow a camel," disproportionately prioritizing the ceremonial details of their own traditions while completely neglecting love for God and moral fairness.
[25-28] The comparison of religious leaders to "whitewashed tombs" illustrates the radical disparity between outward religious appearance and inward depravity. Outwardly they appear beautiful and clean to receive the approval of men, but inwardly they are full of "dead people's bones and all uncleanness." The passage establishes that no clerical position or ceremonial cleansing can purify an unregenerate heart.
[33] The designation of the leaders as "serpents, a brood of vipers" links their spiritual nature directly to the devil (John 8:44; Genesis 3:15). Jesus Christ does not use a diplomatic tone in the face of apostasy; He confronts them with extreme harshness and sharp rebuke. This demonstrates that true preaching includes severe condemnation against those who pervert the truth and lead others to "the condemnation of hell" (Titus 1:13).
[35] The statement "from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah" dogmatically establishes the Old Testament canon recognized by Jesus Christ and Orthodox Jews. The death of Abel is found in Genesis, the first book, and the death of Zechariah is found in 2 Chronicles 24:20, which is the last book in the arrangement of the Hebrew text. By establishing these boundaries, the Lord exclusively legitimizes the traditional Hebrew Scriptures and excludes all the apocryphal books, which He never cites to support doctrine.
[37-39] The lament over Jerusalem exposes the obstinate resistance of the human will to grace, since the Lord wanted to gather His children together "as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing." As a direct consequence of the rejection of His Messiah, the "house" of the temple is left "deserted" and abandoned by the presence of God. The final assertion, "From now on you will not see me until you say, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,'" conditions the physical, visible, and triumphant return of Christ on the future conversion and restoration of the national remnant of Israel during the Second Coming, when they will finally receive him as their King.

[3] The disciples question Jesus Christ about the sign of His coming and the end of the world. The doctrinal and historical context of this chapter is situated entirely within the time of the Tribulation and is addressed exclusively to Jews, since the Church, understood as the Body of Christ, had not yet been revealed nor did it exist at this time. Furthermore, this eschatological discourse was given privately only to Peter, James, John, and Andrew, excluding Judas Iscariot (the son of perdition) from this revelation.
[13] The statement "But he who endures to the end will be saved" does not refer to the physical death of the individual nor does it question the eternal security of the believer in the present Church Age. "The end" here designates the chronological end of the Great Tribulation period. In this coming age, the salvation of Jew or Gentile will be conditioned upon a combination of faith in Jesus Christ and works to maintain that salvation, which includes rejecting the mark of the beast and enduring persecution until the period concludes.
[14] The "gospel of the kingdom" that will be preached as a witness to all nations is not equivalent to the "gospel of the grace of God" later revealed to the apostle Paul (Acts 20:24). It is the specific proclamation that the physical, messianic King will soon return to earth to establish a literal, political, and visible kingdom in Jerusalem. The end of the age will come only after this gospel has been proclaimed to all nations.
[15-16] The "abomination of desolation" mentioned by the prophet Daniel will be fulfilled in the middle of the Tribulation, when the Antichrist sets up his image in "the holy place" of the rebuilt temple in Jerusalem. In light of this sign, the command to flee to the mountains has a literal application for the Jewish remnant in Judea. This remnant will escape to the mountains of Edom, specifically to the rocky city of Selah-Petra, where God will supernaturally sustain them for three and a half years (Revelation 12:6, 14; Micah 7:14-15).
[20-22] The instruction to pray that the flight will not take place on the Sabbath underscores the doctrinal reality that the individuals in this context are again under the covenant of the Law (Exodus 20) and not under the grace of the present dispensation. The "great tribulation" described here will surpass any tragedy known to humankind, far exceeding the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD, the Holocaust, and even the universal flood. The "chosen ones" for whose sake the days are shortened are the Jews, not the New Testament church (Isaiah 45:4, 65:9; Zechariah 2:5-6).
[29-30] The catastrophic astronomical events that will occur "after the tribulation of those days" are detailed, with the darkening of the sun and moon, and the falling of the stars (Revelation 6:12-13). Following these heavenly signs, "the sign of the Son of Man in heaven" will appear. The title "Son of Man" is an exclusively Jewish designation that points to the earthly and physical return of Christ to establish His kingdom over Israel; therefore, the Gentile apostles never used this term to refer to Him in the epistles to the church. At this event, all the tribes of the earth will weep as they see Him return visibly on the clouds of the first heaven.
[31] The sending of angels with "trumpet and loud voice" to gather the elect points to a post-tribulation rapture of Jewish saints (and those saved during the Tribulation) moments before the Second Coming. Attempting to place here the rapture of the Body of Christ described in 1 Thessalonians 4 and 1 Corinthians 15 is a serious exegetical error, as it inserts the Church into a period of wrath and earthly judgments designed to test and deal with the nation of Israel.
[32-34] The parable of the fig tree functions as a prophetic clock, representing the national restoration of Israel in the land of Palestine, an event that began to be fulfilled historically in 1948 (Jeremiah 8:11-13; Isaiah 66:8). The generation that witnesses this event unfolding will not pass away until the entire prophesied eschatological discourse reaches its culmination.
[42-51] The final warnings about the Lord coming like a thief in the night are directed strictly to the Tribulation servants awaiting the Second Coming. Unlike a blood-washed believer in the Church Age, the servant who is unwatchful, who gets drunk and mistreats his fellow servants, faces the loss of his salvation. When the Lord returns, He will cut him in two and assign him his portion with the hypocrites in weeping and gnashing of teeth, again demonstrating a system of salvation conditioned by works.

[1-13] The parable of the ten virgins belongs doctrinally and historically to the Tribulation period, not the church age. Scripture describes the body of Christ as a single "pure virgin" (2 Corinthians 11:2), whereas here it refers to "virgins" in the plural, which typologically corresponds to the Jewish remnant (Revelation 14:4). The text indicates that these virgins go out to meet the bridegroom, not to marry him (Matthew 25:1, 6). Doctrinally, the oil typifies the Holy Spirit. In this future dispensation, the parable demonstrates that it is possible for an individual to lose the Holy Spirit, as illustrated by the foolish virgins whose lamps go out (Matthew 25:8; Psalm 51:11), unlike the born-again believer who is eternally sealed (Ephesians 4:30). The foolish virgins are told, “I do not know you” (Matthew 25:12). This establishes a post-tribulation divided rapture, where only those Tribulation saints who are prepared and persevere to the end ascend to be present at the wedding feast.
[14-30] The parable of the talents focuses on the kingdom of heaven and is addressed to the Jew in the Tribulation, in contrast to the parable of the minas in Luke 19, which deals with the kingdom of God and has an application for Gentiles in the church age. Each servant is given according to his ability (Matthew 25:15). The main exegetical emphasis is on the worthless servant, who does not suffer a mere loss of rewards, but is cast “into the outer darkness,” where “there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 25:30). This proves that, during the Tribulation period, salvation requires a combination of faith and works. A servant of the Lord in that dispensation loses his salvation if he does not bear fruit and does not obey the commandments.
[31-46] The statement "When the Son of Man comes in his glory" establishes the inescapable context of the Second Coming of Jesus Christ to sit upon the throne of David literally, physically, and visibly on earth, in the city of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 3:17, Jeremiah 14:21). This event is the judgment of the nations, which should not be confused with the Great White Throne judgment that occurs in outer space after the Millennium (Revelation 20:11-15). In this earthly judgment, three groups are clearly distinguished: the sheep, the goats, and the "brothers" of the King (Matthew 25:40). The "brothers" are not the New Testament Christians, but the Jews in the flesh who have been persecuted during the Great Tribulation. The basis of this judgment is strictly works; there is no mention of salvation by grace through faith or of the new birth in the entire passage. The Gentile nations are judged and separated according to the physical treatment they gave to the Jewish remnant persecuted by the Antichrist: feeding, giving drink, clothing, shelter, and visiting in prison or in sickness. Inheriting the kingdom (Matthew 25:34) operates here as an earthly reward earned for these good works. In contrast, the goats, who ignored the Jews' affliction and refused to help them, are condemned without mercy and thrown "into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels" (Matthew 25:41).

[14-16] Judas Iscariot's pact with the chief priests to betray Jesus Christ for thirty pieces of silver fulfills with pinpoint accuracy the prophecy established in the Old Testament (Zechariah 11:13). This sum is not arbitrary; it corresponds precisely to the price stipulated by law to compensate for the death of a slave (Exodus 21:32) and to the legal valuation of a woman under a singular vow (Leviticus 27:4). Motivated by greed and the love of money, the "root of all evil" (1 Timothy 6:10), Judas betrays the King of the Jews for the lowest and most humiliating price that could be assigned to a person in Hebrew culture.
[20-25] During the Last Supper, the Lord reveals the impending betrayal. While the disciples ask in pain and sorrow, “Is it I, Lord?”, Judas uses a completely different designation when he inquires, “Am I perhaps, Teacher?” (Matthew 26:22, 25). Judas is the only disciple who consistently refuses to address Christ as Lord, always preferring the title of Teacher. This refusal to submit to the deity and lordship of Jesus Christ is evidence of his identity as the “son of perdition,” an incarnate devil who lacks the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, since no one can call Jesus Lord except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3).
[26-29] The New Testament institution establishes that the elements employed do not confer inherent saving grace, but rather constitute a commemorative act. The cup contains the "fruit of the vine," which typifies the pure and divine blood of Jesus Christ (Deuteronomy 32:14), not a fermented liquor like that used in pagan rites (Proverbs 23:31). Taking the bread, He breaks it, establishing that the word of God must be broken to be distributed and that man himself must be broken (Luke 24:45). The ecclesiastical teaching that the Lord's Supper literally reproduces the Savior's ongoing, physical sacrifice is invalidated in this passage and throughout the rest of Scripture, since Christ is not physically broken at the table, but rather His sacrifice would be offered once and for all on the cross of Calvary (Hebrews 10:10-14). The direct purpose of this communion is to proclaim His death until His Second Coming (1 Corinthians 11:26).
[31-35] Jesus Christ warns all His disciples that they will be offended by Him that very night, basing His statement on the authority of Scripture by quoting Zechariah 13:7. Peter responds by directly contradicting the written prophecy based on his good intentions and excessive carnal confidence. By asserting that he will never be offended, Peter demonstrates the human tendency to reject or alter the word of God when it contradicts one's own feelings, acting with the same spirit that questioned God's authority in the Garden of Eden (Genesis 3:1).
[36-46] The suffering of Jesus Christ in the Garden of Gethsemane is a suffering of an emotional and spiritual nature that leads Him to agonize in prayer. The "cup" mentioned does not represent the fear of physical death in the garden or the crucifixion itself, both of which He joyfully endured (Hebrews 12:2). Doctrinally, the "cup" in Scripture symbolizes the fury and wrath of God poured out upon sin (Jeremiah 25:15; Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17). By becoming a sin offering and being "made sin" in place of men (2 Corinthians 5:21), Christ had to experience God's wrath poured out upon sin and utter helplessness. During this event, two clearly defined wills are evident: "not as I will, but as you will," proving that the Savior experienced a genuine temptation to evade the cross from the perspective of His human will, even though His submission to the Father was absolute (Hebrews 5:7-8).
[47-50] Judas seals the Messiah's betrayal with a kiss, subverting an expression of loyalty and love into the seal of treason. The Lord, fully aware of His enemy's hidden intentions, calls him "Friend," thus historically fulfilling Psalm 41:9. Once again, Judas approaches, saying "Master," and kisses Him, showing not the slightest reverential fear of the Creator.
[51-54] The Lord rebukes Peter's attempt to defend Him with a sword and declares that He has the authority to summon twelve legions of angels for His imminent deliverance. A single angel possesses the power to annihilate entire armies (2 Kings 19:35). His surrender to the Roman and Jewish authorities is not due to powerlessness, but to a deliberate and voluntary submission so that "the Scriptures might be fulfilled" (Matthew 26:54). The integrity, inerrancy, and fulfillment of God's word take precedence over the temporal preservation or physical dignity of Jesus Christ himself in his humanity.
[59-68] The tribunal assembled in Caiaphas's palace represents the total corruption of justice and the law of Israel. The high priests seek false witnesses against Jesus in order to justify a death sentence decreed beforehand (Exodus 20:16). Faced with the fabricated accusations, the Savior remains absolutely silent, fulfilling the role of the lamb led to the slaughter who does not open his mouth (Isaiah 53:7). The High Priest is forced to conjure him legally by the living God, demanding that he declare whether He is the Christ. By pronouncing, “In a little while you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power,” Christ merges Psalm 110:1 with Daniel 7:13, undeniably professing His absolute deity and His future millennial kingdom. This declaration causes Caiaphas to tear his garments—an action forbidden by the Law for a sitting high priest—and Christ to be slapped, punched, and spat upon, fulfilling with mathematical precision the mockery prophesied in Isaiah 50:6.
[69-75] The end of the chapter illustrates the moral failure of a disciple who relies on his own strength. Peter, who previously followed the Lord “at a distance” (Matthew 26:58), ends up sitting and warming himself in the fire of Christ’s enemies. The denial progresses gradually: it begins with evasion, then incorporates an oath (taking God's name in vain), and culminates in open cursing and swearing. The rooster's crow triggers the immediate recollection of the words spoken by Jesus Christ, and Peter's bitter weeping exemplifies real and painful repentance and contrition in the face of conviction of sin.

[3-10] Judas Iscariot returns the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests after seeing Jesus Christ condemned. The sum of thirty pieces corresponds precisely to the legal compensation price for an injured slave (Exodus 21:32) and to the valuation of a woman under a singular vow (Leviticus 27:4). Judas hangs himself, and the apparent contradiction with his fall documented in the Book of Acts (Acts 1:18) is resolved by understanding that the great earthquake that occurred during the crucifixion (Matthew 27:51) broke the branch or threw his body down into the city's garbage dump in the Valley of Gehenna. Regarding the quotation attributed to Jeremiah in verse 9, the sacred text indicates what was "spoken" by the prophet, not necessarily what was written in his canonical book, establishing a valid theological distinction between oral prophetic transmission and the written record, although details of the passages are found in Zechariah 11:12-13.
[15-25] Pilate attempts to evade his responsibility by appealing to the Passover custom and offering to release either Jesus Christ or Barabbas. Theologically, the name Barabbas means "son of the father" (Bar-abbas). He illustrates the doctrine of substitutionary atonement literally, for the true Son of the Father takes the place on the cross of a guilty murderer, seditious, and thief who deserved death (Galatians 3:13). Pilate washes his hands, attempting to absolve himself of the guilt of shedding innocent blood based on the law (Deuteronomy 21:6-7), but the physical act is useless in cleansing his conscience. The Jewish crowd assumes responsibility, saying, "His blood be on us and on our children!" (Matthew 27:25). This declaration brought disastrous historical consequences for the nation, including the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE, global persecutions, the Holocaust, and sets the prophetic stage for the nation's future judgments during the time of Jacob's trouble (Jeremiah 30:7).
[27-31] Roman soldiers place a scarlet (or purple, symbolizing false kingship) robe and a crown of thorns on his head. Since the "thorns and thistles" were the direct result of God's curse on the earth in Eden (Genesis 3:18), the crown doctrinally demonstrates that the Redeemer bears upon His head the curse imposed on natural creation. This anticipates the future regeneration and redemption of nature itself during His millennial reign (Romans 8:18-23; Isaiah 11:1-10).
[34-38] They give Him vinegar mixed with gall to drink, strictly fulfilling Psalm 69:21; the traditional text specifies vinegar and not wine. The soldiers cast lots for His garments, fulfilling Psalm 22:18. The inscription placed by Pilate above the cross (Matthew 27:37) was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin (Luke 23:38). These three languages ​​represent the three main divisions of humanity descended from Shem (Hebrew), Japheth (Greek), and Ham (Latin/North African). The cross demonstrates that the King of the Jews dies for all humanity. Jesus Christ is crucified between two thieves, fulfilling the prophecy that He would be "numbered with the transgressors" (Isaiah 53:12).
[39-44] The religious leaders mock Him as He hangs on the cross, saying, "He saved others; He cannot save Himself" (Matthew 27:42). Although they pronounce this with sarcasm and hostility, the statement constitutes a profound theological truth: in order to effect the salvation of humanity and fulfill the Father's will, the substitutionary sacrifice required that the Son of God not save himself.
[45-46] From the sixth hour to the ninth (from noon to three in the afternoon) there is darkness over all the land. During these three hours of dense darkness, God's wrath is poured out upon sin. Jesus Christ cries out, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" quoting Psalm 22:1. In this moment of extreme agony, He does not address God as "Father," but as "God," since it is the human nature of Jesus Christ enduring divine judgment and utter abandonment by becoming the very personification of sin for the sake of humanity (2 Corinthians 5:21).
[50-53] At the moment the Lord gives up His spirit, the veil of the temple is torn in two from top to bottom. Typologically, the veil represents the flesh of Christ (Hebrews 10:20), and its miraculous and divine tearing (from top to bottom) indicates that direct access to the Most Holy Place has been opened through His atoning death (Hebrews 10:19). The earthquake opens the literal tombs, and many bodies of Old Testament saints are resurrected and enter the holy city after Christ's resurrection. These saints who slept in Abraham's bosom (Luke 16) ascend as firstfruits, demonstrating physically and spiritually that Jesus Christ led "captivity captive" (Ephesians 4:8) after descending to the heart of the earth (Matthew 12:40) and obtaining the keys of hell and death (Revelation 1:18).
[57-60] Joseph of Arimathea, a wealthy disciple and member of the council who did not consent to the condemnation, claims the body of Jesus Christ. As it is wrapped in clean linen and placed in a new tomb hewn out of the rock, belonging to a rich man, the prophecy of Isaiah 53:9 ("and his death with the rich") is fulfilled exactly. The burial ensures that His body did not see corruption (Acts 2:27), and the great stone sealed by the Romans establishes the human impossibility of altering the event of the coming resurrection.

[1] The text mentions the end of the Sabbath, using the plural form in the original language. The strict biblical chronology of three days and three nights places the resurrection at the end of the Sabbath, at approximately six in the evening. This conclusively establishes that the resurrection event itself preceded the women's arrival at the tomb at dawn on the first day of the week by several hours.
[2-4] A great earthquake marks the descent of the angel of the Lord, who rolls away the stone and sits upon it outside the tomb. The Roman guards, being seasoned soldiers trained for military combat, faint from terror, demonstrating the absolute supremacy of divine power over human strength. The stone is not rolled away to allow Christ to leave, since his resurrected body has the ability to pass through physical matter (John 20:19), but so that the witnesses can enter, observe, and verify that the tomb is empty.
[6] The angelic declaration, "He is not here; for he has risen, as he said," constitutes the irreplaceable historical and doctrinal foundation of the Christian faith. Unlike any other world religion whose founders remain in the tomb, the empty tomb of Jesus Christ assures the believer's justification, grants victory over sin, and guarantees the future bodily resurrection of all who die in him (Romans 4:25; 1 Thessalonians 4:14-16).
[9] Upon encountering the resurrected Christ on the road, the women prostrate themselves, embrace his feet, and worship him. Jesus Christ accepts this worship without offering any correction or rejection. Since Scripture expressly forbids the worship of any creature or angel and reserves this act of veneration exclusively for God (Revelation 19:10; Matthew 4:10), the Lord's unconditional acceptance of this worship irrefutably validates His absolute deity.
[11-15] The chief priests bribe the Roman soldiers to spread the theory that the disciples stole Jesus' body while the guard slept. This fabrication lacks logical consistency, given that a group of twelve frightened and poorly armed disciples could not have overcome an experienced Roman guard, and the soldiers, if they had truly been asleep, would not have had the visual capacity to witness who took the body. This perpetuated lie demonstrates the degree of hardness and blindness of the religious leaders who, faced with the undeniable evidence of the resurrection, preferred cover-up to repentance.
[18-20] The Great Commission is established, directed to the Gentile nations, commanding baptism "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." The use of the word "name" in the singular to identify the three divine persons underscores the unity of the Godhead, with "Lord" being the title that unites them (Romans 10:9-13; 2 Corinthians 3:17). This passage theologically rules out the use of the exclusive formula "in the name of Jesus," which was provisionally employed with the Jews in the book of Acts (Acts 2:38). Furthermore, Christ's promise to be with his own "until the end of the age" demonstrates that this mandate remains valid throughout the present dispensation of the church and is not restricted solely to the future tribulation period, which categorically refutes the arguments of hyperdispensationalist systems.

[1-4] The historical heading places Isaiah's ministry under the reign of four monarchs of Judah, establishing a prophetic and doctrinal parallel that extends to the end of time. By calling heaven and earth as witnesses to Israel's rebellion, the Lord appeals directly to the order of physical creation (Genesis 1:1). The prophet's name, meaning "Save, O Lord," doctrinally foreshadows the character and ministry of the Messiah, who will be visibly manifested at Christ's Second Coming to redeem his earthly people. These passages should not be spiritualized or confined to the past, since the apostle Paul states in the New Testament that the historical experiences of the Jewish nation were written as examples and types for our own spiritual admonition in this dispensation (1 Corinthians 10:11). Israel, by not knowing or considering God, behaves in a manner inferior to the beasts of the field, acting as a nation burdened with iniquity and corrupting children who walk backward in obstinate apostasy (Jeremiah 3:14).
[5-9] The description of the moral and physical ruin of the Hebrew people presents the painful reality of a nation under God's judgment. From the sole of their feet to the top of their heads there is no soundness in them, but wounds, bruises, and festering sores that have not been closed or soothed with oil. This condition of national desolation, where cities are burned by fire at the hands of foreigners and the daughter of Zion is left like a hut in a vineyard or like a besieged city, prophetically points to the great tribulation. The Jewish remnant will experience this extreme anguish just before the Second Coming, when God's intervention will prevent Israel from being completely destroyed like Sodom and Gomorrah (Romans 9:29). Amillennial theology errs in allegorizing these physical judgments, for the prophecies guarantee that the preservation of a small seed on the land of Palestine is part of God's unconditional decrees for the national restoration of the Jewish people in the last days (Jeremiah 30:11).
[10-15] By comparing the rulers of Jerusalem to the princes of Sodom, the prophecy strikes a blow against the self-justification of formal and ritualistic religions. The Lord directly declares that He is weary of the multitude of ram sacrifices and the fat of fattened animals, categorizing liturgical incense as an intolerable abomination in His presence (Isaiah 1:13). Religious solemnities, new moons, and Sabbath observance are described as distasteful to God's soul, revealing that outward worship without inward obedience lacks spiritual validity. The text solemnly indicates that the Lord will hide His eyes from the fervent prayers of a people whose hands are stained with blood. This severe judgment is practically applicable to the apostate church systems of the present dispensation that seek to substitute ritual formalities for true faith, forgetting that true communion with God will be restored on earth after the Second Coming of Christ (Colossians 2:16).
[16-20] The command to wash, cleanse, and remove the evil of one's deeds from before the divine eyes prepares the way for sovereign reconciliation under the new covenant. The invitation, "Come now, let us reason together," says the Lord, establishes the basis for a justification that operates unconditionally (Isaiah 1:18). Even if the sins of the people are as fiery red as scarlet or crimson, the Lord promises to supernaturally make them as white as snow and wool. However, a proper division of the word of truth shows that this promise has governmental conditions on the earthly plane; if the people are willing and obedient, they will eat the good things of the land, but if they refuse and rebel, they will be devoured by the sword. This national judicial retribution will be fully realized at the Second Coming, when the Gentile nations and the Jewish remnant will be judged according to their submission to God's direct rule (Matthew 25:31-34).
[21-26] The lament over the faithful city turned harlot exposes the moral decay of Jerusalem, where silver has become dross and wine has been mixed with water. The justice that once dwelt there has been displaced by murderers, and its princes have become companions of robbers who covet bribes and refuse to defend the cause of widows and orphans. In the face of this profound apostasy, the Mighty One of Israel angrily declares that He will take satisfaction from His enemies and avenge Himself on His adversaries. Through the purifying judgments of the great tribulation, the Lord promises to literally cleanse the dross and remove all the tin from the nation (Isaiah 1:25). This restoration will culminate after Christ's return, when God powerfully declares, "I will restore your judges as at the first, and your counselors as at the beginning" (Isaiah 1:26), establishing Jerusalem as the geographical and political center of millennial theocratic justice on earth, just as the apostles indicated in the days of the early church (Acts 3:19-21).
[27-31] Zion will be redeemed with judgment and its converts with justice, demonstrating that Israel's liberation from the oppression of Gentile powers will be accomplished through sovereign military and judicial intervention. Rebels and sinners will be destroyed together, and those who forsake the Lord will be consumed physically.
