The prophecy severely rebukes those who are ashamed of the oak trees they loved and the idolatrous gardens they chose for pagan worship mingled with nature (Isaiah 1:29). By comparing transgressors to an elm tree whose leaves wither and a garden that lacks water, Scripture illustrates the utter fragility of human self-sufficiency. The strong will be like tinder and their work like a spark, both burning together in an eternal fire that no one can quench, foreshadowing the punishment of rebels in the lake of fire (Revelation 20:15).

[1-2] The vision is set “in the last days” (Isaiah 2:2), a plural expression that denotes a direct application to the Second Coming of Jesus Christ and the Millennial era. The prophecy declares that “the mountain of the Lord’s temple will be established as the highest of the mountains,” which figuratively and literally establishes the absolute supremacy of the nation of Israel and Mount Zion over all other kingdoms and governments on earth. The text indicates that “all nations will stream to it,” demonstrating that during this period the Gentile nations that survive the judgments of the Great Tribulation will submit and flock to Jerusalem to seek God’s guidance.
[3] The Gentile multitudes will express a desire to learn God’s ways, saying, “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the temple of the God of Jacob.” The divine declaration, “For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem,” proves that, during the coming kingdom, the law of the Old Testament is not annulled or discarded, but is reinstated as the moral and civil code that will govern the whole earth. This earthly jurisdiction will proceed strictly from Jerusalem and not from other Gentile capitals.
[4] The promise of global peace, where the nations “will beat their swords into plowshares… nor will they train for war anymore,” is conditioned exclusively on the return of the Prince of Peace. The human attempt to institute this prophecy without the physical presence and rule of Jesus Christ is an eschatological failure. The motto inscribed on the United Nations building takes this verse while ignoring its millennial context; The appropriate prophetic guidance for rebellious nations in the present pre-Advent age is found in the contrary instruction to forge swords from plowshares (Joel 3:10).
[9-11] The text traces a transition to the judgments of the Great Tribulation and the Second Advent. Because of idolatry, a decree of divine judgment without mercy is issued: “Therefore you will not spare them” (Isaiah 2:9). Subsequently, men are instructed: “Go into the rock, hide in the dust, from the dreadful presence of the Lord” (Isaiah 2:10). This points to the terror of mankind in the last days, literally foreshadowing men’s flight into caves and underground shelters to escape God’s wrath (Revelation 6:15). Human pride and arrogance will be humbled, and “only the Lord will be exalted in that day.”
[16-18] God’s judgment will fall upon human commerce, represented by “all the ships of Tarshish,” and upon the visual appeal of idolatry, identified as “all the precious paintings” (Isaiah 2:16). Images and paintings are part of a religious and idolatrous system that corrupts the human eye, which is the lamp of the body (Luke 11:34). Therefore, when the Lord rises to shake the earth terribly, He will “completely remove the idols” (Isaiah 2:18), utterly abolishing any representation or image that competes with His glory.

[1-3] The Lord prophesies severe judgments against the nation of Judah and Jerusalem, warning that He will withdraw their sustenance of bread and their sustenance of water. This signifies the removal of everything upon which the people rely and depend for their earthly survival. This prophecy of scarcity and loss of resources establishes a historical and doctrinal principle applicable to any nation that rejects God and His words. What is written in the Old Testament, including these national judgments, serves as an admonition and teaching for the believer of the present dispensation not to covet evil things (1 Corinthians 10:6-11; Romans 15:4).
[4-5] It is declared that God will appoint boys as princes and that children will rule over the people. Social anarchy is manifested when immaturity and inexperience take control, an event that represents a national catastrophe. The natural order and respect are reversed, resulting in mutual oppression where the young rise up in pride against the old. Doctrinally, this radical alteration of authority points to the time of Tribulation and reflects the profound moral and social decay of a nation in decline.
[8-9] The ruin of Jerusalem and the fall of Judah have one direct cause: their tongues and their deeds have been against the Lord, provoking the eyes of His glory. The rebellion is so open that the appearance of their faces testifies against them, declaring their sin brazenly like Sodom, without making the slightest attempt to hide it. The most severe divine judgment in this context is that the Lord allows the individual or nation to repay themselves with the same evil they have committed, reaping exactly what they have sown, for God cannot be mocked (Galatians 6:7).
[12] The text indicates that the oppressors of the people are boys, and that women ruled over them. Unlike pious and biblical exceptions such as Deborah, who judged righteously based on God's words, the general rule of women over men contravenes the established divine order. The imposition and exaltation of the rights of children and women over established authority is seen as a sign of social oppression that destroys the path and leads the people astray.
[13-15] The Lord rises up to plead and judge the elders of his people, and their princes. Political and religious leaders are condemned for devouring the vineyard and for hoarding the spoils of the poor in their homes. The corruption of rulers and the wealthy is exposed, as they increase their wealth at the expense of the needy, trampling on the poor and oppressing the helpless instead of administering fair judgment.
[16-24] The judgment is specifically directed at the pride and vanity of the daughters of Zion. Their pride is manifested in their posture: necks held high, eyes unfocused, and their feet tapping. Excessive clothing, jewelry, and ostentatious adornments designed solely to attract carnal attention are condemned, a stark contrast to the New Testament mandate to adorn oneself with modesty and a gentle spirit (1 Timothy 2:9; 1 Peter 3:3-4). As punishment for this worldly ostentation and pride, the Lord promises to exchange their perfume for stench, their well-groomed hair for baldness, and their luxurious clothes for sackcloth, revealing their nakedness and bringing profound humiliation and shame upon their vanity.

[1] The phrase "in that day" consistently refers to the Day of the Lord and the Second Coming of Christ, a period that overlaps both the Great Tribulation and the Millennium. The prophecy of seven women taking hold of one man reflects a drastic shortage of the male population, a ratio of seven to one, due to the destructive judgments of the end times. These women offer to provide their own bread and clothing, seeking only to bear the man's name to remove his reproach, which foreshadows a social condition in which mortality leaves a large number of women without husbands and multiplies births outside of marriage.
[2] The "branch of the Lord" is a direct designation for Jesus Christ, establishing that He will be beautiful and glorious during His millennial reign. The "fruit of the land" refers primarily to the literal and abundant harvests that the land will produce in the Millennium (Joel 2:21-24), which will be excellent for those of Israel who have escaped the Tribulation and remain safe in the land of Palestine.
[3-4] Those who remain in Zion and Jerusalem will be called saints, specifically those whose names are written among the living. The purification of this remnant occurs when the Lord washes away the defilement and cleanses Jerusalem of the blood by means of the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning. This purifying and judicial event is strictly linked to the Second Coming, when Christ returns to execute judgment and fire upon the earth (Malachi 3:1-3).
[5-6] The promise that Jehovah will create a cloud and darkness by day, and by night a brightness of flaming fire upon Mount Zion, indicates that the miraculous manifestations of the book of Exodus will be literally repeated in the future. The glory of God will be visible day and night over the temple and will defend His assemblies. Additionally, the provision of a tabernacle for shade from the heat and shelter from the storm applies to the physical needs of the remnant seeking to hide during the judgments of the Great Tribulation (Revelation 7:15-16), since in the eternal state there will be no need to take shelter from storms or the heat of the sun.

[1-2] The prophet sings a song about the vineyard of his beloved, situated on a fertile hillside that geographically represents the land of Palestine. Jehovah fenced this vineyard, removed its stones, and planted it with choice vines, expecting it to produce good grapes; however, it produced wild grapes because foreign seeds were planted mixed in with it. The construction of a watchtower and a winepress establishes a direct typological connection with the parable of the wicked tenants in the New Testament (Matthew 21:33).
[3-7] The text doctrinally defines the identity of the vineyard: "the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel," and the men of Judah constitute its "pleasing plant." The divine question about what more could have been done "in" His vineyard underscores a deep and internal work of God, which can be devotionally applied to the work of Christ in the believer (Isaiah 5:4). Because of the stubborn production of wild grapes, the inescapable judgment is pronounced: to remove His hedge so that the vineyard may be consumed, and to tear down His fence so that it may be trampled.
[8] A woe is pronounced upon material greed and monopolistic territorial expansion. Judgment falls upon those who "join house to house, and gather field to field" until they occupy all available space, illustrating a condition of unbridled greed that invariably brings ruin upon a nation.
[11] The text severely condemns the vice of drunkenness, declaring: "Woe to those who rise early in the morning to pursue drunkenness, who stay up late into the night, until wine inflames them."
[13] National destruction and captivity are directly based on ignorance of divine truth. The passage declares: "My people are taken captive because they have no knowledge." The leaders, described as honorable men, perish from hunger because they lack knowledge of God's words, accurately outlining the state of decay of a nation before God's judgment falls upon it.
[20] A stark divine judgment is established against the subversion of absolute moral values: "Woe to those who call evil good and good evil."
[26-28] This passage projects eschatologically toward the Second Coming of Jesus Christ. The description of the whirlwind and the relentless advance of armies with drawn bows and sharp arrows constitutes a prophetic typology of the destructive forces and judgments that will operate on the earth at the end of times.

[1] In the year of the death of King Uzziah, who died a leper for attempting to usurp the priestly office in the temple (2 Chronicles 26:19), the prophet Isaiah received a vision of the Lord seated on a high and exalted throne. The New Testament revelation directly identifies this Lord with Jesus Christ, as the apostle John declares that Isaiah saw the glory of Christ and spoke of Him in this passage (John 12:41). The "skirts" that filled the temple represent the royal robes or train that extends backward, establishing the absolute sovereignty and majesty of the monarch.
[2-3] Above the throne are the seraphim, whose title, in its Hebrew etymological root, means "the burning ones." These beings possess six wings, clearly distinguishing them from the cherubim, who appear with four wings in Ezekiel's visions (Ezekiel 1:6). With two wings they cover their faces, with two they cover their feet, and with two they fly, indicating that, unlike the cherubim who move in conjunction with the throne, the seraphim have independent mobility, flying above it. The profound reverence of these creatures establishes an undeniable lesson about the holiness of God: if supernatural beings associated with purifying fire must cover their faces and feet before the divine presence, fallen humanity has no justification whatsoever for boasting before its Creator. As he cried out, “Holy, holy, holy, O Lord of hosts,” the vibration and power of his voice shook the doorposts of the temple.
[5] The exclamation, “Woe is me! For I am ruined; for I am a man of unclean lips,” demonstrates that a proper vision of God’s holiness invariably produces a profound conviction of one’s own depravity and the corruption of human sin. This same theological principle operates in the experience of the apostle Peter, who falls at the Lord’s knees, immediately recognizing his sinful condition upon perceiving a manifestation of divine power (Luke 5:8).
[6-7] A seraph takes a burning coal from the altar using tongs. Doctrinally, this altar does not correspond to the altar of incense, which typifies prayer, but to the altar of burnt offering, which is strictly connected with the shedding of blood and the atoning sacrifice. By touching the prophet's lips with the coal that consumed the sacrifice, iniquity is removed and sin is purged. In the Old Testament dispensation, fire operates as a physical agent of purification; however, in the New Testament, the purification of the soul and spirit is effected exclusively through the blood of Jesus Christ (Hebrews 1:3, 9:14), refuting any sacramental doctrine that teaches spiritual purging of sins through literal fire or in a state of purgatory after death.
[8] When the Deity asks whom to send, the prophet responds with immediate personal submission: "Here I am, send me." This commission covers a broad timeframe, beginning with the preaching at Christ's first coming and extending prophetically through time to the events of the Tribulation.
[9-10] A judicial judgment is issued, commanding that the people hear without understanding and see without perceiving. This passage is of paramount importance in dispensational development, being cited four times throughout the New Testament (Matthew 13:14-15; John 12:40; Acts 28:25-27; Romans 11:8) to explain Israel's national rejection of its Messiah. The hardening of the heart and blindness do not occur in a deterministic vacuum, but rather God, through His foreknowledge, seeing from eternity that the nation would willfully reject the truth and the signs of His Son, decrees to darken their understanding and harden them as a just judgment for their unbelief.
[11-13] The prophet's question, "How long, O Lord?", places the final eschatological fulfillment in the judgments of the Great Tribulation, when the cities will be laid waste and without inhabitants. The surviving remnant of Israel (referred to as "the tenth") will return to the land of Palestine but will face extreme suffering. The Hebrew text indicates that this remnant "will be eaten," prophesying literal events of cannibalism that accompany the sieges under the reign of the Antichrist, in addition to the slaughter of the Jewish saints offered on the altar during the Tribulation (Revelation 6:9). Finally, the "holy seed" will subsist as the substance and future hope of the nation.

[1-2] During the days of Ahaz, king of Judah, a military confederation is formed against Jerusalem. The ten northern tribes of Israel, under King Pekah, ally themselves with Syria, under King Rezin, to attack the southern kingdom. The prophecy in this chapter is given to Ahaz, a king who rebelled against divine instructions, to encourage him in the face of this imminent threat of destruction.
[14] The text presents one of the most important messianic prophecies in Scripture concerning the virgin birth of Jesus Christ. The Hebrew term used in the original text is "almah," which strictly designates a virgin. Rabbinic traditions, such as the Babylonian Talmud, and textual critics attempt to alter the meaning by translating it as "young woman" to apply it to the mother of King Hezekiah; However, this is historically impossible since Hezekiah was already twelve years old when this prophecy was uttered. The name "Emmanuel" means "God with us," establishing that the child to be born was not merely a human, but God incarnate. Although the sign is given in the context of the war against Judah as a guarantee of deliverance, God postponed the literal fulfillment of the sign of the virgin birth for 750 years to apply it to a future generation because of Ahaz's unbelief and disobedience.
[16] The declaration that the land of the two kings feared by Ahaz (Syria and Israel) would be deserted before the child learns to reject the evil and choose the good establishes a divided chronology of events. God caused the military defeat of Rezin and Pecca to occur shortly thereafter to fulfill the promise of protection to Judah, while the full sign of the virgin birth in verse 14 was moved into the future for its fulfillment in the New Testament.
[17] Immediately after giving a sign of deliverance, days of calamity are pronounced, the likes of which had not been seen since the division of the kingdom (when Ephraim separated from Judah), indicating that the Lord would bring upon them the "king of Assyria." Typologically, the Assyrian king (Sennacherib) operates throughout the book of Isaiah as a direct type of the Antichrist who will invade the earth during the Tribulation period.
[18-19] The phrase "in that day" places the final doctrinal and prophetic fulfillment of this event at the Second Coming of Christ and the Tribulation. Jehovah's act of hissing at the fly of Egypt and the bee of Assyria uses figurative language to describe the swarm of enemy troops that will invade the earth. These armies will rest in the desert valleys, in caves, and on the thickets, wreaking havoc and annoyance upon the earth in the same way that a plague of aggressive insects devastates everything in its path.
[21-25] This final portion of the chapter alternates between descriptions of the Millennial and Great Tribulation eras. Verses 21 and 22 detail conditions of abundance and provision corresponding to the restoration of the millennial kingdom, while verses 23-25 ​​return to the description of territorial desolation during the pre-Millennium tribulation. In that time of judgment, the whole land will be filled with "thorns and thistles," forcing men to go in with "bows and arrows" to defend themselves or hunt, and the mountain areas that were previously cultivated will be abandoned, serving only for the grazing of oxen and small livestock.

[3] The text indicates that the prophet approached the prophetess, referring to his own legitimate wife, not a woman within the temple precincts. She conceived a son whose name serves as a prophetic sign that, before the child could learn to say "my father" or "my mother," the riches of Damascus and Samaria would be taken by the king of Assyria.
[8] It is prophesied that the king of Assyria (a type of the Antichrist) will pass over and spread out upon Judah, and that "he will spread out his wings and fill the breadth of your land, O Emmanuel." The use of the term "wings" prophetically points to an airborne army or a force attacking from the air. In this passage, the name Emmanuel, meaning "God with us," is applied directly to the land of Palestine, which agrees with the name the city will receive in the millennium, "Jehovah-shammah" (Ezekiel 48:35).
[9, 12] Comparing these verses with Zephaniah 3:8 reveals a precise prophetic construction that uses contemporary ecumenical terms such as "gather together," "association," and "confederation." These passages describe the effort of the United Nations and human confederations to establish a new world order without God. It is decreed that these political and ecumenical efforts will result in the nations being broken.
[14-15] The Lord of hosts promises to be a "sanctuary" for those who trust in Him, but "and to the two houses of Israel a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense." This apparent paradox is resolved in the New Testament, where it is established that the stone is Jesus Christ. During His first coming, Israel rejected the stone and stumbled over it (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:8), taking offense at the word. Verse 15 indicates that "many among them will stumble, and fall, and be broken," pointing to a judicial judgment upon those who disobey and stumble over the word.
[16-17] The command to "Bind up the testimony, seal the law among my disciples" refers to New Testament times and the church age, the term "disciples" being a New Testament term. Verse 17 underscores this temporary dispensation by declaring, “I will wait for the Lord, who has hidden his face from the house of Jacob,” describing the present condition where Israel has been temporarily blinded after rejecting its Messiah (Romans 11:7-8).
[18] The statement “Here I am, and the children the Lord has given me” is quoted verbatim in Hebrews 2:13, applying it to Jesus Christ and the believers given to him by the Father. In the prophetic framework of Israel, Isaiah's two sons operate as signs of the two advents: Maher-shalal-hash-baz typifies the judgment and destruction of Jerusalem at the first coming (70 CE), while Shear-jashub (a remnant will return) typifies the conversion and return of the Jewish remnant during the Second Coming after the tribulation.
[19] A stark warning is issued against consulting "diviners and soothsayers," prohibiting spiritism and contact with the dead. The principle is established that a people must consult their God (the law and the testimony), demonstrating that seeking spiritual direction or inner voices outside of God's words leads to deception, false guidance, and death.
[20] The final and absolute authority for examining any teacher, scientist, philosopher, or religious leader is established: "The law and the testimony." The doctrine declares: "If they do not speak according to this word, it is because there is no light in them." This is one of the most rigorous verses in Scripture for testing any system of human knowledge, revealing that a lack of alignment with the written words of God amounts to a total lack of spiritual light, regardless of the individual's education or supposed revelation.

[1-2] The passage is partially quoted in the New Testament in reference to the earthly ministry of Jesus Christ, being fulfilled at that time only in a spiritual sense (Matthew 4:14-16). Matthew's omission of twenty-five words demonstrates that the literal and complete fulfillment of this passage corresponds to the Second Coming. The people who walked in darkness and saw a great light prefigure the illumination and restoration of the nation of Israel at the Second Advent, an eschatological event that was historically typified by the conversion of the apostle Paul when he was struck down by a heavenly light on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:3).
[3] The statement "Though you increased the nation, you did not increase its joy" contains the word "not," which is fundamental in the original Hebrew text and should be preserved as correct, despite the unjustified omissions often made in modern versions. The first half of the verse points to the multiplication of the nation of Israel during an extended period of pain and affliction spanning from the crucifixion to the tribulation, which parallels the birth pangs described in Isaiah 26:15-18. The punctuation in the text dispensationally divides the two advents. The statement following the punctuation mark, indicating that "They shall rejoice before you as people rejoice at the harvest," points to the temporal transition and literal joy that the remnant will experience at the Second Coming, when the Lord divides the spoil and brings in the harvest of the earth (Revelation 14:14-16).
[6] The assertion "for unto us a child is born" refers directly to the incarnation and humanity of Jesus Christ, establishing him as the Son of Man born of the Virgin Mary. The consecutive phrase "a son is given unto us" dogmatically points to His deity, presenting Him as the Son of God freely given for the world (Romans 8:32). The prophetic indication that "the principality is upon his shoulder" was not fulfilled at His first appearance, but demands the strict fulfillment of His political, physical, and literal reign on earth at His return. Likewise, the title "Wonderful" testifies to the miraculous and unfathomable nature of His birth, His atoning death, and His immense power to save.
[7] The promise that "The multitude of dominion and peace will have no end" assures the establishment of an earthly and eternal government. This government will be instituted under the authority of the Lord Jesus Christ in the Millennium and will continue to spread throughout the eternal state. The throne of David will be affirmed and sustained forever, which requires that the fulfillment occur in a fully physical and literal way over the nation of Israel.

[5-15] The text declares: “O Assyrian, the rod of my anger, and a staff, my wrath in their hand” (Isaiah 10:5). The historical Assyrian, Sennacherib, functions typologically as a representation of the Antichrist in the end times. In the same way that Nebuchadnezzar is compared to a lion that breaks the bones of the scattered sheep of Israel (Jeremiah 50:17), the Assyrian is an instrument of judgment in the Lord’s hand. God uses this rebellious ruler simply as a tool—like an axe, a saw, or a rod—to punish the hypocritical nation. “As my hand has found the kingdoms of idols” (Isaiah 10:10) points to the origins of post-flood idolatry established in Babylon under Nimrod, the founder of that kingdom and the original prototype of the Assyrian (Genesis 10:10). Despite being the instrument of divine punishment against the idols of Samaria and the transgressions of Jerusalem, the Assyrian king’s attitude is one of pure arrogance, attributing his victories to his own power and not to the God who wields it. “But it shall come to pass, when the Lord has finished all his work on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, that I will punish the fruit of the proud heart of the king of Assyria” (Isaiah 10:12). This event foreshadows the destruction of the Antichrist at the Second Coming of Christ, establishing the principle that the Lord will first purify His people and then destroy the proud instrument He used to discipline them.
[17] "And the light of Israel shall be a fire, and its Holy One a flame that shall burn up and consume in one day its briers and thorns." In this judgment, what is light and glory to Israel becomes a consuming fire to its enemies. The passage describes the total destruction of the Assyrian, consuming both soul and body in fire, which establishes a strict doctrinal parallel with the warning to fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell (Matthew 10:28). Purification by fire will burn away the thorns and thistles that represent rebellious humanity.
[20] "And it shall come to pass at that time, that those who are left of Israel... shall no more stand on him who struck them, for they shall stand on the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, in truth." The phrase "at that time" places the ultimate fulfillment of this promise at the Second Coming. The remnant of Israel will cease to rely on political alliances or leaders like the Assyrian king who ultimately oppressed them. They will stop relying on the flesh and instead genuinely rely on the Lord.
[22-23] Although the covenant guaranteed the patriarchs numerous descendants (Genesis 22:17), prophecy indicates that only a very small remnant will survive the eschatological judgments and return to the Lord. This text fully agrees with the statement that the nation has multiplied without increasing its joy (Isaiah 9:3), illustrating a population increase accompanied by pain and affliction prior to deliverance. The consummation or destruction that the Lord of hosts has determined upon the earth will finally overflow in justice when the remnant is saved.
[24] "Therefore thus says the Lord God of hosts: 'Fear not, O my people, who dwell in Zion, in Assyria; He will strike you with a rod, and lift up His staff against you by the way of Egypt.'" This is a direct instruction to the Jewish remnant inhabiting the land, urging them not to fear the Assyrian invasion, which typifies the Antichrist. Israel will again experience conditions of slavery and oppression identical to those it suffered under the pharaohs in Egypt. The prophecy anticipates the extreme persecution of the Jewish remnant who will hide and flee during the great tribulation (Revelation 12:6, 14), an event that will immediately precede the Second Coming of Christ.
[26-27] "And the Lord of hosts will raise up a scourge against him, as the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Horeb..." God's punishment against the oppressor will be as miraculous and absolute as Gideon's victory over Midian and the judgment upon Egypt when the staff was raised over the Red Sea. In the context of the Second Coming, the burden imposed by the Antichrist will be lifted from the shoulders of Israel, and the yoke of slavery will be destroyed because of the anointing, freeing the nation forever.

[1-3] This eschatological renewal points directly to the Second Coming, when the Spirit of the Lord will rest upon Him. Verse 3 dogmatically establishes that the Lord “will not judge by what his eyes see, nor decide by what his ears hear.” This indicates that carnal sight and hearing often hinder correct judgment in human affairs, so the incarnate God will judge with perfect justice and absolute equity, completely disregarding outward appearances.
[4-5] The act of striking the earth with the rod of His mouth and slaying the wicked with the breath of His lips is an unmistakable mark of Christ’s Second Coming. Just as God spoke at creation so that there would be light (Genesis 1:3), the word that proceeds from His mouth has the authority to execute physical and literal judgment upon the nations. Justice will operate as the belt around his loins and faithfulness as the girdle around his kidneys, these being the unshakeable virtues that control and sustain his actions on the throne.
[6-9] These verses describe the literal redemption and regeneration of creation itself that will accompany the millennial reign. Nature will be restored in such a way that the wolf will dwell with the lamb, the leopard will lie down with the goat, and the lion will eat straw like the ox. The prophecy declares that animals will lose their wild instincts and will not harm or destroy on all "my holy mountain," referring to Mount Zion in Jerusalem (Psalm 2:6). The passage certifies that the physical earth, and not heaven, will be filled with the knowledge of Jehovah as the waters cover the sea.
[10] The phrase "in that day" places the prophetic fulfillment of this passage strictly within the Second Coming. The root of Jesse, Jesus Christ, will be raised as a banner to the nations. During this coming dispensation, the surviving Gentile nations will look to this banner for guidance and help from Israel, making the Lord's rest on earth glorious.
[11-12] The Lord will again lay His hand "a second time" to recover the remnant of His people. The first time a remnant returned from captivity to their land was under the leadership of Ezra and Nehemiah, following the Babylonian invasion and exile. This second occasion prophesies the modern national restoration that began to materialize after 1948, when the exiles of Israel and the scattered of Judah began to be gathered from the four corners of the earth. The text details specific places from which they will return for the millennium, including Assyria or Asshur, Egypt, Parthia, Ethiopia, Elam (Iran), Shinar (Iraq), Hamath (Syria), and the islands of the sea.
[16] A highway will be opened for the remnant of his people who remain from Assyria, just as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt. This illustrates that the liberation and national gathering of the Jewish people during the Second Coming of Christ will have miraculous characteristics and parallels comparable to those they experienced during the literal exodus described in the Old Testament.

[1] The doctrinal context of this chapter is immediately established by the opening phrase "In that day," which prophetically situates the passage in the Day of the Lord and the Second Coming of Christ. The entirety of chapter twelve functions as a song of redemption and a complementary scriptural commentary illustrating the events and joy of the Messianic return, paralleling the prophecies of national restoration described in other minor prophets (Zephaniah 3:14).
[2-3] The assertion "Behold, O God, my salvation" and the promise that "with joy you shall draw water from the wells of salvation" address the future period when the nation of Israel will experience its true and final deliverance. Although the text has a wonderful and rich spiritual application for the Christian today who finds comfort and salvation in the Lord, its doctrinal and literal fulfillment is strictly anchored in the Second Advent and the millennial kingdom.
[6] The command "Rejoice and sing, O inhabitant of Zion" finds its fulfillment and justification in the final declaration of the text: "for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel." The praise demanded of the nation is not based on an abstract concept, but on the dogmatic fact that the King and Messiah will dwell literally, physically, and visibly in the midst of his people in the city of Jerusalem.

[1] The chapter introduces the burden of Babylon, the first of twelve prophetic burdens recorded by the prophet in this book. Historically and doctrinally, chapters 13 and 14 focus on divine judgment upon this empire, but their primary prophetic application points to future events surrounding the Second Coming. The designation of "burden" implies that the Lord places an inescapable weight of judgment upon a nation because of its wickedness.
[6-9] The passage describes "the day of the Lord" as an imminent time of destruction from the Almighty, characterized by cruelty, wrath, and burning fury (Zephaniah 1:14-15). The explicit purpose of this period is to devastate the earth and destroy its sinners. In contrast to a complacent view of judgment, the text dogmatically states that God will punish the world for its wickedness, the arrogance of the proud will cease, and the haughtiness of the powerful will be humbled during the Second Coming of Christ.
[10] Astronomical phenomena are detailed, in which the stars of the sky and their constellations will not give their light, and the sun and moon will be darkened. This celestial event accompanies the world judgment and marks a total cosmic upheaval (Matthew 24:29). The specific mention of the constellations, of which there are twelve main ones, emphasizes the magnitude of the universal darkening on the day of God's wrath and at the Second Coming of Christ.
[15-16] A relentless physical punishment is decreed, in which all who are found will be pierced and fall by the sword. The prophecy further warns that children will be dashed to pieces and young men torn to pieces. These verses outline the violent nature of earthly judgments when nations face merciless destruction because of their rebellion.
[17] The Lord declares that He will raise up the Medes against Babylon. This verse illustrates God's absolute foreknowledge, as the prophecy was uttered approximately 180 years before Babylon emerged as a world power and the Medo-Persian Empire took control in 536 BC. It emphasizes that these invaders will be a divine instrument, impossible to bribe, for they will not value silver nor delight in gold as they carry out their mission.
[19-20] Babylon, considered the glory of kingdoms, faces perpetual destruction comparable to that of Sodom and Gomorrah. The prophecy guarantees that it will never again be inhabited or dwelled there from generation to generation, to the point that not even the Arab will pitch his tent there, nor will the shepherds make their fold there. Historically, the site was reduced to ruins, foreshadowing the ultimate destruction of spiritual Babylon at the Second Coming (Revelation 18:2).
[21-22] It is prophesied that the ruins of future Babylon will be inhabited by wild desert beasts and peculiar entities, specifically “fauns” and “dragons.” While secular zoology dismisses the existence of the faun or satyr (a half-man, half-goat figure) and the dragon, the sacred text mentions them literally. The presence of these beings underscores that the place becomes a dwelling place of unclean spirits and demonic powers, linking this desolation to scenarios such as the lake of fire and the judgment on Edom (Isaiah 34:13-14).

[1-2] The promise that God will have mercy on Jacob and settle them in their own land points eschatologically to the Second Coming. Although the nation experienced historical restorations, the declaration that foreigners will join them and the house of Israel will possess them as male and female servants (Isaiah 14:2) demands a future literal fulfillment where the Jewish nation will rule politically over the Gentiles in the Millennium. This demonstrates that, in the coming kingdom, Israel will cease to be the oppressed people and will directly rule over those who were formerly their oppressors, reversing the earthly political order.
[4] The command to raise up this proverb against the king of Babylon establishes a theological principle where the Lord addresses a spiritual entity through a human monarch. Historically, the addressee is Nebuchadnezzar, but he operates as a direct typology of Satan and the Antichrist in the last days. Nebuchadnezzar constructed an image related to the number 666, persecuted the Jewish remnant, and acted like a lion (Jeremiah 50:17), prophetically anticipating the actions of the son of perdition.
[9-11] The description of hell stirring to receive this king illustrates a literal scene where the dead shudder and welcome him into the underworld after his fall. Verse 11 mentions that his pride descends into the grave along with the sound of his lyres (stringed instruments). This intimately associates Satan with music, demonstrating that instruments and melodies fall with him into the grave, a detail that aligns with the description of the anointed cherub in Ezekiel 28, who had the work of his tambourines and fifes prepared within himself on the day of his creation.
[12-15] This passage presents the literal fall of "Lucifer, son of the morning." Although this fall is commonly placed exclusively in eternity past, before Genesis 1, it prophetically describes a future event in the middle of the Great Tribulation, when Satan is cast down to earth in great wrath (Revelation 12:7-9). The statements beginning with "I" ("I will ascend to heaven," "I will raise my throne above the stars of God," etc.) expose the fundamental ambition to usurp the throne of the universe. The mention of sitting "on the sides of the north" reveals the actual location of the Lord's throne, to the north. This being's ultimate destiny is not the deity he longs for, but to be cast down "to hell, to the sides of the pit" (Isaiah 14:15).
[16-17] Those who see this individual in his humiliation will be astonished to behold the "man" who made the earth tremble and who "made the world like a desert." This confirms that Satan will be incarnated as a man, assuming a physical form in the person of the Antichrist. During his world dominion, the destruction of the planet will be so devastating that it will turn cities into desolate wastelands. His brutality and lack of mercy are evidenced by the fact that he "never opened the prison" for his prisoners.
[19-20] The Antichrist is cast out of his tomb "like an abominable branch" and like a trampled corpse. At the Second Coming of Christ, this individual will not receive a proper burial like other kings; his body will be left exposed on the battlefield. The text explicitly states the reason for his condemnation: "because you destroyed your land, you killed your people." This proves doctrinally that the Antichrist has a direct connection to Israel and will be Jewish, having destroyed his own nation.
[24-27] The oath of the Lord of hosts to break the "Assyrian" in His land and trample him on His mountains definitively links this Assyrian with the king of Babylon and with Lucifer, demonstrating that they are figures of the same individual. The Lord Himself will see to the crushing of the final oppressor on the mountains of Palestine at the conclusion of the Tribulation. God's purpose to judge the nations and destroy the yoke of slavery on Israel is unshakeable, for "the Lord of hosts has determined it, and who can reverse it?" (Isaiah 14:27).

[1] The prophecy begins with the declaration of the burden upon Moab. A burden in this context represents an inescapable weight of judgment that God imposes upon a nation. The cities of Ar of Moab and Kir of Moab are devastated and silenced during the night. Doctrinally, the entirety of these physical and national judgments that fall upon the territory of Moab find their prophetic fulfillment during the time of the Second Coming.
[3-4] The text describes the population girding themselves with sackcloth in the streets, which constitutes an outward sign of deep sorrow and repentance. The judgment upon the nation is so severe that everyone howls and weeps abundantly, both in the squares and on the rooftops of their houses. The weeping extends to cities located east of the Jordan River, such as Heshbon, Elealeh, and Jahaz, causing even the armed soldiers of Moab to cry out in anguish at the devastation. The entire nation experiences an unprecedented level of terror and pain in preparation for the Second Coming of Christ.
[5-6] The Lord speaks of Moab as if it were an individual, expressing that its heart cries out for him while its life is burdensome. Faced with destruction, the nation's fugitives flee to Zoar. Zoar is the same historical city to which Lot fled when God poured out fire and brimstone to destroy Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:22-24), and was spared by the Lord on that occasion. The Moabites' flight continues up the ascent of Luhith with constant weeping, and along the road to Horonaim they raise a cry of anguish. These locations represent cities geographically situated south of the Dead Sea. Likewise, the waters of Nimrim, another town in Moab, are left completely deserted as part of the territorial devastation.
[9] Divine judgment intensifies by declaring that the waters of Dimon will be filled with blood. The retribution does not stop there, for the Lord promises to bring even greater evils upon Dimon, specifically sending lions upon those fugitives who manage to escape from Moab and upon the remnant that remains inhabiting the land.

[1] The prophetic command states: “Send a lamb to the ruler of the earth, from Sela in the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.” Geographically, the point of origin is Sela, identified with Petra in the region of Seir, or the desert. The instruction to send a lamb as a tribute to Mount Zion in Jerusalem points to the earthly submission that the nations will have to offer to the King. This context frames the future submission of the surrounding kingdoms in preparation for the Second Coming, when the absolute authority that will rule from God’s holy mountain will be recognized.
[2-4] The text illustrates forced displacement and terror by comparing the daughters of Moab to a “frightened bird fleeing its nest” at the fords of the Arnon River. This river constitutes a crucial natural border that the refugees must cross. Doctrinally and prophetically, this passage traces the escape route that the remnant of Israel will take during their flight into the wilderness (Revelation 12:6) during Jacob's time of trouble. The prophetic path will lead them through the territories of Moab and Edom until they descend to the land of Uz (Lamentations 4:21). There, the nation of Israel will suffer its final trial and purification, typologically mirroring the sufferings of Job, before receiving its ultimate restoration from the Lord. The request to provide shade and shelter for the exiles reflects the conditions of extreme persecution that this remnant will face. It is important to note that prophetic literature frequently alternates abruptly between laments of utter desolation and promises where the firstborn of the poor is securely fed, which requires careful consideration of the passage to understand the transitions to the kingdom.
[6] The basis of divine judgment against Moab is its immense pride. The text exposes the pride, arrogance, and haughtiness of the nation that trusted in itself. The ideal biblical commentary for understanding the magnitude of this sin is found in Jeremiah 48:29, which confirms the condemnation by detailing how Moab exalted itself with great pride against the Lord and His people. God detests pride of spirit, and this judgment on Moabite national pride establishes an inescapable eschatological principle: every human power that exalts itself will be humbled, crushed, and judged without mercy at the Second Coming of Christ.

[1] The burden of Damascus absolutely decrees that the city will cease to be a city and will become a heap of ruins. Since Damascus has historically and to this day continued to be an inhabited and prosperous city, the desolation described points to a strictly future prophetic fulfillment.
[2-6] The passage alternates abruptly between statements of judgment and promises of restoration. While verses 2 and 3 describe a positive millennial condition where the cities of Aroer will be for the flocks and the Gentile kingdom of Damascus will cease, verses 4 and 5 return to the tone of judgment, indicating that the glory of Jacob will be dimmed and his fatness will be thinned. The text compares this scarcity to a reaper who gathers a few ears of grain with his arm in the Valley of Rephaim, a site where David historically fought (2 Samuel 5:22). Verse 5, speaking of the vineyard and the harvest when the grapes are ripening, connects directly to the reaping of the earth at Armageddon described in Revelation 14:15. This destructive harvest preceding the Second Coming of Christ will leave corpses lying in wait upon which the birds of the mountains and the beasts of the earth will spend summer and winter (Job 38:41), cleaning up the remnants of the battle.
[7-8] The statement "In that day man will look upon his Maker" dogmatically places the fulfillment of this event at the Second Coming. The text establishes that the Creator will appear physically and visibly on earth, and the eyes of men will behold the Holy One of Israel (Hebrews 12:14). Humanity will directly see the wounds in His hands and feet, recognizing the One they pierced (Zechariah 12:10). Before the majesty of this appearance, humanity will completely abandon humanistic religion and idolatry, for "they will not look to the altars" nor to the work of their own hands.
[13-14] The text illustrates the annihilation of the nations gathered against the Lord, describing them as being chased like the dust of the mountains and "like dust swirling in the wind." The Second Coming of Christ will be a swift destruction. Verse 14 declares: "At evening time, behold, trouble; but before morning he is no more." In the prophetic and doctrinal context, the pronoun "he" refers directly to the figure of the Antichrist and his governmental system (Revelation 13). Before dawn on the Second Coming, the final oppressor of the earth will be completely destroyed. The chapter concludes by stating that this is the inescapable portion and fate of all those who seek to plunder and rob the nation of Israel.

[1-2] A “Woe” is pronounced upon the land that casts shadows with wings, geographically located “beyond the rivers of Ethiopia.” This places the territory in central Africa, where the headwaters of the Nile originate. This land sends ambassadors by sea “in reed boats upon the waters” to a nation “spread out and bare,” describing a tall, polished people. Although there is a historical context related to Egypt and Africa, the development of the passage demands a strictly future prophetic fulfillment associated with the events of the Second Coming.
[3] The divine call is broadened and addressed to “All the inhabitants of the world, and the dwellers of the earth.” This instruction establishes that the message is not dispensationally limited to the nation of Israel alone, but is directed to every individual or occupant of the world, encompassing Jews, Gentiles, or church members. All humanity is called to be attentive when a banner is raised on the mountains and to listen when the trumpet is sounded.
[4-5] The Lord declares, “I will rest and look down from my dwelling place,” remaining still “like clear heat on the grass, and like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.” This stillness anticipates the eschatological judgments, for before the harvest, at the end of the tribulation and when the cluster is ripening, the Lord will cut off the branches with pruning shears. This destructive action doctrinally points to the harvest of Christ’s Second Coming, illustrating a direct parallel with the harvest and the winepress of God’s wrath (Revelation 14:15).
[6] The physical outcome of divine judgment is detailed, where the bodies of the enemies will be left “to the birds of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth.” The specific prophecy that the birds of the air will spend the summer on them and the beasts of the earth will winter on them illustrates an immense accumulation of corpses at Armageddon. This carnage will provide literal food for the birds of prey for at least six consecutive months.
[7] The chapter culminates with the restoration and submission of the nations following the Second Coming of Christ. The text assures that "At that time the offering will be brought to the Lord of hosts" by that scattered and stripped people. This offering will be brought "to the place of the name of the Lord of hosts, to Mount Zion." This shows that the nations will come to Jerusalem to pay tribute and submit to the King's authority during his earthly reign at the Second Advent.

[1] The burden of Egypt has both historical and doctrinal fulfillment; since Egypt functions as a typology of the world, the judgments pronounced apply eschatologically to all nations. The text states that "the Lord rides on a swift cloud, and will enter Egypt," which physically and literally describes the divine means of transportation during the Second Coming (Psalm 104:3). On that occasion, the idols of Egypt will be shaken in His presence, marking God's intervention against the false deities of the land.
[4] The prophecy indicates that the Egyptians will be delivered "into the hand of a harsh lord, and a violent king will rule over them." Historically, this applied to the land of Egypt, but doctrinally, it is a strict reference to the figure of the Antichrist. This event illustrates a firm principle: since the nations of the world speak of peace but in their hearts reject the Lord's rule, He will allow them to be ruled by the worst possible man, just as Israel chose the murderer Barabbas over Christ.
[5] It is announced that "the waters of the sea will be cut off, and the river will be parched and dried up." Drought and violent upheaval of nature accompany these divine judgments, refuting human ideas about flooding and establishing that the water level will indeed drop.
[11] God's judgments expose the folly of human education and leadership, declaring that "Surely the princes of Zoan are foolish," an ancient Egyptian city known as Tanis. The counsel of the wise men turns brutal, showing that neither princes nor supposed inherited wisdom can deliver the nation from the purpose the Lord of hosts has determined.
[17] The text declares that "the land of Judah will be a horror to Egypt," an event that marks the preparation for the Second Coming of Christ. In those days, the mere mention of Judah will cause dread because of the counsel God has decreed against the nation.
[18] The repeated phrase "In that day" places the dogmatic fulfillment of this passage at the Second Coming (Isaiah 19:18, 19, 21, 23, 24). Five cities in Egypt are prophesied to speak "the language of Canaan," the number five being associated with the number of death in biblical numerology. The language of Canaan is Hebrew, the heavenly language, which will be restored during this coming age so that the peoples may call upon the name of God (Zephaniah 3:8-9).
[21-22] It is noted that Egypt will know God on that day and “will offer sacrifice and offering,” proving that during the millennial kingdom there will be a restoration of literal sacrifices on the earth. The Lord “will strike Egypt, striking and healing,” demonstrating that divine retribution will be followed by national restoration when they turn to Him.
[23-25] In the coming kingdom there will be “a highway from Egypt to Assyria.” The Assyrians will enter Egypt and the Egyptians will enter Assyria, crossing the Euphrates River, which will be dried up for this purpose (Revelation 16:12), and both peoples will serve together. Israel will be the "third with Egypt and Assyria," geographically situated as a blessing in the center of both territories with a road running through them. Surprisingly, God will bestow upon two Gentile nations that historically oppressed the Jews titles He normally reserves for His own people. The Second Coming of Christ will bring about the submission and blessing of these nations when the Lord declares: "Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance."

[1] The story recorded in this passage takes place before the destruction of the northern tribes. The text mentions that Tartan came to Ashdod, a Philistine city on the coast, sent by Sargon, king of Assyria. The word "Tartan" is not a proper name, but an official title designating a governor or chief leader. This military movement indicates that the Assyrians were dangerously close to Judah by attacking the coastal cities.
[2] The Lord commands the prophet to untie the sackcloth from his loins and remove his sandals from his feet, which he obeys, walking "naked and barefoot." Isaiah had been wearing sackcloth as a sign of fasting and mourning. "Nakedness" in this biblical context does not imply a total lack of clothing, but refers to wearing only the basic undergarment, similar to the linen ephod worn by David (2 Samuel 6:14), which would be equivalent to modern underwear. God frequently used prophets as living, objective illustrations to convey His message, rather than simply delivering verbal speeches. By obeying this commission, Isaiah loses his reputation by walking in these conditions.
[3] The prophet's act serves as a sign and wonder over Egypt and Ethiopia for three years. This period provided a time of warning, so that any Egyptian or Ethiopian who communicated with Jerusalem would learn that the prophet's strange behavior foreshadowed their future captivity at the hands of Assyria. In this statement, the Lord calls Isaiah "my servant Isaiah," a title that throughout the book of the prophet is supremely applied to the Lord Jesus Christ.
[4-6] The prophecy dictates that the king of Assyria will take the Egyptians and Ethiopians, young and old, into captivity. This Assyrian king operates doctrinally as a direct type of the Antichrist, who will rule before the Second Coming. Unlike the nakedness described by Isaiah, the nakedness of these captives is of an aggravated kind, as they will be led away "with their buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt." This illustrates the characteristic cruelty of the Assyrian Empire and its ultimate oppression of nations. The inhabitants will be filled with fear and shame as they witness the fall of Ethiopia and Egypt, nations in which they had placed their hope and glory. The verse refers to the "inhabitant of this island," describing those who sought deliverance and refuge from the oppression of the Assyrian king. The defeat of these powers demonstrates the futility of seeking help from nations that will also be dominated and judged, an event that typifies the conditions of the world and the destruction of the oppressor at the Second Coming of Christ.

[1] The burden of the desert of the sea places a weight of judgment upon this geographical region (Isaiah 21:1). This expression seems to have a connection with the African continent, given that the text describes the invasion by comparing it to "whirlwinds at noon" sweeping across the land.
[2-4] The text reveals a harsh vision where the transgressor transgresses and the destroyer destroys. The command "Go up, O Elam; draw near, O Media" (Isaiah 21:2) is a prophetic indication that the Medo-Persian Empire is preparing to attack and besiege Babylon. Upon the revelation of this judgment, the prophet recounts that his loins were filled with pain and he experienced "pains like those of a woman in labor" (Isaiah 21:3). Doctrinally and prophetically, these birth pangs are a strict typology of the affliction and terror the world will experience during the Great Tribulation (1 Thessalonians 5:3; Isaiah 66:7-8).
[9] The announcement that “Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the idols of her gods he has broken to the ground” has a twofold fulfillment. Historically, the prophecy was fulfilled when the Medo-Persian Empire conquered the city of Babylon and defeated its idols (Daniel 5:28-31). Prophetically, this event points to the ultimate destruction of spiritual, idolatrous Babylon that will take place just before the Second Coming of Christ (Revelation 18:2).
[11-12] The burden of Dumah, located south of the Dead Sea, is presented, where a voice cries out from Seir: “Watchman, what about the night? Watchman, what about the night?” Seir is the geographical area of ​​Edom through which God will march and pass during the Second Coming. The watchman’s response, “Morning comes, and then night,” sets out a precise dispensational framework. The initial “night” typifies the present church age (Romans 13:12), which will be followed by the “morning” of the rapture. However, this morning will be followed by another “night” corresponding to the time of tribulation, which in turn will precede the Second Coming when the Sun of Righteousness rises (Malachi 4:2). The final response, "If you wish to ask, ask; return, come," functions doctrinally as a plea for the Second Coming of Christ, in the same way that the final prayer of the New Testament concludes (Revelation 22:20).
[13-17] The chapter concludes with the burden on Arabia, indicating that the companies of Dedan will lodge in the forest in Arabia (Isaiah 21:13). The inhabitants of the land of Tema, also located in Edom, are instructed to bring water to the thirsty and bread to the fleeing (Isaiah 21:14). This provides a prophetic picture of the remnant of Israel, who will flee from the sword of war and persecution, finding refuge in the wilderness (Matthew 25:35). Finally, God decrees that within a year, counted as the years of a "soldier of war," all the glory of Kedar will fail, and the remnant of the archers will be diminished, since the Lord God of Israel has spoken it unfailingly (Isaiah 21:16-17).

[1-15] This chapter introduces the burden of the valley of vision (Isaiah 22:1). Negative judgments are pronounced upon Jerusalem before its historical fall to Nebuchadnezzar, as well as upon the northern kingdom of Israel in the face of the Assyrian attacks of Sennacherib and Sargon. The Lord God of hosts directs his attention directly to Shebna, the treasurer “who is in charge of the house.” This individual seized the temple treasury and kept the goods for himself, instead of distributing them legitimately to the Levites, the scribes, and others who performed the work in the temple.
[16] Shebna is severely confronted by the Lord because of his presumption: “What have you here, or whom have you here, that you have hewn out a tomb for yourself here…?” Instead of seeking repentance or trusting in God, this leader attempts to secure himself by carving out a kind of air-raid shelter or hurricane-proof cellar from the rock to hide from the impending judgments. Shebna's attitude illustrates the treachery of those who form ungodly alliances with foreigners seeking their destruction, operating in a manner identical to the corrupt partnership with Tobiah the Arab in the days of rebuilding (Nehemiah 13:4-5).
[17-19] Divine judgment decrees that Shebna will be taken into a powerful captivity and violently tossed like a ball into a spacious land. This large land is Babylon, a territory roughly six times the size of Palestine, where Shebna will ultimately die. "The chariots of your glory" (Isaiah 22:18), representing the army on which the leadership relied to defend Jerusalem, will become the utter shame of their master's house. The Lord will push him from his position and cast him down from his status, demonstrating man's utter inability to evade divine justice.
[20-25] Beginning with the phrase "And it shall be in that day" (Isaiah 22:20), the structure of the passage marks an eschatological transition toward the events of Christ's Second Coming. God calls his servant Eliakim, son of Hilkiah, to replace the deposed administrator. Throughout the passage spanning verses 20-25, the figure of Eliakim functions as a direct and evident typology of Jesus Christ. All the honor, authority, and burden of his father's house will fall upon his shoulders, which will have its literal and definitive fulfillment at the Second Coming, when the Lord will rule the nations of the earth.

[1] The "burden of Tyre" addresses God's judgment on this prominent seaport on the Mediterranean coast. Historically, Tyre was besieged and conquered by Alexander the Great, who built an earthen rampart to attack it. The mention of the "ships of Tarshish" refers to the merchant fleet that sailed between Phoenicia and Tarshish, a territory generally identified with Spain. The destruction of the city is revealed to the sailors from "the land of Chittim," which geographically points to Cyprus or Greece. Prophetically and doctrinally, the wisdom, materialism, and destruction of Tyre operate as a direct typology of the destruction of great Babylon and the Antichrist system that will occur at the Second Coming.
[2-6] The text commands silence from the inhabitants of the island, which had been enriched by the merchants of Sidon. The cities of Tyre and Tarshish are historically connected to Sidon, being described as its daughters, since the Phoenicians crossed the sea and established these colonies along the coast. Divine judgment on this trade network forces its inhabitants to flee to Tarshish as refugees, lamenting deeply and fleeing their homeland.
[8-9] The Lord has decreed this judgment against Tyre, described in the text as "the city that bestows crowns." The immense political and commercial influence of the city is evident in the fact that its merchants are princes and its traders the nobles of the land. Prophetically, this trading city and its global system align closely with the description of the harlot in Revelation 17 and 18, who dominates world trade before the Second Coming of Christ.
[14] The command to "Wail, ships of Tarshish" is a figure of speech indicating the financial collapse and economic ruin of the merchant fleet upon losing its main port and strength. The judgment states that Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, a period defined in the text as "like the days of a king." Although the exact historical application of this seventy-year span is enigmatic to many exegetes, it marks a literal period of inactivity in which the city is rendered completely inactive.
[15-17] At the conclusion of the seventy years, Tyre will return to its former practices and is likened to a harlot who sings and takes up the harp to lure her clients back. Scripture frequently uses prostitution as a type of unscrupulous global trade and international commerce. This city will again commit adultery with all the kingdoms of the earth on the face of the world, consolidating its position as the leading global economic power before the Second Coming.
[18] In the fulfillment of the prophecy, the profit and wages of this city “will be consecrated to the Lord.” Its immense wealth will not be hoarded by the wicked forever, but, similar to how the spoils of Jericho were set apart by divine command, this abundance will become “holy to the Lord.” After the Second Coming of Christ, the Lord will definitively destroy this corrupt commercial system and transfer all its merchandise to His people. These resources will be intended so that those who dwell before the Lord in the Millennium may eat their fill and be provided with lasting clothing.

[1-3] The Lord decrees a devastating judgment upon the earth, leaving it empty, desolate, and in turmoil. The physical alteration where the earth is turned upside down suggests a literal change in the tilt or axis of the planet that accompanies eschatological cataclysms. The judgment is universal and without exception, affecting people and priest, servant and master, buyer and seller alike.
[5] The pollution of the earth is the direct result of human rebellion. The inhabitants have transgressed the laws, falsified the law, and broken the everlasting covenant. This covenant refers to the agreements given to Noah, or the Adamic covenant, which humanity has systematically violated by altering the laws of the earth.
[10] The sentence declares that "the city of confusion is broken." Doctrinally, this points to Babel or Babylon, whose etymological root in Genesis 11 means confusion. It is a picture of the inescapable collapse of urban systems and human government without God, reducing the city to ruins because of its rebellion.
[13-16] Despite the worldwide devastation, God tempers his judgment with mercy, leaving a remnant that is compared to gleanings after the grape harvest. This remnant will glorify the Lord in the fires and on the islands of the sea. However, the contrast is sharp in verse 16, where the prophetic voice cries out in the midst of tribulation, “My weakness, my weakness, woe is me!” indicating the conditions of extreme scarcity, famine, and pain that characterize the end times when the transgressors operate with great disloyalty against God’s people.
[17-18] A dread, a pit, and a snare are pronounced upon the inhabitants of the earth. This is a snare that will catch the inhabitants of the entire world suddenly and inescapably (Luke 21:35). Furthermore, the text declares that “the windows of heaven were opened,” suggesting that elements or judgments descend from the second heaven, trapping and punishing those who try to escape earthly destruction.
[19-20] The earth will be utterly broken and shaken exceedingly, reeling like a drunkard and being removed. These cosmic and geological disturbances demonstrate that the planet is knocked out of its normal orbit, falling under the heavy yoke of human transgression and the iniquity of the world, unable to rise again.
[21-22] At the Second Coming, the Lord will punish not only human kings on earth, but also "the host of the exalted ones on high," a reference to the invisible demonic principalities and powers in the constellations or heavenly places. These beings, along with earthly leaders, will be gathered together as if imprisoned in a dungeon or pit. The text states that "after many days they will be visited," establishing a precise doctrinal parallel with the imprisonment of Satan and his hosts in the abyss for a thousand years, only to be released for a short time at the end of the millennium (Revelation 20:1-3).
[23] The glory of God will completely eclipse natural light and current energy sources in the solar system. The moon will be ashamed and the sun confounded before the divine radiance. This event marks the establishment of the earthly kingdom, when "the Lord of hosts will reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem." At the Second Coming of Christ, the text concludes dogmatically by presenting the Lord ruling visibly and gloriously before his elders, confirming that the promised throne is not celestial nor operating from Washington or Rome, but a political and physical reality of absolute dominion on earth.

[3] The text declares that the strong people will glorify God and that the city of formidable nations will fear Him. Doctrinally and prophetically, this indicates that before the Second Coming of Christ, the nations of the earth will gather and submit to the authority of a particular city to be governed globally. The expression distinguishes a singular “city” that houses and dominates plural “nations.” This urban and power structure is explicitly identified in the New Testament as Babylon the Great, the religious and political system established on seven hills (Revelation 17:9, 18).
[4] The Lord claims to be a stronghold for the poor, a stronghold for the needy in their affliction, a refuge from the storm and a shade from the heat. The subsequent description, “when the fury of the violent is like a storm against a wall,” literally illustrates the judgment events that precede the Second Coming. The language used in the original text describes a sudden, destructive blast or explosion that strikes a wall, accompanied by such extreme heat that it demands protective shade. Far from describing ancient weapons like bows or spears, this devastation typologically points to the nature of modern weapons, illustrating the physical effects of a holocaust or atomic attack. In the midst of this literal devastation on earth, God assures us that He is the refuge that protects His people.
[8] The divine promise that God will swallow up death in victory is directly quoted by the apostle Paul when describing the transformation of believers' corruptible bodies in the resurrection of the present age (1 Corinthians 15:54). However, the second part of the verse adds the statement that the Lord God will wipe away every tear from every face. Although the establishment of justice and judgment occurs at the Second Coming of Christ, the complete elimination of weeping and the absolute cessation of pain are not historically fulfilled there. The final fulfillment of that clause occurs much later, and is doctrinally confirmed in the New Testament when God wipes away the tears from human faces only at the beginning of the eternal state and the new creation (Revelation 21:4). The passage illustrates how biblical prophecy frequently groups events or statements belonging to different dispensations into a single verse, linking the initial victory over physical death with the state of consummated joy that follows the Second Coming.

[5-10] The text describes the humiliation of the haughty city, which is trampled underfoot by the poor and needy during the Second Coming of Christ. As the kingdom is established, the Jewish remnant declares that they have waited on the Lord in the path of His judgments. A fundamental theological principle regarding the Millennium is established: “For when your judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness” (Isaiah 26:9). However, verse 10 demonstrates that the establishment of a perfect environment does not eradicate the sinful nature of fallen humanity. Even if mercy is shown to the wicked and the King physically reigns in the “land of righteousness,” some will refuse to learn righteousness, act unjustly, and refuse to behold the majesty of God. This aligns with the prophecy concerning the nations that will rebel and refuse to go up to Jerusalem to worship the King during the Millennium (Zechariah 14:16-19).
[14-15] An absolute contrast is drawn between the Gentile oppressors and the nation of Israel. The dead enemies “will not live” or “be resurrected” at the beginning of the millennial kingdom, for God has caused their memory to perish. In contrast, God has “increased the nation” of Israel, even though He had previously scattered them “to the ends of the earth.” This increase of the nation occurs during a period of deep sorrow and affliction in the Tribulation, which doctrinally interprets the statement that God multiplied the people, but “did not increase their joy” (Isaiah 9:3).
[16-18] The nation of Israel confesses its inability to have brought salvation or deliverance to the world during its dispersion in the church age. Their affliction under divine punishment is compared to a pregnant woman nearing the time of delivery, crying out in her pain. Despite their suffering, they acknowledge that they have not wrought any deliverance on earth nor caused the inhabitants of the world to fall, recognizing that world dominion has remained in Gentile hands.
[19] The passage presents an explicit promise of a literal, bodily resurrection. Unlike verse 14, where it is declared that the ungodly oppressors will not be resurrected, here it is prophesied: “Your dead will live; they will rise with my dead body.” This is the hope of a Second Coming where the Old Testament saints and the Tribulation martyrs (Revelation 20:4–5) will physically rise from the dust, an event foreshadowed and assured by Christ’s own bodily resurrection. The exclamation “Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust!” It certifies that the earth will cast out the dead, pointing directly to the event where a remnant is resurrected to enter the kingdom.
[20] The command, “Go, my people, enter your rooms and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the wrath has passed by,” is directed strictly to the Jewish people. Doctrinally, this event describes a post-Tribulation rapture of the Jewish saints that occurs a few days or months before the Lord literally descends to earth. The people are temporarily hidden in the chambers of the third heaven to be protected from the coming wrath, while divine indignation falls upon the empire of the Antichrist and the United Nations.
[21] The justification for the hiding in the preceding verse is revealed by declaring that “the Lord is coming out of his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their sins.” This marks the precise moment of Christ's Second Coming, when God abandons His throne to execute physical vengeance upon the world. The declaration that the earth "will disclose its blood, and will no longer cover its slain" establishes the principle that unjustly shed blood cries out from the earth demanding divine retribution. At the Second Coming, the earth will be unable to absorb or conceal the slaughter of the righteous, and the blood of the slain will demand the Lord's absolute and final judgment upon the murderers.

[1] The Lord declares a direct judgment upon a supreme spiritual entity: “In that day the Lord will punish with his fierce, great, and powerful sword Leviathan the coiling serpent, and Leviathan the writhing serpent; he will slay the dragon that is in the sea.” This verse destroys any modern attempt to categorize Leviathan simply as a crocodile or a natural sea creature, for the Scriptures explicitly identify it as the ancient serpent and dragon. Doctrinally, the passage connects directly with the last book of the Bible, where the devil is described as a great red dragon with seven heads (Revelation 12:3, 9), and with the sea creature described in detail in Job 41. This spiritual power, which rules over the children of pride, will be physically punished by the literal sword of the Lord at the Second Coming.
[2-6] In contrast to the vineyard described in previous chapters that produced wild grapes and was destroyed because of its rebellion (Isaiah 5:1-7), this passage presents the nation of Israel as a fruitful vineyard of red wine that the Lord guards and waters at all times. The divine promise that Jacob will take root, blossom, and "fill the face of the world with fruit" refers to the house of Judah and Israel dwelling securely in their land during the Millennium. After the Second Coming of Christ, the land of Palestine will experience unprecedented material and physical productivity, being perfectly irrigated and restored from all previous desolation.
[8-9] The cleansing of the nation from iniquity is described through a fierce east wind that burns and cleanses like fire. Verse 9 establishes the condition for national remission and the removal of idolatry: “By this the iniquity of Jacob will be purged, and this will be the full fruit of the removal of his sin: when he makes all the stones of the altar like crushed lime stones…” When the nation of Israel finally repents, it will destroy its idolatrous altars by reducing them to dust, an act of purification historically foreshadowed by King Josiah during his revival (2 Chronicles 34:7). Doctrinally, this complete forgiveness and cleansing of the nation of Israel from sin demands strict future fulfillment at the Second Coming.
[12] A literal, physical gathering of the nation is prophesied, stating that “the Lord will strike from the riverbed to the Wadi of Egypt, and you, O children of Israel, will be taken one by one.” God marks the original geographical boundaries promised to the seed of Abraham and assures that He will gather His people individually from the dispersion. This miraculous and meticulous gathering of the seed of Jacob precedes the establishment of the earthly kingdom at the Second Coming of Christ.
[13] The chapter concludes by declaring that “a great trumpet will sound” to gather the outcasts who were about to perish in the lands of Assyria and Egypt. This great trumpet is the same trumpet that will sound to gather the elect from the four winds of the earth (Matthew 24:31). This eschatological event points to a post-Tribulation gathering and rapture in which the scattered and persecuted Jews return to their promised land. The ultimate result of this call is that the remnant will come to prostrate themselves and worship God on the holy mountain in Jerusalem, which undeniably certifies that the temple will be rebuilt and Levitical worship within it will be restored in the age to come.

[4] The “fading flower of his glorious beauty that is on the head of the fertile valley” and the “early fruit before summer” illustrate the sudden destruction that will fall upon the proud and the drunken of Ephraim. The beauty and status that human leaders possess are not permanent and will quickly disappear, consumed by the impending judgment without a trace.
[5-6] The phrase “In that day” doctrinally frames the prophecy within the Second Coming. At that time, the Lord of hosts will be “a crown of glory and a diadem of beauty to the remnant of his people.” He promises to be a spirit of judgment upon those who sit to judge, which aligns with the New Testament promise that the Lord’s followers will sit upon twelve thrones to judge the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew 19:28).
