Additionally, God will give strength to those who "push back the battle to the gate," providing the necessary power for the remnant's military victory in their conflict against the nations (Zechariah 14:1-3).
[9-11] The text details God's method of biblical teaching through "precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line." Faced with the rejection of this clear and simple instruction, the Lord warns that "with stammering tongues and with another tongue he will speak to this people." The apostle Paul directly quotes this verse in the New Testament when regulating the gift of tongues in the local church (1 Corinthians 14:21). This passage doctrinally establishes that speaking in tongues or stammering tongues was primarily given as a sign of judgment directed at the unbelief of the nation of Israel and the leaders who ruled in Jerusalem.
[14-15] The Lord severely rebukes "the scoffers who rule over this people in Jerusalem." The nation's declaration that "we have made a covenant with death, and with hell we have made an agreement" prophetically points to the false peace treaty that Israel's leaders will sign with the Antichrist during the tribulation (Daniel 9:27). In their arrogance, the nation will mistakenly believe that lies and deception will protect them from invasion and punishment.
[16] "See, I lay a stone in Zion, a stone of strength, a cornerstone, a precious stone, a sure foundation." This chief and precious stone is none other than the Lord Jesus Christ. The New Testament dogmatically identifies Him as the stone over which Israel stumbles, but which also serves as their absolute refuge (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:6). The command “let him who believes not be put to shame” guarantees the eternal and physical security of those who place their faith in Him. Although Christ was rejected by the builders at His first appearance, He will establish this literal and perfect foundation on earth during Christ’s Second Coming.
[17-18] Divine judgment is relentless against human falsehood: “Hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and waters will flood the hiding place.” The political covenant that Israel made with death will be completely annulled, and the agreement with hell will not stand. When the “storm of the scourge” passes over the earth, the nation will be trampled underfoot. This “flood” describes the severe judgments of the great tribulation, a holocaust that will break every corrupt alliance and purify the nation, preparing it for the Second Coming.
[21] “For the Lord will arise as at Mount Perazim… to do his work, his strange work; and to perform his task, his strange task.” God’s strange work is military retribution and literal devastation upon his earthly adversaries. Just as the Lord intervened physically using natural phenomena and hail in the days of Joshua (Joshua 10:11–14), nature itself will become his arsenal of war (Revelation 16:21). This conflict culminates in the inescapable punishment and annihilation of the armies united under the man of sin at the Second Coming of Christ.

[1-4] The prophecy is addressed to "Ariel," meaning the lion of God, a direct reference to Jerusalem, the city where David lived. The Lord will bring anguish, affliction, and sorrow upon Ariel, raising a siege and siege walls against it. This siege has a historical fulfillment through Nebuchadnezzar (Jeremiah 52:4) and Titus in 70 CE, but it doctrinally points to a final siege under the Antichrist. The text describes a voice speaking from the dust, like that of a whispering spirit or familiar, which contrasts sharply with the still, small voice of the Spirit of God.
[5-8] The multitude of foreign nations and the terrible ones who fight against Ariel will be reduced to fine dust and passing chaff. The Lord uses enemy nations to discipline His people, but then executes final judgment upon those same nations. The attack on Mount Zion is likened to a starving man who dreams of eating but awakens with an empty soul. Enemy nations will dream of riches and conquest after besieging the city (Revelation 11), but upon awakening from their illusion at the Second Coming of Christ, they will find themselves in utter ruin and have nothing.
[9-10] The Lord has poured out a spirit of deep sleep and closed the eyes of the prophets, rulers, and seers of the nation. This is the judgment of God Himself blinding the nation of Israel after it willfully rejected the truth. By covering the prophets and seers after the days of the apostles, the Lord plunged the nation into total spiritual blindness.
[11-14] God's vision becomes to the people like the words of a sealed book. The book is given to an educated man who claims he cannot read it because it is sealed, and to an illiterate man who excuses himself by citing his lack of education. The nation approaches God with its mouth and honors Him with its lips, but its heart is far away, and its fear of God is taught by the commandments of men. Consequently, God promises to do a marvelous work in which the wisdom of the wise will perish and the prudence of the prudent will be hidden. This passage establishes the divine principle by which God confounds the intellectuals of the world (1 Corinthians 1:19).
[16] The text severely condemns human pride by questioning whether the clay will say of its maker, “He did not make me.” This exposes the inescapable folly of those who contend with God and refuse to acknowledge His work and His sovereign power over creation.
[17-18] A millennial promise is established where Lebanon will become a fertile field, and the fruitful field will be valued as a forest. The statement "in that day" places this fulfillment strictly within the Second Coming. At that time, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see, emerging from darkness and gloom. During this earthly reign, all the promises of God's word will be visibly fulfilled.
[24] Those who erred in spirit will come to understanding, and those who murmured will learn doctrine. This points to an absolute millennial transformation where previous unbelief and ignorance will give way to a real understanding of the Lord's doctrine upon His return to earth.

[1-4] The rebuke is directed against the "rebellious children... who take counsel, but not from me" (Isaiah 30:1). The nation of Israel seeks political help by turning to Egypt, as evidenced when "their princes went to Zoan, and their ambassadors came to Hanes" (Isaiah 30:4). This illustrates the failure of relying on human alliances and a nation that cannot provide aid or benefit, instead of consulting God first.
[8] The command “Go now, and write it before them on a tablet, and make it plain in a book” applies doctrinally to the instructions for the nation of Israel, but at the same time establishes immutable principles concerning the Lord’s dealings with any nation on earth.
[21] The promise “Then your ears will hear a word behind you, saying, ‘This is the way; walk in it’” shows that the Holy Spirit often interrupts a general discourse addressed to a multitude to speak directly to a single individual. God guides one’s steps personally to prevent them from straying to the right or left.
[25] The prophecy that “on every high mountain and on every lofty hill there will be rivers and streams of water on the day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall” points to literal eschatological events. The physical collapse of tall towers precedes the Second Coming, marking the time of a great slaughter of enemy nations.
[26] This passage functions as a literal meteorological and astronomical report of conditions on earth during the Millennium. In that period of restoration, the sunlight will be seven times greater than it is now, providing unprecedented physical radiance that will accompany the healing of God's people.
[27-28] The text declares that "the name of the Lord comes from afar, his countenance burning, and he is heavy with suffering; his lips are full of wrath, and his tongue is like a consuming fire" (Isaiah 30:27). This destructive description, where the breath of the Lord reaches up to the neck like a torrent to shake the nations, describes the judgments of Christ's Second Coming. Verse 28 adds that there will be "a bridle that causes the jaws of the peoples to stumble." Eschatologically, the Antichrist imposes an iron grip on the nations; the Lord uses this restraint and places a hook in their jaws to gather them toward their inevitable destruction.
[30-33] The passage recounts the Lord's intervention in the battle of Armageddon. God will make the majesty of his voice heard and show the descent of his arm with the indignation of his wrath and the flame of consuming fire. The text concludes by establishing the ultimate fate of the Assyrian, a direct typology of the Antichrist or the Son of Perdition, who will finally enter the Lake of Fire, which here is called "Topheth," prepared beforehand by the Lord for the oppressive king.

[4-5] The comparison of the Lord of hosts descending to fight for Mount Zion “like a young lion, and a young lion roaring over its prey” sets a picture of military retribution. Simultaneously, the promise that “like birds hovering overhead, so the Lord of hosts will protect Jerusalem, to protect and deliver, to pass over and save” points to a literal and physical fulfillment. God will descend from on high and pass over the city in the air to protect it from its enemies. This event, where the Lord defends the city and the nation, will take place at the Second Coming. Historically, Satan attempted to use and distort a similar promise of angelic preservation in Jerusalem by tempting the Lord to throw himself down from the pinnacle of the temple (Luke 4:9-11), thus anticipating the divine protection that will accompany the Second Coming of Christ.
[7] The statement, “For in that day men shall cast away their idols of silver and their idols of gold, which your hands have made to sin” describes humanity’s inescapable reaction to God’s judgment. During the Second Coming, humanity will finally rid itself of the idolatry, wealth, and materialism in which it had trusted, casting aside everything it made with its own hands upon seeing the terror of the Lord (Revelation 6:15–17).
[8] The text dogmatically declares, “Then the Assyrian shall fall by the sword, but not by man; and the sword shall devour him, but not by man.” The “Assyrian” in this passage functions strictly as a typology of the Antichrist (Isaiah 10:5). The knife or sword that devours this adversary does not belong to an earthly soldier, neither strong nor weak, but is the sharp sword that comes out of the mouth of God (Revelation 19:15). At the Second Coming of Christ, the word that comes from the lips of the Lord will act like a consuming fire that will destroy the son of perdition with the brightness of His coming (2 Thessalonians 2:8).
[9] The fate of the oppressor and his armies is sealed when it is declared: “His stronghold will pass away in fear, and his princes will be terrified at the banner, says the Lord, whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem.” Before the visible manifestation of the Lord’s banner at the Second Coming, the Antichrist will try to flee cowardly to his hiding place, overcome by fear. God will literally set fire and a furnace in the city of Jerusalem, guaranteeing that the punishment at the Second Coming of Christ upon the adversaries of Israel will be a scorching and inescapable judgment.

[1-2] The prophecy begins by establishing the framework of a perfect earthly government, declaring that “a king will reign in righteousness, and princes will rule with justice.” The king described here is the Lord Jesus Christ, who will establish this righteous government at Christ’s Second Coming. The text describes this king as a “man” who will be “like a hiding place from the wind, and a shelter from the storm,” using poetic imagery to illustrate the literal protection and refreshment the Lord will provide for the earth, comparing him to rivers of water in a dry land and the shade of a great rock in a hot land.
[6-8] The passage describes the actions of the “wicked one” who “speaks wickedness” and whose heart “devises iniquity, to do ungodliness, and to speak mockery against the Lord.” Doctrinally, these verses may refer to the tribulation period just before the Second Coming, or they may describe the conduct of the Lord's enemies during the Millennium. The text shows that even under millennial conditions and after having been fed by God, there will be vile individuals who will practice hypocrisy and attempt to empty the soul of the hungry and cause the drink of the thirsty to fail. In contrast, it states that "the generous person will devise generous deeds" and by them will be affirmed.
[9-11] The message is specifically directed to women with a stern warning: "You serene women, rise up and hear my voice; you confident daughters, listen to my words." This rebuke points to the conditions that women will face during the tribulation years. This is a direct prophetic parallel to the warning Jesus Christ gave on the way to the cross, when He instructed the daughters of Jerusalem not to weep for Him, but for themselves and their children, anticipating the days when people will ask the mountains to fall on them (Revelation 6:16). The command to strip off, to be naked, and to put on sackcloth (Isaiah 32:11) demands a literal change of garments as a sign of profound terror, mourning, and repentance in the face of the coming affliction.
[13-15] Negative judgments are pronounced where "thorns and thistles" will grow up on the land, and the palaces and the city will be abandoned. However, the word "until" in verse 15 marks a strict dispensational division regarding the time of desolation: "Until the Spirit is poured out on us from on high." This outpouring of the Spirit will put an end to the desolation described in the preceding verses, dividing the passage to make room for the promises of restoration that follow.
[17-18] It is declared that “the effect of righteousness will be peace; and the effect of righteousness, quietness and confidence forever.” This passage establishes the proper biblical order by which true peace is attained, inexorably preceded by the work of righteousness. Although the verse offers an excellent spiritual application for the life of a believer, doctrinally it describes the state of the Jewish nation in the land. God promises that the nation will dwell “in a peaceful habitation, in secure dwellings, and in quiet resting places,” guaranteeing that they will have an immovable and secure abode.
[20] The chapter concludes with a specific blessing: “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters, and pass the hooves of oxen and donkeys through them.” In accordance with the principle where the Bible itself interprets its own symbols, the "waters" represent peoples, multitudes, nations, and languages ​​(Revelation 17:15). Spiritually, the text declares a blessing upon all who carry and sow the word of God among all nations, a parallel to the instruction to cast bread upon the waters to find it after many days (Ecclesiastes 11:1).

[3-4] At the sound of the tumult, the peoples flee, and when the Lord arises, the nations are scattered. This illustrates the panic of humanity trying to flee at the sight of God coming to execute His vengeance from the heavens (Revelation 6:16). The spoil is gathered as the caterpillar gathers its provisions, and the Lord tramples His enemies at the Second Coming (Revelation 14:18-20).
[5-6] God is exalted because He dwells on high, and He fills Zion with judgment and justice. Scripture indicates that wisdom and knowledge will be the stability of "your times," referring strictly to the future times when the Lord will physically rule on earth, in contrast to the instability of the present times. The fear of the Lord is His treasure and the beginning of true wisdom.
[9] The land mourns and languishes; Lebanon is ashamed, and Sharon, Bashan, and Carmel are devastated. This passage describes the physical deterioration of the land and the devastation of nature during the tribulation period. This condition of drought and ruin contrasts sharply with the regeneration experienced in later passages, where these same places flourish and receive divine excellence at the Second Coming of Christ (Isaiah 35:1-2).
[10] Following the desolation of the land, the Lord declares directly, “Now I will arise… now I will be exalted.” This verse marks the prophetic moment when God ends His apparent inactivity and rises up to take absolute dominion over the world.
[13-14] Those who are “far off,” typifying the Jews in the Dispersion scattered among the nations, and those “near,” the inhabitants of Jerusalem, are summoned to acknowledge God’s power. The sinners and hypocrites in Zion are filled with terror at the consuming fire of God. These events of judgment and fiery wrath set the eschatological stage for the Second Coming.
[15-16] The text lists requirements for salvation based strictly on works: walking righteously, speaking uprightly, refusing bribes, and turning a blind eye to evil. In the prophetic context, this illustrates faith coupled with works operating as the doctrinal standard for the remnant during the tribulation. Spiritually, for the believer in the present age, the only one who has perfectly fulfilled these requirements is Jesus Christ, who is made our righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30). The promises of dwelling in "fortresses of rock" with provision of "bread" and "water" point to the literal protection and secret hiding place of the remnant in the wilderness before the Second Coming of Christ.
[17] The promise assures: “Your eyes will see the King in his beauty.” This is a literal declaration that the remnant will physically behold the Lord Jesus Christ in His reigning glory and will be in full doctrinal agreement after the Second Coming. Furthermore, they will behold a land that is far away, indicating a prospect of cosmic glory that transcends any reach of present human vision.
[22-24] The Lord reveals Himself in a manifestation of legislative, judicial, and executive authority by being called Judge, Lawgiver, and King. He Himself is the inescapable guarantee of salvation. The ropes of the enemy ships loosen, making their escape impossible and leaving a great plunder that will be divided even among the weak and lame who were formerly persecuted. The chapter concludes with the divine guarantee that the inhabitant of Zion will not say, “I am sick,” and their national iniquity will be forgiven and completely forgotten. This healing of the land and unconditional purification for Israel culminates definitively in the Second Coming of Christ.

[1-2] The command, “Come near, you nations, gather together to hear; and you peoples, listen,” establishes that this prophecy is addressed to all the nations of the earth universally, not limited to Israel. The “indignation of the Lord against all the nations” and his “wrath against all their host” dogmatically places the fulfillment of this passage at the Second Coming. The Lord has determined to deliver the united armies to slaughter in order to utterly destroy them.
[3] The description of the slain, where “their corpses will send up a stench; and the mountains will melt with their blood,” portrays the literal magnitude of the devastation. The accumulation of massacred bodies will be so immense that blood will run down the mountains as if they were physically melting under the punishment.
[5-6] It is declared that the sword of God, filled with blood, "will descend upon Idumea, and upon the people of my accursedness for judgment." This region is Edom, and the sword of the Lord will execute a great sacrifice in Bozrah and in the land of Idumea. The descendants of Esau (Idumea) mingled with Canaanite blood and brought upon themselves the ultimate divine accursement. This physical judgment will occur literally when the Lord marches in fury through Edom at the Second Coming of Christ.
[7] The text mentions that "with them will descend unicorns, and calves with bulls" to be an integral part of this slaughter where the dust of the earth will be greased with fat. The explicit inclusion of the unicorn points to a literal, one-horned animal that will inhabit the region and perish in this severe judgment event.
[8] The root cause of this universal judgment is established: “For it is the day of the Lord’s vengeance, the year of recompense for the cause of Zion.” The “contest of Zion” refers to the ongoing international controversy over the city of Jerusalem and to whom it rightfully belongs. God Himself will settle this worldwide dispute through absolute retribution and inescapable physical vengeance at the Second Coming.
[9-10] The streams of Edom will be turned to pitch, its dust to sulfur, and the land to “burning pitch” that “will not be quenched night or day” and whose smoke “will rise forever and ever.” This marks the creation of a literal lake of fire in the land of Edom, south of the Dead Sea, which will remain burning throughout the millennial kingdom. The ceaseless smoke and torment bear a strict doctrinal correspondence with the punishment of those who receive the mark of the beast (Revelation 14:10-11) after the Second Coming of Christ.
[11-15] Divine judgment designates this devastated land as the perpetual dwelling place of specific birds and beasts: the pelican, the little owl, the raven, dragons, and satyrs. Since these unclean birds (Leviticus 11) operate as direct typologies of unclean spirits and demons (Mark 4:4, 15; Revelation 18:2), the presence of dragons and satyrs, which are half-man, half-goat creatures, unmistakably describes the literal dwelling of demonic powers upon these ruins.
[16] The passage concludes with a direct command rebuking unbelief: “Search the book of the Lord, and read.” The Lord challenges men to search and confirm that none of these prophecies will fail and none of these strange creatures will lack its mate, for the Spirit of God has gathered them together through His own mouth in a sovereign act of condemnation and confinement.

[1-2] This entire chapter deals with the millennial conditions and the physical restoration of the land of Palestine. The prophecy that "the wilderness and the solitary place will be glad" and "bloom like the rose" is not fulfilled merely through modern agricultural irrigation, but describes how God will transform the desert between the Jordan and Euphrates rivers into something like the Garden of Eden. This passage stands in direct contrast to the desolation of Isaiah 33:9, where Lebanon, Sharon, and Carmel are destroyed during the tribulation. Here, these same regions flourish abundantly and receive divine excellence and glory. The manifestation of "the glory of the Lord" literally and visibly places the fulfillment of these events at the Second Coming of Christ.
[3-4] The instruction to comfort the tenderhearted, saying, "Your God will come with vengeance, with recompense," points strictly to the Second Advent. The Lord's first coming was intended to save sinners, but here a physical and literal retribution is promised upon the enemy nations that oppress the remnant in tribulation, guaranteeing that the Lord will intervene to save His people.
[5-6] Physical healing is promised where "the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped," and "the lame will leap like a deer." Although the Lord performed these miracles as signs to Israel during His first appearance on earth, the complete physical restoration and removal of the nation's diseases will not occur fully until the Second Coming of Christ. Simultaneously, the text declares that "waters will be brought forth in the wilderness." These are literal waters that will flow from the millennial sanctuary to bring healing to the parched land and the Dead Sea (Ezekiel 47:8-12).
[7] The “dry place will become a pool,” indicating profound geographical and ecological changes. “The dwelling place of dragons” refers to the desolate areas inhabited by demonic creatures or powers described in the judgments on Edom and the Dead Sea (Isaiah 34:13). In the coming age, these places of physical and spiritual desolation will be transformed into a place of reeds and rushes with an abundance of literal water.
[10] The chapter concludes with the promise that “the redeemed of the Lord will return and come to Zion.” This describes the permanent, physical, and political return of the nation of Israel to the land, where the Israelites will enter the city with perpetual joy upon their heads. The statement that “pain and sighing will flee away” will be finally fulfilled when the Messiah establishes his kingdom of righteousness on earth after the Second Coming.

[1] The passage marks an abrupt transition in the book, where direct prophetic preaching ceases and a historical record is introduced, spanning to chapter 39. Historically, it recounts how Sennacherib, king of Assyria, marches against and captures all the fortified cities of Judah. ​​Doctrinally and prophetically, the events recorded here serve as a stark picture of the events that will take place during the tribulation. Sennacherib is a direct typology of the Antichrist, while Hezekiah represents the besieged Jewish remnant before the Second Coming. Although the cities of Judah in ancient times relied on physical walls for defense, in the end times, invasions will target unwalled villages due to the nature of modern warfare with artillery and bombardment (Ezekiel 38:11).
[2-3] The king of Assyria sends Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem with a large army, positioning himself "by the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the Washerman's Field." The Jewish delegation, composed of Eliakim (steward), Shebna (scribe), and Joah (recorder), goes out of the city to meet him.
[4-7] Rabshakeh questions Judah's trust and mocks its military alliance with Egypt. He compares this alliance to "a staff of broken reed... on which, if anyone leans, it will pierce his hand and pass it through." This illustrates the futility of placing trust in Gentile nations or human confederations. Furthermore, Rabshakeh cleverly twists the facts by accusing Hezekiah of removing God's altars, when in reality Hezekiah had destroyed the altars of demons and the high places of idolatry to restore legitimate worship in Jerusalem.
[10] The Assyrian envoy claims to have a divine commission: “Have I now come to this land without the Lord to destroy it? The Lord said to me, ‘Go up to this land and destroy it.’” God uses pagan kings and ungodly empires as the rod of His wrath to discipline His people. Just as Nebuchadnezzar is called a servant of God and the devil operates under God's sovereign control, the king of Assyria has a mandate to attack. This foreshadows how the Lord will permit the military invasion of the world oppressor just before the Second Coming of Christ.
[11-12] The Jewish leaders ask Rabshakeh to speak in Syriac (Aramaic) so that the people on the wall will not understand the conversation. The enemy deliberately refuses, seeking to use the Jews' own language (Hebrew) to shout, instill terror, and completely demoralize the city's inhabitants in the face of the impending siege. The Assyrians were known for their cruelty and the total annihilation of the inhabitants if a city refused to surrender in time.
[13-16] Rabshakeh stands and cries out in a loud voice in the language of the Jews, warning them not to trust Hezekiah or the promise that the Lord will deliver them. He demands that the nation submit to his terms: "Make peace with me, and come out to me." This offer of an agreement or alliance through a gift or bribe ("present") is a dogmatic foreshadowing of the false peace treaty that the Antichrist will confirm with the nation of Israel before the Second Coming (Daniel 9:27). Rabshakeh promises to transport them to a land of abundance identical to their own if they capitulate.
[18-20] The Assyrian discourse attempts to equate God with the worthless idols of the pagan nations already conquered by Assyria, asking: "Which of all the gods of these lands have delivered their land from my hand, that the Lord should deliver Jerusalem from my hand?" This is the insolent reasoning of the ungodly leader who trusts in his own military power and does not recognize the absolute supremacy of the God of Israel over false deities.
[21-22] The people's response is absolute silence: "But they remained silent and did not answer him a word, for the king had commanded, 'Do not answer him.'" This stillness in the face of provocation and enemy slander shows strict obedience to their leader's instruction. Later, the Jewish delegates appear before Hezekiah with their clothes torn as a sign of deep mourning and grief, awaiting the divine intervention that will typologically culminate in the destruction of the Assyrian army, prefiguring the Lord's final victory at the Second Coming of Christ.

[1-13] Chapters 36-39 of the book introduce a transition, moving from direct prophetic discourse to a strictly historical record. This passage recounts the siege of Judah by Sennacherib, king of Assyria, and its account is almost identical to that found in 2 Kings 19, although they maintain sufficient textual differences to avoid being considered identical copies. Doctrinally, Sennacherib and his siege operate as a direct typology of the Antichrist, while King Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem prefigure the Jewish remnant besieged during the time of tribulation, awaiting divine intervention before the Second Coming. [Image of ancient Assyrian siege warfare and the city of Jerusalem]
[14-16] Upon receiving the letter containing Assyrian threats and blasphemies delivered by messengers, Hezekiah went up to the house of God and literally spread the letter before the Lord. The prayer was addressed to "the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, who dwells between the cherubim" (Isaiah 37:16). This designation identifies the Lord as the one and only sovereign God over all the kingdoms of the earth, in direct contrast to Sennacherib's perspective, who considered Him merely another tribal deity, incapable of defending his territory. [Image of Hezekiah spreading the letter before the Lord in the temple]
[17-20] Hezekiah asked God to incline His ear and hear the words Sennacherib had sent to reproach the living God. The Jewish king acknowledges a historical fact: the Assyrians had indeed destroyed other nations and cast their gods into the fire. However, the reason they could be consumed was because "they were not gods, but the work of human hands, wood and stone" (Isaiah 37:19). Finally, Hezekiah presents his plea for salvation, basing his request not on his own merits, but on the purpose that "all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the Lord" (Isaiah 37:20). A prayer that openly seeks God's glory so that the world may acknowledge Him is a plea that ensures a divine response.
[21-22] The Lord responds by sending a message to Hezekiah through the prophet Isaiah, stating, "Because you have prayed to me against Sennacherib king of Assyria" (Isaiah 37:21). In the biblical framework, prayers can be made for or against individuals and nations that are enemies of God. God describes the remnant of his people as "the virgin, the daughter of Zion," who despises and mocks the oppressor, a title that prophetically fits the tribulation passages where the elect resist the son of perdition, awaiting imminent deliverance at the Second Coming of Christ.
[36] Divine intervention and retribution occur physically, suddenly

[1] The narrative pauses from the general prophecy to record a historical event in Hezekiah's personal life, which occurs during the days of the Assyrian king's siege. The declaration that Hezekiah was "sick to death" and the divine instruction to put his house in order signify that the Lord is the ultimate authority over life and death. Faced with such a stern warning, the text underscores the importance of having both spiritual and earthly affairs prepared for God's imminent call.
[2-3] Instead of seeking medical help as a first option, Hezekiah turns his face to the wall and prays directly to God. Doctrinally, his plea reflects the nature of the believer's relationship with God in the Old Testament under the law; Hezekiah bases his request on his own works and on having walked with a "perfect heart," a legal justification that differs diametrically from the salvation by grace without works taught in the New Testament.
[4-6] The Lord answers Hezekiah's prayer by sending the reply through the prophet Isaiah, adding fifteen years to his life (Isaiah 38:5). In addition to physical healing, God promises to deliver Hezekiah and the city from the hand of the king of Assyria, confirming that this illness occurred in the midst of the crisis of the Assyrian invasion. This deliverance of Jerusalem from the Assyrian yoke (this king being a doctrinal type of the Antichrist) foreshadows the physical deliverance the city will experience at the Second Coming of Christ.
[7-8] God grants a miraculous and physical sign to confirm His promise: causing the shadow on Ahaz's sundial to go back ten degrees. Unlike Joshua's request where the sun stood still, this miracle involves the movement being temporarily reversed, equivalent to about forty minutes of time physically going back on the clock (Isaiah 38:8).
[9-11] The text presents King Hezekiah's writing after recovering from his illness (Isaiah 38:9). This record details the intimate exercise of a man's soul facing the gates of death. Hezekiah laments being deprived of the "remnant of my years," expressing the deep anguish of being cut off before reaching the seventy years commonly allotted to a man on earth.
[20-21] The passage demonstrates Hezekiah's gratitude and his intention to sing his songs in the house of God, indicating that Hezekiah is the author of some of the Psalms recorded in Scripture. Furthermore, the command to take "a lump of figs" to apply as a poultice to the ulcer and draw out the infection is detailed (Isaiah 38:21). This establishes the biblical principle that, in the Old Testament, divine healing could be accompanied by the legitimate use of medicine and physical remedies, working in conjunction with prayer to the Lord. The complete restoration and healing of Israel as a nation awaits its absolute completion at the Second Coming.

[1] Merodach-baladan, king of Babylon, sent envoys and gifts to Hezekiah after his miraculous recovery. The interest of these emissaries was not purely diplomatic; as observers of the heavens, the Babylonian astrologers noted the celestial phenomenon where the shadow of the sun went back ten degrees (Isaiah 38:8), so they traveled to inquire about the prodigy that had occurred in the land (2 Chronicles 32:31).
[2] Hezekiah, in an act of self-indulgence, displayed all his wealth, including silver, gold, spices, and his armory. The Lord allowed this visit to test the king and reveal all that was in his heart (2 Chronicles 32:31). Spiritually, this passage warns against the danger of pride after receiving a divine blessing; Hezekiah failed by seeking the admiration of men instead of giving glory to God. Displaying treasures to a nation that typifies the world system is an imprudence that foreshadows the nation's future plunder.
[3-4] Under questioning from the prophet Isaiah, Hezekiah admits that the visitors come from a "far land," Babylon. In biblical structure, the "far land" often represents a state of estrangement from divine justice (Luke 15:13), but it is also the place from which the Lord returns to call His servants to account (Luke 19:12, 15). Hezekiah confesses to having displayed all his possessions, holding nothing back, thus exposing his fathers' heritage to a rapacious enemy.
[5-7] The Lord pronounces a sentence of judgment prophesying the Babylonian captivity. God declares that everything Hezekiah displayed will be taken to Babylon and that his descendants will be eunuchs in the palace of the Chaldean king. This word found its literal fulfillment when Nebuchadnezzar sacked Jerusalem (2 Kings 24:12-13; 2 Chronicles 36:18). Specifically, Hezekiah's royal lineage was taken captive, including figures such as Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, who served in the Babylonian court (Daniel 1:3-7).
[8] Hezekiah's response, "The word of the Lord that you have spoken is good," reflects an acceptance of the judgment, but tempered by personal relief at knowing that there would be "peace and truth" in his days. This attitude ignores the fact that the absence of truth in subsequent generations negates any possibility of lasting peace; the true restoration of both will only be fully realized after the Second Coming.
[Book Structure] This chapter concludes the historical section and the first block of Isaiah. The fact that it contains 39 chapters before a radical transition in chapter 40 mirrors the division of the Bible, which has 39 books in the Old Testament. Just as the New Testament begins with the announcement of John the Baptist, Isaiah chapter 40 begins with the voice crying out in the wilderness to prepare the way for the Second Coming of Christ (Isaiah 40:3; Revelation 19:11-16).

[1-2] This passage begins the second major section of the book of Isaiah, marking a shift in tone after the preceding historical section. Doctrinally, the declaration "Comfort, comfort my people" (Isaiah 40:1) and the announcement that "their service is completed, their sin forgiven" point to a future time beyond the present age. Although historically Judah awaited relief, these promises are fully realized after the Second Coming, when the iniquity of the nation of Israel is finally removed and they are restored (Romans 11:26-27). The mention of receiving "double for all their sins" from God indicates that the nation has undergone a severe judgment before its final restoration at the Second Coming of Christ.
[3] Historically identified with the ministry of John the Baptist at the Lord's first coming (Matthew 3:3; John 1:23), the verse also serves as a foreshadowing of the end times. The "voice of one crying in the wilderness" demands preparing "the way of the Lord," referring to a literal highway by which the King will travel at the Second Coming. This highway is associated with the King's Highway leading from Mount Sinai to Jerusalem (Numbers 20:17).
[4-5] The revelation that "all flesh" will see "the glory of the Lord" (Isaiah 40:5) is a promise that was not fully realized at the first coming, since at that time only a few saw His glory (Matthew 17:1-4; 1 John 1:1-3). These geographical changes where "every valley shall be raised up, and every mountain and hill made low" will occur literally when the Lord returns to establish His earthly kingdom (Revelation 6:14, 16:20). The event will mark the beginning of God's visible reign on earth after the Second Coming.
[6-8] The passage establishes a stark contrast between human frailty and the permanence of God's Word. Man is compared to the “hay” that withers and the “flower” that fades (Isaiah 40:7-8), underscoring the futility of human glory in the face of eternity. While human institutions and nations collapse, “the word of our God endures forever” (1 Peter 1:24-25), serving as the only sure foundation before the Second Coming of Christ.
[9-11] Zion and Jerusalem are exhorted to go up to a high mountain and say to the cities of Judah, “Here is your God!” (Isaiah 40:9). This recognition of the Messiah’s deity by the Jewish remnant occurs at the close of the tribulation. The Lord is presented as a strong ruler who “will rule with his arm” in the millennium, but also as a shepherd who “will tend his flock” and “gather the lambs in his arms” (Isaiah 40:10-11), showing the balance between His judicial authority and His tender care after the Second Coming.
[12-17] God appeals to His power as Creator to humble human pride. He is the one who measured the waters in “the hollow of his hand” and weighed the mountains in “scales” (Isaiah 40:12). In contrast to His immensity, “the nations are regarded as a drop in a bucket” and are “esteemed as nothing” and “vanity” (Isaiah 40:15, 17). This divine perspective diminishes the significance of Gentile confederations and the United Nations, which will be shattered at the Second Coming of Christ (Daniel 2:44-45).
[18-20] The text ridicules idolatry and human attempts to represent God through cast or carved images that “cannot move” (Isaiah 40:20). The Lord challenges humanity by asking, “To whom then will you liken God?” (Isaiah 40:18), reaffirming that there is no possible parallel between the Creator and the works of human hands, which will perish at the Second Coming.
[21-22] Isaiah declares that God “sits enthroned above the boundary of the earth” (Isaiah 40:22). The use of the term "hedge" (from the Hebrew chug) indicates a sphere or globe, revealing the planet's roundness long before modern discoveries. From His position in the third heaven, the inhabitants of the earth appear to Him as "locusts," emphasizing the divine sovereignty that will be fully manifested at the Second Coming of Christ.
[25-26] The Lord challenges us to look at the heavens and consider who created the stars, which He "brings out their host by number" and "calls them all by name" (Isaiah 40:26). His omniscience and omnipotence ensure that "not one shall be missing," guaranteeing that His promises of national restoration for Israel will be faithfully fulfilled at the Second Advent.
[27-31] God rebukes Jacob and Israel for thinking that their way is "hidden from the Lord" (Isaiah 40:27). A God is described who “does not grow tired or weary” and who “gives strength to the weary” (Isaiah 40:28-29). The chapter concludes with the promise that those who “wait on the Lord shall renew their strength” and “sow their wings like eagles” (Isaiah 40:31). This renewal of strength is both a spiritual reality for the believer today and a physical promise for the remnant who will enter the kingdom after the Second Coming of Christ.
[Structure and Authorship] The transition in chapter 40 mirrors the structure of the Bible: after 39 chapters (like the 39 books of the Old Testament) comes the announcement of the Messiah’s forerunner, similar to the beginning of the New Testament. Although modern criticism proposes multiple authors, the New Testament consistently attributes this section to the prophet Isaiah (Matthew 3:3; John 12:38-41; Romans 10:16).

[1-4] In this passage, the Lord calls upon the nations and islands to listen in silence to His judgment and appeal based on His power as Creator. God asks who stirred up “the righteous one from the east,” referring to Abraham, whom He called to follow Him and to whom He gave dominion over kings and nations (Isaiah 41:2). The Lord identifies Himself as the absolute sovereign who is with the first and the last, stating, “I myself am He” (Isaiah 41:4). This section establishes that no political or historical force occurs outside of His eternal decree.
[5-7] The text describes the Gentile nations as terrified by God’s works, which leads them to band together in a cooperative, ecumenical effort. This banding together foreshadows the world unification under the Antichrist’s system that will be fully revealed before the Second Coming. Men "help" one another under a false concept of brotherhood, while rejecting the first commandment to focus exclusively on making idols and statues (Isaiah 41:6-7). This effort to secure social and religious "image" through human works is the prelude to the worship of the image of the beast described in the book of Revelation.
[8-13] In contrast to the nations that will perish, Israel is identified as God's "servant" and the seed of Abraham, His friend. Although the nation has experienced temporary abandonment during the present age, the Lord assures them that He has not rejected them and that He will uphold them with His righteous right hand (Isaiah 41:10). The promises of "Do not fear, for I am with you" have a literal fulfillment for the Jewish remnant who will be delivered from all their adversaries at the end of the great tribulation. In the millennial kingdom established after the Second Coming of Christ, the enemies of Israel will be reduced to nothing and will not be found (Isaiah 41:12).
[14-16] God refers to His people as "the worm of Jacob," highlighting their inherent weakness in the face of the divine power that will strengthen them. The Lord promises to transform Israel into "a new threshing sledge, and a toothed scythe" to break down the mountains, which typify the enemy nations and the kingdoms of the world (Isaiah 41:15). This act of physical judgment and military annihilation occurs during the battle of Armageddon at the Second Coming. The scattering of the wicked by wind and whirlwind will allow the redeemed to rejoice only in the Holy One of Israel.
[17-20] This segment describes the conditions of extreme deprivation for the poor and needy, applying doctrinally to the Jewish remnant besieged in tribulation. God answers their spiritual and physical thirst by opening rivers in the highlands and springs in the valleys (Isaiah 41:18). The transformation of the desert into pools of water and the supernatural planting of cedars, pines, and myrtles are geographical realities that will characterize the land of Palestine during the Millennium. These interventions are intended to make the world recognize that the Lord's hand is what has created these wonders for His glory.
[21-24] The Lord issues a direct challenge to the nations and their false deities, demanding that they present their "strong arguments" (Isaiah 41:21). The standard of deity is established by the ability to declare the future and explain the meaning of past events, something only God can do through the spirit of prophecy. The text employs a tone of contempt and sarcasm against those who trust in idols, calling men and their vain deeds an "abomination" (Isaiah 41:24). Ultimately, any religious system that cannot accurately predict the future is exposed as a fraud before divine judgment.
[25-29] The prophecy concludes by announcing the rise of a deliverer who comes "from the north" and "from the rising of the sun," which points directly to the Messiah. His appearance will bring the fulfillment of the good news for Jerusalem and the end of the Gentile rulers who are like mud before His feet (Isaiah 41:25). This event culminates in the Second Coming of Christ, when the King of kings descends from heaven to establish His absolute authority. While human counselors and false images are revealed as wind and confusion, the word of the Lord remains as the only source of truth and hope (Isaiah 41:29).

[1] This verse introduces the figure of the servant of the Lord, a direct and inescapable reference to the Lord Jesus Christ, and not to the nation of Israel. The quotation is dogmatically confirmed in the New Testament (Matthew 12:17-18). God identifies this servant as his "chosen one," in whom his soul delights, establishing a parallel with the divine declaration at the Lord's baptism (Matthew 3:17). The Spirit of God is placed upon him for the specific purpose of bringing judgment to the Gentiles.
[2-4] The nature of this servant's earthly ministry is described. He does not act like a political revolutionary raising his voice in the streets seeking to overthrow the civil government. His dealings operate with tender mercy; he will not break the bruised reed or quench the smoldering wick, but will preserve the remaining flame until he sends forth judgment for victory. He will not rest until He has established absolute judgment on the earth, an event that will be consummated at the Second Coming.
[5] God presents Himself with absolute power. He is the one who stretches out the heavens, expands the earth, and gives breath to the people who inhabit it. Man's life and breath are not a product of chance, but depend directly on the hand of the Lord.
[13-14] The tone changes radically toward the Second Coming of Christ. The Lord no longer presents Himself as the suffering servant, but as a man of war going forth to battle. He cries out and roars like a lion over its prey, executing vengeance on His enemy nations (Revelation 5:5). For a long time, the Lord has been silent and restrained, but that period ends when He awakens and cries out like a woman in labor to destroy and devour His adversaries at once.
[15-16] The physical judgments upon the earth include laying waste to the mountains and drying up the rivers, which doctrinally corresponds to the lack of rain during the three and a half years of tribulation. Afterward, the Lord will guide the blind along paths they have not known, turning the darkness into light before them and making straight what is crooked. This is a literal promise of restoration and guidance for the remnant of Israel after the Second Coming.
[19-20] The term "servant" in this context changes its application and is directed toward the nation of Israel, now described as a blind and deaf servant. Unlike the Lord Jesus Christ, Israel sees many things but does not observe them, and has open ears but does not heed divine correction.
[21] It is established that the Lord delights for the sake of His justice. This incarnate justice is the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, who kept the law perfectly, magnified it, and made it honorable.
[22-25] The chapter concludes by describing the historical and prophetic condition of Israel as a plundered people, trapped in caves and prisons with no one to deliver them. This desolation and persecution is not accidental, but the direct judgment of the Lord against a people who sinned against Him. God poured out upon the nation the fury of His wrath and the force of battle, typifying events of extreme persecution and physical destruction. Despite being burned and consumed by this judicial fire throughout the centuries, they did not take it to heart to repent. The final redemption of the Jewish nation necessarily awaits the Second Coming of Christ.

[1-7] The Lord addresses Jacob and Israel, reminding them that He created and formed them, promising to redeem them and call them by name. The promise of protection through water and fire has a dual application: it applies spiritually to the believer in their afflictions, and physically and literally to the nation of Israel. The passage directly prophesies the gathering of the Jews from the east, west, north, and south, indicating the future restoration of the nation to its promised land, an event that will inevitably be fulfilled at the Second Coming.
[6] The divine command to the cardinal points to bring "my sons from afar, and my daughters from the ends of the earth" applies dogmatically to the Jews who will be gathered geographically from the nations where they were scattered. The theological interpretation that uses this verse to try to prove that the "sons of God" in the antediluvian era (Genesis 6:2) are the descendants of the line of Seth lacks biblical foundation, since the context of Isaiah deals strictly with the Israelites.
[10-11] The Lord declares Israel as His witnesses and His chosen servant. The text establishes the absolute deity and oneness of God by stating, "Before me no god was formed, nor will there be one after me" (Isaiah 43:10). Immediately, Scripture sets forth a fundamental truth to refute those who deny the deity of Christ, declaring, "I, even I, am the Lord, and apart from me there is no savior" (Isaiah 43:11). Since the Bible teaches that the Lord Jesus Christ is the Savior of the world, biblical doctrine dictates that He must be the Jehovah of the Old Testament.
[20-21] The beasts of the field, the dragons, and the owls will honor God because He will provide water in the desert and rivers in the wilderness. This regeneration of nature and the animal kingdom will literally occur on earth during the Second Coming of Christ. The central purpose of this provision is for His chosen people, God declaring, “This people I formed for myself; they shall declare my praise” (Isaiah 43:21). Although the historical and prophetic promise belongs to Israel, the doctrinal principle applies to the believer in the present dispensation, who has been formed to show praise to the One who called them.
[22-25] The text presents a direct accusation against Jacob and Israel for not calling on God and for growing weary of Him (Isaiah 43:22). Despite the disobedience and sins with which the nation made the Lord serve and wearied Him, He offers unconditional forgiveness based strictly on His own grace. God declares, “I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and remembers your sins no more” (Isaiah 43:25). This promise to cleanse and forget the transgressions of the nation will be fully fulfilled when the King returns at the Second Coming to forgive and restore the remnant of Israel. At the same time, the verse illustrates the undeserved cleansing experienced by every sinner who comes to the cross for salvation before the Second Coming of Christ.

[1-2] The Lord addresses His people and establishes a direct identification by saying, “Hear now, O Jacob, My servant, and Israel, whom I have chosen.” It is crucial to draw a careful doctrinal distinction throughout this prophetic book regarding the title of “servant.” While in passages such as Isaiah 42 and 53 the suffering “servant” is a direct and inescapable reference to the Lord Jesus Christ, in this chapter the term is applied dogmatically to the nation of Israel, which was formed from the womb to serve God.
[5-6] The text presents a claim of belonging where one will say, “I am the Lord’s,” and another will call himself by the name of Jacob. Immediately afterward, the Lord of hosts, the King of Israel and its Redeemer, utters one of the most absolute declarations of deity in Scripture: “I am the first, and I am the last; and apart from Me there is no God.” This statement proves the deity of Jesus Christ, since in the book of Revelation, the Lord Jesus takes for Himself the exact same exclusive title, declaring, “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last” (Revelation 22:13, 16). The Jehovah of the Old Testament and the Savior of the New Testament are the same God.
[7-8] God issues a direct challenge to any other false power or deity, demanding, “And who shall call as I do, and declare it, and set it in order before me…?” The standard of true deity is the ability to declare the future with absolute accuracy. Then the Lord comforts His people and rhetorically asks if there is any other God besides Him, to which He Himself replies, “There is no Rock; I know of none.” There is only one God with a consistent moral standard, and He does not recognize the existence of any other deity.
[9-17] One of the most extensive, logical, and scathing condemnations of idolatry in the Bible is presented here. The makers of carved images are described as vanity, and their works, however delightful they may be, are of no benefit whatsoever. The passage exposes the irrational folly of the natural man who cuts down a tree from the forest, uses some of the wood to make a fire, keep warm, and bake bread, and from the remainder of the same trunk carves a god before which he bows down, crying, "Deliver me, for you are my god." This worship of inanimate matter is a direct denial of the One who formed the heavens and the earth, demonstrating that the idol makers are as blind and worthless as the statues in which they place their trust.
[20] The spiritual state of the idolater is summed up in profound blindness: “He feeds on ashes; his deluded heart leads him astray, so that he cannot deliver himself, nor say, ‘Is there no lie at my right hand?’” The unregenerate man is so blinded by the deceitfulness of his own heart that he clings to a false system or a material idol without realizing that his religion is a sham that cannot save him.
[21-23] Despite the rebellion and obstinacy of Jacob and Israel, the Lord offers redemption based strictly on His grace and mercy, promising: “I have swept away your transgressions like a cloud, your sins like the morning mist. Return to me, for I have redeemed you.” This promise of national forgiveness and absolute cleansing will be physically fulfilled in the nation during the Second Coming of Christ. Because of this undeserved redemption, all creation, including the heavens, mountains, and forests, is called to sing for joy because the Lord has glorified Himself in Israel.
[26-28] The chapter concludes with one of the most compelling prophetic proofs in Scripture. The Lord confirms the word of His messengers and decrees that Jerusalem will be inhabited and the cities of Judah will be rebuilt. To accomplish this purpose, God calls upon the Persian king Cyrus ("Cyrus") by name, approximately two hundred years before Cyrus was born. The Lord designates him as His shepherd, indicating that this Gentile monarch would issue the decree for the temple to be laid and the city restored after the Babylonian captivity. This return from captivity under Cyrus's decree operates as a historical pattern that anticipates the final gathering of Israel prior to the Second Coming.

[1] God calls Cyrus by name approximately 175 years before his birth, specifically designating him as His "anointed one." Historically, Cyrus's decree for the Jews to return to Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity foreshadows the eventual restoration of Israel. Cyrus functions in the text as a type of the Lord Jesus Christ and also typologically illustrates the role that England would play in issuing a mandate to facilitate the Jewish return to Palestine through the Balfour Declaration in 1918.
[5-6] The Lord declares His absolute deity and exclusivity, stating: "I am the Lord, and there is no other; there is no God besides me." The prophetic promise that His name will be known from the rising of the sun to the setting of the west points to a universal and absolute recognition of His sovereignty among the Gentile nations, a momentous event that will culminate in the Second Coming of Christ.
[7] The text dogmatically establishes that God is sovereign over all circumstances of earthly existence, stating: “I form the light and create darkness, I make peace and create evil. I, the Lord, do all these things.” The Lord controls and permits the judgments and consequences of sin in the world, demonstrating His unquestionable power to overthrow empires and preparing the stage for judgment at the Second Coming.
[11] God invites humanity and Israel to inquire about the future and trust in His creative work, declaring: “Ask Me about things to come.” The Lord demonstrates that He possesses complete knowledge of the future and authority over His children by issuing a divine challenge that exposes the inability of human wisdom and false deities to discern the future.
[13] Although the historical context refers to the work of Cyrus, the passage has a profound prophetic application directly to the Lord Jesus Christ. Scripture declares, “I have raised him up in righteousness… he shall build up my city, and set my captives free, not for a price or a gift.” Unlike the nation of Israel or any natural leader who does not operate under perfect obedience, the Lord Jesus Christ was raised up in absolute righteousness and offers spiritual deliverance to the lost as a free gift without any earthly price or charge.
[15] The exclamation, “Truly you are a God who hides yourself, O God of Israel, who saves,” doctrinally illustrates how the Lord conceals His direct dealings with the nation of Israel and does not work visibly and openly during the present dispensation. This concealment will cease, only to be revealed again to the remnant of the nation during the tribulation period, immediately preceding the Second Coming of Christ (Revelation 1:7).
[17] The prophecy guarantees the perpetual national restoration of the Jews by emphatically declaring that "Israel is saved in the Lord with eternal salvation." This unconditional salvation, applicable to the literal nation entering the millennium, will be physically consummated on earth after the Second Advent, a time when Israel will not be shamed "for all ages" nor suffer destruction at the hands of its oppressors.
[18] A monumental theological statement is made regarding the purpose of creation, saying of the earth that the Lord "did not create it in vain; he formed it to be inhabited." The divine plan envisions the future occupation of the new heavens and the new earth by a race freed from the curse of sin, thus decisively destroying the notion that the earth was formed by chance without an eternal purpose for habitation.
[20-21] The command, “Assemble yourselves and come; draw near, all you who have escaped from the nations,” rebukes the useless idolatry of the Gentiles and dogmatically summons the Jewish remnant scattered among the nations. The Lord reaffirms His deity by declaring, “A righteous God and a Savior: there is none besides me.” Since the Lord Jesus Christ is the only Savior of mankind (Acts 4:12), sound doctrine inescapably demands that He is the same Jehovah of the Old Testament.
[23] The Lord swears by His own being with a word of righteousness that “to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall swear.” The apostle Paul applies this decree directly to the Lord Jesus Christ in the revelation of the New Testament (Romans 14:11; Philippians 2:10), confirming His inscrutable deity and demanding the total submission of every creature in the coming judgment.

[1] This chapter directs its prophetic warnings directly against Babylon. Although historically the prophet preaches in the days of Kings Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, a time when the imminent threat was Sennacherib, the Lord allows him to look across the centuries and see the future moment when Nebuchadnezzar will attack Jerusalem. Consequently, judgment is prophesied upon the Babylonian gods, specifically mentioning Bel and Nebo. Bel operates as the tutelary deity of the Babylonian empire and is considered the son of Mercury, the supreme god of that idolatrous system. The collapse of these deities foreshadows the fall of the religious and commercial system at the end of times, an event outlined in Revelation that will culminate in the Second Coming.
[5-8] The text presents a direct challenge to idolatry, rhetorically asking to whom God can be likened or compared (Isaiah 46:5). After exposing the profound folly of those who spend their gold and hire goldsmiths to fashion lifeless deities, the Lord confronts the transgressors, demanding: “Remember this, and show yourselves, O men; I will remember, you transgressors” (Isaiah 46:8). This exhortation condemns the human endeavor to create useless images that can neither answer nor save, exposing the blindness of natural man to divine majesty.
[9-10] The Lord demands that the past be remembered, dogmatically affirming His exclusive deity by saying: “For I am God, and there is no other; there is none like me” (Isaiah 46:9). The ultimate proof of the inspiration of Scripture and the supremacy of God lies in His ability to declare “the end from the beginning, and from ancient times things that were not yet done” (Isaiah 46:10). No man, religious system, or earthly device can duplicate this knowledge of the future. Knowing future events with absolute accuracy is the unmistakable mark of true deity.
[12-13] The chapter concludes by addressing the hard-hearted and self-righteous in Jerusalem, who are far from righteousness. God declares to them, “I will bring my righteousness near, it will not be far off; and my salvation will not be delayed” (Isaiah 46:13). Doctrinally, this nearing righteousness is embodied in the person of the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4). Although the Lord appeared in the flesh in Zion during His earthly ministry to bring salvation, the full manifestation and unconditional restoration of Israel await their fulfillment at the Second Coming of Christ, at which time absolute justice will be established over the enemy nations.

[1] The text addresses the "virgin daughter of Babylon," commanding her to descend and sit in the dust. The loss of her throne forces this entity to sit on the ground, losing her title of being called "tender and delicate," which historically indicated a royal status where not even the soles of her feet touched the ground. Although the verse points to the literal empire of Babylon, it prophetically foreshadows the impending judgment on the corrupt religious and political system of the end times ("Revelation" 17:5).
[3-5] The Lord of hosts, the Redeemer of Israel, declares that He will not find her as an ordinary man, but executing divine judgment and strict retribution. Subsequently, the daughter of the Chaldeans is commanded to enter into darkness, for she will no longer be called "lady of kingdoms" (Isaiah 47:5). This title identifies her doctrinally and prophetically with the great harlot who reigns over the kings of the earth (“Revelation” 17:18), who will face annihilation and be stripped of her authority just before the Second Coming.
[6] God explains the reason why Babylon had temporary power over Israel: He was angry with His people and defiled His inheritance, handing it over to the Babylonians as punishment. However, Babylon acted with unrestrained cruelty, showing no mercy even to the elderly, going so far as to hang the princes of the defeated nation by their hands (Lamentations 5:11-12). Here is set forth the biblical principle where God uses a pagan or adversarial nation to discipline His people, but subsequently judges that nation inescapably for the wickedness and sadism it has exercised.
[7-8] Babylon's attitude overflows with pride as she declares, "I will forever be a mistress," affirming in her heart that she will never sit as a widow, nor know orphanhood. This stance illustrates the deceptive and arrogant confidence of one who depends on their own greatness. The Lord dogmatically warns that both calamities, widowhood and the complete loss of children, will come upon her suddenly in a single day, reflecting the sudden collapse that spiritual Babylon will suffer according to biblical prophecy ("Revelation" 18:8).
[9-10] The confidence of the Babylonian system resided in its own iniquity, believing that it acted in secret, saying, "No one sees me." It is established that the multitude of sorceries and enchantments have their cradle directly in Babylon (Daniel 2:2). Her earthly wisdom and knowledge corrupted her (Isaiah 47:10), just as beauty and wisdom originally corrupted Satan (Ezekiel 28:17). The passage condemns humanity's effort to hide from divine omniscience by relying on evil.
[13-15] The chapter culminates with a direct and ironic challenge against astrology and the occult. God commands astrologers, stargazers, and those who predict the months to rise up and try to save the city from the approaching disaster. The text decrees that these diviners will be like tinder, consumed by fire, unable to save even their own lives from the flames. It is established that none of these occult practices will provide escape from the judgments and wrath that will fall upon the earth at the Second Coming of Christ.

[1-2] The Lord addresses the house of Jacob, identified as those who came out of the waters of Judah, who swear by God's name and remember Him, "but not in truth or in righteousness." Doctrinally, this illustrates the condition of a nation that invokes God and relies on its belonging to the holy city, but, ignoring God's righteousness, seeks to establish its own righteousness (Romans 10:3).
[6-8] God confronts the people's unbelief and hardness of heart by declaring that He has shown them new and hidden things they did not know. Faced with the human tendency to justify themselves by claiming prior knowledge of events, the Lord responds dogmatically that they had neither heard nor known, nor had their ears been opened since ancient times.
[9-11] The passage forcefully establishes that divine mercy toward Israel is not based on the people's goodness, but strictly on divine glory and sovereignty. The Lord declares, "For my name's sake I will defer my anger," withholding his wrath so as not to cut them off completely. The nation's purification process occurs "in the furnace of affliction," demonstrating that when God forgives and preserves his people, he does so solely out of love for himself, ensuring that his name is not profaned nor his honor given to another.
[13] A direct appeal to absolute power over material creation is presented. God states, "My hand also laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand measured the heavens." Such is His authority that, when He calls them, heaven and earth appear together.
[16] This is one of the most profound verses in the Old Testament because of its dogmatic reference to the Trinity. The speaker declares, “From the beginning I have not spoken in secret; from the time it was made, I was there; and now the Lord God and His Spirit have sent me.” The pronoun “me” (has sent me) is an inescapable reference to the Lord Jesus Christ, who is sent by God the Father and the Holy Spirit. This same divine presence affirms having been there from the beginning of time (Genesis 1:1; Job 38:2), demonstrating the co-eternity of the Godhead before the incarnation.
[17-19] The text continues with another manifestation of the divine persons, mentioning the Lord, the Redeemer, and the Holy One of Israel. God presents Himself as the one who teaches for profit and the one who governs the way in which one should walk. Verse 18 expresses the cry of God's heart for the obedience of His people, desiring that they had heeded His commandments so that His peace would flow like a river. Had they obeyed, their offspring would have been like the sand and their descendants like pebbles (Isaiah 48:19).
[20-21] The command "Come out of Babylon, flee from the Chaldeans" brings a shift in focus. Historically, it refers to the command given to the Jewish remnant to leave Babylonian captivity. However, the prophetic application aligns with the future command set forth in Revelation 18:4, ordering the redeemed to come out of spiritual Babylon before the judgments of the Second Coming. The redemption of the servant Jacob is proclaimed with a joyful voice, recalling how the Lord did not let them thirst in the deserts and how He made water flow from the rock. This physical care during the exodus from Egypt functioned as a doctrinal type of the literal provision that God will give to his remnant besieged in the wilderness during the great tribulation, which will inevitably culminate in the Second Coming of Christ.

[1, 5-6] The text directly identifies the servant of God. Although in previous chapters the term "servant" has been applied to the nation of Israel, in this passage the servant is undoubtedly the Lord Jesus Christ. Verse 5 declares that God formed him from the womb to "restore Jacob to himself" (Isaiah 49:5). Since the servant's mission is to restore the tribes of Jacob, it is impossible for the servant to be the nation itself. This doctrinal distinction is fundamental to refuting the orthodox Jewish teaching that claims the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 represents Israel.
[7] The Lord addresses "the one whom the soul despises, the abomination of the nation, the servant of tyrants" (Isaiah 49:7). This is a description of the earthly ministry of the Lord Jesus Christ during His first coming, when He was rejected and despised by men (Isaiah 53:3). The verse also presents the Deity in Trinitarian form by mentioning "Jehovah," the "Redeemer of Israel," and "His Holy One." Despite His initial humiliation, the promise is that "kings will see, and princes will rise and worship," an event of exaltation that will occur at the Second Coming.
[8-9] God the Father speaks to the Son, saying, "In an acceptable time I heard you, and in a day of salvation I helped you" (Isaiah 49:8). Although the apostle Paul applies this verse spiritually to the church age (2 Corinthians 6:2), the prophetic context reveals two ministries of the Lord. The first is saying “to the prisoners, ‘Come out’” (Isaiah 49:9), which typifies His work of freeing the captives, and the second is “to restore the land, to lay waste the desolate inheritances,” a physical restoration of the land that will take place at the Second Coming of Christ.
[12] The gathering of the Jewish remnant from distant lands is prophesied, specifically mentioning those coming “from the north and from the west, and these from the land of Sinim” (Isaiah 49:12). Historically and etymologically, the term “Sinim” has been associated with the territory of China, underscoring a global and literal gathering of Israel to its promised land. This grand event of national restoration directly precedes the Second Advent.
[18] The Lord commands Israel to lift up their eyes to see the nations gathering toward them, guaranteeing this promise with an absolute oath: “As surely as I live, declares the Lord” (Isaiah 49:18). This prophetic gathering, in which the Gentile nations will seek the Lord in Jerusalem and enrich Israel with their strength, will find its literal fulfillment during the millennial kingdom.
[24-26] The chapter closes with a rhetorical question about whether prey can be taken from the mighty (Isaiah 49:24). God answers in the affirmative, promising to contend with those who contend with Israel and save his children (Isaiah 49:25). The judgment of making the oppressors eat “their own flesh” (Isaiah 49:26) is a retributive and literal judgment upon the nations that have persecuted the Jewish people throughout the centuries. This divine vengeance will culminate definitively when the Lord destroys the enemies of Israel at the Second Coming of Christ.

[1] The Lord addresses the people, asking, “Where is your mother’s certificate of divorce, by which I divorced her? Or who are my creditors, to whom I sold you?” Doctrinally, this passage illustrates a fundamental distinction: the Father has a wife who was temporarily divorced but will return—the nation of Israel—while the Son has a wife, a virgin bride, who is the church.
[2-3] The Lord confronts humanity’s lack of response to his call and defends his absolute power, exclaiming, “Is my arm too short to redeem? Or am I powerless to deliver?” The text indicates that through his rebuke, God can dry up the sea and control creation. The full demonstration of this power on earth and the redemption of the remnant will literally occur at the Second Coming of Christ.
[5] This verse unequivocally introduces the servant of Jehovah, who is the Lord Jesus Christ, declaring: “The Lord God opened my ear, and I was not rebellious, nor did I turn back.” Unlike natural human rebellion, the Son manifests absolute submission and obedience to the will of God, prepared to face the suffering for which he was sent without flinching.
[6] The prophecy moves on to a graphic and anticipated description of the crucifixion and torture inflicted on the Lord Jesus Christ. He testifies: “I gave my back to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who plucked out my beard; I did not hide my face from insult and spitting.” This shedding of blood, scourging, and mockery was literally fulfilled when He was beaten and spat upon by ungodly men and Roman soldiers (Matthew 26:67).
[7-9] The text allows us to enter into the thoughts and words of the suffering servant as He endures physical pain. The Lord affirms His resolve, declaring, “For the Lord God will help me… therefore I set my face like a flint” (Luke 9:51). Seated in His humiliation, the Lord directly challenges Satan (Colossians 2:15), His adversary, saying, “Come near to me,” demonstrating that no spiritual or human power can overcome Him or cause Him to abandon His redemptive work. Despite the attacks, Christ declares his innocence and the future ruin of his accusers, saying, “Who is he that condemns me? Behold, they shall all wear out like a garment; the moth shall eat them up.”
[10] The chapter closes with a call that summarizes the plan of salvation for the lost sinner or for the religious person who still walks in darkness. The question is posed as to who fears the Lord and obeys his voice, but who “walks in darkness, and has no light.” The divine remedy and command is established dogmatically, saying, “Trust in the name of the Lord, and rely on your God.” The soul that places its trust individually and rests in the salvation provided will obtain forgiveness and not perish under the judgments of the Second Coming.

[1] The Lord addresses His word to Israel, to the remnant seeking righteousness, commanding them: “Look to the rock from which you were hewn, and to the pit from which you were dug.” Historically, this points to Abraham and Sarah as the progenitors of the nation. Spiritually, the principle applies directly to the New Testament believer, who must remember the Rock of salvation, who is Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4), and the pit of condemnation from which the Lord rescued and cleansed him.
[3] The divine promise that declares, “Surely the Lord will comfort Zion… and make her wilderness like Eden, and her desert like the garden of the Lord,” is a literal prophecy concerning the regeneration of the land of Israel. The land will flourish and experience joy, gladness, and the voice of melody. This physical and geographical regeneration of nature, where deserts bloom, will be an absolute reality on earth that will take place during the Second Coming of Christ.
[9] The prophet's cry, "Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the Lord," is an invocation addressed to the Lord Jesus Christ, who is dogmatically identified in Scripture as the arm of God that brings salvation and judgment (Luke 1:51). The question of whether it was not He who cut Rahab and wounded the dragon carries a profound prophetic weight. Doctrinally, the dragon typifies Satan (“Revelation” 12:3), and the cutting of Rahab and the dragon foreshadows the judgment events upon the corrupt world system at the Second Coming.
[10-11] The Exodus is alluded to in the question: “Are you not the one who dried up the sea… who made the depths of the sea a path, that the redeemed might cross over?” Although historically it points to the crossing of the Red Sea, it typifies the future time when the heavens and the waters above will part to make way for the Lord and the redeemed. It is then promised: “Surely the redeemed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with singing.” This guarantees the literal return of the Jewish remnant to Jerusalem, an event that begins an era where sorrow and groaning will perpetually flee after the Second Coming of Christ.
[12-13] God rebukes man's tendency to fear mortals with the declaration: "I, I am your comforter. Who are you that you should fear man, who is mortal... and have forgotten the Lord your Maker, who stretched out the heavens and laid the foundations of the earth...?" The text contrasts the immensity of God's power in the past creation with the fragility of man, who is cut down like grass. This reminder of God's creative power establishes that there is no reason to fear oppressors, who will inevitably perish at the Second Coming.
