[16] The text explicitly states: "and in the shadow of my hand I hid you, that you might set the heavens and lay the foundations of the earth, and say to Zion, 'You are my people.'" The phrase "my people" in the Old Testament refers strictly and exclusively to the nation of Israel. This passage not only looks back to the original foundation of the world, but prophetically reveals the purpose of establishing new heavens and a new earth under divine rule after the Second Coming of Christ.
[17] The exhortation, “Awake, awake, arise, O Jerusalem, that drank from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath,” is addressed to the city that has endured divine anger. Jerusalem has drunk the cup of trembling to the dregs because of its historical rebellion. The doctrine here states that, although the Jewish nation is disciplined by the Lord, God will subsequently take this cup from Israel’s hand and deliver it inescapably to the Gentile nations that oppressed them (Jeremiah 25:15–17), thus completing the vengeance promised for the Second Coming.

[3] The text states that the nation was sold for nothing and will be redeemed without money. Doctrinally, this indicates that Israel's redemption will not be accomplished through a human commercial transaction, but as an exclusive act of divine salvation without price or earthly reward.
[7] The announcement of "good news" and "peace" culminating in the declaration "your God reigns" points directly to the establishment of the earthly and visible kingdom at the Second Coming. Although the apostle Paul applies this verse spiritually to those who preach the gospel of grace in the present dispensation (Romans 10:15), its doctrinal and literal fulfillment requires the Lord to rule physically from Zion. There will be no lasting or true peace on earth until absolute justice is imparted at the Second Coming of Christ.
[8] It is promised that the watchmen will see "eye to eye" when the Lord brings Zion back. This indicates that the leaders and believers of Israel will be in perfect doctrinal agreement. In turn, literally, it means that they will see the Lord physically, confirming the parallel prophecy in which the nation will look upon the One they pierced (Zechariah 12:10) at the visible event of the Second Coming.
[10] The Lord bares His holy arm "in the sight of all the nations," promising that all the ends of the earth will see God's salvation. The "arm of the Lord" is a prophetic title explicitly applied to the person of the Lord Jesus Christ. Unlike His first incarnation, where few believed the report and His arm was not recognized by the masses (Isaiah 53:1), at the Second Coming of Christ, every eye will literally see Him ("Revelation 1:7").
[11-12] The command “Depart from me, depart from me, come out of her, touch no unclean thing” is a strict and purifying command. Although the New Testament draws out and applies this principle spiritually to the believer’s separation from iniquity and unequal yoke (2 Corinthians 6:17), the dogmatic prophetic application instructs the Jewish remnant to come out of spiritual Babylon (“Revelation” 18:4) before the judgments of the Second Coming. Unlike the ancient deliverance at the Red Sea, this departure will not be hasty, for the Lord will go before them, leading the way.
[13-14] These verses introduce and open the context for the great passage about the Suffering Servant, who is undeniably the Lord Jesus Christ and not the nation of Israel. It is declared that the Servant will be "exalted and lifted up, and highly exalted," pointing to His absolute exaltation at the Second Coming of Christ, which immediately contrasts with the extreme humiliation described below. The awe before Him stems from the fact that "his appearance was so marred beyond human likeness" (Isaiah 52:14). This accurately portrays the physical brutality of the crucifixion and the preceding tortures suffered by the Lord's earthly body, whose face and form were beaten and mutilated more than that of any other man.

[1] Immediately following the crucifixion and atonement detailed in the previous chapter, the text moves on to the future restoration of Israel. The barren woman is commanded to sing, a figure typifying the nation of Israel, which has been spiritually fruitless for a long period in comparison with the Gentiles. Unlike the Church, which is presented in the New Testament as a chaste virgin betrothed to the Lord (2 Corinthians 11:2), Israel is systematically compared in the Old Testament to a wife who was temporarily repudiated for her unfaithfulness but who will later be restored to her husband (Hosea 2:14-20). Although the apostle Paul makes a spiritual application of this passage to the new covenant (Galatians 4:27), the inescapable doctrinal context points to the national restoration of the Jews at the Second Coming.
[3] The promise that the seed of Israel will inherit the Gentiles and inhabit the desolate cities marks a complete change of dominion on the earth. While in the present dispensation the Gentiles exercise political supremacy, this situation will be reversed. The rebuilding of the cities, which will be devastated and inhabited during the judgments of the tribulation (Isaiah 6:11), will take place under the authority of the throne of David at the Second Coming of Christ.
[4-6] The Lord directly identifies Himself as the husband, the Maker, and the Redeemer of the nation. Israel is seen as a widow or a wife repudiated in her youth who has suffered disgrace. She is assured that she will no longer remember the affront of her widowhood because God, who is the Holy One of Israel and will be called the God of all the earth, calls her back with compassion at the Second Coming.
[7-8] God declares that He abandoned the nation with the phrase, "For a brief moment I left you." Doctrinally, this moment of abandonment encompasses the current church age, during which God has hidden His face and divine wrath rests upon the unbelieving nation to the extreme (1 Thessalonians 2:16). However, this judgment is not final. The Lord assures her that with great mercies He will gather her and with everlasting mercy He will have compassion on her—national promises that are literally fulfilled after the Second Coming of Christ.
[9-10] A parallel is drawn with the "waters of Noah" and God's unconditional covenant never to flood the earth again (Genesis 9:11). Likewise, God vows never to be angry with Israel again nor to rebuke them forever. Even if the mountains move and the hills tremble—a catastrophic geological event that will occur at the end of the great tribulation (“Revelation” 16:20)—divine mercy and the covenant of peace will not be withdrawn from the remnant at the Second Coming.
[11-12] The city of Jerusalem, described here as afflicted and tempest-weary, will be rebuilt with foundations of sapphires, windows of agate, and gates of carbuncles. This description details the earthly capital city of the millennium, built for the nation of Israel on earth. It should be clearly distinguished from the heavenly New Jerusalem, which is not the earthly capital of the Jews, but the bride of the Lamb who comes down from heaven (“Revelation” 21:2, 9-10) after the Second Coming of Christ.
[13] The promise that “all your children shall be taught by the Lord; and great shall be the peace of your children” contrasts with the historical and current state of the Jewish nation, which has been plagued by wars, sieges, and spiritual blindness. This absolute condition of universal divine knowledge from the least to the greatest, accompanied by unbreakable national peace, can only be fulfilled through the physical presence of the King on earth, culminating in the Second Coming.
[15-17] The chapter concludes with a guarantee of absolute divine protection where the Lord decrees that “No weapon formed against you shall prosper” (Isaiah 54:17). Every confederation of nations or military coalition that assembles against Israel will be crushed because of them (Zechariah 12:3). The basis of this security and redemption does not lie in the works or merits of the Jewish people, but in imputed divine righteousness, affirmed in the declaration "and their righteousness is mine, says the Lord" (Isaiah 54:17). This principle establishes that the restoration of the nation depends entirely on the grace of God, which will be poured out upon Israel at the Second Coming of Christ.

[1] The chapter begins with a universal invitation to salvation. The call is to partake of the water, wine, and milk "without money and without price," indicating that salvation and eternal life are free gifts that cannot be earned through works or human merit (Romans 5:18). Doctrinally, water represents the Holy Spirit, wine is a type of the blood of Christ, and milk typifies the word of God. Any attempt to put a price on these gifts directly contradicts God's unconditional offer ("Revelation" 22:17).
[2] The futility of human effort is questioned by asking why people spend their money on what is not bread and their labor on what does not satisfy. In the biblical context, the true bread that nourishes the soul is identified with the word of God, which produces "seed for the sower and bread for the eater" (Isaiah 55:10). The world, with all its material and professional progress, is incapable of supplying the true spiritual needs of the individual.
[3] The Lord promises to make an "everlasting covenant" that includes "steadfast mercies to David." In the New Testament, the apostle Paul applies this passage dogmatically to the salvation and eternal security of the believer through the resurrection of Jesus Christ (Acts 13:34). These unconditional mercies were promised to David and his descendants (Psalm 89:28-36), guaranteeing that even if they are disciplined for disobedience, divine faithfulness and mercy will not depart from them in any way.
[4-5] David is presented as a witness, leader, and commander for the people, operating here as a direct type of Jesus Christ, the true leader and captain. Furthermore, the calling of the Gentile nations is foretold, a momentous event where nations unknown to Israel will run to the Lord God because of His glorification. This integration of the Gentiles into the promises given to Israel will find its ultimate fulfillment when the Messiah establishes His visible kingdom at the Second Coming.
[6-7] A command is issued to seek the Lord while He may be found and to call on Him while He is near. The path to God demands an abandonment of sin, commanding the ungodly to forsake their ways and the wicked their thoughts, and to turn to the Lord for mercy and abundant forgiveness.
[8-9] An unbridgeable gap is established between the mind of God and the reasoning of natural man. God states unequivocally, “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways” (Isaiah 55:8). God’s omniscience is as far superior to that of man as the heavens are to the earth. This strips man of any ability or authority to judge God's works based on his own earthly logic or philosophy.
[10-11] The word of God is compared to the rain and snow that come down from heaven and do not return until they have watered the earth, making it sprout and produce seed for the sower and bread for the eater. The Lord guarantees that the word that goes out from His mouth will not return to Him empty, but will " accomplish what I please and achieve the purpose for which I sent it." When a believer sows the word of God, it invariably accomplishes its spiritual work and never returns without effect.
[12-13] The prophecy concludes with a description of great joy and peace, where the elements of nature themselves participate in the redemption. The mountains and hills will burst into song, and the trees of the field will clap their hands. Geographically, instead of the bramble and the nettle (which typify the curse of sin), the beech and the myrtle will grow. These literal and regenerative alterations of nature signify the removal of the curse from the earth, an event that will be definitively realized at the Second Coming of Christ.

[1-2] The context of this passage is prophetically situated in the time of the Second Coming, when the land and nature in the land of Israel will be restored. The Lord commands us to uphold justice and do righteousness, announcing that His salvation and His righteousness are imminent, which points directly to the earthly establishment of His kingdom. A blessing is pronounced upon the person who maintains this conduct and who keeps the Sabbath day from profaning it. The Sabbath observance commanded in the text literally extends from six o'clock Friday evening to six o'clock Saturday evening, a Jewish statute that God never granted to any nation outside a hundred-mile radius of Palestine. Doctrinally, the Sabbath observance in this chapter corresponds to the Sabbaths of the millennial kingdom described by the prophet Ezekiel (Ezekiel 45-46) and mentioned by the apostle Paul (Colossians 2:16-17). Various religious groups, such as Seventh-day Adventists, mistakenly attempt to impose this observance in the present age, ignoring that the passage deals strictly with the conditions established after the Second Coming of Christ.
[3-4] The text offers promises of comfort to the "son of the foreigner" and the eunuch, detailing God's provision for those Gentiles who join the Lord and choose to keep His Sabbaths. A historical and practical example of a Gentile proselyte guided by the Old Testament is found in the highly authoritative Ethiopian eunuch who traveled to Jerusalem specifically to worship (Acts 8:27). On his way back, this man was reading the section of the prophets from Isaiah 53 to 56, where God declares a covenant and direct promises for eunuchs who hold fast to His word.
[6-7] The children of foreigners who choose to join God in serving Him and loving His name will be brought to His “holy mountain,” Mount Zion in Jerusalem (Psalm 2:6), to be recreated in His house of prayer. In this passage, the Lord promises, “Their burnt offerings and sacrifices will be accepted on my altar.” These offerings have no connection to the church age but point to the literal sacrifices that will be reinstated in the millennial temple (Ezekiel 41-46) after the Second Coming. During the millennium, the sacrifices operate as a form of corporate atonement for the restored nation in fellowship with its Messiah, and those Gentiles who desire to offer worship and service to the Lord will need to gather in Jerusalem to participate.
[8] God, who “gathers the outcasts of Israel,” promises to gather still others who will join those already gathered. This underscores a biblical teaching about two different gatherings or congregations of the Gentiles. There is a spiritual gathering of people taken from among the nations for God's name during the present age, but later there will be a literal and physical gathering of the Gentile nations to the nation of Israel. This second gathering of global proportions will take place definitively and unconditionally at the Second Coming of Christ.
[9-12] The end of the chapter marks a dramatic change in tone, pronouncing direct judgments against the nation's leaders by summoning "all the beasts of the field" to devour. A strong condemnation is issued against the spiritual leaders, stating, "Their watchmen are blind, all of them ignorant." These watchmen represent the preachers and religious leaders who, lacking regeneration or being blinded by the god of this age, do not possess the capacity to understand the Scriptures. The Lord identifies them as "dumb dogs" because they fail in their duty to warn the people about the danger of impending judgment. Likewise, the final verse portrays the reprehensible attitude of these leaders who prophesy based on wine and strong drink to ensure prosperity, which directly links them to the class of false prophets described in Micah 2:11, who lead the nation to its own destruction.

[1-2] The text observes that the merciful one is removed before the evil comes, which refers contextually to the generation in the prophet's day, illustrating how God preserves his own from impending judgment.
[3-4] The Lord summons the "children of the sorceress, the offspring of the adulterer and the fornicator" (Isaiah 57:3). Doctrinally, these designations apply directly to the harlot of Babylon the Great described in the book of Revelation, chapter 17. The condemnation operates generally for the unsaved person, who, regardless of the moral background of their earthly family, is by nature a child of wrath and a seed of falsehood (Ephesians 2:3). The text exposes the depraved condition of those who mock, calling them children of transgression.
[6] The judgment prophecies at this point are directed toward unregenerate man, associating him with idol worship and the smooth stones of the brook. Although it has prophetic application to unsaved individuals who will go through the tribulation period, the principle condemns any lost man who is by nature a child of wrath and perdition.
[7-8] The nation's idolatry is graphically described as spiritual adultery. By setting up her bed on a high mountain and placing her memory behind doors and thresholds, the nation is illustrated as an unfaithful wife who has abandoned her husband. She has revealed herself to other gods, enlarging her bed and making repeated covenants with pagan nations.
[9-10] The mention of going to the king with ointment and increasing the perfumes represents Israel's political alliances with Gentile kings, such as those of Syria or Assyria, in times of crisis. This typifies the nation's humiliation in flirting with secular power to make a good impression, selling its allegiance to God to achieve this. Despite tiring itself over the grandeur of its own path, the nation refuses to confess that there is no hope in purely human solutions.
[13] An absolute contrast is established between the vanity of idols and the reward of faith in God. Idols will be carried away by the wind, but he who puts his trust in the Lord will possess the land and inherit the holy mountain. Doctrinally, this promises tribulation believers that they will possess the land of Palestine and the millennial Mount Zion after the Second Coming. At the same time, in a practical sense, it illustrates how the afflicted individual who trusts in the Lord receives an answer and deliverance, reminding us that the meek will inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5).
[14] The command to level and prepare the way by removing the stumbling blocks from the people connects with the proclamation to make a straight highway in the wilderness (Isaiah 40:3). This ordinance points to the literal geographical alterations where every valley will be exalted and every mountain made low before the Second Coming of Christ.
[15] This is one of the most magnificent verses in the Old Testament concerning the nature of God. It declares that God is the "High and Lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy." Scripture reveals that the divine essence completely transcends everything visible in the universe, for He dwells in eternity. However, God's immanence permeates all creation in such a way that He also dwells with the contrite and humble in spirit, knowing perfectly the mental attitudes of His creatures (1 Chronicles 28:9).
[16] God declares, “For I will not contend forever, nor will I always be angry; for then the spirit would fail before me, and the souls whom I have created.” This passage details the times when the Lord hides His face in discipline. At the same time, the declaration that God made souls is fundamental, because it demonstrates that the soul is a direct creation of God that takes place at the moment of birth (Genesis 2:7). The divine promise not to contend eternally sets the stage for the Second Coming, when His anger will turn away from Israel.
[19] The Lord promises comfort and the fruit of the lips, declaring peace to those who are far off and to those who are near. Although the prophetic context is strictly directed to the nation of Israel before the Second Coming of Christ, the text also has a personal and immediate application. This promise of peace extends comfort to the straying or wayward Christian, assuring them that God provides healing when there is a genuine return to Him.

[1] The command to “cry aloud, do not hold back; raise your voice like a trumpet” is a direct instruction to God’s herald, requiring an audible and confrontational message before the congregation. This ordinance precedes the exposure of the people’s true condition, for before declaring the iniquity of the house of Jacob, the preacher must be willing to raise his voice without fear. There is a close spiritual link between the final warning of the previous chapter that “there is no peace for the wicked” (Isaiah 57:21) and the beginning of this chapter, indicating that the denunciation of sin is the indispensable preliminary step for any spiritual restoration.
[3] The nation’s complaint, expressed in the question, “Why have we fasted, they say, and you have not seen it? Have we humbled ourselves, and you have not noticed?” reveals the spiritual blindness of a people who seek to compel God through external rituals. The Lord responds with sharp irony, demonstrating that on the very day of their physical abstinence, they continue to seek their own pleasures and oppress their workers with unjust burdens. This passage exposes the futility of fasting when it is done for selfish reasons and without true inner humility before God.
[5] God harshly rebukes hypocritical formalism by asking if true fasting consists merely in "a person afflicting his soul by day, and bowing his head like a reed, putting sackcloth and ashes under his head." This outward attitude of sadness and physical penance is comparable to that of the Pharisees in the New Testament, whom the Lord warned against because they changed their faces to show others they were fasting (Matthew 6:16). The Scriptures teach that there is no intrinsic merit in simply abstaining from food or in punishing the physical body if there is no genuine brokenness of heart (Joel 2:12-13).
[6] Fasting that pleases God is manifested in "loosing the bonds of wickedness, undoing the bundles of oppression, and letting the oppressed go free." Doctrinally, true godliness requires the practice of justice and practical mercy toward one's neighbor (Zechariah 7:9). Intimate communion with God is inconceivable while yokes of oppression remain or the cries of the needy, the widow, and the orphan are ignored (Zechariah 7:10).
[8] The promise that “then your light will break forth like the dawn, and your healing will quickly appear” directly links moral obedience with the manifestation of physical health and divine guidance. This verse supports the doctrine of providential healing and the physical care that the Lord bestows upon His people when they walk in righteousness. Likewise, the statement that “your righteousness will go before you, and the glory of the Lord will be your rear guard” teaches that God Himself acts as a rear guard, protecting the path of His servants wherever they go.
[9] The promise that “then you will call, and the Lord will answer; you will cry for help, and he will say: Here I am” is conditional upon the removal of the yoke of oppression and strict legalism. The Lord requires His people to eliminate all behavior that involves subjugating or imposing unbearable burdens on others—practices that characterized the Pharisees in their eagerness to tie heavy loads on men's shoulders without lifting a finger to alleviate them (Matthew 23:4; Acts 15:10).
[10] The instruction to "pour out your soul to the hungry and satisfy the afflicted soul" emphasizes that piety must transcend the intellectual realm and manifest itself in the material and spiritual relief of one's neighbor. The result of this self-giving is that "your light will rise in the darkness, and your gloom will become like midday," guaranteeing that the Lord will continually guide the obedient, satisfying their soul in times of physical or spiritual drought and making them like a "well-watered garden" whose waters never fail. This typifies the righteous person who trusts fully in the Lord and whose roots extend along streams of water (Jeremiah 17:7-8).
[13] The commandment, “If you turn back your foot from the Sabbath, from doing your pleasure on my holy day,” is an instruction under the Law directed to the physical nation of Israel. Doctrinally, the Sabbath is a perpetual covenant and an exclusive sign between God and the children of Jacob (Ezekiel 20:12, 20), which extends from six o’clock in the evening on Friday until six o’clock in the evening on Saturday, and should not be confused with Sunday, the day on which the Lord rose from the dead (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2). Under the present dispensation of grace, Sabbath observance has been abolished for the Church, deliberately omitted from the Pauline epistles (Romans 13:8-10; Colossians 2:16-17). Nevertheless, the principle of setting aside a day to delight in the Lord and abstain from worldly pleasures contains immense devotional application for the believer today.
[14] The blessing reserved for those who honor the Lord's holy day includes the promise that "I will make you ride on the heights of the earth, and feed you with the heritage of Jacob your father." Doctrinally and prophetically, this statement anticipates the restoration of Israel's national promises in the earthly kingdom. While the believer in the Church enjoys a heavenly and incorruptible inheritance, the geographical and physical promises given to Jacob will be literally fulfilled after the Second Coming. In that future period, which corresponds to the Second Coming of Christ, the nation of Israel will be restored to its land and the Gentile nations will come to Jerusalem to worship the King (Zechariah 14:16; Revelation 20:4).

[1-2] Behold, the arm of the Lord is not shortened, that it cannot save; nor his ear heavy, that it cannot hear. The prophet begins by declaring that the ineffectiveness in communication with God is not due to a limitation of divine power, but to the spiritual rebellion of the people. It is the iniquities of men that build a barrier of separation between the creature and its God (Isaiah 59:1-2). Doctrinally, the total depravity of man under the law is observed, a reality that the apostle Paul will apply in the Epistle to the Romans to describe the universal condition of sinners under divine wrath (Romans 3:10-18). The hand of God remains powerful, but his holiness prevents him from having fellowship with sin without adequate atonement.
[3-4] The moral degradation of society is evident in the description of its actions and words. The fact that hands are stained with blood can be understood in a direct physical sense of violence, but also in a spiritual dimension of ministerial negligence. In the book of Acts, the apostle Paul declares himself clean from the blood of all men because he did not shrink from proclaiming to them the whole counsel of God (Acts 20:26-27); consequently, spiritual silence and lack of witness constitute a form of blood guilt (Ezekiel 3:17-20). Commercial, religious, and social lies flow from lips that have abandoned the truth, establishing a condition in which no one cries out for justice or pleads for the truth.
[5-6] The images of hatching asp eggs and weaving spider webs illustrate the futility and poisonous nature of human efforts to achieve self-justification. A spider's web can never become a garment to cover the sinner's nakedness, representing that the works of the flesh are utterly insufficient for salvation. From a dispensational perspective, this contrasts with Adam and Eve's original attempt to cover themselves with fig leaves after their fall (Genesis 3:7), an example of humanistic religion that God had to reject in order to provide garments of skin through the shedding of blood (Genesis 3:21).
[7-8] The path of those who are quick to shed innocent blood and whose thoughts are wicked describes the path of the followers of the Antichrist (Isaiah 59:7). The apostle Paul quotes these verses verbatim in Romans to diagnose the spiritual ruin of the natural man (Romans 3:15). Lacking knowledge of the path to peace, humanity seeks to establish pacifist utopias through political agreements or global confederations, but such efforts are destined to fail (1 Thessalonians 5:1-3). True peace is impossible without divine justice, a reality that will only materialize when the Lord returns bodily to reign on the throne of David at the Second Coming (Isaiah 9:6-7).
[9-11] When human wisdom attempts to supplant the words of God, humanity stumbles in darkness, and its understanding is darkened. People long for light, but see only darkness and gloom, groping like the blind and stumbling at midday as if it were night (Isaiah 59:9-10). In this state of despair, two extremes of human behavior are observed: roaring like bears in anger and moaning sadly like doves in pain (Isaiah 59:11). Man seeks judgment and salvation by his own means, but these remain far from him because he insists on making his own light instead of submitting to the Lord.
[12-15] The confession of the people's many transgressions exposes the character of an apostate nation, a condition that will reach its peak during the Great Tribulation (Jeremiah 30:7). The declaration that "truth has stumbled in the street" (Isaiah 59:14) completely shatters the illusions of postmillennial optimism that assumes the world will gradually improve through human effort. The popular notion that God's truth continues to march victoriously in this age is refuted by prophecy, which shows that truth is lacking and falls in the street (2 Timothy 3:1-5). This utter moral collapse sets the stage for divine intervention at the Second Coming of Christ.
[16-19] When the Lord saw that there was no intercessor or man to stand up for the truth, He intervened directly through His own arm, which is the Lord Jesus (Isaiah 53:1). Unlike His first coming in humiliation, where He wore a crown of thorns, this passage describes a physical and literal battle that will occur at the Second Coming. The Lord clothes Himself in vengeance and zeal as a garment to pour out His wrath upon the nations at the Second Coming of Christ (Revelation 19:11-16). When the enemy comes like a raging flood, the Spirit of the Lord will raise a banner against him, crushing every attempt at satanic rebellion on the battlefield (Isaiah 63:1-6).
[20, 21] The passage concludes with the promise of God's covenant with the remnant of Jacob who turn from iniquity. The apostle Paul quotes this text to confirm the national salvation of Israel at the Second Coming of Christ (Romans 11:26-27). The Redeemer will come to Zion and establish an everlasting covenant in which His Spirit and His words will never depart from the mouths of His descendants (Isaiah 59:21). Although this promise applies spiritually to the church in this age, its literal and doctrinal fulfillment will take place at the establishment of the Millennial Kingdom after the Second Advent, when the whole earth will be filled with the knowledge of the Lord (Hebrews 8:10-11).

[1-3] The call to arise and shine is chronologically situated at the Second Coming of Christ, specifically in a glorious manifestation that occurs during the tribulation period (Matthew 24:29-30). While the nations of the earth experience the physical and spiritual darkness of divine judgment (Zephaniah 1:15), the glory of the Lord rises literally and visibly upon the remnant of Israel (Isaiah 60:2). This momentous event finds its typological counterpart in the conversion of Paul on the road to Damascus, where a heavenly light brighter than the sun struck him to the ground (Acts 9:3-4). It is incorrect to spiritualize this prophecy to apply it exclusively to the church or to the first coming, for the nations still walk in darkness and Jerusalem has not yet experienced the final restoration decreed for the end times (Romans 11:25-26). Scripture associates this literal light with the visible manifestation of the Messiah, who will rise from his heavenly throne to defend his earthly people (Psalm 102:16).
[4-7] The gathering and return of the scattered children of Israel from the ends of the earth will take place after the judgments that will purge the nation (Ezekiel 20:38). In this context, the wealth and strength of the Gentiles will be channeled toward Jerusalem to honor the Lord and his earthly people. The historical allusions to the arrival of camels from Midian, Ephah, and Sheba bringing gold and frankincense find their ultimate fulfillment in the Second Coming, when the pagan nations will render material submission to the Davidic throne (Psalm 72:10-11). Solomon here functions as a precise type of the millennial reign; Just as the queen of Sheba came before him with spices, gold, and gifts (1 Kings 10:1-2), the kings of the earth will bring their offerings to the restored sanctuary. The offerings of Kedar and Nebaioth on the altar demonstrate the reinstitution of sacrifices in the millennial temple, which will operate as national memorials and not as atonement for individual salvation (Ezekiel 43:27).
[8-11] The question about those who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows remarkably foreshadows the aerial transport of the saints and the sovereign regrouping of Israel. The ships of Tarshish and the naval forces of the nations will be used at the Second Coming of Christ to repatriate the children of Jacob with their silver and gold (Isaiah 60:9). The gates of Jerusalem will remain open uninterrupted, signifying a state of absolute security and constant trade in which Gentile kings will be treated as vassals before the Hebrew theocracy. Amillennial and historicist theology err in claiming that these descriptions are allegories of the spiritual expansion of the church, for the New Testament maintains that Israel's blindness is temporary and that the covenant of possession of the land of Palestine is perpetual and unconditional (Romans 11:25-29). The Lord Himself will reestablish the geographical boundaries originally promised to the patriarchs in ancient times (Genesis 15:18), since prophetic scripture teaches that the physical restoration of the nation is an unalterable divine plan (Revelation 11:15).
[12-14] The divine decree states that any Gentile nation or kingdom that refuses to submit to and serve Israel in the millennial age will be utterly destroyed and laid waste (Zechariah 14:17-18). The glory of Lebanon, represented by fine woods such as cypress, pine, and boxwood, will be physically employed to rebuild and beautify the temple in Jerusalem, making the place of His feet glorious (Isaiah 60:13). This literal earthly sanctuary will rise upon the ruins of the past and will possess a material splendor surpassing that of the ancient tabernacle or Solomon’s temple (Haggai 2:9). Furthermore, the descendants of Israel’s historical oppressors—empires that persecuted and massacred the Jews throughout the dispensations—will come prostrate and humbled to the feet of the restored remnant, acknowledging that Jerusalem is the geographical and spiritual center of God’s rule after the Second Coming (Isaiah 60:14). This demonstrates that God’s kingdom on earth possesses a political and military character that will destroy the pride of the global coalitions represented by the United Nations (Psalms 2:8-9).
[15-18] The transition from a state of abandonment and reproach to one of eternal excellence underscores God’s faithfulness to his earthly consort. By using the metaphor of suckling the milk of nations and the breast of kings, the prophecy figuratively indicates the economic sustenance and material wealth that the Gentiles will willingly provide to Israel (Isaiah 60:16). The declaration that Jehovah is the Savior and Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob, constitutes an insurmountable obstacle for Unitarian sects that deny the deity of Jesus, since the New Testament unequivocally reveals Christ in this role (Titus 2:13-14). Likewise, the substitution of base metals with precious metals reverses the historical decline of the Hebrew monarchy, just as when Rehoboam replaced his father's gold shields with bronze ones because of Egypt's plunder (1 Kings 14:25-27). With the Second Coming of Christ, absolute peace will reign, abolishing all forms of violence and destruction within the borders of the promised land (Isaiah 60:18).
[19-22] The statements concerning the sun and moon no longer being the primary source of light do not imply the physical annihilation of these celestial bodies, for Scripture teaches that new moons and Sabbaths will continue to be observed during the millennium and into eternity (Isaiah 66:23). The meaning of the text indicates that the radiance of God's personal glory will so surpass physical creation that humanity will no longer depend on the natural order for enlightenment. After the Second Coming, Israel's mourning and brokenness will cease completely, and all its inhabitants will be made righteous through the Lord's sovereign intervention in the new order (Jeremiah 31:33-34). The promise of inheriting the land forever confirms that the eternal destiny of Jacob's physical descendants is not dissolution into the heavenly church, but perpetual possession of the land on this restored earthly soil (Genesis 17:8). The multiplication of the little one into a thousand illustrates the immense demographic expansion and theocratic blessing that will characterize the Messiah's kingdom in its earthly phase (Zechariah 10:8).

[1-2] The anointing of the Spirit of God upon the Messiah directly points to His twofold ministry, encompassing both His first coming in humiliation and His glorious return. In the synagogue at Nazareth, the Lord Jesus read this prophecy but deliberately stopped reading at the midpoint of verse two (Luke 4:18-20). By proclaiming only the year of the Lord’s favor and closing the scroll before uttering the day of God’s vengeance, He demonstrated the correct division of the word of truth, revealing that there is a time gap of over two thousand years between the two events (Genesis 49:11). This time span corresponds to the dispensation of grace, or church age, which remained a mystery hidden from the Old Testament prophets, including Isaiah (Ephesians 3:1-6). Thus, the first section details the mission of the suffering servant who came to bind up the brokenhearted and proclaim freedom for the spiritually captives, while the subsequent clause will be fulfilled literally at the Second Coming of Christ, when the Lord descends in wrath to execute judgment on the rebellious nations (Revelation 19:11-15).
[3-4] The comfort decreed for those who mourn in Zion introduces a regeneration that encompasses both the spiritual and material realms of creation. Those who receive the divine anointing are constituted as trees of righteousness and a planting of the Lord for the manifestation of his own glory, establishing the righteousness that precedes peace in the coming kingdom (Romans 14:17). The text immediately transitions to the events of the Second Coming through a shift in the literal sense, indicating that the restored will rebuild the ancient ruins and raise up the desolations of the past. This regrouping and physical and political restoration of the nation of Israel on the land of Palestine constitutes the central theme of Old Testament prophecy, which cannot be allegorized in a spiritualizing way to be applied to the church (Ezekiel 36:10). God Himself will rebuild the fallen tabernacle of David and restore the desolate cities in the end times (Acts 15:16-17).
[5-6] In the millennial era that will begin after the Second Coming of Christ, the power relations between the Gentile nations and Israel will undergo a complete reversal. Foreigners and the children of foreigners will serve as shepherds, farmers, and vineyard workers, providing the economic and material sustenance for the chosen nation (Isaiah 60:9-10). While the Gentiles will be occupied with farming and livestock, the remnant of Jacob will be officially designated as ministers of God and priests of the Lord. Scripture teaches that, in this period of literal righteousness on earth, any Gentile who wishes to approach the throne of the Lord will have to do so through the channel and mediation of the Jewish people, since millennial salvation operates by sight and not by faith (Zechariah 8:23). Thus, the riches and glory of the Gentile nations will be channeled to honor the Lord's earthly sanctuary in Jerusalem.
[7-9] The promise of receiving double for the historical shame and confusion suffered by Israel will be fulfilled literally when the Lord releases His earthly people from captivity. God, who loves judgment and detests the plundering of burnt offerings, will ratify with the seed of Jacob an eternal and definitive covenant that differs from the conditional Mosaic covenant (Jeremiah 31:31-34). This Second Coming will mark the unconditional restoration of the nation, making its descendants clearly distinguished and recognized among all the nations of the earth as the Lord's blessed lineage. Unlike the reproach experienced during the dispersion in the church age, the inhabitants of the world will testify that Israel is the nation the Lord has materially and physically blessed on the earth (Genesis 17:8).
[10-11] The supreme rejoicing expressed in the garment of salvation and the robe of righteousness uses wedding analogies of profound doctrinal relevance. The adornment of the bridegroom wearing a crown and the bride adorned with her jewels foreshadows the glorious union between the Lord Jesus and his heavenly church at the wedding of the Lamb, which chronologically precedes the establishment of the earthly kingdom (Revelation 19:7-9). Likewise, just as the earth brings forth its shoots and the garden causes its seed to sprout, the Lord God will cause justice and praise to spring forth visibly before all the nations of the world. This universal flowering of truth is not achieved through the scientific progress of secular education, but through the manifestation of the Messiah as the absolute military and political ruler of the earth (Psalm 110:5-6).

[1-2] God Himself declares that He will not be silent or rest for Jerusalem's sake until its righteousness shines forth like the brightness of a blazing torch (Genesis 15:17). The Lord will physically and literally restore the earthly city, since His own honor and glory are tied to its destiny (Ezekiel 36:22). Although the Lord allowed the Babylonian armies and Titus' Roman legions to completely destroy it in the past, His unconditional mercy demands its final rebuilding at the Second Coming (Titus 2:13). On that glorious day, the Gentile nations will see His justice, and Jerusalem will receive a new name determined directly by the mouth of God, which later prophecy accurately identifies as "the Lord is there," indicating the Messiah's presence in His earthly temple at the Second Coming of Christ (Ezekiel 48:35).
[3-4] The promise that the restored nation will be a crown of glory and a royal diadem in God's hand points to the theocratic exaltation of the remnant in the coming kingdom (Psalm 2:6). The Lord will reign on Mount Zion as the absolute monarch decreed by the Father in the divine decrees. Furthermore, the geographical inheritance of Palestine will no longer be called desolate or forsaken, but will be called Beulah, for the land will be married (Hosea 2:19-20). A correct division of the word of truth shows that this marriage union differs from the heavenly wedding of the church; here, at the Second Coming, God the Lord is re-married to his former earthly bride who had been temporarily repudiated because of her historical unfaithfulness (Romans 11:25-29). This reveals the mystery that there are two distinct brides and two distinct grooms in the eternal plan: the church as the chaste virgin betrothed to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2), and Israel as the earthly bride reconciled to God the Father (Isaiah 54:5).
[5] By employing specific wedding analogies, the prophecy illustrates in parallel how the young man betroths a virgin and how the bridegroom rejoices in his bride. In the heavenly realm, Christ is betrothed to his purified church, a mystery not explicitly revealed in the Old Testament prophecies (Ephesians 5:25-32). On earth, the children of Israel are united to their own land in perpetual possession of the geographical boundaries originally promised to the patriarchs in ancient times (Genesis 15:18). While Christ eternally rejoices over the heavenly church that is his body, God the Father lovingly rejoices over the physical remnant of Jacob after Christ's Second Coming, solidifying the unconditional restoration of the earthly covenant.
[6-7] The Lord has established spiritual watchmen on the walls of Jerusalem who will never be silent day or night, fulfilling a ministry of continuous witness that extends throughout the dispensations, as recorded in the book of Acts (Acts 13:46-47). These watchmen and guardians of truth, including ancient prophets and the apostle Paul, have consistently warned the Jewish people to prepare for the re-establishment of the kingdom. This unbroken witness has persisted even during the darkest centuries of the Church, when men attentive to the Scriptures pointed out that the Roman system was acting as the antichrist on earth. The divine command to all those who make mention of the Lord is clear and of direct practical application to the believer: do not be silent or give God rest until Jerusalem is physically and materially re-established as a universal praise throughout the earth before the Second Coming (Psalm 122:6).
[8-9] God's oath by His right hand and by the arm of His might guarantees that the grain and new wine of Israel will never again be given as plunder to their Gentile enemies. These promises of agricultural prosperity and material sustenance must be understood literally in the millennial kingdom that will be established after the Second Coming of Christ (Amos 9:13-14). The amillennial interpretation that spiritualizes these material blessings to apply them to the church in this age commits a serious exegetical transgression by depriving the descendants of Abraham of the national blessings promised (Genesis 12:1-3). Abundant harvests, wine in the winepresses, and peace on the soil of Palestine are physical realities that the Jewish remnant will enjoy under the rule of their King, who will reign with an iron rod over the nations (Psalm 2:8-9).
[10-11] The command to pass through the gates, prepare the way, and raise a banner for the peoples signifies the final preparation for the manifestation of the earthly Savior. The salvation that comes to the daughter of Zion constitutes a physical and military deliverance from the oppression of the armies of the Antichrist in the final period of the great tribulation (Revelation 12:6-14). By declaring that the Lord's reward comes with Him and His work before her, the text aligns with the New Testament prophecies in the book of Revelation (Revelation 22:11-12). This judgment and reward according to works is chronologically situated at the Second Coming, operating under dispensational principles distinct from those of Christ's judgment seat for the church, since the Jewish remnant must persevere in faith and works to inherit the earthly promises of salvation (Matthew 24:13).
[12] The restored remnant of Jacob will finally be called the Lord's holy and redeemed people, forever ridding themselves of the reproach and spiritual blindness they endured during the Gentile dispersion in the church age (Romans 11:25-26). Jerusalem will cease to be a desolate and trampled city and will be established as the geographical, political, and spiritual center of the entire earth after the Second Coming of Christ (Zechariah 14:16-21). In this period of millennial justice, the Gentile hosts who formerly persecuted the Jewish people will come in submission to Zion, bringing their riches and gifts of gold and silver to honor God's sanctuary on earth (Isaiah 60:9-12).

[1-3] The prophet beholds a majestic warrior approaching from Edom and Bozrah, regions historically identified with the territory of Esau (Genesis 36:8). His garments are not stained with his own blood, but with the blood of his enemies after a battle of catastrophic proportions. A correct division of the word of truth teaches that this passage does not describe the sufferings of the crucifixion at Calvary, where the Lord willingly shed his blood for redemption, but rather foreshadows the Second Coming (Revelation 19:11-13). In this momentous event, the Lord will literally tread the winepress of God's wrath, crushing the rebellion of the United Nations' armies gathered against Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:2-3). He who speaks in righteousness and is mighty to save will march in the greatness of his strength, executing the physical judgment decreed against the ungodly nations (Psalm 110:5-6).
[4-6] The declaration that the day of vengeance is in the heart of the Lord places this prophecy chronologically within the great tribulation, a period characterized by Jacob's trouble (Jeremiah 30:7). Faced with the utter desolation and helplessness of Israel, when none of the earthly powers rise to the aid of God's earthly people, the personal arm of the Lord will sovereignly intervene to bring deliverance. While the first coming was a manifestation of love and grace for individual salvation, the second coming of Christ will constitute an act of military and political judgment (Zephaniah 3:8). The Lord will trample the nations in his wrath, causing the blood of his adversaries to literally flow on the soil of Palestine up to the bridles of the horses, demonstrating that God will not tolerate the pride of the human empires that sought to usurp his earthly sovereignty (Revelation 14:19-20).
[7-9] Following the manifestation of divine wrath in the judgment of the nations, there is a beautiful transition to a song of praise for God's mercies and goodness toward the house of Israel. In the period of the millennial kingdom, the remnant of Jacob will recognize the Lord as their national Savior, establishing a relationship of unwavering faithfulness under the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33-34). The mention of the angel of His presence who saved and redeemed them in His love and mercy does not refer to a created heavenly messenger, but to the visible manifestation of Christ Himself, who led His people through the wilderness in ancient times (Exodus 23:20-23). ​​This passage typifies the rejoicing of the Gentile nations who will be saved and will flock to Jerusalem to worship the King during the Second Coming, acknowledging the preeminence of the Jewish people on earth (Zechariah 8:23).
[10-14] Israel's historical rebellion against God grieved His Holy Spirit, resulting in the Lord becoming their enemy and fighting against them, as also noted in the book of Acts (Acts 7:51). Rigorous dispensational study demonstrates that the Holy Spirit operated differently in the Old Testament economy; He dwelt in men selectively (Exodus 31:3) and could withdraw because of disobedience, as happened with King Saul (1 Samuel 16:14). The prophet recalls the exodus from Egypt when God placed His Spirit in their midst and parted the waters of the Red Sea through Moses to make an eternal name for Himself. This crossing of the chasm foreshadows both the deliverance of Israel in the wilderness and the future preservation of the remnant at the Second Coming of Christ, when the Lord will again lead His people into their millennial rest (Revelation 12:6).
[15-16] The fervent plea for God to look down from heaven and behold the affliction of His earthly people is doctrinally situated at the moments of greatest anguish during tribulation. The Jewish remnant cries out directly to God, calling Him “Father,” acknowledging that although Abraham and Jacob ignored them because of their historical dispersion and unfaithfulness, the Lord remains their eternal Redeemer. This prayer of national repentance is offered at the end of the dispensation of grace, when Israel’s blindness is about to be removed following the Second Coming (Romans 11:25–27). The appeal to the Lord’s name as Redeemer demonstrates that the forgiveness and restoration of the physical nation of Jacob are firmly guaranteed by the unconditional covenant God swore to the patriarchs in ancient times (Genesis 15:18).
[17–19] The perplexing question of why God caused them to stray from His ways and hardened their hearts reflects God’s sovereignty in judicial retribution against the nation’s unbelief. When the people of Israel persistently rejected the miracles and words of the Lord at His first coming, God executed a judgment of spiritual blindness upon them, hardening their hearts so that they could not believe (John 12:37-40). The remnant pleads for the Lord's return out of love for His servants, lamenting that the Gentile adversaries have profaned and trampled underfoot the earthly sanctuary in Jerusalem. This prayer will be gloriously answered at the Second Coming of Christ, when the Messiah descends to destroy the system of the Antichrist, cleanse the temple, and restore the Jewish theocracy over all the nations of the earth (Revelation 11:15).

[1-3] The fervent plea for God to rend the heavens and descend is one of the most vivid prayers of the Jewish remnant in the midst of the great tribulation (Isaiah 63:17-19). This plea does not describe a purely mystical or spiritual visitation, but rather the physical and literal Second Coming of the Messiah to judge the enemy hosts. The trembling of the nations and the melting of the mountains at his visible presence coincide with the heavenly and earthly cataclysms prophesied for the end times (Revelation 6:12-14). Upon descending, the Lord will unleash a conflagration that will shatter the geopolitical arrogance of the Gentile empires confederated against Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:3-4). It is a violent interruption of history where God Himself assumes the role of warrior to rescue His earthly people.
[4-5] The revelation of what no eye has seen and no ear has heard, although applied spiritually by the apostle Paul in his epistles, is doctrinally associated with the glorious manifestation of the Son of God (1 Corinthians 2:9). Those who actively await the Lord will experience a physical encounter with His majesty at the Second Coming of Christ. The text emphasizes that God meets those who rejoice and do what is right, but since humanity under the law fell short of this standard, the true righteousness that saves the sinner is imputed directly through the person of Christ (Romans 4:5-6). In prophetic economics, the final salvation of the remnant of Jacob is not achieved through cooperative human effort, but through God's free and sovereign intervention in the last days.
[6-7] The collective confession of the nation's spiritual ruin stands as one of the most powerful testimonies against the theology of human self-justification. By declaring that all of humanity's meritorious works are equivalent to filthy rags, the prophet destroys the notion of salvation by moral works separate from divine sacrifice (Genesis 15:6). During this period of national blindness, God has hidden His face from the house of Jacob because of their historical rebellion at the first coming (Romans 11:25). This lack of fellowship and sincere prayer, where no one awakens to lean on the Lord, leaves the people helpless in the face of the destructive consequences of their iniquities (Ezekiel 22:30). Only repentance and the acknowledgment of their utter spiritual bankruptcy will pave the way for national restoration.
[8-9] Despite the profound rebellion of the children of Israel, the remnant appeals to God's concerted relationship and paternal right over them, calling Him "Father." The recognition that the Lord is the potter and the nation is the clay accurately illustrates divine sovereignty in the election and preservation of the instruments of His grace (Romans 9:21). The cry pleads that the Lord's anger not be perpetual and that He remember the unconditional inheritance promised to the seed of Abraham (Genesis 17:7-8). This intercession is situated at the end of the dispensation of grace, preparing the stage for the Second Coming, where God's wrath will cease to give way to the promised mercy in the new national order (Hebrews 8:10-12).
[10-12] The painful description of the desolation of the land of Palestine and the destruction by fire of the temple in Jerusalem details the historical and prophetic conditions of the great tribulation. The holy cities turned into a desert and the beautiful millennial sanctuary burned by the armies of the Antichrist represent the culmination of Gentile oppression (Revelation 11:1-2). The prophet questions whether, in the face of such destruction, the Lord will remain silent and continue to afflict the people of Jacob. This prolonged retribution will end definitively with the Second Coming of Christ, when the Messiah breaks his heavenly silence to tread the winepress of wrath, destroy the tyranny of the satanic system, and permanently establish the throne of David on earth (Acts 15:16-17).

[1-5] The Lord's manifestation to those who did not seek Him directly prophesies the calling and conversion of the Gentiles during the present dispensation of grace (Romans 10:20). The apostle Paul applies this truth to illustrate how God would reveal Himself to a people who did not bear His name, while the nation of Israel remained in a state of rebellion and apostasy. The ritual sacrifices in gardens and on brick altars symbolize the perversion of the theocratic worship of Mosaic Law. This attitude of hypocritical self-justification, where the rebels demand that others stay away while pretending to be holier, constitutes a constant provocation in the eyes of the Lord, like irritating smoke in His nostrils. It is not permissible to spiritualize this historical judgment to accommodate the church in this century, since Jacob's blindness will continue until the Gentile nations have fully entered the world before the Second Coming of Christ (Romans 11:25-26).
[6-10] The analogy of the must preserved within the grape cluster illustrates how the Lord preserves a faithful remnant in the midst of an apostate generation decreed for judgment. Doctrinally, the new wine represents the pure, unfermented juice of the grape, containing a blessing of physical and literal life (Genesis 40:11). The Lord promises that He will not destroy the entire Jewish nation, but will raise up a seed from Jacob and Judah to perpetually inherit their mountains in the promised land (Genesis 15:18). This geopolitical and geographical legacy in Palestine will be fully consolidated after the Second Coming, when Sharon and the Valley of Achor will be transformed into resting pastures for the livestock of its people. Amillennial theology errs in allegorizing these territorial blessings, for the prophetic scriptures guarantee that the physical restoration of Israel to its land is irrevocable (Jeremiah 31:35-36).
[11-12] Those who abandon the holy Mount Zion to worship pagan deities of fortune and destiny receive a severe admonition under the irony of divine judgment. The allusion to providing libations and offerings for "that number" is doctrinally connected to the mystery of iniquity and the political-religious system of the Antichrist (Revelation 13:18). Because the Lord called through the preaching of His messengers and the nation refused to listen, God Himself will judicially condemn them to physical slaughter and the sword during the great tribulation. This decree of retribution demonstrates that those who willingly choose what displeases the Lord will experience military and governmental punishment at the Second Coming of Christ, when the rebellious coalitions are crushed by divine judgment (Zechariah 14:2-3).
[13-16] An absolute antithesis is established between the rebellious portion and the submissive remnant during the purges that precede the establishment of the millennial kingdom. While God's servants will enjoy physical sustenance, water, and spiritual joy, the transgressors will suffer hunger, thirst, and a deep anguish that will cause them to howl with the anguish of their own spirit. The apostate offspring will leave their name as a curse among the elect, and the Lord will destroy the unbelieving faction to name His servants with a new name, foreshadowing the dispensational distinction observed today in the body of Christ (Acts 11:26). After this judgment, every blessing and oath on earth will be fulfilled by the God of truth, since the anxieties of the past will have been definitively covered up and forgotten in the presence of God at the Second Coming (Revelation 21:4).
[17-20] The promise of the creation of new heavens and a new earth places the climax of God's plan in the eternal state following the great white throne judgment (Revelation 21:1). However, the text presents an immediate dispensational overlap by contrasting this eternity with the restoration of earthly Jerusalem in the millennium, where physical death and sin will still operate in a limited way. In this restored city on the soil of Palestine, human longevity will be restored to pre-flood levels, so that anyone who dies at one hundred will be considered merely a child, and the sinner who reaches that age under a curse will be cast out. This demonstrates that the millennial Jerusalem established at the Second Coming of Christ constitutes a period of physical transition before the complete renewal of the material cosmos (2 Peter 3:13).
[21-25] The material blessings of building homes, planting vineyards, and enjoying the fruits of their labor guarantee the uninterrupted stability and security of Israel under the Messiah's rule. God's chosen people will enjoy such intimate fellowship that their prayers will be answered before they are even uttered, operating fully under the terms of the new national agreement (Jeremiah 31:33). This restoration also encompasses the pacification of the animal kingdom, where the wolf and the lamb will graze together and the lion will adopt one of the herbivorous diets of the beginning (Isaiah 11:6-7). However, the curse imposed on the serpent in Eden will remain unchanged, with the dust of the earth being its exclusive food during this theocratic reign that will be physically inaugurated at the Second Coming (Genesis 3:14).

[1-4] The statement that heaven is God's throne and the earth his footstool establishes divine transcendence in the face of human-made temples (Isaiah 66:1). This declaration is used doctrinally by the martyr Stephen in his final address to confront the carnal trust of the Jewish theocracy in the physical sanctuary (Acts 7:48-49), and the Lord Jesus himself alludes to it when forbidding hypocritical oaths (Matthew 5:34-35). God, who sustains all creation by his personal power, does not find his rest in material structures, but rather fixes his gracious gaze on the humble, poor, and contrite person who trembles before his holy word (Isaiah 66:2). In stark contrast, the worship of the self-righteous is categorized as an abomination; For God, the formal sacrifice of an ox by a rebel is equivalent to the murder of a man, and the offering of a lamb to the slaughter of a dog (Isaiah 66:3). Because these men preferred their own ways and delighted in idolatry, the Lord decreed to send them judicial disappointments and bring upon them their greatest fears, for when God called, no one answered or listened to His voice (Isaiah 66:4).
[5-9] The call to listen to the word of the Lord is directed to those who tremble before it, suffering the rejection and hatred of their own countrymen for the sake of the divine name (Isaiah 66:5). At the Second Coming of Christ, the Lord will manifest Himself visibly for the comfort of the persecuted and the confusion of the unbelievers, who sought to invoke divine glory with hypocrisy. The thunder of judgment emanating from the city and the temple signifies the literal military retribution God will execute against the rebel coalitions gathered in Jerusalem at the Second Coming (Isaiah 66:6). Likewise, the miraculous prophecy that Zion would give birth before experiencing labor pains represents the sudden and sovereign birth of the restored nation in a single day (Isaiah 66:7-8). This physical and spiritual regrouping of the Jewish remnant at the end of the great tribulation constitutes a design of unconditional restoration that cannot be spiritualized to be applied to the Gentile church (Romans 11:26). The Lord Himself, who opens the national womb of Israel, guarantees that He will not prevent the final birth of His earthly people, thus thwarting the extermination plans of the world's empires (Isaiah 66:9).
[10-14] The exhortation to rejoice and be glad in Jerusalem calls to all those who have loved the city and mourned its historical ruin (Isaiah 66:10). Those who assist the Jewish remnant during its final persecution will be admitted to partake of the material blessings and comfort of Zion after the Second Coming of Christ (Matthew 25:34). Under the Messiah's shepherding, God's earthly people will be nourished by the abundance of riches and economic glory that the Gentile nations will willingly pour upon Jerusalem in the age of the kingdom (Isaiah 66:11-12). The divine metaphor comparing the Lord’s comforting visitation to a mother’s solace illustrates the tenderness of His preservation, without justifying the inclusion of female deities in the canon (Isaiah 66:13). The inner joy of the restored people will literally revitalize their bodies, causing their bones to flourish like fresh grass, while God’s mighty hand is manifested benevolently in His servants and unleashes His destructive wrath upon His implacable enemies at the Second Coming (Isaiah 66:14).
[15-18] The Lord’s arrival with heavenly fire and chariots like a whirlwind describes the violent physical intervention that will characterize the Second Coming (Isaiah 66:15). On this day of military judgment, God will pour out His furious anger and rebuke the enemy hosts with literal flames of consuming fire. Through the judgment of His sword and His purifying fire, the Lord will contend judicially against all flesh, resulting in a universal slaughter unprecedented in human history (Isaiah 66:16). This scenario of physical judgment and great tribulation finds its literal counterpart in the coming of the heavenly rider to tread the winepress of wrath (Revelation 19:11-15). Divine judgment will severely consume those idolaters who hypocritically sanctify themselves in pagan gardens behind a central tree, participating in ritual abominations and consuming unclean foods (Isaiah 66:17). The Lord, knowing the rebellious works and thoughts of the inhabitants of the earth, will ultimately gather all nations and languages ​​to appear before His earthly tribunal and behold His visible glory at the Second Coming of Christ (Isaiah 66:18).
[19-21] The reestablishment of the Jewish theocracy includes the placement of a miraculous sign among them and the dispatch of Jewish survivors to the farthest Gentile nations that have never heard of the name of the Lord or beheld His majesty (Isaiah 66:19). These messengers of the remnant, typified in the book of Revelation as the witnesses of the twelve tribes of Israel, will governmentally declare divine glory among the Gentiles (Revelation 7:4). As a result of this powerful testimony, the Gentile nations will cooperate in the physical repatriation of the scattered Israelites, transporting them with honor and gifts by various earthly means to the holy mountain of Jerusalem (Isaiah 66:20). This offering of Jacob’s brothers to the earthly sanctuary is likened to the ritual purity required in the ancient offerings of the Mosaic Law. Finally, the Lord will restore the literal priesthood and select from among them ministers and Levites for the service of the millennial temple, where material sacrifices will be reinstated as national memorials after the Second Coming, operating under specific kingdom dispensational principles (Ezekiel 44:15).
[22-24] The solemn promise that the seed and name of Israel will endure forever before God is grounded in the permanence of the new material cosmos (Isaiah 66:22). This guarantee of Jewish national preservation will extend physically into the eternal state following the destruction of the present heavens and earth (Revelation 21:1). In this coming order, millennial and eternal worship will be literally structured around the New Moon festivals and the observance of the Sabbaths, events at which all flesh will come to prostrate itself before the Lord, signifying the reinstatement of certain ceremonial decrees that do not apply to the church in the age of grace (Colossians 2:16). Finally, the worshippers will leave the sanctuary and visibly and literally behold the corpses of the rebellious transgressors suffering eternal condemnation in the lake of fire, where their worm will not die and their fire will never be quenched (Isaiah 66:24). The Lord Jesus himself repeatedly quoted this passage during his earthly ministry to attest to the conscious and literal punishment that awaits unbelieving sinners after the Second Coming of Christ (Mark 9:44-48).

[1-4] The apostle Paul presents himself as a servant of Jesus Christ, called to the apostolic ministry, having been set apart for the Gospel of God (Romans 1:1). The term "servant" is his preferred designation for identifying himself in his letters (Philippians 1:1, Titus 1:1, James 1:1, 2 Peter 1:1). Regarding the divine sonship of Jesus Christ, the resurrection from the dead is the ultimate proof of his virgin birth and divinity, since the nature of his blood depends on his Father (Acts 20:28). This incorruptible blood prevented his body from undergoing any corruption in the tomb. Although the Son's preexistence is eternal, the full manifestation of his lordship over the nations of the earth will be consummated at the Second Coming of Christ.
[5-7] Through Jesus Christ, grace and apostleship were received for the obedience of faith among all nations for his name's sake (Romans 1:5). True obedience to the Gospel does not consist of external ceremonies like water baptism, but in exercising genuine faith in the finished work of the cross (Romans 10:16-17), recognizing that no work of the flesh can purchase salvation (Ephesians 2:8-9). God purifies the hearts of believers through faith (Acts 15:7-9). This epistle is addressed to God's beloved who reside in Rome, called to be saints, who enjoy the grace and peace of the Lord (Romans 1:7). The phrase "of God" is the doctrinal axis of this chapter, appearing repeatedly to emphasize that the Lord is the source and sustainer of all spiritual life (Romans 1:7, 10, 16-18, 25, 32).
[8-10] First, thanks are given to God through Jesus Christ concerning all the believers in Rome, since their faith is witnessed throughout the world (Romans 1:8). In the geography of the time, the expression "the whole world" referred to the territory of the Roman Empire, where the news spread of those saints who refused to worship the idols of the pagan pantheon. The term "faith" acquires great importance in the New Testament, in marked contrast to the Old Testament, where the word appears only twice (Deuteronomy 32:20, Habakkuk 2:4). The apostle serves God with his spirit in the Gospel of His Son, ceaselessly interceding in his prayers for the steadfastness of the congregation (Romans 1:9-10).
[11, 12] The apostle's keen desire to see the brothers and sisters in order to impart some spiritual gift to them is evident, so that they may be strengthened in their walk (Romans 1:11). This sharing of gifts is intended to strengthen the mind and doctrinal stability of the collective faith, thus ruling out any mystical interpretation referring to complete sanctification or the total eradication of the old carnal nature (2 Corinthians 1:15, 2 Corinthians 8:6). The confirmation of the believer comes through the mutual consolation and encouragement that shared faith provides (Romans 1:12).
[13] Paul explains that he often intended to visit them, but has so far been hindered, desiring to bear spiritual fruit among them as well, just as he has with the other Gentiles (Romans 1:13). The word “hindered” or “stopped” is associated with the concept of preventing or obstructing a purpose (Isaiah 43:13). The Lord uses biblical language with absolute precision, demonstrating that human plans are always subordinate to God’s control and providence. The gathering of spiritual fruit involved both the edification of already converted saints and the evangelization of unconverted Gentiles.
[14, 15] The apostle acknowledges his debt to both Greeks and barbarians, as well as to the wise and the ignorant (Romans 1:14). Likewise, every believer redeemed by the Lord's free grace incurs an inescapable spiritual obligation to witness to the lost around them (Ephesians 2:10). The fervent willingness to preach the Gospel in Rome extends to the entire community without distinction (Romans 1:15). It is essential to remember that the first believers in Rome were originally converted under the preaching of the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:10), when the revelation concerning atonement by blood had not yet been fully expounded as it was later through the Pauline epistles (Acts 15:7-11).
[16, 17] The Gospel of Jesus Christ is not a cause for shame for the believer, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, first to the Jew and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16). In the message of the cross, the righteousness of God is progressively revealed "from faith to faith" (Romans 1:17). This represents the transition from the faith of the Old Testament to the faith of the New Testament. In quoting the prophecy of Habakkuk, the Holy Spirit makes a free quotation by omitting the personal pronoun (Habakkuk 2:4), teaching that the justification of the sinner is a free gift received only through faith in the finished work of Jesus Christ on the cross (Romans 4:5, Ephesians 2:8-9).
[18, 19] The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who suppress the truth by their unrighteousness (Romans 1:18). Modern translations that change the term "suppress" to "suppress" attempt to veil the severity of this warning directed at those who know the truth but persist in their disobedience. God has made manifest what can be known about him in human beings, so that no one has an excuse (Romans 1:19). This passage underscores the constant witness of the Lord’s justice and judgment in the conscience of humanity.
[20, 21] God’s invisible perfections, such as his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, ever since the creation of the world, through what has been made (Romans 1:20). This revelation in nature points to God’s sovereignty, which will be undeniably manifested at the Second Coming of Christ. The historical decline of the Gentile nations began in the post-flood period when, having known God, they neither glorified him as God nor gave thanks to him (Romans 1:21, Genesis 11:6). By turning away from the truth revealed to Noah, the nations’ understanding was darkened, and they fell into the futility of their own reasoning (Genesis 10:25). Faced with this carnal inclination, the believer's response is to submit every thought to the obedience of Christ (2 Corinthians 10:5).
[22, 23] By boasting of their wisdom, men became fools (Romans 1:22). The most evident symptom of this intellectual folly was the formulation of evolutionary theories that diminish human dignity and worship matter, inverting the divine order by placing corruptible man at the top, followed by birds, four-legged animals, and reptiles (Romans 1:23). This idolatry and worship of the creature rather than the Lord represents the original rebellion (Genesis 3:5). When a culture magnifies the creature or glorifies the image of woman above the established order, it is exalting human glory and not God's (1 Corinthians 11:7). This widespread apostasy of the Gentile nations will receive its final retribution during the judgments of Christ's Second Coming.
[24-27] As a consequence of their stubborn idolatry, God gave the Gentiles over to the impurity of their hearts (Romans 1:24). They exchanged the truth of God for a lie and worshiped created things rather than the Lord (Romans 1:25). The culmination of the moral degradation of these societies was manifested in shameful passions and sexual perversion (Romans 1:26-27). This state of extreme depravity, historically exemplified by Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:1-5), represents God's judgment, which delivers humanity to its own depraved mind when it refuses to retain divine knowledge (Revelation 18:1-5).
[28-32] By refusing to retain the knowledge of God, the Lord gave them over to a depraved mind (Romans 1:28). This depraved state is not the result of a decree of eternal predestination, but rather the consequence of the Gentile nations' rejection of the light in history (Genesis 11:6-9). From this comes the list of sins that infest fallen nature, including pride, ungodliness, and disobedience to the parents (Romans 1:29-31). The sin of lacking spiritual understanding reflects the blindness of the natural man who cannot discern the things of the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 2:14). Those who commit such acts know God's judgment and know they deserve death, yet they not only practice them but also take pleasure in those who do them (Romans 1:32). The only way out for the sinner under this just condemnation is repentance and faith in the atoning sacrifice of Jesus Christ (Titus 3:5).

[1-3] The apostle confronts the presumption of the natural man who, by setting himself up as judge of others' conduct, signs his own sentence of condemnation (Romans 2:1). This admonition is not directed at the believer who expounds on divine judgment according to Scripture (1 Corinthians 2:15), but at the unregenerate individual who judges others while committing the same sins. The sinner deceives himself by supposing that he will escape God's judgment, which is inescapable and in accordance with the truth (Romans 2:2-3). Unlike the ungodly moralist, the redeemed person has previously recognized their spiritual ruin and has turned to the sacrifice of Jesus Christ on the cross, thus escaping the coming wrath (Romans 5:9, 1 Corinthians 1:18).
[4, 5] God's kindness, patience, and generous forbearance should not be despised by the natural person, who ignores that the purpose of such kindness is to lead them to repentance (Romans 2:4). The obstinacy of the unrepentant heart only accumulates wrath for the day of wrath and the revelation of God's righteous judgment (Romans 2:5). God demonstrates His patience by temporarily limiting His wrath against the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction (Romans 9:22), extending the day of salvation before consummating judgment at His Second Coming (2 Peter 3:7-9).
[6-10] Divine judgment will repay each individual according to their works (Romans 2:6).
