Under the historical dispensation that governed the Gentiles from Noah until the coming of Christ, moral righteousness and the constant pursuit of glory, honor, and immortality were rewarded with the granting of eternal life by God (Romans 2:7). This describes a dispensational plan based on faithfulness and works (Acts 13:48, Luke 7:3-5). However, for those who act with contention and disobey divine truth, the retribution will be wrath, distress, and tribulation (Romans 2:8-9). This structure of faith and works is distinct from the New Testament salvation by pure grace (Ephesians 2:8-9, Romans 6:23), but it will be revealed again for the saints who go through the great tribulation (Revelation 12:17, 14:12).
[11-13] Before God there is no partiality, for both Jews and Gentiles are measured by the same standard of justice (Romans 2:11). Those who sinned without the written law will perish without it, while those who sinned under the law will be judged by the law itself (Romans 2:12). Justification before God does not belong to mere hearers of the law, but to doers of it (Romans 2:13). In contrasting this section with the Epistle of James, it is observed that James is addressing himself primarily to Jewish believers in the Diaspora (James 1:1, 2:1), while Paul defines the doctrinal impossibility of man being justified by the works of the law in the present age (Romans 3:20, Galatians 2:16).
[14-16] When Gentiles, lacking external legislation, naturally carry out the moral precepts of the law, they become a law to themselves (Romans 2:14). In this way, they demonstrate that the work of the law is engraved on their hearts, their conscience testifying and their own thoughts either accusing or excusing them (Romans 2:15). A historical example of this internal moral law is found in the integrity shown by Abimelech (Genesis 20:3-6). All the hidden things and secrets of men will be judged by Jesus Christ according to the gospel proclaimed by Paul (Romans 2:16). This final scrutiny will take place before the great white throne (Revelation 20:11-15), where each individual will give a personal account before God (Romans 14:10-12, 2 Corinthians 5:10).
[17-24] Addressing the Jewish people specifically, the apostle points out the folly of boasting in the law and in the knowledge of God without possessing an internal moral correspondence (Romans 2:17-20). The Jew who instructs others but engages in theft, adultery, and sacrilege dishonors God by transgressing the very law he boasts of (Romans 2:21-23). This inconsistency causes the name of God to be blasphemed among the Gentiles, as it is written in the prophets (Romans 2:24, Isaiah 52:5). Mere intellectual instruction is useless if conduct contradicts the standard of holiness required by the Lord.
[25-27] Physical circumcision has value only if the entirety of the law is observed and kept; otherwise, transgression turns circumcision into uncircumcision (Romans 2:25). If an uncircumcised Gentile fulfills the requirements of the law's righteousness, his uncircumcision will be considered as circumcision (Romans 2:26). In this way, the Gentile who keeps the law by nature will judge the Jew who, possessing the letter of the law and circumcision, breaks the divine commandment. External rites lack salvific value in themselves (1 Corinthians 7:19, Galatians 5:6).
[28, 29] A true Jew is not one who is one outwardly in the flesh, nor is true circumcision merely visible and physical (Romans 2:28). Rather, a Jew is one who is one inwardly, and true circumcision is that of the heart, performed by the Spirit and not according to the letter of the law (Romans 2:29). Doctrinally, this spiritual circumcision of the heart in the Old Testament required a determination of the human will (Deuteronomy 10:16). In contrast, in the present dispensation of grace, the circumcision of Christ is effected without hands through the regeneration of the Holy Spirit, permanently separating the soul from the body of sin (Colossians 2:11-13). The praise for this inner transformation does not come from men, but solely from the Lord.

[1, 2] The apostle raises the question of the advantage of the physical Jew and the usefulness of external circumcision, concluding that his primary privilege lies in having received the deposit of God's oracles (Romans 3:1-2). Although true circumcision is that of the heart in the Spirit and not according to the letter of the law, God assigned historical value to the descendants of Abraham by entrusting them with the preservation of the Holy Scriptures (Romans 2:28-29, 3:2). These divine oracles constitute the foundation of the plan of salvation that will be fully revealed after the resurrection of Jesus Christ. God reveals himself through what he has spoken, establishing that knowledge of his being is linked to what is written in his Word (1 Samuel 3:7, John 1:1-3).
[3, 4] The unfaithfulness of some Jews to God's oracles does not nullify the Lord's faithfulness or his covenant with the people of Israel (Romans 3:3). Faced with human objections, the guiding principle is that every person should be considered a liar before admitting that God has broken his word (Romans 3:4). When quoting King David's song of repentance, a free quotation is used, introducing the passive voice "so that you may prevail when you are judged," indicating that at the great white throne, lost sinners will attempt to judge and condemn divine justice to justify their own wickedness (Psalm 51:4, Revelation 20:11-15). In that final judgment, the Lord will present the record of His written oracles to justify His words and definitively silence the mouths of the wicked, who will be forced to confess that their condemnation is just (Philippians 2:10-11, Job 40:8).
[5-8] If human injustice serves to highlight divine justice by contrast, this does not mean that God acts unjustly in pouring out His wrath on the sinner (Romans 3:5). The Lord cannot compromise His holiness and, therefore, will judge the world severely at the Second Coming of Christ (Romans 3:6, 2 Thessalonians 1:7-9). The fallacy of those who claim that human lies amplify God's truth for His glory, or who promote the slander of doing evil so that good may come, is rejected (Romans 3:7-8). This erroneous assumption is typical of the natural man who seeks to excuse his wickedness by resorting to private interpretations of grace (Galatians 5:4). The final retribution and condemnation of those who teach and practice such conduct is entirely just before the Lord.
[9-18] No Jew possesses an intrinsic moral superiority over the Gentile, since the entire human race is subject under the yoke of sin (Romans 3:9). The verdict of God's oracles is universal and declares that "there is no one righteous, not even one" (Romans 3:10). The Holy Spirit links various portions of the Old Testament to demonstrate the total depravity that affects the members of the human body, describing the throat as an open grave, the tongue as deceitful, the lips as dripping with viper's venom, and the feet as swift to shed blood (Romans 3:13-15, Psalms 5:9, 140:3, Isaiah 59:7). This physical and intellectual ruin prevents the natural man from perceiving the things of the spirit, manifesting a complete lack of filial fear in the presence of God (Romans 3:18, Psalms 36:1). The condition of the ungodly is one of utter moral bankruptcy, so their paths are marked by destruction and misery.
[19, 20] The Law of Moses speaks directly to those under its rule with the specific purpose of silencing every boastful mouth and declaring the whole world guilty before God (Romans 3:19). Therefore, no one will be justified in God’s sight by the works of the law, since the instrument of the law was provided only to give accurate knowledge of sin (Romans 3:20). The law acts like a mirror that reveals the filth on the sinner’s face, but it is completely powerless to cleanse him (James 1:23-24). Justification, understood as a legal declaration of righteousness before the divine tribunal, is unattainable through human works in the present dispensation of grace (Galatians 2:16, Ephesians 2:8-9).
[21, 22] In this age the righteousness of God has been made known independently of the law, with the consistent testimony of the Law and the Prophets (Romans 3:21). This divine righteousness is granted through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe in him, without any distinction between Jew and Gentile (Romans 3:22). The Lord Jesus Christ is the very personification of God's righteousness, so that the believer receives the imputation of his perfect holiness entirely free of charge (1 Corinthians 1:30, 2 Corinthians 5:21). Before the standard of the Lord's holiness, social, cultural, or national differences are spiritually meaningless, for both Jew and Gentile require the same provision for salvation.
[23-26] For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified freely by his grace (Romans 3:23-24). God presented his Son as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to demonstrate his righteousness by the forgiveness of past sins, which had been tolerated in his forbearance (Romans 3:25). The forgiveness of past sins refers to the transgressions committed from Adam's fall in the Garden of Eden until the sacrifice at Calvary, which God temporarily forgave under the system of animal sacrifices without definitively erasing them, until the divine blood effected perfect atonement (Genesis 3:21, Exodus 34:7, Hebrews 9:15, 10:4). In this way, God demonstrates his righteousness in the present time, remaining just while justifying those who exercise faith in the work of Jesus Christ (Romans 3:26).
[27, 28] Man's boasting is entirely excluded, not by the law of works, but by the law of faith (Romans 3:27). It is firmly concluded that man is justified by faith without needing to resort to the works of the law (Romans 3:28). The salvation of the sinner is effected sovereignly and freely without the intervention of external rites such as water baptism or ecclesiastical sacraments, which add no value whatsoever to the redemption accomplished on the cross (Acts 15:11, Ephesians 2:8-9). The redeemed have no reason to boast in their own flesh or personal righteousness, but only in the Lord Jesus Christ (Galatians 6:14, 1 Corinthians 1:31).
[29-31] The Lord is not only the God of the Jews, but also of the Gentiles, since there is one God who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith (Romans 3:29-30). Far from nullifying God's moral law through faith, the gospel of grace establishes and confirms the holy purpose of the law by revealing that Jesus Christ perfectly fulfilled all its demands on behalf of the believer (Romans 3:31, Galatians 3:24). The Lord's moral law remains as a manifestation of His eternal righteousness and holiness, which will be fully vindicated when the kingdom of God is established on earth.

[1-3] The apostle Paul raises the question of what Abraham, the father of faith according to the flesh, found (Romans 4:1). If Abraham had been justified by works, he would have had something to boast about, but not before God (Romans 4:2). Scripture declares that Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6, Romans 4:3). Here, an exegetical contrast is presented with the Epistle of James, since James states that Abraham was justified by works by offering his son Isaac on the altar (James 2:21). However, this latter event occurred in Genesis 22, many years after Abraham received the imputed righteousness in Genesis 15 entirely freely and without works. The patriarch is a type or figure of salvation by grace, but his salvific process is not identical to that of the New Testament believer, since the believer is justified, sanctified, and regenerated immediately upon believing, looking to the cross and not to the stars (Genesis 15:5). Abraham's definitive justification was not completed until his obedience on the cross perfected his faith (James 2:22-23).
[4, 5] To the worker, wages are not credited as a gift of grace but as an obligation the employer is forced to pay (Romans 4:4). However, to the one who does not work to gain entry to heaven, but places his faith in the Lord who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness (Romans 4:5). The justification of the sinner is a free gift obtained only by ceasing to rely on self-righteousness and resting fully in the finished work of Jesus Christ on the cross (Ephesians 2:8-9). Any religious system that attempts to mix faith with human works for salvation is rejected, since by trying to add merits of the flesh, the sufficiency of divine grace is nullified (Galatians 5:4). The unregenerate person must renounce their own moral effort in order to receive the imputation of divine righteousness sovereignly.
[6-8] David describes the blessedness of the person to whom God imputes righteousness apart from works, declaring blessed those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered (Romans 4:6-7, Psalm 32:1-2). David is the supreme example of this mercy, for he committed adultery and murder, moral transgressions for which the Law of Moses prescribed no sacrifice, inexorably demanding capital punishment (Leviticus 20:10, Numbers 35:31). Despite this, the Lord set aside his sin and did not impute iniquity to him (2 Samuel 12:13). In the present dispensation, the redeemed believer enjoys this blessedness permanently, since God considers their sinful body as dead and buried with Christ in the tomb, and does not impute sin to their spiritual account, guaranteeing their eternal security.
[9-12] This blessedness of imputed righteousness is not limited to circumcision, but extends also to uncircumcision (Romans 4:9). The faith was revealed to Abraham while he was uncircumcised, still a Gentile in God's eyes (Genesis 15:6, Romans 4:10). The ordinance of physical circumcision was later given in Genesis 17 as an outward sign and seal of the righteousness of the faith he already possessed while uncircumcised (Romans 4:11). This demonstrates that the physical rite has no regenerative power, but rather serves as the seal of a pre-existing relationship. Furthermore, it is explained that water baptism does not replace circumcision, since baptism is a symbol of spiritual salvation and is administered to believers of both sexes after they receive the Holy Spirit, whereas circumcision was limited to male offspring and applied to the physical body (1 Peter 3:21, Acts 10:47-48). Thus, Abraham became the spiritual father of all uncircumcised believers and of those circumcised believers who walk in the footsteps of his original faith (Romans 4:11-12).
[13-15] The promise made to Abraham and his descendants that he would be heir of the world was not given through the moral law, but through the righteousness of faith (Romans 4:13). If those who belong to the law were the only heirs, faith would be worthless and the promise completely nullified, since the law of Moses only brings wrath and condemnation upon the transgressor (Romans 4:14-15, Deuteronomy 28:63). The Lord's moral law reveals the immense sinfulness of man without providing him with the spiritual strength to fulfill its demands, acting as a mirror of his moral ruin (Romans 3:20, Galatians 3:24). Since where there is no law there is no transgression, the provision of divine grace is the only way by which the sinner can evade just condemnation and receive the promised inheritance (Romans 4:15, Romans 5:13).
[16-22] Therefore, the inheritance of the promise is by faith, so that it may be by grace and be assured to all the offspring of Abraham, who is the father of all believers in the sight of God (Romans 4:16-17). God raises the dead and calls into being things that do not exist (Romans 4:17). Upon receiving the promise that his descendants would be countless, Abraham believed against all human hope (Romans 4:18, Genesis 15:5). His faith did not waver when he considered his own body, already dead, at almost a hundred years old, nor the barrenness of Sarah’s womb (Romans 4:19). Far from doubting the divine promise through unbelief, he grew stronger in faith, giving glory to God, fully convinced that the Lord was able to fulfill what he had promised (Romans 4:20-21). For this reason, his unshaken confidence was credited to him as righteousness (Romans 4:22). These steps describe the growth of progressive faith.
[23-25] This declaration of imputed righteousness was not written solely for Abraham, but also for the benefit of New Testament believers (Romans 4:23-24). God’s righteousness will likewise be imputed to us if we believe with our hearts in him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead (Romans 4:24). He was delivered over to death because of our moral transgressions and gloriously raised to life for our legal justification (Romans 4:25). Unlike Abraham's process, which required years for his works to perfect his faith before men, the justification of the saints in the present dispensation is immediate and complete at the moment of receiving the sacrifice of Calvary by faith (Romans 5:1, Colossians 2:11).

[1, 2] Justification by faith constitutes the legal foundation that grants the believer peace with God through Jesus Christ (Romans 5:1). This state of grace in which one perseveres steadfastly represents an absolute transition from condemnation to eternal life (John 3:36). Likewise, rejoicing in the hope of God's glory points to an unshakable future certainty, since the reconciliation effected by the Lord ensures that the destiny of the justified is eternally fixed (2 Corinthians 5:5). This spiritual rest contrasts with the anxiety of man under the law.
[3-5] The path to the believer's spiritual maturity unfolds through tribulations, which produce patience, experience, and a firm hope that does not disappoint, because the love of God is poured into the heart by the Holy Spirit (Romans 5:3-5). This process of moral refinement is consistent with the scale of growth set forth by the apostle Peter (2 Peter 1:5-7). By adding virtue, knowledge, and temperance to faith, the believer practically manifests the fruit of the Spirit in their daily conduct, demonstrating God's transforming work in the new creation (Galatians 5:22-23).
[6-8] The manifestation of divine love is distinguished from human justice in that Christ died for the ungodly when they still lacked spiritual strength (Romans 5:6). While on a human level, hardly anyone would offer to die for a righteous or good person (Romans 5:7), God demonstrates his love for humanity by giving his Son to death on Calvary when people were still sinners (Romans 5:8, 1 John 4:10). Man in his fallen condition is considered spiritually hopeless (Ezekiel 16:4-6), therefore redemption is not based on any merit, but on the pure benevolence of the Lord.
[9-11] Having been justified by the blood of Christ, believers enjoy the full assurance of being saved from the coming wrath through Him (Romans 5:9). The doctrine of salvation establishes that justification has a threefold dimension: it is by grace (Romans 3:24), by faith (Romans 5:1), and by the blood (Romans 5:9), which completely excludes water baptism or church rites as instruments of salvation (Titus 3:5). Though enemies, reconciliation with God was effected through the death of His Son, ensuring that the Savior's life will preserve the redeemed (Romans 5:10-11).
[12] Sin entered the earthly realm through one man, and death was introduced as a direct consequence of sin, thus extending to the entire human race because all sinned (Romans 5:12). Doctrinally, the number five is linked to death, as recorded in the genealogy of Adam, where the first natural death occurs precisely in the fifth verse of the fifth chapter of Scripture (Genesis 5:5). Under the principle of the federal head, corruptible blood transmits the sinful nature and death to all Adam's descendants immediately (1 Corinthians 15:22).
[13, 14] Although sin was already at work in the world before the promulgation of the law, it was not formally imputed where there was no written legislation (Romans 5:13). Nevertheless, death exercised its sovereign dominion from Adam to Moses, reaching even those who did not transgress under the same pattern of disobedience as Adam, who is a type of the one who was to come (Romans 5:14). Adam prefigures Christ by way of contrast (1 Corinthians 15:45), and the formation of Eve from his side typically illustrates the origin of the Church as the mystical body of the Savior (Ephesians 5:22-32). Even without the Mosaic Law, the testimony of conscience and the moral law written on the heart either accused or excused people (Romans 2:15).
[15-17] Adam's transgression is not comparable in magnitude to God's free gift, for if by the trespass of the one man many died, how much more did the grace and gift of the one man, Jesus Christ, abound sovereignly for many (Romans 5:15). In Adam, humanity inherited death without any choice, while in Christ, the sinner exercises his will to receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness (Romans 5:17). The notion that salvation is automatic or consists of mere passive assent is rejected, for it requires the personal reception of the Son of God (John 1:12).
[18, 19] Just as through the offense of one man the judgment of condemnation was pronounced upon the whole human race, so through the righteousness of one man justification of life is offered to all (Romans 5:18). The use of terms referring to the free gift highlights that salvation is an undeserved gift that cannot be bought or supplemented by the works of the flesh (Galatians 3:13). Through the disobedience of the first man, many were made sinners, but through the obedience of the last Adam, many will be declared legally righteous before the judgment seat of God, their debt having been canceled on the cross (2 Corinthians 5:21).
[20, 21] The law of Moses intervened so that transgression might abound and become evident, but as sin abounded, God's grace abounded infinitely (Romans 5:20). The law acts as a mirror that reveals the moral defilement of the sinner, leading him inexorably to the perfect provision of Calvary (Galatians 3:24). Thus, just as sin reigned, bringing physical and spiritual death, grace reigns sovereignly through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ (Romans 5:21, Revelation 22:14).

[1, 2] The apostle addresses the carnal objection of man who intends to continue in sin under the premise that this magnifies divine grace (Romans 6:1). This assumption is categorically rejected by declaring that the believer has died to sin (Romans 6:2). Doctrinally, death to sin represents a legal and unalterable position in Jesus Christ, since the justified no longer belongs to the sphere of Adamic condemnation (Colossians 3:3). Although sin remains present in the believer's physical members, its relationship to legal guilt has definitively ended (1 John 4:17).
[3, 4] The reality of the believer's spiritual identification is explained, clarifying that it is not a regeneration through water baptism, which only wets the physical body (1 Peter 3:21). True baptism is an operation of the Holy Spirit that directly incorporates the sinner into the mystical body of Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 12:13). Through this heavenly union, the old self of the Adamic nature is buried with Christ in His death, so that the new creation may rise from the dead to walk in newness of life (2 Corinthians 5:17). This threefold legal position of death, burial, and resurrection ensures the redemption of the soul.
[5-10] Practical victory over sin is based on the certainty of having been united with Christ in the likeness of His death, ensuring that we will also be united with Him in the likeness of His resurrection (Romans 6:5). The old self was crucified with Him so that the body of sin might be destroyed, freeing the believer from moral bondage (Romans 6:6). The justified person must know that their new life resides in the resurrection of Christ, who, having risen from the dead, will never die again, for death no longer has dominion over Him (Romans 6:9). Unlike human religious rites such as the Mass, where the Savior is repeatedly sacrificed, Christ's sacrifice was made once and for all (Hebrews 10:10-12), establishing the believer's glorious hope (Titus 2:13).
[11-13] The process of moral victory is established through the instruction to consider oneself dead to sin but alive to God in Jesus Christ our Lord (Romans 6:11). The verb "consider" denotes a mental exercise of faith where the believer takes as fact the truth of their heavenly position, treating the old nature as a buried corpse. The presence of both natures in the justified person generates a constant conflict, since the soul has been separated from the physical body through spiritual circumcision performed without hands (Colossians 2:11-12). We are exhorted not to allow sin to reign in the mortal body and not to present our physical members as instruments of iniquity, but rather to present them to God as those who have been brought from death to life (Romans 6:12-13).
[14-16] Sin will not have dominion over the believer, because the believer is not under the regime of the moral law of Moses, but under the dispensation of grace (Romans 6:14). The freedom that grace provides is not a license to sin, but the spiritual power to obey the Lord out of love and not out of fear of judgment (John 14:15). The transgressions committed by believers in their physical weakness do not nullify their legal justification, since the old, sinful, carnal nature has already been judged on the cross, while the new self in the Spirit remains free from guilt (Romans 7:17-20). By submitting to obedience for righteousness, believers practically demonstrate which Lord they have chosen to serve in their daily walk (Romans 6:16).
[17-20] The apostle gives thanks to God because, having been slaves to sin in the past, believers wholeheartedly obeyed the form of doctrine that was delivered to them (Romans 6:17). This form of doctrine constitutes the glorious message of the Gospel, which offers free salvation to all who believe, freeing them from the power of darkness (Acts 26:18). Having been freed from sin, believers were made servants of righteousness, and therefore must use their bodies with the same intensity with which they previously served impurity (Romans 6:18-19). The former moral condition of the Gentiles kept them completely alienated from divine righteousness, in a state of ruin that inexorably led them to eternal condemnation (Ephesians 2:12).
[21-23] The fruit of the two paths is contrasted, pointing out that the works of the flesh produce shame and death, while service to God produces sanctification and eternal life (Romans 6:21-22). The dogmatic conclusion of this section is summarized in the solemn warning that "the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Jesus Christ our Lord" (Romans 6:23). Wages represent the just recompense that the sinner deserves for his works, while eternal life is an undeserved gift that cannot be bought or maintained by human effort (Ephesians 2:8-9). If a believer persists in sowing to his flesh, it may provoke the Lord to decree his premature physical death as a disciplinary judgment (1 Corinthians 11:30, 1 John 5:16), but his soul remains eternally secure in Christ (Revelation 20:11-15).

[1-3] The apostle introduces a legal analogy addressed to those who know the moral law, establishing that it exercises dominion over the individual only while that person lives (Romans 7:1). To illustrate this truth, he uses the figure of marriage, where the married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if the husband dies, she is freed from this legal obligation (Romans 7:2). This instruction does not contemplate civil divorce as an option, but only the dissolution of the bond through physical death (Deuteronomy 24:1, 1 Corinthians 7:39). If the woman unites with another man while her husband is still alive, she is declared an adulteress; however, the death of her spouse completely emancipates her from the marriage law, allowing her to remarry without incurring any moral transgression (Romans 7:3). This typology illustrates the state of the human soul before experiencing spiritual regeneration.
[4-6] Likewise, believers have died to the moral law through the sacrifice of Christ's body on Calvary, in order to be spiritually united with Him who rose from the dead to bear fruit for God (Romans 7:4). Before conversion, the soul was united to the Adamic flesh, but under the dispensation of grace, the Holy Spirit performs a spiritual circumcision that separates the soul from the physical body (Colossians 2:11-13). When the individual was in the flesh, the sinful passions stimulated by the law operated in the bodily members to produce the fruits of death (Romans 7:5). However, the believer has been freed from the law by dying to that which held him captive, enabling him to serve in the newness of the Spirit and not under the old rigidity of the letter (Romans 7:6).
[7-9] The moral law is not sin in itself, but the holy instrument that exposes the true nature of human transgression (Romans 7:7). The apostle declares that he would not have known covetousness if the moral law had not explicitly prohibited it (Exodus 20:17, Romans 3:20). Moral sin, taking advantage of the written commandment, stirred up all kinds of lust in natural man, demonstrating that without legislation, transgression remained dormant (Romans 7:8). In the stage of childhood innocence, the individual lived without the imputation of the moral law; But when the commandment was presented with its standard of holiness, sin took root in the conscience, and humanity experienced spiritual death (Romans 7:9). This awakening of guilt demonstrates that regeneration is essential to stand spotless before the Lord.
[10-13] The moral commandment, originally intended to lead to life, resulted in a death sentence for the sinner (Romans 7:10). Sin exploited the holiness of the commandment to deceive the natural man and decree his moral ruin (Romans 7:11). Therefore, the moral law is intrinsically holy, and the particular commandment is righteous, holy, and good in its divine purpose (Romans 7:12). God did not ordain the commandment to destroy humanity, but to demonstrate the extreme gravity of sin, using what is good to manifest death in the transgressor and show that rebellion is exceedingly sinful (Romans 7:13). The law functions as a spiritual mirror that diagnoses the disease but lacks the power to heal it.
[14-17] Although the moral law is eminently spiritual, the natural person is in a carnal state and sold under the dominion of sin (Romans 7:14). The believer experiences a daily conflict where their practical actions contradict their deepest spiritual desires (Romans 7:15). This constant struggle demonstrates that the justified person consents to the goodness of the Lord's moral law, recognizing its divine perfection (Romans 7:16). Doctrinally, when a believer acts contrary to justice, the fault is not attributed to their new spiritual self, but to the sin that still dwells in their physical members (Romans 7:17).
[18-20] In the Adamic flesh of humankind, no moral virtue or good resides (Romans 7:18, Philippians 3:8). Although the will to please God is present in the believer's new spirit, the physical capacity to do good is unattainable through human strength alone (Romans 7:18). The spiritual good that the redeemed person desires to do is often postponed, while the moral evil they detest is what ends up manifesting itself in their daily walk (Romans 7:19, Galatians 5:19). If a believer does what his mind hates, the legal guilt does not fall on the newly regenerated man, but on the old sinful nature that still resides in his mortal body (Romans 7:20).
[21-23] Thus, a constant law in the earthly walk is revealed: when the believer intends to do good, the inclination to evil is present in his members (Romans 7:21). The inner man, who has been renewed by divine grace, truly delights in God's moral law (Romans 7:22, 1 Corinthians 2:15). However, in the physical members, another opposing law operates, actively combating the law of the mind and leading the believer captive to the law of sin that resides in his flesh (Romans 7:23, Romans 8:2).
[24, 25] Faced with the anguish of this internal conflict, the apostle would burst forth in a cry for deliverance from this body of death that oppresses him (Romans 7:24, Philippians 1:23). The Lord Jesus effected a legal separation on the cross to free the believer, so that, although with his mind he serves God's law with his heart, with his flesh he inevitably serves the law of sin (Romans 7:25). This paradox of the Christian life finds its ultimate consolation in the fact that the blood of Christ has canceled the sinner's moral debt.

[1-4] It is emphatically established that no eternal condemnation rests on those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). The final portion of the verse is omitted in many modern revisions, but the sacred text accurately preserves it, since the believer who walks according to the flesh does experience a condemnation of a temporary and corrective nature, which can even lead to premature physical death (1 Corinthians 11:30). The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus definitively emancipates the justified from the law of sin and death, operating instantaneously through the new birth, the baptism of the Holy Spirit, and the spiritual circumcision that separates the soul from the body of sin (Colossians 2:11). What was impossible for the law of Moses, due to the inherent weakness of Adamic flesh, God accomplished by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh (Romans 8:3). In this way, the Lord condemned sin in the flesh so that the justice of the moral law might be fulfilled in us, who walk under the guidance of the Spirit and not according to the dictates of the flesh.
[5-8] The apostle makes a clear distinction between the natural birth and the new birth, indicating that those who live according to the flesh are concerned exclusively with carnal things, while the regenerate attend to the things of the Spirit (Romans 8:5). Being concerned with the flesh produces death and destroys the peace of daily life, while being concerned with the Spirit is life and peace (Romans 8:6). The carnal mind of the natural man is a declared enemy of God, since it does not submit to the divine law nor does it have the moral capacity to do so (Romans 8:7). Therefore, those who remain in their natural, ungodly state in the flesh cannot please God under any circumstances, since they lack the faith necessary to please Him (Hebrews 11:6).
[9-11] The saints are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, under the inescapable condition that the Spirit of God dwells in their bodies (Romans 8:9). Scripture states unequivocally that if anyone lacks the Spirit of Christ, they do not belong to the Lord. This reception of the Holy Spirit is universal for all the redeemed and takes place at the moment of conversion, completely refuting erroneous theories that consider it a second work of grace evidenced by speaking in tongues or mystical gibberish (1 Corinthians 12:13). Although the physical body remains dead and subject to temporary corruption because of sin, the spirit enjoys divine life due to the imputed righteousness of Christ (Romans 8:10). If the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in the believer, the Lord will also give life to their mortal bodies at the glorious event of the bodily rapture, employing the same power that raised the Savior.
[12, 13] The congregation of the saints incurs no debt to the flesh to live according to the disordered desires of the old nature (Romans 8:12). If a believer persists in sowing to his flesh and living according to it, he will suffer the loss of his already blessed fellowship and experience physical death as the Lord's disciplinary measure (Galatians 6:8). However, if through the work of the Spirit the justified person puts to death the works and desires of the flesh, he will enjoy a fruitful and abundant spiritual life (Romans 8:13). The old Adamic nature tends to constantly rise from its legal grave, which is why a daily exercise of faith is required to consider oneself dead to sin and alive to God (Romans 6:11).
[14, 15] All those who are automatically and sovereignly led by the Spirit of God are made true children of God (Romans 8:14). This guidance of the Spirit does not refer to a mystical or hesitant direction, but to the Lord's irrevocable decree to preserve the justified and bring them safely to heavenly glory. The believer has not received a spirit of bondage to be immersed in the fear of judgment or hell, but has received the Spirit of adoption (Romans 8:15). Through this legal adoption, the redeemed enjoy the glorious privilege of crying out in an intimate and filial way, “Abba, Father,” using a tender Hebrew term that denotes a closeness that no angel, nor even Adam in his innocence, could experience.
[16, 17] The Spirit Himself testifies directly to our human spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:16). The use of the neuter pronoun in sacred grammar is extremely precise, as it alludes to the work of the Holy Spirit in contrast to the physical realities of the flesh (John 3:6). As children, believers are declared legitimate heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). This heavenly inheritance of dwelling in the New Jerusalem is entirely free and secure for every redeemed person (Revelation 21:1-4). However, the portion concerning reigning with Christ in the Millennium and receiving crowns of glory is conditional upon willingly suffering with Him in this age of wickedness (2 Timothy 2:12).
[18-22] The sufferings and afflictions of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed in the saints (Romans 8:18). Because of the original human rebellion in Eden, the earth and animal nature suffered the divine curse and were subjected to futility (Genesis 3:17-18). Creation groans and experiences collective birth pangs to this day, waiting to be freed from the bondage of corruption and brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God (Romans 8:21-22). This regeneration of material creation and the restoration of the peaceful order of the animal kingdom will be fully consolidated after the Second Coming of Christ (Isaiah 11:6-9).
[23-25] Not only does physical creation suffer the scourge of the Fall, but believers, possessing the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as they await bodily adoption, which consists in the redemption of our bodies (Romans 8:23). The soul of the justified has been redeemed instantaneously at Calvary, but the corruptible body of flesh must await its glorious and incorruptible transformation on the day of the Rapture at the Second Coming of Christ (1 Corinthians 15:51-53). Salvation is awaited in hope, knowing that true biblical hope is not a secular doubt, but the sure and patient expectation of the final redemption from the cross (Titus 2:13).
[26, 27] The Holy Spirit admirably helps us in our weaknesses in our daily struggles (Romans 8:26). In the midst of afflictions, the human mind often doesn't know how to pray properly, but the Spirit himself intercedes for the saints with inexpressible groanings that defy all human expression. This rules out any charismatic claim to associate these groanings with intelligible tongues or emotional displays, since Scripture teaches that such groanings cannot be expressed in words. He who searches hearts with absolute knowledge fully understands the mind of the Spirit, who intercedes for the elect according to the perfect will of God (Romans 8:27).
[28-30] One of the most sublime promises of the sacred text is proclaimed: all things work together unconditionally for the good of those who love God, who are called according to his holy purpose (Romans 8:28). Those whom God foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that Christ might be the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29). The doctrine of predestination applies exclusively to the eternal destiny of the redeemed after their conversion, which exegetically refutes the Calvinist decrees of unconditional reprobation or condemnation to hell. Those whom he predestined, he also called; those whom he called, he also justified; And those whom he declared righteous, he also glorified in his sovereign presence (Romans 8:30).
[31-34] In light of these eternal truths, the believer can confidently exclaim that if God is for us, no one can successfully prevail against us (Romans 8:31). The Lord, who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, will also freely give us all things with him (Romans 8:32). No one can bring any accusation against God's elect, since God is the supreme Judge who effects sovereign justification (Romans 8:33). There is therefore now no condemnation for the righteous, because Christ died, rose again in power, and remains at the right hand of God, continually interceding for our souls before the heavenly throne (Romans 8:34).
[35-39] Nothing has the moral power to separate us from the love of Christ, whether tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, or the sword of the executioner (Romans 8:35). In the midst of all these extreme trials, the saints are made more than conquerors through him who loved us infinitely (Romans 8:37). It is declared with absolute certainty that neither death, nor life, nor fallen angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor the present, nor height, nor depth, nor anything else in all creation will ever be able to separate us from the love of God, which is permanently in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 8:38-39).

[1-3] The apostle Paul expresses deep sadness and continuous pain in his heart for the spiritual condition of his brothers, his kinsmen according to the flesh (Romans 9:1-2). Such is his concern for the salvation of the Jewish nation that he would wish to be accursed himself, separated from Christ, for the love he has for them (Romans 9:3). This declaration of filial love underscores the great distinction between Israel's temporary unbelief and its permanent standing before God. Although many stumble in their spiritual blindness, the Lord has not definitively rejected his people (Romans 11:1-2, 11:25-26).
[4, 5] The eight great privileges that God granted to the Israelites are described: adoption as sons, the visible glory of the divine presence, the covenants, the promulgation of the law, the service of worship, the messianic promises, the patriarchs, and, above all, the birth of Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all (Romans 9:4-5). These national privileges should have led the people to receive their Messiah, but by rejecting him historically in order to accept Roman rule, they turned his blessings into a cause for judgment (John 19:15).
[6-8] The word of God has not failed despite the national apostasy, since not all the physical descendants of Israel belong to the true spiritual Israel, nor are all descendants of Abraham children of the promise (Romans 9:6-7). It is clarified that the true seed is counted in Isaac, representing the children of the promise and not those of the flesh (Romans 9:8). The apostle later applies this same truth in the letter to the Galatians to point out how believing Gentiles are made children of Abraham through faith, receiving the spiritual inheritance (Galatians 3:14, 3:29).
[9] God's sovereign plan is revealed in the promise made to Abraham regarding the birth of Isaac, establishing that the birth of the chosen seed would depend entirely on divine power and not on human efforts (Romans 9:9). Sarah conceived miraculously when her body was considered dead, typifying the spiritual regeneration that occurs freely in the believer (Romans 4:19).
[10-13] Before the twins Jacob and Esau were born or had done any good or bad work, it was prophesied that the older would serve the younger, so that the purpose of God’s election would stand firm, not by works but by him who calls (Romans 9:11-12). This prophecy, given in Rebecca’s womb in historical time (Genesis 25:23), is based on divine foreknowledge and not on an unconditional decree prior to creation (1 Peter 1:2). The subsequent judgment of hating Esau and loving Jacob (Romans 9:13, Malachi 1:2-3) describes the national destiny of Edom and Israel as federal heads, demonstrating that God chose the most spiritual lineage to bring forth the Redeemer without this implying the unconditional condemnation of individuals to hell.
[14-16] There is no injustice in God exercising His sovereignty, for He declared to Moses that He would have mercy and compassion on whomever He chose (Romans 9:15, Exodus 33:19). Divine mercy does not depend on the desire of the one who wills or the effort of the one who runs, but on God who has mercy (Romans 9:16). This means that the Lord sovereignly determines the conditions under which He grants forgiveness, having established that the only place to find mercy is at the cross of Christ, which rules out the possibility of man purchasing salvation or righteousness through works (Ephesians 2:8-9).
[17, 18] Scripture presents the example of Pharaoh, whom God raised to the Egyptian throne for the purpose of manifesting His power and declaring His holy name throughout the earth (Romans 9:17). Pharaoh's hardening of heart was not the result of a capricious decree preventing him from being saved, but rather the consequence of his own willful hardening of his heart in the face of the plagues (Exodus 3:19, 8:15). Thus, God has mercy on whom He wills and hardens whom He wills, applying His judgment according to man's moral response to the truth.
[19-21] In response to the carnal objection of how God can find fault if no one resists His will, the natural man is rebuked for arguing with the Lord (Romans 9:19-20). Like the potter who has power over the clay to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor, God forms His vessels in historical time (Romans 9:21). Clay represents fallen and visible humanity, which, if it repents of its wickedness according to the moral standard of Scripture, has its destiny of judgment altered and becomes a useful vessel for the Lord's service (Jeremiah 18:8, 2 Timothy 2:21).
[22-24] God demonstrates his justice by patiently enduring the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy prepared beforehand for glory (Romans 9:22-23). ​​This patience temporarily limits God's wrath against the ungodly nations before executing his final judgments and manifesting his sovereign power. These vessels of mercy are the believers called by grace, from both the Jewish people and the Gentile nations in the present dispensation (Romans 9:24).
[25, 26] The apostle quotes the prophecies of Hosea to illustrate that those who were not considered God's people are now called children of the living God (Romans 9:25-26, Hosea 2:23, 1:10). Although these prophecies literally point to the physical and national restoration of the ten tribes of Israel after the Second Coming of Christ (Hosea 1:11), the Holy Spirit applies them here by way of accommodation to the salvation of the Gentiles during the time when Israel remains blind (Romans 11:25).
[27-29] Isaiah cries out concerning the nation of Israel that, even if the number of its children were like the sand of the sea, only a remnant would return and be saved through a shortened work of righteousness on earth (Romans 9:27-28, Isaiah 10:22-23). ​​If the Lord of Hosts had not preserved a seed for the Jewish people, the nation would have perished permanently under God's judgment, like Sodom and Gomorrah (Romans 9:29, Isaiah 1:9). This national preservation guarantees the physical survival of the Jewish remnant who will be converted in a single day upon seeing the Messiah descend from heaven at the end of the Tribulation (Zechariah 12:10).
[30-32] It is concluded that the Gentiles attained justification through faith in the finished work of the cross, while Israel, by striving to follow the law of righteousness, did not attain it because they sought it by the works of the law and not by faith (Romans 9:30-32). By ignoring the imputed righteousness that God freely offers, they stumbled over the stumbling stone represented by the message of the cross, which is scandalous to the pride of the carnal man (Romans 10:3, 1 Corinthians 1:23).
[33] Jesus Christ is the stumbling stone and the rock of offense placed in Zion, so that whoever believes in Him will not be put to shame (Romans 9:33, Isaiah 8:14, 28:16). For the unbeliever, this rock represents the sovereign judgment that will completely crush him (Matthew 21:44). On the other hand, for the redeemed believer, the Lord's faithfulness constitutes his eternal security and glory.

[1-4] The apostle's longing and intercession before God for the people of Israel are directed toward their salvation, recognizing that they possess a fervent zeal for divine things, though lacking knowledge in accordance with scriptural truth (Romans 10:1-2). Ignoring the righteousness that comes from God, the Israelites have sought to establish their own righteousness through human efforts, refusing to submit to divine provision (Romans 10:3). God's righteousness is personified in Jesus Christ, who is the end and fulfillment of the law to grant justification to all who believe, thus invalidating any attempt at self-justification by the works of the flesh (Galatians 2:16, 2 Corinthians 5:21). In this sense, the Mosaic law ceased to serve its purpose of demanding an unattainable standard for natural man once the Savior perfectly fulfilled all its moral requirements (Romans 8:3-4).
[5-8] In contrasting legal righteousness with righteousness based on faith, the prescription given by Moses is cited: that the person who keeps the commandments will live by them (Deuteronomy 30:16, Romans 10:5). However, righteousness based on faith rejects any human claim to make extraordinary efforts, such as ascending to heaven to bring Christ down, or descending into the abyss to raise Him from the dead (Romans 10:6-7). The abyss, or place of the dead, represents the state of Sheol from which Christ has already been raised in power (Acts 2:27). The word of faith is not found in an unattainable realm, but is exceedingly close to the sinner, providentially placed in his mouth and heart (Romans 10:8, Deuteronomy 30:14).
[9-13] The solemn declaration of the Gospel stipulates that if a person confesses with his mouth that Jesus is Lord and believes in his heart that God raised him from the dead, he will obtain salvation for his soul (Romans 10:9). Genuine faith is exercised in the heart, resulting in the imputation of divine righteousness, while the public confession that testifies to this salvation is made with the mouth (Romans 10:10). Faith of the heart transcends mere intellectual assent, implying absolute rest in the atoning sacrifice of the cross (Ephesians 2:8-9). By invoking the name of the Lord, it is guaranteed that no believer will be put to shame, for before the Lord there is no difference between Jew and Greek (Romans 10:11-12). This universal promise assures that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Romans 10:13, Joel 2:32).
[14, 15] The development of faith presupposes a sovereign order where people cannot call on the one they have not believed in, nor believe in the one they have not heard, nor hear without a witness to preach to them (Romans 10:14). Likewise, the proclamation of the message requires that messengers be sent by God, as the Scriptures testify when they declare how beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news and proclaim peace (Romans 10:15, Isaiah 52:7). Although these Old Testament prophecies originally address the establishment of the literal kingdom in Jerusalem when the Lord reigns visibly, the apostle applies them spiritually to the spread of the Gospel of grace in this time of visitation to the Gentiles (Nahum 1:15, Acts 13:42-44). Every member of the body of Christ is constituted a herald of this divine peace.
[16, 17] The disobedience to the Gospel by the majority of the nation of Israel was anticipated by the prophet Isaiah when he cried out about who had believed the divine message (Romans 10:16, Isaiah 53:1). From this comes the immutable principle that faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God (Romans 10:17). This spiritual hearing requires an inner and receptive disposition to receive the divine words as absolute truth and not as mere human reasoning (John 8:47). When God's words are received with meekness, they work effectively in the believer, purifying their heart through faith without the need for ritual works (Acts 15:9).
[18-21] In response to the question of whether the nation of Israel has stopped hearing God's revelation, it is argued that His voice has gone out throughout the earth through the testimony of the material creation, which constantly proclaims the glory and eternal power of the Lord (Romans 10:18, Psalms 19:1-4). Israel cannot plead ignorance, for Moses prophesied that God would provoke His chosen people to jealousy through a foolish nation that lacked covenants, referring to the salvation granted to the Gentiles (Romans 10:19, Deuteronomy 32:21). Similarly, Isaiah speaks with great boldness when he declares that God was found by those who were not seeking him, while regarding Israel he affirms that he has stretched out his hands all day long to a rebellious and contradictory people (Romans 10:20-21, Isaiah 65:1-2). This unbelief of the Jewish nation does not nullify the promises made to the patriarchs, which will be fulfilled literally when their rebellion is removed from Jacob (Romans 11:25-27, Revelation 12:17).

[1-6] The initial question of whether God has rejected his earthly people receives a resounding no, demonstrated first by the apostle Paul's own testimony as a physical Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, and belonging to the tribe of Benjamin (Philippians 3:5). The Lord has not rejected the nation he foreknew (1 Peter 1:2). The sacred record refers to the historical intercession of Elijah on Mount Horeb (1 Kings 19:10-18), where the prophet believed he was the only faithful servant left in the face of judgment and apostasy. The divine response revealed the providential reserve of seven thousand men who did not bow their knees to the image of Baal. Similarly, in the present dispensation of the church, there is a Jewish remnant that is preserved according to the election of grace through faith in Jesus Christ (Galatians 3:22). This election operates exclusively by free grace and not by the works of the Mosaic Law, for if it were by works, grace would cease to be grace, establishing the absolute theological and doctrinal incompatibility between the two systems in the justification of the believer (Romans 4:4-5, Ephesians 2:8-9).
[7-10] The corporate mass of Israel did not attain the legal righteousness it sought through its own religious efforts, while the chosen remnant obtained it by receiving God's imputed righteousness (Romans 10:2-4). The remaining majority was hardened and judicially blinded as a result of their prior and deliberate rejection of the Messiah (John 12:37-40, Acts 28:25-27). Old Testament prophecies are cited to support this sovereign judgment, indicating that the Lord gave them a spirit of lethargy, eyes that could not see, and ears that could not hear, even to this day (Isaiah 29:10, Deuteronomy 29:4). Likewise, the Davidic curse is invoked (Psalm 69:22-23), where the table of ordinances, feasts, and ceremonial sacrifices became a snare, a trap, a stumbling block, and just retribution (1 Corinthians 1:23). Their spiritual eyes were darkened so that they could not behold the Redeemer in the Scriptures, their backs bent under the weight of a spiritual bondage that will persist until the end of the present age (2 Corinthians 3:14-16).
[11-15] The stumbling of the Jewish nation was not intended as a final or irrevocable fall from divine favor, but rather, through their corporate transgression, salvation was sent and formally granted to the Gentile nations for the providential purpose of provoking the Hebrew seed to jealousy (Deuteronomy 32:21, Romans 10:19). If Israel's transgression constituted an immense source of spiritual riches for the Gentile world, the millennial restoration and fullness of the nation will result in an incomparably greater earthly blessing (Isaiah 60:1-5). Paul exercises and magnifies his office as apostle to the Gentiles to encourage his own people, seeking to redeem some of them through the witness of grace (Acts 9:15, 1 Corinthians 9:22). If the temporary exclusion of Israel brought about the reconciliation of the world and the opening of the gospel to all nations, the readmission and restoration of Jacob to his land will literally amount to life from the dead, foreshadowing the national resurrection prophesied for the coming kingdom (Ezekiel 37:1-14).
[16-24] The sanctity of the firstfruits of the harvest guarantees the consecration of the entire batch, just as a holy root sustains the branches (Leviticus 23:10, Numbers 15:19-21). The root of the covenant rests on the patriarchal promises given to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Genesis 12:1-3, Genesis 17:7). The olive tree symbolizes the privilege of spiritual witness and the divine promises entrusted to Israel (Jeremiah 11:16, Hosea 14:6). As the natural branches broke off due to unbelief, the Gentile believer, being a wild olive tree by nature, was grafted in among them to partake of the root and the rich sap of the olive tree (Ephesians 2:11-13). Gentile Christianity is sternly warned not to boast about the broken branches, remembering that it is the root that sustains the branch, not the branch the root. The natural branches fell because of their lack of faith, while the Gentile stands only by faith (Hebrews 3:12). If God did not forgive the original branches for their apostasy, neither will He forgive the Gentile powers if they stray from His goodness, decreeing that apostate Christendom will be cut off before the Lord's return (2 Thessalonians 2:3, Revelation 3:16). In contrast, the Lord has the power to graft natural branches back onto His own olive tree when they abandon their state of rebellion (Zechariah 12:10).
[25-27] The doctrinal mystery concerning the prophetic destiny of Israel is declared to prevent Gentiles from falling into theological pride or mistakenly assuming that the church has permanently replaced the Hebrew nation (Proverbs 3:7). Spiritual hardening and blindness have befallen Israel only partially and temporarily, extending only until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered the body of Christ (Luke 21:24). Once the rapture of the church is complete, the promise that all surviving Israel will be saved at the conclusion of the great tribulation will be fulfilled (Isaiah 45:17, Jeremiah 31:31-34). This national redemption will occur according to the prophecy that the Deliverer will come out of Zion and remove all iniquity from Jacob during the Second Coming (Isaiah 59:20-21, Psalm 14:7). The Lord's unchanging covenant with His earthly people will be consummated when their national sins are finally blotted out and forgiven at the establishment of the millennial kingdom (Jeremiah 50:20, Hebrews 8:10-12).
[28-32] Regarding the proclamation of the gospel in the present dispensation, the Jews remain in a position of temporary enmity for the benefit of the Gentiles; Nevertheless, with regard to sovereign election, they continue to be greatly loved because of the promises sworn to the patriarchal fathers (Deuteronomy 7:7-8, Deuteronomy 10:15). God's gifts and calling concerning Israel's national destiny are irrevocable and beyond divine repentance (Numbers 23:19, Malachi 3:6). Just as the Gentiles lived in disobedience and idolatry in times past and have now attained divine mercy through Jewish unbelief, so too will they experience God's mercy as they witness the forgiveness bestowed upon the Gentiles. The Lord imprisoned all corporate humanity in disobedience and unbelief so that He could extend His sovereign mercy to all who come in faith to the atoning sacrifice of His Son (Galatians 3:22, Romans 3:9-19).
[33-36] The revelation of the redemptive plan culminates in solemn praise before the unfathomable depth of the riches, wisdom, and knowledge of God (Psalm 92:5, Ephesians 3:8-10). His judgments are beyond comprehension, and His ways are inscrutable to the understanding of the flesh (Job 11:7-9, Isaiah 40:13-14). No earthly creature has ever known the mind of the Lord or acted as His spiritual counselor (1 Corinthians 2:16, Jeremiah 23:18). Likewise, no one has given to God first so as to demand a reward or consider themselves entitled to His justice (Job 41:11). All created things proceed from Him as their original source, subsist by His providential power, and are directed toward Him as their ultimate end (Colossians 1:16-17, Hebrews 2:10). To God be the glory forever and ever, in the present time and throughout all eternity.

[1, 2] The apostle Paul pleads with the brothers and sisters, by the mercy of God, to present their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, which constitutes their spiritual service (Romans 12:1). The transitional term directly links this practical exhortation with the concluding doxology of the previous chapter (Romans 11:36). Unlike the self-justifying asceticism of monks and gurus who punish the flesh to gain heaven, the consecrated believer offers their physical members—head, hands, feet, tongue, and eyes—in active condition for the service of the Lord (Romans 6:13). This spiritual sacrifice is pleasing to God because the offerer is already legally justified in Jesus Christ and sanctified by the Holy Spirit (1 Peter 1:2, 2:5). The mind of the natural person cannot comprehend this spiritual offering, for it lacks the regenerating work of the new birth (1 Corinthians 2:14). The transformation of the believer is effected through the renewal of the mind, which is equipped by the Holy Spirit with the mind of Christ to discern God's perfect will (Philippians 2:5, 1 Corinthians 2:16).
[3-5] Each member of the congregation is admonished not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think of himself with sober judgment, according to the measure of faith that God has assigned to each one (Romans 12:3). Sobriety of thought is the antidote to the spiritual pride and boasting that often threaten fellowship in the local church (2 Corinthians 10:12). The analogy of the human body illustrates that, just as a body has many members with diverse functions, so believers, though many, form one body in Christ and are members of one another (Romans 12:4-5, 1 Corinthians 12:12). This truth about the mystical body excludes any preeminence or carnal division, for each part has been sovereignly placed to function in mutual interdependence (1 Corinthians 12:25). The organic unity of the body highlights the Lord's sovereignty.
[6-8] Spiritual gifts differ according to the grace given to us, and they must be exercised with absolute fidelity to the scriptural standard (Romans 12:6). The Holy Spirit distributes these abilities individually for the purpose of building up and establishing the congregation, not for the personal exaltation of the bearer (1 Corinthians 12:7-11). While the gifts of signs granted to the Jewish apostles gradually ceased with the end of the apostolic age (2 Corinthians 12:12, 1 Timothy 5:23), the gifts of teaching, service, and exhortation remain active for the stability of the saints (Romans 1:11). Those who preside must do so diligently, and those who exercise mercy, with joy, reflecting the fruit of the Spirit in their character and not a display of carnal power (Galatians 5:22-23).
[9-13] Christian love must be sincere, abhorring what is evil and clinging to what is good with brotherly affection (Romans 12:9-10). The saints should prefer one another in honor, showing an attitude of humility that imitates the Savior's example (Philippians 2:3). In serving the Lord, fervent diligence in the spirit is required, joy in hope, patiently enduring tribulation, and persevering in constant prayer (Romans 12:11-12, 1 Thessalonians 5:17). Practical compassion is shown by distributing to the saints' needs and practicing heartfelt hospitality (Romans 12:13, Philemon 7). Sharing material possessions to help a brother or sister in need is outward evidence that God's love dwells in the believer (1 John 3:17, 1 Timothy 6:18).
[14-16] The believer's conduct in the face of the world's hostility should be characterized by blessing persecutors and not cursing them (Romans 12:14, 1 Peter 2:23). Likewise, it requires empathetic identification with the circumstances of others, rejoicing with those who rejoice and weeping with those who weep (Romans 12:15, 1 Corinthians 12:26). Spiritual unity is maintained by not harboring pride of mind, but by being considerate of the humble and avoiding being wise in one's own eyes (Romans 12:16, Philippians 2:2). The shepherd and the flock must walk in the same spirit of meekness, recognizing that intellectual pride is a direct affront to the Lord's holiness (Acts 20:19, Colossians 3:12). This mutual submission and renunciation of carnal arrogance is indispensable for presenting oneself approved before the Lord in His glorious manifestation.
[17-21] One should not repay anyone evil for evil, striving to do what is right in the eyes of all (Romans 12:17, 2 Corinthians 8:21). As far as possible, and depending on the believer, one should maintain peace with all people (Romans 12:18, Hebrews 12:14). Personal vengeance is strictly excluded from the Christian life, since the Lord has decreed that the retribution of justice belongs exclusively to Him (Deuteronomy 32:35). Therefore, if the enemy is hungry, he should be given food, and if he is thirsty, drink, thus heaping burning coals on his head by exposing his injustice (Romans 12:20, Psalms 140:9-10). Moral victory consists in not being overcome by evil, but overcoming evil with good (Romans 12:21, 1 Peter 3:9).

[1, 2] Every soul must submit to the higher powers, since there is no authority except that which comes from God, and those that exist are ordained by the Lord (Romans 13:1). God grants power and governance to rulers whom He does not necessarily approve of in a moral sense, such as Pharaoh, Nero, Hitler, or Stalin, who operate under divine permission to fulfill sovereign purposes in the history of nations (Genesis 10:8-10, Exodus 10:1-2, John 19:11). Whoever opposes civil authority resists the design established by God, bringing judgment upon themselves in the earthly realm (Romans 13:2). This establishes the principle that human governments are instituted to restrain social chaos while awaiting the Second Coming of Christ.
[3-5] Magistrates are not meant to instill fear in those who do good, but in those who do evil, acting as servants of God for the welfare of society (Romans 13:3-4). The magistrate wields the sword of justice as a legitimate instrument of deterrence and physical punishment against wrongdoers (Romans 13:4). Submission is prescribed not only out of fear of physical punishment, but also for reasons of conscience before the Lord (Romans 13:5). However, there are clear exceptions to this obedience when government decrees openly contradict the written word of God, at which point the believer must obey God rather than men (Acts 4:19-20, Acts 5:29). Civil submission to government should not be confused with approval of ungodly conduct, but rather is observed for the sake of spiritual witness.
[6, 7] For this reason, taxes are also paid, since the authorities are ministers of God who continually attend to this social service (Romans 13:6). It is commanded to give to each what is due, whether it be tribute, taxes, respect, or honor (Romans 13:7). The payment of civil taxes does not represent ideological adherence to the ruler of the day, but rather the fulfillment of a civic obligation that avoids legal judgment by the magistrate (Matthew 22:21). The Lord Jesus Christ and the apostle Paul modeled peaceful submission to the financial demands of the empire, clearly separating the sphere of state sovereignty from the absolute loyalty owed to God (Acts 25:11). Thus, the church renders its financial service to the earthly state while awaiting its final redemption at the Second Coming.
[8-10] The commandment to owe no one anything, except to love one another, indicates that mutual love represents the perfect fulfillment of God's law (Romans 13:8). When listing the precepts of the Decalogue, such as not committing adultery, not murdering, not stealing, not bearing false witness, and not coveting, it is observed that the Sabbath commandment is intentionally omitted in the epistles addressed to the church (Romans 13:9, Colossians 2:14-16). The Sabbath was granted as a ceremonial sign exclusively for the nation of Israel under the Mosaic covenant (Ezekiel 20:20, Nehemiah 9:14), and therefore the believer under grace is not bound by this ordinance. Christian love does no harm to one's neighbor, constituting the practical fulfillment of the justice of the moral law (Romans 13:10, Galatians 5:14, James 2:8). Thus, obedience to mutual love safeguards the believer from apostasy before the Second Coming of Christ.
[11, 12] It is time to awaken from spiritual slumber, for bodily salvation is nearer than when it was initially believed (Romans 13:11). The expression "the night" alludes to the present age of moral darkness and spiritual gloom where Satan temporarily operates as the prince of the power of the air (Ephesians 2:2, John 9:4-5). In contrast, the solemn declaration that "the night is past, the day is at hand" (Romans 13:12) indicates that the manifestation of Jesus Christ is at hand and will dispel all darkness from creation. Therefore, believers are exhorted to definitively cast off the works of darkness and to put on the armor of light (Ephesians 6:11-13). This expectation of bodily redemption purifies the daily walk of the justified as they long for the Second Coming of Christ (1 John 3:1-3, 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18, Revelation 12:11).
[13, 14] The believer's walk should be characterized by honesty and decency appropriate to the day, abstaining from gluttony, drunkenness, lust, debauchery, strife, and envy (Romans 13:13). Practical victory over the disordered desires of the flesh is not achieved through human effort or ascetic legalism, but by putting on the Lord Jesus Christ through faith (Romans 13:14). Putting on Christ involves considering the old Adamic nature as dead and buried, allowing the life of the Savior to manifest itself in the physical members of the new creation (Galatians 2:20, Colossians 3:5-10). The provision for the Adamic flesh is entirely canceled in the spiritual aspect through circumcision performed without hands, ensuring the preservation of the redeemed soul (Colossians 2:11-12, Philippians 3:20-21).

[1-4] The apostle Paul instructs us to welcome the weak in faith, but not to argue over opinions or doubtful disputes (Romans 14:1). The believer who is weak in faith chooses to eat only vegetables, while the one who possesses firm faith understands that it is permissible for him to eat everything (Romans 14:2). It is strictly forbidden for the one who eats everything to look down on the one who abstains, and likewise, it is forbidden for the one who does not eat to judge the one who does, since God has already accepted him (Romans 14:3). In the present dispensation of grace, physical diet is irrelevant for the justification of the soul before the Lord (1 Corinthians 8:8). Each servant stands or falls to his own master, and the Lord is able to make him stand.
[5, 6] The regard for the days is addressed, noting that while some consider one day more important than another, others regard all days equally (Romans 14:5). Paul's instruction states that each individual must be fully convinced in his own mind (Romans 14:5). Whoever regards one day as special does so to the Lord; and whoever does not regard one day as special does not regard it to the Lord (Romans 14:6). It is crucial to note that the ceremonial commandment of the Jewish Sabbath was deliberately excluded from the letters addressed to the church (Colossians 2:16, Galatians 4:10). The Sabbath was a national sign exclusive to Israel (Ezekiel 20:20, Nehemiah 9:14), therefore the believer under grace is not bound by this physical ordinance (Galatians 5:4).
[7-9] None of the believers live for themselves, and none of them die for themselves (Romans 14:7). If we live, we live for the Lord; and if we die, we die for the Lord (Romans 14:8). For this reason Christ died, rose again, and lived again, so that he might be the Lord of both the dead and the living (Romans 14:9). In practical terms, the believer's decisions are often influenced by the circumstances of their family environment or mixed marriages, as evidenced in Timothy's journey (Acts 16:3, 1 Corinthians 13:5). Nevertheless, the soul's spiritual union with the Savior guarantees that its legal standing remains unchanged.
[10-12] The apostle challenges the reader regarding the folly of judging or despising a brother or sister in the faith, since all believers will appear before the Judgment Seat of Christ (Romans 14:10). Multiple modern church revisions have altered this passage to read as the judgment seat of God, obscuring the direct connection with the examination of God's servants in heaven (2 Corinthians 5:10). By quoting Old Testament prophecy, Scripture affirms that every knee will bow before the Lord and every tongue will confess God (Romans 14:11, Isaiah 45:23). Thus, each of the redeemed will give a personal account of themselves before God (Romans 14:12). This examination is not the great white throne judgment reserved for the ungodly (Revelation 20:11-15), but rather an evaluation of the believer's motives and works for reward.
[13-16] We are exhorted to no longer judge our brothers and sisters, but to resolve not to place any stumbling block or cause of offense in their way (Romans 14:13). The believer knows and trusts in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but rather it is unclean to the one who considers something unclean (Romans 14:14). If a brother or sister is grieved over food, we are no longer walking in love (Romans 14:15). We must not destroy with food the one for whom Christ died, thus preventing the good of the saints from being reproached (Romans 14:15-16). On the cross, the spiritual circumcision of the heart severed the union between the soul and the physical body (Colossians 2:11-12), meaning that what enters the body does not contaminate the spiritual condition of the regenerate (Acts 10:15, 1 Timothy 4:3-5). Nevertheless, the believer must voluntarily limit their moral freedom out of love for the conscience of the weaker brother.
[17, 18] The doctrinal definition of the Church Age is established by declaring that "the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit" (Romans 14:17). This spiritual kingdom differs markedly from the literal, geopolitical theocracy that the Lord will establish through the judgment of the nations and the exercise of armed force after His Second Coming (Revelation 11:15, Matthew 25:31-46). He who serves Christ in these things pleases God and is approved by men (Romans 14:18). The presence of the Holy Spirit in the believer's body is the seal of his legal justification, which enables him to manifest the fruit of peace.
[19-21] We are exhorted to pursue what contributes to peace and to mutual edification in the congregation of the saints (Romans 14:19). Believers should not destroy the work of God for the sake of food, since although all things are clean, it is wrong for a person to eat with offense (Romans 14:20). It is right and noble not to eat meat, nor drink wine, nor do anything by which a brother or sister stumbles, is offended, or is weakened (Romans 14:21). This testimony of practical consideration constitutes a voluntary removal of every obstacle in the Christian walk.
[22, 23] He who has faith must keep it to himself before the presence of God, and blessed is he who does not condemn himself in what he approves (Romans 14:22). However, he who doubts is condemned if he eats, because he does not do so by faith, since everything that does not come from faith is sin (Romans 14:23). The condemnation or judgment mentioned in this passage does not refer to eternal damnation in hell, but to the erosion of peace of mind and the contamination of the believer's conscience (Titus 1:15). When the redeemed act with hesitation, he violates the principle of faith of the new man, exposing his walk to divine rebuke.

[1, 2] Believers who are strong in faith should bear with the failings of the weak, seeking to please their neighbors for their edification (Romans 15:1-2). This excludes the attitude of spiritual arrogance and carnal selfishness that often disrupt practical fellowship in local churches, promoting instead the mutual edification of the body of Christ (Ephesians 4:11-12).
[3, 4] Christ did not please himself, but the reproaches of those who reviled God fell upon his forehead (Romans 15:3, Psalm 69:9). In facing the afflictions of the cross, the Lord wore the crown of thorns, bearing the curse of creation (Genesis 3:17-18). The things written in the Old Testament were recorded for the comfort of the New Testament saints in the midst of their tribulations (Romans 15:4). This instruction demonstrates that the study of divine truth should not be limited to the New Testament, since the prophecies of the Old Testament spiritually sustain the believer during their earthly pilgrimage.
[5-7] God grants patience and comfort so that the saints may live in harmony with one another according to Jesus Christ (Romans 15:5). The purpose of this spiritual harmony is to glorify with one mind and one mouth the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 15:6). Believers should receive their brothers and sisters in the faith just as Christ received them, for the glory of the Lord (Romans 15:7). This unification of the redeemed into one mystical body was definitively accomplished on the cross of Calvary, legally destroying the dividing wall that previously existed (Ephesians 2:14-16).
[8-12] The Lord Jesus was appointed minister to the circumcised to confirm the divine promises made to the Hebrew patriarchs (Romans 15:8, Matthew 15:24). In His first earthly ministry, God sent His Son exclusively to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, under the Mosaic Law and before His blood was shed on the cross (Matthew 10:5-6). However, because of God's mercy, the Gentiles also glorify God, fulfilling the Scriptures that foretell that the nations will rejoice with His people (Romans 15:9-11, Deuteronomy 32:43). The prophet Isaiah foretold that from the root of Jesse would arise the one who would rule the Gentile nations, who would place their trust in Him (Romans 15:12, Isaiah 11:10).
[13-15] The God of hope fills the believer with joy and peace in believing, so that they may abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit (Romans 15:13).
