Paul expresses his conviction regarding the goodness and knowledge that reside in the saints in Rome, enabling them to admonish one another in the faith (Romans 15:14). The apostle writes resolutely to remind them of the doctrine of grace entrusted to him by God (Romans 15:15).
[16-19] Paul was called to be a minister of Jesus Christ to the Gentiles, exercising the service of God's gospel so that the offering of the nations might be acceptable and sanctified by the Holy Spirit (Romans 15:16). Unlike Simon Peter, whose primary commission focused on circumcision using the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Acts 15:7-8), Paul was set apart as the apostle to the Gentiles to reveal the mystery of the church in one body (Ephesians 3:1-6). The signs, wonders, and miracles performed by the apostle through the power of God's Spirit spread from Jerusalem to Illyricum, fully proclaiming the gospel of Christ (Romans 15:19). These sign gifts confirmed the dispensational transition in the book of Acts, gradually ceasing once the written revelation of Scripture was complete (2 Timothy 4:20).
[20-22] The apostle endeavored to preach the Gospel in those territories where the name of Christ had not previously been proclaimed, so as not to build on someone else's foundation (Romans 15:20). In this way, what was written in the prophet Isaiah was fulfilled: that those who had not heard of Him would see Him, and those who had not heard would understand (Romans 15:21, Isaiah 52:15). This evangelistic outreach was the main reason why the apostle was often hindered from visiting them (Romans 15:22, Romans 1:13).
[23, 24] Having no more fields of work in those regions, and having long desired to see them, the apostle planned his journey to Spain via Rome (Romans 15:23-24). He expected to be guided by the brothers in Rome after having enjoyed their company for a while (Romans 15:24). All of the apostle's planning is subordinate to the submission to the Lord's will, a practice that safeguards the believer's mind from falling into human pride (James 4:15-16).
[25-29] Immediately, the apostle sets out for Jerusalem to minister to the needs of the saints (Romans 15:25). The churches of Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to make a voluntary offering to help the poor saints residing in Jerusalem (Romans 15:26). This material contribution represents the fulfillment of a moral debt of spiritual gratitude from the Gentiles to the Jews (Romans 15:27). By citing this historical event, the truth of the saving visitation in the present dispensation is highlighted (Acts 11:29-30). After completing his service in Jerusalem, Paul assures them that he will go to Rome with the abundant blessing of the Gospel of Christ (Romans 15:29). Faithful stewardship of the offerings and mutual service will be duly rewarded before the judgment seat of Christ before the Second Coming of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10).
[30-33] The apostle pleads with the brothers and sisters, through our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Holy Spirit, to help him by earnestly interceding in their prayers before God (Romans 15:30). His request is to be delivered from the rebellious and unbelieving people residing in Judea, and that his service in Jerusalem may be well received by the saints (Romans 15:31, Acts 21:11-12). Paul longs to arrive in Rome with joy by the Lord's will and to be refreshed together with them (Romans 15:32). The God of peace remains permanently with all the saints (Romans 15:33).

[1-4] [1, 2] The apostle Paul begins by recommending Phoebe, whom he identifies as a servant of the church in Cenchreae, requesting that she be received into the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints (Romans 16:1). It should be noted that some ecclesiastical versions attempt to translate her as minister or deaconess to justify hierarchical or monastic positions, but the sacred text simply calls her a servant (Romans 16:1). This woman's faithfulness in the practical service of hosting the saints and assisting the apostle illustrates that true work in the body of Christ does not consist of holding titles of authority, but in mutual support out of love for the Lord.
[3-5] Greetings are sent to Priscilla and Aquila, fellow workers in Jesus Christ who risked their lives for Paul, to whom not only he gives thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles (Romans 16:3-4). Likewise, greetings are extended to the congregation that meets in her home (Romans 16:5). This clearly establishes that in the present dispensation, the church of God is not limited to a physical temple or stone cathedral, but can legitimately meet in private homes (Colossians 4:15, Philemon 1:2).
[6-16] An extensive list of greetings to various saints residing in Rome is detailed, among whom Andronicus and Junia, relatives of the apostle and his fellow prisoners, stand out. It is testified that they were in Christ before Paul (Romans 16:7). This statement forcefully refutes the error of those who maintain that the mystical body of Christ did not exist before Paul's conversion, demonstrating that the church was already in formation before the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 15:11, Romans 16:7). Concluding the personal greetings, the apostles are exhorted to greet one another with a holy kiss, declaring that the churches of Christ send their greetings (Romans 16:16). The use of the plural "the churches" is highlighted in contrast to systems that seek to establish a human and exclusive denomination under the singular title of the church of Christ (1 Corinthians 16:19), a sectarian error that will be severely judged. Thus, the preservation of local churches as independent and autonomous entities guarantees the collective witness.
[17, 18] The apostle urges the brothers to watch out for those who cause divisions and stumbling blocks contrary to the doctrine they have learned, ordering them to separate themselves from them (Romans 16:17). These false teachers are exposed, as they do not serve our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own appetites, using smooth talk and flattery to deceive the hearts of the simple (Romans 16:18). This pattern of behavior is characteristic of intellectuals and scholars who dedicate themselves to correcting the written Word of God under the pretext of clarifying the original texts (Colossians 2:8, 1 Timothy 6:20). By altering divine words to justify their own interests or evade rebuke for their sins, these men act with hypocrisy and impiety, leading the unwary into spiritual confusion.
[19, 20] The obedience of the believers in Rome has been proclaimed to all, which brings joy, exhorting them to be wise in what is good and innocent in what is evil (Romans 16:19). The promise is added that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet (Romans 16:20). This statement places the crushing of the serpent's head prophesied in Eden as a strictly future event relative to the apostle's time, thus refuting those who erroneously claim that the enemy's mortal wound was definitively inflicted at Calvary (Genesis 3:15, Revelation 12:7-9). The final and irreversible defeat of the adversary will be carried out literally and physically on earth at the events of Christ's Second Coming.
[21-24] Greetings from Paul's co-workers are conveyed, including Timothy, Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater (Romans 16:21). In this context, Tertius is introduced as the scribe who wrote the epistle at the apostle's dictation (Romans 16:22). This scribe's work illustrates how the Lord used faithful servants to commit his inspired words to writing, as happened with Onesiphorus in other letters (Philemon 1:19, 2 Peter 1:21). Gaius, host of the whole church, and Erastus, the city treasurer, also send their greetings, testifying to the fellowship and practical order that prevailed among the believers.
[25-27] The epistle concludes with a doxology to the only God who is able to confirm believers according to the gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that had been kept hidden for ages past (Romans 16:25). This mystery has now been made known through the prophetic writings to all the Gentile nations for the obedience of faith (Romans 16:26). The obedience of faith denotes absolute rest in the atoning sacrifice of Christ's cross, in total opposition to water baptism or the works of the flesh by which the natural man futilely tries to buy salvation (Ephesians 2:8-9, Galatians 5:4).

[1, 2] The historical context of Judah's exile in Babylon begins under the reign of Jehoiakim and the invasion of Nebuchadnezzar. An apparent chronological discrepancy with the records of the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 25:1) is resolved either by Nebuchadnezzar's co-regency with his father or by the Babylonian calendar's methods of calculation. Jehoiakim, originally named Eliakim, was the son of King Josiah (2 Kings 23:24). The vessels of the house of God were taken to the land of Shinar to be placed in the temple of a pagan god, symbolizing the initial fall of the Hebrew theocracy. This introductory account was written in Hebrew, which comprises the first section of the book.
[3, 4] The selection of young men from the royal family and princes to be trained in the royal palace directly fulfills the prophecy announced by Isaiah (Isaiah 39:7, 2 Kings 20:18). These young men were required to possess intelligence and an aptitude for "knowledge," this passage being one of the few places in Scripture where that term is used (1 Timothy 6:20). The Babylonian system aimed to instruct them in their own language and wisdom, but the ability of these young men to stand tall before the monarch reflects the diligence that should characterize God's servants (Proverbs 22:29).
[5-7] The Babylonian monarch assigned a daily ration of the king's food and wine for the three-year training period (Daniel 1:5). Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah received new names of pagan origin: Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego (Daniel 1:6-7). This alteration of their Hebrew names, which directly referenced the Lord (Genesis 30:6), was an attempt at cultural assimilation to erase their spiritual identity. However, in their private lives, the young men maintained their brotherly fellowship and their devotion to the God of their ancestors (Daniel 2:17).
[8-10] Daniel resolved not to defile himself with the king’s food or wine. This determination represents a model of holiness and nonconformity with the ways of the world (Romans 12:2). The defilement of food stemmed both from the dietary prescriptions of Mosaic Law (Leviticus 11) and from the pagan practice of offering food to idols before eating it. Divine favor allowed Ashpenaz, the chief eunuch, to treat Daniel with kindness, despite expressing understandable fear of the monarch's anger should the Hebrews' appearance deteriorate (Daniel 1:9-10).
[11-14] Daniel proposed a ten-day test to Melzar, the steward in charge of his custody, based on vegetables and water. The number ten is dispensationally associated with the Gentiles in the biblical design (Genesis 10:10, Acts 10:1, Romans 10:1). Since Daniel was a prophet whose ministry was primarily before pagan courts, this ten-day probationary period foreshadows the trials and tests to which the saints will be subjected under Gentile powers (Revelation 2:10).
[15, 16] After the ten days had passed, the Hebrew youths looked healthier and more robust than those who consumed the monarch's rations. Consequently, Melzar permanently withdrew the royal delicacies and supplied them with vegetables (Daniel 1:16). This physical vitality was not the result of a natural diet or contemporary fasting, but of God's sovereign blessing upon their faithfulness to the law. The use of the expression "the end" in this section typologically anticipates the preservation of the remnant in the end times (Daniel 12:4, 12:13).
[17, 18] God granted the four young men extraordinary knowledge and aptitude in all literature and wisdom, endowing Daniel with a unique understanding of visions and dreams. This spiritual training likens Daniel to the patriarch Joseph (Genesis 41:14-15) and constitutes the sign of the true prophetic gift (Numbers 12:6). At the end of the three-year period appointed by the king, the young men were formally presented before the court of Babylon.
[19-21] When examined by Nebuchadnezzar, none was found to be comparable to the four Hebrews, who proved to be ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers in the province. Magicians resorted to demonic incantations, while astrologers attempted to decipher the future through stellar occultism—abominable practices that the Lord severely forbids (Deuteronomy 18:10-12). Daniel remained active at court until the first year of King Cyrus of Persia, demonstrating that a decision for holiness made in youth ensures the preservation of spiritual testimony throughout an entire earthly existence.

[1-13] In the second year of Nebuchadnezzar's reign, the monarch had dreams that troubled his spirit and prevented him from sleeping. This chronological date, compared to Jeremiah 25:1, is calculated from the beginning of his sole reign and not from his two-year co-regency with his father, thus corresponding to the fourth year of Daniel's captivity after the completion of his three-year training (Daniel 1:5). God troubled the Babylonian monarch with a nightmare, just as He had done with Pharaoh in the past (Genesis 41:4-7), with the purpose of warning the Gentile king, discrediting the false diviners, and validating His own prophet. The king summoned magicians, astrologers, sorcerers, and Chaldeans, who represented the intellectual and spiritualist elite of Babylon (Daniel 2:2). Sorcery or sorcery in Scripture is etymologically associated with the use of drugs and potions in magical or occult practices (Revelation 18:23). Suspecting the fraud of these wise men, whom he had previously deemed inferior (Daniel 1:20), the monarch imposes a final test upon them, demanding that they reveal both the dream itself and its interpretation under penalty of being dismembered and having their houses reduced to dung heaps. When the Chaldeans confess their complete inability and claim that only gods whose dwelling is not with the flesh can reveal such a secret, the king furiously decrees the death of all the wise men, extending the sentence to Daniel and his companions. This crisis reveals the bankruptcy of worldly wisdom in contrast to the revelation that comes from the Lord (1 Corinthians 3:19).
[14-23] Daniel prudently and wisely intervenes with Arioch, captain of the royal guard, upon learning of the hasty execution decree (Daniel 2:14-15). Granted a reprieve by the monarch, Daniel meets at his house with his companions Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah to implore the mercies of the God of heaven concerning this mystery (Daniel 2:17-18). The united prayer of the Hebrews is answered when the secret is revealed to Daniel in a night vision (Daniel 2:19). Daniel bursts into a doxology, acknowledging that wisdom and absolute power belong to God, who has sovereign control over time, history, and earthly dynasties, deposing and enthroning monarchs according to His eternal designs (Daniel 2:20-21). The Lord searches the depths and the hidden, and light dwells unchangingly beside Him (Daniel 2:22). This direct revelation dismisses any human method of divination, demonstrating that the God of the fathers is the sole giver of true spiritual intelligence, which protects the righteous from physical destruction (Proverbs 2:6-8).
[24-30] When Daniel appears before Arioch, he pleads with him not to destroy the wise men of Babylon and asks him to guide him into the presence of the sovereign to reveal the matter. Hastily brought before Nebuchadnezzar, the prophet is questioned about his ability to decipher the mystery (Daniel 2:25-26). Daniel responds by disclaiming all personal glory and declaring the utter powerlessness of the astrologers, magicians, and soothsayers of the Gentile court. With great boldness, he testifies that there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets and makes known to the monarch what will happen in the last days (Daniel 2:28). The God of heaven uses the king's dream to reveal the prophetic panorama of human history leading up to the Second Coming of Christ. Daniel humbly emphasizes that the revelation was not granted to him because he possessed wisdom superior to that of other living beings, but for the sovereign purpose that the interpretation be revealed to the king so that he might understand the thoughts of his heart (Daniel 2:30). God uses his servants as instruments of national and international witness, preserving the lives of his people in the midst of ungodly empires (Esther 10:3).
[31-35] The monarch sees in his vision a great image of excellent brilliance and terrible appearance standing before him (Daniel 2:31). The metal structure of the statue represents a progressive moral and physical degradation of empires, progressing from the head of fine gold, the chest and arms of silver, the belly and thighs of bronze, the legs of iron, culminating in the feet and ten toes made of an unstable mixture of iron and baked clay (Daniel 2:32-33). This material gradation represents the decline in the specific gravity of metals, making the statue extremely unstable and heavy at its peak (Daniel 2:35). As the monarch watches, a stone is cut out without human hands, which descends violently to strike the image precisely on its feet of iron and clay, shattering them completely (Daniel 2:34). After this impact, all the metals and clay are reduced to fine dust, resembling chaff on a summer threshing floor, and are scattered by the wind without leaving a trace (Daniel 2:35). Finally, the striking stone is transformed into a great mountain that fills the expanse of the entire earth (Daniel 2:35). This event describes the Second Coming of Christ, who will overthrow the world system of the Antichrist (Revelation 19:11-15).
[36-39] Daniel presents the interpretation of the dream, revealing that Nebuchadnezzar has been appointed by the God of heaven as king of kings, having received dominion, power, strength, and glory (Daniel 2:37-38). The Babylonian monarch is personified by the golden head in the image, initiating the period of Gentile domination over the earth in 606 BC (Daniel 2:38, Jeremiah 27:6). The golden head represents an absolute monarchy, the highest form of governmental authority, whose perfect design will be fulfilled only when the Lord Jesus reigns sovereignly over the nations (Zechariah 14:9). After the Babylonian Empire, a second, lesser kingdom will arise, represented by the silver chest and arms, which historically corresponds to the coalition of the Medes and Persians from 536 BC (Daniel 2:39, Daniel 5:28). This government exercises a lesser, military authority, governed by inflexible laws that limit even the monarch (Daniel 6:15). Later, a third bronze empire would emerge, corresponding to Greece under Alexander the Great in 330 BC, which would extend its military dominion over the geography of the known world (Daniel 2:39, Daniel 8:5-7).
[40-43] The fourth empire, symbolized by the legs of iron, possesses an implacable hardness that crushes and breaks everything in its path, historically corresponding to the Roman Empire in its two branches, East and West (Daniel 2:40, Luke 2:1). This empire maintains its influence throughout history through ecclesiastical and legal systems, and will manifest itself in its final stage as a confederation of ten kings represented by the toes (Daniel 2:41, Revelation 17:12). The potter's clay typifies humanity in its weakness and earthly condition, for the human body comes from the dust and mud of the earth (Job 33:6, Job 10:9, 2 Corinthians 4:7). The incomprehensible mixture of iron and clay reveals a profound mystery in which fallen and demonic spiritual entities will attempt to mingle with the human race (Daniel 2:43). This supernatural infiltration evokes the antediluvian rebellion in which fallen angels cohabited with the daughters of men to corrupt the human race (Genesis 6:1-4). Thus, the final Gentile confederation will combine the weakness of human democracies with the strength of spiritual forces of evil, which will be suddenly dismantled by divine judgment before the Second Coming of Christ (Ephesians 6:12).
[44, 45] In the days of this final confederation of ten kings, the God of heaven will establish an eternal kingdom that will never be destroyed or transferred to another nation, which will crush and consume all the world empires (Daniel 2:44). The stone cut out of the mountain without human intervention typologically represents Jesus Christ at His Second Coming (Daniel 2:45, 1 Peter 2:4). The exegetical error of Catholicism and amillennialism, which attempts to see in this stone the first coming of Christ or a gradual spiritual spread of the church, is rejected, since in the first coming the Savior did not strike the nations, but was struck on the cross (Isaiah 53:5). Furthermore, when Christ came the first time, the Roman Empire was in the stage of the legs of iron, and the federation of the ten toes or kings on the feet did not yet exist (Daniel 2:43-44). Jesus Christ will descend like a striking stone to instantly shatter the world system of the nations of the earth, establishing a visible kingdom and a military theocracy on this earthly plane (Psalm 110:1-2, Revelation 11:15). This glorious event is certain, and the divine prophecy will be fulfilled with absolute literal precision at the Second Coming of Christ.
[46-49] Upon hearing the astonishing revelation of the mystery, King Nebuchadnezzar prostrates himself before Daniel and orders that gifts and incense be offered to him (Daniel 2:46). The monarch wholeheartedly confesses that the God of the Hebrews is the God of gods, Lord of kings, and revealer of secrets (Daniel 2:47). However, this declaration by the king constitutes mere intellectual admiration and not a genuine inner conversion, as is evident when shortly afterward he decides to build a statue entirely of gold to defy the design the Lord had revealed to him (Daniel 3:1). The king exalts Daniel by bestowing valuable gifts upon him and appointing him governor of the province of Babylon and chief of all his wise men (Daniel 2:48). Daniel assumes a governmental position equivalent to that of a prime minister or chief judge, sitting at the gate of the royal palace (Daniel 2:49). At the prophet's request, his companions Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego are placed in charge of the administration of the affairs of the province of Babylon (Daniel 2:49). This elevation of the young Jewish men in exile shows how the Lord uses historical circumstances to position his own in spheres of authority, ensuring the witness and preservation of the people of Israel until the end of time.

[1-3] King Nebuchadnezzar erects a statue made entirely of gold on the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon (Daniel 3:1). Having previously received the revelation in the preceding chapter that he represented only the head of gold (Daniel 2:38), the monarch acts with open rebellion and pride by building an image made entirely of this precious metal, attempting to declare that his empire would be eternal and would never be replaced by other powers (Daniel 4:30). The statue's physical dimensions, sixty cubits high and six cubits wide (Daniel 3:1), create a symmetrical design that implicitly evokes the number six hundred and sixty-six (666), which constitutes the mark and number of the beast in the time of the end (Revelation 13:15-18). Likewise, the number six takes on singular significance in this portion, since the act of setting up the image is mentioned six times in the opening verses, and exactly six musical instruments that make up the Babylonian orchestra are detailed (Daniel 3:5). The sovereign summons the governmental and political elite of his provinces, including princes, governors, captains, judges, and constables, to attend the inauguration and pay homage before the monument of the empire (Daniel 3:2-3).
[4-7] A herald loudly proclaims the imperial ordinance addressed to all the peoples, nations, and languages ​​of the earth (Daniel 3:4). It is decreed inexorably that upon hearing the sound of the horn, flute, harp, tambourine, psaltery, pipes, and all kinds of musical instruments, every soul must fall down and worship the golden statue (Daniel 3:5). The punishment for refusing to submit to this ecumenical and state-sanctioned worship is to be immediately thrown into a blazing furnace (Daniel 3:6). This globalized government structure under a single Babylonian religion is a perfect example of the system the false prophet will establish during the tribulation, forcing humanity to worship the image of the Antichrist under penalty of death (Revelation 13:11-15). The orchestra and worldly music act as the primary instruments of moral seduction to bend the will of the masses and drag them into collective apostasy (Ephesians 2:2). As the music plays, the vast majority of nations prostrate themselves before the idol, demonstrating the frailty of man without God (Romans 3:23).
[8-12] Certain Chaldean men, driven by envy and national resentment, appear before the throne to formally accuse the exiled Jews (Daniel 3:8). These accusers had previously seen their own egos humbled when Daniel and his companions demonstrated wisdom ten times greater than that of the entire spiritualist elite of Babylon (Daniel 1:20, 2:10). The historical hostility and antisemitism are specifically directed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, whom the king had placed in high administrative positions over the province of Babylon (Daniel 2:49, 3:12). The informers reveal that these Hebrew men have disobeyed the royal decree, refusing to serve the court gods and worship the golden statue (Daniel 3:12). Just as will happen in the end times, the faithfulness of the saints to the Word of God becomes the only pretext the wicked find to persecute them and seek their physical destruction (Daniel 6:5, Revelation 12:17).
[13-18] Nebuchadnezzar, overcome with anger and fury, orders the three young Hebrew men to be brought before him to confront them directly (Daniel 3:13). Although the monarch is offended by their disobedience, he unusually grants them a second chance to recant their doctrinal position upon hearing the music again (Daniel 3:14-15). The king launches a defiant challenge against the Most High, arrogantly asking who the God would be who could deliver them from his hand (Daniel 3:15). With admirable composure, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego respond respectfully yet firmly, declaring that they have no need to deliberate on their answer (Daniel 3:16). They testify firmly that the God they serve has the absolute power to rescue them from the fiery furnace and from the king's hand (Daniel 3:17). However, the young men add a declaration of unwavering faith, affirming that even if the Lord decides not to deliver them physically, they will by no means worship their deities or bow down to the golden statue (Daniel 3:18). This resolution illustrates that true devotion is not based on the guarantee of temporary deliverance, but on unconditional obedience to divine sovereignty (Hebrews 11:35).
[19-23] Nebuchadnezzar's face contorts with indignation, losing all trace of mercy, and he orders the furnace to be heated seven times hotter than usual (Daniel 3:19). This urgent order to raise the temperature to its maximum capacity represents the severity of the judgment and foreshadows the intense trials of the great tribulation (Daniel 12:1). The king commands the strongest and most vigorous men of his army to tie up the three young Hebrew men, fully clothed in their robes, trousers, turbans, and other garments, and throw them into the fire (Daniel 3:20-21). Due to the urgency of the royal command and the extreme heat emanating from the entrance of the furnace, the flames instantly consumed the elite soldiers transporting the three Hebrews (Daniel 3:22). Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego fell bound into the blazing furnace, descending into the place of punishment without offering any physical resistance, typifying the submission of martyrs throughout the ages (Revelation 20:4).
[24-30] The Babylonian monarch was astounded and rose hurriedly upon witnessing an event that defied the laws of nature, asking his advisors if they had not thrown three bound men into the fire (Daniel 3:24). Upon confirmation from his court, the king declared that he saw four men loose, walking freely through the fire without suffering any harm, and emphasized that the fourth man's appearance was like the Son of God (Daniel 3:25). This wondrous apparition constitutes a theophany, or pre-incarnate presence of Jesus Christ, who descends into the furnace to accompany and deliver his servants in their suffering (Isaiah 43:2). The flames consumed the Hebrews' physical bonds but did not harm their bodies or their garments, showing that the Lord uses trials to break the chains of sin without diminishing the believer's spirit (Galatians 5:1). As they approach the mouth of the furnace, the sovereign calls them servants of the Most High God and commands them to come out (Daniel 3:26). The entire imperial court observes with astonishment that the fire had no power over their bodies, that not a single hair on their heads was singed, and that they did not even retain the smell of smoke (Daniel 3:27). Nebuchadnezzar bursts into praise of the God of Israel, acknowledging that He sent His Angel to deliver those who trusted in Him, and decrees the death penalty for anyone who blasphemes against the Lord, subsequently promoting the three young men in the province of Babylon (Daniel 3:28-30). This miraculous preservation of the faithful remnant foreshadows the glorious restoration of Israel after the Second Coming of Christ.

[1-3] This chapter constitutes both a personal testimony and an official decree issued by the Gentile monarch Nebuchadnezzar, addressed to all peoples, nations, and languages. Unlike his previous edicts, which uttered threats of death and punishment, on this occasion the sovereign pronounces a greeting of peace. The king publicly acknowledges the signs and wonders of the Most High God, declaring that His kingdom is everlasting and His dominion endures from generation to generation (Psalm 145:13). This radical change of attitude demonstrates a profound transformation in the monarch's heart following divine intervention in his life.
[4-9] While the sovereign rested and prospered in his palace, he experienced a second dream that filled him with great fear. If the first dream revealed the course of world empires (Daniel 2), this new vision concerned him directly. When the wise men of the court failed, Daniel was brought into the royal presence. The monarch addresses him, acknowledging that the spirit of the holy gods dwells within him. The assertion that no mystery is hidden from him does not imply an absence of emotional turmoil, but rather the supernatural ability to discern the hidden through the illumination of the Holy Spirit.
[10-18] The night vision shows a tree of immense stature in the middle of the earth, whose top reached the sky and was visible to the ends of the world. In biblical typology, large trees represent monarchs and their empires, ultimately foreshadowing the son of perdition (Ezekiel 31:2-18). A watcher or angel descends from heaven, ordering the tree to be cut down, leaving only the stump of its roots bound with iron and bronze. It is decreed that the king's human heart be changed into that of a beast for seven periods of time, for the sovereign purpose that the living may recognize that the Most High God rules over the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever He determines.
[19-27] Upon understanding the meaning, Daniel is astonished for an hour, and his thoughts deeply trouble him. Demonstrating loyalty to civil authority (Romans 13:1), the prophet expresses his desire that the dream and its interpretation fall upon the monarch's enemies. The tree represents Nebuchadnezzar himself in his greatness and pride. Daniel advises him to redeem his sins with justice and his iniquities by showing mercy to the poor. This admonition demonstrates that under the Old Testament dispensation, the salvation of the Gentiles included the component of works, which differs from the salvation by grace through faith without works of the present dispensation (Ephesians 2:8-9).
[28-33] Twelve months later, as the king was walking around the royal palace, his heart swelled with pride as he boasted of having built great Babylon by the might of his power and for the glory of his majesty. At that very moment, a voice descended from heaven declaring the inescapable fulfillment of the judgment. The kingdom is taken from him, and he is driven from among men to live with the beasts of the field and eat grass like oxen, until the seven times are fulfilled and he acknowledges the sovereignty of the Lord.
[34-37] When the appointed time is fulfilled, Nebuchadnezzar raises his eyes to heaven, and his understanding is restored. He blesses the Most High and praises the One who lives forever, confessing that all the inhabitants of the earth are considered as nothing before him. The king is restored to his throne with greater majesty and concludes by praising the King of heaven, experiencing a genuine conversion according to the Gentile model of the Old Testament. This experience establishes the doctrinal principle that God has the power to humble those who walk in pride. The more exalted a person is, the more severe the disciplinary process becomes, so the believer must voluntarily humble themselves before the Lord (James 4:10) to avoid being overcome by divine judgment.

[1-4] The sacred record places Belshazzar's banquet as the culminating event in the fall of the Babylonian empire. Historically, critics have questioned the text, arguing that Nabonidus was the last king, but Scripture shows that Belshazzar ruled as co-regent in Babylon while Nabonidus was in the southern part of the kingdom. Belshazzar, being the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar (Jeremiah 27:7), organizes a great feast for a thousand of his princes, during which he commits the sacrilege of desecrating the vessels of God's temple by drinking wine and praising pagan idols. This conduct illustrates how carnal celebrations often conclude in slaughter and divine judgment (Proverbs 6:15).
[5-16] In the midst of the feast, the fingers of a human hand write on the palace wall, terrifying the monarch. The wise men, astrologers, and soothsayers of Babylon again fail to read or interpret the message, demonstrating the utter ineffectiveness of worldly wisdom in discerning divine revelations without the illumination of the Spirit. The queen mother intervenes and advises summoning Daniel, who is testified to possess an excellent spirit. Upon being brought before the king, Daniel is offered the position of third ruler in the kingdom, since Nabonidus was the first and Belshazzar the second. In biblical typology, this third governmental position foreshadows the work of the Holy Spirit, the Third Person of the Trinity.
[17-24] Daniel initially rejects the monarch's gifts and rewards, knowing that the empire represented by the head of gold has come to an end and is about to be replaced by the chest of silver. Before delivering the interpretation, the prophet severely admonishes Belshazzar. He reminds him of the Lord's dealings with his grandfather Nebuchadnezzar, whom God humbled until he acknowledged His absolute sovereignty. Belshazzar is condemned because, despite knowing all this, he did not humble his heart, but rather rose up in pride against the God of heaven, profaning his sacred vessels.
[25-29] The writing traced on the wall is "MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN." The prophet explains that "MENE" means that God has numbered the kingdom and set limits to it. The repetition of the word affirms the certainty of the judgment, even though ancient translators in Alexandria tried to suppress one of these words in the Septuagint to accommodate the text to their own reasoning. "TEKEL" indicates that the monarch has been weighed in the scales of divine justice and found wanting. "PERES" is a singular participial form derived from the root "UPHARSIN," meaning division, thus creating a play on words that directly identifies the Persians as the designated executors of the empire's division.
[30, 31] That very night, the prophecy is fulfilled with literal precision. Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, is killed, and the kingdom is transferred to Darius of Mede. The transition from the Babylonian Empire to the Medo-Persian Empire occurs suddenly, confirming what was prophesied in the vision of the great image (Daniel 2:38-39). This judgment underscores the immutable principle that pride goes before destruction (Proverbs 16:18) and demonstrates how the Lord intervenes in human history to remove and establish rulers according to His sovereign decrees.

[1-3] The Medo-Persian Empire, under the reign of Darius, was organized into 120 provinces administered by princes, over whom three governors were appointed. Daniel was designated as the chief of these because he possessed an excellent spirit (Daniel 6:1-3). In the typological design of Scripture, just as in the previous chapter Daniel represents the Third Person of the Trinity, in this account he prefigures Jesus Christ, symbolically passing through death, burial, and resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:1-4).
[4, 5] Daniel's exaltation provoked the envy of the other governors and princes, who sought an opportunity to accuse him in matters of the kingdom (Daniel 6:4). However, finding no fault or error in his administration, they concluded that the only way to incriminate him would be through the law of their God (Daniel 6:5). This hostility reflects the opposition that divine justice faces in a fallen world, just as the religious leaders rose up against the Savior driven by envy (Mark 15:10).
[6-9] The magistrates approach Darius with flattery and propose that he issue an unalterable royal edict. The decree forbids anyone from addressing a petition to any god or man for thirty days, except to the monarch, under penalty of being thrown into a den of lions (Daniel 6:6-7). By appealing to Darius's pride, they persuade him to sign the document according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be revoked (Daniel 6:8-9). This maneuver of uniting state civil power with forced religion to persecute the faithful clearly foreshadows the system of the Antichrist that will operate during the tribulation (Revelation 13:15).
[10, 11] Upon learning of the publication of the decree, Daniel does not change his behavior or organize a public protest, but goes into his house and, with the windows open toward Jerusalem, kneels down to pray and give thanks to God three times a day, just as he had done before (Daniel 6:10). This consistency in prayer—morning, evening, and noon—reflects unwavering spiritual discipline (Psalm 55:17). The accusers, lying in wait, find him praying and pleading with the Lord, thus obtaining the legal evidence they had been deliberately seeking (Daniel 6:11).
[12-15] The conspirators go to the king to remind him of the immutability of his decree and formally accuse Daniel of ignoring the imperial ordinance (Daniel 6:12-13). Upon hearing this, Darius is deeply saddened and strives until sunset to free him, but the magistrates insist that the law of the Medes and Persians demands the inescapable execution of the sentence (Daniel 6:14-15). The rigidity of pagan and human law contrasts with grace, demonstrating the inability of earthly rulers to save the innocent in the face of an inflexible legal system engineered by envy.
[16, 17] The king orders that Daniel be thrown into the lions' den, expressing the hope that the God whom the prophet continually serves will deliver him (Daniel 6:16). A stone is brought and placed over the entrance to the den, sealing it with the ring of the monarch and his princes to ensure that the sentence will not be altered (Daniel 6:17). This sealed tomb directly foreshadows the burial of the Lord Jesus Christ, whose tomb was also secured with a stone and an official seal provided by the ruling empire of his time (Matthew 27:66).
[18-23] Darius spends the night fasting, forbidding musical instruments, and sleep eludes him (Daniel 6:18). At dawn, he rushes to the den, calling out to Daniel in a sorrowful voice, asking if the living God has been able to deliver him (Daniel 6:19-20). Daniel responds reverently, stating that God sent his angel to shut the lions' mouths, because he was found innocent before God and the king (Daniel 6:21-22). The Lord preserved his servant from the lion's mouth, demonstrating his victory and power over the principalities that seek to devour believers (1 Peter 5:8) and miraculously intervening, as he would later do to deliver other servants (Acts 12:11). When he was pulled from the den, he was found without injury because he trusted in his God (Daniel 6:23).
[24] By order of the monarch, the men who falsely accused Daniel were brought and thrown into the same lions' den, along with their children and wives (Daniel 6:24). Before their bodies reached the bottom, the lions seized them and broke all their bones. This severe retribution manifests God’s vindictive justice and reaffirms the biblical principle that the wicked inevitably fall into the same trap they set for the righteous (Psalm 7:15-16).
[25-28] King Darius issues a new decree addressed to all the peoples, nations, and languages ​​of the earth, commanding that men fear and tremble before the God of Daniel (Daniel 6:25-26). This official testimony proclaims that the Lord is the living God, whose kingdom will not be destroyed and whose dominion will endure to the end, acknowledging the signs and wonders He has performed in heaven and on earth (Daniel 6:26-27). This proclamation demonstrates how the Lord sovereignly uses Gentile monarchs to magnify His name internationally. Finally, Daniel prospers during the reigns of Darius and Cyrus the Persian, illustrating divine preservation of the remnant in the midst of captivity until the restoration (Daniel 6:28).

[1-3] In the first year of the reign of Belshazzar, the last monarch of Babylon, the prophet Daniel receives a night vision on his sickbed, which he records in Aramaic. This vision extends to the end of the chapter (Daniel 7:1). The four winds of heaven clash over the great sea, identified in biblical geography as the Mediterranean Sea (Daniel 7:2). From this turmoil emerge four great creatures, each different from the others (Daniel 7:3). While the waters represent multitudes in later prophetic portions (Revelation 17:15), in this passage the singular term "the great sea" literally denotes the Mediterranean basin, pointing to the geographical origin of the empires that will succeed one another in the history of Gentile domination before the Second Coming of Jesus Christ.
[4-6] The first animal is like a lion with eagle's wings, whose wings are torn off until it is made up on its feet like a man and given a human heart (Daniel 7:4). The second is like a bear that rises up on one side with three ribs between its teeth, and it is commanded to devour much flesh (Daniel 7:5). The third is like a leopard with four wings of a bird on its back and four heads, receiving dominion over the earth (Daniel 7:6). Contrary to the traditional interpretation that likens these animals to the metals of Nebuchadnezzar's great statue (Daniel 2:32-33), Scripture solemnly states that these four kings "will arise" in the future (Daniel 7:17). Since Belshazzar is the last king of Babylon, the golden head belongs to the past, and therefore the animals represent powers that emerge after the fall of Babylon: the lion represents Persia, the bear Greece, and the leopard Rome.
[7-8] After this, a fourth beast arises, dreadful, terrible, and exceedingly strong, equipped with large iron teeth with which it devours and crushes, trampling the remains underfoot (Daniel 7:7). This monster, which bears no resemblance to any earthly animal, has ten horns on its head (Daniel 7:7). Upon seeing the horns, another small horn emerges among them, uprooting three of the horns of the first beast (Daniel 7:8). This small horn has eyes like those of a man and a mouth that speaks blasphemous words (Daniel 7:8). This structure represents the final confederation of nations under the control of the Antichrist, who will rise in the end times to unite Roman harshness and Greek subtlety, acting as the global dictator before the Second Coming of Jesus Christ. The three uprooted horns signify the fall of three superpowers that will attempt to oppose his material hegemony (Daniel 7:24).
[9-12] The prophet contemplates the heavenly scene until the earthly thrones are overthrown and the Ancient of Days takes his seat (Daniel 7:9). His clothing is as white as snow, and the hair of his head is like pure wool; His throne is a flame of fire, and its wheels are burning fire, from which flows a river of fire (Daniel 7:9-10). Thousands upon thousands serve him, and ten thousand times ten thousand appear before him; judgment is established, and the books are opened (Daniel 7:10). This description coincides with the judgment at the great white throne where the wicked will appear after the Millennium to be judged according to their works (Revelation 20:11-12). The fourth beast is killed in historical time, and its body is given over to the burning fire because of the blasphemous words of the little horn (Daniel 7:11). In contrast, the dominion over the other three animals is taken away, although their lives are prolonged for a time as vassal kingdoms subordinate to divine authority on earth (Daniel 7:12).
[13-14] In the night visions, one like the Son of Man is seen coming with the clouds of heaven, approaching the Ancient of Days to be presented before Him (Daniel 7:13). The Son of Man is given dominion, glory, and an eternal kingdom so that all peoples, nations, and languages ​​may serve Him (Daniel 7:14). This absolute dominion constitutes the establishment of the literal, theocratic kingdom on earth at the Second Coming of Jesus Christ. The heresies of amillennialism and postmillennialism, which attempt to spiritualize this kingdom by presenting it as the church of grace in this age, are rejected, since the Lord did not assume this political dominion at His first coming, but was crucified by the Gentiles under the Roman Empire, represented by the legs of iron.
[15-18] The prophet's spirit is troubled within his physical body, and the visions disturb him, so he approaches one of the heavenly ministers to inquire about the truth of what he has seen (Daniel 7:15-16). The heavenly messenger declares that the four great beasts are four kings who will arise from the earth (Daniel 7:17). However, the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom and possess it for all eternity (Daniel 7:18). These saints do not correspond to the believers of the present dispensation of the church who will be raptured before the beginning of Daniel's seventieth week (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17), but to the Jewish remnant who will suffer persecution from the Antichrist and keep God's commandments during the period of the great tribulation (Daniel 7:25).
[19-22] Daniel desires to know the truth about the nature of the fourth beast, whose iron teeth and bronze claws destroyed and crushed everything in its path, as well as the ten horns on its head and the little horn that felled three of them (Daniel 7:19-20). It is noted that this little horn was more robust in appearance than its companions and waged war against the saints, prevailing over them in the physical realm (Daniel 7:21). This persecution and martyrdom of the righteous in the tribulation will persist relentlessly until the glorious coming of the Ancient of Days, at which time divine judgment will be handed over to the saints of the Most High and the time will be fulfilled for them to take possession of the earthly kingdom (Daniel 7:22). The armed intervention of Jesus Christ at His Second Coming will abruptly end the tyranny of the son of perdition.
[23-28] The messenger explains that the fourth beast represents a fourth kingdom on earth, different from all the previous kingdoms, which will devour, trample, and crush the whole earth (Daniel 7:23). The ten horns denote ten kings who will arise from that kingdom, after whom the little horn, different from the first ones, will emerge and humiliate three kings (Daniel 7:24). This dictator will speak against the Most High, break the saints, and attempt to alter the festival times and the moral law for "a time, and times, and half a time," which exactly equates to three and a half years of persecution under the reign of the beast (Daniel 7:25). The heavenly court will remove his dominion to destroy it definitively at the Second Coming, and the greatness of the kingdom under all heaven will be given to the people of the saints, whose kingdom is eternal (Daniel 7:26-27). Daniel concludes by treasuring these words in his heart with deep mental turmoil (Daniel 7:28).

[1, 2] The prophet Daniel receives his second prophetic vision during the third year of King Belshazzar's reign, being transported in spirit to the stronghold of Susa, in the province of Elam, by the bank of the Ulai River (Daniel 8:1-2). From this section onward, the sacred text returns to the Hebrew language, as the Lord resumes His direct dealings with the national restoration of Israel, its sacrifices, and its temple. The geographical location places the prophetic scene outside the confines of Babylon, indicating that the empire represented by the golden head of the great image now belongs to the past under God's sovereign decrees (Daniel 2:38-39).
[3, 4] The prophet sees a ram standing by the Ulai River with two high horns, the second of which grows higher at the end (Daniel 8:3). The ram charges with great force toward the west, the north, and the south, and no other beast can withstand its power or deliver it from its dominion (Daniel 8:4). The heavenly messenger reveals that this two-horned ram literally represents the kings of Media and Persia (Daniel 8:20). The smaller horn that arises first symbolizes Darius the Mede, while the larger horn that springs up later represents the final consolidation of the empire under Cyrus the Persian, whose military conquests were sovereignly directed by the Lord (Ezra 1:1-3).
[5-8] A male goat advances swiftly from the west across the face of the whole earth with such lightness that it seems not to touch the ground, possessing a prominent horn between its eyes (Daniel 8:5). This animal attacks the ram with fury, breaks off its two horns, knocks it down, and tramples it to the ground (Daniel 8:6-7). The male goat represents the king of Greece, and its prominent horn is the first monarch of that empire, Alexander the Great, who defeated the Persian army in historical times (Daniel 8:21). Upon consolidating his immense power, the large horn is suddenly broken off, and in its place four prominent horns spring up, pointing toward the four winds of heaven. This represents the division of the Greek empire after Alexander's death into four dynasties led by his generals, not by his biological descendants (Daniel 8:8, Daniel 11:4).
[9-12] From one of these four prominent horns emerges a small horn that grows extraordinarily large toward the south, the east, and the desirable land of Palestine (Daniel 8:9). This figure grows so powerful that he reaches the host of heaven, casting down some of the heavenly hosts and stars to the earth to trample them underfoot (Daniel 8:10). The little horn is not historically limited to Antiochus Epiphanes, since its description properly belongs to the time when humanity's rebellions reach their peak before the Second Coming of Christ (Daniel 8:23). It is a supernatural entity, Satan incarnate, who will drag down a third of the fallen angels, typified as stars in the Scriptures (Revelation 12:3-4, Job 38:7). With unprecedented arrogance, the adversary will magnify himself against the Prince of princes, suspending the daily sacrifice and profaning the earthly sanctuary during the tribulation (Daniel 9:27).
[13, 14] One holy being asks another how long the scourge against the daily sacrifice and the desolating transgression that delivers the sanctuary and the host to be trampled underfoot will last (Daniel 8:13). The heavenly answer establishes a precise period: “For two thousand three hundred evenings and mornings; and the sanctuary shall be cleansed” (Daniel 8:14). Doctrinally, these evenings and mornings denote literal twenty-four-hour days and not prophetic years, as is confirmed by defining revelation as the evening and morning vision (Daniel 8:26, Genesis 1:5). This period of approximately six years and four months takes place during the great tribulation, encompassing the Beast's interruption of worship until the cleansing of the temple that the Lord will physically inhabit after His Second Coming (Revelation 11:2).
[15-19] Daniel seeks to understand the meaning of the vision and beholds the likeness of a man, hearing a human voice that commands the angel Gabriel to make him understand the revelation (Daniel 8:15-16). Gabriel addresses the prophet as "son of man," a title of testimony that likens Daniel to the saints who will testify during the tribulation period (Daniel 8:17, Ezekiel 2:1). The heavenly messenger emphasizes that the vision belongs to the end times and the final period of divine wrath against human rebellion (Daniel 8:17, Daniel 8:19). The two horns of the ram represent the kings of Media and Persia, while the male goat is the king of Greece, whose horn is broken to give rise to four weak kingdoms (Daniel 8:20-22).
[20-22] The two horns of the ram literally represent the kings of Media and Persia, while the rough male goat is the king of Greece, whose large horn between its eyes represents the first king of that nation (Daniel 8:20-21). When this main horn is broken, the four horns that arise in its place symbolize four kingdoms that will emerge from the same nation, although without possessing the absolute power of the first monarch (Daniel 8:22). This geopolitical division prepares the historical platform from which the final Gentile confederation will emerge before the Second Coming of Christ.
[23-25] In the final period of these kingdoms, when the transgressors have reached the full measure of their wickedness, a king will arise, haughty in countenance and skilled in intrigue, whose power will be formidable, though not by his own might (Daniel 8:23-24). This dictator will prosper by miraculously destroying the strong and the holy people of the Jews, using his cunning and a false policy of peace to ruin many (Daniel 8:24-25). With satanic pride, he will rise up against the Prince of princes, Jesus Christ, but he will be destroyed without human intervention (Daniel 8:25). This physical destruction will be carried out directly through the word from the mouth of the Savior at His Second Coming, crushing the enemy under the feet of the saints (Revelation 19:15, Romans 16:20).
[26, 27] Gabriel commands the prophet Daniel to close the vision because its full fulfillment is reserved for a very distant time (Daniel 8:26, Daniel 12:4). After receiving this tremendous vision of destruction and judgment, the aged prophet faints and remains ill for several days (Daniel 8:27). Upon regaining his physical strength, he rises to attend to the affairs of the monarch of Babylon, still troubled by the vision, since no one in the Gentile court possessed the spiritual capacity to comprehend such a profound mystery (Daniel 8:27, 1 Corinthians 2:14). This patience teaches the believer to rest with absolute confidence in the words of the Lord, knowing that God's truth will inexorably make its way through human history until the Second Coming of Christ.

[1, 2] In the first year of Darius, son of Ahasuerus, of the lineage of the Medes, Daniel understands from the Scriptures the number of years prophesied by Jeremiah concerning the desolations of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 25:11-12, 29:10). God decreed that the Babylonian captivity would last seventy years because the Hebrew people never observed the Sabbath year for the land required by the Mosaic Law (Leviticus 25:2-4). The Lord promised that the captivity would last one year for each Sabbath year that the nation had neglected (Leviticus 26:34-35, 2 Chronicles 36:21). In this sense, the 490 years that elapsed from the beginning of Saul's reign until the start of the captivity represent a cycle of seventy times seven Sabbaths, establishing a numerical parallel with the prophecy of the seventy weeks that Gabriel would later reveal (Genesis 15:18, Daniel 9:24).
[3, 4] The aged prophet Daniel sets his face to seek the Lord God in prayer and supplication, accompanying his petition with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes as a testimony of his profound humility. Daniel addresses Jehovah under the solemn title of Adonai, recognizing that this word perfectly expresses the divine Trinity in contrast to erroneous interpretations that attempt to separate the divine names (Psalm 110:1, Genesis 18:26-27). Daniel's preparation through severe spiritual discipline demonstrates that the servant of the Most High must cultivate personal holiness to intercede effectively and receive the revelations of Scripture in times of crisis (Philippians 4:6, 1 Thessalonians 5:17-18).
[5-15] Daniel's confession constitutes a national intercession in which he assumes the collective guilt of the chosen people, declaring "we have sinned" before God (Daniel 9:5). The prophet sharply contrasts God's spotless justice with the confusion of countenance that weighs upon the men of Judah, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and all Israel, both those near and those scattered in distant lands, which accurately foreshadows the visitation of Pentecost (Acts 2:39). The sacred text employs multiple synonyms to describe the Hebrew rebellion, such as sin, iniquity, transgression, rebellion, and turning away from the commandments. It also acknowledges the fulfillment of the curse and oath that Moses wrote in the law, since the national disgrace represented just divine retribution for their systematic disobedience (Leviticus 26:14-33, Deuteronomy 29:25-28).
[16-19] Daniel bases his plea for mercy solely on God's justice and faithfulness, and in no way on the supposed merits of the Jewish people or his own personal righteousness (Daniel 9:18). The prophet implores that the Lord's face shine upon the sanctuary, desolate because of the divine testimony before the Gentiles, since the pagan nations mocked the ashes of the temple in Jerusalem (1 Kings 9:7-9). This petition has a background that points toward the great tribulation, a period in which the sanctuary will again be desecrated and plunged into desolation by the Antichrist (Revelation 11:2, 16:10). Israel's national repentance and its cry for the manifestation of divine justice will be fully answered at the Second Coming of Christ (Isaiah 60:1-2, Romans 11:25-27).
[20-23] As the prophet continues praying and confessing his sin and the iniquity of his people Israel, the angel Gabriel interrupts his intercession, appearing in the form of a man at the time of the evening sacrifice (Daniel 9:21). This moment, equivalent to three o'clock in the afternoon in our reckoning, coincides exactly with the time of the Savior's atoning death on the cross (Mark 15:34-37, Acts 3:1). Gabriel was sent swiftly to grant Daniel wisdom and understanding concerning the earlier vision that still remained veiled in his understanding (Daniel 8:27). The heavenly messenger affectionately calls the prophet "greatly beloved," denoting both God's esteem for Daniel and Israel's position as the Lord's beloved people in His sovereign purpose (Psalm 108:6, Romans 11:28).
[24] Seventy weeks of years, equivalent to four hundred and ninety literal years, are determined exclusively for the Jewish people and the holy city of Jerusalem (Daniel 9:24). The error of attempting to include the church of grace or the New Testament period within this chronological calculation is rejected, since divine dealings are strictly directed toward the Hebrew remnant (1 Corinthians 12:13, Romans 11:25-26). The purpose of this time frame encompasses six fundamental objectives: to conclude the national transgression by destroying the idol of the Antichrist, to put an end to sin, to atone for iniquity, to bring in the enduring righteousness of the millennial kingdom, to seal up vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most holy sanctuary of the millennial temple that the Lord will physically inhabit (Ezekiel 40–48, Revelation 20:1–6).
[25] The starting point of the prophetic chronology is established with the promulgation of the decree to restore and rebuild Jerusalem (Daniel 9:25). Among the four edicts issued by Persian monarchs recorded in Scripture (Ezra 1:1-4, 6:7-12, 7:11-26, Nehemiah 2:1-8), the ordinance issued by Artaxerxes in his twentieth year of reign marks the definitive beginning of the seventy weeks, as it specifies the physical reconstruction of the plaza and the wall. The sixty-nine-week period, equivalent to four hundred and eighty-three years, extends until the Messiah, the Prince. Traditional dispensational doctrine places the end of this portion at Christ's triumphal entry into Jerusalem at the first coming (Matthew 21:1-9), while other commentators place its end at his baptism, the moment when the Savior was publicly anointed by the Holy Spirit (Luke 3:21-22, John 1:41).
[26] After the sixty-two weeks have elapsed, which, added to the initial seven, make a total of sixty-nine weeks, it is decreed that "the Messiah will be put to death, but not for himself" by virtue of the vicarious atonement for the Jewish nation (Daniel 9:26, Isaiah 53:8, John 11:49-51). Later, the people of a prince who is to come will destroy Jerusalem and the sanctuary, a prophecy historically fulfilled when the legions of the Roman Empire under Titus razed the city in the year 70 (Luke 21:20-24). However, the end of Jerusalem's desolation will be consummated with a flood and a devastating war during the great tribulation, a period in which the Antichrist, personified as the Roman prince who is to come, will invade Jewish territory (Ezekiel 21:25, Revelation 12:15-16).
[27] The prince who is to come, who represents the Roman Antichrist, will make a firm agreement with many Jews for one week, which constitutes the seventieth week of Daniel (Daniel 9:27). In the middle of that week, which is equivalent to three and a half years of persecution, the dictator will violate the covenant, violently suspending the sacrifice and offering of the rebuilt temple to erect the abomination of desolation in the holy place (Mark 13:14, 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4). While traditional dispensationalists place the entirety of this week in the future after the rapture of the church, another doctrinal perspective suggests that the first three and a half years were fulfilled during Christ's earthly ministry before his crucifixion (Luke 3:23). However, the final three-and-a-half-year period of the great tribulation remains undeniably future, concluding with the judgment and destruction of the desolator at the Second Coming of Christ (Revelation 19:11-21, Romans 16:20).

[1-3] In the third year of Cyrus, king of Persia, a revelation is granted to Daniel, whose Babylonian name is Belteshazzar. The sacred text indicates that the word is true and that the announced conflict is long-lasting (Daniel 10:1). The prophet spends three full weeks in a state of spiritual affliction and mourning, abstaining from choice foods, meat, wine, and ointments (Daniel 10:2-3). This affliction of the elderly prophet in his retirement from public service coincides with the period of strong Samaritan opposition that weakened the hands of the Jews who had returned to Jerusalem to rebuild the temple (Ezra 4:4-5). Thus, Daniel's intercessory prayer demonstrates the profound burden that God's servants experience.
[4-6] On the twenty-fourth day of the first month of Abib, while Daniel was standing by the bank of the great river Hiddekel, which corresponds to the Tigris River, he looked up and saw a man clothed in linen, girded with pure gold from Uphaz (Daniel 10:4-5). The physical description of this extraordinary figure, with a face like lightning, eyes like blazing torches, limbs like polished bronze, and a voice like the sound of a great multitude (Daniel 10:6), coincides with the glorious manifestation of Jesus Christ described in the New Testament (Revelation 1:13-15). This is a theophany, or pre-incarnate appearance of the Lord in his role as the Angel of the Lord, revealing his absolute sovereignty and foreshadowing the judgments that will be executed against the nations at his Second Coming.
[7-9] Only Daniel witnesses the vision, while the men who accompany him are overcome with fear and flee to hide (Daniel 10:7). Left alone before the magnificent presence, the prophet completely loses his physical strength, describing how his vigor turns into corruption and faintness (Daniel 10:8). This extreme weakness and the subsequent falling into a deep sleep on his face (Daniel 10:9) typify the death-like condition of carnal man before divine holiness, similar to what happened to the apostle Paul on the road to Damascus in the book of Acts (Acts 9:3-4). No one can stand before the Lord on their own merits; divine grace is required to be enabled in the service of the Kingdom.
[10-12] A heavenly hand touches the prophet, raising him trembling to his hands and knees (Daniel 10:10). The divine messenger calls him a man greatly beloved, commanding him to stand with understanding, since his prayers were heard from the first day he humbled his heart to gain wisdom before God (Daniel 10:11-12). This readiness of the Lord to hear the cry of His servants highlights that sincere prayer is answered immediately in the heavenly court, although practical results may be temporarily hindered by battles fought in the invisible dimensions of the cosmos (Philippians 4:6).
[13, 14] The divine messenger reveals that the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted him for twenty-one days in the heavenly realms, aided by Michael, one of the chief princes, so that he could prevail alongside the kings of Persia (Daniel 10:13). This prince of Persia does not represent a human ruler of flesh and blood, but a satanic and demonic spiritual power that operates in the heavenly realms, influencing the politics of the Gentile nations (Ephesians 6:12). Michael, identified exclusively as the archangel of the Jewish people (Jude 1:9), intervenes to defend the Hebrew remnant. The revelation brought is intended to help Daniel understand what will happen to his people in the last days, so the full scope of the vision is reserved for the time of the end (Daniel 10:14).
[15-17] Faced with the weight of these solemn declarations, the prophet falls silent and bows his face to the ground (Daniel 10:15). However, one resembling a son of man touches his lips, allowing him to open his mouth to confess his utter weakness before the Lord, declaring that the vision has brought him spiritual pain and deprived him of all physical breath (Daniel 10:16-17). Daniel's muteness and his restoration through divine touch foreshadow the spiritual regeneration of Israel, a nation that in this present age remains blind and mute under dispensational hardening, but which will be made alive by looking upon the pierced Messiah at the Second Coming of Christ (Zechariah 12:10, Romans 11:15).
[18, 19] The One who appeared to be a man touches Daniel again to strengthen him, speaking the words of grace and comfort: “O man greatly beloved, do not be afraid; peace be with you, be strong and courageous” (Daniel 10:19). Upon receiving divine strengthening, the prophet confesses that he is ready to hear his Lord's message. The words used to comfort the prophet evoke the solemn terms with which the Lord promises to restore the remnant of Jacob, both nationally and individually, after the period of tribulation and anguish (Isaiah 43:1-5, Isaiah 61:2-3).
[20, 21] The heavenly messenger inquires whether Daniel understands the purpose of his visitation, announcing that he must return immediately to battle against the prince of Persia, and warning that after his departure the prince of Greece will arise (Daniel 10:20). These spiritual entities invisibly control the successive Gentile empires that will strike the land of Palestine. Finally, the envoy promises to declare what is unalterably recorded in the scripture of truth, noting that he has no other collaborator in this heavenly battle but Michael, the prince of Israel (Daniel 10:21).

[1-4] The revelation brought to the aged prophet Daniel is initially set against the historical backdrop of the Persian Empire and its subsequent clash with the Greek Empire (Daniel 11:1-2). The heavenly messenger announces that three more kings will arise in Persia, and that the fourth will amass extraordinary wealth to mobilize the entire empire against the kingdom of Greece (Daniel 11:2). This fourth wealthy monarch corresponds historically to Xerxes I, whose military campaigns against the Greeks paved the way for the later Western counterattack. The prophecy then jumps to the rise of a powerful king, Alexander the Great, who will rule with immense dominion and execute his sovereign will (Daniel 11:3). However, at the height of his military power, his kingdom will be fragmented and scattered to the four winds of heaven, with divine precision specifying that his empire will not pass to his descendants nor retain the same power he possessed (Daniel 11:4). The conquered territory is divided among his generals, thus preparing the geopolitical stage from which the northern and southern dynasties will emerge, serving as historical types for the final confederation of Gentile nations before the Second Coming of Christ.
[5-9] The military campaigns and political alliances between the king of the south, represented by the Ptolemaic dynasty in Egypt, and the king of the north, corresponding to the Seleucid dynasty in Syria, are described with astonishing prophetic detail (Daniel 11:5-6). Despite attempts to consolidate peace through dynastic marriages, such as the offering of the southern king's daughter to secure an agreement, these human plans failed due to internal betrayals and assassinations (Daniel 11:6). The text specifies that the southern king would outlive the northern king, a prediction that was literally fulfilled when Ptolemy III outlived Seleucus II by four years (Daniel 11:8-9). Dispensational doctrine teaches that this intricate web of political intrigue and territorial invasions has a dual application (2 Peter 1:20-21). What was historically fulfilled during the intertestamental period spiritually foreshadows the deceptive diplomatic treaties that will be made in the territory of Palestine before the Second Coming of Christ.
[10-20] The descendants of the Syrian monarchs continue the military campaigns to strip the Egyptian kingdom of its coastal possessions in Asia Minor (Daniel 11:10-15). The rise of Antiochus III the Great is described, who manages to march with a large army to establish himself triumphantly in the desirable land of Palestine, which is consumed under the weight of his destructive battles (Daniel 11:16). With political cunning, the Syrian monarch gives his own daughter in marriage to corrupt and neutralize the Egyptian king, but she does not remain on his side nor support his geopolitical interests (Daniel 11:17). Later, the prophecy foretells the rise of a tax collector in the glory of the kingdom, historically fulfilled by Seleucus IV Philopator, who attempted to plunder the treasures of the Temple in Jerusalem to pay the war debts imposed by the Roman Empire, only to be suddenly eliminated without anger or military battle (Daniel 11:20). These historical events underscore the instability of earthly thrones in contrast to the unchanging Kingdom that the Lord will establish after His Second Coming.
[21-30] In place of the slain monarch, a vile man arises, to whom the nobility initially does not grant the dignity of the kingdom, but who manages to usurp the throne through intrigue and peaceful flattery, historically identified with Antiochus IV Epiphanes (Daniel 11:21). In the typology of Scripture, this figure is the most accurate type of the New Testament Antichrist, who will present himself to the world as a harmless peacemaker riding a white horse with a bow but no arrows (Revelation 6:2). The biblical term "vile man" is directly associated with practices of sexual perversion (Romans 1:26, Judges 19:24), which foreshadows the morally disordered condition of the end-time global dictator (Daniel 11:37). This usurper will forge a deceitful alliance with the leaders of the earth and break the Prince of the covenant (Daniel 11:22-23). ​​In his southern campaigns against Egypt, the desolator will prevail thanks to the treachery of the very courtiers who feasted at the Egyptian monarch's table (Daniel 11:25-26). Both kings will sit at the same diplomatic table to utter mutual lies in sham peace conferences that will not succeed, for the sovereign end is decreed for the appointed time (Daniel 11:27). Upon returning to his territory, the naval fleets of Chittim, associated in prophetic geography with forces of Roman origin and from the western Mediterranean, will come out to meet him and humiliate him (Daniel 11:30, Numbers 24:24). Filled with indignation, the usurper will return to unleash his fury against the holy covenant, making deals with the apostate Jews who abandon God's law (Daniel 11:30).
[31-35] The usurper's troops will desecrate the temple in Jerusalem, forcibly suspending the daily sacrifice to place the abomination of desolation in the holy place (Daniel 11:31). This event did not find its definitive fulfillment under Antiochus Epiphanes, since the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, during His first earthly ministry, warned His disciples that the abomination of desolation foretold by Daniel was a strictly future event in relation to their time (Matthew 24:15, Mark 13:14). Consequently, the military desecration of the Hebrew sanctuary belongs to the seventieth week of Daniel and will be carried out under the reign of the Roman Beast (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4, Revelation 11:1-2). The apostate Jews who act ungodly against the covenant will be definitively corrupted through flattery and flattery (Daniel 11:32). In contrast, the saints who know their God will stand firm and perform great feats of faith, spiritually instructing the multitudes in the midst of severe persecution (Daniel 11:32-33). This faithful remnant, foreshadowed by the 144,000 sealed ones (Revelation 7:4-8), will suffer martyrdom by sword, fire, captivity, and plunder in order to be purified and made white until the time of the end (Daniel 11:33-35). The perseverance of these saints in observing God's law will be indispensable during this period of judgment that will precede the Second Coming.
[36-39] The text emphasizes the description of the final dictator by directly calling him the king, an absolute ruler who will act according to his own sovereign will (Daniel 11:36). This usurper will become so proud that he will exalt himself above any earthly deity, uttering unheard-of blasphemies against the God of gods (Daniel 11:36, 2 Thessalonians 2:4). The sacred text reveals that the Antichrist will show no regard for the God of his fathers (Daniel 11:37), a Hebrew idiom used exclusively to designate the line of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Exodus 3:15, Romans 11:28). This doctrinal precision demonstrates that the son of perdition will have a Jewish ethnic origin, acting as a false Hebrew messiah who will betray his own nation and devastate his own land (Ezekiel 21:25, Isaiah 14:20). He will also have no regard for the desires of women (Daniel 11:37), which indicates his condition as a sexually perverted and utterly homosexual man in rebellion against the natural order established by God (Genesis 2:24). Instead, the destroyer will pay homage to the god of strength in his military stronghold, a deity his ancestors never knew, worshipping him with gold, silver, and precious stones (Daniel 11:38). This mysterious god corresponds spiritually to the fallen heavenly hosts and to Satan himself (Ephesians 6:12, 2 Corinthians 4:4). The dictator will divide the land of Palestine for material gain and political expediency, foreshadowing modern proposals for geopolitical partition and international peace treaties that threaten divine sovereignty over the inheritance of Jacob (Joel 3:2), judgments that will be swiftly corrected at the Second Coming of Christ.
[40-45] When the time of the end arrives, the king of the south, leading a large Islamic coalition that includes the forces of Egypt, Libya, and Ethiopia, will attack the dictator (Daniel 11:40, 11:43). The king of the north, leading the renewed Roman confederation, will respond with a swift and destructive military offensive, like a whirlwind, invading the territories with chariots, cavalry, and a vast naval fleet (Daniel 11:40). The destroyer will violently sweep into the glorious land of Israel, overthrowing numerous nations and bringing Egypt's economic resources and treasures under his control (Daniel 11:41-43). However, the eastern territories of Edom, Moab, and the main part of Ammon will escape his physical control (Daniel 11:41). This providential exemption of the Transjordanian peninsula foreshadows the safe haven of the rock city of Selah-Petra, where the remnant of Israel will flee to be divinely sustained during the three and a half years of the great tribulation (Matthew 24:16, Revelation 12:6, 12:14). While he is on the military campaign, alarming news from the east and the north will trouble the usurper (Daniel 11:44). The news from the east concerns the march of the two hundred million horsemen of the kings of the east who will cross the Euphrates River (Revelation 16:12), while the news from the far north of the universe points to the opening of heaven and the imminent descent of God's army with the King of kings on his white horse (Revelation 19:11-14, Job 26:7). The destroyer will march out in great fury to exterminate the multitudes, pitching the tents of his royal palace between the seas, on the holy mountain of Zion in Jerusalem (Daniel 11:45). Despite his immense military and satanic deployment in the valleys of Palestine, the Antichrist will meet his end suddenly and irreversibly before the glorious manifestation of Jesus Christ, without any human or demonic power being able to help him before the judgment of the Most High (Revelation 19:19-21, 2 Thessalonians 2:8).

[1] The angel Gabriel reveals to Daniel that in the time of the end, Michael, the great prince who defends the children of the Jewish people, will arise, unleashing a time of distress such as has never been since the existence of nations (Daniel 12:1). This period of extreme affliction on earth corresponds to Daniel's seventieth week and is doctrinally identified as the time of Jacob's trouble (Jeremiah 30:7).
