During this terrible dispensation of judgment, the remnant of Israel whose names are found written in the book of life will be miraculously preserved from physical and moral destruction (Malachi 3:16, Revelation 12:17). This national salvation and the defeat of the Antichrist's forces will be accomplished through God's sovereign intervention at the Second Coming of Christ (Romans 11:26-27).
[2, 3] Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt (Daniel 12:2). This prophetic passage points to the physical resurrection that will take place after the great tribulation, distinguishing it from the pre-tribulation resurrection of the church (1 Thessalonians 4:13-18). The judgment of these Old Testament and tribulation saints is based on their faithfulness and their works of obedience to God's commandments under extreme conditions (Revelation 14:12, James 2:24). Those who are wise, who teach righteousness to the multitude, will shine gloriously like the stars for all eternity, illustrating the sovereign reward the Lord will bestow upon His faithful servants (1 Corinthians 15:41-42). This national resurrection of Israel is also foreshadowed in the prophetic visions of the Old Testament (Ezekiel 37:11-14, Isaiah 26:19).
[4] The Lord commands the prophet to shut up the words and seal the book of prophecy until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4). The truths contained in this book of Daniel will remain veiled from human understanding until the present dispensation of grace concludes (Ephesians 3:1-6). It is foretold that in the last days many will run to and fro, and knowledge will increase extraordinarily (Daniel 12:4). This astonishing increase in human knowledge and the speed of land transportation and communication is an unmistakable sign of the end times, preparing the geopolitical platform for the world control that the Antichrist will exercise before the Second Coming of Christ (Revelation 13:16-17).
[5-7] The prophet sees two heavenly messengers standing on either side of the Tigris River, and a man clothed in linen standing on the waters of the river (Daniel 12:5-6). When asked about the duration of these wonders, the man clothed in linen swears by Him who lives forever that the judgment will last for a time, times, and half a time (Daniel 12:7). This solemn oath defines the three-and-a-half-year period of the great tribulation, during which the desolator will trample the Hebrew sanctuary underfoot and scatter the power of the holy people (Revelation 11:2-3, Revelation 12:14). The man on the water is a theophany of Jesus Christ, who manifests his absolute dominion over the nations before the Second Coming of Christ (Ezekiel 1:26-28, Revelation 10:5-6).
[8-10] Daniel confesses to hearing but not understanding the outcome of these events, receiving the heavenly command to continue on his path, since the words are closed up and sealed until the time of the end (Daniel 12:8-9). It is declared that many will be purified, made white, and tested in the midst of suffering, while the wicked will act wickedly, and none of them will understand the written revelation (Daniel 12:10). This spiritual blindness of the rebels is a just judgment from the Lord for their deliberate rejection of the truth (2 Thessalonians 2:10-12). In contrast, those who understand the Scriptures will perfectly grasp the design of God's timing (Proverbs 2:6, Matthew 24:15).
[11-13] It is established that from the time the daily sacrifice is taken away and the abomination of desolation is placed in the rebuilt temple, 1,290 days will pass (Daniel 12:11). A blessing is pronounced upon the believer who waits for and reaches the 1,335 days (Daniel 12:12). These literal time lapses add thirty and forty-five additional days to the three-and-a-half-year tribulation period, presumably encompassing the judgments of the nations and the cleansing of the temple in Jerusalem for millennial worship (Matthew 25:31-32, Ezekiel 40-48). The Lord commands Daniel to rest in the grave, promising him that he will rise to receive his spiritual inheritance at the end of days, thereby guaranteeing the prophet's bodily resurrection at the Second Coming of Christ (Isaiah 26:19, Job 19:25-27).

[1-3] The ancient Greek word translated as revelation is apo-kalupsis (apocalypse), which means "to reveal" or "to unveil." It is the act of exposing something hidden in the past, the apo-kalupsis being the very person of the Lord Jesus Christ visibly manifested in power to the future inhabitants of the Earth. Revelation comes from the incarnate Word, the Son of Man, manifested in absolute and supreme power as God Himself (John 1:18; Acts 1:2), acting as the one sent by the Father, who remains on His throne in the third heaven. The book consists of 22 chapters, was written between 90 and 95 AD, and constitutes a vision granted to the apostle John during his exile on the island of Patmos. The author is the same as that of the Gospel of John and the First, Second, and Third Epistles of John. The phrase "things that must soon take place" points to the brief window of time in which the sequence of judgments will unfold once initiated, emphasizing its inevitability. Throughout two millennia of church history, humanity has remained on the brink of prophetic fulfillment. The text establishes a sequence of four agents in the transmission of the message: God → Jesus Christ → Angel → John → believers. Through this order, God imparts a revelation concerning past, present, and future events, encompassing the Millennial Kingdom and eternity after the Great White Throne Judgment. In Revelation 19:10, the "testimony of Jesus Christ" is defined as the "spirit of prophecy," that is, the ability to predict the future beforehand. The Word of God and its 66 books support their infallibility in the prophetic element (Isaiah 41:23-26). Although during his earthly ministry the Lord stated that no one knew the day or hour of the judgments on Jerusalem except the Father (Mark 13:1-31), after his ascension he received the complete information from the Father, transmitting it to John before the end of the first century. The apostle describes the events using literal imagery presented in chronological sequence, recording visions of the three heavens and the Earth in the language available to him. Finally, the expression "the one who reads" in the singular and "those who hear" in the plural alludes to the public reading in the congregation. Although various schools of thought omit the teachings of this book, Scripture promises an explicit blessing to those who heed its words, warning that once the events begin, the remaining time will be short.
[4-5] John writes from the island of Patmos to seven real churches located in Asia Minor. The number seven appears repeatedly in the book (7 churches, 7 spirits, 7 stars, 7 lampstands). The phrase "who is, who was, and who is to come" emphasizes the eternity of God, who transcends earthly temporal limitations (Exodus 3:14-15). The "seven spirits before his throne" correspond to the manifestations of the Holy Spirit listed in Isaiah 11:1-2 (the spirit of wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, and the fear of the Lord). Likewise, Jesus Christ is described as the "faithful witness" (a word etymologically linked to the concept of martyr) and as the "firstborn from the dead." This latter title does not imply that he was the first to be resurrected chronologically—since others were resurrected before him only to die later (Luke 7, John 11, Jonah 2)—but rather that he was the first man to be resurrected with an immortal body, never to die again (John 11:25). Furthermore, he is proclaimed "ruler of the kings of the earth," a title that will be fully and visibly realized at the end of the Great Tribulation with the establishment of his earthly kingdom. The amillennialist view, which holds that the Kingdom of God is already present through the gradual improvement of the world, is refuted by clarifying that Scripture often speaks in the present tense of future prophetic events whose consummation is certain. The passage concludes by exalting the blood of Christ as the source of eternal salvation.
[6-7] Every believer is assigned two future offices: kings and priests. The priesthood will be exercised by representing God before humanity during the millennial reign, while the royal dignity will be manifested by ruling alongside Christ in that same thousand-year earthly reign (Revelation 5:9-10). Regarding His coming, the text declares that the Lord "is coming with the clouds," indicating a visible return through the Earth's atmosphere, in accordance with His ascension (Acts 1:9-11, Zechariah 9:1, Matthew 24:30, Psalm 104:3, Matthew 26:64). This manifestation should not be confused with the rapture or translation of the Church, which occurs "in the twinkling of an eye" without prior warning to believers, whereas the Second Coming is a public event visible to the entire unbelieving world. At his manifestation, two groups will express lamentation: "those who pierced him," referring to the Jewish people (Zechariah 12:10), and "all the tribes of the earth," alluding to the Gentile nations (Matthew 24:30).
[8] Jesus Christ himself proclaims to be "the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end," using the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet to affirm his preexistence and eternity above creation (Revelation 22:13). After his ascension, the Lord took his place in the third heaven, beyond the limitations of time and cosmic space, directing human history from Eden. His three offices are summarized in the phrase "he who is (priest), who was (prophet), and who is to come (king)." The title "Almighty" is literally translated as "the one who has his hand over all things," confirming that, although he was born in Bethlehem in historical time, he possesses a prior eternal existence with God the Father (John 1:1-14).
[9-10] Patmos was a rocky and desolate island used by the Roman Empire as a penal colony. The apostle John was exiled there under the reign of Emperor Domitian (81-96 AD) because of his biblical testimony. The expression "was in the Spirit on the Lord's Day" does not refer to Sunday worship or the habitual presence of the Holy Spirit in the believer, but to a spiritual transport or vision in time. The "Lord's Day" constitutes an Old Testament prophetic period encompassing the future judgments of the Tribulation (Joel 2:31, Isaiah 13:9, Jeremiah 46:10). John was spiritually transported to witness and record the end-time events as an eyewitness. The “voice like a trumpet” he hears behind him is the glorified voice of Jesus Christ in majesty, similar to the manifestation witnessed on the Mount of Transfiguration (Matthew 17).
[11] The Lord reiterates His eternal sovereignty as “the first and the last” and commands John to write the vision in a book to send to seven local churches in Asia Minor: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. In addition to their historical existence in the first century, these seven congregations prophetically represent seven successive periods in the history of the Church: Ephesus (90-200 AD), Smyrna (200-325 AD), Pergamum (325-500 AD), Thyatira (500-1000 AD), Sardis (1000-1500 AD), Philadelphia (1500-1900 AD) and Laodicea (from 1900 AD until the rapture, characterized by apostasy; Revelation 3:15-17). Chapters 2 and 3 thus have four levels of application: historical (first-century churches), doctrinal (congregations in the future Tribulation), prophetic (Church Ages), and practical (moral instruction for the contemporary believer).
[12-13] Turning around, the apostle sees seven golden lampstands, which symbolize the seven churches according to the interpretation of verse 20. In the midst of them is the "Son of Man," clothed in a priestly robe reaching to his feet and girded with a golden sash around his chest. The designation "Son of Man" directly evokes the messianic vision of the prophet Daniel in the third heaven (Daniel 7:13-14), recorded approximately six centuries earlier.
[14-15] Jesus' earthly appearance corresponded to that of a first-century Jew; However, in his glorified state, his hair is shown as white as wool or snow, and his eyes as a flame of fire, denoting eternal holiness and penetrating judgment. He is no longer presented merely as the sacrificial Lamb, but as the "Lion of the tribe of Judah" (Revelation 5:5, Genesis 49:9-10). His feet, like fine brass glowing in a furnace, evoke the burnished bronze associated with judgment and the altar of sacrifice (Exodus 27:1-6). His voice, compared to the sound of many waters, reflects the divine power manifested in the Old Testament.
[16] The Lord holds seven stars in his right hand, identified in verse 20 as the angels of the churches. In biblical language, the term "star" is sometimes used to refer to angelic beings (Genesis 1:16, Revelation 6). From Christ's mouth comes a "sharp two-edged sword," a metaphor for the living and effective Word of God that judges and exercises justice (Hebrews 4:12, Ephesians 6:17). His face, shining like the sun, evokes the prophecies about the "Sun of Righteousness" on the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:2).
[17-18] Upon seeing the glory of the resurrected Christ, John falls as though dead at his feet. The impact of heavenly glory on the mortal body is a phenomenon previously documented in Scripture (Luke 9:28-36, Daniel 10:8-9, Isaiah 6:4-5), underscoring the necessity of bodily transformation at the rapture to inhabit the heavenly realm (1 Corinthians 15:51-53). Jesus strengthens the apostle by touching him with his right hand (just as he did with Daniel in Daniel 8:17-18) and declares his victory over death. The statement "I hold the keys of death and Hades" indicates his authority to release the souls held in Hades, a place described in Luke 16:19-31 as having two separate compartments (John 10:9).
[19-20] Verse 19 provides the key to the book's chronological structure in three sections: "the things you have seen" (Christ's vision in chapter 1), "the things that are" (the messages to the churches in chapters 2 and 3), and "the things that will take place after this" (the future events following the rapture of the Church, from chapter 4 to 22). Finally, the mystery of the symbols is interpreted: the seven stars represent the angels or messengers of the churches, and the seven lampstands correspond to the seven churches. The word "angel" (aggelos) designates a messenger function, and can be applied to both human leaders and celestial beings, with the most coherent exegesis leaning towards the latter supernatural option.

[1] Jesus Christ, presented as "the one who holds the seven stars in his right hand," begins sending separate messages to each of the seven churches, starting with Ephesus. This city housed the temple of Diana, a fertility goddess worshipped through a pagan, sexually charged cult. The messages to the seven churches share a recurring structure: they begin with an attribution or description of Christ introduced in chapter 1 and conclude with a promise of eternal life and immortality in the Millennial Kingdom. Historically, the message to Ephesus typologically represents the early apostolic church.
[2-3] Doctrinally, the messages to the seven churches are directed to congregations that will go through the Great Tribulation under a soteriological system of faith plus works. When the present Church is taken to heaven before the Tribulation, the age of grace ends, and the Church returns to its previous operating principles. Ignorance of this multidimensional framework leads to interpretive confusion, such as the false premise that salvation is lost in the present dispensation (2 Timothy 2:15). Therefore, it is essential to distinguish between the historical, doctrinal, and spiritual applications. By declaring "I know your works," the Lord highlights the work, patience, and discernment of Ephesus in testing and exposing false apostles, a characteristic of the apostolic age that contrasts sharply with the passivity toward self-proclaimed contemporary leaders. The early church remained steadfast in protecting sound doctrine without wavering.
[4-5] Despite its doctrinal soundness, the church in Ephesus declined into a ritualistic state, abandoning its "first love" (1 Corinthians 13:1-3). The exhortation to repentance—present in five of the seven letters—responds to the demand for faithfulness for congregations during the Tribulation. The removal of the lampstand symbolizes the loss of their status as witnesses to Christ within the faith system and the works of that future period.
[6] The word "Nicolaitans" comes etymologically from nikao (to conquer) and laos (common people). Their doctrine establishes a priestly or hierarchical caste that exercises dominion over the membership, perverting the biblical teaching of the priesthood of all believers. This pyramidal model, with Babylonian roots and present in the Roman Catholic system as well as in Gnostic secret societies, is explicitly abhorred by Jesus Christ.
[7] The expression "he who has an ear, let him hear" extends the scope of the instruction to the entire Church throughout the ages. The promise to the overcomer includes access to the "tree of life," which was present in Eden (Genesis 2:9) and was guarded by cherubim with flaming swords after the Fall to prevent eternity in a corrupt body (Genesis 3:24). In the Tribulation dispensation, victory involves practical perseverance, while the tree of life will be fully restored during the Millennium (Revelation 22).
[8] The message to Smyrna (a term derived from myrrh, associated with bitterness and death) is addressed to a persecuted church that typifies the ecclesial period between 200 and 325 AD, a time when pagan Rome unleashed violent persecutions. Faced with the imminent martyrdom of believers, Christ presents himself as "the first and the last, who was killed and is alive again," offering the foundation for facing physical death in the Roman Colosseum (John 11:25).
[9] Although Smyrna considered itself poor in earthly matters, the Lord declares it rich in faith (James 2:5). Likewise, the passage denounces the blasphemy of the "synagogue of Satan," made up of those who claim to be Jews without being so. In doctrinal and spiritual terms, this judgment condemns so-called "replacement theology" (the basis of amillennialist and postmillennialist positions), which erroneously maintains that the Church has replaced Israel and that God has ended his covenant with the physical descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Romans 2). Scripture reaffirms that the twelve literal tribes of Israel retain a definitive prophetic role that will be fulfilled at the Second Coming.
[10-11] Smyrna represents the church purified by martyrdom in the Tribulation, which is guaranteed preservation (1 Corinthians 1:7-9). The historical reference to the "ten days" of tribulation is associated with the ten decrees of persecution under the Roman emperors: Nero, Domitian, Trajan, Hadrian, Septimius Severus, Maximinus, Decius, Valerian, Aurelian, and Diocletian. The "crown of life" alludes to the rewards given to believers at the Judgment Seat of Christ after the rapture. For their part, the promise of being freed from the "second death" guarantees that the redeemed will not experience Gehenna or the Lake of Fire after the Great White Throne judgment (Revelation 20:6, 13-14), a clear distinction between the first death (physical and temporary in Hades) and the second death (eternal condemnation in the Lake of Fire).
[12-13] Pergamum (whose name evokes union or marriage) represents the period between 325 and 500 AD, characterized by the syncretism between Christianity and the Roman Empire. Christ is depicted wielding the "sharp two-edged sword," an instrument of divine judgment and of the Word of God (Numbers 22:22-25). The mention of Pergamum housing the "seat of Satan" refers to the relocation of the Babylonian high priesthood (worship of Semiramis, Tammuz, and Nimrod) to that city in 133 BC, as well as the presence of the monumental throne-shaped altar dedicated to Zeus. Despite this pagan environment, the church maintained its faith without denying the name of the Lord, highlighting the martyrdom of Antipas, a faithful witness.
[14-16] The Lord rebukes Pergamum for tolerating the "doctrine of Balaam," referring to the prophet who advised King Balak to lead Israel into idolatry and fornication through alliances with the Moabites to provoke divine judgment (Numbers 25:1-8). In the church of Pergamum, this compromise with the world manifested itself in participation in pagan and immoral rites. Likewise, the persistence of the Nicolaitan doctrine is condemned. The command to repent warns that, without correction, the Lord will confront them with the sword of His mouth (1 Peter 4:17).
[17] The promises to the overcomer present a twofold dispensational dimension. The "hidden manna" spiritually represents Jesus Christ as the bread of life (John 6:35), while doctrinally it alludes to God's provision for the Jewish remnant during the Tribulation persecution (Micah 7:12-14). Similarly, the "white stone" with a new name has a spiritual application for the believer of the present age (1 Peter 2:5) and a doctrinal meaning linked to the new name given to Israel (Isaiah 62:1).
[18-19] Thyatira (meaning "continual sacrifice") prophetically represents the period between 500 AD and the time of the Crusades (11th-12th centuries), a time characterized by the ecclesiastical dominance of Roman Catholicism and the persecution of the faithful remnant. Christ reaffirms himself with the title "The Son of God," emphasizing his absolute deity and divine origin. His eyes "like a flame of fire" manifest his omniscient light, and his feet of "fine brass" symbolize the firmness of his imperishable judgment. The Lord acknowledges Thyatira's growing works in love, faith, service, and patience.
[20-23] The rebuke to Thyatira points to the tolerance shown toward "Jezebel," a figure reminiscent of the idolatrous queen of the Old Testament (1 Kings 16-21, 2 Kings 9:30-37). This false prophetess introduced idolatry, paganism, and spiritual fornication into the church. Because of her refusal to repent, the divine judgment declares that she and her spiritual lovers will be cast into the "great tribulation," a doctrinal reference to the judgment on Jewish unfaithfulness. The execution of their children and the searching of hearts confirm God's sovereign justice and the evaluation of works (2 Corinthians 5:10).
[24-25] The text distinguishes the remnant that has not participated in the "depths of Satan" (occult and sorcery practices that oppose "the depths of God" expressed in 1 Corinthians 2:10). This faithful group is burdened with no other obligation than to hold fast to sound doctrine until the Lord's coming.
[26-29] The overcomer who keeps good works until the end is promised authority over the nations during the Millennial Kingdom (Revelation 20:4-6), ruling with a "rod of iron" through a system of strict justice where rebellion will be broken like a potter's vessel. Likewise, he is promised "the morning star," a title Christ himself uses in Revelation 22:16 to symbolize the light of his glorified presence before the dawn of eternity. The chapter concludes by reiterating the universal call to hear what the Spirit declares to the churches.

[1-3] The prophetic period of Sardis spans from approximately 1000 AD, placing it in the heart of the Middle Ages, marked by the Crusades and the invasions of figures like Saladin and Genghis Khan. This church represents a spiritually dead body that retains only the reputation of life. Doctrinally, the call to vigilance and the warning that the Lord will come like a thief connect with the seventieth week of Daniel (Revelation 16:15) and the prophecies of the Olivet Discourse (Matthew 24-25). Those who ignore the sobriety of His coming will be caught off guard by the judgments, unlike the believers of the present age, who are constituted as children of light and not of darkness (Ephesians 5:8, Matthew 24:42-44).
[4-6] Despite the widespread spiritual death in Sardis, the text highlights a faithful remnant that has not defiled its garments with the corruption of the world. The white garments symbolize the righteousness of the saints (Revelation 3:18, Revelation 16:15, Psalm 45). Doctrinally, the warning against being blotted out of the Book of Life does not apply to the present Church—which possesses the eternal assurance of salvation by grace through faith (Romans 3:24)—but to the Tribulation saints who will be under a soteriological system of faith plus works. The failure to properly divide Scripture leads to theological errors by extrapolating these dispensational warnings to the present age (2 Timothy 2:15). The section concludes by instructing the entire Church to heed the admonition of the Spirit.
[7-9] Philadelphia, a Greek term meaning brotherly love, prophetically represents the church period between 1500 and 1900 AD. It is the only one of the seven churches that receives neither rebuke nor exhortation to repentance. Christ is presented as the holder of the key of David (Isaiah 22:20-23), exercising absolute sovereignty over the gates of salvation. Unlike Laodicea, which is depicted as the church with the closed door, Philadelphia is the church with the open door that guards the Word of God. Their lack of strength is not a slight, but rather a demonstration of divine power perfected in human weakness, in the manner of the apostle Paul (2 Corinthians 12:7-10). Likewise, the Lord promises the vindication of Philadelphia against the synagogue of Satan, a false group already denounced in Smyrna (Revelation 2:9) that promoted the replacement of Israel and postmillennial theology, forcing the persecutors to acknowledge God's love for his faithful church.
[10-13] Verse 10 contains the explicit promise to keep the Church from the hour of trial, that is, the Great Tribulation that will come upon the inhabitants of the earth, a term that designates unredeemed humanity that will suffer divine wrath (Luke 21:36). The warning to hold fast to what one has so that no one takes the crown indicates that the rewards and prizes for service can indeed be lost through negligence (2 John 8). The victor is guaranteed the dignity of being a pillar in the temple of God and citizenship in the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:1-5). This passage has a twofold application: spiritual for the present Church that will inhabit the heavenly Jerusalem (Galatians 4:26-27), and literal for the Jewish remnant that prevails during the Tribulation. The bestowal of the new name seals the believer's eternal belonging to the Lord.
[14-18] Laodicea, whose name means the rights or justice of the people, represents the apostate church of the last days. The expression "the beginning of God's creation" does not suggest that the Son is a created being, but rather that he is the origin, cause, and primacy of all creation (Colossians 1:16-17). Laodicea is an opportunistic church that compromises the truth with the world, remaining lukewarm between spiritual fervor and complete coldness. Their material prosperity has generated a false sense of self-sufficiency, which contrasts sharply with the divine diagnosis that declares them wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked (Luke 18:9-14, Matthew 6:24). Faced with this deception, the Lord advises them to acquire from Him the true gold refined in the fire of tested faith (1 Peter 1:7), the white garments of righteousness (Revelation 16:15), and the spiritual eye salve to restore sight (John 9:8, 2 Corinthians 5:3).
[19-22] Divine discipline toward Laodicea confirms His paternal status, for the Lord rebukes and chastises those He loves (Hebrews 12:5-6), prescribing spiritual zeal and repentance as a cure for lukewarmness. In the final stage of the church age, Christ is excluded from the apostate institution, standing at the door and inviting individual communion with whoever hears his voice. Even the most degraded church is offered the singular promise of sitting with Christ on his throne during the millennial reign. The chapter concludes by reiterating the need to heed the lessons of the seven churches, whose practical summary includes: the preservation of first love in Ephesus, faithfulness in persecution in Smyrna, steadfastness in sound doctrine in Pergamum, rejection of worldly compromise in Thyatira, constant vigilance in Sardis, persevering obedience in Philadelphia, and renunciation of carnal lukewarmness in Laodicea.

[1-3] This passage begins the third section of the book of Revelation, which deals with events that will take place after these events in the future prophetic dimension. As the Great Tribulation begins on Earth, the apostle John hears a voice like a trumpet commanding him to "come up here," and he is suddenly transported to heaven. The open door in heaven, a figure that reappears in Revelation 19:11 with the public descent of Christ, is a typology of the future rapture of the Church, which is removed from Earth before the Tribulation judgment (1 Thessalonians 4:15-18). John's immediate translation in the spirit reflects the nature of both the physical and spiritual rapture (1 Corinthians 15:49-52), since flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of heaven (1 Corinthians 15:50-51). The apostle contemplates God seated on his throne in majesty (Psalm 11:4), a physical, real, and tangible place located in the third heaven, above the material universe. The divine radiance is described as jasper and sardonyx stones, characterized by a crystalline brilliance of purple and blood-red hues, surrounded by an emerald-green rainbow around the throne.
[4-5] Around the throne are arranged twenty-four thrones occupied by twenty-four elders clothed in white robes and with golden crowns on their heads. Regarding their identity, exegesis proposes three main positions: 1) Representatives of the redeemed Church, whose white garments evoke the saints (Revelation 19:8) and whose golden crowns correspond to the awards bestowed at the Judgment Seat of Christ; 2) Representatives of the saints of the Old and New Testaments, that is, the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve apostles; or 3) Heavenly beings created specifically for this ministry around the throne. In any case, Scripture identifies them as beings with human dignity (Revelation 4:9-10). Likewise, from the divine presence emanate lightning, thunder, voices, and seven lamps of fire, physical phenomena that represent the irruption of God's majesty into the created realm, just as occurred on Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:16-19, 20:18-19). The seven lamps correspond to the fullness of the seven Spirits of God (Isaiah 11:1-3, Revelation 1:4).
[6-8] Before the throne stretches a sea of ​​glass resembling crystal, a literal liquid plane that separates the second heaven from the third heaven. Beside the throne dwell four living beings covered with eyes in front and behind, identified as cherubim in Ezekiel 1, Ezekiel 10, and Genesis 3:24, and related to the seraphim of Isaiah 6:2-6. These supernatural hybrid figures find satanic and idolatrous counterparts in ancient mythology and Babylonian, Assyrian, and Egyptian monuments. In biblical exegesis, the four appearances of the cherubim reflect the facets of Christ in the four Gospels: Matthew presents him as the lion of the tribe of Judah, Mark as the suffering calf or servant, Luke as the Son of Man, and John as the eagle, a symbol of divinity. They possess six wings and a multitude of eyes that allow them simultaneous vision in four directions. Unlike the vision in Ezekiel 1:15-26—where these beings moved the divine throne on wheels—in Revelation they are fixed in the heavenly realm. Originally, there were five guardian cherubim, with Lucifer, identified as Satan, being the fifth cherub before his fall, representing the reptilian and fiery realm (Ezekiel 28:14). Their ceaseless acclamation, "Holy, Holy, Holy," proclaims the holiness of the Trinity and its unchanging eternity.
[9-11] Whenever living beings render glory, honor, and thanksgiving to the eternal God, the believer's posture finds its supreme model: the twenty-four elders prostrate themselves before the One who lives forever and ever and cast their crowns before the throne. By this act, they acknowledge that dignity, majesty, and the right to rule belong solely to the Creator, by whose sovereign will all things exist. This cosmic scene of heavenly worship is the glorious panorama that the apostle John beholds when he is transported in the spirit to the third heaven.

[1-4] John sees in the right hand of the One seated on the throne a book written on both sides and sealed with seven seals. Exegesis raises various possibilities regarding its identity: the Book of Revelation itself, the entirety of Sacred Scripture, the book given to the prophet in Daniel 12, or even the title deed to the Earth lost by Adam after the Fall. The command of the mighty angel to open the book implies not only a visual inspection but also the ability to understand its divine mystery (Luke 24:45, Acts 16:14). The inability to find anyone worthy, neither in heaven among the angels and saints, nor on earth among ministers, scholars, or rulers, nor beneath the earth among the demonic hosts, moves John to tears, demonstrating that no creature possesses the merit to release the revelation.
[5-7] One of the twenty-four elders comforted the apostle by identifying Jesus Christ as the Lion of the tribe of Judah and the Root of David, a messianic lineage supported by his human genealogy (Matthew 1:1). Christ's victory over temptation in the wilderness, over sin on Calvary, and over death in the resurrection establishes him as the only one worthy to take the scroll. In the center of the throne appears a Lamb standing as if slain, a physical representation of the Savior bearing the eternal marks of the crucifixion. Its seven horns symbolize the fullness of divine power and rule, representing the horn of salvation (Luke 1:68-69), while its seven eyes represent omniscience and the full wisdom transmitted through the seven Spirits of God. The scene in which the Son takes the scroll from the Father's right hand constitutes an explicit manifestation of the Trinity in the heavenly realm (Psalm 110:1).
[8-10] The act of taking the scroll triggers the immediate worship of the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders, who prostrate themselves, holding harps and golden bowls filled with incense, identified as the prayers of the saints. The new song they sing proclaims the redemption through the blood of Christ of people from every tribe, language, people, and nation—an exclusive hymn of the redeemed Church that takes place in heaven before the opening of the first seal and the beginning of the earthly Tribulation. The promise to establish a kingdom of kings and priests will be fulfilled literally on Earth after the Second Coming (Zechariah 14:4), rejecting allegorical interpretations that confine this dominion to a purely spiritual kingdom in the heavens.
[11-14] Worship expands to include an innumerable multitude of angels around the throne, proclaiming the dignity of the slain Lamb to receive power, riches, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing (Hebrews 1:6). To this cosmic doxology are added all creatures of heaven, earth, sea, and the depths, enabled by divine sovereignty to praise the Creator, just as in the Old Testament the mouth of Balaam's donkey was opened (Numbers 22:21-33). The chapter culminates with the assent of the four living creatures and the prostration of the twenty-four elders before the eternal God, marking the prelude to the execution of redemption and the reclaiming of creation.

[1] When Jesus Christ takes the scroll and proceeds to open the seals, the judgments upon the Earth are progressively unleashed. The events described from chapter 6 through 19 are prophetically identified in the Old Testament as Daniel's seventieth week (Daniel 9), Jacob's time of trouble (Jeremiah 30:7), and the time of trouble (Daniel 12:1). This nomenclature demonstrates theologically that the Tribulation period is intended for the redemption and purification of the Jewish people as the chosen nation, and is not meant for the Gentile Church, which belongs to the dispensation of grace and is removed before these events.
[2] The appearance of a white horse whose rider rides out conquering and destined to conquer has been misinterpreted by Catholic, Mormon, Adventist, Jehovah's Witness, Charismatic, and Neo-Evangelical denominations as a manifestation of Jesus Christ. If such a premise were true, it would imply that Christ already reigns on earth and that his kingdom expands gradually through human conquests, giving rise to the heresy of postmillennialism developed by Augustine, Eusebius, and Origen between 200 and 500 AD. This perspective suggests a humanistic spiritual Darwinism that affirms the world's ceaseless progress. True Christian doctrine depends on correctly identifying this rider. In Scripture, there is only one man with characteristics so similar to Christ that he could supplant him before the deceived masses: the Antichrist. The popular image that reduces Satan to a grotesque being ignores that his nature allows him to manifest as an angel of light, wielding supreme power in the universe after God and possessing the ability to perform miracles and deceptive signs. Satan's counterfeit is evident when comparing Christ and the devil. While Jesus possesses a city that descends like a bride (Revelation 21), Satan also has a city described in the same way (Revelation 17). Jesus declares himself the light of the world (John 8:12, John 9:5), but Satan is called an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14). Jesus Christ holds the title of King of kings (Revelation 19:16), and Satan is king over all the children of pride (Job 41:34). Christ is recognized as the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6), while Satan operates as the prince of this world (John 14:30). Jesus is Lord and true God (John 20:28), but the devil acts as the god of this age (2 Corinthians 4:4). Finally, Christ is called the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5), and the apostle describes Satan as a roaring lion seeking someone to devour (1 Peter 5:8).
[3-4] The second living creature, previously described as having the appearance of a calf (Revelation 4:7), heralds the opening of the second seal. The appearance of the red horse ushers in bloodshed on Earth, taking away peace and causing people to kill one another with a great sword. This event represents the devastating consequences of global warfare, marking the fulfillment of the Lord’s prophetic warning about the outbreak of wars and rumors of wars.
[5-6] The opening of the third seal and the command of the third living creature reveal a black horse whose rider holds a pair of scales in his hand. The weight in the hand indicates extreme rationing where staple foods like wheat and barley must be meticulously measured against the exorbitant cost of a denarius per ration. The command not to harm the wine or the oil reflects a stark social contrast where luxury items remain available to the wealthy while the lower classes perish from hunger, a phenomenon foreshadowed by the oppression described in Job (Job 24:11). This extreme scarcity confirms the worldwide pestilences and famines foretold for the last days (Matthew 24:7, Ezekiel 4:11).
[7-8] The fourth cherub announces the opening of the fourth seal, giving way to the pale horse whose rider is named Death, closely followed by Hell. The destructive sequence initiated by the Antichrist, war, and famine culminates in the annihilation of a quarter of the world's population, perishing by the sword, starvation, plagues, and wild beasts. This unprecedented extermination will wipe out billions of people, imposing a judgment of inconceivable magnitude.
[9-10] After the opening of the fifth seal, John observes under the altar the souls of the martyrs beheaded for the sake of the Word of God and the testimony they held. The passage demonstrates that the human soul is not an incorporeal energy or an ethereal spark, but an entity with a specific bodily form that possesses a voice, memory, and the capacity to wear white robes. The soul retains anatomical characteristics invisible to the flesh. As evidenced in the parable of the rich man in Hades, the soul possesses eyes, a tongue, and vocal cords while the physical body lies inert in the tomb (Luke 16). This refutes the doctrine of annihilationism or the notion that hell is merely an earthly grave. These souls under the altar do not constitute the Church, since the redeemed of this age have already been glorified and worship the Lamb in heaven (Revelation 5). This new group, martyred during the Tribulation, cries out for divine vengeance against the inhabitants of the earth, assuming their heavenly position in Revelation 7.
[11] Upon receiving white garments, they are commanded to rest for a while until the number of their fellow servants and brothers destined for martyrdom is complete. The persecution of the Tribulation will intensify when the Antichrist and the false prophet demand the worship of the image of the beast under penalty of death (Revelation 13:15). Alongside this demand, an angel will fly through the sky warning humanity to avoid the mark of the beast at all costs (Revelation 14:9-11). Anyone who receives the mark will irrevocably lose their chance of redemption, which is why countless people will turn to Christ and suffer martyrdom. The predominant form of execution will be beheading, echoing the capital punishment of pagan Rome suffered by figures such as James and the Apostle Paul (Acts 12, Romans 16:4). This capital punishment typologically fulfills the sacrificial regulations of the Old Testament, where every expiatory victim had their head cut off (Leviticus 1:8, Leviticus 1:15).
[12-13] The sixth seal introduces the upheavals that precede the climax of the Tribulation, materialized in precise astronomical cataclysms already foretold in the Gospels (Matthew 24:29, Mark 13:24-26, Luke 21:25, Acts 2). A great earthquake shakes the planet, the sun turns black, and the moon takes on the appearance of blood. The prophets of the Old Testament had already described how the Earth would wobble, losing its stability (Isaiah 13:13, Isaiah 24:20) and how the heavenly powers would darken their radiance (Joel 2:30-31, Joel 3:15-16). The falling of the stars from the sky like unseasoned figs (Luke 21:26) could allude to a meteor shower upon the Earth's surface, but in the prophetic context, the term "stars" frequently identifies angelic beings. This interpretation aligns with the expulsion of Satan and his hosts described later, when the dragon's tail drags a third of the fallen angels to Earth (Revelation 12:4). The materialization of the impact of angelic bodies resisting the earthly shock coincides with the fall of Lucifer (Luke 10:18), creating a scenario where mortal inhabitants must necessarily coexist with spiritual entities banished from heaven.
[14-16] The commotion continues when the sky recedes like a rolled-up scroll, an unprecedented phenomenon that could open a visual breach from Earth into the dimension of the third heaven (Matthew 24:29). Simultaneously, the relocation of every mountain and island suggests a catastrophic shift in the Earth's axis. Faced with such desolation, the kings, magnates, and wealthy individuals who sustained the Antichrist's empire attempt to evade divine scrutiny by hiding in caverns and fortified underground structures. In their desperation, they cry out to the rocks, begging to be buried before facing God's face and the wrath of the Lamb. This statement reveals that world leaders acknowledge the coexistence of at least two persons of the Trinity in heaven (Revelation 3:21). Such distorted theological understanding could stem from the pronouncements of the resurrected Antichrist himself, who will rule through deception and riddles (Daniel 8:23).
[17] The confirmation of the great day of his wrath corresponds to Old Testament prophecy uttered more than seventy-five times throughout Scripture. This is the definitive time when divine holiness executes judgment on the wickedness and rebellion of human history (Isaiah 2:12, Isaiah 13:6, Ezekiel 13:5, Ezekiel 30:3, Joel 1:15, Joel 2:1, Joel 3:14, Amos 5:18, Obadiah 15, Zephaniah 1:7, Zephaniah 1:14-15, Zechariah 14:1, Malachi 4:5, Acts 2:20, 1 Thessalonians 5:2, 2 Thessalonians 2:2, 2 Peter 3:10). God's wrath does not represent an uncontrollable emotional outburst, but rather the perfect application of His justice upon those who deliberately reject salvation. The Lord will judge the living wicked with equity and will raise the unredeemed dead to pronounce their final sentence (Revelation 21:8). While the world is in the Age of Grace and benefits from divine mercy, the day of sovereign wrath is inexorably advancing.

[1-3] The book of Revelation presents four parallel accounts of the Tribulation period, structurally corresponding to the four Gospels that narrate the first coming of Christ. The first account spans chapters 5 and 6 and focuses on the seals. The second account extends from chapter 8 to 11 and describes the trumpet judgments. The third account begins in chapter 12 and concludes in Revelation 14:20, detailing the activities of the Antichrist. The fourth and final account comprises chapters 15 through 19, culminating in the seven bowls and the destruction of Babylon the Great. This pattern demonstrates that the prophetic events do not follow a strictly chronological and consecutive order from the first chapter to the last. Chapter 7 functions as a prophetic interlude situated between the opening of the sixth and seventh seals. In this scenario, four angels are positioned at the four cardinal points of the Earth to halt the destructive winds. These winds represent the divine judgment manifested regularly in the Old Testament (Hosea 13:15), likely alluding to the temporary withholding of devastating weather phenomena such as tornadoes and hurricanes. A fifth angel bursts forth from the east to halt the action of the previous four angels. A delay in the judgments upon the Earth is imposed for the specific purpose of sealing God's servants on their foreheads. This seal literally consists of inscribing the Lord's name upon them.
[4-8] The designation of the 144,000 individuals from all the tribes of the children of Israel constitutes a key doctrinal passage frequently misrepresented by groups such as Seventh-day Adventists, Mormons, and Jehovah's Witnesses. These groups misappropriate a future dispensation by applying to their members a promise that belongs exclusively to the Hebrew people in the midst of judgment. The text rejects all spiritualization and affirms that these sealed ones are not Christians or spiritual Jews, but literal Israelites. The prophecy confirms that God will resume direct dealings with the nation of Israel during this final seven-year period known as Daniel's seventieth week and Jacob's time of trouble (Daniel 9:24-27, Jeremiah 30:7). The designation of servants of our God is historically applied to Israel, and the method of sealing refers to the ink mark on the forehead described by the prophet Ezekiel with the sacred name of Jehovah (Ezekiel 9:1-8). The apostle lists twelve thousand sealed ones from the tribes of Judah, Reuben, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, and Benjamin. This list presents a notable variation from the Old Testament records, omitting the tribes of Dan and Ephraim and inserting Levi and Joseph. The exclusion of Dan and Ephraim corresponds to the divine punishment established against any tribe or family that led the people into idolatry, warning that they would be wiped out from among the nations (Deuteronomy 29:18-21). It was precisely in the territories of Dan and Ephraim that Jeroboam erected the golden calves. Furthermore, Scripture prophetically describes Dan as a serpent and a lion cub (Genesis 49:17, Deuteronomy 33:22), figures that typify Satan and suggest a prophetic connection with branches of apostate Judaism serving dark agendas. Having been removed from this list of special protection, the descendants of Dan and Ephraim will have to face the ravages of the Great Tribulation without the immunity the seal grants against the demons of the abyss described later (Revelation 9:4).
[9-12] After witnessing the sealed Israelites, the vision reveals a second group comprised of an innumerable multitude of Gentiles from every nation, tribe, people, and language. While the 144,000 represent the protected Jewish remnant on Earth, this great multitude corresponds to the Gentiles martyred during the Tribulation who are now in the third heaven. It is imperative to connect these believers clothed in white robes with the souls under the altar who previously cried out for justice (Revelation 6:11) and with the promises of cleansing mentioned to the churches (Revelation 3:4, 18). The white garments symbolize the righteous and human justice of the saints (Revelation 19:8), while the palm branches in their hands evoke the praise of the Savior and King during His triumphal entry into Jerusalem (John 12:12-16). This group comprises those who rejected the mark of the beast, refused to worship the image of the Antichrist, and steadfastly bore witness to Jesus Christ by giving their lives. The dispensational distinction is clear when we observe that this multitude remains before the throne as servants, while the Church is in heaven as the Bride of Christ, destined to reign and rule with Him. The loud acclamation of these martyrs acknowledges God and the Lamb as the only source of salvation, a stark contrast to the false system of peace offered by the Antichrist. In response to this testimony of redemption, all the angels, living beings, and elders prostrate themselves to join in a doxology of blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honor, and power toward the Creator, exalting the saving work accomplished in the midst of the greatest judgment on Earth.
[13-17] The interaction between one of the elders and the apostle contains a fascinating prophetic mystery. If we assume that the twelve apostles are part of the twenty-four heavenly elders, there is a theoretical possibility that the glorified John, seated on his throne, was questioning the earthly John caught up in the vision. When asked about the identity and origin of the multitude, the apostle responds with complete submission, declaring that the answer belongs to the elder. Divine revelation identifies this multitude as those who have come out of the great tribulation and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb. This statement prevents the passage from being applied doctrinally to Christians of the present age. The Church itself has been washed directly in the blood of Christ (Revelation 1:5), while this group washes its garments through the act of its own martyrdom and faithful resistance. Although the modern believer faces afflictions necessary to enter the kingdom (Acts 14:22), the text explicitly specifies the prophetic Great Tribulation, making any spiritualization of this event a false teaching. Further compelling evidence that this is not about the Church lies in its role of continuous service within the heavenly temple. In the present dispensation, the Christian's body is the temple of the Holy Spirit, and in the eternal state of the New Jerusalem, no physical temple will exist. The promise of never again suffering hunger, thirst, or extreme heat corresponds to the literal sufferings this multitude endured on Earth, especially in the context of the coming plagues where the sun will scorch humanity with great intensity (Revelation 16:8-9). Finally, the ultimate comfort is that the Lamb will shepherd them and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes. This divine act of consolation is mentioned only twice after the close of the Church Age, this being the first instance and Revelation 21:4 the second. The literal record of tears in heaven refutes the popular notion of immediate and unwavering joy after death, for there will be sorrow and weeping at the Judgment Seat of Christ over lost rewards, wasted opportunities, and burned works (1 Corinthians 3:12-14), as well as profound and inevitable grief after the Great White Throne Judgment as they behold the eternal fate of unredeemed friends and family falling into the Lake of Fire (Revelation 20:11-15).

[1-2] In this verse begins a new account of the Tribulation period, developed from chapter 8 to 11 under the imagery of the trumpets. The silence in heaven for almost half an hour represents a period of awe at the severity of the coming judgments. The seven angels receive seven trumpets, instruments that in the Old Testament sounded the alarm of war and caused panic in the enemy, here announcing God's direct intervention.
[3-4] The mention of the censer and the golden altar before the throne confirms the existence of a real heavenly temple or tabernacle, which served as the original model for the earthly sanctuary of Moses (Hebrews 8:5). The daily work of the Hebrew priest in offering incense was an imitation of heavenly actions, where the prayers of the saints ascend before God accompanied by the smoke of incense.
[5-6] The angel fills the censer with fire from the altar and throws it to Earth, unleashing voices, thunder, lightning, and an earthquake. This act responds to the prayers of the saints ascending like incense (Psalm 141:2, Luke 1:10), connecting directly with the cry of the souls of the martyrs pleading for justice in Revelation 6:9-10. Following this, the seven angels prepare to sound their trumpets in unbroken sequence.
[7] The first trumpet affects the earth's vegetation: hail and fire mixed with blood are hurled down, burning up a third of the trees and all the green grass. The detail that the hail comes with blood is evidence of a retributive divine judgment that reminds the world of the blood of the martyrs shed on Earth.
[8-9] The second trumpet describes a great fiery mass—similar to a volcano erupting in the middle of the sea—that turns a third of the waters into blood. The term “the sea” frequently refers to the Mediterranean Sea, from which the Beast will later emerge (Revelation 13:1). This judgment results in the death of a third of the sea creatures and the destruction of a third of the ships.
[10-11] The third trumpet impacts the sources of fresh water. A great burning star called Wormwood, a term associated with bitterness and sorrow, falls upon a third of the rivers and springs, bittering and poisoning the water supplies, causing the death of many people who drink it.
[12] The fourth trumpet strikes the celestial luminescence, darkening a third of the sun, moon, and stars. This may be due to a dense atmospheric disturbance following the first trumpets in the middle of the Tribulation, or it may be due to the celestial signs preceding the second coming of Christ in accordance with Revelation 6:12. Although the exact chronology is complex, the event literally alters the astral light.
[13] An angel flies through the midst of heaven—referring to outer space or the atmospheric region within the doctrine of the three heavens—proclaiming in a loud voice a threefold “Woe!” about the inhabitants of the Earth, emphasizing the terrible gravity of the three remaining trumpets that astonishes even the celestial creation.

[1-2] The fallen star represents a person or human-like being from outer space who is given the key to the abyss. This abyss is literally a bottomless pit sealed in the Earth's surface that leads to the planet's center, where Hades, a Greek term often translated as hell, is located (Matthew 4:29). Hell is a tangible place, not an allegory. In the Old Testament, it was the abode of souls divided into two sections, as Jesus confirmed in the story of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31). Paul teaches that after his death, Christ descended to the lowest parts of the Earth and, upon ascending, led captivity captive (Ephesians 4:8-10), a heavenly event that will be imitated in the future by the Beast when it rises from the abyss (Revelation 17:8). The entity that opens the pit could be an angel sent by God to execute judgment, or it could be Satan or a fallen angel seeking destruction, the latter being the most likely since it is described as an entity that fell from heaven. The opening of the pit releases a dense cloud of smoke similar to that of a large furnace or volcanic eruption, which pollutes the air and obscures the sun.
[3-6] From the smoke emerge supernatural locusts endowed with the power of scorpion venom. Unlike ordinary biological locusts that die in the smoke and lack a leader (Proverbs 30:27), these have a king over them (Revelation 9:11). They are forbidden to harm vegetation or trees, receiving the explicit command to torment only those men who lack the divine mark on their foreheads, thus protecting the 144,000 who are sealed. The punishment inflicted lasts exactly five months for the purpose of leading the inhabitants of the earth to repentance (Revelation 9:20-21). The torment will be so unbearable that people will seek death but will not find it. This phenomenon aligns with the current advance of transhumanism, where the integration of biotechnology and technological components into the human body will prevent a person from dying even if they wish to.
[7-12] John describes the appearance of these beings as horses prepared for war, with crowns like gold and human faces. Their long, woman-like hair evokes the androgynous figure of Baphomet and ancient pagan goddesses used in occultism. Their iron armor and the thunder of their wings like chariots reveal a hybrid and mechanical nature. In biblical prophecy, iron has a negative connotation and symbolizes the mixing of technology with humanity or with angelic seed in the final empire (Daniel 2:41, 43). The reiteration of the five-month timeframe confirms the literal fulfillment of the event. These locusts obey a king called the angel of the abyss, known as Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek, names that mean the Destroyer and are associated with the son of perdition (2 Thessalonians 2:3, John 17:12). There is a connection with the fourth horseman of death at the beginning of the judgments (Revelation 6) and with the delegation of the power of death (Hebrews 2:14), indicating that after the period of torment without the possibility of suicide, death will once again strike humanity en masse at the end of this first woe corresponding to the fifth trumpet.
[13-19] When the sixth trumpet sounds, a voice comes from the four horns of the golden altar of heaven, ordering the release of four angels bound at the Euphrates River, a historical region linked to Babylon and the origin of the world's false religious systems. These beings are fallen angels of extreme danger, held captive by God in chains of darkness in the depths of Tartarus (Jude 6, 2 Peter 2:4). Their release at the appointed hour, day, month, and year is intended to exterminate the third of humanity remaining after the previous judgments (Revelation 6:8), using the immense destructive power that a single angel possesses against thousands of people (Isaiah 37:36). These angels are accompanied by an army of two hundred million riders on supernatural horses with breastplates of fire, hyacinth, and sulfur (Isaiah 5:26-30, Psalm 57:4, 2 Kings 2:11). This military force that crosses the Euphrates is also linked to the kings of the east in the final battle (Revelation 16). The horsemen spew fire, smoke, and sulfur from their mouths and harm with serpent-like tails, combining the ferocity of the lion (1 Peter 5:8) with the deceitful nature of the serpent (Revelation 12:9).
[20-21] Despite the death toll and the magnitude of the plagues, the survivors stubbornly refuse to repent of the works of their hands, persisting in the worship of demons and inanimate idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood. The works of their hands represent their science, their technological development, and a civilization built without God. They also show no remorse for their murders, thefts, fornications, or sorcery, a term derived from the Greek word referring to the use of drugs and medicines. With their consciences seared (1 Timothy 4:2), humanity rejects repentance and prepares for direct confrontation with the Creator.

[1-2] Like chapter 7, Revelation 10 serves as a prophetic prelude to the sounding of the seventh trumpet. The mighty angel surrounded by a cloud, with a rainbow above his head, his face like the sun, and his feet like pillars of fire, typifies Jesus Christ in his manifestation as the Angel of the Lord. The cloud is consistently associated with the Son of Man (Revelation 1:7, Acts 1:9), while his radiant face coincides with the vision of Christ at the opening of the scroll (Revelation 1:14-15). The rainbow evokes the divine covenant and the throne of God (Revelation 4, Hebrews 9, Hebrews 10). The open scroll in his hand corresponds to the scroll that only the Lamb was worthy to open (Revelation 5:1-7). By placing his right foot on the sea and his left on the land, the Lord claims sovereignty and absolute authority over creation.
[3-4] The loud cry, like the roar of a lion, alludes to Old Testament passages describing Christ's triumphant return in majestic power (Isaiah 42:13, Jeremiah 25:30, Hosea 11:10, Joel 3:16). Following this cry, the voices of the seven thunders utter a message that the apostle prepares to write down; however, a voice from heaven commands him to seal up what the thunders have spoken and omit its written record (Isaiah 58:1, Psalm 29). This passage confirms the existence of divine decrees and mysteries reserved exclusively for God's counsel, which were not revealed to humanity in the Scriptures.
[5-7] The angel's posture of gigantic proportions over the Mediterranean Sea and the land of Palestine demonstrates the power to manifest colossal dimensions, exposing the crude imitation that Satan attempted with the antediluvian giants (Genesis 6). Raising his hand to heaven, the angel swears by the eternal Creator of the heavens, the earth, and the seas that the divine delay will be no longer prolonged. This oath announces the direct fulfillment of the prayer for the coming of the Kingdom (Matthew 6:10). With the sounding of the seventh trumpet (Revelation 11:15), the mystery of God will fulfill its purpose as announced to the prophets, ushering in the physical and visible dominion of Christ on Earth.
[8-11] The command to take the little book from the angel's hand and devour it constitutes a mandate for the spiritual assimilation of God's Word (Ezekiel 2:9). The parchment is sweet as honey in the mouth upon receiving the magnificent divine promises, but it produces bitterness in the stomach upon digesting the terrible judgments and afflictions that must occur before the consummation of the kingdom. After assimilating this message, the apostle receives the commission to prophesy again before peoples, nations, languages, and kings, a task accomplished through the recording of the book of Revelation.

[1-2] The command to measure the temple, the altar, and the worshippers establishes the existence of a literal third temple on Earth during the Tribulation period. This earthly precinct is distinct from the heavenly sanctuary mentioned in other passages and will be the stage where the Antichrist will seek to be worshipped (2 Thessalonians 2:4, Matthew 24:15, Daniel 11:31). The text specifies that the outer court is given to the Gentiles, who will trample the city underfoot for forty-two months. Although Jerusalem is called the holy city because of the promises and the future restoration of the remnant of Israel, its present spiritual condition during this period of apostasy equates it with Sodom and Egypt because of its rejection of Jesus Christ.
[3-6] During the 1,260 days, equivalent to the second half of the Tribulation, God grants authority to two witnesses clothed in sackcloth. Identified in the prophecy as the two olive trees and the lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth (Zechariah 4:11-14), the text affirms their nature as real human beings endowed with extraordinary abilities, such as breathing fire to consume their enemies. Their ministry, through the power to shut the heavens to prevent rain, turn water into blood, and strike the earth with plagues, identifies these two figures with Moses and Elijah. Moses and Elijah represent the Law and the Prophets, having manifested identical powers in the Old Testament (1 Kings 17:1, 2 Kings 1:10, Exodus 7:17-25, Exodus 10:14-15) and having appeared together at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:3-4, Malachi 4:5).
[7-10] Upon concluding their testimony, the Antichrist, first designated as the beast that rises from the abyss, engages in physical combat against the two witnesses and kills them. Scripture confirms that the beast primarily represents a resurrected man infused with infernal power and not merely a political structure (Daniel 7:17, Revelation 13:18). The bodies of the two prophets are publicly displayed for three and a half days in the square of Jerusalem, spiritually identified as Sodom and Egypt because of the city's covenant with the world ruler (Daniel 9:27). The literal fulfillment of peoples, lineages, languages, and nations simultaneously viewing their bodies is explained by modern global technological coverage via satellites and digital screens. Unrepentant humanity celebrates the event by exchanging gifts, relieved by the temporary cessation of the torment caused by the plagues and the proclamation of the Kingdom message.
[11-14] After the three and a half days, the Spirit of life sent by God enters the two prophets, causing their resurrection and instilling profound awe in the observers. The designation of the Spirit of God, rather than the formulas of the Church Age, underscores the dispensational nature of the period. A great voice summons them from heaven, and both ascend on a cloud before the eyes of their enemies, constituting a literal ascension of two servants and not the rapture of the Church. Simultaneously, a devastating earthquake destroys a tenth of Jerusalem and causes the death of seven thousand people, prompting the surviving remnant to fear and give glory to the Creator. With these events, the second woe concludes.
[15-19] The sounding of the seventh trumpet triggers the third woe and proclaims that the kingdoms of the earth become the sovereign possession of the Lord and his Christ. This declaration confirms that world government did not previously belong directly to God but to Satan (2 Corinthians 4:4, Luke 4:5-6). In response to this manifestation, the twenty-four elders prostrate themselves in worship, prophetically framing the events that extend from the Tribulation and the Millennial Kingdom to the Great White Throne Judgment (Revelation 20:8-12). The scene culminates with the opening of the heavenly temple and the manifestation of the ark of the covenant amidst flashes of lightning, voices, thunder, an earthquake, and hail, revealing God's original dwelling place.

[1-2] The vision of the woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars frames the identity of the nation of Israel during the Tribulation. Exegesis rejects the Roman Catholic interpretation that identifies the woman with Mary, as well as the amillennial or Protestant position that attempts to equate her with the Church. The Church is referred to in the New Testament as wife, bride, or virgin (2 Corinthians 11:2, Revelation 21:9), while Israel is historically typified as the woman. The hermeneutical key to the passage lies in Joseph's dream, where the sun represents Jacob, the moon his mother, and the stars his brothers of the twelve tribes (Genesis 37:9-10). The woman, being pregnant, gives birth to the Lord Jesus Christ, the offspring of Abraham and David (Galatians 3, Romans 1:1-6), a passage that applies to the Hebrew nation within the dispensational framework of Jacob's time of trouble.
[3-4] The second sign reveals a great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns, explicitly identified as the ancient serpent, the devil, and Satan (Revelation 12:9). Scripture distinguishes Lucifer as an anointed cherub with wings (Ezekiel 28:14) and not as an ordinary angel, describing his true reptilian form as the multi-headed Leviathan that dwells in the depths (Job 41, Psalm 74:14, Isaiah 27:1). The seven heads allude to the great historical kingdoms and empires subdued under Satan's power. The dragging of a third of the stars represents the physical fall of a third of the angelic beings to Earth during the Tribulation. This massive descent of fallen celestial entities will promote the ultimate end-times deception, presenting these beings as extraterrestrial intelligences or gods to captivate rebellious humanity, similar to the days of Noah (Genesis 6, Luke 17:26-27).
[5-6] The male child born to the woman is Jesus Christ, prophesied to rule all nations with an iron rod and raptured to God's heavenly throne after his resurrection. Following this redemptive event, the prophecy contemplates the time of Tribulation, where the woman, the nation of Israel, flees to the desert to a place prepared by God, a region historically associated with Petra in Jordan, to be sustained for 1,260 days, equivalent to three and a half years (Hosea 2:14-19).
[7-12] A great battle erupts in the second heaven between Michael with his angels and the dragon with his demonic forces. Defeated by the heavenly army, Satan is definitively expelled from the heavenly realms and cast down to Earth along with his angels, constituting the third of his five prophetic falls (Ezekiel 28:14-16, Luke 10:18, Revelation 20). Having lost his access as the accuser of the brethren before the divine throne (Job 1, Job 2), the devil descends in great wrath, knowing that his time is short. While the heavens rejoice, the heavenly voice pronounces a woe upon the inhabitants of the earth and the sea, highlighting that the Tribulation saints overcome the serpent through the blood of the Lamb, the word of their testimony, and the offering of their lives unto martyrdom.
[13-17] Upon being cast down to the earth, the dragon unleashes a fierce persecution against the woman who gave birth to the male child. Israel is given the two wings of a great eagle to fly into the wilderness, an allusion to the divine supernatural help and transport that evokes the Exodus from Egypt and protection in times of crisis (Exodus 19:4, Matthew 24:20). There, she is preserved from the presence of the serpent for a time, times, and half a time, equivalent to three and a half years. The serpent spews forth a river of water from its mouth to drown the woman, a cataclysm or torrent of armies recorded in Scripture (Daniel 9, Jeremiah 47:2), but the earth opens its mouth and swallows the flood. Filled with fury, the dragon wages war against the remnant of the seed of Israel who keep God's commandments. The observance of the law during the Tribulation corresponds to the framework of the Old Testament reinstated for Israel (Leviticus 27:34), differing from the Church Age where the Christian is saved exclusively by grace through faith apart from works of the law (2 Timothy 2:15).

[1-4] The beast that emerges from the sea represents the Antichrist manifested as a political and military leader backed by the dragon. The seven heads allude to the historical empires dominated by satanic power—Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome, and the final alliance of ten nations—whose rulers have functioned as types of the prophetic dictator. The ten horns with ten diadems symbolize the ten kings who will confederate their dominion with the beast during the Tribulation (Daniel 2:31-47, Revelation 17:11-14). Its appearance combines features of the leopard, the bear, and the lion, assuming the sum of the might of the powers described by the prophet Daniel (Daniel 7:1-7). The mortal wound of one of its heads and its subsequent healing stage a false resurrection through possession by a demonic spirit that rises from the abyss (Revelation 11:7). This wound and resurrection marks the transition of the character from a man of sin to the son of perdition (2 Thessalonians 2:3), provoking global admiration and explicit worship of both Satan and the beast.
[5-10] The beast is granted a mouth that utters blasphemies against the name of God, His heavenly tabernacle, and the believers raptured before the Tribulation, exercising direct dominion for a period of forty-two months, equivalent to the second half of Daniel's seventieth week. During this time, it wages persecution and physical warfare against the Tribulation saints until it overcomes and kills them by beheading (Revelation 20:4). Its totalitarian rule extends to every tribe, people, language, and nation, receiving worship from those whose names were not written in the Lamb's book of life, the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world (1 Peter 1:20, Revelation 20:15). The warning to the inhabitants of the Earth emphasizes that there will be no neutrality toward the regime: resistance will entail martyrdom or total exclusion, constituting the ultimate test of faith and patience for the saints of this period.
[11-15] The vision introduces the second beast that rises from the earth, the False Prophet, completing the satanic trinity alongside the dragon and the Antichrist. Appearing as a harmless lamb but speaking like a dragon, this religious and occult leader wields the authority of the first beast and induces humanity to worship him. The False Prophet performs great wonders and calls down fire from heaven in the sight of men (Matthew 24:24), imitating the miracles of Elijah and Moses to legitimize himself before the world (1 Kings 18, Exodus 7:10-11). Following the temporary death of the first beast, which leaves permanent marks on its right eye and arm (Zechariah 11:15-17), the False Prophet promotes the creation of an image with the breath of life. This talking, autonomous statue represents the convergence of technology, robotics, and sorcery, ordering the execution of anyone who refuses to worship it (Daniel 3:1-25).
[16-18] The beast's totalitarian system imposes a literal, physical, and visible mark on the right hand or forehead as a mandatory requirement for conducting business transactions. The spiritual interpretation of the passage, attempted by groups such as Seventh-day Adventists regarding Sabbath observance, is dismissed, confirming that the mark imitates the divine sealing (Revelation 7:3-4) and corresponds to the elimination of physical money in a digital financial system. The number of the beast, 666, is the number of man and reflects humanity's attempt to elevate itself to the divine status of the Trinity. The typology of King Solomon, who received 666 talents of gold annually before his apostasy (2 Chronicles 9:13), illustrates the dual nature of the prophetic figure. The mark will not only restrict trade but will also be linked to transhumanist advances aimed at altering human biology, binding humanity to prolonged suffering before divine plagues without the possibility of death (Revelation 9:6, Revelation 16:2).

[1-5] The Lamb standing on heavenly Mount Zion with the 144,000 sealed represents the translation of this remnant of Israel to the third heaven (Hebrews 12:22, Galatians 4). The passage distinguishes heavenly Mount Zion, the Jerusalem above, from earthly Mount Zion, which remains in bondage. The sound like the roar of many waters, thunder, and harps accompanies the divine presence and the voice of Christ (Psalm 29:3, Ezekiel 43:2, Exodus 19:16-20, Revelation 1:15, Revelation 4:5, Revelation 15:2-3, Revelation 19:6). The 144,000 sing a new song—the song of Moses and of the Lamb (Deuteronomy 32, Revelation 15:3)—that intertwines law observance with faith in Christ, reflecting the dispensational system of salvation by faith and perseverance through works active during the Tribulation (Revelation 12:17, Revelation 14:12). The description of these servants as virgin men in the plural identifies them as the Israelite saints of the Tribulation (Matthew 25), distinguishing them from the Church, which is a single, pure virgin in the singular (2 Corinthians 11:2, Psalms 45:13–14, Song of Solomon 6:8–9). These men are presented as pure and undefiled firstfruits before the throne of God.
[6–8] An angel flying through the sky proclaims the everlasting gospel to the Gentile inhabitants of the earth. Scripture confirms that angels appear in human form without wings, unlike the winged cherubim (Genesis 18:1-2, Ezekiel 10:3-22, Hebrews 13:2). The eternal gospel differs from the gospel of grace preached to the Church by the Apostle Paul (Acts 20:24, 1 Corinthians 15:1-4), constituting one of the four expressions of good news in the Bible, along with the gospel of the kingdom and the glorious gospel (Matthew 24:14, Romans 2:16, Titus 2:13). This message exhorts the nations to fear God, give Him glory, and worship the Creator in the face of the imminent divine judgment (Galatians 1:8-11). Next, a second angel announces the fall of Babylon the Great, the corrupt metropolis that intoxicated the nations with the wine of her spiritual fornication, revealing the nonlinear nature of the book of Revelation by foreshadowing later events (Revelation 17).
[9-13] The third angel loudly warns of the irrevocable condemnation for all who worship the beast, its image, or receive its mark on their forehead or hand. Such individuals will drink the undiluted wrath of God and suffer eternal torment with fire and sulfur in the presence of the angels and the Lamb, refuting the doctrine of annihilationism by stating that the smoke of their torment rises forever and ever, without rest day or night (Revelation 20:10). In this trial scenario, the patience of the saints who keep the commandments and the faith of Jesus is required through a combination of faith and works. A voice from heaven proclaims blessed the martyrs of this period who die in the Lord, whose labors are finished and whose deeds follow them to be evaluated at the subsequent judgment (Revelation 11:18), unlike the Church whose believers have already been judged at the Judgment Seat of Christ.
[14-20] The vision of the figure like the Son of Man sitting on a white cloud with a golden crown and a sharp sickle represents a previous manifestation of Jesus Christ in his power as executioner (Numbers 22:21-33, Mark 9:2, Luke 24:13). This appearance precedes the equestrian descent recorded at the Second Coming (Zechariah 14:1-21, Ezekiel 44:1-3, Revelation 19:11). The passage describes two distinct agricultural harvests: the first reaping, prompted by the heavenly command, corresponds to the wheat harvest or the post-tribulation rapture of the saints (Deuteronomy 16:9, Isaiah 17:6, Matthew 13:39, James 5:7); the second harvest represents the grape harvest of the earth, where an angel with authority over fire gathers the clusters of the wicked (Revelation 14:17-18).
