The grapes are thrown and trampled in the great winepress of God's wrath outside the city of Jerusalem, unleashing a literal massacre where the blood reaches the height of the horses' bridles along 1,600 stadia (Isaiah 63:1-6, Joel 2:2-3, Revelation 18:13-16). This violent intervention consummates the execution of the wrath of the Lion of the tribe of Judah upon the rebel armies gathered in Palestine.

[1] Chapter 15 introduces the fourth and final account of the Tribulation period under the figure of the seven bowls or flasks, concluding the sequence previously presented through seals, trumpets, and the actions of the Antichrist. The seven final plagues constitute the consummation of God's wrath upon unrepentant humanity, manifesting signs and wonders in the heavenly realm as a divine response to the rejection of the Messiah before the establishment of the millennial kingdom.
[2-4] The vision of the sea of ​​glass mingled with fire places the conquerors of the beast, its image, its mark, and its number in the third heaven, above the starry regions, moments before Christ's return to Earth. These Tribulation saints sing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb (Deuteronomy 32, Revelation 14:12), articulating the Mosaic law with faith within the faith-and-works framework of this dispensation. The proclamation of Christ as King of the nations anticipates His literal reign from Jerusalem (Zechariah 14, Isaiah 2:1-4, Micah 4:1-2, Psalms 72, Psalms 110), dismissing the premise that He is called king over the Church in the present age and refuting prosperity theology, which distorts this distinction. The present Church forms its spiritual body under His head as it bears the cross in a world temporarily ruled by Satan, reserving the literal reign for the glorious coming upon the throne of David.
[5-8] The opening of the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony in heaven reveals the original heavenly pattern that served as the model for the sanctuary of Moses (Hebrews 8:5). From it emerge seven angels clothed in pure linen and girded with golden sashes around their chests, wearing garments similar to those of Christ in the initial vision (Revelation 1:13-14). One of the four living creatures gives the seven angels seven golden bowls filled with the wrath of the eternal God. Divine glory and power fill the temple with smoke, preventing any being from entering until the full execution and consummation of the plagues upon the inhabitants of the Earth, in analogy with the historical manifestation in the earthly tabernacle (Exodus 40:34-35).

[1-2] The commanding voice emanating from the heavenly temple orders the seven angels to pour out the flasks or bowls of divine wrath upon the Earth, unleashing a series of judgments parallel to the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 9). The first plague consists of painful and pestilent boils or sores that afflict exclusively those who received the mark of the beast and worshipped its image, carrying out the direct retribution announced in chapter 14 upon the followers of the Antichrist.
[3-7] The second and third angels pour out their flasks upon the sea, the rivers, and the springs of water, turning all the water into thick blood, like that of a dead body. This mass destruction brings about the death of every living soul in the oceans, a term that can refer to both biological marine life and the emergence of submerged hybrid civilizations, analogous to the pre-flood creatures of Genesis 6, in accordance with the warning of judgment upon the inhabitants of the sea (Revelation 12:12). The angel of the waters proclaims the absolute justice of this retributive plague: since ungodly humanity shed the blood of the saints and prophets, they are now given blood to drink. A voice from the altar confirms that the judgments of Almighty God are true and just, dismantling the ancient satanic accusation that questions divine righteousness (Genesis 3:4-5).
[8-11] The fourth bowl is poured out upon the sun, altering its radiation to scorch humanity with fire. This cataclysm, potentially resulting from the destruction of the ozone layer or a stellar disturbance (Isaiah 30:26), intensifies humanity's physical torment. The fifth angel pours out his flask directly upon the throne of the Antichrist, whether in rebuilt Babylon, Rome, or Jerusalem, plunging his empire into dense darkness (Exodus 10:20-23). ​​Amidst sunburn, darkness, the stench of blood, and sores, people gnaw their tongues in agony. However, upon crossing the point of no return in their depravity, they reject repentance and blaspheme the name of the God of heaven (Jeremiah 17:9).
[12-16] With the pouring out of the sixth bowl, the Euphrates River dries up completely, opening a vital geographical corridor for the advance of the armies from the East (Daniel 11:44), a massive contingent of two hundred million troops (Revelation 9:16). Simultaneously, from the mouths of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet—the satanic trinity—emerge three unclean spirits in the form of frogs. These demonic entities perform deceptive wonders and miracles to gather world kings and leaders, promoting a unified global resistance against the imminent arrival of the Lord (Psalm 2:2-5). At this critical juncture, Jesus Christ issues an interpolated warning about his surprise return as a thief. This return does not describe the rapture of the Church, but rather the post-tribulation rapture of the Israelite saints, prior to the direct military confrontation (Matthew 24:29-31, Psalm 50:3-5, Isaiah 26:12-21). The nations are thus gathered in the valley of Megiddo, a place designated in Hebrew as Armageddon.
[17-21] As the seventh angel pours out his bowl into the air, the voice from the throne proclaims, "It is done," marking the consummation of divine wrath, in parallel with the Savior's redemptive declaration on the cross (John 19:30). The event is accompanied by flashes of lightning, voices, thunder, and a global earthquake of unprecedented magnitude (Isaiah 24:1-23). The seismic wave fragments Jerusalem into three parts, collapses the Gentile capitals of the world, and sinks islands and mountains, leveling the earth's surface in preparation for the geological renewal of the Millennium (Isaiah 35). Babylon the Great, the seat of the world religious system, receives the final cup of wrath. Finally, hailstones weighing approximately twenty-five kilograms lash rebellious humanity, replicating the historical judgments executed during the conquest of Canaan and against Egypt (Joshua 10:8-13, Exodus 9:24, Ezekiel 38:22). Despite the force of the plagues, people persist in their blasphemy against God, culminating the conflict in total rebellion.

[1-2] One of the seven angels of the bowls reveals the judgment of the great harlot seated on many waters, a figure symbolizing a real metropolis and a globally influential apostate religious system (Ezekiel 16:26). The expression “many waters” represents multitudes, nations, and languages ​​under her influence (Revelation 17:15). The kings of the earth commit spiritual fornication through alliances and idolatry with her, while the inhabitants of the planet become intoxicated with the wine of her corruption and the fruits of her commercial network (Revelation 18:11-13).
[3-6] John is taken in the spirit to the wilderness where he sees a woman seated on a scarlet beast full of blasphemous names, with seven heads and ten horns. The vision exposes the satanic pattern of counterfeiting, contrasting the heavenly Jerusalem with the corrupt Babylon backed by the political and religious power of the Antichrist (Revelation 12:3, Revelation 13:1). Clothed in purple, scarlet, gold, precious stones, and pearls, the woman displays great wealth and regal pretensions (Ezekiel 28:13-17). In her hand, she holds a golden cup filled with abominations, alluding to the global Tribulation religion. On her forehead is written the name MYSTERY: BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF FORNICATIONS AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH, linking her origin to the ancient rebellion at Babel (Genesis 11:1-8) and the pagan systems that arose from it. The woman appears drunk with the blood of the saints and the martyrs of Jesus, demonstrating that the false religious structure will be the main persecutor of God's people.
[7-11] The angel explains the mystery of the woman and the beast. It is declared that the beast was, is not, and is about to rise from the abyss to go to destruction (2 Thessalonians 2:3, John 17:12, Acts 1:25). This ascension describes a spirit or principality emerging from the abyss within Hades (Luke 16:19-31) to possess the Antichrist after his mortal wound and subsequent resurrection (Revelation 11:7-8, Zechariah 11:15-17). The seven heads represent seven mountains on which the woman sits, denoting the geography of Rome and a historical sequence of seven empires: Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, the Roman Empire in John's day, and the future confederation of ten nations. The beast is also an eighth king belonging to the seven, reflecting his dual existence as the man of sin before his death and the son of perdition after his resurrection (2 Thessalonians 2:3).
[12-14] The ten horns represent ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom but who will receive authority as kings for one hour alongside the beast. In keeping with the mixture of iron and clay in Daniel 2:41-43, these rulers represent an alliance with non-human or fallen angelic seed during the Tribulation (Genesis 6, Revelation 12:4). With a shared purpose, they surrender their power and authority to the Antichrist and gather to physically fight against the Lamb in Palestine. The Lamb will defeat them because He is Lord of lords and King of kings, accompanied by His called, chosen, and faithful saints (Luke 1:68-69, Revelation 19:11-21).
[15-18] The angel confirms that the waters represent peoples, multitudes, nations, and languages ​​under the harlot's dominion. After his resurrection and proclamation of self-deification (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4), the Antichrist and the ten kings betray the harlot, strip her of her skin, eat her flesh, and burn her with fire, destroying the ecumenical system to impose exclusive worship of the beast. God places it in their hearts to carry out His sovereign purpose until the divine words are fulfilled (John 17:17). Finally, the woman is identified as the great city that reigns over the kings of the earth, the resurrected Babylonian global capital.

[1-3] The descent of an angel endowed with great authority, whose radiance illuminates the Earth, heralds the final fall of Babylon the Great. This metropolitan entity represents the commercial pillar of the Antichrist's world government, which operates in alignment with the religious pillar described in the previous chapter. The prophetic passage connects the building of this metropolis with the vision of the prophet Zechariah concerning the woman in the metal container taken to the land of Shinar (Zechariah 5:5-11). The declaration that the city becomes a dwelling place of demons, a haunt of every unclean spirit, and a refuge for detestable birds anticipates the visible manifestation and physical intrusion of fallen celestial entities and hybrid beings who will populate the Earth during the Tribulation (Genesis 6:4, Luke 17:26, Matthew 8:28-34). All nations and rulers of the planet succumb to idolatrous fornication and the illicit enrichment derived from their system of opulence.
[4-8] A voice from heaven exhorts the remnant of God's people to leave the corrupt city so as not to share in its sins or receive its plagues, in analogy with the historical deliverance of Lot before the destruction of Sodom (Genesis 19:1-26). The sins of Babylon pile up to heaven as at the ancient Tower of Babel (Genesis 11:1-4). In the moments before the Second Coming, after the pouring of the seventh bowl (Revelation 16:19), God judges the iniquities of the city, decreeing a double and relentless retribution according to its deeds (Hebrews 8:12). The pride of the harlot, who proclaims herself invulnerable queen in her heart, is broken in a single day through plagues, famine, mourning, and consuming fire.
[9-19] The kings and powerful of the earth watch from afar as the smoke of the burning city burns, lamenting the sudden collapse of their commercial ally in the span of a single hour. The world's merchants join in the weeping as the flow of goods of opulence comes to a standstill. These goods include precious metals, royal robes, exotic woods, spices, choice foods, vehicles, slaves, and human souls. This catalog of merchandise reflects the level of extreme consumption and plutocratic exploitation imposed by the regime on impoverished nations (James 5:1-3). The rulers and sailors of the port metropolis watch in dismay as judgment is carried out, throwing dust on their heads as a sign of mourning for the total loss of the wealth and power the city held.
[20-24] While the Earth mourns, the heavens, the holy apostles, and the prophets are summoned to rejoice at the execution of divine vengeance. A mighty angel hurls a great millstone into the sea to symbolize the violence and irreversibility with which Babylon is buried, never to be found again. All artistic activity, musical production, creative expression, milling, and the city's light are permanently silenced. The cessation of the voices of husband and wife confirms the end of the corrupt unions imposed on antediluvian society (Genesis 6:4, Matthew 24:38). The ruin of the great city is a response to the global deception exercised through its sorcery, a term linked to the use of potions, drugs, and alchemical or transhumanist manipulation, and to its historical culpability in the shedding of the blood of prophets, saints, and all those martyred on Earth (Matthew 23:35-36).

[1-6] After the destruction of Babylon the Great, heaven bursts into praise with the Hebrew exclamation Hallelujah, reaffirming the incorruptibility of divine judgment in avenging the blood of the martyrs. The rising smoke of torment confirms the perpetuity of the soul's condemnation (Revelation 14:11). The twenty-four elders and the four living creatures prostrate themselves before the heavenly throne above the sea of ​​glass, joining their voices with a multitude proclaiming the visible manifestation of God's kingdom. The prophecy envisions the transition from the present spiritual realm to the earthly and tangible dominion of Christ after the ephemeral reign of the Antichrist (Luke 17:20-22, 2 Thessalonians 2:4, 2 Peter 1:11, Revelation 11:15).
[7-10] The Wedding of the Lamb celebrates the heavenly union of Christ with his Bride, the Church, after she has been purified at the Judgment Seat of Christ (1 Corinthians 3:10-16, 2 Corinthians 5:10-11, Ephesians 5:27). Typified in the Old Testament in the story of Isaac and Rebekah (Genesis 24:1-17) and developed in the Song of Solomon and Psalm 45, the vision distinguishes the roles in the family of God: the Bride, the Bridegroom, the Bridegroom's friends, the Israelite maidens, and the Gentile guests. The garments of fine white linen represent the righteous works of the saints approved after the judgment. The wedding supper of the Lamb formally contrasts with the bloody supper of the great God (Matthew 26:29, Revelation 19:17). When John attempts to worship, the angel refuses, reminding him that only God should be worshiped (Exodus 20:3-5) and that Jesus' testimony constitutes the essence of all prophecy (John 5:39).
[11-16] The opening of heaven reveals Christ as the rider on a white horse called Faithful and True, waging the righteous war in the context of the final battle (Genesis 3:15, Isaiah 63:1-5). His eyes, like flames of fire, reflect the radiant energy of his glorified body (Matthew 17:1-8, Hebrews 1:3), while his many diadems and his garments stained with the blood of his enemies confirm his absolute dominion. Known as the Word of God (John 1:1), he is followed by the heavenly armies composed of the glorified saints of the Church Age, riding on white horses (2 Corinthians 10:4, Jude 1:14, Joel 2:1-11). From his mouth comes a sharp sword to strike down the nations and to rule them with a rod of iron (Psalm 2:9, Isaiah 11:4). His robe displays the title KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS, marking his prophetic journey from Sinai, Edom, and the Jordan River to the Mount of Olives, where he crosses the eastern gate of the temple (Zechariah 14:4, Ezekiel 44:1-3).
[17-21] An angel in the sun summons all the carrion birds to the great God's dinner to feed on the corpses of kings, captains, and warriors (Ezekiel 39:1-20, Job 39:19-30). The beast, the ten kings, and the world elite—comprised of marked men, transhumanist forces, and genetic hybrids—gather in the Valley of Megiddo to resist the Creator (Psalm 2:2-5, Jude 1:6-7). The intervention of the heavenly King is swift: the Antichrist and the False Prophet are arrested and thrown alive into the lake of fire burning with sulfur, the place corresponding to the second death (Matthew 25:41, Revelation 20:14-15). The rest of the rebel armies are destroyed by the word from the mouth of Christ, their flesh being devoured by birds at the consummation of the Day of the Lord (Proverbs 12:18, Zechariah 14:3).

[1-3] The descent of the angel with the key to the abyss and a great chain signifies the beginning of the millennial reign of Jesus Christ on Earth, replacing the defeated world government of the Antichrist (Luke 21:24). The text highlights the corporeal and material nature of heavenly beings, confirming that both the angel and Satan possess a visible physical existence that allows for literal chaining with heavenly chains (Daniel 8:15, 1 Kings 19:7-15, Genesis 32:24-32, 2 Peter 2:4, Jude 6). Lucifer receives four distinct names: the dragon, because of his reptilian form; the ancient serpent, because of his intrusion into Eden; the devil, as the accuser; and Satan, as the supreme adversary. Satan's confinement in the abyss for a literal thousand years guarantees a period free from demonic influence (Daniel 2:45). This event fulfills the premillennial covenants established with Abraham (Genesis 12:2-3, Genesis 17:4-8, Isaiah 65:8-10, Jeremiah 30:22, Micah 7:19-20), with David regarding his throne in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 7:16, Jeremiah 23:5-8, Ezekiel 37:23-24, Luke 1:32-35, Jeremiah 23:5, Isaiah 9:7, Habakkuk 2:14, Micah 4:2, Micah 4:6-7, Zechariah 14:17), and with Israel concerning the geographical possession of the promised land (Deuteronomy 30:1-10, Isaiah 65:9, Ezekiel 36:28-29), refuting amillennial positions and Historical postmillennials. At the end of this millennium, Satan will be released for a brief time to test the generations born during the Messianic theocracy.
[4-6] The vision presents the establishment of thrones granted to the saints to exercise judgment and reign with Christ for a thousand years. The passage distinguishes between the believers of the Church Age, who were promised thrones and crowns for their faithfulness (Matthew 19:27-30, Romans 8:17, 2 Timothy 2:12, Revelation 1:6, Revelation 5:10), and the Tribulation saints who suffered martyrdom by beheading for refusing the mark of the beast (Matthew 25:31, 34). All of them participate in the first resurrection, which unfolds in three stages according to the pattern of the Hebrew festivals (Deuteronomy 16:16, 1 Corinthians 15:22-25): the firstfruits, composed of Christ and the Old Testament saints (Matthew 27:52-53); the harvest, represented by the rapture of the Church (2 Timothy 2:19, Ephesians 5:30, 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18); and the ears of grain corresponding to the resurrection of the Tribulation martyrs and Old Testament saints (Ezekiel 37, Revelation 7:9-14, Revelation 14:1-3). The second death has no power over these victors. In contrast, the other ungodly dead remain in Hades until the end of the millennium, at which time they will experience the second resurrection, or resurrection of condemnation (John 5:29), to face final judgment and eternal separation in the lake of fire.
[7-10] When the thousand years are completed, Satan is released from his prison and begins his final revolt by deceiving the nations located in the four corners of the earth, collectively known as Gog and Magog. During the millennium, the Earth will experience a theocratic restoration where the animal creation will regain its original meekness (Genesis 1:29, Isaiah 2:4, Isaiah 11:6-9, Isaiah 35:9, Isaiah 65:25, Jeremiah 31:8, Zephaniah 3:19, Zechariah 14:8-10). However, the mortal populations who survived the Tribulation and their descendants (Isaiah 65:20, Zechariah 14:16-19, Matthew 25:34, 40, 46), who outwardly obeyed Christ's iron rod, will manifest their latent Adamic rebellion (Revelation 2:27, 12:5). Satan gathers this countless multitude to surround the beloved city of Jerusalem and the camp of the saints, which is connected to the heavenly suspended New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:23-27). The rebellion is instantly crushed by fire from heaven that consumes the invaders (2 Peter 3:10). Next, the devil is thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur to be tormented eternally alongside the beast and the false prophet, culminating the five stages of his prophetic fall (Ezekiel 28:14-16, Luke 10:18, Revelation 12:9, Revelation 20:1-2, Matthew 25:41).
[11-15] The Great White Throne Judgment is the final appearance before the Creator seated on the throne, in whose presence the present earth and heaven are dissolved by fire (Daniel 7:9-10, 2 Peter 3:7, 2 Peter 3:10). This judgment is distinct from the Judgment Seat of Christ for the Church and the judgment of the living nations (Matthew 25:31-46), focusing exclusively on the condemnation of the ungodly dead. The sea delivers the dead or spiritual entities confined since the flood (Genesis 6:4, 1 Peter 3:20), while death and Hades deliver the souls that remained in them. The dead are judged by the things written in the books according to their works (Exodus 32:32, Daniel 12:1, Malachi 3:16, Philippians 4:3, 2 Timothy 2:13, Revelation 3:5-6). Anyone whose name is not found written in the Book of Life is thrown into the lake of fire along with death and hell, thus experiencing the second death (Hebrews 9:22, Leviticus 4, Leviticus 17:11, Genesis 2:17, 1 Corinthians 6:3, Jude 6). Scripture suggests a final physical degradation of the condemned wicked into an inextinguishable reptilian or worm-like form in the midst of eternal fire (Psalms 22:6, Isaiah 13:19-22, Isaiah 34:6-17, Isaiah 35:7, Isaiah 66:24, Ezekiel 20:47-49, Mark 9:44).

[1-4] The vision of the new heaven and the new earth reveals the renewal of existing creation through divine intervention (Ecclesiastes 1:4, Psalms 78:69, 2 Peter 3, Hebrews 1:10-12). The disappearance of the sea alludes to the withdrawal of the watery barrier or sea of ​​glass that separated the stellar regions of the third heaven (Job 38:30, Job 41:31-33), restoring direct communication after the tearing of the veil (Matthew 27:51). The New Jerusalem descends as a bride prepared for the Lamb, spiritually linking itself to the victorious Church (Galatians 4:26, Revelation 19:7-8) in the typology of Adam and Eve (Genesis 2:21-23), distinguishing itself from Israel as the bride of Jehovah (Jeremiah 3:14, Isaiah 54:5). The heavenly city constitutes a physical metropolis and antithesis of Babylon (Revelation 17, Revelation 18), framing the dispensational distinction between Jews, Gentiles and the Church (1 Corinthians 10:32). God establishes his ultimate dwelling place with humanity (Exodus 25:8-9, 2 Samuel 7:1-17, 2 Chronicles 3:1-2, Ezra 1:2-3, Ezekiel 40:2, 2 Corinthians 5:1-4), eradicating the weeping, pain, and spiritual and immaterial death that began after the Fall (Genesis 3:5, Genesis 3:22, Genesis 5:5, 1 Corinthians 15:42-44).
[5-8] The Creator, seated on the throne, proclaims the absolute renewal of all things, completing the final purification of creation (Genesis 1:1-2, Genesis 7:17-24, Daniel 2:44, Proverbs 22:17). The Father's declaration as the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end (Isaiah 41:4, Isaiah 44:6, Isaiah 48:12) aligns with the divine attributes and shared eternity of Jesus Christ (Revelation 1:8, Revelation 1:17, Revelation 22:12, 1 John 1:1-2, John 1:3, Colossians 1:15-16, Revelation 3:14, Matthew 1:25). Salvation and access to the fountain of the water of life are offered freely to all who suffer spiritual thirst (Revelation 22:17). The victorious inheritance and divine sonship are promised to the overcomers who persevere (Revelation 2-3, 1 John 4:4, 1 John 5:4), while the cowardly, the unbelieving, the vile, the murderers, the sexually immoral, those who practice magic arts, idolaters, and liars receive their portion in the lake of fire and sulfur, which constitutes the second death (Mark 8:36, John 3:16).
[9-14] One of the seven angels of the bowls shows the vision of the Bride, the wife of the Lamb, revealing the holy city of Jerusalem descending out of heaven (2 Corinthians 11:2, Revelation 19:7). The heavenly metropolis is envisioned as a resplendent structure furnished with the dwellings prepared for the Church (John 14:2, Revelation 20:9, Revelation 21:23-27), its luminosity resembling crystal jasper. A towering wall protects the city with twelve gates guarded by twelve angels (Genesis 3:24, Revelation 21:27), three facing each of the four cardinal directions and inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel. The twelve foundations of the wall bear the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb, harmoniously intertwining the Old Testament dispensation with the New Testament Church in the city's structure.
[15-21] The golden reed used by the angel determines the exact and literal proportions of the New Jerusalem. The city rises as a cubic structure, twelve thousand stadia on each side, equivalent to one thousand nine hundred and thirty kilometers in length, width, and height, evoking the proportions of the Most Holy Place (Ephesians 3:18). The wall is one hundred and forty-four cubits thick, according to the human measurement used by the angel, confirming the masculine and anthropomorphic appearance of angelic beings (Genesis 6:1-6, Genesis 18:1-22, Genesis 19:1-26, Judges 13:1-13, Galatians 4:14, Luke 24:3-6). The wall is made of jasper, and the city of pure gold, transparent as crystal. The twelve foundations are adorned with twelve precious stones corresponding to the breastplate of the high priest (Exodus 28), unlike the incomplete ornamentation of the fallen cherub (Ezekiel 28:13-14), while the twelve gates consist of individual pearls leading to streets of translucent gold.
[22-27] The absence of a physical temple in the city is because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb constitute its living sanctuary. The New Jerusalem does without celestial luminaries such as the sun and moon, being perpetually illuminated by the radiance of God's glory and the presence of the Lamb (Genesis 1:3, Isaiah 24:23, Isaiah 60:1, Zechariah 14:7, 1 John 1:5, Revelation 22:16). The saved nations and the kings of the earth walk in its light and bring honor to it during the millennial period (Psalm 72:12, Isaiah 60:14, Isaiah 66:23-24, Zechariah 8:22-23, Zechariah 14:16-17, Revelation 20:13). Its gates remain continually open, for there is no night in it. The absolute holiness of the city prevents the entry of any impure being or practitioner of abomination, guaranteeing exclusive access for those whose names remain written in the Lamb's book of life (Revelation 20:8-10).

[1-2] The river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and the Lamb describes the inner glory of the New Jerusalem, distinguishing it from the earthly waters of the millennial temple described in Ezekiel (Ezekiel 47:1-11, Zechariah 14:8). While the earthly sanctuary has priestly ordinances and animal sacrifices (Ezekiel 46:3), the heavenly metropolis lacks a physical temple, as the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple itself (Revelation 21:22), confirming two seats in the Messianic government. The tree of life located in the plaza and on the banks of the river produces twelve fruits each month, associated with the cycle of twelve prophetic divisions in Scripture (Deuteronomy 32:8), and its leaves provide healing for the nations. The Church, already endowed with a glorified and immortal body (1 Corinthians 15:52-55), does not require these leaves; they benefit the mortal survivors of the Tribulation and their descendants who participate in the millennial order.
[3-5] The eradication of the curse in the New Jerusalem reverses the judgment pronounced in Eden (Genesis 3:17-19), dissolving physical death and spiritual separation. Unlike in the Old Testament, where mortal man could not behold the face of God without dying (Exodus 33:20-23, Daniel 10:8-11), the redeemed servants will see His face in resurrected and incorruptible bodies capable of bearing His glory (1 Corinthians 13:12), bearing His name on their foreheads (Revelation 14:1). The absence of night and artificial or solar lights in the city is due to the direct radiance of the Lord God and the Lamb (Revelation 21:23, John 8:12), without this negating the physical permanence of the sun and moon as eternal lights for the cosmos (Psalm 89:36-37). His servants will reign eternally, definitively fulfilling the promises of life and dominion given to the body of believers (Romans 6:22-23, Titus 1:2).
[6-10] The words of the vision are ratified as faithful and true by the Lord God of the prophets, emphasizing the imminent execution of the events for those who go through the period of judgment. The expression of an imminent return resonates as an encouragement of perseverance for the saints persecuted during the Tribulation. Faced with John's prostration, the angel refuses to be worshipped and declares himself a fellow servant of the prophets and those who observe the Scriptures, reaffirming that worship belongs exclusively to God (Exodus 20:3-5, Matthew 8:2, Hebrews 1:6). Unlike the prophet Daniel, who was commanded to seal up the vision until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4), John is instructed not to seal up the words of the book because of the imminence of their prophetic fulfillment.
[11-15] The proclamation concerning the fixing of moral status points to the irreversibility of spiritual destiny once the Lord is revealed, leaving the unrighteous in their wickedness and the holy in their eternal sanctification. Christ proclaims his coming with the reward to repay each person according to their works (2 Corinthians 5:10), assuming the titles of Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, attributed to God the Father (Isaiah 41:4, Revelation 1:8, Revelation 21:6) and confirming his eternal deity and pre-existent presence (John 1:1-3, Colossians 1:15-16). Mortals inhabiting the earth during the Millennium must keep God's commandments to maintain their right to the tree of life and enter the city through the pearly gates (Leviticus 23, Zechariah 14:16-19, Ezekiel 43:18-27). Those designated as dogs, a biblical term for ungodly Gentiles (Matthew 15:26-28), along with sorcerers, fornicators, murderers, idolaters, and liars, are excluded from the heavenly realm (Revelation 21:27), coexisting outside on the ruined earth during the Millennium until the final rebellion of Gog and Magog (Revelation 20:7-9).
[16-21] Jesus Christ testifies to his message to the churches by proclaiming his messianic titles as the root and offspring of David (Isaiah 11:1, Matthew 22:41-46, Romans 1:3) and the bright morning star, whose physical radiance is a manifestation of his glorified body (Malachi 4:2, Matthew 17:2). The Holy Spirit and the Bride issue a joint call to invite all who are thirsty to receive the free water of life (Revelation 22:1). The text concludes with a solemn threefold warning against adding to or subtracting from the prophetic words, connecting the warning in the Pentateuch (Deuteronomy 4:2) and the Writings (Proverbs 30:6) with the closing of the New Testament. Adding doctrines brings about the plagues of the book, while subtracting them deprives the individual of their share in the holy city. Scripture culminates with the affirmation of the Savior's imminent return and the blessing of the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ upon all believers.

[1-4] The book of Exodus begins with a continuation of the historical and theological events of the book of Genesis (Genesis 50:26). The sons of Jacob who entered Egypt are recorded by name, precisely arranged according to their respective mothers in the order of wives and servants. Doctrinally, this descent of Abraham's seed into Egypt represents the people's immersion in the world system (Ephesians 2:1-3). In the typology of Scripture, Egypt typifies this evil age from which the church is rescued through redemption (Galatians 1:4).
[5, 6] The total number of souls descended from Jacob amounts to seventy, including Jacob in the count and acknowledging that Joseph was already in Egypt (Genesis 46:26-27). Some spurious versions, influenced by the codices of the Alexandrian school, alter the original order of this passage by moving fragments of verse five to the beginning of the genealogy, thus exposing the corruption of those manuscripts. With the death of Joseph and that entire generation, an era of providential preservation concludes, giving way to a period of transition where the people will experience the loss of their earthly privileges under Gentile rule.
[7-10] The people of Israel experience extraordinary multiplication that fills the land of Goshen, fulfilling the sovereign promises of national expansion (Genesis 12:1-3). When a new monarch arises over Egypt who was unaware of Joseph's legacy, hostile state opposition is introduced (Exodus 1:8). This foreign ruler, historically identified as an Assyrian and not a native Egyptian (Isaiah 52:4, Isaiah 10:5), is a precise type of the Antichrist who will reign during the great tribulation (Revelation 13:1-4). The imperial proposal to deal shrewdly with the Hebrew people stems from the political fear that the Israelites might join enemy powers in the event of war and then abandon earthly servitude.
[11, 12] The empire imposes tax collectors on the Jewish people to burden them with heavy loads, forcing them to build the store cities of Pithom and Raamses (Exodus 1:11). Several modern commentators have attempted to destabilize the biblical chronology of the Exodus from Egypt by arguing that the name of the city of Raamses necessitates a later dating linked to subsequent dynasties; However, the Scriptures document the use of this place name from much earlier times (Genesis 47:11). Despite the severity of the oppression, the more the Israelites were afflicted, the more they multiplied and grew, which caused deep fear and annoyance in the Egyptians.
[13, 14] The Egyptians intensified the slavery of the children of Israel by imposing extremely harsh and bitter servitude upon them (Exodus 1:13-14). The forced labor in preparing mud, bricks, and various agricultural tasks represents the severity of the yoke of sin under the dominion of Satan (Galatians 4:3-5). The description of these brutal working conditions is not mere Eastern hyperbole, but a historical reflection of the ruthless treatment that imperial powers inflict on defenseless minorities, typifying the moral captivity from which the sinner needs to be freed by the grace of Jesus Christ (Romans 6:16-18).
[15-17] When the measures of labor oppression failed, the ruler of Egypt ordered the Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, to secretly murder the male children at the moment of their birth on the birthing stools (Exodus 1:15-16). These midwives represented the chief supervisors of the nation's medical service. By refusing to carry out the orders of infanticide out of fear of God, the midwives set a legitimate precedent of civil disobedience against human laws that contradict the Lord's absolute commandments (Acts 4:19-20, Matthew 22:21). Satan's attempt to destroy only the male children reveals the enduring desire to cut off the seed that would bring forth the Redeemer and crush the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15, Revelation 12:4-5).
[18-21] The monarch confronts the midwives for having spared the male children, receiving in response that Hebrew women are not like Egyptian women, for they possess a physical strength that allows them to give birth before the midwife arrives (Exodus 1:18-19). The Israelite women's industrious, outdoor life set them apart from the dissolute, sedentary lifestyle of the Gentile court. Because of the reverent fear they showed toward God, the Lord blessed the midwives by granting them offspring and strengthening their own families, while the Hebrew people continued to multiply in a sovereign manner (1 Samuel 2:20-21).
[22] Faced with the ineffectiveness of the previous directives, the monarch issued a general decree ordering all his people to throw every newborn male child into the Nile River, reserving life only for daughters (Exodus 1:22). This measure of state extermination foreshadowed the future murderous edicts issued by Herod in the New Testament (Matthew 2:16-18). The retribution of divine justice will later be manifested under the immutable law of sowing and reaping, as Egypt will lose its own firstborn and its army will perish, drowned in the waters of the Red Sea during the national exodus (Exodus 12:29-30, Exodus 15:4-5).

[1, 2] A man from the family of Levi takes as his wife a daughter of the same tribe, and she conceives and gives birth to a son. Seeing that he is a beautiful child, she hides him for three months (Hebrews 11:23). Typologically, Moses figures as the great lawgiver and prophet to whom the Lord Jesus Christ is directly compared (Deuteronomy 18:15). The faith of the parents, who acted without fear of the severe royal decree, ensures the initial preservation of the deliverer whom the Lord had chosen.
[3, 4] When she could no longer hide him, the mother takes a basket made of reeds, caulks it with bitumen and pitch, places the child in it, and sets it among the reeds by the bank of the river. The child's sister, Miriam, stands at a distance to see what will happen to him. The sealed chest spiritually foreshadows the ark of salvation, a refuge provided by faith in the midst of a system doomed to death, while the child is entrusted entirely to the Lord's providence.
[5-10] Pharaoh's daughter goes down to the river to wash and discovers the chest. Upon opening it and seeing the crying child, she has compassion on him and recognizes that he belongs to the Hebrews. The Lord's sovereign intervention allows the child's sister to suggest the mother herself as a wet nurse, even receiving a salary from the Gentile empire to raise her son. When the child grows up, he is taken to the princess, who adopts him and names him Moses, declaring that she drew him from the waters. The rescue of this child and his subsequent adoption into the royal household typify the ministry of Jesus Christ, who was called to come out of Egypt at his first coming and will deliver his people at the end of time (Matthew 2:15).
[11-14] Upon reaching the age of forty (Acts 7:23), Moses visits his brethren and witnesses their heavy burdens. Seeing an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, he intervenes, kills the Egyptian, and hides his body in the sand. The next day, he attempts to mediate a dispute between two Hebrews, but the offender rejects him, questioning who made him prince and judge over them, and revealing that his violent act of the previous day is public knowledge. This rejection typologically illustrates the nation of Israel rejecting the ministry of the Lord Jesus Christ when He came to liberate them at His first coming (Acts 7:35), preferring their own misery to submitting to the authority of God's appointed liberator.
[15] When Pharaoh learned of the murder, he sought to kill Moses. However, Moses fled from the monarch's presence and settled in the land of Midian, sitting by a well. This flight began an extensive period of forty years in which the rejected savior remained hidden from His earthly people, dwelling among the Gentiles.
[16-22] The priest of Midian had seven daughters who were being harassed by shepherds as they tried to water their flocks. Moses intervened, defending them from the oppression and giving water to their sheep. As a token of gratitude, he is invited to the priest's house, agrees to live with him, and takes his daughter Zipporah as his wife, with whom he fathers a son named Gershom. Moses' life in Midian is a strikingly accurate picture of Jesus Christ's position in the present dispensation: rejected by his Hebrew brethren, he takes a Gentile wife and shepherds a foreign flock while patiently awaiting the time when the Lord will make his enemies a footstool for his feet (Psalm 110:1). The name Gershom reflects this position of a stranger in a foreign land.
[23-25] After a long period of time, spanning almost forty years according to the inspired record (Acts 7:30), the king of Egypt dies. The children of Israel groan because of the harsh servitude, and their cry rises to God. In these final three verses, the text uses God's name five times consecutively, underscoring the deity's sovereign intervention upon a nation dead in its sins. God hears the groaning, remembers his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, looks upon the children of Israel, and acknowledges them. This glorious divine preparation anticipates the imminent deliverance of the oppressed, foreshadowing the final restoration of Israel when the remnant cries out to the Lord in the midst of the affliction of the great tribulation before being rescued at the Second Coming of Christ.

[1-3] Moses tends Jethro's flock in the desert and arrives at Mount Horeb, where he witnesses the miracle of the burning bush that is not consumed (Exodus 3:1-3). During his time in Midian, Moses spends forty years in spiritual preparation, a period in which he writes the book of Genesis and assimilates the lessons of the book of Job concerning the suffering of the righteous (Job 1:1-2). The thorn bush historically represents the nation of Israel in the midst of the furnace of Gentile affliction (Genesis 15:13-17). Despite the attempts of empires such as Egypt, Syria, Babylon, Rome, and modern European powers to exterminate the Hebrew people, the remnant survives because God Himself is in their midst, fulfilling the principle that the children of Jacob are not consumed (Malachi 3:6). The burning bush constitutes the first national symbol of Israel, distinct from later pagan symbols such as the six-pointed star, which the deacon Stephen identifies as the star of the god Remphan (Acts 7:43).
[4-6] The Lord repeatedly calls Moses by name to capture his attention and commands him not to approach without first removing his sandals, for the ground he is standing on is holy (Exodus 3:4-6). The repetition of Moses' name follows a heavenly pattern documented in Scripture where God calls his chosen servants twice, as with Samuel (1 Samuel 3:10), Martha (Luke 10:41), Simon (Luke 22:31), and Saul (Acts 9:4). The command to remove one's shoes, "Take off your sandals" (Exodus 3:5), introduces the concept of divine holiness into earthly geography, foreshadowing the geographical itinerary of Christ's Second Coming through the regions of Sinai, Seir, and Paran (Deuteronomy 33:2, Habakkuk 3:3). Moses is confronted by the theophany of the Angel of the Lord, who assumes the identity of the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, instilling a holy awe that compels the prophet to cover his face (Exodus 3:6). This encounter demonstrates that God is a consuming fire (Hebrews 12:29), which acts as a purifier for his servants (Isaiah 6:1-7) but represents a scorching and intolerable judgment for the wicked (Malachi 4:1). The presence of the thorn bush evokes the curse of nature that the Savior will later bear on his forehead on the cross (Genesis 3:18, Hebrews 6:8, 2 Samuel 23:6).
[7-10] God declares that he has beheld the suffering of his people in Egypt and heard their lament at the cruelty of the Gentile oppressors (Exodus 3:7-10). The provision of divine grace in this descent will bring about the physical liberation of the seed of Jacob, establishing Egypt as a historical type of the world system from which the sinner is rescued through redemption (Galatians 1:4). The Lord commissions Moses to appear before Pharaoh, who embodies the type of the political Antichrist of the great tribulation (Revelation 13:1-4). Just as the people were preserved by the blood of the Passover lamb in their exodus from Egypt (Exodus 12:13), the final deliverance of the remnant of Jacob will be accomplished when the Savior descends in power at His Second Coming to judge the Gentile nations (Revelation 19:11-16).
[11, 12] In response to Moses' doubt about his own suitability for the mission, God promises him His abiding presence and grants him a future sign: the congregation will serve the Lord on that very mountain (Exodus 3:11-12). The promise that "For I will be with you" (Exodus 3:12) constitutes the unshakeable foundation of all prophetic ministry in Scripture (Joshua 1:5, Matthew 28:20). The theocratic worship on Mount Horeb represents a progressive revelation that transcends the mandate to inherit the land of Canaan, teaching that congregational worship on the mountain of God is the ultimate goal of redemption (Exodus 19:1-6).
[13-15] Moses inquires about the specific name he should announce to the Israelites in Egypt, receiving in response the solemn revelation of "I AM WHO I AM" and the command to declare that "I AM" has sent him to them (Exodus 3:13-15). This designation constitutes the definitive definition of the unchanging essence of the deity, denoting an eternal and self-existent existence that transcends the categories of past, present, and future (Revelation 1:8). The claim of modern translators and critics who attempt to render this expression as a future tense is rejected, since the designation "I AM WHO I AM" describes God's present. The Lord Jesus Christ claims this absolute deity for Himself by declaring to the Pharisees that before Abraham existed, “I am” (John 8:58). Likewise, in the Garden of Gethsemane, the mere pronouncement of this truth causes the multitude of captors to recoil and crumble to the ground (John 18:6). The name reveals that the Lord is a blank check for the believer, providing power, comfort, and redemption according to the needs of His people (Matthew 28:18, John 14:16).
[16, 17] Moses is commanded to summon the elders of Israel to announce God’s visitation and the promise to rescue them from Egyptian bondage and lead them to a land flowing with milk and honey (Exodus 3:16–17). The meeting with the elders represents the establishment of the governmental order of the Hebrew theocracy before their physical departure. The faith with which the elders receive this message demonstrates that the Spirit of God sovereignly prepares the hearts of believers to accept the visitation of their Redeemer (Exodus 4:31, John 1:12-13).
[18-20] Moses and the elders of Israel must request from the ruler of Egypt a three-day period of travel through the desert for the purpose of offering sacrifices (Exodus 3:18-20). This request for three days represents a literal request that tests the pride of the pagan court, refuting modernist interpretations that attempt to spiritualize the text or dilute its historical character. God's omniscience absolutely anticipates Pharaoh's rebellion before hardening his heart, demonstrating that divine sovereignty operates with perfect justice and foreknowledge (Exodus 3:19, Romans 9:17). The judgment of plagues and wonders upon Egypt manifests the Lord’s just retribution upon the Gentile powers that oppress the saints (Exodus 7:3–5).
[21, 22] The Lord assures them that He will grant the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians so that they will not leave empty-handed, commanding that every woman demand silver and gold jewelry and garments to plunder the oppressing nation (Exodus 3:21–22). This sovereign plunder constitutes just retribution for centuries of unpaid servitude and typologically foreshadows the plundering of the ungodly nations on the day of divine judgment following the great tribulation (Zechariah 14:14, Zephaniah 2:9). God's justice balances the accounts of history, ensuring that his people are enriched and provided with the necessary elements for the building of the sanctuary in the desert (Exodus 35:21-24).

[1-5] When Moses objected to the people's unbelief, the Lord instructed him to throw his staff to the ground, where it transformed into a snake, causing the prophet to flee. When God commanded him to grasp the snake by the tail, Moses obeyed, which served as a moral lesson about resisting the adversary in the spiritual realm. The snake flees when the believer confronts it directly and transforms back into a staff in his hand (James 4:7). This portent demonstrates the authority God delegates to His servants over Satan's deception.
[6-9] The Lord gave him a second sign, commanding the prophet to put his hand inside his bosom. When he withdrew it, his hand was leprous, like snow, and upon repeating the action, his flesh was restored and completely healed. This constitutes the first recorded instance of physical illness and healing in Scripture, establishing the doctrinal principle that signs of healing begin with the nation of Israel, since the Jews require a sign (1 Corinthians 1:22). These miracles are designed to validate the commission before the Hebrew congregation.
[10-17] Despite divine assurances, Moses objects to his commission, claiming to be slow of speech and tongue, demonstrating the doubts of the flesh in the face of a sovereign command. The Lord responds by affirming His sovereignty over the creation of human faculties and ultimately delegates Aaron as Moses' spokesman and prophet, while Moses will act in God's place before the king, carrying in his hand the staff with which he is to perform the miraculous signs.
[18-23] Moses returns to his father-in-law Jethro to request permission to return to Egypt, receiving his blessing to depart in peace. The Lord assures him in Midian that those who sought his death have already perished, thus typifying the experience of the Lord Jesus Christ upon his return from Egypt during his first coming (Matthew 2:20). The prophet takes his wife and sons, placing them on a donkey and carrying with him the staff of God. The Lord then reveals a profound dispensational truth by sending word to the monarch: “Thus says the Lord: Israel is my son, my firstborn.” This solemn declaration elevates the Hebrew nation to the position of son on a corporate level, warning that if the Gentile king refuses to let God’s firstborn go, the judgment of death will fall directly upon the firstborn of Egypt himself.
[24-26] On the journey, the Lord meets Moses at an inn and seeks to kill him because he had not circumcised his son. Moses had failed to keep the strict ordinance of the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17:14), showing how a servant can be in imminent danger of judgment for disobedience in his own home. Zipporah quickly intervenes by cutting off the boy's foreskin and throwing it at Moses' feet, thus appeasing divine wrath. This event demonstrates that disobedience to the Lord's commandments can bring severe punishment, reminding us of the unbreakable sanctity of the divine covenants.
[27-31] God sends Aaron into the wilderness to find Moses, and they meet on the mountain of God, where they kiss each other. It is a geographical error to confuse this Mount Horeb with Mount Hor, as they are a great distance apart. After the meeting, they gather the elders of the Israelites; Aaron pronounces the words dictated by God and performs the signs in the sight of all the people. Upon witnessing the wonders and hearing that the Lord had visited the children of Israel and looked upon their affliction, the congregation bows their heads and worships. This act precisely fulfills the Lord's earlier promise concerning the faith with which the elders would initially receive Moses' commission.

[1-3] Moses and Aaron appear before Pharaoh with the demand to let the people go to celebrate a festival in the desert. However, the text reveals that Moses dilutes the original message, omitting the solemn warning about the death of Egypt's firstborn. Pharaoh responds arrogantly, declaring that he does not know the Lord and has no intention of freeing Israel. The request for a three-day journey to offer sacrifices is a genuine demand, but the pagan monarch, acting according to the nature of the prince of this world, rejects divine authority over the enslaved nation.
[4-9] The monarch accuses the liberators of letting the people rest from their burdens and orders the taskmasters to stop providing them with straw for brickmaking, while maintaining the daily production quota. Pharaoh fiercely opposes the first promise of freedom for the captives, imposing a religion based solely on works. Meanwhile, Moses backs down and abandons the confrontation without displaying the divine signs that were granted to him, and this indecision results in extremely bitter days and severe physical punishments for the Hebrew people.
[10-14] The taskmasters and governors of the empire issue the merciless decree, forcing the Israelites to spread throughout the land of Egypt in search of stubble instead of straw. Unable to meet the previously established daily production quotas, the Hebrew taskmasters who had been placed over the work crews suffer severe beatings, illustrating the brutality of the world system against those who seek to serve God.
[15-19] The officers of the children of Israel cry out directly to Pharaoh for justice, but are met with mockery and scorn. The monarch calls them idle for wanting to offer sacrifices to the Lord, demonstrating that true worship in spirit and in truth is considered foolishness by the rulers of this world (1 Corinthians 2:6). Pharaoh acts under the influence of the prince of the power of the air (Ephesians 2:2), foreshadowing the absolute dominion of the Antichrist in the coming global system (Revelation 13:3-8).
[20, 21] Upon leaving Pharaoh's presence, the Hebrew officials encounter Moses and Aaron, confronting them with deep bitterness and resentment. They accuse them of having made their name abominable before the empire and of having placed a sword in the hands of the Egyptians to destroy them. This hostility reveals the instability of the multitudes and foreshadows the temporary rejection experienced by God's servants when circumstances turn adverse before the manifestation of divine victory.
[22, 23] Moses turns to the Lord in prayer, complaining that since he spoke in God's name, the people have been afflicted and have not experienced any deliverance. However, the root of this temporary crisis lies in the fact that Moses himself altered and softened the original message, failing to declare the precise words concerning the firstborn. This portion teaches the unchanging lesson that the Lord's servants must convey God's exact words without adding or taking away, trusting in His absolute sovereignty to execute judgment and redemption.

[1-3] The Lord responds to Moses' complaint by announcing that deliverance will be accomplished with a mighty hand, which points both to divine intervention and Pharaoh's eventual desire to expel them from his territory (Exodus 11:1). God reveals himself to Moses, confirming his covenant and declaring that, although the patriarchs knew him as the Almighty God, his name "JEHOVAH" was not revealed to them in its full manifestation. The fallacy of modern critics who attempt to use the change in divine names to divide the text among different authors is rejected, since the theological unity of Scripture is absolute and the revelation of the divine name is progressive.
[4-8] The patriarchal covenant is ratified along with seven divine promises, each preceded by the absolute declaration of the Lord's will. The text details the purposes of redemption: to free them from heavy burdens (Matthew 11:28), to deliver them from bondage to millennial rest (Isaiah 14:1-7), to redeem them with an outstretched arm in clear foreshadowing of the redemption accomplished on the cross, to take them as his people (Romans 9:26), to be their God (John 20:28), and finally to bring them into the promised land to possess as their inheritance (Revelation 5:10). This portion illustrates how God's grace intervenes directly before the formal giving of the law at Mount Sinai.
[9-13] Moses conveys these sublime promises to the congregation, but the children of Israel do not listen because of the anguish of their spirits and the harshness of their bondage. The material afflictions of the world often blind the oppressed sinner, preventing them from trusting in heavenly realities. Faced with this initial rejection, the prophet again expresses his reservations to the Lord, arguing that he has uncircumcised lips and questioning how Pharaoh will listen to him if even his own people do not pay attention. Nevertheless, the divine mandate remains unchanged, and the responsibility for carrying out the great deliverance falls jointly and formally upon the prophet and the priest.
[14-25] The sacred record interrupts the main narrative to present, in an orderly fashion, the genealogy of the heads of the ancestral houses, focusing on the families of Reuben, Simeon, and primarily Levi. Within this Levitical lineage, figures relevant to the later history of the nation are detailed, such as Korah (Numbers 16:1-3), and strategic marriage alliances are documented, such as the marriage of Aaron to Elisheba, from the tribe of Judah (Numbers 2:3). This genealogical census establishes the immutable priestly foundation that will govern the Hebrew congregation during their wilderness wanderings.
[26-30] The chapter concludes by formally identifying Moses and Aaron as the human instruments appointed by God to lead the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt “by their divisions.” The inclusion of this military term reveals that the descendants of Jacob are beginning to be recognized and organized as a military and political unit, despite not yet having fought any physical battles (Exodus 13:17). Finally, the text returns to the narrative of the divine command and Moses’s complaint regarding his slowness of speech, setting the theological stage for the impending judgments upon the gods of the Gentile nation.

[1-7] The Lord establishes Moses as a "god" to Pharaoh, appointing Aaron as his prophet to declare the divine commandments. God announces beforehand that he will harden the heart of the Egyptian monarch in order to multiply his signs and wonders on the earth, ensuring that the Egyptians recognize Jehovah's omnipotence. Moses was eighty years old and Aaron eighty-three when they appeared before the throne. The ten successive plagues, which begin at this point, constitute literal judgments that typify the severe punishments that will be poured out globally during the great tribulation (Revelation 16:1-21).
[8-13] When Pharaoh demands a miracle to validate his commission, Aaron throws down his staff, which transforms into a snake. The monarch summons the wise men and sorcerers of Egypt, doctrinally identified in the apostolic text as Jannes and Jambres (2 Timothy 3:8), who, through their enchantments, manage to imitate the portent by throwing down their own staffs. However, Aaron's staff devours the magicians' staffs, demonstrating God's absolute superiority over satanic magic. Despite witnessing this powerful manifestation, the Gentile monarch's heart hardens, and he refuses to obey, fulfilling the Lord's prophetic word with precision.
[14-18] The Lord instructs Moses to confront Pharaoh in the morning by the banks of the Nile River, intercepting the monarch during his routine descent into the sacred waters. Moses is commanded to present himself with the staff that had become a serpent and reiterate the divine demand to let the people go. Faced with persistent obstinacy, the warning is given that the river waters will turn to blood, causing the fish to die and producing a great stench, which constitutes a direct assault on the pantheon of false river deities worshipped in Egypt.
[19-25] Divine judgment is executed by extending over all the streams, rivers, ponds, and water reservoirs of the nation, affecting even domestic wooden and stone vessels. When Aaron raises his staff and strikes the river in Pharaoh's sight, the waters literally turn to blood, establishing an inescapable doctrinal parallel with the future judgments that the world system will suffer during the tribulation (Revelation 8:8, Revelation 16:3-4). The Egyptian sorcerers replicate the plague with their occult arts, providing the king with an excuse to return to his palace with a hardened heart, dismissing the severity of the warning. The water crisis persisted for exactly seven full days, forcing the Egyptians to dig around the river to find drinking water, thus cementing the first major defeat of the pagan empire.

[1-7] The Lord commands Moses to warn Pharaoh to let the people go to serve Him, under threat of afflicting the entire land with frogs (Revelation 16:13). When Aaron stretches out his staff over the streams and ponds, frogs come up and cover the land of Egypt, invading palaces, chambers, ovens, and kneading troughs. The magicians of Egypt, through their enchantments, manage to replicate the plague and cause more frogs to come up, demonstrating that the adversary can imitate judgments but lacks the power to relieve them.
[8-15] Pharaoh summons Moses and Aaron and asks them to plead with the Lord to remove the frogs, promising to let the congregation go to offer sacrifices. Moses allows the monarch to set the time, so that it is clear that there is no deity like God. Following the prophet's cry, frogs die in the villages and fields, piled up in such large numbers that the land reeks. However, seeing the relief, Pharaoh hardens his heart and refuses to keep his word, demonstrating that his promises are as deceptive as his spiritual nature (John 8:44).
[16-19] Without prior warning, the Lord instructs Aaron to strike the dust of the earth with his staff, transforming it into lice upon men and beasts throughout the nation. The magicians attempt to reproduce this plague through their occult arts, but they fail miserably, unable to imitate the act of producing life from the dust of the earth (Genesis 2:7). Faced with this crushing defeat, the magicians acknowledge the supreme power, confessing, "This is the finger of God." Doctrinally, the finger of God is associated with the direct power of the Holy Spirit operating on the earthly plane (Luke 11:20, Psalm 8:3).
[20-24] The Lord commands Moses to rise early and intercept Pharaoh by the waters to warn him about a swarm of flies. From this plague, God establishes a strict separation or redemption, exempting the land of Goshen from judgment to publicly demonstrate His absolute dominion over the land. A terrible swarm of flies of various species (Psalm 78:45) invades the royal palace, the servants, and the entire land, which becomes corrupted, exposing the impotence of the deities of uncleanness worshipped by the empire (Matthew 12:27).
[25-32] Overwhelmed by the severity of the plague, Pharaoh proposes his first diplomatic compromise, offering that the Hebrews sacrifice to their God within the borders of Egypt. Moses flatly rejects the offer, arguing that sacrificing sheep is an abomination to the Egyptian religion and that such an act would cause the natives to stone them (Genesis 46:34). The prophet remains firm in his demand to travel for three days through the desert. The monarch then offers a second concession: he allows them to go into the desert on the condition that they do not go too far, asking them to pray for him. Moses pleads with the Lord and the flies are completely removed, not a single one remaining, but Pharaoh again hardens his heart and refuses to grant the people their freedom.

[1-7] The Lord commands Moses to again demand the release of the Hebrews, warning of a plague upon the livestock of Egypt. This miracle directly attacks the pagan deities represented by bulls, cows, rams, and goats. A strict separation is established: the livestock of Israel is preserved intact, while all the livestock of Egypt in the fields perishes under a severe plague. Despite witnessing this miraculous distinction through messengers, the heart of the Gentile monarch hardens, and he refuses to let the people go.
[8-12] Without warning, Moses and Aaron are commanded to take ashes from a furnace and scatter them toward the sky, causing boils and malignant sores to break out on both people and animals. The furnace typifies the iron furnace of affliction where the Jewish people suffered severe slavery under Gentile rule (Deuteronomy 4:20). Likewise, this plague foreshadows the malignant and painful ulcer that will afflict the inhabitants of the earth during the great tribulation for bearing the mark of the beast (Revelation 16:2). The magicians of Egypt are incapacitated by the disease and cannot resist the prophet. On this occasion, the text declares that the Lord hardens Pharaoh's heart as a just and judicial retribution for his previous and constant obstinacy.
[13-17] The Lord warns Pharaoh, announcing that He will now send all His plagues directly upon his heart so that he may acknowledge absolute divine supremacy. It is revealed to him that he has been raised to his position as sovereign for the specific purpose that God's power may be displayed in him and the name of the Lord declared universally. This solemn truth is doctrinally expounded by the apostle to demonstrate that divine patience endures the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, Pharaoh's rebellion having been foreknowledged by God before the monarch even acted in his resistance (Romans 9:17-22).
[18-26] A severe hailstorm is prophesied, granting in His mercy an opportunity for those servants of the empire who fear the word of God to shelter their livestock and families in their homes. Those who disregard the divine warning suffer the loss of their servants and animals in the fields. Judgment descends, mixing hail with fire that sweeps across the land, laying waste to people, animals, and vegetation, and shattering the trees of the fields. This historical event accurately foreshadows the trumpet judgments during the great tribulation, where hail and fire mixed with blood will burn up a third of the trees and all the green grass (Revelation 8:7). The land of Goshen is again spared from heavenly punishment, demonstrating God's providential protection over the Hebrew nation.
[27-35] In the face of the storm's devastation, Pharaoh summons Moses and confesses his sin, declaring that the Lord is just and that he and his people are wicked. However, this apparent contrition lacks genuine repentance and resembles the superficial confessions of other reprobate transgressors in Scripture (1 Samuel 15:24, Matthew 27:4). Moses agrees to intercede, stretching out his hands to the Lord to stop the thunder and hail, knowing beforehand that the monarch does not yet truly fear God. The sacred text documents with astonishing agricultural precision that the flax and barley were destroyed by the storm, while the wheat and rye did not perish because they were late crops that had not yet grown. When judgment ceased, the monarch and his servants sinned even more and hardened their hearts, thus fulfilling the Lord's prophetic word literally.

[1-6] The Lord commands Moses to appear again before the Egyptian monarch, revealing that He has hardened his heart and the hearts of his servants in order to manifest His divine signs and so that these wonders may be recounted to future generations. Moses and Aaron warn Pharaoh that if he refuses to let the people go to serve God, a plague of locusts will invade the land the next day. It is prophesied that this invasion will cover the face of the earth, darkening the ground, devouring all the remains that escaped the hail, and filling the houses of the Egyptians—a punishment unprecedented in the nation's history. After pronouncing this solemn judgment, the prophet turns and leaves the royal presence.
[7-11] Pharaoh's servants, realizing the impending ruin, plead with their master to let the men go to serve their God, asking if he still doesn't understand that Egypt is destroyed. Upon being brought back, the monarch asks who will go into the desert. Moses replies firmly that they will go with their young and old, sons and daughters, flocks and herds, for they must hold a festival to the Lord. At this demand, Pharaoh mocks them and offers a deceptive concession: he allows only the adult males to leave, withholding the women, children, and possessions as collateral. When his attempt to divide the families and ensure the eventual return of the slaves to the world order failed, the monarch flew into a rage and violently expelled them from his presence.
[12-15] Following the divine command, Moses stretched out his staff, and the Lord caused a strong east wind to blow across the land throughout that day and night. In the morning, the wind brought an immense swarm of locusts that settled over the entire land, constituting a most severe plague, surpassing any known natural phenomenon. The locusts covered the face of the entire land, darkening the country and relentlessly devouring all the grass and fruit of the trees that the hail had spared. The judgment is total, leaving nothing green in the fields of Egypt, foreshadowing the devastating literal judgments that will consume the resources of ungodly nations during the great tribulation (Revelation 9:1-11).
[16-20] Overwhelmed by the economic and agricultural devastation, Pharaoh hastily summons the deliverers, confessing that he has sinned against the Lord and against them. He begs for forgiveness this time and pleads for God to take away the death from him. After Moses’ prayer, the Lord sends a mighty west wind that stirs up the locusts and drives them into the Red Sea, leaving not one behind on the shores of Egypt. However, once he obtained material relief, the monarch's heart hardened again by divine decree, confirming that his repentance lacked genuine spiritual conversion and was motivated solely by fear of the consequences of divine judgment (1 Samuel 15:24).
[21-23] Without any warning, the Lord commands Moses to stretch out his hand toward heaven, causing thick darkness to descend upon the land of Egypt, so dense it can be felt. For three full days, the Egyptians are immobilized, unable to see one another or rise from their places. This absolute blackout not only constitutes a direct humiliation of the sun god of the Egyptian religion but also foreshadows the literal darkness that will cover the kingdom of the Antichrist when the fifth bowl of wrath is poured out (Revelation 16:10-11). Simultaneously, all the children of Israel enjoy light in their dwellings, demonstrating the sovereign grace that separates and preserves the elect in the midst of the darkness of the world system (Ephesians 5:8).
[24-29] Pharaoh summons Moses one last time in terror and offers a final concession: he allows all the families to go and serve the Lord, requiring only that they leave their flocks and herds behind. Moses flatly rejects this proposal, declaring that the livestock will also go, not even a hoof left behind, since they do not know what specific sacrifices the Lord will require in the wilderness. Filled with rage at having his will rejected, Pharaoh dismisses Moses, threatening him with death if he ever appears before him again. With unwavering resolve, Moses agrees to the decree, solemnly declaring that he will never see his face again. This definitive break sets the historical and theological stage for the execution of the final judgment upon the Gentile land.

[1-3] The Lord announces a final plague upon Pharaoh and Egypt, after which the monarch will expel them from the territory in haste [4, 5]. The people are commanded to ask their neighbors for silver and gold jewelry, which will provide the materials for the future construction of the tabernacle [5]. These earthly riches of Egypt, a typology of the world system, have no redemptive value for the salvation of the soul, as is doctrinally established by declaring that the believer is not redeemed with corruptible things like gold or silver (1 Peter 1:18, Acts 3:6) [5]. The Lord grants favor to the Hebrews before the Egyptians, and Moses is exalted as the true authority on earth, foreshadowing the Lord's absolute dominion over the nations (Matthew 28:18) [4, 6].
[7-9] Moses declares that around midnight the Lord will go out into the midst of Egypt and every firstborn will die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh on his throne to the firstborn of the female slave behind the mill, as well as every firstborn of the beasts [10, 11]. This fatal judgment is carried out by Abaddon or Apollyon, the angel of death, although the Lord Himself assumes sovereignty and responsibility for the act (Exodus 12:12, Hebrews 2:14, Revelation 9:11) [6, 10]. This event equates the heir to the empire with the son of a slave woman in judgment [12], producing a great outcry throughout the Gentile nation, an unprecedented outcry that will never be repeated [11]. Milling is identified in Scripture as labor of slavery (Judges 16:21, Isaiah 47:1-2), and Moses' declaration constitutes a direct affront to the monarch's pride by placing his offspring on the same level of judgment as the Hamite slaves [13].
[14, 15] An absolute separation is established between the Egyptians and the children of Israel, indicating that not even a dog will utter a word against the Hebrew people [11]. This distinction manifests God's authority in instituting a clear divine segregation between his chosen people and the oppressive Gentile nation [12, 13]. Moses warns that Pharaoh's servants will come down and prostrate themselves before him, begging for the people's release—an act of reverence reserved for royalty that confirms the monarch's complete loss of influence [6:16]. After pronouncing this solemn verdict, Moses leaves Pharaoh's presence burning with great anger, revealing that this prophetic portion was declared in the same encounter described in the previous chapter before his final withdrawal from the palace [12:16]. [17:18] The Lord recaps the conflict by declaring to Moses that Pharaoh would not listen, so that divine wonders might be multiplied in the land of Egypt [16]. Moses and Aaron performed all these signs before the monarch, but the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart so that he would not let the Israelites go from his country [16:19]. This conclusion summarizes the entirety of the historical confrontation: the servants perform miracles, obstinacy is sealed by divine judgment after the ruler's prior rejection, and the detention of the people sets the inescapable stage for the night of Passover and the death of the firstborn [19].

[1, 2] The Lord establishes a new calendar for the Hebrew nation, indicating that the month of Abib should be the beginning of the months and the first of the year. Doctrinally, this event teaches that the true spiritual life of an individual or a people does not begin until redemption is accomplished through the blood of the Lamb, marking a new beginning separate from the world system.
[3-6] The assembly is commanded to set apart a lamb without blemish for each family on the tenth day of the month, keeping it under observation until the fourteenth day to be slaughtered at sunset. This four-day period of examination accurately typifies the public entry of the Lord Jesus Christ into Jerusalem, where He was tested and examined before His crucifixion. The sacrifice of the lamb for the entire congregation of Israel prophetically anticipates the nation's corporate responsibility in the death of the Messiah, a sacrifice that constitutes the most momentous event in the history of redemption (Matthew 27:25).
[7-11] The blood of the sacrifice is to be placed on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses. The lamb is to be eaten roasted over a fire with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. The fire is a type of the wrath of God that consumed the Redeemer on the cross, who cried out for thirst and received no relief (John 19:28). The required attitude for partaking of the Lamb—loin girded, sandals on feet, and staff in hand—reflects a pressing urgency, illustrating that salvation must be received without delay and that the redeemed must be prepared to depart and leave the world immediately.
[12-14] The judgment is executed at midnight when the Lord passes through the land to strike down the firstborn and exact vengeance against the gods of Egypt, employing the destroying angel, known in the New Testament as Abaddon or Apollyon (Revelation 9:11). The text stipulates with absolute clarity the basis of divine security: “When I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exodus 12:13). Preservation does not depend on morality, lineage, or good intentions, but purely and exclusively on the blood applied. This principle establishes that no one escapes divine wrath except under the refuge of the shed, atoning blood of Jesus Christ (Romans 5:9).
[15-20] The Feast of Unleavened Bread is instituted, lasting for seven days, with the warning that anyone who eats leaven during that time will be cut off from Israel. Leaven invariably typifies sin, moral corruption, and false doctrine (Matthew 16:12, 1 Corinthians 5:6-8). The complete exclusion of leaven from homes represents the radical separation and purity that should characterize the believer once redeemed by the Passover sacrifice.
[21-28] Moses summons the elders to sacrifice the Passover lamb and apply the blood with a bunch of hyssop, sternly ordering them not to leave their homes until morning. Hyssop is the natural instrument with which the protective blood is sprinkled. The directive not to leave the house underscores that the only protection from the judgment that sweeps away the wicked lies in remaining under the protection of the blood covenant, set apart from the darkness of the world. The people heed these words, bowing their heads in worship.
[29-36] Death visits every Egyptian home at midnight, claiming the lives of all the firstborn, from Pharaoh's household to the captive in the dungeon. This devastating punishment provokes a great national outcry and results in the monarch's temporary surrender, who urges the Israelites to leave immediately. Before departing, the people plunder the Egyptians, demanding silver and gold jewelry and clothing. These treasures would later provide the materials for the construction of the tabernacle, demonstrating that worldly riches, though incapable of purchasing redemption (1 Peter 1:18), could be consecrated by the saints for God's service.
[37-42] The Israelites set out from Rameses toward Succoth, numbering six hundred thousand foot soldiers, not counting their families. Along with them came a mixed multitude of foreigners, who would later cause constant trouble in the desert by coveting the customs of Egypt.
