The sacred record seals this test by affirming that “in all this Job did not sin with his lips,” confirming that true faith submits with equal reverence to the blessings and afflictions ordained by the Lord (James 5:11, Romans 8:28).
[11-13] Job’s three friends, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite, having heard of the calamity, agree to meet together to come and comfort him. Observing him from a distance, his physical disfigurement is so great that they cannot recognize him, which moves them to weep bitterly, tear their garments, and throw dust over their heads toward heaven (Lamentations 2:10). Sitting beside him on the ground for seven days and seven nights in complete silence, they respect the immensity of his spiritual suffering, foreshadowing the solemn mourning for the dead (Genesis 50:10, 1 Samuel 31:13). This providential silence will constitute the only true display of consolation before theological discussions disturb the peace of the sufferer for nineteen chapters.

[1-10] After the prolonged silence of his companions, the suffering man curses the day of his earthly birth, exclaiming, {{quote: Job 3:1|Job opened his mouth, and cursed his day}}. This attitude is spiritually associated with the bitterness of the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 20:14). The name Jeremiah denotes that the Lord will bring down, serving as a type of the nation of Israel under the judgments of the great tribulation (Revelation 11:1-3). By pointing to the conception of a male child, {{quote: Job 3:3}}, the text introduces a crucial prophetic element that points toward the birth and preservation of the male child in the wilderness (Revelation 12:5, Isaiah 66:8-9). The apostle Paul represents this man born out of season (1 Corinthians 15:8). By requesting that their day be darkness, they anticipate the dense darkness of the day of God's wrath (Zephaniah 1:15, Revelation 16:10). Likewise, the plea that that night not be counted among the days of the year or in the number of the months doctrinally reveals how God omits or discountes certain periods of time in history in His dispensational reckoning (Revelation 12:14). Those who are ready to awaken Leviathan are called upon to curse the night—a Hebrew word that modern versions mistakenly translate as mourning or crocodile, but which in Scripture represents the great dragon of the abyss, the ancient serpent (Isaiah 27:1-3, Revelation 12:9). Finally, the mention of the gates of the womb is linked to the birth pangs that precede the manifestation of the Jewish remnant (Jeremiah 13:21, 1 Thessalonians 5:3).
[11-19] In the midst of his affliction, the sufferer questions the reasons for his physical survival, asking {{quote: Job 3:11}}. This question exposes the pain of the creature under a creation subject to futility because of the Fall (Romans 8:20-22). Job prefers the rest of a hidden abortion that never saw the light of day, teaching in harmony with Ecclesiastes that a long earthly existence devoid of spiritual peace is inferior to the rest of an infant who was never born (Ecclesiastes 6:3-5). In the grave, earthly conditions are leveled, for the monarchs who built deserted places and the princes who amassed silver lie in the same stillness. Physical death acts as an absolute leveler of all oppression, where {{quote: Job 3:17|There the wicked leave the tumult; and there the weary find rest}}. In this state of temporary rest in the dust, the prisoners no longer hear the voice of the oppressor, and the servant is definitively freed from his master, foreshadowing the rest from the labors of this evil age before the future bodily resurrection (Genesis 3:19, 1 Thessalonians 4:14-17).
[20-26] The patriarch inquires about the purpose of granting light and life to bitter souls who yearn for death without it coming, digging for it more than for treasures. This state of utter despair foreshadows the agony of the earth's inhabitants during the judgment of the fifth trumpet, where they will seek death but it will elude them (Revelation 9:6). Job laments the condition of the man whose path is hidden, expressing (Job 3:23). Unlike the providential hedge of prosperity that surrounded him at first (Job 1:10), this new hedge represents a barrier of affliction and thorns that encloses the servant of God without offering any human escape (Jeremiah 20:8, Hebrews 6:8). His cries pour forth like water before his daily bread, a profound sorrow that finds a parallel with Christ's cry in His hour of helplessness on the cross (Psalm 22:1, Psalm 32:3). Job confesses that his deepest fears have come upon him (Job 3:25), demonstrating that in his days of abundance he maintained a humble spiritual vigilance and never fell into lethargy or complacency (Job 1:5). In this way, divine testing exposes and consumes all self-righteousness in the human heart so that only the sovereign grace of God may shine forth (Romans 10:3).

[1-5] Eliphaz the Temanite, originally from Edom and traditionally considered the most moderate of the accusers, begins his speech with apparent courtesy (Job 4:2). Eliphaz appeals to Job's past work as an instructor and strengthener of others in times of affliction, implicitly applying the reproach that a counselor should be able to heal his own afflictions (Job 2:11). The tone of the rebuke, noting that Job is faint and troubled now that calamity has touched him personally, typologically anticipates the mockery directed at Jesus Christ during the crucifixion (Matthew 27:42). Although there is practical truth in the observation, the inappropriateness of his words to a man devastated by the loss of his children and his failing health turns the attempt at consolation into a trigger of bitterness (Job 1:21). In this dispensational context, the land of Uz is situated on the borders of Edom, the region of Petra, isolating Job's drama in a barren and prophetic setting that foreshadows the suffering of the nation of Israel during the great tribulation (Lamentations 4:21, Revelation 12:13).
[6-11] Eliphaz's theological argument is based on moral retribution and empirical observation, suggesting that righteousness and the fear of God should be the source of the sufferer's confidence and hope (Job 4:6). Through a series of rhetorical questions, he upholds the traditional thesis that the innocent do not perish nor are the upright ever truly cut off (Job 4:7). Eliphaz argues that those who sow iniquity reap the same, limiting divine justice to immediate, earthly, material retribution (Job 5:17-27). This simplistic perspective ignores divine sovereignty in the processes of testing and associates Job's brokenness with direct punishment from God. To illustrate the destruction of the wicked, the discourse uses the image of lions whose strength and offspring are destroyed under divine wrath, so that the breath of God consumes the rebels (Psalm 2:12, Job 20:22).
[12-16] Eliphaz validates the authority of his doctrine by appealing to a mystical, revelatory experience that occurred during deep sleep (Job 4:12). The description of the night vision evokes an atmosphere of panic and physical trembling that shook the witness's very bones, which is symmetrical with the encounters of sacred terror recorded in other pre-Mosaic manifestations (Genesis 15:12). The appearance of a spirit without discernible form but with a defined image before their eyes establishes a solemn silence before the proclamation of the message (Job 4:15). These spiritual beings act as messengers or ministers in God's plan (Hebrews 1:14). This scene of panic and nocturnal revelation highlights the primitive and patriarchal character of the book, where God routinely communicated directly or through dreams and theophanies before the codification of the written law (Numbers 12:6, Genesis 20:6).
[17-21] The message proclaimed by the spirit directly confronts the fragility and limitations of the human condition in comparison to divine perfection (Job 4:17). The admonition emphasizes that if God does not place absolute trust in his heavenly servants and attributes folly to his own angels, how much more will he judge human beings, poetically described as dwelling in houses of clay founded on dust (Job 4:19). This statement establishes a stark contrast between the holiness of God and the insignificance of humankind, who continually perish from morning till night without anyone noticing. The argument that man's excellence fades and he dies without wisdom emphasizes that no flesh can justify itself before the Lord (Job 15:15, Job 25:4-6, Romans 3:20). Eliphaz uses these legitimate spiritual truths disastrously in the following chapters, diverting the purpose of the message to falsely categorize Job as a foolish sinner under judgment (Job 5:1-4). This emphasis on original creation, the fallen angels, and the flood, to the detriment of themes such as the exodus or the law, confirms that the historical chronology and conversations in the book belong to the patriarchal era before Moses.

[1-5] Eliphaz the Temanite continues his first speech by severely applying the doctrine of moral retribution to Job's afflictions. He begins by challenging the patriarch to seek a mediator or intercessor among the heavenly beings {{quote:Job 5:1|Call now, if there is anyone who will answer you; and to which of the holy ones will you turn?}}. This challenge constitutes a subtle mockery that foreshadows the derision heaped by the chief priests at the foot of the cross (Mark 15:35), suggesting that no faithful servant of the past like Abraham, Noah, or Enoch will intercede for a man under judgment. Eliphaz characterizes Job's agony and desire to die as foolishness, declaring that anger and indignation destroy the fool {{quote:Job 5:2}}. The allusion to the wicked man who takes root only to see his dwelling suddenly cursed is doctrinally connected to the final judgment on the Antichrist (Psalm 52:1-7). However, the most devastating blow against Job is found in the mention of the fool's children, described as helpless and crushed at the gate without a savior (Job 5:4). This merciless statement directly evokes the tragic death of Job's children when his household collapsed (Job 1:19), implying that Job is the foolish one responsible for the family's misfortune. Furthermore, in detailing how the hungry and the plunderers consume his crops and riches, Eliphaz uses the historical robberies perpetrated by the Sabeans and Chaldeans to attest to his friend's supposed impiety (Job 1:15).
[6-16] Eliphaz's philosophical exposition continues by disassociating physical nature from being the primary source of suffering, arguing that affliction and pain do not spring spontaneously from the earth (Job 5:6). If humankind were only to contend with material creation and its elements, it could live free from disease until naturally wasting away, as happened with the patriarchs. Although the earth was cursed because of original sin (Genesis 3:17) and leads to the physical death of the body, real afflictions stem from the depravity of human nature (1 Timothy 6:10, James 4:1-4) and the active intervention of the kingdom of darkness (Ephesians 6:10-16). Thus, the inevitable condition of fallen humanity is stated, born into suffering with the same certainty as lightning bolts soaring upwards (Job 5:7). Humanity enters a creation subject to futility (Romans 8:20) and under the temporary dominion of the god of this age (2 Corinthians 4:4), making existence a fiery trial (1 Peter 4:12). In an attempt at moral superiority, Eliphaz advises Job to seek the Lord, ignoring that the afflicted man had already committed his case to the heavenly tribunal (Job 10:2, Job 13:2). The discourse extols God's sovereignty in thwarting the designs of the cunning and trapping the wise in their own prudence (Job 5:13). This maxim is quoted by the apostle Paul to emphasize that the wisdom of the world is foolishness in God's sight (1 Corinthians 3:19), assuring that the Lord delivers the helpless from the sword of the proud and from their own destructive mouths, providing hope and silencing iniquity.
[17-27] Eliphaz concludes by introducing the paradox of blessedness in divine discipline: {{quote:Job 5:17|Behold, blessed is the man whom God chastenes; Therefore, do not despise the discipline of the Almighty. This statement, reproduced in the book of Proverbs (Proverbs 3:11) and quoted in the Epistle to the Hebrews (Hebrews 12:5-11), highlights that although no discipline seems pleasant at present, but rather painful, God uses it to make us partakers of his holiness. While the Lord chastises everyone he accepts as his child, in the practice of extreme pain, a glimmer of consolation and sympathy is infinitely more valuable than the cold exposition of theological orthodoxy. God employs various methods of instruction: dealing with the Holy Scriptures (2 Timothy 3:16), the thorn in the flesh as a method of humiliation (2 Corinthians 12:7), and ultimately, the scourge of discipline (1 Corinthians 11:32) or the knife of spiritual pruning for the production of fruit (John 15:2). Prophetically alluding to divine deliverance in six tribulations, and noting that in the seventh evil will not touch (Job 5:19), the passage symbolically points to the preservation of the Jewish remnant during the seven years of the great tribulation (Daniel 9:27). Eliphaz outlines a series of apocalyptic plagues such as famine, war, the scourge of the tongue, and wild beasts, which will ravage the earth in the last days (Revelation 6:3-8). Finally, the promises of peace, posterity, and extreme longevity described at the end of the chapter (Job 5:24, 26) are spiritually reserved for three particular classes of the redeemed: the resurrected saints from Adam until the outpouring of the Spirit in the book of Acts (Acts 2:1-4); the Church that attains the New Jerusalem in glory (Revelation 21:4); and the nation of Israel when their captivity is restored on the day of the Lord (Psalm 126:4). This finds a faithful typological reflection in the literal restoration that the Lord granted to Job by doubling all his possessions and prolonging his days by an additional one hundred and forty years (Job 42:10-16).

[1-4] Job responds to Eliphaz by completely ignoring the previous moralistic discourse, focusing instead on the immensity of his personal suffering. The afflicted man expresses his longing for his pain and ruin to be fairly weighed on a scale (Job 6:2), estimating that his calamity would outweigh the sand of the sea. This extreme pressure causes his words to be swallowed or choked by sobs and weeping, reflecting a state of physical and emotional prostration (Job 16:16). Job attributes his condition to a direct punitive action of the Lord, describing how God's arrows have pierced his being (Job 6:4). Divine terrors are arrayed in battle formation against him, a scene that foreshadows Christ's sufferings on the cross (Psalms 22:1-18, Isaiah 53:3-8), the torment of the wicked in hell, and the afflictions of Israel's remnant during the great tribulation (Lamentations 2:4, Ephesians 6:16, Revelation 12:13).
[5-13] The mourner appeals to nature to justify his lamentations, posing rhetorical questions whose answers are necessarily negative. He asks whether the wild donkey brays beside the green grass or whether the ox lows before its full manger {{quote: Job 6:5}}, illustrating that crying arises only in the face of want and extreme need. The comforting words of his friends are compared to bland, unsalted food or the tastelessness of egg white, foods his soul once refused to touch but which now sustain him in his suffering (Job 30:16). Faced with the intensity of his torment, Job implores the Lord to loose His hand and end his physical existence (Job 6:9). This plea for voluntary death, which evokes the limits of human suffering (Lamentations 3:1-20), is based on the recognition of his own physical weakness, for he argues that his body does not possess the hardness of rock or the strength of bronze (Job 13:28). Acknowledging that the Lord has temporarily suspended his help, the grieving man affirms that his only strength lies within himself and that wisdom has not been taken from him, refusing to accept simplistic theological explanations.
[14-21] The psalmist and mourner exposes the betrayal of his close associates, pointing out that whoever denies mercy to a troubled friend effectively abandons the fear of the Lord (see Job 6:14). Job compares the loyalty of his brothers to the seasonal torrents of the desert, which flow impetuously in winter, becoming turbid with ice and snow, but vanish completely with the arrival of summer's heat. The caravans of Tema and the merchants of Sheba divert their routes seeking these watercourses, but find only a dry riverbed, becoming confused and ashamed of having placed their trust in an illusory source of water (Psalms 120:5, Jeremiah 15:18). Job applies this analogy directly to his accusers, declaring that they have become nothing, for upon seeing his appalling physical ruin and prostration they have been seized by panic and distrust (Job 6:21). Instead of providing the expected comfort, his friends distance themselves socially and spiritually, falsely judging him as a reprobate struck by the hand of God.
[22-30] With great indignation, the patriarch launches a series of defensive questions aimed at demonstrating that he has never asked his relatives for material aid or financial rescue (Job 31:13-22). Job expresses his sincere willingness to remain silent if they can show him precisely what his actual transgression has been (see Job 6:24), exclaiming that righteous words possess overwhelming power, unlike the empty and speculative reasoning of his comforters. The grieving man censures the insensitivity of those who presume to judge the excessive complaint of a desperate man, whose expressions should be excused as a passing wind, and accuses them of being capable of oppressing the orphan and digging a grave for their own friend. Finally, Job urges them to look him in the face to verify his honesty, demanding that they desist from their unjust accusations to avoid falling into iniquity, for his cause remains just (Job 6:29). Although Job firmly defends the purity of his moral discernment (Job 13:28), his stance typologically reveals the danger of self-righteousness, resembling the blind trust that the nation of Israel placed in its legalistic works (Romans 10:3, Isaiah 64:6, Acts 1:25). His words appeal to the universal moral principles inscribed by God on the conscience of all humanity (Romans 2:15), closing his intervention with a direct challenge to examine the origin of their affliction instead of multiplying sterile discourses.

[1-6] Job describes the human condition on earth as a time of forced servitude and arduous labor, comparing man's days to those of a hired worker who longs for shade and awaits payment for his work (Acts 17:26, Psalm 79:11, Romans 6:23). Amid his physical anguish, the afflicted man recounts months of futility and nights of toil where rest is denied him, characterized by a tormenting insomnia that stretches until dawn. The degradation of his body reaches abominable extremes, his flesh covered with worms and clods of dust, his skin cracked and despicable (Deuteronomy 28:59-61, Leviticus 26:16). These physical manifestations of judgment typologically reflect the curses pronounced upon the nation of Israel for its disobedience, foreshadowing the horrors the Jewish remnant will experience during the great tribulation (Jeremiah 30:7, Revelation 16:2). The brevity and instability of earthly existence are illustrated by the image of the loom {{quote: Job 7:6 | My days were swifter than the weaver’s shuttle}}, emphasizing how quickly the days of the sufferer are exhausted when he contemplates his life devoid of earthly hope (1 Corinthians 3:13-15).
[7-10] The afflicted person directs his prayer to the Lord, recalling the inherent fragility of human nature {{quote: Job 7:7 | Remember that my life is but a breath}}. Life is defined as a fleeting breath and a passing cloud, teaching the brevity of existence on earth (James 4:14, Psalm 78:39). From the perspective of the Old Testament, prior to Christ's finished work on the cross and his victory over death, the descent into the grave or Sheol implied a departure from earthly life with no return, where the deceased never returns home nor is their place recognized again (Psalm 89:48, Ecclesiastes 9:5). In this dispensational economy prior to the New Covenant, the souls of the dead descended to the lower parts of the earth before the Lord proclaimed the release of the captives and transported Abraham's bosom to the third heaven (Ephesians 4:8-10, Acts 2:27-31). Meditation on the passing of life underscores the urgency of seeking divine favor while still in the flesh, acknowledging that man has no power to retain his spirit on the day of death (Ecclesiastes 8:8).
[11-16] Faced with the severity of God's treatment, Job refuses to remain silent and decides to openly express the bitterness of his soul (Job 7:11). The grieving man questions the Lord, asking if he is perhaps the sea or a sea monster like Leviathan, that such a close guard should be placed around him, alluding to the forces of chaos that God sovereignly represses in creation (Job 41:1-10, Psalms 74:13-14). The nighttime refuge he expected to find in his bed is transformed into a scene of torment, as the Lord terrifies him with dreams and frightful visions that shake his troubled mind (Job 33:15). This extreme anguish leads Job to loathe his physical life and to desire death by suffocation rather than continue in a wasting body (Job 7:15). In his despair, he pleads with the Lord to leave him alone, arguing that his days are vanity and that earthly existence has become unbearable under the weight of incessant affliction (Job 10:20, Psalms 39:13).
[17-21] The chapter concludes with a question that contrasts sharply with the piety of the Psalms (Job 7:17). While David contemplates human greatness under divine grace with awe and gratitude (Psalms 8:4, Hebrews 2:6), Job perceives the magnitude of God's concern as an oppressive watchfulness that examines him every morning and tests him at every moment. The grieving man bitterly laments the time it takes the Lord to turn His gaze away, using the proverbial expression of not even leaving him to swallow his saliva. Nevertheless, Job makes an explicit confession, declaring his sin before the Lord (Job 7:20). Although he acknowledges his fault in general terms, his sense of self-righteousness leads him to question why God has made him the target of His arrows and why He does not immediately forgive his transgression before he sleeps in the dust of the earth (Job 16:12, Job 40:8, Romans 3:20). On a prophetic level, this plea for forgiveness and the pre-death anguish foreshadow the conversion of the Jewish remnant at the end of the great tribulation, when they acknowledge their iniquities and look upon the one they pierced before being restored by the Lord (Hosea 6:1-3, Zechariah 12:10-14, Revelation 1:7).

[1-7] Bildad the Shuhite enters the controversy representing the traditionalist position, appealing to accepted dogmas about divine government. His speech begins with a direct rebuke of Job's vehemence, describing the suffering man's words as a rushing wind and defending God's absolute equity {{quote:Job 8:3|Can God pervert justice, or can the Almighty pervert what is right?}}. Bildad attributes the tragic death of Job's children to direct divine judgment as a consequence of their own transgressions (Job 1:19), asserting unequivocally that calamities are always the result of sin. In his reasoning, he maintains that if Job were to seek the Lord early and make his supplication, and if he were truly pure and upright, the Lord would rouse himself in his favor to prosper the dwelling place of his righteousness {{quote:Job 8:6}}. Although his statements contain general truths about divine justice (Genesis 18:25, Romans 3:5), their application to Job's case is merciless and insensitive, for it ignores the spiritual conflict in the third heaven (Job 1:6-12) and judges affliction as irrefutable proof of guilt. Nevertheless, the promise that Job's latter state would be greatly increased prophetically anticipates the literal restoration that the Lord will grant the patriarch at the end of his trial (Job 42:10-12).
[8-19] To support his theological position, Bildad exhorts the afflicted man to inquire of the past age and to examine the wisdom bequeathed by the fathers of old, referring to the patriarchal instruction prior to the codification of the written law (Genesis 6-9, Deuteronomy 32:7). He argues for the brevity of earthly life by pointing to the fragility of humankind {{quote: Job 8:9|For we are but yesterday, and know nothing; our days on earth are like a shadow}} (Psalm 144:4, Ecclesiastes 6:12). Using analogies from the natural world, he explains that just as the reed cannot grow without mud nor the rush without water, the hope of the wicked and those who forget God is destined to perish. The hypocrite's confidence is compared to a spider's web {{quote: Job 8:14}}, a fragile and unstable structure on which he tries to lean but which cannot sustain his dwelling in the face of judgment. In the dispensational context, this description of plants quickly withering and houses collapsing not only illustrates the vanity of self-righteousness but also prophetically projects toward the destruction of the Antichrist and the ruin of the wicked during the great tribulation (Isaiah 14:22, Ezekiel 28:14, 2 Thessalonians 2:8).
[20-22] Bildad's speech concludes by formulating a general maxim concerning the Lord's moral rule {{quote: Job 8:20|Behold, God will not abhor the blameless, nor will he take the wicked by the hand}}. The accuser argues that if Job proves righteous, the Lord will ultimately fill his mouth with laughter and his lips with shouts of joy, while those who hate him will be clothed in shame and the dwelling place of the wicked will perish. Although Bildad's words carry a veiled sarcasm given the patriarch's present misery, the statement contains a prophetic truth that will be fully realized when the saints are vindicated and their enemies shamed before God's judgment seat (Psalm 35:26, Revelation 19:21). Likewise, the restoration of joy and laughter foreshadows the rejoicing of the Jewish remnant when the Lord returns their people from captivity after the glorious coming of the Messiah (Psalm 126:1-3).

[1-10] Job responds to Bildad's previous speech by first acknowledging the general premise of divine majesty, while nevertheless posing humanity's fundamental dilemma: {{quote:Job 9:2|How can man be righteous before God?}}. The grieving man understands that no created being can argue in court against the Lord's omniscience and power, for if man were to attempt to contend with Him, he could not answer one in a thousand of his accusations (Romans 3:20, 1 Corinthians 1:25). Divine sovereignty is manifested in absolute control over the forces of nature and the cosmos, moving mountains in His fury and shaking the foundations of the earth through cataclysmic judgments that prophetically foreshadow the events of the great tribulation (Revelation 16:20). The Lord commands the sun not to rise and seals up the light of the stars, stretching out the heavens and walking on the waves of the sea—an attribute of divine authority that the Lord Jesus literally demonstrated in his earthly days (Matthew 14:25). Likewise, the text attributes to the Lord the creation of celestial constellations such as Arcturus, Orion, the Pleiades, and the southern chambers (Amos 5:8, Job 38:31–32), astronomical structures that serve as signs of God’s majesty and transcend human understanding.
[11–20] The Lord’s invisibility and incomprehensibility become evident when he passes by humanity unseen, sovereignly disposing of his creatures without anyone being able to oppose or question his actions (Daniel 4:35). Job acknowledges that even if he had a just cause, God's holiness is so overwhelming that he would have no recourse but to plead before his judge (Job 9:15). The physical and emotional ordeal that overwhelms the patriarch is described as a continuous breaking through storms, where his wounds multiply without him perceiving any apparent cause in his earthly conduct (Job 16:12-14). In this internal struggle, the suffering man admits the impossibility of achieving self-righteousness before the divine tribunal, concluding that if he were to try to justify himself, his own words would condemn him, and if he were to declare himself perfect, his words would confirm his wickedness (Job 9:20, Romans 3:19). This despair in the face of divine law demonstrates humanity's inability to save itself through its own carnal merits.
[21-31] In the midst of his profound affliction, Job makes a controversial statement, asserting that in the temporal order of the present world, God destroys both the blameless and the wicked (Job 9:22). The grieving man observes that in human history, the earth is frequently handed over to the wicked, and judges suffer blindness—a practical reality that contrasts sharply with the simplistic explanations of his comforters (Psalms 73:3-12, Jeremiah 12:1). To illustrate the brevity and fleeting nature of earthly life, the text employs three metaphors drawn from everyday life: the swift runner or courier, the light reed boats, and the eagle swooping down on its prey (Job 7:6-7, James 4:14). Attempting to erase the complaint or find comfort through human effort proves futile, for Job understands that ritual washing with snow water and the purification of hands cannot cleanse the stain of original sin. The sinner remains submerged in the pit of corruption until even his own garments abhor him (Isaiah 64:6, Jeremiah 2:22).
[32-35] The chapter culminates by establishing the infinite distance that separates the divine nature from the human condition, for God is not a man who can be brought to trial by his peers (Job 9:32). Given the impossibility of a finite creature appearing directly before the majesty of the Almighty, Job expresses the deepest longing of fallen humanity by pointing out the absence of a mediator: {{quote: Job 9:33|There is no arbiter between us to lay his hand on us both}}. This divine arbiter or mediator, capable of touching divinity with one hand and humanity with the other, is perfectly and definitively fulfilled in the person of the Lord Jesus Christ (1 Timothy 2:5, 1 John 2:1). Only through the Redeemer and the removal of the rod of divine judgment is it possible for humanity to speak before God without being overwhelmed by the terror of His holiness, finding the peace and reconciliation that human justice could never provide (Romans 5:1, Hebrews 4:16).

[1-3] The patriarch's lament expresses his weariness with life, giving free rein to his complaint and instructing others to speak out in the bitterness of his soul {{quote:Job 10:1|My soul is weary of my life}}. Job demands that God not condemn him and inquires about the reasons why He contends with him (Isaiah 1:18), questioning the divine silence in the face of his suffering. By asking whether it pleases the Lord to oppress, to despise the work of his hands, and to enlighten the counsel of the wicked, Job involuntarily assumes the position of adversary and accuser (Proverbs 17:11), attributing to God the conduct of an oppressor in collusion with evildoers.
[4-13] Job questions whether God has eyes of flesh or sees according to human vision, and inquires whether his days and years are short like those of man (Job 10:4-5), an inquiry that seeks to trace his iniquity even though the Lord knows that he is not wicked and that no one can deliver from his hand {{quote:Job 10:7|You know that I am not wicked}}. The passage evokes how divine hands molded humankind like clay (Job 10:8-9), comparing the conception and development of the embryo to pouring milk and curdling cheese (Job 10:10). In the physical structure, the bones function as posts and the nerves as crossbeams, covered by skin and flesh like a tabernacle (Exodus 25:9). After having unfolded such a design and bestowed life and favor (Job 10:12), the dilemma arises of why destroy His own creation or afflict humankind. To understand divine judgments and perceive one's own righteousness, human beings require God to apply spiritual eye salve that opens their eyes (Revelation 3:18), like Hagar (Genesis 16), Elisha (2 Kings 6:17, 2 Kings 2), Abraham (Genesis 22:13), the disciples on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:31), and John (John 1:33).
[14-17] The patriarch's reflections reveal that if he sins, God observes him so as not to absolve him of his iniquity {{quote: Job 10:14|If I sinned, you have observed me}}. Amidst constant fluctuation regarding his moral condition, Job affirms that if he is wicked, he is lost, and if he is righteous, he cannot lift his head either, being overwhelmed with confusion and affliction (Job 10:15). The afflicted man feels that the Lord is hunting him like a fierce lion, attributing to Him the renewal of His witnesses against him and the increase of His indignation and strife (Job 10:16-17).
[18-22] Questioning the reason for having been brought forth from his mother's womb, Job laments not having died before being seen by any eye (Job 3:9-12, Job 10:18), wishing he had been taken directly from the womb to the grave as if he had never existed (Job 10:19). Begging for a brief cessation of affliction to obtain comfort before his departure (Job 10:20), the patriarch longs for rest before descending to the place from which there is no return {{quote:Job 10:21|before I go never to return, to the land of darkness and the shadow of death}}. This place is described as an abyssal realm without order, where even light resembles the density of darkness (Job 10:22), representing the rest of the spirit in the subterranean world of the dead.

[1-6] Zophar the Naamathite enters the debate representing the moralist's position, beginning his speech with a rebuke of Job's abundance of words and accusing him of uttering falsehoods (Job 11:3). The accuser attributes to Job the assertion that his doctrine is pure and that he considers himself clean in the eyes of God (Job 11:4). Although Job had maintained his integrity in the face of accusations of specific crimes (Job 9:22, Job 10:7), he did not utter such words of self-sufficiency. Zophar expresses the desire for God to speak and interact directly to reveal the secrets of wisdom (Job 11:5), assuring Job that the Lord punishes him with less severity than his iniquity truly deserves (Job 11:6). Doctrinally, the premise that every sinner deserves divine judgment is correct (Romans 3:23, Romans 6:23); however, Zophar's application is misguided in ignoring that the patriarch's sufferings were not due to judgments for unrepentant iniquity, but to a test of faith permitted by the Lord (Job 1:1, 1 Peter 3:14).
[7-12] The discourse poses one of the book's fundamental questions about the unattainable transcendence of God {{quote:Job 11:7|Can you reach the footprint of God? Can you reach the perfection of the Almighty?}} (Ecclesiastes 3:11, Romans 11:33). Divine wisdom and immensity surpass the height of the heavens and the depth of hell (Job 11:8), extending beyond the surface of the earth and the breadth of the sea (Job 11:9). If the Lord decides to overthrow, imprison, or summon to judgment, no creature can hinder His sovereign determination (Job 11:10), for He knows human vanity and identifies iniquity without need of inquiry (Job 11:11). The passage concludes by pointing out the spiritual stubbornness of the unregenerate man, declaring that the vain man lacks understanding and divine inclination, being like a wild donkey's colt at birth {{quote:Job 11:12|A vain man will become wise, though he is born like a wild donkey's colt}} (Exodus 13:13, Psalms 32:9).
[13-20] Zophar sets forth the conditions for restoration under the legalistic framework: preparing the heart, stretching out the hands in prayer, and purifying the tent by removing iniquity (Job 11:13-14). It is promised that, by fulfilling these requirements, Job will be able to lift up his face without blemish (Revelation 13:2, 1 Peter 1:19), stand firm, and forget his affliction like waters that have passed away (Job 11:15-16). The declaration that existence will be clearer than midday and brighter than the morning (Job 11:17) contains a prophetic application oriented toward the Second Messianic Coming and the restoration of Israel at the end of the Great Tribulation (Isaiah 60:1-3, Malachi 4:2, 2 Peter 1:19). Conversely, the eyes of the wicked will fail, finding no refuge, their only expectation being the surrender of their last breath {{quote:Job 11:20|But the eyes of the wicked shall fail, and they shall have no refuge}}, foreshadowing the final destiny of the lost in the judgment (Joshua 8:20, Revelation 6:15-17, Revelation 20:11-15).

[1-6] Job responds with biting irony to the supposed intellectual superiority of his interlocutors {{quote:Job 12:2|He does not doubt but that you are the people, and with you wisdom will die}}. The afflicted man affirms that he possesses understanding of equal measure and is not inferior to them (Job 12:3), pointing out that the general truths expressed by his companions result from common knowledge. Despite having invoked God and maintained his integrity, the suffering man has become an object of ridicule (Job 12:4), experiencing the contempt reserved for one on the verge of falling from those who enjoy earthly comfort (Job 12:5). Likewise, Job exposes the paradox observed in the fallen world: the tents of thieves and those who provoke the Lord's anger remain secure and prosper temporarily (Job 12:6, Jeremiah 12:1, Habakkuk 1:13), demonstrating that the absence of material affliction does not constitute automatic proof of piety or divine approval.
[7-11] To confront his friends' reasoning, the patriarch refers them to the testimony of visible creation, urging them to question the beasts, the birds of the air, the earth, and the fish of the sea (Job 12:7-8). All these creatures manifestly declare that the hand of the Lord has made all things, acknowledging that in His sovereign hand is the soul of every living being and the breath of all humanity (Job 12:10). Nature suffers the bondage of corruption after the fall (Romans 8:20-22), a dilemma whose solution will not occur until the establishment of the Messiah's millennial kingdom after the Great Tribulation (Isaiah 11:6-9, Revelation 6:8). Just as the palate tastes food, the ear examines words to discern the truth of speeches (Job 12:11).
[12-25] Although the longevity of the elders and patriarchs of ancient times held human experience (Genesis 5:1-32, Genesis 11:10-32, Job 12:12), supreme wisdom, power, counsel, and intelligence belong absolutely to the Lord {{quote:Job 12:13|With him are wisdom and might}}, identifying the Ancient of Days (Daniel 7:13, Revelation 1:14). God exercises unrestricted dominion over history and human structures: what He tears down cannot be rebuilt, and no door is opened to the man He imprisons (Job 12:14). The Lord governs the natural elements, withholding water to cause drought or sending it forth to disrupt the earth, as happened in the Flood (Genesis 7:11-24, Job 12:15). In His sovereignty, He deprives counselors of counsel, drives judges mad, looses the bonds of kings, leads princes astray, and overthrows the mighty (Job 12:16-21). Likewise, the Lord uncovers the depths of darkness and brings to light the shadow of death (Job 12:22, Psalm 139:12), multiplying or destroying nations according to His will (Job 12:23). Finally, he deprives the leaders of the peoples of the earth of understanding, making them wander through pathless deserts, groping in darkness and staggering like drunkards (Job 12:24-25, Isaiah 19:14).

[1-4] Job declares that he understands divine power on the same level as his comforters and expresses his desire to reason directly with God rather than argue with them (Job 13:1-3). He calls his friends fabricators of lies and worthless physicians (Job 13:4), illustrating the human systems of science, religion, philosophy, and education, which are incapable of healing themselves (Luke 4:23).
[5-16] Job exhorts his listeners to be silent and listen to his reasoning (Job 13:5-6, Proverbs 17:28), questioning whether divine excellence does not inspire fear in them (Job 13:11). He reminds them that the memory of man is like ashes and clay (Job 13:12), since human beings are born into a home of affliction and end up reduced to dust (Job 5:7). Despite the suffering, he expresses his unwavering resolve to trust in the Lord {{quote:Job 13:15|Though he slay me, yet will I hope in him}}, ready to defend his ways and seal his words with his own blood, knowing that no hypocrite will appear in the divine presence (Job 13:15-16).
[17-22] The patriarch orders his cause with the certainty of being justified (Job 13:18). To sustain this dialogue with God, he requests two conditions: that the Lord withdraw his hand of sickness and pain, and that his terror not frighten him (Job 13:20-21).
[23-28] Job poses five specific questions to God about the extent of his faults and iniquities, the reason why he hides his face and considers him an enemy, and the persecution of a dry leaf (Job 13:23-25). Doctrinally, the hiding of the divine face prophesies the condition of the nation of Israel (Deuteronomy 31:18, Matthew 13:44), while the complaint about the persecution of dry chaff evokes David's complaint to Saul (1 Samuel 26:20). The passage concludes by pointing out the bitter decrees received, the marks of the sins of youth, and the decay of the body like a garment eaten away by moths (Job 13:26-28).

[1, 2] Psalm 1 begins with the description of the blessed man, a term that, according to Scripture, denotes the spiritual happiness of one who finds his delight in God (Genesis 30:13). In the Old Testament, this blessedness is presented in the form of practical separation through a threefold negative command regarding a man's walk, stand, and sit, exclaiming {{quote:Psalm 1:1|Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked}}. The wicked man's walk begins with accepting counsel contrary to the divine covenant, progresses by dwelling on the sinful path and sharing common projects (Proverbs 1:10-14), and culminates in sitting in the seat of the scoffers who ridicule the Scriptures (2 Peter 3:3-5). Doctrinally, under the dispensation of grace, the believer's position is defined in a contrasting and glorious way: their walk is in Christ (Colossians 2:6), their strength lies in the power of His might (Ephesians 6:10), and their spiritual seat is established in the heavenly realms (Ephesians 2:6). The blessed person finds their positive delight in God's law, valuing it more than their necessary food (Job 23:12) and rejoicing in it as one who finds a great treasure (Psalm 119:162). This constant meditation prevents the believer from straying from communion, reminding them that it is in God that human beings live, move, and have their being (Acts 17:28).
[3] The righteous person is compared to a tree sovereignly planted by God (Matthew 15:13), whose roots extend along streams of water, typifying the constant presence and fullness of the Holy Spirit (John 7:38). This divine planting is further detailed in the declaration {{quote:Psalm 1:3|will be like a tree planted by streams of water}}, guaranteeing that the tree will bear its fruit in its season (2 Timothy 4:2), manifesting the virtues of the Holy Spirit in the character of the redeemed (Galatians 5:22-23). Its foliage remains green and unaffected by the heat, teaching that the believer who fully trusts in the Lord will not experience anxiety or spiritual dryness when times of drought or trials afflict creation (Jeremiah 17:7-8, James 5:17-18). While the tree of empty and hypocritical profession withers from the roots (Matthew 21:19), the righteous prosper in all they undertake, for their walk is aligned with the divine will and their delight rests in the living Word, confirming that {{quote:Psalms 1:3|its leaf does not wither; and everything he does will prosper (Joshua 1:8).
[4-6] The ultimate fate and nature of the wicked are drastically contrasted with the soundness of the righteous, who are described as chaff or barren straw that the wind scatters from the threshing floor, as Scripture warns: {{quote:Psalms 1:4|Not so the wicked, but are like chaff that the wind blows away}}. This analogy of chaff directly alludes to the judicial separation process that the Lord Jesus Christ will carry out when He purifies His threshing floor (Luke 3:17), where the wheat will be stored in the heavenly barn and the useless chaff will be consumed in the fire of Gehenna (Matthew 13:30, Malachi 4:1). A sentence of absolute exclusion is established by declaring {{quote:Psalm 1:5|Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment}}, which means that the wicked will not remain standing in the final judgment (Psalm 130:3, Romans 3:19), nor will sinners have a part in the glorious congregation of the righteous (Hebrews 12:22-23). ​​While the Lord knows and lovingly guards the path of the righteous, the way of the wicked, characterized by rebellion against His words, is sentenced to eternal destruction and perishment (Proverbs 14:12, Revelation 20:11-15).

[1-3] The rebellion of the Gentile nations and the vain designs of the peoples find an initial historical application in the conspiracy of Herod, Pontius Pilate, and the Jewish rulers against the Savior (Acts 4:25-28). However, the text unveils a conspiracy of a global and eschatological nature, where the forces of the United Nations under the direct control of the Antichrist will gather to shake off God's lordship and discipline, exclaiming Psalms 2:1 and Psalms 2:3. The contemporary ecumenical movement promotes religious and political integration to mask this concerted rebellion against Scripture, paving the way for the time of Jacob's trouble (Jeremiah 30:7, Revelation 17:12-14). The providential order of the books in Scripture, placing Psalm 2 immediately after Job, precisely foreshadows that after the rigors of the great tribulation, the absolute reign of the promised seed will be revealed.
[4-6] God's sovereignty responds with irony and heavenly mockery to the pretensions of earthly rulers who attempt to usurp dominion over the planet. The Lord will speak to the nations in His anger and disturb them with His supreme fury during the consummation of the end-time judgments, immutably establishing His eternal purpose, as declared in Psalm 2:6. The holy hill of Zion is not a mystical metaphor or a spiritualized reference to the church of the present dispensation, but rather represents the physical and geographical hill of Jerusalem in the land of Palestine, where the Messiah will reign bodily and visibly after His second coming (Psalm 48:2, Luke 1:32-33, Micah 4:1-2). The throne of David is an earthly and historical seat that belongs by unconditional covenant to the seed of Jacob, destroying any theological claim that seeks to supplant the national promises of Israel with the spiritual inheritance of the body of Christ (Galatians 3:29, Ephesians 3:1-6).
[7-9] The divine decree that constitutes the legal foundation of the Messiah's lordship over all creation, formulated in Psalm 2:7, is revealed. This passage, historically twisted by church councils to argue for a supposed eternal generation of the Son prior to material creation, finds its true doctrinal interpretation in the bodily resurrection of the Savior and His future enthronement as sovereign of the kings of the earth (Acts 13:33, Hebrews 1:5-6). The Lord Jesus Christ will claim the Gentile nations as His rightful inheritance, not to reform or peacefully integrate them through the gospel of grace, but to subject them to a rigorous rule, declaring (Psalm 2:9). This iron scepter represents an absolute, theocratic military dictatorship that will rule the earth during the millennial kingdom, where any disobedience or insurrection against the Jewish King will be immediately broken without recourse (Zechariah 14:16-19, Revelation 2:27, Revelation 19:15).
[10-12] The admonition is urgently directed to the monarchs and judges of the earth, urging them to submit to the deity of the heavenly Sovereign before the final outpouring of His wrath. The solemn command demands absolute and physical submission, establishing in Psalm 2:12 the only way of preservation to avoid perishing under the judgment of His impending wrath. The act of kissing the Son represents the tribute of vassalage and bodily surrender that the dignitaries of the world must render prostrate before His feet on Mount Zion, completely dismantling the political, economic, and religious systems devised by Gentile humanism (Psalm 72:9-11, Philippians 2:10-11, Revelation 20:11-15). The final beatitude crowns the psalm, guaranteeing refuge and providential security for all those who place their faith in the Redeemer, whose justice inescapably precedes the establishment of true earthly peace (Hebrews 7:2, Romans 5:1).

[1-4] The historical background of this psalm is David's flight from his son Absalom (2 Samuel 15:14). Absalom, whose name means "father of peace," represents one of the most accurate foreshadowings of the son of perdition in Scripture, who will temporarily usurp the kingdom of the earth through flattery (Daniel 11:21, 24). The cry of the afflicted, {{quote:Psalm 3:1|O Lord, how many are my enemies!}}, finds its prophetic counterpart in the distress of the Jewish remnant who will be pursued by the adversary in the wilderness (Revelation 12:13-17). In the midst of this hostile siege, the Gentile nations will scornfully proclaim the spiritual desolation of the covenant people, declaring: {{quote:Psalm 3:2|There is no salvation for him in God}}. The insertion of the word "Selah" at the end of the second verse acts as an indicator of the second coming of Christ, alluding to the rocky fortress of Sela-Petra in the region of Edom (2 Kings 14:7). To this physical refuge in the desert, the Hebrew remnant will escape to be providentially sustained by the divine hand (Revelation 12:6, Micah 7:14). The righteous person confesses that the Lord is their shield and glory (Psalm 27:3), and that when they cry out, they are heard from the mountain of His holiness, which anticipates the millennial enthronement of the Messiah on Mount Zion (Psalm 2:6, Amos 1:2, Joel 3:16).
[5-8] The believer's physical safety and rest are based exclusively on divine preservation, as expressed in the declaration: {{quote:Psalm 3:5|I lay down and slept; I awoke, for the Lord sustained me}}. This tranquility in the midst of adversity empowers the servant of God not to fear the multitude of enemies of the faith, even when it comes to confederated Gentile armies besieging the city (Psalm 83:4-8). Doctrinally, under the Mosaic covenant, faith was accompanied by the manifestation of physical power, where a small number of righteous people could put thousands of opponents to flight, as historically occurred with Gideon's army (Judges 7:15-22, Judges 8:10). The fervent plea of ​​the seventh verse, "Arise, O Lord; save me, O my God," is one of the most frequently repeated prayers in the Psalter to demand the Lord's coming in His wrath (Psalm 7:6, Psalm 9:19, Psalm 10:12, Psalm 17:13). This sovereign judgment will result in the destruction of the ungodly powers that attack the chosen people, whose teeth will be broken by the Lord's mighty arm (Jeremiah 50:17). The psalm concludes by absolutely attributing salvation and blessing to God's sovereignty, sealing this prophetic destiny with a final "Selah" that reveals the consummation of divine purposes for the national restoration of Israel at the sound of the trumpet (Joel 2:31-32, Acts 3:19-21).

[1, 2] The psalmist begins with a cry for help in the midst of anguish, appealing to divine justice through an expression of filial dependence {{quote:Psalms 4:1|Hear my cry, O God of my righteousness}}. This invocation reflects David's awareness of the Lord's involvement in his own practical righteousness (Psalms 22:31, Psalms 89:16). David, possessing steadfast mercies not bestowed upon other Old Testament figures, acts as a type of Christ in his sufferings. His historical experience details multiple episodes of extreme affliction, such as his flight to Nob or Gath, and his grief over Absalom. On a technical level, the instruction for the chief musician regarding Neginoth refers to stringed instruments. Furthermore, the Masoretic Text numbers the introduction as the first verse, resulting in a variation in the chapter divisions compared to Western translations. Finally, the term Selah, which appears in verse two, marks a solemn pause and points doctrinally to future events related to the second coming of Christ (Psalm 3:5).
[3, 4] Men are exhorted to recognize God's sovereign separation of the godly (Psalm 4:3). Textual exegesis shows that critical readings often alter the original Hebrew statements, as occurs when proposing alternative translations for the expression that urges trembling and not sinning in verse four. Several commentators erroneously argue that the apostle Paul quotes an ancient Greek version of the Old Testament when writing to the Ephesians (Ephesians 4:26), omitting the fact that no Greek manuscripts of this psalm existed during Paul's ministry. The use of Selah at the end of verse four is omitted by modern translators, despite appearing in all available Hebrew manuscripts. The instruction to meditate in bed and remain silent establishes a principle of spiritual introspection in times of difficulty (Psalm 3:5).
[5, 6] The liturgy of the Old Testament requires sacrifices of righteousness that must be presented with a broken heart, for the offering of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord (Proverbs 15:8, Proverbs 21:27). Verse five inseparably combines faith and works, demanding both ceremonial sacrifices and absolute trust in God (Psalm 4:5). The cry of verse six constitutes a direct plea for the second coming, where the light of the divine countenance is associated with the national restoration of Israel, the establishment of the millennial temple, and the wedding feast of the Lamb (Psalm 37:6, Psalm 43:3, Psalm 89:15, Revelation 19:6-9). The implications of these prophecies point to the resumption of sacrifices that took place in the Temple of Jerusalem during the millennium (Ezekiel 40-48), a concept that often causes confusion among theologians who attempt to spiritualize the Hebrew text.
[7, 8] The inner joy that the Lord grants far surpasses the earthly, material joy associated with grain and wine harvests (Psalm 4:7). On a national level, this rejoicing will be fully manifested in the Jewish people after the return of the Messiah (Psalm 126:2). On an individual level, it allows the believer to sleep and rest in peace even under extreme anguish, as the apostle Peter experienced in prison the night before his scheduled execution (Acts 12:1-6). Security does not depend on governmental systems, religious alliances, or human protective measures, but on the exclusive preservation that God provides (Psalm 4:8).

[1-3] The dedication to the chief musician on Nehiloth indicates that the liturgical piece was performed with wind instruments or flutes, the Hebrew word for which also alludes to a great inheritance or a whispered request. Regular commentators consider the psalm to represent a morning prayer because of the psalmist's statement {{quote: Psalms 5:3}}; however, King David's devotional practice transcends any time constraints (Psalms 55:17). Prophetically, this morning awakening points toward the dawn of Christ's second coming, which is the great day of the Lord described in the eschatological texts (Malachi 4:2, Matthew 13:43). The act of leading the prayer and then looking upward symbolizes an attitude of expectation and priestly vigilance, awaiting the divine response at a time when ungodliness seems to prevail in the earthly realm.
[4-6] The holiness of God excludes any fellowship with wickedness, explicitly declaring that the foolish will not remain in His presence. There is a contemporary doctrinal tendency to mitigate the statement that the Lord hates evildoers (Psalm 5:5), proposing that such hatred is limited exclusively to actions and not to individuals. However, the Hebrew text and dispensational theology confirm that God experiences a real rejection of the persistently wicked, a principle also evident in the dispensational treatment of Esau (Malachi 1:3, Romans 9:13). This divine abhorrence also extends to liars and bloodthirsty men, who will be destroyed under the Lord's judgment (Proverbs 6:16-19, Psalm 11:5). The psalmist describes an active enmity where the Lord abhors the deceitful man, which refutes humanistic interpretations that attempt to eliminate the reverent fear and severity of God's justice.
[7-10] Access to the house of God is attributed solely to the abundance of His mercy, allowing the psalmist to worship toward the holy temple in an attitude of reverence (Psalm 5:7). Since Solomon's temple had not yet been built in David's time, the mention of the holy temple is historically associated with the Most Holy Place of the tabernacle, or prophetically with the future millennial temple (Ezekiel 41-48). The fear mentioned in this passage has been diluted by various modern translators under the terms of mere reverence or awe, stripping the Hebrew word of its true sense of sacred fear, which is consistent throughout other biblical passages (Genesis 20:11, Deuteronomy 2:25, 2 Samuel 23:3). Regarding the psalmist's enemies, the description of their physical and moral depravity serves as the basis for the universal accusation that the apostle Paul makes against humanity (Romans 3:13). The anatomy of human corruption is laid bare, encompassing the dishonest mouth, inner wickedness, the flattering tongue, and a throat described as an open grave where death and moral decay lie (Matthew 12:34, Mark 7:20-23). Finally, the plea for God to destroy them constitutes a legitimate imprecatory prayer under the rule of law, where rebels suffer the retribution for their own plots, similar to the historical and eschatological judgments that befell oppressors (Psalm 109:6, Psalm 137:8-9, Revelation 19:11-21).
[11, 12] All those who put their trust in the Lord and love his holy name are exhorted to rejoice and be glad forever, for it is God who takes up their defense (Psalm 5:11). Although the saints of the Old Testament did not experience the mystical union of being in Christ characteristic of the mystery of the Church, they enjoyed a particular divine communion and preservation (Acts 17:28). Divine favor surrounds the righteous like a protective shield, guaranteeing their preservation in the midst of conflict. However, the identity of these righteous people under the economy of the law inseparably involves faith and practical works of righteousness, distinguishing them from justification by faith alone, which operates exclusively in the present dispensation of grace (Psalms 15:2-5, Romans 3:20).

[1-4] This psalm, commonly categorized among the penitential psalms of Scripture (Psalms 32:1, Psalms 38:1), begins with a fervent plea in which the psalmist begs not to be rebuked in divine wrath {{quote:Psalms 6:1|O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger}}. Liturgical instruction indicates that it should be interpreted on Sheminith, a Hebrew word that designates the eighth or lower octave in the musical scale, also relating to the eighth day of circumcision under the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17:12). There is a fundamental theological difference between the scourge of wrath and paternal instruction; while punishment in fury reflects divine retribution, the discipline of the believer manifests the Lord's love and care (Hebrews 12:5-9). The psalmist experiences extreme weakness that shakes his bones and deeply troubles his soul, portraying the limit of physical and spiritual suffering where the believer, ravaged by the trial, is tempted to faint at the apparent delay of divine intervention (Lamentations 3:22-39). The plea for deliverance appeals exclusively to divine mercies, recognizing that under the economy of the law, the cry for help rests on God's grace and sovereign favor, which foreshadows the suffering Messiah in his earthly days.
[5-7] In the grave or physical tomb, there is no active memory directed toward the public praise of God {{quote:Psalms 6:5|For in death there is no remembrance of you}}. This statement underscores the somber nature of the state of physical death in the Old Testament, where the soul descends to the earth's core before the resurrection and ascension of the Messiah, who emptied Abraham's bosom and triumphed over the bonds of death (Ephesians 4:8-10, Acts 2:24-31). Modern translations tend to soften the severity of these words by substituting or omitting terms of judgment and condemnation, but biblical revelation maintains a clear distinction between the grave of the flesh and the destiny of the sinful soul. Under the oppression of his adversaries, the psalmist describes a night of deep groaning and weeping that gnaws at his eyes and ages his physical strength, likening his affliction to the despair suffered by Job or by the martyrs of the faith under the persecution of the wicked (Job 16:16, Revelation 6:9-11). This figurative expression details the total breaking of the human system under God's sovereign test, also serving as a foreshadowing of the sufferings of the nation of Israel in times of judgment.
[8-10] The psalmist concludes with an imperative command of separation, urging the evildoers to depart from his presence {{quote:Psalm 6:8|Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity}}. This radical distancing constitutes a public testimony that God has heard the cry of his weeping, enabling the troubled believer to claim by faith future victory in the midst of present adversity. The abrupt shift from lament to song of assurance demonstrates how faith anticipates divine help, counting God's answer as a foregone conclusion {{quote:Psalm 6:9|The Lord has heard my plea}}. Prophetically, the shame and sudden dismay of the psalmist's enemies will be fully realized at the second coming of Christ, at which time the adversaries of the Lord and his people will be put to shame and scattered with the breath of his lips (Psalm 2:5, Revelation 19:11-21). The demand that his enemies be turned to confusion underscores the impending judgment on the wicked, strengthening the confidence of the faithful remnant awaiting the glorious restoration of God's justice.

[1-5] The epigraph cataloged as Sigaion evokes a poetic composition of profound spiritual turmoil, historically linked to the accusations of Cushi the Benjamite. In biblical genealogy, the term Cushi is translated as Ethiopian or descendant of Ham (Genesis 10:6, Numbers 12:1), typologically linking him to King Saul and foreshadowing the figure of the son of perdition or Antichrist, who will possess a Jewish ruling background with Hamite ties (Ezekiel 21:25). David turns to the Most High seeking refuge from persecution, imploring deliverance so that the adversary will not tear his soul apart like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8). Under the Messianic order of Mosaic law, the psalmist submits his conscience to a conditional integrity examination (Psalm 7:3: “O Lord my God, if I have done this”), declaring that if there were iniquity in his hands or betrayal of one who dwelt in peace with him, it would be just for the enemy to trample his life in the earth and lay his honor in the dust. The Selah marker at the close of this section signifies the solemn suspension that precedes the Lord’s intervention to humble the proud on the day of judgment (Revelation 14:19–20).
[6–9] The psalmist’s plea appeals to God’s holy wrath to restrain the fury of the adversaries, demanding that the Lord awaken to execute the decreed judgment (Psalm 44:23, Isaiah 51:9). This prophetic invocation anticipates the Messianic advent when the congregation of Israel will gather around the King restored to his throne on the heights of Zion (Psalm 78:65-68, Luke 1:32-33). By proclaiming that the Most High will judge the nations, David requests to be judged according to his personal righteousness and integrity, a stance characteristic of the dispensation of the Law where earthly vindication was linked to the practical behavior of works (Psalm 18:20-24), in stark contrast to the church age where divine righteousness is imputed by grace through faith apart from works (Romans 3:21-22, Philippians 3:9). The passage yearns for the definitive end of the wickedness of the ungodly {{quote:Psalm 7:9|Let the wickedness of the wicked be consumed}}, reaffirming that God is just and thoroughly examines the hearts and minds of human beings (1 Chronicles 28:9, Jeremiah 17:10).
[10-13] The believer's confidence is grounded in the protection of the Most High, who acts as a shield and preserves the upright in heart. The text establishes the sanctity of divine judgment by proclaiming that the Lord's indignation remains active against the doers of iniquity {{quote:Psalm 7:11|God is angry with the wicked every day}}, confirming that God's wrath remains upon all who refuse to turn to repentance and truth (John 3:36, Romans 1:18). Faced with the rebel's obstinate impenitence, the passage describes the Lord sharpening his sword of judgment (Ezekiel 21:9-10) and drawing his war bow to shoot fiery arrows and instruments of death upon the persecutors of his people (Lamentations 2:4, Habakkuk 3:9, Zechariah 9:14). These images of divine warfare prophesy the fiery judgments that the Messiah will execute at his Second Coming, crushing the resistance of the ungodly nations (2 Thessalonians 1:7-8, Revelation 19:15).
[14-17] The nature of sin is described through the allegory of childbirth, showing how the wicked person incubates iniquity, conceives affliction, and gives birth to lies (James 1:14-15). In his eagerness to destroy the innocent, the wicked man digs a deep pit, but God's retributive justice determines that he will fall into the same trap he set for others (Proverbs 26:27, Ecclesiastes 10:8). Doctrinally, the declaration that the aggressor's violence will fall upon his own head prophesies the final defeat of the Antichrist, who will receive a mortal wound to the head (Judges 9:53-54) in fulfillment of the promise in Genesis where the seed of the woman crushes the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15, Romans 16:20). The Psalm concludes with a song of worship to the Name of the Lord Most High {{quote: Psalms 7:17|I will praise the Lord according to his righteousness}}, celebrating the unchanging equity of divine rule on earth (Psalms 9:2, Psalms 97:1-2).

[1, 2] The title Gittith evokes an instrument or melody associated with the Feast of Tabernacles and the winepress of judgment (Revelation 14:20), introducing a sequence of Psalms with marked prophetic allusions to the Second Coming. The psalmist opens with a proclamation of praise declaring the excellence of the Lord's name throughout the earth and placing His glory above the visible heavens (Psalm 19:1-4). This glory is manifested in material creation, which functions as the garment of the Most High without being confused with His divine essence, refuting all forms of pantheism (Psalm 104:2, Hebrews 1:10-11). Likewise, from the mouths of children and infants the Lord has established strength to silence the enemy and the avenger (Matthew 21:16), demonstrating that divine authority operates through what the world considers weak to thwart satanic opposition {{quote:Psalm 8:1|O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!}}.
[3, 4] By contemplating the celestial bodies—the moon and the stars formed by the fingers of God—the psalmist reflects on the insignificance of mortal humankind in the face of the immensity of the cosmos. However, the question of why the Lord remembers humankind and visits the Son of Man possesses a profound Messianic dimension. In the original order, Adam received earthly stewardship but lost his dominion by falling into transgression (Genesis 1:28, Genesis 3:17-19). Therefore, the prophecy shifts from the first Adam to the last Adam, the Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 15:45-47), who as the Son of Man is visited and exalted by God to fulfill the redemptive purpose {{quote:Psalm 8:4|What is man that you are mindful of him?}}.
[5-8] The Messiah's work required that He be made for a short time shorter than the angels through His incarnation and suffering of death, to be subsequently crowned with glory and honor (Hebrews 2:9). The divine decree establishes the subjection of all things under His feet, guaranteeing a literal, physical, and visible dominion over the works of the Lord's hands. Although the visible subjection of all creation before the eyes of the world is not yet contemplated in the present age (1 Corinthians 15:25-27, Hebrews 2:8), prophetic fulfillment requires that the Messiah reign over the animal kingdom—including sheep, oxen, beasts of the field, birds of the air, and fish of the sea—during the millennial reign (Isaiah 11:6-9, Zechariah 14:9) {{quote:Psalm 8:6|you have put all things under his feet}}.
[9] The Psalm concludes by reiterating the initial doxology, sealing the thematic unity of the passage. This final acclamation anticipates the age when the Lord's kingdom will be established over the entire globe and his name will be recognized as glorious throughout the earth (Isaiah 54:5, Zechariah 14:9, Revelation 11:15). The universal recognition of divine majesty will replace the rebellion of the nations, consummating the exaltation of the Messiah as King of kings and Lord of lords {{quote:Psalms 8:9}}.

[1-4] The epigraph Muthlabben, translated as death to the son, establishes a messianic framework concerning the downfall of the son of perdition—the antichrist—and the consummation of divine judgment at the Second Coming. David begins a doxology of praise on behalf of Israel and the resurrected Messiah, celebrating that the enemies fall and perish before the physical presence of God at his glorious return (Psalms 68:1-2, John 18:6). Messianic vindication is manifested when the Lord sits on the throne of David to judge with equity and uphold the righteous cause of his chosen people {{quote:Psalm 9:4|For you have upheld my right and my cause}}, anticipating the ultimate victory over the rebellion of the kings of the earth (Psalm 2:6-9, Revelation 19:11-16).
[5-8] The text describes the execution of divine wrath upon the Gentiles and the summary destruction of the ungodly, a term that specifically identifies the man of sin (2 Thessalonians 2:8, Habakkuk 2:5). His name is blotted out forever, and the devastations wrought by the enemy—Abaddon or Apollyon, the angel of the abyss (Revelation 9:11)—reach their perpetual end in the battle of Armageddon (Isaiah 14:5-7, Revelation 20:10). While the wicked cities perish and their memory is blotted out from the face of the earth, the Lord's sovereignty remains unchanged, having established his throne in Jerusalem to administer the millennial judgment upon the nations (Isaiah 2:2-4, Daniel 2:44, Zechariah 14:9) {{quote:Psalms 9:5|You rebuked the nations, you destroyed the wicked}}.
[9-12] The Lord reveals himself as a stronghold and impregnable refuge for the oppressed during the time of trouble, a direct allusion to the period of the Great Tribulation or time of Jacob's trouble (Jeremiah 30:7, Matthew 24:21). During this final dispensation, the faithful Jewish remnant is stripped of its material resources by refusing the mark of the beast, being reduced to destitution and depending exclusively on divine assistance (James 5:1-7, Revelation 13:16-17). Those who know the name of the Lord place their trust in Him without being forsaken (Hosea 6:1-2), singing praises to the Messiah who dwells in Zion and who demands the blood of the martyrs sacrificed during the persecution of the antichrist (Psalms 50:2, Revelation 6:9-10, Revelation 16:6) {{quote:Psalms 9:9|And the LORD will be a refuge for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble}}.
[13-16] The plea for divine mercy asks to be delivered from the gates of death to proclaim salvation at the gates of the daughter of Zion, foreshadowing the physical and spiritual restoration of Israel in the millennial kingdom (Isaiah 35:10, Romans 11:26). The passage describes the collapse of pagan nations, which sink into the pit they dug for God's people and are caught in the net they secretly laid (Proverbs 26:27, Ecclesiastes 10:8, Romans 11:9). The manifestation of the Lord's justice causes the wicked to be ensnared in the work of their own hands {{quote:Psalms 9:16|The LORD was known in the judgment he made}}, concluding the section with the indication Higgai Selah, which calls for a slow and solemn meditation on the inevitable ruin of Satan and his empire (Psalms 19:14, Psalms 92:3).
[17-20] The divine sentence decrees that the wicked and all nations that forget God will be taken to Hell, a literal judgment that will fall upon the rebels at the end of the Great Tribulation (Psalms 50:22, Matthew 25:41, Revelation 20:15). In contrast to the fate of the wicked, the hope of the needy will not perish eternally, for the Lord will vindicate his people. The invocation {{quote:Psalms 9:19|Arise, O LORD}} constitutes a characteristic cry of the Second Coming (Psalms 3:7, Psalms 7:6, Psalms 68:1, Isaiah 51:9), by which God is asked to judge the Gentiles and instill fear in the proud so that they may recognize their fragile condition as mere mortals before the Messianic majesty (Psalms 82:7, Zechariah 14:16-19).

[1-3] The entire psalm addresses the figure and career of the Antichrist, beginning with the prayer of the afflicted Jewish remnant during the Great Tribulation (Matthew 24:21, Jeremiah 30:7). This initial plea in the face of God's apparent estrangement reflects the affliction of the saints in times of persecution (Psalm 13:1, Psalm 30:7, Psalm 44:24). The persecutors described are the followers of the man of sin (2 Thessalonians 2:3). Doctrinally, in the time of Jacob's trouble (Jeremiah 30:7), material wealth appears linked to ungodliness, and it is practically impossible to be both rich and righteous simultaneously (James 5:1-9). Therefore, poverty becomes almost synonymous with righteousness (Psalm 69:33, Psalm 107:41, Psalm 140:12, Isaiah 29:19, Job 34:28, Luke 16:19-31). This framework differs from the Church Age, where salvation is granted by grace through faith apart from works of the law (Ephesians 2:8-9). It is also noted that the Septuagint mistakenly combined this psalm with the ninth.
[4-8] The pride of the wicked, or the Son of Perdition, is detailed, who in the haughtiness of his countenance does not seek God nor include Him in his thoughts (Psalm 10:4). His ways are crooked, he despises his enemies, and he affirms in his heart that he will never be shaken nor fall into adversity (Psalm 10:5-6). His mouth is full of cursing, deceit, and fraud, harboring malice under his tongue (Psalm 10:7). Moreover, he acts like an ambushing oppressor who sits in the hiding places of villages to secretly murder the innocent and prey on the poor (Psalm 10:8).
[9-15] The opponent is presented as a lion in his den, lying in wait to catch the helpless (1 Peter 5:8). This adversary shrinks back and humbles himself so that the poor may fall under his power, thinking in his heart that God has forgotten him and hidden his face so as not to see him (Psalm 10:9-11). In response, the persecuted cry out to the Lord to lift up his hand and not forget the humble (Psalm 10:12-14). The passage contains the imperative plea to break the power of the wicked (Psalm 10:15). Doctrinally, this disabling of the wicked one's arm is fulfilled in the judgment of the worthless shepherd who loses the strength of his arm and the sight in his right eye (Zechariah 11:17). This same prefiguration of the broken arm reappears in Moab in connection with Kerioth (Jeremiah 48:24-25), linking it to Judas Iscariot as the man of Kerioth (Ezekiel 30:2, 24, Isaiah 37:17).
[16-18] The Lord is proclaimed King for eternity, decreeing that the Gentiles will perish from his land (Psalm 10:16). This expulsion of the pagan nations from the land of Palestine has not been fulfilled in the historical past, but rather literally points to the establishment of the Millennial Kingdom after the visible return of the Messiah (Psalm 22:28, Psalm 110, Zechariah 14). God hears the desire of the humble and judges the orphan and the oppressed so that the man of the earth may no longer instill terror (Psalms 10:17-18). The term "man of the earth" designates the Antichrist as the ultimate exponent of Adamic and earthly nature (1 Corinthians 15:47) {{quote: Psalms 10:18|so that the man of the earth may no longer do violence}}, whose prefiguration is observed in rulers who manifested impairments in their right arm or limb.

[1-3] The declaration of trust in the Lord opens the passage, emphasizing the main theme of the first group of psalms (Psalms 118:8, Jeremiah 17:5). In response to the exhortation to flee like a bird to the mountains, the question {{quote:Psalms 11:3|If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?}} prophetically points to the Great Tribulation (Jeremiah 30:7). At that time, the appearance of the Son of Perdition destroys the foundations of the law, the economy, freedom, Christianity, and the temple structure (Psalms 137:7, Revelation 11:1-2). Homiletically, the ruin of human institutions compels the believer to proclaim the word and stand firm on the unshakeable foundation of Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3:11, Hebrews 12:27).
[4, 5] The presence of the Lord in his holy temple and his heavenly throne (Habakkuk 2:20) is described by the anthropomorphic image of his eyelids examining the children of men (Proverbs 15:3, Proverbs 20:8, Psalms 66:7). The trial inflicted on the righteous does not necessarily constitute punishment for iniquity, finding its greatest Old Testament illustration in the experience of Job (Job 1:1, Psalms 73:1-4). Furthermore, it is categorically established that the Lord hates in His soul the wicked and the man who loves violence {{quote:Psalms 11:5|his soul hates the wicked and him who loves violence}}, contradicting the theological assumption that the Deity regards all sinners with favor without distinction.
[6, 7] The judgment upon the wicked will be executed by a rain of snares, fire, sulfur, and a scorching wind {{quote:Psalms 11:6|On the wicked it will rain snares; fire and sulfur}}, an event literally fulfilled at the end of the Millennial Kingdom (Revelation 20:9) and foreshadowed in the Great Tribulation (Ezekiel 38:22). Unlike the believer's cup of blessing (Psalms 23:5), the portion of the wicked consists of the retribution of divine wrath. Finally, it is stated that the just Lord loves justice and looks upon the upright, recalling that under the regime of law, the righteousness of the individual was defined by practical obedience to the commandments (Ecclesiastes 12:13), in clear contrast to salvation by grace alone granted in the present age (Ephesians 2:8-9).
