[1-4] Luke begins his writing by addressing Theophilus with a rigorous historical methodology, based on the testimony of eyewitnesses and ministers of the word from the beginning {{quote:Luke 1:3|writing them to you in order, O most excellent Theophilus}}. The gospel perspective highlights the human nature of Jesus Christ as the Son of Man, tracing his genealogy back to Adam to present the perfection of his humanity to a Greek-speaking audience (Luke 3:38, 1 Corinthians 15:45). Unlike Matthew, who emphasizes the Davidic King, and Mark, who presents the Suffering Servant, Luke's narrative highlights the doctrinal certainty of the teachings received, guaranteeing the literal historicity of the events that underpin the believer's faith.
[5-25] The narrative is historically situated during Herod's reign in Judea, introducing the priest Zechariah, of the lot of Abijah, and his wife Elizabeth, a descendant of Aaron. The union of the tribe of Levi with that of Judah through ancient marriage ties foreshadows the convergence of the priestly and royal offices in the person of Jesus Christ (Exodus 6:23, Hebrews 3:1). Both spouses walked blamelessly according to the commandments and ordinances of the Mosaic Law, reflecting the dispensational framework of the Old Testament prior to Calvary. Elizabeth's barrenness places her among the seven barren women in Scripture whose miraculous conception typifies the virgin birth (Genesis 11:30, 1 Samuel 1:2, Judges 13:2). While Zechariah was offering incense in the sanctuary, the angel Gabriel appeared to him at the right of the altar, announcing the birth of John and his Nazarene consecration from the womb (Luke 1:15). The angelic prophecy links John's ministry with the spirit and power of Elijah, combining elements of the first coming with the eschatological preparation for the Day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5-6, Matthew 11:14). The priestly division of Abijah places John's conception in June, which situates his birth at Passover and the subsequent birth of Jesus Christ during the Feast of Tabernacles in September. Doubting the promise because of his advanced age, Zechariah was deprived of speech until the fulfillment of the divine word.
[26-38] In the sixth month of Elizabeth's pregnancy, the angel Gabriel was sent to Nazareth to a virgin betrothed to Joseph, both belonging to the royal house of David. This conception without male intervention directly fulfills the Messianic prophecy of the seed of the woman (Genesis 3:15, Isaiah 7:14, Matthew 1:22-23). ​​The angelic greeting recognizes Mary as favored among women, but biblical doctrine distinguishes her personal need for redemption from later theological elaborations that attempt to attribute to her an immaculate conception or a role as co-redemptrix (Psalm 51:5, Romans 3:23). Gabriel proclaims the scope of the Davidic covenant, announcing that the Lord God will give Jesus the throne of his father David to reign sovereignly over the house of Jacob forever (Luke 1:32). This throne represents a literal monarchy on earth, established in Jerusalem, the ultimate fulfillment of which will occur at the Second Coming (Jeremiah 23:5, Acts 2:30, Revelation 19:11-16). The action of the Holy Spirit overshadowing Mary guarantees the absolute holiness of the incarnation, declaring that the Holy Being conceived in her womb is truly the Son of God.
[39-56] Mary hurried to the hill country of Judah to visit Elizabeth, at which point the child leaped for joy in her womb, filled with the Holy Spirit (Luke 1:15). In response to the greeting, Mary sang the hymn known as the Magnificat, whose theological structure closely corresponds to Hannah's prayer in the Old Testament (1 Samuel 2:1-10). Mary explicitly acknowledges her condition as a creature in need of salvation by rejoicing in God her Savior {{quote: Luke 1:47|and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior}}. This confession confirms that the Lord's earthly mother was subject to the requirements of the law and required the ritual purification prescribed by the Mosaic code (Leviticus 12:2-8, Galatians 4:4). The prophetic declarations of the hymn employ the prophetic past tense to describe future eschatological events, such as the deposition of the powerful and the exaltation of the humble, which will be fully realized with the return of the Messiah to fulfill the perpetual covenant made with Abraham and his descendants (Genesis 15:18, Psalms 105:8-11, Romans 11:26).
[57-80] When the time came for her to give birth, Elizabeth bore a son, and on the eighth day the community gathered for the circumcision according to the precept of the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17:12, Leviticus 12:3). When the relatives insisted on naming him Zechariah, the father confirmed in writing the name John, prompting him to immediately open his mouth to bless God. Filled with the Holy Spirit, Zechariah delivered a national and messianic prophecy known as the Benedictus, extolling the Lord for having visited and redeemed his people (Luke 1:68). The text celebrates the raising of a horn of salvation in the house of David, promising the physical deliverance of Israel from its political enemies and all who hate it (Psalm 132:17, Psalm 106:10). This earthly and spiritual salvation is grounded in the holy covenant and the mercy promised to the patriarchs. Finally, the child's mission is defined as that of the prophet of the Most High who would go before the Lord to prepare his ways and guide the feet of the remnant in paths of peace (Isaiah 40:3, Malachi 3:1). The forerunner grew and became strong in spirit, remaining in the deserts until the day of his public manifestation to the nation of Israel.

[1-7] Divine Providence uses the census decree issued by Caesar Augustus to move Joseph and Mary from Nazareth to Bethlehem of Judea, the city of David, precisely fulfilling the prophecy concerning the birthplace of the Messiah (Micah 5:2). The historical accuracy of the narrative places this census during Quirinius's first term as governor of Syria around 4 BC, refuting the challenges of rationalist criticism. The journey of approximately one hundred miles is physically arduous for the pregnant virgin, revealing Satan's attempt to induce a miscarriage or premature birth outside the prophetic setting; nevertheless, the Lord preserves the promised seed (Genesis 3:15). When the time came, Mary gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling cloths, laying him in a manger because there was no room for them in the inn (Luke 2:7). The stable with animals highlights the humble condition of the incarnation and aligns with the typology of the Lamb of God, whose birth occurs where lambs are born (Genesis 4:2, John 1:29). Likewise, the swaddling evokes the ritual way in which bodies were prepared for burial (John 19:40, Acts 5:6), foreshadowing that this child was born with the express purpose of dying for humanity. The lack of space at the inn is due both to the large influx of people for the census and to the crowds typical of the Feast of Tabernacles in September, the time when the Savior's coming truly occurred, not at the winter solstice.
[8-20] The proclamation of the Messianic birth is made sovereignly to shepherds watching over their flocks during the night vigils in the fields of Bethlehem. The presence of the flocks in the open air confirms that the event did not take place in the harshness of winter, but in autumn during the Feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:34). The angel of the Lord appears surrounded by the glory of God—the Shekinah light manifested at Sinai and in the tabernacle (Exodus 24:16, 1 Kings 8:11)—and imparts a message of comfort intended for all the people. The heavenly host joins the messenger in proclaiming the Trinitarian praise: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.” The structure of this praise establishes that there can be no true peace on earth without first giving glory to God in the highest and acknowledging the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6, Romans 5:1). Doctrinally, this peace on earth points toward the millennial kingdom that will be established at the second coming of Christ (Micah 5:5, Revelation 19:11-16). After the angels depart, the shepherds hurry and find Mary, Joseph, and the child lying in the manger, spreading what they had been told about the Savior. It is worth noting that the wise men from the East mentioned in the first Gospel were not present in the stable, but arrived one or two years later, finding the family settled in a house (Matthew 2:11).
[21-39] In obedience to the Abrahamic covenant, the child was circumcised on the eighth day and given the name Jesus, announced by the angel before his conception (Genesis 17:12, Leviticus 12:3). After the days of purification according to Mosaic law were completed, his parents took him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord. The offering presented by Mary and Joseph—a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons—reveals the family's extreme poverty, since the law stipulated this substitute sacrifice only for those who could not afford a lamb (Leviticus 12:8). Nevertheless, the mother held in her arms the true Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). This ritual need for purification confirms that Mary was subject to Mosaic Law like any other Israelite woman, refuting the notion of an immaculate or sinless conception (Psalm 51:5, Romans 3:23). In the temple, the elderly Simeon, moved by the Holy Spirit, takes the child in his arms and blesses God, declaring that his eyes have seen salvation (Luke 2:32, "a light to be revealed to the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel"). Simeon's prophecy indicates that the Messiah is destined for the fall and rise of many in Israel, announcing to Mary that a sword will pierce her own soul as she witnesses the rejection and crucifixion of her son (Isaiah 8:14, John 19:25). Likewise, the elderly prophetess Anna, of the tribe of Asher, who worshipped night and day with fasting and prayer, gave thanks to the Lord and spoke of the child to all who were awaiting the redemption in Jerusalem. After all the legal rites were completed, the family returned to Galilee, to their town of Nazareth.
[40-52] The child grew and became strong in spirit, filled with wisdom under divine grace as he developed into a sinless human being (Hebrews 4:15). When he was twelve years old, his parents went up to Jerusalem for the Passover festival according to liturgical custom. After the festival, the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem without Joseph or his mother noticing, who assumed he was traveling with the group. After searching for him for a day among relatives and acquaintances, they return to the holy city and find him three days later in the temple, sitting among the teachers of the law, listening to them and asking them questions. His understanding and answers astonish the religious scholars, foreshadowing the theological debates of his earthly ministry (Luke 20:1-8). When lovingly rebuked by his mother, who argues that she and his father Joseph had been anxiously searching for him, Jesus utters his first recorded words in the Gospels: “Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?” (Luke 2:49). In this statement, the young man respectfully corrects Mary’s assertion about Joseph, proclaiming his direct divine sonship with God the Father and manifesting for the first time an awareness of his Messianic mission. Following this event, Jesus goes down with them to Nazareth and lives in obedience to his earthly parents, while Mary treasures these words in her heart. The chapter concludes by noting that Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men, manifesting the perfection of his sinless humanity (1 Corinthians 1:30).

[1-6] Luke's narrative places the beginning of John the Baptist's ministry within a precise chronological framework, citing the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar's reign, the governorship of Pontius Pilate, and the reigns of Herod, Philip, and Lysanias, as well as the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas. This historical contextualization demonstrates the reality of biblical events in the face of the challenges of rationalist criticism (Luke 1:3-4, Acts 4:6). The word of God came to John in the wilderness, sending him to preach a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins throughout the land around the Jordan (Luke 3:3). This ministry literally fulfilled Isaiah's prophecy concerning the voice crying in the wilderness to make straight the highways of the Lord (Isaiah 40:3-5), announcing that all flesh will see God's salvation within the framework of the Messianic dispensation.
[7-14] Before the multitudes who came to be baptized, John delivered a stern warning against false religious security, denouncing the presumption of appealing to the physical lineage of Abraham without demonstrating genuine conversion (Luke 3:8). The forerunner warned that God has the power to raise up children to Abraham even from stones, pointing out that the ax is already at the root of the trees to cut down and throw into the fire every tree that does not produce good fruit (Matthew 3:7-10). When questioned by various social classes, John prescribed practical works of justice and charity, instructing the people to share their tunics and food, the tax collectors not to demand more than required, and the soldiers to avoid extortion and be content with their pay (Romans 3:20, Galatians 3:29).
[15-22] Faced with the people's expectation and wondering if John was the Christ, the Baptist declared the Messiah's transcendence by proclaiming that He would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire {{quote:Luke 3:16|he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire}}. Unlike the Gospel according to Saint Mark, which omits the mention of fire, Luke preserves the full statement that links the Holy Spirit with the grace of the New Testament and fire with the final judgment at the second coming (Matthew 3:11, Mark 1:8, Revelation 19:11-16). After recording John's imprisonment for rebuking Herod's abominations, the text details the baptism of Jesus, where, while he was praying, the heavens opened and the Holy Spirit descended bodily like a dove upon him. This Trinitarian manifestation was sealed by the voice of the Father, who declared divine sonship and absolute delight in his beloved Son (Acts 2:1-4).
[23-38] Jesus Christ began his earthly ministry around the age of thirty, presenting a genealogy that differs from that recorded in the first Gospel by tracing the biological line through Mary {{quote:Luke 3:23|being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, who was from Heli}}. Since Jewish custom traced genealogies through the paternal line, Joseph is recognized as the son of Heli by way of son-in-law, deriving royal lineage from David through his son Nathan and not through Solomon (Matthew 1:16, Romans 1:3-4). Luke extends the Messianic lineage beyond Abraham to Adam, whom he describes as the son of God, thus reinforcing the presentation of Christ as the true Son of Man and the last Adam sent to redeem fallen humanity (Genesis 5:1, 1 Corinthians 15:45).

[1-13] Jesus Christ, filled with the Holy Spirit after his baptism in the Jordan, is led by the same Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil for forty days (Hebrews 2:17-18, Hebrews 4:15). The typology of the forty-day fasting period links the Lord's experience to the journeys of Moses and Elijah on Mount Sinai (Exodus 34:28, 1 Kings 19:8). At the conclusion of the fast, Satan presents three strategic temptations. In the first, he urges Jesus to turn stones into bread; Jesus rejects this selfish, miraculous recourse by quoting Scripture {{quote:Luke 4:4|It is written: Man shall not live by bread alone}}. This provision of food in affliction is prophetically connected to the manna in the wilderness and to the supernatural sustenance God will provide for the Jewish remnant during the great tribulation (Exodus 16:14-15, Micah 7:14, Revelation 12:6). In the second temptation, the devil shows Jesus all the kingdoms of the world in a single moment, offering him their power in exchange for worship (Luke 4:5-7). The Lord refused to take a shortcut without the cross, reserving possession of earthly kingdoms for his second coming (Revelation 11:15), and responds by demanding exclusive worship of the true God (Deuteronomy 6:13). In the third temptation, the adversary takes Jesus to Jerusalem and places him on the pinnacle of the temple, manipulating Scripture by omitting the clause about keeping his ways (Psalm 91:11-12). Jesus triumphs again through the written word {{quote:Luke 4:12|It is said: You shall not put the Lord your God to the test}}. After this battle, the devil departs from Him for a time, leaving the Savior victorious where Adam and the nation of Israel had failed (Genesis 3:6, Numbers 14:22).
[14-30] Jesus returns to Galilee in the power of the Holy Spirit, teaching in the synagogues and winning the acclaim of the people (Luke 4:14-15). Upon arriving in Nazareth, He enters the synagogue on the Sabbath, as was his custom, and stands up to read from the book of the prophet Isaiah (Isaiah 61:1-2). The selected passage proclaims the anointing of the Spirit upon the Messiah to bring good news to the poor, heal the brokenhearted, proclaim freedom for the captives, and give sight to the blind. In a doctrinally relevant way, Jesus stops reading midway through the text of Isaiah just as it proclaims the year of the Lord’s favor, omitting the subsequent phrase concerning the day of God’s vengeance. This division demonstrates the dispensational separation between the first coming in grace and the second coming in judgment (Isaiah 61:2, Revelation 19:11–16). As he closes the scroll, the Lord solemnly declares, “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” Although the crowd admires the grace of his words, a stumbling block soon arises when they question his humble origins as the son of Joseph (Matthew 13:55). Faced with the ungodly demand to replicate there the signs performed in Capernaum, Jesus points out that no prophet is accepted in his own country, illustrating God's sovereign favor through the sending of Elijah to the Gentile widow of Sarepta in Sidon and the healing of Naaman the Syrian by Elisha (1 Kings 17:9, 2 Kings 5:14). This reminder of the grace bestowed upon the Gentiles provokes the fury of the listeners, who drive Jesus out of the city and lead him to the top of the mountain to throw him down the cliff. Nevertheless, the Lord passes through their midst, demonstrating His sovereign authority over His enemies (Psalm 2:1-4, John 8:59).
[31-37] The Lord descends to Capernaum, a Galilean city that served as His ministry headquarters, partially fulfilling the prophecy about the light shed on Zebulun and Naphtali (Isaiah 9:1-2, Matthew 4:13-16). On the Sabbath, Jesus taught the congregation in the synagogue with an unusual authority that contrasted sharply with the teaching of the scribes (Luke 4:32: “And they were astonished at His teaching, for His word was with authority”). In the synagogue was a man possessed by an unclean spirit, who exclaimed with a loud voice, acknowledging Jesus’ divinity and holiness as the Holy One of God (Mark 1:24). Scripture demonstrates that demonic entities hold an intellectual orthodoxy regarding the deity of the Messiah, although they lack salvific submission (James 2:19). Jesus forcefully rejects the testimony of unclean spirits to avoid any association with the forces of darkness, rebuking the demon and ordering it to be silent and come out of the man (Luke 4:35, Acts 16:16-18). The demon throws the man down in the middle of the assembly without causing him bodily harm, causing widespread astonishment among those present, who questioned the nature of a word capable of commanding unclean spirits with authority. This event spread the Lord's fame throughout the surrounding area (Mark 1:28).
[38-44] After leaving the synagogue, Jesus enters the house of Simon Peter, whose mother-in-law is suffering from a severe fever. This detail from the biblical account explicitly confirms Simon Peter's married status, refuting ecclesiastical traditions regarding apostolic celibacy (1 Corinthians 9:5, Mark 1:30). The disciples plead with the Lord for the sick woman, and Jesus, bending over her, directly rebukes the fever, which instantly disappears, allowing the woman to immediately rise and serve them (Luke 4:39). As the sun sets, marking the formal conclusion of the Sabbath rest, the people flock to Jesus, bringing the sick with various ailments and those possessed by demons. The Lord lays his hands on each of them, healing them, while rebuking the demons and preventing them from proclaiming his Messianic status, for they knew that he was the Christ (Mark 1:34, Luke 4:41). In the early morning, Jesus withdrew to a deserted place to seek communion with the Father, but crowds sought him out and tried to keep him in the region. The Lord declared the purpose of his mission, pointing out the need to preach the kingdom of God in other cities {{quote: Luke 4:43|I must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns also}}, continuing his preaching in the synagogues throughout Galilee (Matthew 4:23, Matthew 10:5-6).

[1-11] Jesus Christ's teaching on the shores of the Sea of ​​Galilee draws a crowd eager to hear the word of God, prompting the Lord to board Simon Peter's boat to instruct the congregation from the water. The harmonious sequence of the Gospels demonstrates that this event is not the first contact between the Messiah and the Galilean fishermen, but rather an advanced stage of consecration following a previous introduction and initial calling (John 1:40-42, Matthew 4:18-22). At the conclusion of the discourse, the Lord commands Simon to put out into deep water and let down his nets for a catch, using the technical term diktuon in the Greek text to refer to the three-layered net. In his response, Peter reveals a partial obedience by protesting that they have worked all night without catching anything, agreeing to cast the net in a single instance instead of the multiple nets decreed by the Lord (Luke 5:5). Despite this hesitation, the Lord's sovereign intervention ensnares a multitude of fish that bursts the net and fills two boats to the point of capsizing, a prodigy that differs from the second similar miracle after the resurrection where the net remained unbroken (John 21:6-11). Before this display of omnipotence, Simon Peter falls to his knees before Jesus in awe, manifesting a profound conviction of his own human depravity (Luke 5:8). This vision of God's majesty produces the believer's humility before divine holiness, emulating the experience of the prophet Isaiah before the heavenly throne (Isaiah 6:5). The Lord transforms Simon's fear into a mission of eternal significance by promising him that from then on he will be a fisher of men, leading Peter, James, and John to leave everything to follow him unconditionally (Mark 1:17, Acts 2:41).
[12-16] The appearance of a man covered in leprosy in a Galilean city illustrates the spiritual condition of humanity under the dominion of sin, for in biblical revelation leprosy constitutes the most complete type of moral corruption (Leviticus 13-14, Isaiah 1:5-6). The disease contaminates the victim, demands atonement through blood, and only God has the power to effect healing. The leper prostrates himself on his face before Jesus, acknowledging his deity and sovereignty by calling him Lord {{quote:Luke 5:12|Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean}}. This attitude of faith differs from the skepticism of formal religion, for the afflicted man does not doubt the Messiah's power but submits to his sovereign will. Extending his hand, the Lord touches the unclean man, proclaiming his willingness to cleanse him {{quote:Luke 5:13|I am willing; be clean}}, causing the leprosy to disappear instantly. Touching a leper was strictly forbidden under the Mosaic code because it imparted ceremonial defilement (Leviticus 13:45-46, Numbers 5:2-3). However, Christ acts in his capacity as Great High Priest, taking upon himself the sicknesses and iniquities of his people to purge them through his redemptive sacrifice (Isaiah 53:4-5, Matthew 8:17, Hebrews 3:1). The Lord commands him to remain silent and appear before the priest to offer the sacrifice prescribed by Moses as a testimony before the Jewish leadership (Leviticus 14:12-24). Prophetically, leprosy will reappear on earth during the great tribulation as the pestilent sore that will afflict those who receive the mark of the beast, foreshadowing the purification that the Israelite remnant will obtain under divine judgment (2 Kings 5:14, Micah 7:14, 2 Peter 2:13, Revelation 16:2).
[17-26] Jesus' teaching in Capernaum draws an audience of Pharisees and teachers of the law from all the villages of Galilee, Judea, and Jerusalem, demonstrating the Lord's power to heal. Four men carry a paralytic on a bed or stretcher, and finding themselves unable to enter through the door because of the crowd, they climb onto the roof and tear down the covering to lower the sick man into the midst of the assembly before Jesus. Seeing the faith of the intercessors, the Lord pronounces spiritual absolution for the suffering person (Luke 5:20). This action demonstrates that in the economy of the Old Testament and in the healing ministry of the Gospels, the required faith is usually that of those who intercede for the sick person, not necessarily that of the one suffering (Mark 2:5, James 5:14-16), thus refuting the tenets of the contemporary charismatic movement. The scribes and Pharisees accuse Jesus in their hearts of uttering blasphemies, arguing that no one can forgive sins but God alone (Psalm 103:3). The Lord demonstrates his omniscience by perceiving the secret thoughts of the religious leaders (Romans 2:16), confronting their unbelief by questioning whether it is easier to declare the forgiveness of sins or to command the cripple to rise and walk. To certify to the nation that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, he commands the paralytic to get up, take his mat, and go home (Luke 5:24). The man immediately gets up, glorifying God, plunging the crowd into awe as they recognize the manifestation of extraordinary works in Israel (Acts 3:8).
[27-32] The call of Levi, later known as Matthew, to the service of the Kingdom occurs while he is sitting on the public treasury bench, working as a tax collector for the Roman Empire. Jesus' imperative command transforms the life of the tax collector (Luke 5:27, "Follow me"), leading him to abandon his worldly possessions to rise up and follow the Messiah. Grateful for the grace he had received, Levi hosted a grand banquet at his residence, gathering a multitude of tax collectors and sinners. This prompted the scribes and Pharisees to murmur against the disciples for sharing a meal with such ethically dishonest people. Jesus responded to the religious challenge by using an analogy from the realm of health: {{quote: Luke 5:31|Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick}}. The Lord clarified the primary purpose of his earthly coming by declaring that he had not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance (Matthew 9:13, Romans 3:23). This recommendation of the physician by the Savior validates the earthly medical profession, represented in the New Testament by the evangelist Luke as the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14), dismissing the extreme positions that seek to condemn the use of medicine in the life of the believer (1 Timothy 5:23).
[33-39] Opponents question the conduct of Jesus' disciples, observing that, unlike the followers of John the Baptist and the Pharisees who frequently fast and pray, they eat and drink without observing ascetic discipline. The Lord justifies the rejoicing of his entourage by comparing himself to the Bridegroom at the wedding, declaring that the guests at the banquet cannot fast while the Bridegroom remains with them. However, he prophetically announces the coming of days when the Bridegroom will be taken from them, at which time they will formally fast (Luke 5:35). This statement encompasses the practice of fasting in the apostolic age of the Church (Acts 13:2-3, 2 Corinthians 11:27) and extends dispensationally to the suffering of the Jewish remnant during the great tribulation, when they cry out for the return of the heavenly Bridegroom (Revelation 19:7-9). Jesus illustrates the incompatibility between the two spiritual economies through two parables: He points out that no one cuts a patch from a new garment and sews it on an old garment, for the new garment will be torn and the patch will not match the old; Likewise, no one puts new wine into old wineskins because the boiling wine would burst the dry wineskins, wasting both the liquid and the containers (Luke 5:38). The ceremonial ordinances and legalism of Mosaic law cannot contain the new life imparted by the Holy Spirit under the New Covenant (Galatians 5:1-4, Colossians 2:14). The chapter concludes by observing that those who have drunk the old wine of religious tradition do not immediately desire the new, for human nature prefers the comfort of old systems (Jeremiah 6:16).

[1-5] The controversy over the Sabbath began when the disciples plucked and marked ears of wheat to satisfy their immediate hunger, a practice explicitly permitted under the Mosaic Law to satisfy physical need without incurring deprivation (Deuteronomy 23:25). The Pharisees' objection was not to the action itself, but to performing what they considered servile labor on the Sabbath. Biblical revelation teaches that the Sabbath was granted as a ceremonial sign exclusively for the nation of Israel (Ezekiel 20:12, 20), and was not obligatory for the Church under the dispensation of grace (Romans 13:9, Colossians 2:16). To confront the legalism of the religious leaders, the Lord evokes the historical precedent of David eating the bread of the Presence (1 Samuel 21:6), demonstrating that ceremonial ordinances are subordinate to the preservation of life and to the authority of the Most High. Christ culminates the instruction by affirming his divinity and absolute sovereignty over the law {{quote:Luke 6:5|The Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath}}.
[6-11] In a later session in the synagogue, the scribes and Pharisees watch the Lord to see if he performs healings on the Sabbath, seeking to formulate a formal accusation against him. Knowing the secret thoughts of the human heart (Romans 2:16), the Lord places the man with the withered hand in the middle of the assembly and poses a question that exposes the hypocrisy of the religious system: {{quote: Luke 6:9|Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do evil?}}. By instructing the afflicted man to extend his hand, the limb is instantly restored, emulating the miraculous healing of Jeroboam in the Old Testament (1 Kings 13:6). Far from recognizing the manifestation of divine power, the religious leaders are filled with fury and begin to conspire against the Messiah's life, preferring the rigid observance of their traditions to the well-being of a needy sinner (John 5:16, Acts 3:8).
[12-19] The Lord withdraws to a mountain to spend the entire night in prayer before formally appointing the twelve apostles, demonstrating the dependence of his human nature on the Father at crucial moments in his ministry (Psalm 55:17, Acts 1:13). Upon descending from the mountain, Jesus stops on a plain with his disciples and a large crowd from Judea, Jerusalem, and the coastal region of Tyre and Sidon. The geography of the narrative establishes a distinction from the Sermon on the Mount recorded in the first Gospel, identifying this discourse as the Sermon on the Plain, delivered after the apostolic election (Matthew 5:1, Matthew 10:1-4). The multitudes came not only to hear the doctrines of the Kingdom, but also to be delivered from unclean spirits and physical ailments, for divine power emanated from the Messiah, healing all those present {{quote: Luke 6:19|for power came out from him and healed them all}} (Mark 5:30, Acts 10:38).
[20-26] The exposition of the Beatitudes in the Sermon on the Plain presents a structure that contrasts blessings and curses, evoking the blessings and woes pronounced upon Israel on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal before entering the Promised Land (Deuteronomy 27-28). Unlike the spiritualized version of the first Gospel, which alludes to the poor in spirit and those who hunger for righteousness (Matthew 5:3, 6), Luke's narrative emphasizes direct physical and material conditions (Luke 6:20: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God”). The promises of satisfaction and joy for the needy stand in stark contrast to the woes directed toward the rich and satiated of this present age, whose consolation is limited to earthly prosperity. This reversal of physical conditions foreshadows the fate of the rich man and the beggar Lazarus in the Old Testament economy (Luke 16:25), framed within a predominantly Jewish context prior to the inauguration of the church age (James 5:1-5).
[27-49] The discourse concludes by establishing ethical guidelines for conduct characterized by love for enemies, non-retribution of offenses, and the practice of the Golden Rule in interpersonal relationships (Proverbs 25:21, Romans 12:19-20). The Lord warns against the folly of hypocritical judgment through the illustrations of the blind leading the blind and the plank in one's own eye that prevents one from removing the speck from another's eye (Matthew 7:3-5). Likewise, the nature of the tree is inescapably manifested in the quality of its fruit, for out of the treasure of the heart the mouth speaks. Faced with a merely verbal profession of faith, the Messiah confronts his listeners with an imperative demand for obedience {{quote: Luke 6:46|Why do you call me, Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say?}}. The final parable of the two builders compares the man who hears and puts the word into practice to a wise builder who digs deep and lays the foundation on solid rock, which withstands the force of floods; on the contrary, the one who hears but does not put the doctrine into practice builds on the ground without a foundation, suffering the collapse and total ruin of his house when judgment strikes (Proverbs 10:25, 1 Corinthians 3:11, James 1:22-25).

After concluding his sermons to the people, Jesus Christ enters Capernaum, where a Roman centurion owns a servant who is paralyzed and near death (Matthew 8:6). The centurion sends the Jewish elders to request the servant's healing, the local leaders arguing that the centurion is worthy of this favor because he loves the nation of Israel and has built them a synagogue. In dispensational typology, this approach of a Gentile through the Jewish elders foreshadows the judgment of the nations and the salvation of the Gentiles during the great tribulation and the millennium, where the treatment of the Jewish people determines divine blessing (Genesis 12:3, Matthew 25:31-46, Zechariah 8:21-23). In contrast, under the church's dispensation of grace, no one is worthy by their own works; salvation is received by grace through faith in the one Mediator (Romans 3:23, Ephesians 2:8-9, 1 Timothy 2:5). As the Lord approaches the house, the centurion sends friends, expressing his conviction that he is not worthy for the Master to enter his home, demonstrating his understanding of the military hierarchy and Christ's absolute authority over physical ailments. Recognizing that the Lord requires neither physical presence nor a material point of contact, the centurion requests only a word of command, prompting Jesus to marvel at his faith before the crowd (Luke 7:9: "I have not found such great faith even in Israel"). Upon returning to the residence, the messengers found the servant completely healed. The next day, the Lord traveled to the city of Nain, located about twenty-five miles south of Capernaum, near the valley of Megiddo. As he approached the city gate, he encountered a funeral procession carrying the only son of a widow, accompanied by a large group of townspeople. Moved with compassion, the Lord approached, touched the coffin, and commanded the young man to be raised from the dead (Luke 7:14). The dead man immediately sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him back to his mother. This event constitutes one of the three bodily resurrections performed by the Messiah in the Gospels, along with Jairus' daughter and Lazarus (Luke 8:54, John 11:43), demonstrating his sovereign victory over physical death. The manifestation of this divine power instills awe in the crowd, who glorify God, recognizing that a great prophet has arisen in the midst of the nation and that the Lord has visited his people (Luke 1:68).
John the Baptist, imprisoned by order of Herod, sends two of his disciples to question Jesus about whether he is the expected Messiah or whether they should await another. This inquiry does not stem from a wavering in the forerunner's personal faith, but from the pedagogical purpose of directing his followers toward the Messianic evidence prophesied in the Old Testament (Isaiah 35:5-6, Isaiah 61:1). At that very hour, the Lord healed many of various diseases, plagues, and evil spirits, and gave sight to the blind, instructing the messengers to return to John and testify to the miracles they had witnessed: “The blind receive their sight, the lame walk, and those with leprosy are cleansed.” After the messengers departed, Jesus commended John’s steadfastness and ministry before the crowds, declaring him more than a prophet and confirming him as the messenger sent to prepare the way before the Lord (Malachi 3:1). The text points out that the people and the tax collectors justified God by submitting to John’s baptism, while the Pharisees and experts in the law rejected God’s counsel against themselves by refusing to repent (Luke 3:12). The Lord compares the fickleness of that generation to restless children playing in the marketplace, for they accused John of being possessed by a demon because of his ascetic conduct, while they labeled the Son of Man a glutton and a drunkard for eating with tax collectors and sinners (Luke 5:33-34); nevertheless, divine wisdom is vindicated by all His children. A Pharisee named Simon invites Jesus to eat at his home, and while the Lord is at the table, a woman known in the city for her sinful life enters, carrying an alabaster jar of ointment. Standing behind Him, the woman weeps over the Savior's feet, dries them with her hair, kisses them repeatedly, and anoints them with the perfume. Faced with Simon's inner murmuring, who questions Jesus' prophetic discernment in allowing contact with a sinful woman, the Lord demonstrates his omniscience by answering the host's secret thoughts (Romans 2:16) through the parable of the two debtors. By explaining that a creditor forgave the debt of one who owed five hundred denarii and another who owed fifty, Simon correctly acknowledges that the one forgiven the larger sum will love more. Jesus confronts the Pharisee's neglect of Eastern courtesies of hospitality, noting that the woman has not ceased washing, kissing, and anointing his feet since he entered, and declares the remission of her sins (Luke 7:47). The chapter concludes with the diners' astonishment at God's power to forgive sins, as the Lord dismisses the woman, confirming the efficacy of faith for salvation {{quote:Luke 7:50|Your faith has saved you; go in peace}}, guaranteeing spiritual justification in the face of religious legalism (Romans 5:1, Ephesians 2:8-9).

[1-3] The itinerant ministry of Jesus Christ through cities and villages, proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom of God, unfolds in the company of the twelve apostles and a group of self-sacrificing women who had been delivered from evil spirits and infirmities. Among them, Mary Magdalene stands out, from whom seven demons had gone out, as well as Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's procurator, Susanna, and many others who provided for him out of their resources (Luke 8:3). The presence of these women demonstrates the transformation wrought by divine grace in those who experience spiritual liberation, contrasting with the austerity of traditional religious systems (Mark 16:9, Luke 23:49). The contribution of their material possessions for the physical support of the Lord and His disciples establishes a model of practical stewardship in the service of the Kingdom, distinguishing sincere devotion from the love of money and carnal greed (1 Timothy 6:10, 2 Corinthians 8:9).
[4-15] Before the large crowd gathered from various cities, Jesus Christ presents the parable of the sower, whose key interpretation is explicitly stated by the Lord {{quote: Luke 8:11|The seed is the word of God}}. The incorruptible seed (1 Peter 1:23) is scattered on four types of soil that represent the moral and spiritual condition of the human heart. Those along the path symbolize the hardened hearers where the devil, typified by the birds of the air (Revelation 18:2), comes and takes the word from their hearts so that they do not believe and are saved. Those on rocky ground represent those who receive the word with joy, but lack deep roots, falling away when trials or temptations arise (Matthew 13:21). The seed that falls among thorns illustrates those in whom the word is choked by the cares, riches, and pleasures of this life, preventing the fruit from ripening (Mark 4:19, 1 Timothy 6:9). Finally, the good soil represents those who retain the word in a good and upright heart, bearing fruit with patience through perseverance in the faith (James 1:22-25).
[16-21] The Lord teaches that no one lights a lamp and then puts it in a bowl or under a bed, but sets it on a lampstand so that those who come in may see the light (Luke 8:16). This divine Truth is not meant to remain hidden under human traditions, for there is nothing secret that will not be revealed, nor anything hidden that will not be made known (Luke 12:2, 1 Corinthians 4:5). Therefore, the Savior exhorts us to pay attention to how we hear the word, warning that to those who have, more will be given, and from those who do not have, even what they seem to have will be taken away (Matthew 13:12). When Jesus' earthly mother and brothers come to find him but cannot approach him because of the crowd, the Lord redefines the true spiritual family by proclaiming that his mother and brothers are those who hear the word of God and put it into practice (Luke 8:21). This statement underscores the primacy of spiritual obedience over the bonds of the flesh and dismantles unfounded Marian veneration (Psalm 69:8, Mark 3:31-35, 1 John 2:17).
[22-25] Jesus boards a boat with his disciples and instructs them to cross to the other side of the lake, dozing during the crossing due to the physical exhaustion of his sinless humanity (Hebrews 4:15). Over the lake, he unleashes a windstorm that floods the vessel, placing the lives of the sailors in imminent danger. Awakened by the disciples in their terror, the Lord rises and rebukes the wind and the raging waters, the storm instantly ceasing and a great calm ensuing. When Jesus questions the faith of his followers {{quote:Luke 8:25|Where is your faith?}}, the disciples are filled with fear and awe as they witness the forces of nature obeying the Savior's commanding voice. This manifestation of sovereign authority over the elements reaffirms the Messiah's absolute deity, consistent with the Old Testament revelation that attributes to the Lord alone dominion over the fury of the sea (Psalms 107:28-30, Matthew 8:26-27).
[26-39] Upon arriving in the land of the Gadarenes, a man from the city, possessed by demons for a long time, comes out to meet the Lord, living naked among the tombs without dwelling in any house. Upon seeing Jesus, he falls prostrate before him, crying out and acknowledging his divinity {{quote:Luke 8:28|What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?}}. I beg you not to torment me. The demonic manifestations in the passage expose the characteristics of demonic possession: superhuman strength, nakedness, isolation in places of death, and involuntary submission to the divine presence (Mark 5:1-15, James 2:19). Identifying themselves as Legion because of the multitude of unclean spirits within them, the demons plead not to be sent to the abyss, requesting instead permission to enter a herd of pigs. Upon entering the animals, the herd rushes down a steep bank into the lake and drowns. The inhabitants of the region, terrified to see the man sitting at Jesus' feet, clothed and in his right mind, beg the Lord to leave their area because of their great fear. Jesus sends the healed man away, telling him to return home and tell of the great things God had done for him, making him a living witness to God's redeeming power (Psalm 66:16, 2 Corinthians 5:17).
[40-48] Jairus, the synagogue leader, falls at Jesus' feet, pleading with him to come into his house because his only daughter, twelve years old, is dying. As the Lord walks surrounded by the crowd pressing around him, a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years—and who had spent all her money on doctors without finding any cure—approaches from behind and touches the hem of his garment, and the flow of blood immediately stops. Jesus asks who touched him, and when Simon Peter objects about the crowd pressing around him, the Savior explains that someone touched him out of faith, because power has gone out from him (Luke 6:19). The woman, seeing that she had not gone unnoticed, came trembling and prostrated herself before Him, declaring before all the people the cause of the touch and her immediate healing. The Lord comforted her with words of peace {{quote: Luke 8:48|Daughter, your faith has healed you; go in peace}}. The number twelve prophetically links the young woman's age with the years of the woman's suffering, symbolizing the condition of Israel in its unbelief and need for restoration (Leviticus 15:25, Isaiah 64:6, Matthew 9:20-22). Likewise, the passage rejects the superstitious veneration of relics, demonstrating that healing does not come from the physical cloth but from faith placed exclusively in the person of the Savior.
[49-56] While the Lord was still speaking, a messenger arrived from the house of the synagogue leader, announcing the girl's death and advising them not to trouble the Master any further. Upon hearing this, Jesus exhorts the father to absolute faith (Luke 8:50). Entering the house, the Lord allows only Peter, James, John, and the girl's parents to be present. Confronting the weeping of those present, he declares that the young woman is not dead but asleep, prompting mockery from the grieving family. Taking her by the hand, Jesus calls out, commanding the young woman to rise. At that moment, her spirit returns to her body, and she immediately gets up (Ecclesiastes 12:7, 1 Thessalonians 5:23). The Lord commands that she be given something to eat and instructs the astonished parents not to reveal what has happened. This bodily resurrection constitutes one of the three manifestations of authority over death recorded in the Gospels, foreshadowing the Messiah's ultimate victory over the grave and the call of the rapture at the second coming (Luke 7:14, John 11:43, 1 Corinthians 15:52).

[1-9] Jesus Christ summons the twelve apostles and grants them power and authority over all demons and to heal diseases, sending them to preach the kingdom of God and to heal the sick. In the dispensational framework prior to the cross, the commission requires dependence exclusively on divine provision, instructing them not to take a staff, bag, bread, money, or two tunics (Matthew 10:5-10). If they are not received in any city, the instruction to leave and shake the dust from their feet serves as a testimony against the obstinacy of the listeners (Acts 13:51). As the fame of these works spreads, Herod the tetrarch hears all that the Lord does and is perplexed, for some claim that John the Baptist has risen from the dead, others that Elijah has appeared, and still others that one of the ancient prophets has risen (Luke 9:7). The ruler expresses his desire to see Jesus, anticipating the court appearance that would take place during the crucifixion trial (Luke 23:8).
[10-17] Upon returning, the apostles report to the Lord the works they have done during their mission, withdrawing to a deserted place near the town of Bethsaida. Crowds follow them, and Jesus greets them, speaking of the kingdom of God and healing those who needed medicine. At sunset, the twelve suggest sending the crowd away to find lodging and food in the neighboring villages, but the Lord requires them to take responsibility for providing for them. Having only five loaves and two fish, Jesus orders the crowd to sit down in groups of fifty, taking the food, looking up to heaven, blessing it, breaking it, and giving it to his disciples to distribute. The prior breaking of the bread teaches that brokenness is an indispensable condition for effective service in God's work (Mark 14:22). After five thousand men had eaten their fill, twelve baskets full of the leftover fragments were collected (Luke 9:17), a number that links the abundance to the twelve tribes of Israel and foreshadows the miraculous sustenance the Lord will provide for the Jewish remnant in the wilderness during the great tribulation (Exodus 16:16, Micah 7:14, Revelation 12:6).
[18-27] While Jesus was praying alone with his disciples, he asked them about popular opinions concerning him. After the disciples cited the people's conjectures about John the Baptist, Elijah, or some ancient prophet, the Lord confronted them with a direct question, to which Peter responded with the Messianic confession (Luke 9:20, "The Christ of God"). The Savior forbids them from openly divulging this truth, announcing that the Son of Man must suffer many things, be rejected by the elders, the chief priests, and the scribes, be killed, and rise again on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). He then establishes the demand of unconditional discipleship by pointing to the need to deny carnal selfishness {{quote: Luke 9:23|deny yourself, and take up your cross daily, and follow me}}. The passage warns against the vanity of gaining the whole world if one loses oneself, concluding with the prophetic promise that some of those present would not taste death until they saw the kingdom of God revealed in glory (Matthew 16:28, 2 Peter 1:16).
[28-36] About eight days after these instructions, the Lord went up a mountain with Peter, John, and James to pray, and the Transfiguration occurred in the midst of prayer. His face changed its appearance, and his garments became white and dazzling, manifesting the uncreated light of his deity and his coming in glory (Psalm 104:2, Acts 26:13, Revelation 1:14). Moses and Elijah appear in glory, conversing about the departure or exodus that Jesus would accomplish in Jerusalem, representing the Law and the Prophets who testify to redemption through the blood of the Lamb (Deuteronomy 18:15, Malachi 4:4-5, Romans 3:21). Though overcome by sleep, the apostles remain awake and behold his glory. As the visitors depart, Peter proposes building three tabernacles, failing to grasp his error in equating the Son with creatures; immediately, a luminous cloud covers them, and from it emanates the voice of the Father, consecrating Christ's exclusive authority: {{quote: Luke 9:35|This is my beloved Son; listen to him}}. The vision constitutes a literal foreshadowing of the Messianic kingdom that will be established at the second coming (2 Peter 1:16-18).
[37-45] As Jesus came down from the mountain the next day, a large crowd came out to meet him, and a father cried out in despair, pleading for mercy for his only son, who was possessed by a spirit that made him shout, convulse, and foam at the mouth. The man revealed that he had begged the disciples to cast it out, but they could not, exposing their lack of power due to unbelief. Jesus rebuked the unbelieving and perverse generation (Luke 9:41), ordered the boy to be brought to him, and, while the demon violently threw him to the ground, the Lord rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. Amid the widespread awe at God's majesty, the Messiah gives his disciples a second warning about his being handed over to men (Luke 9:44). However, they did not understand this statement because it was hidden from them, and they were afraid to question him about it (Mark 9:32, Luke 18:34).
[46-50] A dispute arises among the disciples as to which of them would be the greatest in the order of the Kingdom. Perceiving their thoughts, Jesus takes a child, places him beside him, and teaches the true standard of greatness in God's economy: "Whoever is least among you all—this one will be great." The Lord clarifies that receiving a child in his name is equivalent to receiving him and the Father who sent him, rejecting any aspiration to hierarchical preeminence (Matthew 18:3-5, 3 John 1:9). John then reports having seen someone casting out demons in the name of Jesus and having forbidden it because he was not part of the apostolic entourage. The Lord corrects this sectarian zeal and instructs them not to hinder it {{quote: Luke 9:50|For he who is not against us is for us}}, teaching them to recognize the legitimate work of the Holy Spirit performed by other servants who honor the Savior's name (Numbers 11:27-29, Philippians 1:18).
[51-62] As the time drew near for Him to be taken up to heaven, Jesus set His face to go resolutely toward Jerusalem (Isaiah 50:7). Messengers sent to a Samaritan village were turned away because the group was headed for the holy city, highlighting the historical rivalry between the two nations (2 Kings 17:24-34, John 4:9). Faced with this affront, James and John requested permission to call down fire from heaven to consume them as Elijah had done (2 Kings 1:10-12); However, the Lord rebukes them, declaring that they do not know what kind of spirit they are of (Luke 9:55), for the Son of Man did not come to destroy souls but to save them (Luke 9:56). During the journey, three aspirants face the demands of discipleship: to the first, who promises to follow him wherever he goes, the Lord warns him about the lack of an earthly home; to the second, who asks to go first to bury his father, he commands him to let the dead bury their own dead and to proclaim the kingdom of God; to the third, who asks to say goodbye to his family, Jesus responds with a solemn warning: “No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for service in the kingdom of God.” This demand for undivided loyalty condemns indecision and longing for things left behind (Genesis 19:26, 1 Kings 19:20-21, Philippians 3:13-14).

[1-16] The Lord appoints seventy other disciples and sends them out two by two before him to every city and place where he is about to go. In the typology of Scripture, the number seventy relates to the Gentile nations that arose after the dispersion at Babel and to the seventy elders appointed to govern Israel (Genesis 10:1-32, Exodus 24:1, Numbers 11:16), distinguishing them from the group of twelve apostles who symbolize the twelve tribes of the chosen people (Matthew 19:28). By commissioning this host, the Messiah declares the abundance of the harvest and the shortage of laborers, urging them to pray to the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his fields (Matthew 9:37-38). The mission demands an attitude of helplessness and innocence, as they are sent out like lambs among wolves, requiring absolute dependence on divine provision, which forbids carrying a purse, bag, or sandals, or engaging in ceremonial greetings along the way (2 Kings 4:29). Instruction requires ministering peace to the receiving households, remaining in the home of a child of peace to eat and drink whatever is offered, for the worker is worthy of his wages (1 Corinthians 9:7-14, 1 Timothy 5:18). The proclamation of those sent announces the nearness of the kingdom of God, which is dispensationally distinct from the visible, Israelite kingdom of heaven by emphasizing the inner spiritual dimension of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit (Romans 14:17). When a city rejects them, the disciples must go out into its streets and publicly shake the dust from their feet as a testament to the impending judgment. The Lord pronounces severe woes against the cities of Galilee that witnessed most of his miracles without repenting, declaring that on the day of judgment the fate of Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom will be more tolerable than that of Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum (Matthew 11:20-24). Capernaum, having been lifted up to heaven by the presence of the Son of God, will be brought down to Hell. The section concludes by affirming the absolute identification between the Sent One and his messengers {{quote:Luke 10:16|He who hears you hears me}}, so that the rejection of the servants constitutes a direct rejection of the heavenly Father.
[17-24] The seventy disciples return joyfully from their itinerant commission, testifying that even the demons submitted to them at the invocation of Jesus' name. Upon hearing this report, the Lord responds by declaring that he had witnessed the fall of the adversary {{quote:Luke 10:18|I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven}}. In the chronology of Scripture, Satan's fall comprises five successive stages: his initial expulsion from the third heaven after his primordial rebellion (Isaiah 14:12-15, Ezekiel 28:14-17), his expulsion from the second heaven into the earthly atmosphere during the Messianic ministry (Luke 10:18), his final plunge to earth in the midst of the great tribulation (Revelation 12:7-9), his confinement in the abyss during the millennium (Revelation 20:1-3), and his eternal punishment in the lake of fire and brimstone (Revelation 20:10). The Savior grants His messengers authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, as well as over all enemy forces, guaranteeing that nothing will cause them bodily harm (Mark 16:18, Acts 28:3-5). However, the Messiah redirects the believer's ultimate reason for rejoicing, teaching that authority over unclean spirits is secondary to the certainty of eternal salvation (Luke 10:20: "But rejoice that your names are written in heaven"; Exodus 32:32, Philippians 4:3, Revelation 20:15). At that same time, Jesus rejoices in the Spirit and praises the sovereignty of the Father, Lord of heaven and earth, for having hidden the mysteries of the Kingdom from the wise and learned of the earthly world in order to reveal them to children in faith (1 Corinthians 1:26-29). All things have been handed over to the Son by the Father, and no one knows the identity of the Son except the Father, nor who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (John 3:35, John 14:6). Finally, addressing the disciples privately, the Lord proclaims the blessedness of their eyes, assuring them that many prophets and kings of the Old Testament longed to see and hear the revelation of the incarnation but did not attain it in their day (1 Peter 1:10-12).
[25-37] A lawyer stands up to test the Lord, posing the fundamental question about the requirements for inheriting eternal life. The Messiah refers him to the Mosaic Law, and the lawyer responds by appropriately quoting the requirement to love the Lord God with all your heart, soul, strength, and mind, and your neighbor as yourself (Deuteronomy 6:5, Leviticus 19:18). The Lord confirms the validity of the statement by declaring that perfect obedience to the law imparts life (Luke 10:28, “Do this, and you will live”), demonstrating that under the Old Testament economy, justification required the practical observance of the ordinances, in contrast to the church's economy of grace where salvation is received by faith apart from works of the law (Romans 3:20, Romans 10:5, Galatians 3:11-12). Seeking to justify himself to avoid the divine requirement, the interpreter questions the identity of his neighbor (Luke 10:29, “And who is my neighbor?”). In response, the Messiah tells the parable of the Good Samaritan. A man was traveling down from Jerusalem—the holy city and site of the sanctuary—toward Jericho, the city under a curse (Joshua 6:26), symbolizing the moral decline of fallen humanity far from the divine presence. On his journey, the traveler falls into the hands of robbers representing demonic forces (John 10:10, Luke 8:12), who strip him of his clothes, brutally wound him, and leave him half-dead. A priest and a Levite happen to be passing by; however, upon seeing the suffering man, both representatives of formal religion and the Mosaic ceremonial system pass by on the opposite side, demonstrating the law's inability to heal or impart life to the dying sinner (Galatians 3:21, Hebrews 7:18-19). Later, a Samaritan, despised by Jewish orthodoxy—a prophetic type of the Lord Jesus Christ whom the Pharisees insultingly called a Samaritan (John 8:48)—approaches the wounded man, is moved with compassion, and heals his wounds by pouring oil and wine on them, elements that prefigure the anointing of the Holy Spirit and the joy of redemption through blood (Psalm 104:15, Ephesians 1:13). After placing him on his own animal, he takes him to an inn and provides financially for his continued care, promising to pay any additional expenses upon his return. When the interpreter is questioned about which of the three acted as a neighbor to the wounded man, the doctor acknowledges that it was the one who showed mercy. The Lord concludes the instruction by commanding him to imitate this practical compassion toward every human being in need.
[38-42] As Jesus continued his journey, he entered a village in Judea called Bethany, where a woman named Martha welcomed him into her home (John 11:1). Martha had a sister named Mary, who sat at Jesus' feet, listening attentively to his teaching (Luke 10:39). This humble posture of Mary reflects the true attitude of the disciple who reverently worships the Messiah, prioritizing spiritual communion and doctrinal nourishment over material concerns (Psalm 27:4, Matthew 4:4). In contrast, Martha was overwhelmed and distracted by the multitude of household chores, and approaching the Lord, she expressed her discontent by questioning the Master's apparent indifference to her sister's inactivity, requesting that He command Him to help her. The Savior responds to the complaint by affectionately repeating her name and pointing out the inner turmoil that overwhelms her {{quote:Luke 10:41|Martha, Martha, you are worried and upset about many things}}. The Lord teaches that although hospitality has value, the edification of the spirit through the reception of divinely revealed truth is the only absolute need of humankind. The passage concludes with the Messianic vindication of Mary's conduct, declaring that she has chosen the good and lasting portion, which will never be taken away from her, neither in this present age nor in eternity (Psalm 16:5, Philippians 3:13-14).

[1-13] The teaching on prayer in the Gospel of Luke begins when one of the disciples sees the Lord in prayer and asks for instruction, taking as a reference point the practice of John the Baptist's ministry (Luke 11:1). The model of prayer transmitted by the Messiah is situated within a dispensational economy prior to the crucifixion and the advent of the church age at Pentecost, reflecting the framework of Mosaic Law under which the disciples operated. The brevity of Luke's formulation compared to the Sermon on the Mount recorded in the first Gospel reflects the particular scope of each writing: while Matthew directs his message to the nation of Israel, emphasizing the Davidic theocracy, Luke presents the Son of Man in his relationship with humanity (Matthew 6:9-13, Luke 19:10). Doctrinally, Jesus' statement about human nature in describing his own followers as imperfect {{quote:Luke 11:13|For if you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children}} refutes the theological notion of the innate goodness of human beings, ratifying the total depravity that affects the descendants of Adam (Psalms 51:5, Romans 3:10-12, Ephesians 2:1-3). Likewise, the parable of the friend who comes at midnight to ask for three loaves of bread illustrates the principle of importunity in supplication (Luke 11:5-8), teaching that persistent insistence in prayer does not seek to bend the divine will, but to exercise the supplicant's faith until receiving the provision promised by the heavenly Father (Luke 18:1-8, Philippians 4:6, Hebrews 4:16).
[14-26] Jesus Christ's casting out a mute demon provokes opposition from the Pharisees, who attribute the miracle to Beelzebub, the prince of demons (Luke 11:15). In biblical terminology, Beelzebub derives from the name of the Philistine god Baalzebub, meaning "lord of the flies" or of filth (2 Kings 1:2), symbolizing Satan as the head of a hierarchy of unclean spirits represented in Scripture as birds or organisms that pollute creation (Mark 4:4, Ephesians 6:12, Revelation 18:2). The Lord dismantles the religious accusation by demonstrating the impossibility of a kingdom or family divided against itself prevailing, for if Satan were to expel his own hosts, his dominion would have come to an end. By stating that demonic liberation is effected through divine authority {{quote:Luke 11:20|But if I drive out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you}}, the Messiah evokes the manifestation of divine power witnessed in the judgments on Egypt (Exodus 8:19), proclaiming the victory of the Stronger over the armed man who guarded his palace (Colossians 2:15). Likewise, the teaching about the unclean spirit that wanders through dry places and returns to the swept house with seven worse spirits (Luke 11:24-26) has a direct prophetic application to the nation of Israel: after being cleansed of gross idolatry following the Babylonian captivity, the house remained spiritually empty by rejecting the Savior, becoming exposed to a greater apostasy during the period of the great tribulation under the rule of the antichrist (Matthew 12:43-45, 2 Thessalonians 2:9-12, Revelation 13:1-8).
[27-36] As the Lord was instructing the multitude, a woman exclaimed, blessing the Savior's earthly mother because of her physical motherhood; However, Jesus Christ immediately redirects the devotion of his listeners to written revelation (Luke 11:28). This Messianic response establishes the primacy of doctrinal obedience over the bonds of the flesh and constitutes a categorical biblical testimony against Mariolatry and the veneration of creatures, confirming that salvation and divine approval depend on faith in revealed truth and not on human mediations separate from the Lord (Luke 1:47, John 2:4, 1 Timothy 2:5). Faced with the ungodly demand for signs from an unbelieving generation, the Messiah announces that no miracle will be granted to him except the sign of the prophet Jonah (Luke 11:29-30). Jonah's experience in the belly of the great fish directly foreshadows Christ's death, burial, and bodily resurrection on the third day (Jonah 1:17, Matthew 12:40, 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). The Queen of the South and the inhabitants of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment to condemn the Jewish hierarchy, for those pagans recognized the wisdom of Solomon and the preaching of Jonah, while Israel rejected the One who transcends all the prophets of the Old Testament (1 Kings 10:1, Jonah 3:5). The section concludes by comparing the reception of truth to the lamp of the body, teaching that the clarity of the spiritual eye allows divine light to fully illuminate the believer's conscience (Psalm 119:105, Proverbs 4:18-19, 2 Corinthians 4:4).
[37-54] As he concludes his discourse, a Pharisee invites the Lord to eat at his house, marveling that the Master did not perform the ceremonial washing of hands stipulated by rabbinic traditions before sitting down to eat (Luke 11:37-38). Jesus openly confronts the hypocrisy of formal religion, pointing out that the Pharisees prioritize the outward cleanliness of the cup and plate while their interior remains full of greed and wickedness (Matthew 23:25-26, Mark 7:6-8). Divine rebuke pronounces severe woes against the religious leaders for tithing lesser spices like mint and rue, while neglecting the fundamental precepts of God's judgment and love. It also describes them as hidden tombs over which people walk, unaware of their spiritual defilement (Luke 11:44). In response to the protest of a lawyer who feels wronged, the Messiah extends the condemnation categorically: {{quote:Luke 11:46|“Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not lift one finger to help them.”}} The interpreters of the law are accused of building monuments to the prophets executed by their ancestors, condoning the deeds of their fathers and making the blood of all those martyred from Abel to Zechariah a matter of responsibility for that generation (Genesis 4:8, 2 Chronicles 24:20-22, Matthew 23:34-36). Finally, the Lord rebukes them for having taken away the key to knowledge (Luke 11:52), hindering the understanding of the Scriptures and preventing access to salvation. After these declarations, the scribes and Pharisees intensified their hostility, lying in wait for the Savior to utter some word that would allow them to bring a legal accusation against him (Luke 20:20, John 8:6).

[1-12] Jesus Christ first warns his disciples before an immense crowd about the spiritual contamination of religious leaders {{quote:Luke 12:1|Command yourselves to beware of the yeast of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy}}. Pharisaic yeast is doctrinally defined as human doctrine and tradition imposed upon the Scriptures (Matthew 16:12, Mark 7:7), which seeks to appear outwardly pious while concealing inward corruption. Unlike the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection and the spirits (Acts 23:8), the Pharisees upheld formal orthodoxy but added commandments of men. The Lord teaches that there is nothing hidden that will not be revealed, urging us not to fear men who can only take physical life, but to fear God who has the power to judge and condemn (Luke 12:5). This warning confirms the literal reality of Hell as a place of eternal punishment (Mark 9:44, Revelation 20:15). Likewise, the Messiah comforts his followers by reminding them that the value of a believer surpasses that of sparrows and that the hairs of their head are numbered, guaranteeing the assistance of the Holy Spirit when they appear before synagogues and magistrates (Matthew 10:28-31, Acts 4:8).
[13-34] Refusing to intervene as an earthly judge or mediator in a family dispute over an inheritance, Jesus Christ warns the multitude against all forms of greed, declaring that a person's life does not consist in the abundance of their possessions (1 Timothy 6:9-10). To illustrate this truth, the Lord tells the parable of the rich fool, whose only desire was to tear down his barns to build larger ones where he could store his harvest and rest in carnal indulgence. However, divine justice unexpectedly demands his soul {{quote:Luke 12:20|Fool! This very night your soul will be demanded from you, demonstrating the folly of storing up treasure for oneself without being rich toward God (Job 27:8, Job 34:30, James 5:1-3). The Savior then instructs His disciples not to worry about food or clothing, appealing to God's provision regarding the ravens and the lilies of the field (Matthew 6:25-33). Instead of seeking the things that the nations of the world eagerly pursue, the Lord exhorts them to seek the kingdom of God, comforting His people with a promise of encouragement: “Do not be afraid, little flock, for your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom.” (Luke 12:32) On the dispensational level, this little flock represents the faithful remnant of Israel who receive the inheritance of the Kingdom, constituting a spiritual nation set apart for the glory of the Lord (Romans 11:2-5, 1 Peter 2:9).
[35-48] The Messianic exhortation demands an attitude of constant vigilance, requiring the servants to keep their loins girded and their lamps burning as they await the Lord's return from the wedding feast (Luke 12:35-37). The Savior proclaims the blessedness of those found watching, assuring them that the Lord Himself will gird Himself, have them sit at the table, and serve them, foreshadowing the joyful fellowship in the millennial kingdom (Genesis 18:8, Luke 22:27, Revelation 19:9). When Peter asked Jesus whether the parable was directed exclusively to the apostles or to everyone, Jesus described the conduct of the faithful and prudent steward in contrast to the unfaithful servant. Before the Lord's coming at an unexpected hour (Luke 12:40: “You also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect”), the wicked servant who begins to beat the other servants and get drunk will suffer separation and the severity of judgment. Doctrinally, the punishment of the servant who knew his master's will and was unprepared results in being flogged with many blows (Luke 12:47), an assessment of individual responsibility that will be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ (1 Corinthians 3:13-15, 2 Corinthians 5:10), unlike the judgment of the unrepentant sinner who is cast into outer darkness (Matthew 25:30). The section concludes by establishing the principle of divine judgment in proportion to the light received {{quote:Luke 12:48|For to everyone who has been given much, from him much will be required}}.
[49-59] The Lord declares the purpose of his mission by stating that he has come to send fire upon the earth, longing for it to be kindled already {{quote:Luke 12:49}}. While in the present dispensation fire symbolizes the purifications and persecutions that test the believer (1 Peter 4:12), at the second coming it represents the literal fiery judgment that will consume the wicked (Malachi 4:1, 2 Thessalonians 1:8). Jesus also points to the baptism of affliction and death that he must undergo before the completion of his redemptive work (Mark 10:38). Confronting the false expectation of an earthly kingdom of immediate peace without the prior crucifixion, the Savior affirms that His first coming brings division (Luke 12:51). This doctrinal sword fragments homes by dividing fathers against sons and mothers-in-law against daughters-in-law for the sake of faith (Micah 7:6, Matthew 10:34-36), reserving peace on earth for the establishment of His millennial kingdom after the judgment of the saints (Luke 2:14, Isaiah 9:6-7, Revelation 19:11-16). Rebuking the multitude for discerning the meteorological aspects of the wind and clouds while ignoring the fulfillment of Messianic prophecies, the Lord calls their blindness hypocrisy (Luke 12:56). Finally, he advises man to reconcile with his adversary as he walks toward the judge, warning of inescapable imprisonment until the last penny is paid for whoever rejects divine grace (Matthew 5:25-26, Romans 3:19).

[1-5] The news presented to the Lord about the Galileans whose blood Pontius Pilate had mixed with the victims of their sacrifices in the temple serves as a juncture to confront the inclination of formal religion to judge the affliction of others as evidence of greater guilt (Luke 13:1). Jesus Christ dismantles this retributive logic by asking whether those Galileans or the eighteen men on whom the tower of Siloam fell were more sinful than the rest of the inhabitants of Jerusalem. The Messiah categorically rejects the presumption of self-righteousness and proclaims the imperative demand of repentance for all humanity {{quote:Luke 13:3|unless you repent, you will all likewise perish}}. Doctrinally, physical calamity does not necessarily constitute a proportional measure of the afflicted person's personal iniquity, but rather a solemn warning that points to the universal depravity of the human race and the certainty of divine judgment for those who do not seek the Lord's grace (Psalm 51:5, Romans 3:23, Acts 17:30).
[6-9] The parable of the fig tree planted in the vineyard illustrates the Lord's dispensational dealings with the nation of Israel. The owner of the vineyard comes for three consecutive years seeking fruit but finds none, decreeing the sentence of cutting it down because of the tree's barrenness {{quote:Luke 13:7|Cut it down; why does it still use the ground in vain?}}. The vinedresser intercedes, requesting an additional year of grace to dig around the roots and fertilize it, making the plant's survival contingent upon his future response. Prophetically, the vineyard represents the territory of Palestine and the fig tree the Jewish national entity (Isaiah 5:1-7, Hosea 9:10, Matthew 21:19). The three years of inspection symbolize the time of Christ's earthly ministry among his chosen people, while the reprieve granted foreshadows the divine patience extended to Israel through the apostolic preaching recorded in the book of Acts, prior to the judgment of desolation carried out by the Roman legions in 70 AD (Romans 11:20-22, 1 Thessalonians 2:15-16).
[10-17] During the teaching in the synagogue on the Sabbath, the Lord beholds a woman possessed by a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years, who remained bent over and unable to straighten up in any way (Luke 13:11). This physical condition offers a spiritual reflection of fallen humanity, for sin bends the human being and directs their gaze exclusively toward earthly things, preventing them from beholding heavenly glory until Messianic grace brings liberation (Psalm 145:14, Ephesians 2:1-3). Upon laying his hands on her, the woman is instantly made right and glorifies God, arousing the indignation of the synagogue leader for performing healings during the Sabbath rest. The Messiah exposes the hypocrisy of the religious system by pointing out that any Pharisee unties his ox or donkey on the Sabbath to lead it out to water, thus defending the dignity of this afflicted woman—this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan had bound (Luke 13:16). The Lord's triumph shames his adversaries and fills the multitude with joy at the manifestation of divine power over the demonic chains (Luke 14:5, Acts 10:38).
[18-21] The parables about the kingdom of God expounded by the Lord employ the figures of the mustard seed and the yeast to describe the prophetic development of religious profession on earth. The mustard seed sown in the garden experiences disproportionate growth until it becomes a large tree where the birds of the air nest in its branches; in the symbolic language of Scripture, the birds represent unclean spirits and demonic powers that find refuge in the bloated structure of apostate Christendom (Genesis 15:11, Matthew 13:4, Revelation 18:2). Likewise, the parable of the yeast describes the action of a woman who introduces this leaven into three measures of flour until it corrupts the entire dough {{quote:Luke 13:21|it is like yeast, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour}}.
