Biblical typology immutably maintains that leaven never symbolizes the gospel, but rather false doctrine, malice, and hypocrisy (Exodus 12:15, Matthew 16:6, 1 Corinthians 5:6-8, Galatians 5:9), while the woman represents the corrupt ecclesiastical system that will adulterate revealed truth until the end of time (Revelation 17:5).
[22-30] On his journey to Jerusalem, the Lord is questioned about whether few attain salvation, to which he responds by exhorting the multitude to a determined effort {{quote:Luke 13:24|Strive to enter through the narrow door}}. The Messiah warns that many will try to enter when the Master of the house has risen to shut the door, suffering ultimate rejection as they are labeled as workers of iniquity. Mere ceremonial proximity or outward familiarity with the Savior's teaching does not replace spiritual regeneration of the heart (Matthew 7:21-23, Romans 2:28-29). The text anticipates the anguish of judgment, characterized by weeping and gnashing of teeth, when unrepentant religious people behold Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets in the kingdom of God as they are cast out, while multitudes from the east, west, north, and south will take their place at the table of the Kingdom, fulfilling the reversal where the last will be first and the first last (Matthew 8:11-12, Luke 14:23, Romans 9:30-32).
[31-35] In response to a warning from a group of Pharisees about Herod Antipas's murderous intentions, the Lord responds with Messianic sovereignty, calling the ruler cunning and impotent {{quote:Luke 13:32|Go, and tell that fox}}. The Savior affirms the unwavering determination of His divine plan to cast out demons, heal the sick, and complete His work on the third day, pointing to the tragic reality that no prophet should perish outside of Jerusalem (Micah 3:1-3, Acts 4:26-28). The section culminates with Christ's lament over the holy city, expressing His Messianic longing to shelter His children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings and denouncing the nation's obstinate rebellion (Luke 13:34). As a consequence of this rejection, the Lord decrees the judicial abandonment of the temple and the city until His glorious return at the second coming, when the remnant of Israel will recognize Him, exclaiming that blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord (Psalms 118:26, Matthew 23:37-39, Revelation 19:11-16).

[1-6] Jesus Christ's entry into the house of one of the leading Pharisees to eat bread on the Sabbath marks the third instance in the Gospel of Luke where a Pharisee invites the Lord to his table (Luke 7:36, Luke 11:37, Luke 14:1) and the third recorded Sabbath healing in this narrative (Luke 6:6-11, Luke 13:10-17). The scribes and Pharisees were lying in wait for the Savior to find grounds for accusation, but the Lord confronts their ceremonial legalism by asking them if it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath. Before the silent assembly, Jesus heals the man suffering from dropsy—a condition characterized by the excessive accumulation and retention of fluids in the body tissues—and poses a probing question: {{quote:Luke 14:5|Which of you has a donkey or an ox that has fallen into a well}}. The hypocrisy of the religious system is exposed, for while the Pharisees do not hesitate to help their animals on the Sabbath to preserve their material possessions (Exodus 20:8, Deuteronomy 5:12), they deny compassion to a human being in need, ignoring that the Sabbath was made for humankind and that the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath (Mark 2:27-28).
[7-14] Observing how the guests chose the best seats or the ends of the table, the Lord tells a parable about humility at wedding banquets. In the social structure of the time, guests were seated according to their rank and status, and the Pharisees habitually sought places of preeminence to feed their vanity (Matthew 23:6). The Lord instructs that when invited to a feast, the guest should take the lowest place, allowing the host to elevate him to a position of honor before those present, thus establishing the spiritual principle of the Kingdom {{quote: Luke 14:11|for whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted}} (Proverbs 25:6-7, James 4:6, 1 Peter 5:5). Likewise, Jesus exhorts the host not to invite his friends, brothers, relatives, or wealthy neighbors in order to receive a reciprocal earthly reward, but rather to invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind. Although these needy people lack the material means to repay the courtesy, the believer who acts selflessly will be blessed and rewarded at the resurrection of the righteous (Luke 14:14), an allusion to the first resurrection and the millennial rewards reserved for the saints (Revelation 20:4-6, 1 Corinthians 3:11-15).
[15-24] In response to one of the guests' exclamation about the blessedness of eating bread in the kingdom of God, the Messiah tells the parable of the great banquet (Luke 14:15-16). A man prepared a great banquet and invited many, sending his servant at dinnertime to say that everything was ready; However, the invited guests unanimously began to make excuses, citing the purchase of a property, the testing of oxen, or their recent marriage (Luke 14:18-20). Since a king's invitation demands immediate obedience and transcends any earthly commitment, the guests' refusal constitutes a personal affront that provokes the anger of the master of the house (Matthew 22:2-7). Consequently, the master orders his servant to go out quickly into the squares and streets of the city to bring in the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind, and then to the highways and hedges to compel them to come in (Luke 14:23). Prophetically, the first guests represent the Jewish hierarchy that rejected the Messiah, while the poor and the highwaymen symbolize the tax collectors, sinners, and Gentiles incorporated into the banquet of grace (Isaiah 55:1-3, Acts 13:46-48, Romans 11:11), concluding the passage with the pronouncement that none of the men originally invited will taste the Messianic supper (Matthew 21:43, Hebrews 3:18-19).
[25-33] Large crowds accompanied the Lord on his itinerant journey, at which point he expounds on the requirements of discipleship, establishing a clear theological distinction between salvation as a free gift received by grace through faith (Romans 3:24, Ephesians 2:8-9) and discipleship as a consecrated service that demands works and self-denial (1 Corinthians 3:12-14, 2 Timothy 2:4). The Savior declares that whoever does not hate his father, mother, wife, children, brothers, sisters, and even his own life in comparison to his devotion to the Messiah, cannot be His disciple (Luke 14:26). This demand for supreme loyalty requires subordinating the affections of the flesh to the Lordship of Christ (Exodus 32:27-28, Deuteronomy 33:9, Matthew 10:37). Likewise, whoever does not take up his cross and follow the Master cannot be His disciple, which implies the daily mortification of carnal selfishness (Romans 6:11, 1 Corinthians 15:31, Galatians 2:20). The Lord illustrates this cost calculation through two parables: that of a builder who assesses whether he has what is needed to finish a tower before laying the foundation—where the foundation represents salvation and the tower the building of Christian character—and that of a king who considers whether with ten thousand soldiers he can face an enemy of twenty thousand (Luke 14:28-32). The section concludes with the imperative command to renounce all possessions in order to be a disciple worthy of the Kingdom (Philippians 3:7-8).
[34, 35] The teaching of the chapter culminates by addressing the properties of salt, declaring that salt is good, but if it loses its flavor it becomes useless for the earth or the dung heap, being thrown out by men (Matthew 5:13, Mark 9:50). In the symbolism of Scripture, salt represents the preserving function, doctrinal purity, and active witness of believers in the midst of a corrupt world (Colossians 4:6). The loss of salt's flavor does not describe the loss of eternal salvation under the dispensation of grace (John 10:28, Romans 8:38-39), but rather the futility of the disciple's witness and the consequent loss of rewards and inheritance at the judgment seat of Christ and in the millennial kingdom (1 Corinthians 3:15, 2 Timothy 2:12). The Lord closes His discourse by demanding responsible attention to revealed truth {{quote: Luke 14:35|He who has ears to hear, let him hear}} (Luke 8:8, Revelation 2:7).

[1-3] The approach of tax collectors and sinners to Jesus Christ to hear his teaching provoked the immediate murmuring of the Pharisees and scribes, who reproached the Lord's conduct in sharing the table with people considered ethically flawed (Luke 5:30). From the perspective of the religious leaders, the term "sinner" defined a condition of manifest moral defilement (Genesis 13:13, Romans 3:23), and therefore they censured the Savior's grace in welcoming the outcasts of society {{quote:Luke 15:2|This man welcomes sinners and eats with them}}. In response to this challenge, the Messiah presents a comprehensive parable composed of three successive illustrations that depict the search for and recovery of what is lost, exposing the harshness of formal legalism in contrast to the joy that heaven experiences in the salvation of souls (Luke 19:10, 1 Timothy 1:15).
[4-7] The first illustration presents the parable of the lost sheep, highlighting the ministry of God the Son as the Good Shepherd who seeks the stray creature in the wilderness (Psalm 23:1, Isaiah 53:6, John 10:11). The Shepherd leaves the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness to go after the one that has gone astray until he finds it, placing it on his shoulders with rejoicing—a figure that symbolizes God's ability to sustain and impart eternal security to the redeemed (John 10:28). On a doctrinal level, the ninety-nine represent those who consider themselves self-sufficient and righteous in their own eyes without acknowledging their need for repentance (Luke 18:9, Romans 10:3). Upon returning to his dwelling, the Shepherd summons his friends and neighbors to celebrate the finding, the Lord declaring that there is greater joy in the divine presence over the conversion of one sinner {{quote: Luke 15:7|there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people}}.
[8-10] The parable of the lost coin contains a typological application relating to the work of the Holy Spirit, who uses the light of truth to convict the world of sin and reveal salvation (Psalm 119:105, John 16:8-11). The presence of the number ten is biblically linked to the entirety of the Gentile nations (Genesis 10:1-32, Romans 10:12), this teaching being interwoven between two narratives with a Jewish background to signify the inclusion of Gentiles in the economy of grace (Acts 10:45, Ephesians 2:11-13). The woman lights a lamp, sweeps the house, and searches diligently until she finds the piece of silver, which represents the redemption of the soul through the price of divine sacrifice (Exodus 30:12-16, 1 Peter 1:18-19). Upon finding the coin, she calls together her friends and neighbors to share in her joy, the Savior concluding that the restoration of the sinner brings unspeakable heavenly joy {{quote:Luke 15:10|Thus I say unto you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents}}.
[11-24] The story of the younger son profoundly illustrates the sinner's descent into rebellion and the magnanimity of the heavenly Father's grace. The young man demands his share of the inheritance and sets out for a distant province, squandering his wealth through a dissolute life (Proverbs 29:3). When his resources are exhausted and a great famine strikes that region, the young man takes a job with a local man tending pigs, an abject task for a Jew that symbolizes spiritual degradation under the dominion of the world (Leviticus 11:7, James 4:4). Longing to eat the carob pods left by the animals with no one to help him, the young man reflects on his situation and recognizes the abundance that prevails in his father's house (Luke 15:17). When he came to his senses, he said, “How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, and here I am starving to death!” Moved by genuine repentance, he begins his journey home, confessing his unworthiness. However, while he is still far away, his father sees him with compassion, runs to meet him, throws his arms around his neck, and kisses him. The father arranges to dress him in the finest clothes, place a ring on his finger, and shoes on his feet, ordering the fattened calf to be killed to celebrate the young man's restoration (Luke 15:24). In sacred symbolism, the garment represents imputed righteousness (Isaiah 61:10, Romans 3:22), the ring the adoption of sonship (Ephesians 1:13-14), the shoes the new way of life in the truth (Ephesians 6:15), and the fattened calf the satisfaction provided by Christ's atonement (Hebrews 9:12).
[25-32] The final section of the narrative addresses the attitude of the older son, who, upon returning from the fields, hears music and dancing in the house. Learning from a servant of his brother's return and the celebration arranged by their father, the older son is filled with anger and refuses to participate in the feast, forcing his father to come out and intercede for him. The older son justifies his position by claiming impeccable obedience to his father's commands and reproaching his father for not having a young goat to celebrate with his friends, in contrast to the reception given to the one who squandered his wealth on prostitutes (Luke 18:11-12, Galatians 3:10). This reaction portrays the vainglory of the Pharisees and scribes, who trusted in their own works and rejected the mercy shown to sinners (Matthew 23:23, Romans 9:31-32). The father responds by reaffirming his affection for his son but asserting the moral necessity of rejoicing: {{quote: Luke 15:32|But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found}}. The parable concludes without recording the firstborn's final decision, prophetically warning against the self-exclusion of those who despise the banquet of divine grace because of their religious pride (Matthew 21:43, Acts 13:45-46).

[1-12] Jesus Christ presents the parable of the dishonest steward to his disciples, recounting how a steward accused of squandering his master's possessions acts shrewdly in the face of his impending dismissal (Luke 16:1-3). By hastily reducing his master's creditors' debts, the steward secures his place in other households after being removed from his position. The master commends his servant's shrewdness in the worldly realm, the Savior pointing out that the children of this age are more shrewd in their temporal dealings than believers are in their spiritual affairs (Luke 16:8). Doctrinally, material wealth is described as unrighteous or wicked riches, a term associated with worldly greed (Luke 16:9). Money is the least and most foreign thing that God uses to test the faithfulness of his servant; if a person does not demonstrate integrity in the management of temporary financial resources, the Lord will not entrust them with the true riches of the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 4:2, 1 Timothy 6:9-10).
[13-18] Messianic teaching proclaims the impossibility of maintaining a dual spiritual loyalty, for affection for one master results in contempt for the other {{quote:Luke 16:13|You cannot serve both God and money}}. Upon hearing these words, the Pharisees, characterized by their avarice and material greed, mocked the Savior; However, the Lord confronts them, declaring that although they seek to justify themselves before men, God knows their hearts, for what human society extols is an abomination before the Most High (Luke 16:15, Isaiah 65:5, James 4:4). The text establishes the dispensational transition by indicating that the Law and the Prophets extended until John the Baptist, and from then on, the proclamation of the Kingdom of God began (Luke 16:16, Matthew 11:12-13). Nevertheless, the validity of the written Law remains unaltered in its observance; it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one iota of the Mosaic Law to fail (Matthew 5:18). As an illustration of the moral deviation of the religious, the Messiah reaffirms the sanctity of marriage, declaring that whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, as does whoever marries the divorced woman (Malachi 2:16, Matthew 19:9, Romans 7:2-3).
[19-26] Unlike allegories, the narrative of the rich man and the beggar Lazarus constitutes a literal historical account of the Old Testament economy, evidenced by the use of proper names such as Lazarus, Abraham, and Moses (Luke 16:19-20). The rich man was clothed in purple and fine linen, enjoying daily feasts, while Lazarus lay at his gate, hungry and covered with sores that dogs licked. When the beggar died, his soul was taken by angels to Abraham’s bosom, the resting place in the lower parts of the earth where the saints of previous dispensations awaited the atonement of Calvary before the rapture to heaven (Galatians 4:4, Ephesians 4:8-10, Hebrews 10:4). The rich man, on the other hand, died, was buried, and in Hell experienced conscious punishment (Luke 16:23: “And in hell, lifting up his eyes, being in torment”). Biblical revelation teaches that the human soul possesses a spiritual anatomy with eyes, tongue, and limbs, suffering the torment of literal flames (Psalm 139:8, Matthew 12:40, Revelation 20:14). Between Hell and Abraham's bosom lies a great, fixed, and impassable chasm that prevents any transfer or relief between the two compartments of Sheol (Luke 16:26).
[27-31] The rich man begs Abraham to send Lazarus to his mother's house to warn his five brothers and prevent them from descending to the same place of suffering (Luke 16:27-28). The appeal to the patriarch confirms his Jewish origin (Matthew 3:9, Romans 9:4-5); however, Abraham responds that his relatives have sufficient revelation for their salvation {{quote:Luke 16:29|They have Moses and the Prophets; let them listen to them}}. In response to the condemned man's argument that a supernatural miracle would bring about the repentance of his relatives, the text establishes the absolute sufficiency of God's word over any miraculous manifestation, declaring that if they do not listen to the Scriptures, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead (Luke 16:31). This judgment foreshadows the hardness of heart of the nation of Israel, which rejected both the testimony of the resurrection of Lazarus of Bethany and the bodily resurrection of the Lord Jesus Christ (John 11:53, John 12:10, Acts 2:31-32, 1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

[1-4] The Lord instructs His disciples on the inexorability of offenses in earthly experience, declaring the severity of judgment upon those who cause the spiritual downfall of the little ones {{quote:Luke 17:1|It is impossible that no stumbling blocks should come}}. The severity of the warning indicates that it would be preferable for Him to be thrown into the sea with a millstone tied around His neck than to cause one of the believers to stumble (Matthew 18:6-7). This principle establishes the balance between the Lord's permissive will and His retributive justice, demonstrating that God repays with tribulation those who afflict His own (2 Thessalonians 1:6). Likewise, the passage establishes the standard for discipline and reconciliation in the local church, commanding that a brother who sins be rebuked and that he be forgiven without reservation as many times as he repents in a single day {{quote:Luke 17:3|If your brother sins against you, rebuke him}}. This willingness to forgive up to seven times a day seeks the spiritual restoration of the servant and not the satisfaction of the carnal desire for revenge (Matthew 18:21-22, Galatians 6:1, Ephesians 4:32).
[5-10] Faced with the high demands for forgiveness and brotherly conduct, the apostles ask the Lord to impart greater spiritual capacity {{quote:Luke 17:5|Increase our faith}}. Jesus responds by pointing to the power of genuine faith, stating that a tiny portion like a mustard seed has the power to uproot a sycamore tree and plant it in the sea (Matthew 17:20, Mark 11:23). The parable of the servant returning from plowing or tending livestock in the field then illustrates the attitude that should characterize the believer in the face of grace and works. The master does not express gratitude to the servant for fulfilling the assigned tasks, nor does he allow him to eat dinner before serving his master, establishing that the strict fulfillment of duty does not constitute merit or generate boasting before God (Luke 17:10). Doctrinally, this instruction refutes the theology of human merit, teaching that works of obedience are solely the responsibility of the creature and that salvation and blessings are the exclusive result of the Lord's sovereign grace (Romans 3:27, Romans 11:6, Ephesians 2:8-9).
[11-19] On his journey to Jerusalem, the Lord travels along the border between Samaria and Galilee, entering a village where he is met by ten lepers who were kept at a distance as prescribed by the law (Leviticus 13:45-46, Numbers 5:2). Leprosy represents in biblical revelation the most complete type of sin and moral corruption, requiring a divine purification that the Mosaic law could not effect on its own (Leviticus 14:2-3, Romans 8:3). The grieving people cry out for mercy, and Jesus sends them to the priests for ritual inspection without touching them at that moment (Luke 17:14). Healing occurs as they march in obedience, reflecting the faith-and-works system of the pre-Calvary economy (2 Kings 5:14). Upon realizing their restoration, only one of them—a Samaritan—returns, glorifying God with a loud voice and falling at the Savior’s feet to give thanks. The Lord highlights the ingratitude of the nine Jews and the faith of the foreigner (Luke 17:18). “Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?” Doctrinally, the number ten connects this event to all the Gentile nations (Genesis 10:1-32, Acts 10:45), foreshadowing the conversion of the Gentiles in the face of the rejection by the majority of Israel (Romans 11:11). Likewise, leprosy will prophetically reappear during the great tribulation as the evil plague that will strike those who receive the mark of the beast (Revelation 16:2, 2 Peter 2:13, Jude 23).
[20-25] When questioned by the Pharisees about when the kingdom of God would be revealed, the Messiah clarifies that the present phase of the Kingdom will not come with visible signs of outward observation or announcements of geographical location, proclaiming that divine authority was present in his own person {{quote: Luke 17:21|for behold, the kingdom of God is among you}}. Doctrinally, the text establishes the distinction between the Kingdom of God, spiritual and internal in nature, centered on righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit (Romans 14:17), and the Kingdom of Heaven, political, earthly, and visible in nature, centered on the throne of David in Jerusalem (Isaiah 9:6-7, Luke 1:32-33). Then, addressing his disciples, the Lord announces future days when they will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man without attaining it, warning against false messiahs who will arise in the desert or in secret chambers (Matthew 24:23-26). The second coming of the Messiah will not be a private or hidden event, but a glorious and sudden manifestation that will encompass the entire firmament {{quote: Luke 17:24|like lightning flashing from under the sky}}. However, the establishment of this Messianic glory required, first and foremost, the crucifixion of the Savior and the rejection by the nation of Israel (Luke 9:22, 1 Peter 1:11).
[26-37] The Lord characterizes the days before the manifestation of the Son of Man by comparing them to the times of Noah and Lot (Genesis 6:1-8, Genesis 19:1-25). The multitudes before the judgment were engaged in the ordinary activities of eating, drinking, marrying, buying, selling, planting, and building, living in complete spiritual indifference until the flood and the rain of fire and brimstone destroyed them all. The condition of the world before the glorious advent will reflect this same materialism and moral corruption (2 Timothy 3:1-5, 2 Peter 3:3-7). On that day, whoever is on the roof should not go down to retrieve their belongings, the Savior urging them to remember the summary judgment executed upon Lot’s wife for longing for the earthly things she left behind (Genesis 19:26). Likewise, the simultaneous mention of daytime activities on the roof and people sleeping in a bed that night demonstrates that Scripture recognizes the earth’s sphericity, with light in one hemisphere and darkness in the other. The statements about two in a bed, two grinding grain, or two in the field—where one is taken and the other left—describe the summary judgments of the Second Coming (Matthew 24:40–41), where those taken are led to physical destruction and those left are preserved to enter the millennial kingdom. When the disciples inquired about the fate of those taken captive, the Messiah responded by pointing to the gathering of birds of prey over the corpses of the wicked {{quote: Luke 17:37|Where the body is, there the eagles will gather}}, a prophetic reference to the great supper of God at the battle of Armageddon (Job 39:27-30, Isaiah 34:6-8, Revelation 19:17-21).

[1-8] The Lord presents the parable of the unjust judge for the doctrinal purpose of instructing on the need to pray continually and not lose heart (Luke 18:1). The narrative features a magistrate who lacked fear of God and respect for men, who grants justice to a widow only because of her repeated importunity (Luke 18:4-5). In dispensational hermeneutics, the troubled widow represents the persecuted Jewish remnant during the Great Tribulation, who cry out day and night for divine vindication against the dominion of the Antichrist (Psalm 79:1-12, Revelation 6:9-10). The Lord assures that God will swiftly bring justice to His chosen ones, concluding with a prophetic question about the lack of faith at the time of the Second Coming: {{quote: Luke 18:8|But when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on earth?}}. This statement anticipates the state of universal apostasy that will prevail in the world before the glorious manifestation of the Messiah (2 Thessalonians 2:3, 2 Timothy 3:1-5).
[9-14] Jesus Christ directs a second parable to those who trusted in their own righteousness and despised others, presenting the confrontation between a Pharisee and a tax collector in the temple (Luke 18:9-10). The Pharisee prayed to himself, boasting of his fasting, tithing, and moral separation from extortioners and sinners (Luke 18:11-12, Isaiah 65:5); however, his religious profession was worthless before God because it was founded on spiritual pride. In contrast, the tax collector stood at a distance, not daring to lift his eyes to heaven, beating his breast in contrition and pleading for divine mercy (Luke 18:13). The Lord declares that the tax collector went home justified before the Pharisee, establishing the immutable principle of God's economy (Luke 18:14). For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and everyone who exalts himself will be humbled. And he who humbles himself will be exalted (Proverbs 3:34, James 4:6, 1 Peter 5:5).
[15-17] When the crowd presented some little children for the Savior to touch, the disciples rebuked those who brought them. Jesus stops the apostolic rebuke and demands that the children be allowed access {{quote:Luke 18:16|Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them}}, proclaiming that the kingdom of God belongs to those who possess such a condition. The Messianic lesson establishes that entering the Kingdom requires receiving divine truth with the humility, meekness, and dependence of childhood (Matthew 18:3-4, 1 Corinthians 1:26-29), rejecting the self-sufficiency of human wisdom and claims of personal merit in the face of sovereign grace (Romans 3:27, Ephesians 2:8-9).
[18-30] A leading man questions Jesus about the works necessary to inherit eternal life, calling him Good Teacher (Luke 18:18). The Lord responds by questioning the attribution of the term and referring it to the fulfillment of the commandments of the Mosaic Law (Exodus 20:12-16). From a dispensational perspective, this dialogue reflects the pre-resurrection administration, where eternal life under the Law was linked to the practical obedience of its precepts (Leviticus 18:5, Romans 10:5). When the young man declares that he had kept the Law since his youth, the Lord exposes the hidden greed in his heart by instructing him to sell his possessions, distribute them to the poor to obtain treasure in heaven, and take up his cross to follow Him (Luke 18:22). The man's sadness at leaving because of his great wealth prompts the Savior to declare how difficult it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God, using the illustration of the camel passing through the eye of a needle (Luke 18:24-25, Matthew 19:24). To the astonishment of his listeners, the Messiah affirms that what is impossible for men is possible for God (Luke 18:27), assuring his disciples that every sacrifice for the sake of the kingdom of God will receive abundant reward in this present time and eternal life in the age to come (Matthew 19:27-29, 2 Corinthians 9:8).
[31-34] The Messiah gathers the twelve apostles privately to announce the imminent fulfillment of the Old Testament prophecies concerning his passion in Jerusalem (Isaiah 53:1-12, Psalms 22:1-18). The Lord details that the Son of Man will be handed over to the Gentiles, suffering mockery, insults, spitting, flogging, and death, culminating in his resurrection on the third day {{quote:Luke 18:33|And after they have flogged him, they will kill him; But on the third day he will rise again. Despite the clarity of the announcement, the disciples did not grasp the meaning of the discourse, this truth remaining hidden from their understanding due to their expectation of an immediate earthly kingdom without the prior passage through the altar of Calvary (Luke 9:45, Luke 24:25-27, 1 Peter 1:11).
[35-43] As Jesus approached the city of Jericho, a blind beggar sitting by the roadside inquired about the commotion of the crowd and, upon learning that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by, cried out, invoking the divine and royal title of the Savior {{quote:Luke 18:38|Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!}}. Despite the rebukes of the crowd trying to silence him, the suffering man intensified his cry, moving the Lord to stop and command that he be brought into his presence. When Christ questions him about his request, the blind man begs to regain his sight, and the Lord grants him immediate healing by virtue of his faith (Luke 18:42: “Go, your faith has made you well”). The restored man follows Jesus, glorifying God and prompting praise from all the people. Typologically, the blind man's beggary condition portrays the spiritual misery of humanity without Christ and the temporary blindness of Israel, whose physical and spiritual restoration will occur when they recognize their Messiah with repentance at the second coming (Isaiah 35:5, Zechariah 12:10, Romans 11:25-26, Revelation 1:7).

[1-10] The entry of Jesus Christ into the city of Jericho—a place historically subject to a curse (Joshua 6:26)—frames the conversion of Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector who had become wealthy through extortion on behalf of the occupying Roman power (Luke 3:12-13, Luke 19:2). Unable to see the Messiah because of his short stature and the dense crowd, Zacchaeus goes ahead and climbs a sycamore tree in the Savior's path. The Lord sees the man, calls him by name, and commands him to humble himself and come down quickly {{quote:Luke 19:5|Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today}}. The publican's response shows genuine repentance that transforms his economic behavior, arranging to give half of his possessions to the poor and make four times the restitution to those he had defrauded, exceeding the requirements of Mosaic law (Exodus 22:1, Leviticus 6:5). In response to the murmuring of the religious crowd over the hospitality shown to a sinner, the Lord proclaims the arrival of salvation to that house, recognizing Zacchaeus as a true son of Abraham in faith (Romans 4:11-12, Galatians 3:7) and declaring the central purpose of his incarnation {{quote:Luke 19:10|For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost}}.
[11-27] In response to the crowd's false expectation of the immediate manifestation of the Messianic kingdom in Jerusalem, the Lord tells the parable of the ten minas to teach the postponement of the earthly theocracy and the responsibility of the servants during his absence (Luke 19:11). The nobleman who departs for a distant land to claim a kingdom for himself and return represents Christ ascending to heaven after the crucifixion, leaving ten of his servants a mina each with the formal instruction to trade until his return (Luke 19:13). Doctrinally, there is a clear distinction between the talents of Matthew 25—where the servant's unfaithfulness in the Great Tribulation results in the loss of salvation—and the minas of Luke 19, where each servant receives the same portion of grace in the present age; the negligent servant who keeps his mina in a handkerchief suffers the loss of rewards and authority in the millennium, but remains saved (1 Corinthians 3:13-15, 2 Timothy 2:12). In contrast, the citizens who hated him and declared that they did not want him to reign over them symbolize the rebels who reject the gospel, who will be physically executed at the King's glorious return at the second coming {{quote:Luke 19:27|And those enemies of mine who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here, and slaughter them before me}} (2 Thessalonians 1:7-9, Revelation 19:15).
[28-40] The Lord continues his ascent toward Jerusalem, arriving at Bethphage and Bethany on the Mount of Olives, a prophetic location linked to the departure and glorious return of the Messiah (Zechariah 14:4, Acts 1:11-12). Jesus sends two disciples to fetch a donkey on which no one had ever sat, instructing them to tell the owners that the Lord needs it (Luke 19:31). This statement is one of only two instances in the Gospels where the Savior declares an earthly need, symbolizing the untamed sinner set free by the word for Messianic service (John 4:4). The group leads the donkey and places their garments upon it to accommodate Jesus, literally fulfilling Zechariah's prophecy concerning the coming of the humble King to the daughter of Zion (Zechariah 9:9). As they descended the slope of the Mount of Olives, the multitude of disciples burst into loud praise for the wonders they had witnessed, proclaiming the blessing of the King who comes in the name of the Lord and announcing peace in heaven and glory in the highest (Psalms 118:26, Luke 2:14). In response to the Pharisees' protest, who demanded that Jesus rebuke his followers, the Messiah affirms the inevitability of his royal acclamation (Luke 19:40), demonstrating that even inanimate creation would bear witness to his divinity if the people refused to give him glory.
[41-44] As he approaches and beholds the city of Jerusalem from the height of the mountain, the Lord weeps over it, expressing Messianic sorrow at the impending tragedy of his chosen people (Psalm 122:6, Jeremiah 9:1). Jesus laments that the nation had not known, at least in his day, the things pertaining to his peace, which remained hidden from their eyes because of their obstinate unbelief (Isaiah 48:18, Matthew 23:37-38). Consequently, the Savior delivers a detailed prophecy concerning the military destruction of the holy city, announcing that the enemies will surround it with trenches, besiege it on all sides, devastate it along with its inhabitants, and leave not one stone upon another (Luke 19:44, "because you did not recognize the time of your visitation"). This prophetic announcement found literal historical fulfillment in 70 AD. When the Roman legions led by Titus destroyed the temple and the city, executing divine judgment on the generation that rejected the presence of their Savior (Daniel 9:26, Micah 3:12, Luke 21:20-24).
[45-48] Entering the temple precincts, Jesus Christ carries out the second cleansing of his earthly ministry—following the first at the beginning of his public work (John 2:13-17)—by driving out the merchants and money changers who profited from the ceremonial sacrifices. The Messiah vindicates the sanctity of the sacred precincts by confronting the corruption of the priesthood through Scripture {{quote:Luke 19:46|It is written: My house is a house of prayer; But you have made it a den of robbers, summarizing the prophetic declarations of Isaiah and Jeremiah concerning the house of God (Isaiah 56:7, Jeremiah 7:11). After reclaiming the sacred space, the Lord taught daily in the temple, while the chief priests, the scribes, and the leaders of the nation sought a way to kill him. However, the religious authorities were unable to carry out their murderous plans at that time because all the people hung on his every word, listening attentively, foreshadowing the final conflict that would lead to the Savior's arrest and crucifixion at Passover (Mark 11:18, Luke 20:19, John 7:46).

[1-8] Jesus Christ teaches the people in the temple and proclaims the gospel when the chief priests, scribes, and elders of the nation approach him. The religious authorities question the legitimacy of his ministry, demanding to know by what authority he performs his works or who has granted him such power. Instead of directly answering his adversaries, the Lord poses a counter-question about the origin of John the Baptist's baptism, an inquiry that places the leaders in an insurmountable dilemma (Luke 3:2-3, Matthew 21:23-27). If they admitted that baptism came from heaven, they would have to justify their disbelief in the forerunner; if they affirmed that it came from men, they feared the reaction of the crowd, who considered John a true prophet. When the religious leaders declared they were ignorant of the origin of baptism, the Savior refused to reveal to them the source of his power (Luke 20:8). This Messianic refusal exposes the insincerity of the Jewish hierarchy and reserves spiritual enlightenment only for those who seek the truth with humility of heart (Luke 10:21, 1 Corinthians 1:27-29).
[9-19] The Lord presents to the people the parable of the vineyard planted by a man who leases it to tenants and travels to a distant country for a long time (Isaiah 5:1-7). At harvest time, the owner successively sends three servants to collect their share, but the tenants beat them, insult them, and send them away empty-handed, illustrating Israel's historical rejection of God's prophets (Jeremiah 7:25-26, 2 Chronicles 36:15-16). Finally, the owner of the vineyard decides to send his beloved son, assuming he will be respected; however, the tenants identify the heir and agree to kill him to seize the inheritance, foreshadowing the Sanhedrin's conspiracy to execute Christ outside the holy city (Matthew 21:38-39, Hebrews 13:12). The owner of the vineyard will come, destroy the tenants, and give the vineyard to others. To the awe of his listeners, the Messiah quotes Psalm 118 to identify himself as the stone rejected by the builders (Luke 20:17). Doctrinally, the Stone operates in both comings: in the first coming, it is the stumbling block over which the unbeliever falls and is broken; in the second coming, it descends as the Stone of Daniel 2 to strike the image of the Gentile kingdoms and grind the wicked to dust (Luke 20:18). Anyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces; anyone on whom it falls, it will crush him (Daniel 2:34-35, Romans 9:32-33, 1 Peter 2:6-8). Perceiving that the parable was directed against them, the scribes and chief priests sought to arrest him at that very hour, though they feared the people.
[20-26] Watching for the Savior, the religious leaders sent disguised spies, pretending to be righteous, with the purpose of catching him in some statement and handing him over to the power and authority of the Roman governor (Luke 20:20, Matthew 22:15-22). The messengers approached Jesus with flattery, praising his upright and impartial teaching, to pose the trick question about whether or not it was lawful to pay taxes to Caesar. Perceiving the cunning of his opponents, the Messiah asked to see a denarius and inquired whose image and inscription were engraved on the coin. By replying that they belong to Caesar, the Lord pronounces the rule that dismantles the political trap {{quote: Luke 20:25|Give therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and the things that are God’s to God}}. This instruction establishes the distinction between civic duties toward earthly government (Romans 13:1-7, 1 Peter 2:13-17) and the absolute surrender of conscience and soul to God. Unable to rebuke his word before the people, the spies marveled at his answer and remained silent.
[27-40] Some of the Sadducees, the rationalist sect that denied the bodily resurrection, the existence of angels, and the spirit world (Acts 23:8), approach the Lord. They present a hypothetical case based on the law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5-6), where a woman was successively married to seven brothers who died without leaving offspring, asking which of them she will marry in the resurrection. Jesus corrects their ignorance by distinguishing between the conditions of the present age and the order to come: the children of this age marry and are given in marriage, but those considered worthy to attain to the age to come and the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they are like the angels and are children of God, being children of the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:42-53, 1 John 3:2). He also demonstrates the reality of the resurrection from the writings of Moses in the passage about the burning bush, where the Lord is called the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob (Exodus 3:6), concluding that God is not the God of the dead, but of the living (Luke 20:38). Some scribes praised the Master's answer, and no one dared to ask him any further questions.
[41-44] The Messiah takes the initiative and questions the congregation about why it is claimed that the Christ is the son of David. To establish his deity, Jesus quotes Psalm 110, where David, speaking by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, calls the Messiah Lord, declaring that the Lord said to his Lord to sit at his right hand until he made his enemies a footstool for his feet (Luke 20:42). Christ explains that if David calls him Lord, he cannot be merely his son according to the flesh. The resolution of this paradox lies in the dual nature of the Messiah: as a man, he is a direct descendant of David, but according to his eternal divinity, he is the Lord of David (Romans 1:3-4, Revelation 22:16).
[45-47] With all the people listening, the Lord gives his disciples a direct warning to beware of the scribes (Matthew 23:1-7, Mark 12:38-40). These ostentatious leaders liked to wear long robes, coveted respectful greetings in the marketplaces, the best seats in the synagogues, and the places of honor at banquets. However, their outward devotion masked rapacious behavior that devoured widows' houses, pretending to cover up their greed with the appearance of long prayers {{quote:Luke 20:47|They devour widows' houses, and for a show make long prayers}}. Because of this religious hypocrisy and the abuse of the needy, the Savior decrees that these teachers will receive a more severe condemnation in the divine judgment (Luke 11:43-52, James 3:1).

[1-4] Jesus Christ observes the rich casting their offerings into the temple treasury, a system historically established since the days of High Priest Jehoiada (2 Kings 12:9, 2 Chronicles 24:8). Amid the ostentation of the elites, a poor widow deposits two mites, equivalent to a quadrans or half a penny (Mark 12:42). The Lord emphasizes that the woman's contribution surpasses that of the wealthy, for they gave from their abundance without sacrificing their lifestyle, while she gave all she had to live on out of her poverty {{quote: Luke 21:4|for all these out of their abundance gave to the offerings of God, but she out of her poverty put in all she had to live on}}. Doctrinally, this scene serves as a visual illustration of the earlier denunciation of the religious leaders who devoured widows' houses (Luke 20:47), showing how the ceremonial system exploited the vulnerable to adorn a building abandoned by God. It also demonstrates that at the judgment seat of Christ, rewards are not measured by quantity but by the magnitude of personal sacrifice (2 Corinthians 8:12).
[5-9] Faced with the admiration of some disciples for the architectural magnificence of the temple adorned with beautiful stones and votive offerings, the Messiah pronounces the sentence of desolation, announcing that not one stone will be left upon another that will not be thrown down. This prophecy found a literal historical fulfillment in 70 AD when the Roman legions under Titus set fire to the sanctuary and demolished its walls (Daniel 9:26, Luke 19:44). When questioned about the timing and sign of these events, the Savior warns against religious deception, cautioning about the appearance of impostors who will come in his name claiming to be the Christ (Luke 21:8: “See that you are not deceived; for many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Christ’”). The Lord instructs not to follow these false leaders or be terrified by the outbreak of wars and seditions, clarifying that these things must happen first, but that the end of the age will not occur immediately (Jeremiah 14:14, Matthew 24:4-6).
[10-19] The Messiah details the armed conflicts between nations and kingdoms, accompanied by great earthquakes, famines, pestilences, and terrifying phenomena in the sky. Before the full manifestation of these judgments, the disciples would face fierce persecution, being arrested, handed over to synagogues and prisons, and brought before kings and governors for the sake of Christ's name. The Savior promises to impart eloquent and irresistible wisdom to his adversaries (Acts 4:13, Acts 6:10), warning that betrayal would come even from their own parents, siblings, relatives, and friends. Despite the universal hatred and the physical death of some witnesses, the Lord guarantees the divine preservation of the Jewish remnant through a promise of literal protection (Luke 12:7, Matthew 10:30), exhorting them to persevere for physical and spiritual salvation {{quote: Luke 21:19|In your patience you will possess your souls}} (Matthew 24:13, Hebrews 3:14).
[20-24] The Lord indicates that the presence of armies surrounding Jerusalem constitutes the unmistakable sign of its impending desolation, commanding the inhabitants of Judea to flee to the mountains without returning to the city (Matthew 24:15-16). These days are described as days of vengeance for the fulfillment of Scripture, pronouncing a woe upon pregnant women and nursing mothers during that time of tribulation. The passage differentiates the first-century judgment from the final Great Tribulation: while in 70 AD the Jewish people fell by the edge of the sword and were taken captive to all nations during the Church Age, the city of Jerusalem remains under pagan rule until the formal conclusion of the Gentile dispensation {{quote:Luke 21:24|and Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled}}. Doctrinally, the times of the Gentiles encompass the succession of world empires beginning with Nebuchadnezzar in Babylon (Daniel 2:31-45, Daniel 7:1-28) that will culminate in the glorious return of Christ at His second coming (Romans 11:25, Revelation 19:11-16).
[25-28] The narrative describes the cosmic upheavals preceding the glorious advent, characterized by signs in the sun, moon, and stars, as well as anguish and perplexity among the nations at the roaring of the sea and the waves. Terror will paralyze the hearts of men as they witness the upheaval of the heavenly powers (Isaiah 13:9-10, Joel 2:30-31, Acts 2:19-20). In the midst of this planetary catastrophe, they will behold the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory (Daniel 7:13-14, Matthew 24:30, Revelation 1:7). The Lord speaks a word of encouragement and hope to the believing remnant, urging them to stand upright and lift up their eyes at the beginning of these events {{quote: Luke 21:28|and lift up your heads, for your redemption is drawing near}}, pointing to the nearness of Israel's final liberation and the establishment of the millennial kingdom (Psalm 98:1-9, Isaiah 35:4, Romans 11:26).
[29-33] Jesus Christ presents the parable of the fig tree and all the trees, teaching that just as the budding of their blossoms announces the nearness of summer, the contemplation of these prophetic signs confirms the nearness of the kingdom of God. In the typological language of Scripture, the fig tree represents the national restoration of Israel (Hosea 9:10, Joel 1:7, Matthew 21:19), while the other trees symbolize the parallel resurgence of neighboring nations. The Savior solemnly affirms that the generation that witnesses the flourishing of these signs will not pass away until all is fulfilled (Luke 21:32). The passage culminates by proclaiming the eternity and inerrancy of divine revelation in contrast to the transience of the created order: {{quote:Luke 21:33|Heaven and earth will pass away; But my words will not pass away, guaranteeing the perfect preservation of the Scriptures through the ages (Psalm 119:89, Isaiah 40:8, 1 Peter 1:25).
[34-38] The Messiah warns his listeners about the danger of their hearts becoming burdened with gluttony, drunkenness, and the cares of this life, causing that day of judgment to overwhelm them unexpectedly like a snare upon all the inhabitants of the earth (Isaiah 24:17-18, 1 Thessalonians 5:2-3). To avoid spiritual ruin, the Lord commands them to watch and pray at all times so that they may be considered worthy to escape these tribulations and stand before the Son of Man (Luke 12:37, Ephesians 6:18, 2 Thessalonians 1:11). The chapter concludes by outlining the Messianic routine in the days leading up to his passion: he taught during the day in the temple precincts and withdrew at night to spend the night on the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:39, John 8:1). All the people flocked to the temple from dawn to hear his word, demonstrating the Savior's doctrinal authority in the face of the imminent conspiracy of the religious authorities (Mark 11:18, Luke 19:48).

[1-6] The approach of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, called Passover, frames the conspiracy of the chief priests and scribes to eliminate Jesus Christ while avoiding a popular uprising (Exodus 12:8, Matthew 26:3-5). At this juncture, the adversary intervenes directly in the story of redemption (Luke 22:3: “And Satan entered into Judas, called Iscariot”), prompting the apostate apostle to confer with the religious authorities and the temple captains about how to betray the Savior. The Sanhedrin agrees to give him money, stipulating the sum of thirty pieces of silver, which represented the legal value of a slave in the Mosaic economy (Exodus 21:32, Zechariah 11:12-13). Judas accepts the transaction and looks for an opportunity to betray him in the absence of the crowd, demonstrating the spiritual degradation to which the love of money leads in contrast to the consecration required by the Kingdom (1 Timothy 6:10, Acts 1:18).
[7-23] When the day of Unleavened Bread arrived, on which the Passover lamb was to be sacrificed, the Lord commissioned Peter and John to make preparations in the upper room, demonstrating his divine foreknowledge by indicating to them the sign of a man with a water jar (Mark 14:13). While at the table, the Messiah instituted the Lord's Supper through figurative symbols {{quote:Luke 22:19|This is my body, which is given for you: do this in remembrance of me}}, teaching that the bread and the cup spiritually represent his atoning sacrifice and the new testament in his shed blood (Jeremiah 25:15, Psalms 75:8, 1 Corinthians 11:24-25). Judas Iscariot's participation in the banquet before going out to carry out his betrayal confirms that the outward reception of ritual ordinances does not bring about the regeneration of the soul, for the traitor partook of the figurative elements while remaining in a state of perdition (John 6:70-71, John 13:26-30, Acts 1:25).
[24-38] The contention among the apostles regarding hierarchical preeminence in the Kingdom is resolved by the Savior, who establishes that spiritual leadership is based on humble service and meekness, in contrast to the despotic rule of the Gentile rulers (Matthew 20:25-28). The Lord promises the twelve that they will eat and drink at his table in his kingdom, sitting on thrones to judge the twelve tribes of Israel during the millennial age (Matthew 19:28, Revelation 20:4). Next, the Messiah reveals to Simon Peter Satan's attempt to sift him like wheat, assuring him that he has interceded for him so that his faith will not fail and he can strengthen his brothers after their conversion. In the dispensational realm before the crucifixion, the disciples operated under the Old Testament order without yet possessing the permanent regeneration of the body of Christ (Psalm 51:11, Ephesians 4:30). Finally, the Lord modifies the previous itinerant guidelines by ordering the provision of a purse, bag, and sword {{quote: Luke 22:36|Let the one who has no sword sell his clothes and buy one}}, indicating that the prophecy about being numbered among the wicked had to be fulfilled before his departure (Isaiah 53:12, Acts 13:51).
[39-46] After the Last Supper, Jesus Christ proceeds as usual to the Mount of Olives and enters Gethsemane, a place whose name means oil press and which foreshadows the spiritual pressure the Redeemer would suffer (Isaiah 53:10). Withdrawing a stone's throw away, the Lord prostrates himself in prayer, asking for the removal of the cup of judgment {{quote: Luke 22:42|Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me; yet not my will, but yours be done}}. Doctrinally, this cup did not consist of the fear of physical death or a satanic attempt to extinguish his life in the garden, but rather the cup of God's fury and judgment against the sin of humanity (Psalm 75:8, Jeremiah 25:15). Strengthened by a heavenly angel, the Messiah enters into such intense agony that his sweat becomes like great drops of blood falling to the ground, manifesting the sufferings of Him who was made sin for us, though he knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21, Galatians 3:13, Hebrews 5:7-8). At the conclusion of his sermon, the Lord finds his disciples asleep from grief, urging them to rise and pray so they will not fall into temptation (Matthew 26:41).
[47-53] The intrusion of an armed mob into the garden marks the culminating phase of the conspiracy, with Judas going ahead to approach the Savior. The Lord exposes the agreed-upon signal by questioning the infamy of the act {{quote:Luke 22:48|Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?}}, demonstrating that betrayal through a gesture of affection mirrors the deceitful behavior of the adversary (2 Samuel 15:5, Hosea 13:2, Psalm 41:9). As the disciples perceive the outcome, Peter draws a sword and cuts off the right ear of Malchus, the high priest's servant (John 18:10). The Savior represses the armed action and, touching the aggressor's ear, heals the afflicted man; this restoration constitutes Christ's last public miracle before the crucifixion, paradoxically performed on an enemy to illustrate the precept of divine grace (Luke 6:27-28, Romans 5:10). The Lord rebukes the religious leaders for coming at night with clubs and weapons as against a robber, proclaiming that this situation represented the hour of the power of darkness (Luke 19:47, John 8:44, Colossians 1:13).
[54-62] After the arrest, the guards lead the Lord to the high priest's residence, while Simon Peter follows at a distance and enters the courtyard to warm himself by the guards' fire. This closeness to the Messiah's enemies places the disciple in a position of carnal weakness that precipitates his downfall (Psalm 1:1, 1 Corinthians 15:33). Confronted successively by a servant girl and others present who identify him as a Galilean and a follower of Jesus, Peter repeatedly denies Jesus, adding oaths to distance himself from the Master (Matthew 26:72-74). At the moment of his third denial, the rooster crows and the Lord turns to look upon Peter, reminding the apostle of the Savior's warning (Luke 22:34). Contrite in spirit, Peter leaves the compound and weeps bitterly, experiencing the contrition of a godly sorrow that leads to repentance and subsequent restoration, in stark contrast to Judas's worldly remorse that culminated in self-destruction (2 Corinthians 7:10, Acts 1:18, John 21:15-17).
[63-71] During the night captivity, the men guarding the Savior committed physical and verbal abuse against Him, covering His face to beat Him and sarcastically demanding that He prophesy the identity of the assailant, literally fulfilling the prophecies of the Suffering Servant (Isaiah 50:6, Isaiah 52:14, Matthew 26:67-68). At daybreak, the Sanhedrin assembly, composed of the chief priests and scribes, convened to put the Savior on trial in an irregular judicial session (Luke 20:19, Acts 4:5-6). Questioned by the court about his Messianic status, the Lord pointed out the futility of their unbelief and proclaimed the majesty of his heavenly lordship {{quote: Luke 22:69|From now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God}} (Psalm 110:1, Daniel 7:13-14). When the assembly pressed him to confirm whether he was the Son of God, the Messiah affirmed with his word, leading the religious authorities to conclude the summary proceedings and send the accused to the Roman court of Pontius Pilate (Luke 23:1, John 18:31, Acts 4:26-28).

[1-7] The transfer of Jesus Christ before Pontius Pilate by the entire Sanhedrin marks the beginning of the governmental judicial process following the irregular night session (Luke 22:66, John 18:28). The religious authorities avoid entering the praetorium so as not to incur ceremonial contamination before Passover, revealing the hypocrisy of a formal religion concerned with ritual purity while plotting the murder of the Righteous One (Matthew 23:23-24, Acts 7:52). The Jewish hierarchy formulates three false accusations of a political nature to force Roman intervention: corrupting the nation, forbidding the payment of taxes to Caesar, and claiming to be the Messiah King (Luke 23:2). These accusations constitute outright defamation, since the Lord paid taxes, taught to give to Caesar what is Caesar's (Luke 20:25), and refused to be crowned by the crowd (John 6:15). When questioned by the procurator about His royal majesty, the Lord calmly nods; however, after a private examination of the spiritual nature of His Kingdom (John 18:36-37), Pilate pronounces the first verdict of innocence: “I find no fault in this man.” Faced with the renewed fury of the accusers, who point to the unrest stirred up in Galilee, the procurator tries to evade his legal responsibility by sending the accused to the jurisdiction of Herod Antipas, who was in Jerusalem for the festival (Luke 3:1, Acts 4:27).
[8-12] The encounter between the Savior and Herod Antipas exposes the frivolity of carnal behavior in the face of divine truth. Herod is overjoyed to see Jesus, for he had long desired to witness the performance of some spectacular miracle as royal entertainment (Luke 9:9). When confronted with numerous questions, the Messiah remained completely silent, literally fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy about the Lamb who was silent before his shearers (Isaiah 53:7, 1 Peter 2:23). The Lord refused to address a man who had seared his conscience by beheading John the Baptist (Mark 6:26-28). While the chief priests and scribes vehemently accused the Lord, Herod and his guards scorned and mocked him, dressing him in a splendid robe or a mock king's mantle before sending him back to Pilate (Luke 23:11). Doctrinally, the clothing imposed by the Roman soldiers foreshadows the scarlet and purple garments associated with religious corruption (Revelation 17:4), distinguishing them from the Savior's ordinary garments. The day concludes with the reconciliation between Pilate and Herod, two enemy rulers fraternizing in their shared rejection of the Lord's Anointed (Psalms 2:1-2, Acts 4:27-28).
[13-25] Pilate summons the chief priests, rulers, and the people to reiterate the lack of capital punishment in Jesus, confirming that Herod also found no cause for death in Him (Luke 23:14-15). Seeking a compromise to appease the crowd's bloodlust without executing an innocent man, the procurator proposes having the Lord flogged and then releasing him; however, the crowd erupts in a unanimous outcry demanding the release of Barabbas (Luke 23:18). In the typology of Scripture, Barabbas—whose name means "son of the father"—represents the sinner condemned to death for his rebellion, theft, and murder (Mark 15:7, John 18:40), who is literally acquitted because the true Son of the heavenly Father takes his place on the cross (Galatians 3:13, 1 Peter 2:24). After attempting for the third time to free the Savior, Pilate yields to the urgent voices of the religious leaders who demand the Messianic crucifixion {{quote:Luke 23:21|"Crucify him, crucify him!"}}. The governor formally washes his hands (Deuteronomy 21:6-9, Matthew 27:24) and hands the Lord over to the will of His enemies, demonstrating the moral cowardice of human judgment and unleashing a two-thousand-year period of dispersion upon the nation because of the assumed blood guilt (Matthew 27:25, 1 Thessalonians 2:15-16).
[26-31] During the journey to the place of execution outside the city walls (Hebrews 13:12), the Roman soldiers seize Simon of Cyrene, a passerby from North Africa, forcing him to carry the cross behind Jesus (Matthew 27:32). A large crowd of people and women followed the Savior, mourning His suffering; Nevertheless, the Messiah turns to them to deliver a prophecy concerning the nation's future judgments (Luke 23:28: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children”). The Lord announces days of distress when the blessedness of the barren will be proclaimed, and multitudes will cry out to the mountains and hills to fall upon them to cover their ruin (Hosea 10:8, Revelation 6:16). This warning foreshadows both the military destruction of Jerusalem by the Roman legions in 70 AD and the horrors of the Great Tribulation. Through the analogy of the green tree and the dry tree (Luke 23:31), the Lord teaches that if divine judgment allowed the breaking of the innocent Son on the green tree of His presence, the punishment upon the broken and barren nation on the dry tree of apostasy will be devastating (Ezekiel 20:47, 1 Peter 4:17-18).
[32-38] The Savior is led to the place called Calvary—a word derived from the Latin term that translates the Hebrew word Golgotha, meaning "place of the skull" (John 19:17)—and crucified alongside two criminals, one on his right and one on his left. This arrangement fulfills the prophecy of Isaiah that foretold the Servant would be numbered with the wicked (Isaiah 53:12, Mark 15:28). From the cross, Jesus utters the Messianic prayer of intercession, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,” a plea answered in the book of Acts by granting Israel an opportunity for repentance after Pentecost because of their ignorance of sin (Acts 2:38, Acts 3:17). The soldiers divide his garments by casting lots to fulfill the Scriptures (Psalm 22:18), while the rulers and soldiers mock the Messiah, urging him to save himself if he was God’s Chosen One (Psalm 22:7–8). Above his head was placed a title written in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew letters proclaiming the truth of his deity and kingship: THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS (John 19:19–20). This trilingual inscription encompasses all the families of the earth descended from Shem, Ham, and Japheth (Genesis 10:1-32, Zechariah 14:9), testifying to the world of the sovereignty of the Crucified One.
[39-43] One of the hanged criminals was reviling the Lord, demanding that He save himself and them (Matthew 27:44); however, the second criminal is enlightened by the truth upon seeing the Messianic conduct and the inscription of the title. The repentant thief rebukes his companion, reminding him of the fear of God and acknowledging the justice of his own condemnation in contrast to the spotless holiness of Christ {{quote: Luke 23:41|but this man did nothing wrong}}. Turning to the Savior with saving faith, the dying man confesses Jesus' deity and future kingdom {{quote:Luke 23:42|Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom}}. The Messiah's response grants him the immediate assurance of salvation by grace apart from works of the law {{quote:Luke 23:43|Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise}}. Doctrinally, at the time of the crucifixion, Paradise was located in Abraham's bosom in the lower parts of the earth (Luke 16:22, Ephesians 4:8-10), where the souls of the Old Testament saints awaited the consummation of atonement before being taken to heaven after the Lord's bodily resurrection (Matthew 27:52-53, 2 Corinthians 12:4).
[44-49] From the sixth hour to the ninth hour—corresponding to the interval between noon and three in the afternoon—a dense darkness falls over the whole earth because of the darkening of the sun, manifesting the mourning of creation before the judgment of sin (Amos 8:9, Matthew 27:45). At that very hour, the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom, symbolizing the end of the Aaronic ceremonial system and the opening of the new and living way into the Father's presence through the sacrifice of Christ's body (Exodus 26:31-33, Hebrews 10:19-20). Crying out with a loud voice, the Lord uttered his final words, committing his spirit before willingly surrendering his life: "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit" (Psalm 31:5, John 10:18). As the Savior's body descended into the tomb and his soul into Sheol to triumph over death (Acts 2:27, 31, 1 Peter 3:18-19), the Roman centurion in charge of the execution glorified God by declaring the Messiah's righteousness (Luke 23:47, Matthew 27:54). The crowds watched the outcome, beating their breasts in grief, while Jesus' acquaintances and the women of Galilee observed the Messianic fulfillment from a distance (Psalm 38:11, Luke 8:2-3).
[50-56] A man named Joseph, from Arimathea in the region of Judea, intervened to provide a proper burial for the Savior, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy that the Messiah would be with the rich in his death (Isaiah 53:9, Matthew 27:57). Joseph was a member of the Sanhedrin, a man of virtuous and righteous character, who had not consented to the conspiracy or the murderous actions of the religious assembly, waiting in faith for the kingdom of God (Mark 15:43, John 19:38). Boldly appearing before Pontius Pilate, he requested the body of Jesus, which was taken down from the cross and wrapped in fine linen according to Jewish burial custom (John 19:39-40), and placed in a new tomb hewn out of the rock in which no one had ever been laid (Luke 23:53). That day was the eve of Preparation Day, the Sabbath of Passover beginning to dawn (John 19:31, 1 Corinthians 5:7). The women who had accompanied the Lord from Galilee witnessed the tomb and the preparation of the body, returning to their homes to prepare spices and ointments, after which they rested on the Sabbath according to the commandment of the Mosaic Law (Exodus 20:8-11, Luke 24:1).

[1-12] Early in the morning, on the first day of the week, the women went to the tomb carrying the aromatic spices prepared to anoint Jesus' body, finding the stone rolled away and the tomb empty. Two men in dazzling garments—angels in human form (Mark 16:5, Acts 1:10)—appeared, startling the women, and posed the question that forms the cornerstone of faith: {{quote:Luke 24:5|Why do you look for the living among the dead?}}. The heavenly messengers reminded the women of the words spoken by the Lord during his ministry in Galilee regarding the necessity of being handed over to sinful men, being crucified, and rising again on the third day (Luke 9:22, Luke 18:32-33). Recalling these Messianic words, the women returned to announce the events to the eleven apostles and all the other disciples; However, the words of Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and their companions seemed like madness to the apostles, reflecting the initial disbelief of the leadership (Luke 24:11, Mark 16:11). Peter gets up and runs to the tomb, and when he bends down to look inside, he sees only the linen cloths laid side by side. Doctrinally, the arrangement of the wrapped cloths and the cloth placed over the head separately (John 20:7) refutes the false theories about a single burial shroud or the theft of the body, since the resurrected body emerged through the wrappings without unraveling the structure of the bandages (Acts 2:31). Peter withdraws, amazed at what has happened, while the absence of a physical body in the tomb confirms the Messiah's absolute victory over bodily death (Psalm 16:10, 1 Corinthians 15:20).
[13-35] Two disciples—one of them named Cleopas (Luke 24:18)—were walking that same day toward a village called Emmaus, about sixty stades from Jerusalem, discussing the events of the crucifixion. Jesus himself approaches and walks with them; however, the travelers' eyes were closed so that they would not recognize him. When the Lord inquires about the cause of their sadness, Cleopas expresses his astonishment that a stranger in Jerusalem would be ignorant of the events concerning Jesus of Nazareth, whom they considered a prophet powerful in word and deed before God and the people (Luke 7:16, Acts 2:22). The disciples recount the death sentence carried out by the chief priests and rulers, confessing the frustration of their Messianic expectation of political redemption for Israel (Luke 24:21: “But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel”). They also relate the women’s perplexing testimony about the empty tomb and the vision of angels who affirmed that He lives. The Lord rebukes them for their hardness of heart in believing the prophetic writings, asking them if it was not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things before entering His glory (Isaiah 53:1–12, Psalm 22:1–31, 1 Peter 1:11). Beginning with Moses and continuing through all the prophets, the Messiah expounds to them in all the Scriptures the statements concerning Himself, imparting a comprehensive biblical teaching on the fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets. As Jesus approached the village, he pretended to go further to test the disciples' hospitality; when they insisted he stay the night with them, he entered the house. While at the table, the Lord took the bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them, at which point their eyes were opened and they recognized him by the nail marks in his hands (John 20:27), and the Savior vanished from their sight instantly. The disciples recognized the spiritual fervor in their hearts as He spoke to them on the road and opened the Scriptures to them. They rose that very hour to return to Jerusalem, where they found the eleven and their companions gathered together, proclaiming that the Lord had truly risen and had appeared to Simon (1 Corinthians 15:5).
[36-49] As the disciples recounted the events of Emmaus, Jesus appeared in the midst of the assembly in the upper room, pronouncing the Messianic greeting of peace (John 20:19). Terrified by the unexpected intrusion through the locked doors, those present assumed they were seeing a spirit or ghost. The Lord dispelled their doubts by demonstrating the reality of His bodily resurrection and inviting them to verify the tangibility of His limbs {{quote:Luke 24:39|Touch me and see; for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see I have}}. Doctrinally, the formula "flesh and bones"—which omits any mention of blood—defines the nature of the believer's glorified body in the first resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:50, Ephesians 5:30). While Adam's corruptible blood transmits the inheritance of sin and physical death (Genesis 2:23, Romans 5:12), the resurrected body of the Messiah is bloodless, having been shed entirely on the cross of Calvary for the atonement of sins (Hebrews 9:22, Acts 20:28). To dispel any remaining unbelief, the Savior requests food and eats before them a portion of broiled fish and a honeycomb, demonstrating that his resurrected body possesses the physical capacity to eat without being subject to the biological processes of digestion or earthly corruption (Genesis 18:8, Luke 22:16). The Lord reminds the disciples of the words spoken during His earthly ministry, reaffirming the inspiration and tripartite division of the Old Testament canon: the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms (Luke 24:44). Jesus opens the understanding of the congregation—comprised not only of the eleven apostles but of all the disciples gathered there (Luke 24:33, Acts 1:14)—to grasp the meaning of the Scriptures, declaring that it was written that the Christ would suffer and rise from the dead on the third day. The Savior proclaims the commission for the present age, commanding them to preach repentance and the remission of sins in His name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Acts 2:38, Acts 13:38). The disciples are made witnesses of these things, instructing them to remain in the city of Jerusalem until they are clothed with the promise of the Father through the baptism of the Holy Spirit and the power from on high (Acts 1:4-8, Acts 2:1-4).
[50-53] After the instruction in the upper room and the forty days of Messianic appearances (Acts 1:3), the Lord leads the disciples out of the city to the vicinity of Bethany, on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives (Luke 19:29, Acts 1:12). Raising His sacred hands, the Savior imparts His blessing upon the apostolic company, and it came to pass, while He was blessing them, that He parted from them and was taken up into heaven (Luke 24:51). Doctrinally, this bodily ascension to the third heaven constitutes the definitive exaltation of the Son of God to the right hand of the Majesty on high (Mark 16:19, Hebrews 1:3, Ephesians 4:8-10). The unaltered preservation of this reading in the Received Text tradition refutes the omissions of the Alexandrian manuscripts that seek to truncate the testimony of Christ's physical ascension into heaven. After worshiping the Messiah in his glorious departure, the disciples return to Jerusalem filled with great joy, remaining continuously in the temple precincts praising and blessing God (Acts 2:46, Acts 3:1). The Gospel concludes in the same setting of worship where it began its narrative with Zechariah's priestly vision (Luke 1:9-11), closing the revelation of the Son of Man whose resurrection and ongoing intercession guarantee the eternal salvation of believers (Hebrews 7:25, 1 John 2:1).

[1-3] Luke begins the second part of his historical record addressed to Theophilus, connecting the narrative with his earlier treatise where he set forth the works and teachings of Jesus Christ up to his ascension (Luke 1:1-4, Luke 24:50-51). The resurrected Messiah manifested himself to the twelve apostles for a period of forty days through undeniable proofs, instructing them in the truths concerning the kingdom of God (Matthew 28:18-20, 1 Corinthians 15:5-7). In the dispensational scheme, these instructions prepared the disciples to witness the transition from Old Testament administration to the apostolic age, confirming the Savior's deity through His victory over physical death {{quote:Acts 1:3|to whom also, after His suffering, He presented Himself alive by many infallible proofs}}.
[4, 5] Gathered with His apostles, the Lord commands them not to leave the city of Jerusalem until they receive the promise of the heavenly Father (Luke 24:49, John 14:16-17). The Savior contrasts the water baptism administered by John the Baptist with the baptism of the Holy Spirit that would take place in a few days during the Jewish festival of Pentecost {{quote:Acts 1:5|For John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days later}}. Doctrinally, this event marks the coming of the Holy Spirit to form the spiritual body of Christ and initiate a new dispensation (1 Corinthians 12:13, Ephesians 4:5), differing from baptismal water, which constitutes a mere testimony and external identification (1 Peter 3:21).
[6-8] The apostles question the Lord about the immediate restoration of the Davidic theocracy in Israel {{quote:Acts 1:6|Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?}}. This inquiry did not arise from carnal ignorance, but from knowledge of the Old Testament prophecies that linked the outpouring of the Spirit with the establishment of the Messianic kingdom in Jerusalem (Isaiah 32:15-18, Joel 2:28-32, Zechariah 14:9). The Lord clarifies that the setting of times and seasons belongs solely to the Father's authority (Daniel 2:21, 1 Thessalonians 5:1), but He promises them the investiture of divine power to be His witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea, in Samaria, and to the ends of the earth (Luke 24:47-48, Acts 8:1, Acts 13:47).
[9-11] After completing His instructions, the Lord Jesus Christ is physically taken up to heaven while the apostles gazed upon Him, being received by a heavenly cloud that hides Him from their sight (Psalm 68:18, Ephesians 4:8-10). While they stood gazing intently at the heavens, two men in white robes—angels in human form (Mark 16:5, Acts 10:30)—appeared beside them to proclaim the Messianic promise of the glorious return {{quote:Acts 1:11|This same Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen him go into heaven}}. This declaration guarantees the literal, bodily, and visible Second Coming of Christ on the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4, Matthew 24:30, Revelation 1:7).
[12-14] The apostolic entourage returns to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, located a Sabbath day's journey away (Exodus 16:29). Upon entering the city, they went up to the upper room where the eleven apostles were staying: Peter, James, John, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James (Luke 6:13-16). They all persevered with one accord in prayer and supplication, together with the believing women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and the Lord’s earthly brothers (Acts 1:14), who, after the resurrection, had acknowledged the deity of their kinsman according to the flesh (Matthew 13:55, John 7:5, 1 Corinthians 15:7).
[15-20] In those days, Peter stood up in the midst of an assembly of about one hundred and twenty disciples to address the defection of Judas Iscariot.
