The apostle explains that the traitor's apostasy had to be fulfilled according to what the Holy Spirit had prophesied through David (Psalms 69:25, Psalms 109:8). Judas acquired a field with the price of his iniquity, and suffering a tragic death by falling headlong and bursting open, the place was called Aceldama or Field of Blood (Matthew 27:3-8). The text indicates that Judas fell through transgression to go to his own place {{quote:Acts 1:25|to take the part of this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas fell through transgression, to go to his own place}}, pointing to his unique destiny in the eternal judgment (John 6:70, Revelation 9:11).
[21-26] To fill the vacancy in the apostolic college, Peter sets the required qualifications: having accompanied the group from John's baptism until the day of the ascension, to be a direct witness of Christ's resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:5-8). The assembly proposes Joseph called Barsabbas, surnamed Justus, and Matthias. After entrusting the decision in prayer to the Lord who knows the hearts of all men, they cast lots according to the custom of Mosaic Law (Leviticus 16:8, Proverbs 16:33), the lot falling on Matthias {{quote:Acts 1:26|And they cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias; so he was numbered with the eleven apostles}}. This appointment completes the number of the twelve apostles of the Lamb destined to judge the twelve tribes of Israel in the millennial kingdom (Matthew 19:28, Revelation 21:14), distinguishing it from Paul's later apostleship to the Gentile nations (Romans 11:13, Galatians 2:7-8).

[1-13] The fulfillment of the day of Pentecost brings the disciples together in unity of spirit in Jerusalem. The coming of the Holy Spirit is accompanied by a heavenly sound like a rushing mighty wind that fills the house where they are sitting (Acts 2:1-2). The visible manifestation includes divided tongues that rest on each of them {{quote:Acts 2:3|and divided tongues as of fire appeared to them}}, all of them being filled with the Holy Spirit and beginning to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance. Devout Jews from every nation under heaven crowd together in amazement as they listen to the Galilean apostles proclaim the wonders of God in their own native languages ​​(Acts 2:5-11). Doctrinally, this event marks the coming of the Holy Spirit to baptize and incorporate believers into the spiritual body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:13, Ephesians 4:5). The tongues spoken at Pentecost were real, legible human languages ​​(Acts 2:8-11), granted as a divine sign to the people of Israel to convict them of their unbelief (1 Corinthians 1:22, 1 Corinthians 14:22, Isaiah 28:11). The text specifies that the tongues were like fire, a concept distinct from the baptism of fire, which represents the purifying and condemning judgment that will consume the wicked at the Second Coming (Matthew 3:11-12, 2 Thessalonians 1:8). Likewise, the manifestation of tongues in this passage was limited to the initial apostolic group, with none of the three thousand subsequent converts speaking in tongues upon receiving the word (Acts 2:41).
[14-21] Simon Peter stands up with the eleven apostles and exhorts the Jewish crowd to listen to their words, refuting the accusation of drunkenness by pointing out that it was only the third hour of the day (Acts 2:14-15). The apostle explains the phenomenon by referring to the prophetic testimony of the Old Testament {{quote:Acts 2:16|But this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel}}, citing the outpouring of the Spirit on all flesh, the dreams and visions in the last days, as well as the wonders in heaven and on earth before the great and glorious day of the Lord (Joel 2:28-32). From a hermeneutical perspective, Peter's statement does not imply that Joel's prophecy reached its full and unconditional fulfillment on the day of Pentecost, but rather that it served as an announcement and illustration of the Messianic order. The cosmic wonders of blood, fire, smoke, the darkening of the sun, and the turning of the moon to blood described by Joel (Joel 2:30-31, Revelation 6:12-13) did not occur at Pentecost, but belong to the judgments of the Great Tribulation preceding the Second Coming (Isaiah 13:9-10, Matthew 24:29-30). In the dispensational economy, Peter was offering Israel the opportunity for national repentance for the restoration of the Kingdom (Acts 3:19-21). Faced with the nation's definitive rejection, the Messianic kingdom was postponed, and God proceeded to call the Church (Romans 11:11-25, Ephesians 3:1-9).
[22-36] Addressing the Israelite men explicitly, Peter presents Jesus of Nazareth as a man approved by God through miracles, wonders, and signs (Acts 2:22). The apostle affirms that the Messiah was handed over by God's predetermined plan and providence, crucified and killed by the hands of wicked men, but raised by God, freeing him from the agony of death, since it was impossible for death to hold him (Acts 2:23-24). Citing Psalm 16, Peter demonstrates that David prophesied the bodily resurrection of Christ by declaring that his soul would not be left in Hell nor would his flesh see corruption (Psalm 16:10, Acts 2:27-31). The preacher testifies that Jesus has been exalted to the right hand of God and that, having received the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this visible and audible manifestation, concluding with the proclamation of his glorious Lordship (Acts 2:36). The discourse emphasizes the responsibility of the Jewish people in rejecting their King and grounds their faith in the Messianic resurrection. Doctrinally, when the Savior's soul descended into Sheol or Hell during the three days following His death (Psalm 16:10, Ephesians 4:8-10, 1 Peter 3:18-19), He did not experience torment or corruption, but proclaimed His victory and led the Old Testament saints to heavenly Paradise (Luke 23:43, 2 Corinthians 12:4), cementing His exaltation to the right hand of the Father until the final subjugation of His enemies (Psalm 110:1, Hebrews 1:13).
[37-41] Upon hearing these words, the listeners were cut to the heart and inquired of Peter and the other apostles what course of action they should take in light of His guilt (Acts 2:37). The apostle responds with the formal instruction of the passage {{quote:Acts 2:38|Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of your sins; and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit}}. Peter adds that the promise is for them, for their children, and for all who are far off, as many as the Lord our God will call, resulting in approximately three thousand souls willingly receiving his word and being baptized (Acts 2:39-41). Doctrinally, the ordinance of Acts 2:38 belongs to a historical context of transition administered to the house of Israel (Acts 2:22, 36). At that time, water baptism functioned as a public manifestation of national repentance and identification with the crucified Messiah for the reception of the gift of the Holy Spirit, continuing the tradition of John's baptism (Luke 3:3, Acts 19:4). However, this verse does not constitute the standard of salvation for the Church Age under the gospel of God's grace, where justification and the seal of the Holy Spirit are obtained through faith in the blood of Christ without the prerequisite or causal condition of water baptism (Acts 10:43-48, Acts 16:30-31, Romans 3:24-25, Ephesians 2:8-9, 1 Corinthians 1:17). Attempting to impose Acts 2:38 as the universal formula for salvation leads to the error of baptismal regeneration (Galatians 1:8-9, Titus 3:5).
[42-47] The first community of believers devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer (Acts 2:42). Awe came over everyone as many wonders and signs were performed through the apostles (Acts 2:43). The believers remained united and shared everything in common, selling their possessions and goods to distribute the proceeds to all, according to each one's need (Acts 2:44-45). Continuing with one accord in the temple every day and breaking bread from house to house, they partook of food with gladness and simplicity of heart, praising God and enjoying the favor of the people, while the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved (Acts 2:47). This picture describes the initial constitution of the local church in Jerusalem. Signs and wonders were performed exclusively by apostolic hands as Messianic credentials directed to Israel (2 Corinthians 12:12, Hebrews 2:3-4). The practice of selling possessions to share resources was a temporary and local measure adopted in Judea in anticipation of persecutions and imminent judgments upon the city, not representing an ecclesiastical mandate or a normative model of communism for the Gentile churches of the apostolic era (Romans 15:25-26, 1 Corinthians 16:1-2, 2 Thessalonians 3:10-12).

[1-3] Peter and John go up together to the temple at the ninth hour, the time designated for evening prayer in Jewish piety (Psalms 5:7, Daniel 6:10). In front of the temple gate called Beautiful—an entrance overlaid with Corinthian bronze—lay a man crippled from birth, placed there to beg alms from those entering the sacred precinct (Acts 3:2). Typologically, the condition of this man, disabled from birth and over forty years old (Acts 4:22), portrays the misery and powerlessness of fallen humanity under the condemnation of sin, deprived of the strength to fulfill the law or enter God's presence on its own (Romans 5:6, Ephesians 2:1-3). Upon seeing the apostles about to enter, the crippled man begs them for alms, expecting fleeting material assistance without realizing that the Messianic provision was about to manifest a higher restoration {{quote:Acts 3:3|Which, seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, begged them for alms}}.
[4-10] Peter, fixing his eyes on the needy man along with John, commands him to look toward them, generating an expectation of earthly gain in the beggar (Acts 3:4-5). The apostle then pronounces the Messianic declaration of faith {{quote:Acts 3:6|I have neither silver nor gold, but what I do have I give you: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk}}, and taking him by the right hand, he raises him up instantly. The healing performed was not a gradual process or an emotional suggestion, but an immediate bodily restoration where his feet and ankles regained strength, allowing him not only to stand and walk, but to leap for joy and enter the temple praising God (Isaiah 35:6). This miracle constitutes one of the Messianic apostolic signs granted to the twelve to confirm the testimony of the resurrection before the house of Israel (1 Corinthians 1:22, 2 Corinthians 12:12, Hebrews 2:3-4). The crowd recognizes the former beggar from the Beautiful Gate and is filled with awe and wonder at the manifestation of divine power over a clinically incurable man (Acts 3:9-10).
[11-16] While the healed man clung to Peter and John, the astonished crowd pressed toward them in Solomon’s Portico, located in the eastern outer court of the temple (1 Kings 6:3, Acts 5:12). Peter seized the opportunity presented by the commotion to deliver an expository speech to the crowd, addressing his listeners as Israelite men and categorically rejecting any attribution of personal merit or piety in the performance of the miracle (Acts 3:12). The apostle attributes glory to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, affirming that He has glorified His Son Jesus, whom the nation handed over and denied in the presence of Pontius Pilate when the Roman governor had resolved to release Him (Luke 23:16, John 19:12). Peter confronts the guilt of the people by pointing out that they rejected the Holy and Righteous One to ask for a murderer, killing the Author of life (Acts 3:15). The apostle testifies to the bodily resurrection of the Messiah and proclaims that it was faith in his name that restored this man's complete health in their presence (Acts 4:10, Romans 1:4).
[17, 18] The apostolic discourse addresses the moral responsibility of the Israelites and their rulers, acknowledging that they carried out the crucifixion of the Messiah out of spiritual ignorance {{quote:Acts 3:17|But now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your rulers}} (Luke 23:34, 1 Corinthians 2:8). This ignorance did not absolve the people of guilt, but it opened the door to divine mercy in response to Christ's intercession on the cross. In this way, God sovereignly fulfilled the Old Testament prophecies that foretold Christ's suffering for the atonement of sins (Psalm 22:1-18, Isaiah 53:5-10, 1 Peter 1:11). The Savior's suffering did not represent a circumstantial defeat before the Sanhedrin or Roman power, but rather the fulfillment of God's predetermined plan and providence to offer salvation to His chosen people (Acts 2:23, Acts 13:27-29).
[19-21] Peter exhorts the nation to genuine repentance and conversion in view of the Messianic restoration {{quote:Acts 3:19|Repent therefore, and turn to God, that your sins may be blotted out, when times of refreshing come from the presence of the Lord}}. From a dispensational perspective, the final erasure of Israel's national sins is temporarily contingent upon Christ's return at His Second Coming, as prophesied in the Old Testament (Isaiah 43:25, Isaiah 44:22, Jeremiah 50:20, Romans 11:26-27). The passage announces that God will send Jesus Christ, whom heaven must receive until the time of the restoration of all things (Acts 1:11, Hebrews 9:28). This restoration encompasses the theocratic, physical, and environmental renewal of the earth during the millennial kingdom (Isaiah 11:6-9, Isaiah 35:1-10, Matthew 19:28, Romans 8:19-22), an event proclaimed by all the holy prophets since ancient times and distinguished from the Church Age (Acts 15:14-17, Revelation 20:4-6).
[22-26] To establish the Messiah's authority, Peter quotes the passage in Deuteronomy where Moses prophesied the coming of a Messianic Prophet from among the brothers of Israel {{quote:Acts 3:22|The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers; you shall listen to him in all that he tells you}} (Deuteronomy 18:15-18). The apostle solemnly warns that any soul who refuses to listen to this Prophet will be cut off from the people, a sentence of final judgment according to the Mosaic order (Leviticus 23:29, Deuteronomy 18:19). All the prophets from Samuel onward announced these Messianic days (1 Samuel 3:20), the Jewish hearers being the heirs of the prophets and of the covenant made with Abraham concerning the blessing of all the families of the earth (Genesis 12:3, Galatians 3:8). For this reason, God, having raised his Son Jesus, sent him first to Israel to bless the people by turning each one away from their iniquities, granting them priority in the offer of Messianic grace before the dispersion and the calling of the Gentile nations (Acts 13:46, Romans 1:16, Romans 2:10).

[1-4] Peter and John's speech to the people in the temple precincts is abruptly interrupted by the priests, the captain of the temple guard, and the Sadducees (Acts 4:1). The determining cause of the apostles' arrest lies in the hierarchy's indignation at the doctrinal proclamation of the Messianic resurrection {{quote:Acts 4:2|Resentful because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead}}. The sect of the Sadducees constituted the dominant theological group in the Sanhedrin and categorically rejected the bodily resurrection, the existence of angels, and the spiritual world (Acts 23:8), so the apostolic teaching threatened the structure of their religious system. Although the authorities imprisoned the apostles until the next day, the proclaimed word could not be chained (2 Timothy 2:9), and the number of male believers grew to approximately five thousand (Acts 4:4). Within the dispensational framework, this extraordinary growth occurred through the direct preaching of Messianic truth, without any of the new converts speaking in tongues or any immediate baptismal rites being administered at that time (1 Corinthians 1:17, 1 Corinthians 15:1-4).
[5-12] The next day, the Sanhedrin was established in Jerusalem, composed of the rulers, elders, scribes, and the high priestly leadership represented by Annas, Caiaphas, John, and Alexander (Acts 4:5-6). The authorities brought the apostles to trial, demanding to know the power or name by which they had healed the cripple. Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit according to God's promise of assistance before the judges (Matthew 10:19-20, Luke 21:14-15), boldly declared that the man's restoration was accomplished in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom the nation crucified but whom God raised from the dead (Acts 2:24, Acts 3:15). The apostle quoted Psalm 118 to identify the Savior as the stone rejected by the builders, which has become the cornerstone (Psalm 118:22, Matthew 21:42). Doctrinally, the Stone operates in both advents: in the first advent it acts as a stumbling block where the unbeliever stumbles and is broken, while in the Second Coming it will descend as the Stone of Daniel 2 to crush the pagan kingdoms of the earth (Daniel 2:34-35, Matthew 21:44, 1 Peter 2:7-8). Peter concludes by proclaiming the absolute exclusivity of Messianic redemption {{quote: Acts 4:12|And there is salvation in no one else; because there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved, thus rejecting all human priesthood or religious syncretism (John 14:6, 1 Timothy 2:5).
[13-22] The council authorities observe with astonishment the boldness of Peter and John, perceiving that they were uneducated and common men, that is, people without formal rabbinic instruction or credentials from the theological schools of the time (John 7:15). This transformation demonstrates that communion with Jesus Christ and the fullness of the Holy Spirit impart a spiritual authority superior to any academic qualification from human institutions (1 Corinthians 1:26-29). Upon seeing the healed man standing beside them—who was over forty years old (Acts 4:22)—the judges are unable to refute the fact. After ordering the apostles to leave the building, the members of the Sanhedrin deliberated, acknowledging that the miracle was common knowledge among all the inhabitants of Jerusalem. However, instead of submitting to the truth, they resolved to threaten them to prevent the spread of the Messianic name. Peter and John responded by establishing the unalterable principle of the subordination of human authority to God's commands (Acts 4:19), affirming the impossibility of silencing the evidence of the resurrection (Acts 5:29, 1 Corinthians 9:16). The Sanhedrin released them after reiterating their threats, held back by fear of the people's reaction, who were glorifying God for the miracle.
[23-31] Once freed, Peter and John returned to the congregation of believers and recounted the threats made by the chief priests and elders. The assembly responded by offering a sovereign prayer to the Lord who made the heavens, the earth, the sea, and everything in them (Genesis 1:1, Nehemiah 9:6). The faithful turned to Psalm 2 to interpret the opposition of the Jewish hierarchy and the Roman authorities as the prophetic fulfillment of the conspiracy of kings and rulers against the Lord and his Anointed One (Psalm 2:1-2, Luke 23:12). The biblical text highlights the deity and sonship of the Savior (Acts 4:27), vindicating the Son's dignity against textual alterations that seek to degrade his status to that of a mere servant. The church recognizes that the persecution only carried out what God's hand and plan had predetermined for the atonement of sins (Acts 2:23, Acts 13:27-29). Instead of asking to be spared the trials, the disciples implore boldness to proclaim the word and the manifestation of signs by the divine hand (Acts 5:12, 2 Corinthians 12:12). At the conclusion of the prayer, the place shook, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit (Acts 4:31), and they spoke the word of God boldly. Doctrinally, this event teaches that while the baptism of the Holy Spirit is an initial and unrepeatable experience that incorporates the believer into the body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:13, Ephesians 4:5), the filling of the Holy Spirit for courageous service must be constantly renewed throughout the Christian life (Ephesians 5:18).
[32-37] The community of believers manifested a profound spiritual unity, characterized by the selfless and voluntary stewardship of their material possessions (Acts 2:44). The apostles bore witness to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus with great power, and abundant grace rested upon the entire congregation. The distribution of resources ensured that no one among them was in need, for those who owned land or houses sold them voluntarily and placed the proceeds at the apostles' feet for distribution according to individual needs (Acts 2:45, Acts 6:1). In theological and dispensational hermeneutics, this practice did not constitute a social system of mandatory communism nor the abolition of private property, since the giving of goods was strictly voluntary and administered within the local church (Acts 5:4). The believers of the early church in Judea adopted this act of self-denial in the face of imminent persecution and the expectation of the Messianic return, representing a testimony of charity that was not established as a universal legislative mandate for the Gentile churches in the Pauline epistles (Romans 15:25-26, 1 Corinthians 16:1-2, 2 Thessalonians 3:10-12). The chapter concludes by highlighting the example of Joseph, whom the apostles named Barnabas—meaning son of encouragement—a Levite from Cyprus {{quote:Acts 4:37|Having a piece of property, he sold it, brought the money, and laid it at the apostles' feet}}, foreshadowing the ministry of encouragement and apostolic accompaniment that he would later perform in building up the church (Acts 9:27, Acts 11:22-26, Acts 13:2-3).

[1-11] Ananias and his wife Sapphira sell a property and commit the crime of embezzling part of the price through a secret agreement, presenting a fraction of the amount to the apostles as if it represented the entire sale (Acts 4:37, Acts 5:1-2). The apostle Peter confronts Ananias, revealing the satanic temptation in his heart to lie to the Holy Spirit (John 13:2, 1 Timothy 6:10). Doctrinally, the apostolic declaration in verse four—where Peter affirms the nature of the deception {{quote: Acts 5:4|you have not lied to men but to God}}—constitutes a categorical testimony to the absolute deity and personality of the Holy Spirit (Psalm 139:7, 1 Corinthians 3:16). The severity of divine retribution brings about the immediate physical death of Ananias and, three hours later, that of Sapphira for relapsing into falsehood {{quote:Acts 5:9|Why have you conspired together to test the Spirit of the Lord?}}. This summary judgment does not represent the eternal damnation of souls, but the execution of the extreme discipline upon the believer known as the sin unto death or the surrender of the flesh to destruction for the preservation of purity in the assembly (1 Corinthians 5:5, 1 Corinthians 11:30, 1 John 5:16). The event instilled profound fear in the entire congregation, and this passage contains the first formal mention of the term "church" in the book of Acts to designate the body of the redeemed (Acts 2:47, Ephesians 1:22-23).
[12-16] Through the apostles, numerous signs and wonders were performed among the people, and the community gathered together in Solomon's Portico (Acts 3:11, Acts 4:32). The reverent fear instilled by the judgment on hypocrisy prevented insincere sympathizers from joining the assembly, while the multitude of true believers in the Lord continued to grow (Acts 2:47, Acts 6:7). The inhabitants carried the sick into the streets, placing them on beds and stretchers, hoping that Peter's shadow would fall upon the suffering as he passed by {{quote:Acts 5:15|at least Peter's shadow would pass by and shelter some of them}}. Doctrinally, the mass healings and deliverance from unclean spirits in the cities surrounding Jerusalem constituted the Messianic credentials granted to the apostolic college to convince the unbelief of the nation of Israel (1 Corinthians 1:22, 2 Corinthians 12:12, Hebrews 2:3-4). The projection of the shadow did not possess inherent magical power, but rather operated as a visible instrument of the manifestation of divine power in the apostolic transitional economy (Acts 19:11-12).
[17-26] The high priestly hierarchy and the sect of the Sadducees, driven by envy at the popular support for the apostolic message, arrested the twelve apostles and imprisoned them in the public jail (Acts 4:1-3, Acts 17:5). However, during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and led them outside, instructing them to proclaim the message of salvation in the temple {{quote:Acts 5:20|Go, and standing in the temple, speak to the people all the words of this life}}. Obeying the divine command, the apostles entered the sacred precinct early in the morning and resumed teaching (Psalm 119:46, Acts 4:20). Meanwhile, the Sanhedrin and the council of elders met and sent guards to the prison, discovering that the building remained securely locked and the sentries at their posts, but finding no prisoners inside (Psalm 2:2-4). Upon receiving the report that the apostles were teaching publicly in the temple, the captain of the guard brought them before the court without violence, fearing the reaction of the crowd (Acts 4:21, Acts 5:26).
[27-33] The high priest questioned the accused, rebuking them for having broken the formal prohibition against teaching in the name of Jesus and for attempting to blame the council for the Savior's death (Acts 4:18, Matthew 27:25). Peter and the apostles responded by proclaiming the fundamental axiom of Christian conscience in the face of earthly authorities: {{quote:Acts 5:29|We must obey God rather than men}}. The apostolic declaration affirms the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, whom God has exalted to his right hand as Prince and Savior in order to grant Israel repentance and forgiveness of sins (Acts 2:33, Acts 3:15, Philippians 2:9-11). The apostles assert themselves as direct witnesses to these facts in conjunction with the Holy Spirit, given by God to those who obey him (John 15:26-27, Acts 2:38). The confrontation with divine truth enrages the council, which deliberates privately to decree the execution of the preachers (Acts 7:54, Acts 22:22).
[34-42] Gamaliel, an eminent doctor of the law from the sect of the Pharisees and Paul's teacher (Acts 22:3), intervenes in the council, ordering the temporary removal of the accused. The rabbi exhorts prudence, citing the precedents of Theudas and Judas the Galilean, whose insurrections were quelled after the death of their leaders (Acts 5:36-37). Gamaliel advises against persecution, arguing the futility of fighting a work if it comes from God (Acts 5:39). Doctrinally, although Gamaliel's recommendation demonstrates political wisdom, his argument does not constitute an absolute theological rule, since various movements of falsehood thrive in the present age under the dominion of the adversary (2 Corinthians 4:4, 2 Timothy 3:13). The council accepts the ruling, but subjects the apostles to flogging before reiterating the prohibition against speaking in the name of Jesus (Matthew 10:17, Luke 20:11). The apostles withdrew from the presence of the Sanhedrin rejoicing at having been judged worthy to suffer shame for the sake of the Name (Matthew 5:11-12, 1 Peter 4:13-16), and continued teaching and preaching Jesus Christ daily in the temple and from house to house (Acts 2:46, Acts 20:20).

[1-4] The growth of the local church triggers murmuring from the Greeks against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. The reading of the received text preserves the distinction of the Greeks against the critical alterations that sought to reduce them to Hellenistic Jews. Faced with this administrative conflict, the twelve apostles summon the multitude to establish the service of seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, to serve at the tables. The word deacon designates one who runs through the dust to serve at the table, establishing the biblical pattern for this role. This delegation of material tasks allows the ministers to dedicate themselves continuously to the two essential priorities of New Testament ministry: prayer and the ministry of the Word.
[5-8] The proposal satisfies the congregational crowd, which chooses Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, along with Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas, a proselyte from Antioch. The selection made by the entire assembly sets the precedent for congregational authority in the local church in choosing its own ministers, who are then presented to the apostles for the laying on of hands. The required qualifications do not correspond to worldly financial or political criteria, but rather to spiritual maturity and godly testimony. As a result of this order in the church, the Word of the Lord multiplies greatly in Jerusalem, producing the conversion of a large company of Jewish priests who obey the faith, while Stephen performs great wonders and signs among the people.
[9-15] Opposition arises from the synagogue of the Libertines, the Cyrenians, the Alexandrians, and those from Cilicia and Asia, who dispute with Stephen. In this passage, Antioch and Alexandria are mentioned for the first time in Scripture: Antioch linked to Spirit-filled and qualified deacons, and Alexandria associated with a center of opposition and resistance to divine truth. Unable to withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which Stephen spoke (Acts 6:10), his adversaries bribe false witnesses to accuse him of uttering blasphemous words against Moses, God, the temple, and the law. As he was brought before the council, all those seated in the Sanhedrin fixed their eyes on him and beheld his face as the face of an angel, reflecting the dazzling presence of the Lord before his accusers (Exodus 34:30).

[1-16] Before the high priest's questioning, Stephen begins his defense by tracing the patriarchal history from Abraham in Mesopotamia before his time in Charran (Genesis 12:1). God granted him the covenant of circumcision, and the line of Isaac, Jacob, and the twelve patriarchs followed (Genesis 17:10, Genesis 21:4). Driven by envy, the patriarchs sold Joseph into Egypt, a man who constitutes the most complete type of the Lord Jesus in the Old Testament, having been sold for silver and preserved by God for the salvation of his family (Genesis 37:28, Genesis 45:5). The figure of seventy-five souls summoned by Joseph does not come from a spurious copy of the Septuagint, but from an inclusive count of all of Jacob's relatives (Genesis 46:27). Likewise, Abraham's acquisition of the burial place in Shechem from the sons of Hamor corresponds to a separate historical real estate transaction from the purchase of the cave of Machpelah in Hebron (Genesis 23:16, Genesis 33:19, Joshua 24:32), demonstrating the absolute accuracy of the biblical record.
[17-36] As the time of the promise drew near, the people multiplied in Egypt until a king arose who did not know Joseph (Exodus 1:8). During this period, Moses was born, raised by Pharaoh's daughter, and instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, becoming powerful in word and deed (Exodus 2:2). At the age of forty, Moses decided to visit his brothers and assumed they would understand that God would deliver them by his hand, but they did not understand (Exodus 2:11-14). After fleeing to the land of Midian for another forty years, the Angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the burning bush on Mount Sinai (Exodus 3:2). The manifestation of the Angel of the Covenant as a divine theophany commissioned Moses as ruler and redeemer of Israel, whom the nation had previously rejected.
[37-43] Moses prophesied to the children of Israel about the coming of the Messiah, declaring that the Lord would raise up a prophet like himself from among their brethren (Deuteronomy 18:15). This same Moses was in the church in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:3). However, the ancestors refused to obey, turned their hearts toward Egypt, and fashioned a golden calf to offer sacrifices to the work of their hands (Exodus 32:4). In response to this apostasy, God withdrew and gave them over to worshiping the host of heaven, carrying the tabernacle of Moloch and the star of the god Remphan, pagan figures for which the Lord transported them beyond Babylon in fulfillment of prophetic warnings (Amos 5:25-27).
[44-50] The patriarchs possessed the tabernacle of the testimony in the wilderness, erected according to the heavenly pattern revealed to Moses (Exodus 25:40), which they brought into the inheritance of the Gentiles under Joshua. Although Solomon built a house for God (1 Kings 6:1), divine revelation establishes that the Most High does not dwell in temples made by human hands, as the prophet proclaimed: {{quote:Acts 7:49|Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool}} (Isaiah 66:1-2). The earthly temple cannot contain the unlimited presence of the Lord, pointing to the primacy of spiritual truth over the physical structure of the sanctuary in Jerusalem.
[51-53] Stephen concludes his speech by directly confronting the Sanhedrin, accusing them of being stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears. The religious hierarchy continually resisted the Holy Spirit in the same way their ancestors had (Isaiah 63:10). The forefathers of the Jewish leaders persecuted and killed the prophets who announced the coming of the Righteous One, whom the Sanhedrin betrayed and murdered (Matthew 23:34-35). Having received the law through the guidance of angels (Galatians 3:19), the religious leaders demonstrated their ungodliness by not keeping it.
[54-60] Upon hearing these words, the members of the council were cut to their hearts and gnashed their teeth at him. Stephen, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and beheld the glory of God, exclaiming: {{quote: Acts 7:56|Look! I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God}}. The Lord Jesus' position standing at the right hand of God indicates that He was upright and ready to return to earth at His Second Coming if the nation of Israel had repented nationally (Psalm 110:1); with Stephen's testimony being rejected, the offer of the kingdom was postponed, and the church age began. The judges turned a deaf ear, turned on Stephen, and dragged him out of the city to stone him. The witnesses laid their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul (Acts 22:20). As they stoned him, Stephen called upon the Lord, asking to receive his spirit, and cried out with a loud voice, pleading that this sin not be imputed to them, after which he fell asleep in the Lord.

[1-4] Saul consents to Stephen's death and unleashes a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem. All are scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except for the apostles. Devout men carry Stephen to his burial, wailing bitterly over him. Saul ravages the church, entering houses and dragging off men and women to imprisonment, punishing them violently (Acts 22:19, Acts 26:11). However, the scattering of the believers spurs the spread of the Gospel in fulfillment of the divine command to take the testimony out of Jerusalem into Judea and Samaria (Acts 1:8), with the dispersed going everywhere proclaiming the Word.
[5-13] Philip, one of the seven deacons previously chosen (Acts 6:5, Acts 21:8), goes down to the city of Samaria and preaches Christ to them. Accompanied by apostolic signs, unclean spirits came out crying out with loud voices, and many paralytics and lame people were healed, bringing great joy to that city. In the same city, Simon the magician practiced sorcery and astonished the people by claiming to be some great person and the great power of God. Believing Philip's message about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus, the Samaritans and Simon himself were baptized in water. However, the Samaritans' experience demonstrates a dispensational transition where the miracles and healings performed by Philip in Samaria subsequently ceased in Jerusalem after the national rejection recorded at the trial of Stephen.
[14-25] When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the Word of God, they sent Peter and John. Upon arriving, they prayed for the Samaritans to receive the Holy Spirit, since it had not yet descended upon any of them; they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Because of the Samaritans' historical, ethnic, and idolatrous background (2 Kings 17:24-41, John 4:9), the apostolic authority and ratification from Jerusalem through the laying on of hands was required to bestow the Holy Spirit and preserve the unity of the church. Seeing that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of hands by the apostles, Simon offered them money to acquire this power, thus giving rise to the concept of simony. Peter rebukes him severely, declaring that his money should perish with him for thinking that the gift of God could be obtained with money (Acts 8:20), pointing out that his heart was not right before God and urging him to repentance.
[26-40] An angel of the Lord commands Philip to go at midday to the deserted road from Jerusalem to Gaza. There he finds an Ethiopian man, a eunuch of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who managed her treasury and had gone to Jerusalem to worship (Isaiah 56:3-7). As he returns in his chariot reading the messianic passage of the prophet Isaiah about the lamb led to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7-8), the Spirit prompts Philip to approach him. Philip asks him if he understands what he is reading and, starting from that same Scripture, proclaims to him the Gospel of Jesus and the atonement by His blood. Upon the eunuch's declaration of faith, confessing that Jesus Christ is the Son of God (Acts 8:37), Philip baptizes him by immersion in water. This eunuch is the first Gentile converted and saved by grace through faith in the blood of the Lord in the book of Acts. After coming up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord takes Philip away, and the eunuch goes on his way rejoicing, while Philip is found in Azotus preaching the Gospel throughout the cities until he reaches Caesarea.

[1-9] On his way to Damascus, Saul breathes threats and demands against the Lord's disciples, obtaining letters from the high priest to extradite the believers to Jerusalem (Acts 9:1-2). Near the city, a heavenly light brighter than the sun (Acts 26:13) suddenly surrounds him, causing him to fall to the ground as he hears the voice of the Lord Jesus questioning him about his persecution of Him (Acts 9:4). By persecuting the members of the church, Saul was directly attacking the Body of Christ itself (1 Corinthians 12:26). Astonished and trembling, Saul responds by acknowledging the Lord's deity by asking what He wants him to do, while the men accompanying him hear a sound but do not understand the words or see anyone (John 12:28-29, Acts 22:9). Saul wakes up blind and spends three days fasting and in darkness, a period that constitutes a prophetic type of the three thousand years of spiritual blindness of the nation of Israel until the coming of the Messiah, as well as the figure of a Jew converted out of time (1 Corinthians 15:8, Isaiah 60:1-3).
[10-19] In Damascus, the Lord speaks in a vision to Ananias, a Jewish proselyte of good reputation (Acts 22:12), instructing him to go to the street called Straight, to the house of Judas, to look for Saul of Tarsus, who is praying. Despite Ananias's initial objections about the harm Saul caused to the saints in Jerusalem, the Lord declares that Saul is a chosen vessel to carry His name before the Gentiles, kings, and the children of Israel (Acts 9:15), announcing to him the sufferings he will endure for His sake. Ananias comes and lays his hands on him, calling him "Brother Saul," demonstrating that Saul's new birth occurred three days earlier when he saw the resurrected Christ on the road (1 Corinthians 15:8), and not through water baptism. At that moment, something like scales fall from his eyes, he regains his sight, is filled with the Holy Spirit, and is baptized in water.
[20-31] Immediately, Saul preaches Christ in the synagogues, declaring that He is the Son of God. After a period in Arabia and three years of preparation in Damascus (Galatians 1:17-18, 1 Kings 19:8), Saul grows stronger and confounds the Jews by demonstrating that Jesus is the Messiah. Faced with a Jewish conspiracy to kill him and the constant surveillance of the gates, the disciples lower him at night through an opening in the wall in a basket (2 Corinthians 11:33). Upon arriving in Jerusalem, the believers feared him until Barnabas presented him to the apostles, testifying to his conversion and bold preaching. Saul spoke openly in Jerusalem and argued against the Greeks, who sought to kill him. Therefore, the brothers took him to Caesarea and sent him to Tarsus. As a result, the churches throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria experienced peace, were strengthened, and multiplied, walking in the fear of the Lord.
[32-43] During his travels, Peter visited the saints in Lydda, where he found Aeneas, paralyzed for eight years, and healed him in the name of Jesus Christ, leading the inhabitants of Lydda and Sharon to convert to the Lord. In Joppa, a disciple named Tabitha (which, when translated, means Dorcas, meaning gazelle), who was abundant in good works and almsgiving, became ill and died. The disciples sent two men to summon Peter, who, upon arriving in the upper room, was surrounded by widows who showed him the tunics made by Dorcas. Peter sent them all out, knelt down, prayed, and, uttering the command "Tabitha, arise," presented the woman alive after she had been raised from the dead. This miracle foreshadowed the future national restoration of Israel, leading to the conversion of many in Joppa, where Peter stayed for several days at the house of Simon the tanner.

[1-8] In Caesarea, Cornelius, a centurion of the Italian Company, is presented as a devout and God-fearing man, living in abundance at his home, giving alms, and praying continually. Despite his devout and irreproachable character in the eyes of society, Cornelius represents the condition of an unsaved man who requires the proclamation of the gospel to obtain eternal salvation (Romans 2:6-7, Acts 11:14). The mention of chapter ten highlights the biblical significance of the number ten in association with the dispensation and the call to the Gentiles (Genesis 10:10, Romans 10:1). At the ninth hour of the day, an angel of God appears to him in a vision, declaring that his prayers and alms have ascended as a memorial offering before God, and instructing him to send men to Joppa to bring back Simon, who is also called Peter. Immediately obeying the heavenly command, Cornelius sends two of his servants and a devout soldier to locate the apostle. The next day, as the messengers approach the city, Peter goes up to the rooftop to pray at the sixth hour. Experiencing intense hunger, he falls into a trance and beholds heaven opened and a large sheet woven at its four corners descending to earth, containing all kinds of four-footed animals, wild beasts, reptiles, and birds of the air. A voice commands him to rise, kill, and eat, to which Peter firmly refuses, stating that he has never eaten anything common or unclean, in observance of the Mosaic dietary laws (Leviticus 11:2-8) that had already been nailed to the cross (Colossians 2:14). The heavenly voice replies a second time, declaring that what God has cleansed should not be called common, and the scene repeats itself three times before the sheet is taken up into heaven. The three repetitions and the inclusion of unclean animals typologically represent the union of Jews and Gentiles in one spiritual body (Ephesians 3:1-6). While Peter doubts the meaning of the vision, the Holy Spirit commands him to go down and accompany the three men sent by Cornelius without hesitation.
[24-33] Peter sets out on the journey accompanied by six Jewish brothers from Joppa (Acts 11:12), bringing the total number of members in the group to Caesarea. Upon entering the centurion's house, Cornelius comes out to meet him and prostrates himself at his feet to worship him; however, Peter immediately raises him up, declaring himself a mortal man and rejecting any idolatrous veneration or claim to hierarchical supremacy. Before the assembled crowd of Gentiles, Peter declares that, although it is an abomination for a Jewish man to associate with or go into contact with a Gentile (John 4:9), God has shown him not to call any common or unclean man. Cornelius recounts the angel's appearance four days earlier during his fasting and prayer, expressing the readiness of all present to hear the Lord's commandments.
[34-43] Opening his mouth, Peter proclaims divine truth by declaring: {{quote:Acts 10:34|I now realize how true it is that God shows no partiality}}, teaching that divine grace does not consider racial distinctions or national privileges, but that in every nation he who fears Him and does what is right is acceptable (Romans 2:11). The apostle summarizes the earthly ministry of the Lord Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power, and how He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil. After witnessing His crucifixion on the cross and His resurrection on the third day, manifested not to all the people but to the witnesses chosen by God, Peter concludes his message by stating: {{quote:Acts 10:43|To him all the prophets bear witness, that whoever believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name}}.
[44-48] While Peter is still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit miraculously descends upon all who hear the message, effecting salvation and spiritual regeneration before water baptism or any sacramental rite. The circumcised believers who had accompanied Peter are astonished to see the gift of the Holy Spirit poured out also upon the Gentiles, hearing them speak in tongues and magnify God as a miraculous sign granted to the Jews (1 Corinthians 1:22, 1 Corinthians 14:22). Reaffirming the divine testimony, Peter asks if anyone can withhold water from those who have received the Holy Spirit, just as the apostles did (Acts 2:38), ordering them to be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.

[1-18] Upon Peter's return to Jerusalem, the circumcised believers confronted him, reproaching him for having entered the house of uncircumcised men and eaten with them (Acts 11:2-3, Galatians 2:11-14). In response, Peter systematically recounts the events that took place in Joppa, relating the ecstasy in which he beheld the sheet descending from heaven with four-footed animals, wild beasts, reptiles, and birds, the heavenly voice that commanded him to kill and eat them, and the divine declaration not to call common what God has cleansed. He also narrates the arrival of the three men sent from Caesarea, the instruction of the Holy Spirit to accompany them without hesitation, and the presence of six Jewish brothers (Acts 11:12), bringing the total number of members in the group to ten. Upon entering Cornelius's house, Peter recounted how an angel had instructed him to send for Simon to Joppa to hear words by which he and his entire household would be saved (Acts 11:14). As Peter began to speak, the Holy Spirit descended upon the Gentiles in the same way it had descended upon the apostles at Pentecost (Acts 2:4). This event recalled the Lord's words concerning spiritual baptism (Acts 11:16). Recognizing that God bestowed the same gift upon the Gentiles through faith in the Lord Jesus, Peter could not oppose this divine work. Upon hearing this, the circumcised believers were appeased and glorified God, exclaiming, “So even to the Gentiles God has granted repentance leading to life,” acknowledging the granting of dispensational privileges to the nations (Romans 11:11).
[19-26] The persecution unleashed in the wake of Stephen’s martyrdom led to the scattering of the believers, who traveled to Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, proclaiming the Word only to the Jews (Acts 11:19). However, some men from Cyprus and Cyrene, upon arriving in Antioch, spoke to the Greeks, preaching the Lord Jesus, resulting in a great number of people believing and being converted to the Lord by divine intervention (Acts 11:20-21). When this news reached the church in Jerusalem, they sent Barnabas to Antioch. Upon witnessing God's grace, he rejoiced and urged everyone to remain faithful to the Lord with all their hearts (Acts 11:22-23). ​​Barnabas, described as a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, went to Tarsus to find Saul and brought him to Antioch, where they met for a whole year, teaching a large crowd (Acts 11:25-26). In this city, the historic center for the preservation of the pure biblical text against Alexandrian corruption, the disciples are first called Christians (1 Peter 4:16).
[27-30] In those days, prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch, among whom one named Agabus foretold through the Spirit that a great famine would come upon the whole inhabited world, which occurred during the reign of Claudius Caesar (Acts 11:27-28, Acts 21:10-11). This famine was the eleventh mentioned in the record of Scripture (Genesis 12:10, Ruth 1:1, Revelation 6:6). In response to the prophetic warning, the disciples in Antioch resolved to send aid to the brothers and sisters living in Judea, each contributing according to their means, following the New Testament principle of giving (1 Corinthians 16:2, 2 Corinthians 9:7). This material aid was sent to the elders in Jerusalem by Barnabas and Saul (Acts 11:30, Romans 15:25-27).

[1-5] Herod Agrippa I extends his hand to afflict certain members of the church and executes James, the brother of John, with the sword, a landmark event marking the last appearance of this apostle without a successor being appointed to his office, as occurred with Judas (Acts 1:26). Perceiving that the execution pleases the Jewish hierarchy, he arrests Peter during the days of Unleavened Bread with the intention of presenting him to the people after Passover. The mention of the term "Passover" at this time corresponds to the Roman festival of Ishtar or Ostara observed by the Roman ruler Herod, distinct from the sacred reckoning of the Jewish Passover (Exodus 12:2-8). Peter remains in prison under the guard of four squads of soldiers, while the church perseveres in continuous prayer to God {{quote:Acts 12:5|So Peter was kept in prison, but the church was earnestly praying to God for him}}. In this intercession, the congregation does not invoke Mary or human intermediaries, but rather implores the apostle's faithfulness in the face of imminent martyrdom.
[6-11] On the night before his public trial, Peter sleeps peacefully between two soldiers, bound with two chains and guarded by sentinels at the gate, manifesting the peace of the Lord in the face of death (Psalm 127:2). Suddenly, an angel of the Lord appears surrounded by heavenly light, strikes Peter on the side to awaken him, and causes the chains to fall from his hands. Obeying the angel's commands to gird himself, put on his sandals, and wrap himself in his cloak, Peter follows him, unaware that the event is real and assuming he is seeing a vision. After passing the first and second guards, they arrive at the iron gate leading to the city, which opens by itself. Once outside, the angel disappears, and Peter regains consciousness, recognizing that the Lord sent His angel to deliver him from Herod's hand and the expectations of the Jewish people—an event that typologically illustrates the spiritual liberation and salvation of the sinner.
[12-17] Upon understanding his liberation, Peter goes to the house of Mary, the mother of John, also called Mark, where the church was gathered in prayer. When he knocks on the courtyard gate, a servant girl named Rhode comes to listen, and upon recognizing Peter's voice, she hesitates to open the door in her joy and runs to announce that the apostle is at the entrance. The believers call her mad (Acts 26:24) and, unable to conceive of his physical liberation, they assume it is his angel or spirit after his martyrdom. At the apostle's insistence on knocking, they open the door and are astonished to realize that their prayers for strength had been surpassed by divine intervention. Peter signals them to be quiet, recounts how the Lord brought him out of prison, sends word to James and the brothers, and departs for another place, refuting Roman traditions that claim his destination was Italy.
[18-25] At daybreak, a great commotion arises among the soldiers over Peter's disappearance, leading Herod to order the execution of the guards after questioning them. Later, Herod goes down to Caesarea and, being enraged against the inhabitants of Tyre and Sidon, they bribe Blastus, the king's chamberlain, to sue for peace, given their economic dependence on him. On an appointed day, Herod dressed in royal robes, sat on the tribunal, and delivered a public speech, to which the crowd acclaimed, proclaiming that his voice was that of a god and not a man. Immediately, the angel of the Lord struck him down for not giving glory to God (Acts 12:23). He perished, consumed by worms, in a judgment that foreshadowed the fall of the Antichrist (Revelation 13:5). Despite the fury of the persecution, the Word of the Lord grew and multiplied, while Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem after completing their ministry, bringing John Mark with them.

[1-3] In the church gathered in Antioch, a center for preserving the pure biblical text against the Alexandrian corruption, prophets and teachers ministered, including Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen, and Saul. While these men worshipped the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit directed the separation of Barnabas and Saul for the missionary work to which He had destined them (Acts 9:15). After persevering in prayer and fasting, the church laid hands on them and sent them forth, beginning the first missionary journey that shifted the focus of revelation from Jerusalem to the Gentile nations.
[4-12] Sent directly by the Holy Spirit, the missionaries went down to Seleucia and sailed to Cyprus, proclaiming the Word of God in the synagogues of Salamis alongside John Mark. Upon crossing the island to Paphos, they encountered a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus or Elymas, who was trying to turn the Roman proconsul Sergius Paulus away from the faith. Saul, also called Paul for the first time in the biblical record, filled with the Holy Spirit, fixed his eyes on the sorcerer and pronounced a judgment of temporary blindness upon him for resisting divine truth (Acts 9:8). Upon witnessing this apostolic miracle and the teaching of the Lord, the proconsul believed, demonstrating the power of the Gospel in the face of satanic opposition.
[13-15] Sailing from Paphos, Paul and his companions arrived at Perga in Pamphylia, where John Mark left the group and returned to Jerusalem. Continuing their journey, Paul and Barnabas arrived in Pisidian Antioch and entered the synagogue on the Sabbath. After the public reading of the Law and the Prophets, the synagogue leaders invited them to address the people with a word of exhortation, providing an opportunity for the proclamation of Messianic truth.
[16-41] Standing up, Paul addressed the Israelite men and the God-fearing Gentiles, tracing the history of Israel from the exodus from Egypt, the journey through the desert, the conquest of Canaan, and the establishment of the monarchy to David. From the line of David, God raised up Jesus as Savior according to the promise, whose coming was preceded by the baptism of repentance preached by John the Baptist (Matthew 3:1-3). Although the inhabitants of Jerusalem and their rulers ignored the voices of the prophets and condemned the Lord, demanding His crucifixion from Pilate, God raised Him from the dead on the third day so that He would not see corruption, fulfilling Psalm 2:7, the firm mercies of David (Isaiah 55:3) and Psalm 16:10. Through this sacrifice, the remission of sins and justification by faith are proclaimed (Acts 13:39: “And by him everyone who believes is justified from every sin, a justification you could not be obtained from under the law of Moses”), warning against rejecting God’s work (Habakkuk 1:5).
[42-52] As they left the synagogue, the Gentiles begged that these same words be preached to them the following Sabbath, while many devout Jews and proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas, who persuaded them to continue in God’s grace (Acts 11:23). On the following Sabbath, almost the entire city gathered to hear the Word of God; however, seeing the crowds, the Jews were filled with jealousy and contradicted Paul’s teachings with blasphemous insults. Paul and Barnabas boldly declared that it was necessary to speak the Word of God to the Gentiles first, but upon their rejection and judgment of themselves unworthy of eternal life, they turned to the Gentiles in fulfillment of the divine mandate (Isaiah 49:6, "I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth"). The Gentiles rejoiced and glorified the Word, all those ordained for eternal life believing, while the truth spread throughout the province. Faced with persecution instigated by the Jews, the apostles shook the dust from their feet (Matthew 10:14) and departed for Iconium, the disciples remaining filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.

[1-7] In Iconium, Paul and Barnabas enter the Jewish synagogue together, preaching so effectively that a large crowd of both Jews and Greeks believe. However, unbelieving Jews stir up the Gentiles and corrupt their minds against the brothers. The apostles remain there for a long time, speaking boldly in the Lord, who testifies to the word of His grace by granting signs and wonders through them, demonstrating that Barnabas possessed the apostolic signs (2 Corinthians 12:12) and is recognized as an apostle (Acts 14:14). The proclamation of the Gospel divides the city's crowd between those who are with the Jews and those who follow the apostles (Luke 12:51). Realizing that the Gentiles and the Jews, along with their rulers, were preparing an attack to harass and stone them, they fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding region, where they continued to preach the gospel.
[8-18] In Lystra, a man lame from birth, who had never walked, heard Paul speaking. Looking intently at him and perceiving that he had faith to be healed, Paul commanded him in a loud voice to stand upright on his feet, whereupon the man leaped up and walked. Seeing Paul's work, the crowd raised their voices in the Lycaonian language, declaring that the gods had come down in human form, calling Barnabas Zeus because of his appearance and Paul Hermes because he was the one who carried the message. The priest of Zeus, whose statue stood before the city, brought bulls and garlands to the gates to offer sacrifices. Upon hearing this, the apostles Barnabas and Paul tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, rejecting human deification (Acts 10:26), proclaiming that they were men of similar passions, subject to the same diseases (James 5:17), and urging them to turn from these vanities to the living God who made the heavens, the earth, the sea, and everything in them (Exodus 20:11). They barely managed to prevent the mob from offering them sacrifice.
[19, 20] Then unbelieving Jews arrived from Antioch and Iconium, who persuaded the crowd and instigated a lynching of Paul. After stoning him, they dragged him out of the city, leaving him for dead. However, surrounded by the disciples, Paul got up and went back into the same city where he had been stoned, leaving the next day with Barnabas for Derbe. Doctrinally and chronologically, this stoning in Lystra coincides with the experience in which Paul was caught up to the third heaven or Paradise (2 Corinthians 12:1-4), where he experienced physical death before being sent back to earth to continue his apostolic ministry.
[21-28] After preaching the Gospel in Derbe and teaching many, the apostles returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, strengthening the disciples and encouraging them to remain in the faith, teaching that {{quote:Acts 14:22|We must go through many hardships to enter the kingdom of God}} (1 Thessalonians 1:6). After appointing elders in each local church through prayer and fasting, they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed. Passing through Pisidia, they arrived in Pamphylia, and having preached the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia. From there they sailed to Antioch in Syria, the sending church from which they had been commended to the grace of God (Acts 13:1-3). When they gathered the congregation together, they reported all the things God had done with them and how he had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles, remaining there a long time with the disciples.

[1-5] Some men who came down from Judea to Antioch taught the brothers that circumcision according to the custom of Moses was essential for salvation. This claim raises the two fundamental false doctrines that plague the faith: requiring human works to obtain salvation and requiring ceremonial works to maintain salvation (Galatians 2:4, Galatians 5:1-4). Paul and Barnabas had a considerable discussion with them, agreeing to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders to address this issue. As they traveled through Phoenicia and Samaria, they reported the conversion of the Gentiles, causing great joy among the brothers. Upon arriving in Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church, the apostles, and the elders; However, some believers from the sect of the Pharisees arose, asserting the necessity of circumcising the converts and commanding them to keep the Law of Moses.
[6-12] The apostles and elders met to consider the matter. After intense discussion, Peter stood up and recalled how God had chosen him in Caesarea so that the Gentiles might hear the word of the Gospel and believe (Acts 10:44). God, knowing the hearts of men, bore witness to them by giving them the Holy Spirit in the same way as the apostles, without making any distinction between Jews and Gentiles, purifying their hearts by faith (Acts 10:47). Peter confronts the assembly, questioning why they are testing God by placing on the disciples' necks a yoke that neither their ancestors nor they themselves could bear (Exodus 20:1-17, Romans 8:3), concluding with the doctrinal declaration of grace: {{quote:Acts 15:11|But we believe that it is through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ that we are saved, just as they are}}. The entire crowd falls silent and listens to Barnabas and Paul relate the great signs and wonders that God had performed through them among the nations (Acts 14:27).
[13-21] At the conclusion, James, the Lord's brother and moderator of the meeting, takes the floor to summarize the matter, pointing out how Simon Peter declared the first divine visitation to the Gentiles to take from them a people for His name (Acts 10:45). This aligns with the words of the prophets, for it is written that after these events the Lord will return and re-establish the tabernacle of David that had fallen (Amos 9:11-12), so that the rest of humanity may seek the Lord and all the Gentiles upon whom His name is invoked. This revelation establishes two callings or gatherings of Gentiles in the divine plan: the gathering of the church in the present age to form the Body of Christ (Acts 15:14) and the gathering of Gentiles in the Millennium after the Second Coming (Isaiah 2:2-3, Zechariah 8:22-23). James judges it best not to trouble the Gentile converts, but to write to them instructing them to abstain from things polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from what has been strangled, and from blood (Genesis 9:4, Leviticus 17:10-14), noting that Moses has had men in every city from ancient times to preach to him in the synagogues on the Sabbath.
[22-35] The apostles, the elders, and the whole church agree to choose men from among them—Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, leading men among the brothers—to send to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They write official letters denouncing the legalists who went out without a mandate and subverted people's minds by demanding circumcision and the law. The formal decree confirms that they will not impose any burden beyond these necessary recommendations {{quote:Acts 15:28|For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us not to impose on you any burden beyond these essential requirements}}. These guidelines for conduct do not constitute commandments for salvation nor do they condition the believer's eternal security (Romans 14:1-6, 1 Corinthians 10:25-29), but rather seek to preserve the testimony and avoid stumbling blocks with the Jews in the synagogues. Upon arriving in Antioch and delivering the letter, the congregation rejoices in the consolation; Judas and Silas, being prophets, comfort and strengthen the brothers, continuing the teaching of the Word of God.
[36-41] After some days, Paul proposes to Barnabas that they revisit the brothers in each city where they had proclaimed the Word of the Lord to examine their condition. Barnabas tries to take John, also called Mark, with him; however, Paul does not think it appropriate to take someone who had separated himself from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work (Acts 13:13). Such a sharp conflict erupts between them that they separate from each other: Barnabas takes Mark and sails to Cyprus, while Paul chooses Silas and departs, commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord, traveling through Syria and Cilicia and imposing confirmation in the churches.

[1-5] In Derbe and Lystra, Paul adds Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman and a Greek father, to his missionary team (Acts 16:1). Despite advocating justification by faith apart from ceremonial works of the law (Galatians 2:16, Acts 15:11), Paul circumcises Timothy because of the Jews in that region, who knew his father was Greek (Acts 16:3). This practical measure sought to remove an obstacle to evangelism among the Jews without compromising the doctrine of grace. As they traveled through the cities, they delivered the decrees issued by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem (Acts 15:28), which strengthened the local churches in the faith and increased their numbers daily.
[6-10] As they passed through Phrygia and the region of Galatia, the Holy Spirit forbade the missionaries from preaching the Word in the province of Asia (Acts 16:6). When they attempted to go to Bithynia, the Spirit prevented them, guiding them sovereignly through northwestern Asia Minor until they reached Troas. In that coastal city, Paul received a vision that night in which a man from Macedonia pleaded with him for help. The grammatical shift to the pronoun "we tried" in the biblical account (Acts 16:10) indicates the personal incorporation of Luke, the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14), into the missionary group composed of Paul, Silas, and Timothy. Responding immediately to the divine call, they set sail from Troas, sailing directly to Samothrace and the next day to Neapolis, introducing the Gospel to the European continent for the first time.
[11-15] From Neapolis, the missionary party traveled to Philippi, the principal city of that part of Macedonia and a Roman colony (Acts 16:12). Instead of finding a Jewish synagogue—which required a minimum quorum of ten adult men to be constituted—on the Sabbath they went outside the city gate by the river, where prayer was usually held. Among the women gathered was Lydia, a purple cloth merchant from the city of Thyatira, who feared God. Upon hearing the message, the Lord opened her heart to heed Paul's teachings (Revelation 3:20). Lydia believes and is baptized in water along with her household, demonstrating that New Testament baptism presupposes the believer's conscious faith and refutes the practice of infant baptism. Grateful for her salvation, Lydia compels the ministers to stay at her house.
[16-24] On the way to the place of prayer, they are met by a young woman possessed by a spirit of divination or python, who brought her masters great profit through occult practices. The girl follows Paul and his companions, shouting that they are servants of the Most High God who proclaim the way of salvation (Genesis 14:18). Although her verbal testimony expressed true words, Paul is annoyed and commands the spirit in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her, since the truth of the Gospel does not permit demonic promotion or patronage. When their masters saw that their hope of financial gain had vanished, they arrested Paul and Silas and dragged them to the forum before the Roman magistrates. They falsely accused them of stirring up the city, being Jews, and of teaching customs unlawful to the Romans. The magistrates ordered their clothes to be torn, they were beaten with rods, and they were imprisoned in the innermost cell, their feet fastened in the stocks.
[25-34] At midnight, Paul and Silas prayed and sang praises to God from the cell, and the other prisoners heard them (Psalm 42:8). Suddenly, a great and miraculous earthquake shook the foundations of the prison, instantly opening all the doors and unfastening the chains of all the prisoners. The jailer, upon waking and seeing the open doors, drew his sword to kill himself, knowing that Roman law punished with death any guard who allowed prisoners to escape (Acts 12:19). Paul shouted at him, pleading with him not to harm himself, as everyone was present. The jailer called for a light, entered trembling, and prostrated himself before Paul and Silas, bringing them out and questioning them: “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” (Acts 16:30). The apostles proclaimed the Gospel of grace: “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household,” teaching the Word to the jailer and all his men. That same night, the jailer washed their wounds and was baptized along with all his family after believing in God.
[35-40] At dawn, the magistrates sent officers with orders to release the prisoners. When the jailer conveyed the news so they could leave in peace, Paul refused to be secretly released, denouncing the fact that they had been publicly flogged without a trial, even though they were Roman citizens (Acts 22:25-28). He demanded that the magistrates themselves come and formally remove them. Upon hearing Paul's words, the Roman rulers were filled with fear for having violated the sacred rights of Roman citizenship, and they came in person to plead with them, remove them, and ask them to leave the city. Leaving the prison, Paul and Silas went to Lydia's house, where they saw the brothers, comforted them, and departed to continue their missionary work.

[1-4] In Thessalonica, traveling along the Roman road known as the Via Egnatia, Paul enters the Jewish synagogue on three Sabbaths to reason with them from the Scriptures. He explains and declares that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and rise from the dead, proclaiming that Jesus is the Messiah. A large crowd of devout Greeks and prominent women believe and join Paul and Silas (Acts 13:14).
[5-9] Unbelieving Jews, driven by envy, recruit idle and wicked men from the marketplace to stir up trouble in the city and attack Jason's house in order to hand the missionaries over to the people. Unable to find them, they dragged Jason and some other believers before the city officials, accusing them of turning the world upside down and acting against Caesar’s decrees by claiming there was another king, Jesus (Acts 16:21). The authorities and the people were disturbed to hear this, but after receiving bail from Jason and the others, they released them.
[10-15] The believers immediately sent Paul and Silas away that night to Berea, where they entered the Jewish synagogue. The Bereans proved to be more noble than the Thessalonians, for they received the Word with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so (1 Thessalonians 2:13). Because of this, many of them believed, along with prominent Greek women and quite a few men. However, when the Jews of Thessalonica learned of this, they also went to Berea to stir up trouble and incite the crowds, so the brothers escorted Paul to the sea for Athens, while Silas and Timothy remained in Berea.
[16-21] While Paul waited in Athens, the philosophical center of Western education, his spirit was inflamed as he beheld the city completely given over to idolatry. He argued in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout, and daily in the marketplace with those who frequented it. Certain philosophers of the Epicureans, dedicated to hedonistic pleasure, and of the Stoics, defenders of self-sufficient pride, confronted him; some accused him of being a verbose, and others claimed that he was promoting foreign gods because he preached Jesus and the resurrection (1 Corinthians 1:22). They then led him to the Areopagus, or Mount of Mars, to inquire about this new doctrine, since the Athenians and the resident foreigners occupied their time with nothing but saying or hearing some novelty. Standing in the middle of the Areopagus, Paul confronted Athenian religiosity, pointing out its extreme superstition and identifying an altar with the inscription: {{quote:Acts 17:23|TO THE UNKNOWN GOD}}. He proclaimed the sovereign God who made the world and all things in it, who, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made by human hands, nor is served by human hands as though he needed anything (Acts 7:48). He announced that from one blood he made all the nations of humankind to inhabit the whole earth, having determined their times and the boundaries of their dwelling place. He urges them to abandon idolatry and ignorance, declaring that {{quote:Acts 17:30|God... now commands all people everywhere to repent}}, having set a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by the Man whom he has appointed, giving proof of this to all by raising him from the dead.
[32-34] Upon hearing about the resurrection of the dead, some openly scoffed, while others postponed their decision, saying they would hear him again on the matter. Paul left the group; however, some men joined him and believed, among whom were Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman named Damaris, and others with them (1 Corinthians 1:26).

[1-4] Paul leaves Athens and moves to Corinth, a commercial and industrial center distinguished by its idolatrous worship of Aphrodite. There he finds a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, and his wife Priscilla, recently arrived from Italy because of Emperor Claudius's edict ordering the expulsion of all Jews from Rome. Since Paul was a tentmaker, he stays and works with them, attending the synagogue every Sabbath to reason with and persuade both Jews and Greeks.
[5, 6] When Silas and Timothy arrive from Macedonia, Paul is compelled in spirit and vehemently testifies to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ. Faced with the Jews' continued opposition and insults, Paul shakes out his clothes and confronts them, declaring: {{quote:Acts 18:6|Your blood be on your own heads; I, being cleansed, will now go to the Gentiles. This event constitutes the third dispensational turning point in the book of Acts (Acts 7:58, Acts 13:46), where the collective rejection by the Jewish nation prompts the official shift of apostolic preaching toward the Gentiles.
[7-11] Leaving there, Paul goes to the house of a man named Justus, a God-fearing man, whose house was next to the synagogue. Crispus, the chief dignitary of the synagogue, believes in the Lord with all his household, and many of the Corinthians who hear the message believe and are baptized in water. The Lord strengthens the apostle in a night vision, saying to him: {{quote: Acts 18:9-10|Do not be afraid, but speak, and do not be silent; for I am with you}}, revealing to him that He has many people in that city, referring to the elect who were to be converted. As a result of this divine support, Paul remained in Corinth for a year and six months teaching them the Word of God.
[12-17] When Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews unanimously rose up against Paul and brought him before the tribunal, accusing him of persuading men to worship God contrary to Mosaic Law. When Paul was about to answer, Gallio interrupted and dismissed the charge, declaring that if it were a matter of a crime or a criminal offense, it would be reasonable to hear them, but since it was a dispute about words, names, and instructions of Jewish law, he would not judge such matters. Gallio expels the accusers from the tribunal, and immediately the Greeks seize Sosthenes, the new leader of the synagogue, and flog him before the tribunal, without the Roman proconsul showing any concern for the case.
[18-23] After remaining in Corinth for many days, Paul bids farewell to the brothers and sails for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila, having shaved his head in Cenchreae because of a Nazirite vow (Numbers 6:18). Upon arriving in Ephesus, he leaves his companions there and enters the synagogue to reason with the Jews, who beg him to stay longer; however, Paul refuses, stating the necessity of celebrating the festival in Jerusalem and promising to return if God wills. Landing at Caesarea, he went up to Jerusalem to greet the church and then went down to Antioch, beginning his third missionary journey by traveling through the regions of Galatia and Phrygia to strengthen all the disciples.
[24-28] Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, well-versed in the Scriptures. Apollos had been instructed in the way of the Lord and, being fervent in spirit, taught diligently the things concerning the Lord, though he knew only the baptism of John the Baptist. When Aquila and Priscilla heard him speaking boldly in the synagogue, they took him aside and instructed him more fully in the way of God. When Apollos wanted to go to Achaia, the brothers wrote to him urging the disciples to receive him, and when he arrived in Corinth he greatly helped those who had believed by grace, publicly convincing the Jews with great vehemence by demonstrating from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.

[1-7] In Ephesus, while Apollos was in Corinth, Paul arrived after traveling through the upper regions and found twelve disciples of Apollos. When he asked them if they had received the Holy Spirit upon believing, they replied that they had not even heard that the Holy Spirit existed, having been baptized only with the baptism of repentance of John the Baptist. Paul explained to them that John baptized pointing to the Messiah who was to come, Jesus Christ. Upon hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, and when Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.
