While the disciples urged him to eat some of the food they had bought, the Messiah revealed the source of his divine strength: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to finish his work” (Job 23:12, Psalm 40:8, John 6:38). Seeing the multitudes of Samaritans flowing in from Sychar, the Lord exhorted the apostles to lift their eyes to the spiritual fields that were ripe for harvest (Matthew 9:37-38). In the work of evangelism, the one who reaps receives a reward and gathers fruit for eternal life, so that the sower and the reaper rejoice together in the Messianic reward (Proverbs 11:30, 1 Corinthians 3:6-9, Galatians 6:9).
Many Samaritans in that city believed in the Lord through the woman's testimony, and when they asked Him to stay with them, the Savior remained there for two days, resulting in an even greater multitude believing through hearing His word directly (John 17:20, Romans 10:17). The inhabitants profess the confession of faith that recognizes Jesus not only as the Jewish King, but as the Savior of the world (John 1:29, 1 John 4:14). After two days, the Lord departed for Galilee, pointing to the maxim that a prophet is not honored in his own country (Matthew 13:57, Luke 4:24). Upon arriving in Cana of Galilee, a royal official came from Capernaum to beg him to come down and heal his dying son. The Savior tested the crowd's inclination by pointing to their desire for visible miracles (1 Corinthians 1:22); however, in response to the father's persistent plea, the Lord performed the healing from a distance by the sole authority of his word (John 4:50). The officer believes the Messianic word and verifies the next day that the fever left the young man at the seventh hour—one in the afternoon—, leading to the conversion of his entire household and recording this event in the text as the second miracle performed by Jesus upon returning from Judea to Galilee (John 2:11, Acts 16:31).

[1-9] Jesus Christ ascends to Jerusalem for a Jewish festival, going to the pool called Bethesda near the Sheep Gate, which had five portals (John 5:1-2). In biblical symbolism and scriptural numerology, the number five is associated with physical death and a tendency toward decay rather than grace (Genesis 5:5, 2 Samuel 2:23, Revelation 9:5). The five portals housed a multitude of sick, blind, lame, and barren people awaiting the movement of the water caused by an angel. In that enclosure lay a man afflicted with an illness for thirty-eight years, a period that typologically evokes the thirty-eight years of wandering and helplessness of the nation of Israel in the desert from Kadesh-barnea (Deuteronomy 2:14). Perceiving his condition and knowing the length of his affliction, the Lord inquired if he desired to be healed. The paralytic, discouraged by the lack of human assistance to enter the pool, expressed the futility of his attempts. The Savior dispensed with the ritual water and performed the healing by the sole authority of His word (John 5:8), and the man was instantly restored on the Sabbath (John 5:9, John 9:14, Acts 3:6).
[10-16] The Jewish religious leaders confronted the healed man, rebuking him for carrying his mat on the Sabbath, which they considered unlawful according to traditional interpretations of Mosaic law (Exodus 20:8-11, Jeremiah 17:21-22). The man justifies his behavior by stating that the same man who restored his health ordered him to take up his bed and walk. Initially, the man was unaware of the healer's identity, as Jesus had withdrawn from the crowd gathered there. After some time, the Lord finds the man in the temple precincts and gives him a spiritually significant warning: {{quote: John 5:14|See, you have been healed; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you}}, revealing that physical affliction can be linked to moral condition and warning of divine judgment (1 Corinthians 11:30, James 5:15). The man goes before the Jews to declare that Jesus was the one who healed him, triggering the persecution of the religious authorities against the Savior for performing these works on the Sabbath (John 7:19, John 9:16, Acts 4:1-2).
[17-23] Faced with the rebuke for Sabbath observance, the Messiah bases his actions on the uninterrupted activity of the divine {{quote: John 5:17|My Father is always at work to this very day, and I too am working}}. This response intensifies the hostility of the Jewish leaders, who sought to kill him not only for breaking the Sabbath law according to their dogmas, but also for calling God his own Father, making himself equal to God (John 8:58, John 10:30-33, Philippians 2:6). The discernment of the first-century listeners confirms that the sonship proclaimed by Christ entailed a direct affirmation of absolute deity, refuting the arguments of liberal theology or of sects that deny his divinity. The Lord expounds on the perfect unity of will and essence between the Father and the Son: the Son does nothing of his own accord but what he sees the Father do, and the Father shows him all things and entrusts him with the power to give life to whomever he wills (John 3:35, John 11:25, 1 Corinthians 15:45). Likewise, the Father judges no one, but has entrusted all judgment to the Son so that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father (Psalm 2:11-12, John 14:9, 1 John 2:23), establishing that the rejection of Jesus Christ invalidates any claim to worship God.
[24-30] The Savior pronounces the declaration of the eternal security of salvation in the present age {{quote: John 5:24|Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into condensation, but has passed from death to life}}. Doctrinally, the possession of eternal life constitutes a present reality for the believer justified by faith apart from works of the law (Romans 3:28, Romans 8:1, Ephesians 2:8-9), having been transferred from spiritual death to life without danger of falling into the condemnation of Hell. The Messiah announces that the hour has come and is now when the spiritually dead hear the voice of the Son of God and live (Ephesians 2:1-5, Colossians 2:13), the Son possessing life in himself and the power to execute judgment because he is the Son of Man (Daniel 7:13-14, Acts 17:31). The Lord then distinguishes the physical resurrection of humanity, revealing that all who are in the tombs will hear his voice: those who have done good will come out to the resurrection of life, while those who have done evil will come out to the resurrection of condemnation (Daniel 12:2, Matthew 25:46). In the unfolding of prophetic revelation, these two resurrections are separated by a thousand-year interval (Revelation 20:4-6, 11-15): the first resurrection encompasses the redeemed in the rapture and at the end of the Great Tribulation (1 Corinthians 15:51-52, 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17), while the second resurrection brings the wicked before the Great White Throne to receive the sentence of the second death (Revelation 20:14-15).
[31-47] To satisfy the requirements of the law regarding the validity of testimony (Deuteronomy 17:6, 19:15), the Lord presents four converging testimonies that attest to his Messiahship. First, he cites John the Baptist, whom he describes as a burning and shining lamp (John 1:6-8, John 3:28); however, the Messiah possesses a superior testimony to John's, consisting of the works the Father gave him to complete, which testify that the Father sent him (John 9:3-5, John 10:37-38). Third, the Father himself has testified about him (Matthew 3:17, 1 John 5:9-10). Fourth, the Lord refers to the authority of Scripture (John 5:39). Jesus rebukes the hierarchy for their refusal to come to him for life and for the lack of God's love in their hearts. By announcing that, having come in his Father's name, they did not receive him, he pronounces the prophecy concerning the coming of the Messianic imposter {{quote: John 5:43|if another comes in his own name, you will receive him}}, anticipating the acceptance of the antichrist or son of perdition by the apostate nation in the Great Tribulation (2 Thessalonians 2:3-10, Revelation 13:1-8). The chapter concludes by pointing to Moses as the accuser of the people before the Father, for Moses wrote about Christ in the law (Genesis 3:15, Genesis 22:8, Deuteronomy 18:15); thus, those who refuse to believe in the writings of Moses are unable to believe in the words of the Savior (Luke 16:31, Acts 26:22-23).

[1-14] The miracle of feeding the five thousand men—not counting women and children—constitutes a test of faith for the disciples, in which the Lord asks questions knowing beforehand what He would do (John 6:5-6). From the delivery of five barley loaves and two small fish provided by a boy, the Lord blesses, breaks, and distributes the food through the apostles (John 6:9-11). Doctrinally, the miraculous multiplication of food in the hands of the servants illustrates that the minister must be broken by God to be a blessing and transmit the Bread of Life to the multitudes (1 Corinthians 3:9, 2 Corinthians 5:20). When the multitude is satisfied, twelve baskets full of leftover fragments are collected so that nothing is wasted (John 6:12-13). Faced with the magnitude of the sign performed in the desert, the spectators recognize the Messiah as the prophet foretold by Moses in the Scriptures {{quote:John 6:14|This is truly the prophet who was to come into the world}} (Deuteronomy 18:15, Acts 3:22).
[15-20] As the multitude traveled in boats to Capernaum seeking the Lord again, the Savior confronted the carnal motivation of the crowd, rebuking them for seeking him not for the understanding of the miraculous signs, but for the temporary satisfaction of their physical needs (John 6:26). In contrast to the pursuit of perishable earthly goods, we are exhorted to work for the spiritual food that endures to eternal life, which is given by the Son of Man sealed by the Father (John 6:27, Romans 16:18, Philippians 3:19).
[21-28] In response to the Jews' question about the works required by God, the Lord clarifies that the ultimate divine work does not consist of legal merits or works of the law, but in believing in the One whom the Father has sent {{quote:John 6:29|This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent}}. In response to the demand for a sign similar to the manna given to the ancestors in the desert (Exodus 16:15, Psalm 78:24), the Savior clarifies that Moses did not provide the true bread from heaven, but that God the Father gives the true heavenly Bread that imparts life to the world (John 6:32-33). The Lord categorically identifies Himself as the Bread of Life, guaranteeing that whoever comes to Him will never go hungry and whoever believes in Him will never be thirsty (John 6:35, John 4:13-14).
[29-33] Despite having visibly witnessed the manifestations of the Messiah, unbelief prevails among the crowd (John 6:36). The doctrine of the divine purpose in redemption is established: all that the Father gives to the Son will come to Him, and whoever comes to Him He will never cast out (John 6:37). The Savior's incarnate mission does not seek to execute human will, but to fulfill the Father's design (John 6:38), guaranteeing the preservation and bodily resurrection on the last day of all who see the Son and believe in Him for eternal life (John 6:39-40, 2 Corinthians 5:5).
[34-45] The Lord reiterates His status as the Bread of Life, contrasting the nature of the manna in the desert—whose consumers died physically—with the living Bread that came down from heaven and imparts spiritual immortality (John 6:48-51). The statement about eating His flesh and drinking His blood (John 6:53-56) does not contemplate a literal practice of cannibalism nor does it establish the dogma of transubstantiation in the Roman Mass, since the physical ingestion of matter does not confer eternal salvation (Exodus 16:20, Leviticus 3:17, Acts 15:20). The expression constitutes a spiritual metaphor for the union through faith with the Savior, in the same way that the Son lives by the Father {{quote:John 6:57|as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so he who feeds on me, he also will live because of me}}.
[46-51] The harshness of the discourse provokes murmuring among many of the disciples who followed him superficially, who call the teaching a hard word (John 6:60-61). The Lord anticipates his future heavenly ascension to demonstrate the spiritual nature of his words (John 6:62), establishing the fundamental anthropological and soteriological principle: the Spirit is the one who gives life and the flesh profits nothing {{quote:John 6:63|the Spirit is the one who gives life; the flesh profits nothing: the words that I have spoken to you, they are spirit, and they are life}}. It is reaffirmed that the divine words are spirit and life, and that access to the Son requires the sovereign grant of the Father (John 6:64-65).
[52-57] Confrontation with doctrinal truth produces a mass defection among the carnal followers, who turn back and no longer walk with the Lord (John 6:66). When questioned about their continued commitment, Simon Peter responds by acknowledging that only the Messiah possesses the words of eternal life and the revelation of his deity (John 6:67-69). Finally, the Lord warns that, although he chose the twelve, one of them is a devil {{quote: John 6:70|Have I not chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?}}, prophetically pointing to Judas Iscariot, the Son of Perdition who would betray him (John 17:12, 2 Thessalonians 2:3, Acts 1:25).

[1-13] This passage records the Lord Jesus' journey through Galilee and his refusal to travel openly through Judea due to persecution by the religious authorities in Jerusalem (John 7:1). Historically, the apostle John wrote his Gospel approximately two decades after the destruction of the temple in 70 CE, using the term "Jews" to specifically refer to the church leadership opposed to the truth. It is also documented that his own siblings—those born of Mary after the virgin birth—did not believe in his messiahship during his earthly ministry (John 7:5, Matthew 1:25, Mark 6:3). Faced with pressure to appear publicly at the Feast of Tabernacles, the Savior declares that His time had not yet come (John 7:6, John 7:8), demonstrating that no earthly power could hasten His arrest before the time appointed by the Father (John 8:20). The world cannot hate His own, but it hates the Son for bearing witness to the wickedness of its works {{quote:John 7:7|The world cannot hate you; but it hates me, because I bear witness about it, that its works are evil}}.
[14-24] In the middle of the festival, the Lord goes up to the temple and teaches, causing astonishment among the leaders who questioned His academic authority since He had not graduated from rabbinical schools (John 7:14-15). In response, the Savior clarifies that His doctrine comes directly from the Father (John 7:16), establishing the fundamental soteriological and epistemological rule: “Anyone who chooses to do God’s will will find out whether the teaching is from God.” This statement makes it clear that humanity’s spiritual blindness is not due to agnosticism or a lack of information, but rather to the rebellion of the will and to sin (Romans 1:17–20, Acts 10:1–22). To expose the hypocrisy of His accusers regarding the Sabbath, the Lord reminds them that the law authorizes circumcision on the Sabbath, rebuking their unfounded indignation at having completely healed a man on the Sabbath (John 7:22–23). The section concludes with the commandment on spiritual discernment {{quote:John 7:24|Do not judge by appearances, but judge rightly}}, reminding us that right judgment is not based on carnal impressions, but on the systematic comparison with the inspired word (1 Corinthians 2:15, 1 Samuel 16:7).
[25-36] Among the inhabitants of Jerusalem, perplexity arose upon seeing the boldness with which the Messiah preached without being stopped by the rulers (John 7:25-26). However, popular unbelief argued that they knew his earthly origin, advocating the false premise that no one would know where the Christ would come from (John 7:27); this stance reveals the blindness of the nation, which was perfectly aware of Micah's prophecy about the birth in Bethlehem of Judah (Micah 5:2, Matthew 2:5-6). Jesus cries out in the sanctuary, reaffirming his heavenly origin and the truth of the Father whom they ignore (John 7:28-29). Although they sought to arrest him, no one laid a hand on him because his hour had not yet come (John 7:30). Faced with the sign of faith shown by the crowd (John 7:31), the Pharisees and chief priests send officers to arrest him (John 7:32). The Lord announces his imminent heavenly ascension, warning of the impossibility of his persecutors finding him: “You will look for me, but you will not find me; And where I am, you cannot come (John 8:21), while the Jews were mistakenly speculating about a possible departure into the dispersion among the Greeks (John 7:35-36).
[37-39] On the last and great day of the Feast of Tabernacles, the Lord Jesus stands and proclaims the invitation to salvation {{quote: John 7:37|If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink}} (John 4:10-14). It is promised that from within those who believe in Him will flow rivers of living water, in fulfillment of the Old Testament typology of the pierced rock and the provision of manna (Psalm 1:3, Exodus 17:6). The Scripture text explicitly explains that this promise alluded to the Holy Spirit whom believers would receive (John 7:39). Doctrinally, the impartation and permanent indwelling of the Spirit in the Body of Christ was contingent upon the glorification of the Redeemer, requiring the completion of the atoning work on the cross and His subsequent resurrection (Acts 2:1-4, John 20:22, Colossians 2:11).
[40-53] The Savior's teachings caused a division among the people: while some recognized Him as the Prophet promised by Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15) and others as the Christ, objections arose regarding His Galilean origin in light of the prophecies concerning the lineage of David and the village of Bethlehem (John 7:40-42, Micah 5:2). When the officers returned empty-handed, they justified their omission to the priests by declaring the impact of divine preaching: {{quote: John 7:46|“No one ever spoke the way this man does!”}}. The Pharisees responded by appealing to the pride of academic and institutional consensus: {{quote: John 7:48|“Have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed in him?”}}, illustrating the inclination of carnal scholars to subordinate biblical truth to the approval of their peers and to human hierarchies (John 12:42-43). Following Nicodemus's moderating intervention regarding the procedural guarantees of the law (John 7:50-51), the leaders rebuke him, falsely claiming that no prophet arises from Galilee (John 7:52), ignoring, through historical blindness, the origin of the prophet Jonah in Gath-hepher (2 Kings 14:25, Joshua 19:13). The narrative concludes by recording that each went home (John 7:53), marking the boundary of the traditional passage about the adulterous woman in chapter 8 (John 8:1-11), whose authenticity in the preserved Reina Valera 1865 text is vindicated against the omissions of the Alexandrian manuscripts.

[1-3] Elkanah, a man residing in Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim, belonged to the priestly lineage of the Kohathite Levites (1 Chronicles 6:33-38), although his home was in Ephraimite territory. Elkanah had two wives: Hannah and Peninnah. Peninnah had children, while Hannah was barren, reflecting the polygamy of the time and the family tensions characteristic of the moral decline during the period of the judges (Judges 21:25). The family went up annually from their city to Shiloh to worship and offer sacrifices to the Lord of hosts, the site where the tabernacle of meeting with the ark of the covenant was kept (Joshua 18:1, Psalms 78:60). In that sacred precinct, Hophni and Phinehas, the two sons of Eli, exercised the priestly ministry, and their abuses and immoralities profaned the divine worship (1 Samuel 2:12-17). Doctrinally, this passage records the first appearance in Scripture of the title "Lord of Hosts" (1 Samuel 1:3), revealing God's absolute sovereignty over the heavenly hosts in the midst of Israel's spiritual apostasy.
[4-8] When the day of the annual sacrifice arrived, Elkanah distributed the portions to Peninnah and all her sons and daughters; however, he gave Hannah a double portion because of the special love he had for her, even though the Lord had closed her womb (Genesis 29:31, Luke 1:7). Her rival irritated and distressed her with constant reproaches to anger her because of her barrenness, repeating this provocation every year when they went to the house of the Lord, which led Hannah to weep and refuse food. Typologically, Hannah represents the faithful and powerless remnant in the flesh awaiting divine intervention (Isaiah 54:1, Galatians 4:27), while Peninnah embodies formal religion that boasts of its earthly fruits. Elkanah tries to comfort his wife by offering her his personal affection, but human relief proves insufficient to alleviate the pain of spiritual barrenness.
[9-18] After the meal at Shiloh, Hannah gets up and goes into the tabernacle. With bitterness of soul and overwhelmed with tears, she prays to the Lord and makes a solemn vow: if God will look upon the affliction of his servant and grant her a son, she will dedicate him to the Lord for all the days of his life, pledging that no razor will touch his head under the condition of a lifelong Nazirite vow (Numbers 6:1-5, Judges 13:5). Eli the priest, sitting on his chair by a pillar of the temple at Shiloh—a term applied to the structure of the tabernacle (1 Samuel 3:3)—observes Hannah praying silently, moving her lips without uttering a word, and mistakenly concludes that she is drunk. This lack of discernment on the part of the high priest demonstrates the insensitivity of the religious leadership of the time to genuine suffering (Acts 2:13-15, Ephesians 5:18). Hannah meekly clarifies that she is not a wicked woman, but rather pours out her soul before the Lord in her sorrow, receiving the priestly blessing {{quote: 1 Samuel 1:17|Go in peace, and may the God of Israel grant you the petition you have made to him}}, which restores her inner peace and her countenance.
[19-23] In the morning, the family worships before the Lord and begins their return to their residence in Ramah. Elkanah goes to his wife Hannah, and the Lord remembers her (Genesis 8:1, 1 Samuel 1:19). Hannah conceives and gives birth to a son, naming him Samuel because she had asked the Lord for him {{quote: 1 Samuel 1:20}}, testifying that his birth was a direct answer to her prayer of faith. The following year, when Elkanah went up to Shiloh to offer the annual sacrifice and fulfill his vow, Hannah remained in Ramah until she had weaned the child, declaring her intention to later take him to dwell permanently in the sanctuary. Elkanah approved of his wife's decision, praying that the Lord would confirm her word. Doctrinally, Hannah's conduct highlights faithfulness in fulfilling sacred vows and the family's consecration to divine service (Psalms 116:12-14, Ecclesiastes 5:4-5).
[24-28] Once Samuel was weaned, Hannah took him to Shiloh accompanied by three calves, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine, entering the house of the Lord. After sacrificing the calf, the mother presented the child to the priest Eli and identified herself as the woman who years before had prayed in that same place. Hannah declares that the Lord heard her plea and granted her request {{quote: 1 Samuel 1:28|I also give him up to the Lord; all the days that he lives he will be the Lord’s}}. The scene culminates with the worship of the Lord in Shiloh, marking the beginning of Samuel’s ministry as prophet and priest who will prepare the transition from theocracy to the establishment of David’s Messianic monarchy (1 Samuel 2:35, Acts 3:24, Acts 13:20).

[1-10] Hannah offers a prayer of praise and prophecy after the surrender of Samuel at Shiloh, whose poetic structure foreshadows Mary's song in the New Testament (Luke 1:46-55). Doctrinally, the declarations about the breaking of the bows of the mighty, the exaltation of the hungry, and the humiliation of the proud have a twofold scope that transcends the personal experience of overcoming barrenness, projecting itself toward the judgments of the Great Tribulation and the establishment of the Messianic kingdom at the Second Coming (Psalm 18:14, Revelation 19:11-16). The song proclaims the Lord's incomparable holiness, divine sovereignty over life and death (Deuteronomy 32:39), and the lifting up of the needy from the ash heap to inherit the throne of glory (Psalm 113:7-8). The section concludes with the first explicit biblical mention of the Messianic king and his anointing {{quote: 1 Samuel 2:10|the LORD will judge the ends of the earth, and will give strength to his King, and exalt the horn of his Anointed}}, prophesying the exaltation of Christ as King of kings on earth (Psalms 2:6-8, Zechariah 14:9).
[11-17] After Samuel's consecration, Elkanah returns to Ramah while the young man remains in Shiloh ministering to the Lord before the priest Eli (1 Samuel 1:28). In stark contrast to the boy's faithfulness, Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are identified as wicked men or sons of Belial who did not know the Lord or respect the priestly order established in the Mosaic Law (Leviticus 7:30-34, Deuteronomy 18:3). The corrupt practice of the priests was to send their servant with a three-pronged fork while the sacrificial meat was cooking, arbitrarily taking for himself what the fork pulled out, and demanding that the offerer hand over the raw meat before burning the fat required for God's altar. This profanation of the sacred ordinances undermined worship and led the people to abhor the Lord's offerings, bringing great guilt upon the priestly house (Malachi 2:7-9, 1 Timothy 6:10). {{quote:1 Samuel 2:17|So the sin of the young men was very great in the sight of the Lord; because men despised the sacrifices of the LORD.
[18-21] In the midst of the moral degradation of the sanctuary, Samuel continued his service before the Lord wearing a linen ephod, a garment proper to the priestly ministry that symbolized purity and separation for sacred service (Exodus 28:6, 1 Samuel 22:18). Annually, his mother Hannah made him a small tunic and took it with him when she went up with her husband to offer the customary sacrifice (1 Samuel 1:3). Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife, invoking divine restitution for the offering of the son given to the Lord. Hannah's faithfulness in fulfilling her vow is rewarded by divine grace {{quote:1 Samuel 2:21|And the LORD visited Hannah, and she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters}}, while young Samuel grew up in the presence of the Most High, becoming strong in grace and knowledge (Luke 1:80, 2 Peter 3:18).
[22-26] Eli's old age coincides with the complete breakdown of discipline at the tabernacle of Shiloh, and news reaches him of the excesses of his sons, who even slept with the women who kept watch at the entrance to the tent of meeting (Exodus 38:8). Despite the gravity of these abominations, Eli's admonition to his sons proved weak and ineffective, limited to verbal rebukes without exercising judicial authority or suspending them from priestly duties (Deuteronomy 21:18-21, 1 Samuel 3:13). The young men refused to listen to their father's voice {{quote: 1 Samuel 2:25|But they would not listen to their father's voice, for the Lord wanted to put them to death}}, demonstrating the judicial surrender to the hardness of heart that precedes the execution of divine punishment upon the unrepentant (Proverbs 29:1, Romans 1:28). In contrast to the ruin of Eli's house, the text highlights the holistic development of Samuel {{quote: 1 Samuel 2:26|And the boy Samuel grew, and advanced in the sight of God and man}}, a phrase that foreshadows the earthly growth of the Lord Jesus Christ (Luke 2:52).
[27-36] A prophet or man of God appears before Eli to deliver the divine judgment against his dynasty, reminding him that God chose the house of his father Aaron in Egypt to serve as priests, wear the ephod, and offer sacrifices on the altar (Exodus 28:1, Numbers 18:1-7). The divine messenger rebukes Eli for having honored his sons more than God, fattening himself on the choicest offerings of the people of Israel. The Lord proclaims the law of spiritual retribution (1 Samuel 2:30), announcing the end of the covenant of perpetual priesthood for the house of Ithamar (1 Kings 2:27) and decreeing that Eli's descendants will die in their prime and beg for a piece of bread. As an imminent sign of judgment, Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, will both perish on the same day during the battle against the Philistines (1 Samuel 4:11). Finally, God announces the establishment of a new priestly line {{quote: 1 Samuel 2:35|And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will do according to what is in my heart and in my soul}}, a promise that finds partial historical fulfillment in the appointment of Zadok during the reign of Solomon (1 Kings 2:35, 1 Chronicles 6:8), and its full fulfillment in the eternal and unchanging priesthood of Jesus Christ according to the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 110:4, Hebrews 7:23-28).

[1-3] In the days of Samuel’s youth, the word of the Lord was precious and rare, and there was no open vision (1 Samuel 3:1). The young man served at the sanctuary at Shiloh, where the biblical text refers to the tabernacle or portable tent as a “temple” before the construction of the building during Solomon’s reign (1 Samuel 1:9, 1 Samuel 3:3). This earthly structure was called a temple because it was erected according to the pattern of the heavenly temple (Hebrews 8:5, Revelation 11:19, Revelation 14:17). It is also recorded that Samuel was resting in the sanctuary before the lamp of God went out before the ark of the covenant (1 Samuel 3:3, Exodus 27:21).
[4-11] The Lord began revealing himself to Samuel at a time when the young man had not yet directly heard the divine voice nor had the word been formally revealed to him (1 Samuel 3:7). In response to the divine call, the servant's submissive and obedient disposition is expressed in the declaration of submission: {{quote: 1 Samuel 3:10|Speak; for your servant is listening}} (Amos 3:7). The first commission given to the prophet consisted of a direct message comprised of three points of judgment and condemnation against the house of the high priest Eli (1 Samuel 3:11-14). This initial commission illustrates the minister's responsibility to faithfully proclaim the negative message of divine rebuke and warning, without yielding to the position or fear of men (Amos 7:16-17).
[12-16] In Eli's demand of Samuel to know the vision, the formula of oath and solemn imprecation common in the Old Testament is employed (1 Samuel 3:17, 1 Samuel 14:44, Ruth 1:17). As Samuel grew, the Lord was with him and did not let any of his words fall to the ground, making him a prophetic type of Christ and John the Baptist in his development and divine support (1 Samuel 3:19, Luke 1:80, Luke 2:52). All Israel, from the northernmost point in Dan to the southern border in Beersheba, recognized Samuel as a faithful prophet, confirmed by the Lord (1 Samuel 3:20, Judges 20:1, 2 Samuel 3:10). Finally, the Lord manifested himself again in Shiloh, revealing himself to Samuel {{quote: 1 Samuel 3:21|by the word of the Lord}}, demonstrating that God uses inspired words to reveal himself to humanity (1 Samuel 3:7, 2 Timothy 3:16).

[1-6] In the military confrontation against the Philistines at Ebenezer, Israel decided to move the ark of the covenant of the Lord from the sanctuary at Shiloh to the battlefield (1 Samuel 4:3-4). The sources indicate that the people engaged in idolatrous behavior by treating the ark as if it were a divine amulet or fetish, presuming that its mere physical presence would guarantee them military victory (1 Samuel 4:3, Joshua 6:6). Upon the ark's arrival at the camp, Israel uttered a great cry that terrified the pagan troops (1 Samuel 4:5-8). [7] In the face of the panic caused by the presence of the ark, the Philistine leaders exhorted their troops to take courage {{quote: 1 Samuel 4:9|Be strong, and be men, O Philistines}}, preferring to fight with determination rather than fall under Hebrew servitude. Although these words came from pagans and idolaters, the sources highlight the validity of the attitude of fighting steadfastly in the midst of adversity, serving as a parallel to the apostolic exhortation given to believers to conduct themselves manfully in the spiritual warfare (1 Corinthians 16:13, 2 Samuel 10:12). [8] The resulting divine judgment on the house of Eli was fulfilled with the defeat of the army of Israel, the capture of the ark of God by the Philistines, and the death of the two wicked priests, Hophni and Phinehas (1 Samuel 4:11). Because of the desecration of the priesthood and the corruption of the people, the Lord abandoned the tabernacle located at Shiloh, withdrawing His glorious presence from that historic place (Psalm 78:60, Jeremiah 7:12). [9, 10] Upon receiving the news of the loss of the ark and the death of her father-in-law and her husband, Phinehas' wife bent over and gave birth in the midst of labor pains (1 Samuel 4:19). This event records the experience of a Jewish widow who perishes in childbirth following the national disaster (1 Samuel 4:19-20, Job 39:3). [11, 12] Before she died, the mother named the newborn Ichabod, expressing that glory had departed from Israel because of the capture of the ark of God (1 Samuel 4:21-22). From an ecclesiological perspective, the term Ichabod describes the condition of a church or institution where the Holy Spirit has departed due to apostasy, carnal formalism, human control, and the abandonment of the biblical message (2 Timothy 3:5, Revelation 3:1-2).

[1, 2] Paul presents himself as an apostle of Jesus Christ by the directive will of God (Acts 9:15) and not by the permissive will (James 4:15). Sources point out that the words "in Ephesus" were omitted by Marcion, Origen, and in manuscripts such as the Vatican and Sinaiticus, although the letter maintains its apostolic authority to the saints and faithful in Christ Jesus. The greeting conveys the grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
[3] A hymn of praise is sung to God the Father for blessing believers with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ. The text comprises seven specific and individual blessings expressed in this first chapter (Ephesians 1:4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 13, 14). The expression concerning the heavenly places points to the spiritual and exalted position that the Christian occupies in the mind of God, united with his Head in heaven above the physical universe (Ephesians 1:20, 2:6, 3:10, 6:12).
[4-6] In addressing the statement {{quote:Ephesians 1:4|according to which he chose us in him before the foundation of the world}}, the Calvinist position of unconditional and irresistible election is rejected. Sources maintain that no one was in Christ before the creation of the world or before Genesis 1:1, since all people were born in Adam, alienated and dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1, Ephesians 2:12, Galatians 4:7-9). Election is in Him, so that a person becomes part of the elect only by being placed in Christ by the Holy Spirit upon hearing and believing the gospel (Ephesians 1:13, 1 Corinthians 12:13, 2 Timothy 1:9). Likewise, predestination focuses on the future destiny of believers for adoption and future glorification in the image of the Son (Romans 8:29).
[7-10] The passage teaches that spiritual redemption and forgiveness of sins are obtained exclusively through the blood of Jesus Christ, manifesting the abundant riches of divine grace. God has made all wisdom and prudence abound in revealing the mystery of his will, whose divine design is to unite all things in Christ, both heavenly and earthly, in the dispensation of the fullness of time (1 Corinthians 15:28, Revelation 21).
[11-14] Believers are constituted as a predestined inheritance according to the Lord's purpose. The soteriological order is precisely established: {{quote: Ephesians 1:13|having heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and having believed in him, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise}}, which demonstrates that the sealing occurs after hearing and believing the message, refuting regeneration prior to faith (John 1:12-13). The Holy Spirit dwells in the Christian as the earnest or guarantee of the inheritance until the physical redemption of the body at the rapture (Romans 8:23, 1 Peter 1:4-5, 2 Corinthians 5:5).
[15-18] Upon learning of faith in the Lord Jesus and the love shown to all the saints, the apostle expresses his constant gratitude and intercession. The apostolic prayer asks that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ grant a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of Him, enlightening the eyes of our understanding to comprehend the hope of His calling and the glorious riches of His inheritance in the saints (Psalm 33:12).
[19-23] The surpassing greatness of the divine power available to believers is proclaimed, which was demonstrated in raising Christ from the dead and seating Him at His right hand in the heavenly realms, far above all principality, authority, and dominion. God put all things under His feet and appointed Him to be head over everything for the Church, which is His body and the fullness of Him who fills all in all (Colossians 1:18, Ephesians 5:23).

[1-7] The natural state of the unsaved human being is death in trespasses and sins, walking according to the course of this world and under the dominion of the prince of the power of the air (Ephesians 2:1-3). Upon being made alive together with Christ, the believer does not at that instant receive his resurrected physical body, but is positionally placed in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus (Ephesians 2:5-6). This heavenly position demonstrates the spiritual union with the Head before the physical bodily resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:50, Revelation 20:5).
[8-10] Salvation is effected solely by grace through faith, faith itself being a gift bestowed by God and not a human work {{quote: Ephesians 2:8|for by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God}} (Romans 6:23). Good works are presented in the divine order as the fruit following salvation, not as its cause, since the believer is God's handiwork, created in Christ Jesus to walk in them (Ephesians 2:10, Titus 3:5).
[11-18] In the past, the Gentiles were separated from the citizenship of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, without hope and without God in the world (Ephesians 2:11-12). However, they were brought near through the blood of Christ, who broke down the dividing wall of hostility and abolished the law of commandments to reconcile Jews and Gentiles {{quote: Ephesians 2:16|in one body through the cross}} (Colossians 1:20). This reconciliation accomplished at Calvary demonstrates that the formation of the one body was provided on the cross, refuting the positions of hyperdispensationalism that postpone its origin to later revelations (Galatians 3:28).
[19-22] The redeemed Gentiles are no longer foreigners or strangers, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Ephesians 2:19). The church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets of the New Testament, with Jesus Christ as the chief cornerstone upon which the whole well-coordinated building grows to become a holy temple in the Lord and a dwelling place of God in the Spirit (Ephesians 2:20-22, 1 Corinthians 3:11, 1 Peter 2:5).

[1-6] Paul presents himself as a prisoner of Jesus Christ for the sake of the Gentiles (Ephesians 3:1). When addressing the expression {{quote: Ephesians 3:2|the dispensation of God's grace}}, the sources point out that the term dispensation does not designate a specific era or period of time, but rather the grace bestowed directly upon Paul to carry out his ministry and impart the revelation of the mysteries (Colossians 1:25, Ephesians 3:7). Divine grace was granted to believers before the apostle's conversion, as was the case with Noah, the criminal on the cross, and Cornelius (Genesis 6:8, Luke 23:42-43, Acts 10:44). Through divine revelation, the mystery hidden in past ages was made known (Ephesians 3:3-5), which establishes that Gentiles are co-heirs and members of the same body, sharing in the promise in Christ through the gospel (Ephesians 3:6, Romans 16:25). The positions of hyperdispensationalism are refuted by demonstrating that the spiritual body, composed of Jews and Gentiles, was constituted at Calvary through the cross (Ephesians 2:16, 1 Corinthians 12:13), and that the apostle was already teaching and writing about the existence of this body before the writing of this letter (Galatians 2:2, 1 Corinthians 12:13, Romans 12:4).
[7-13] The apostle was appointed a minister according to the gift of God’s grace received through the working of his power (Ephesians 3:7). Recognizing himself as less than the least of all the saints, he was given the task of proclaiming to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ and making clear to all people the communion of the mystery hidden for ages in God (Ephesians 3:8-9). The formation of the Church is intended to manifest the manifold wisdom of God before the principalities and powers in the heavenly realms (Ephesians 3:10), serving as a spiritual witness before the cosmic hosts (Ephesians 1:23, Ephesians 6:12, Isaiah 24:21). This design corresponds to the eternal purpose fulfilled in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom we obtain security and access with confidence through faith (Ephesians 3:11-12, Romans 5:2). Therefore, believers are exhorted not to lose heart because of the tribulations suffered in ministry, which are His glory (Ephesians 3:13, 2 Corinthians 1:4).
[14-21] Paul kneels before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom the entire family in heaven and on earth derives its name (Ephesians 3:14-15). The sources emphasize that the family of God encompasses various groups in different spheres, including the Father, the Son, the Bride who is the Church, the Old Testament saints, and those redeemed from the Tribulation (Galatians 4:26, Revelation 19:7-9). We ask that the Lord grant us to be strengthened with power through the Spirit in our inner being, so that Christ may dwell in our hearts through faith (Ephesians 3:16-17, Colossians 1:27). We also ask to understand, with all the saints, the four spatial dimensions {{quote: Ephesians 3:18|width, length, depth, and height}}, which describe the vastness of the physical and spiritual universe in relation to God (Romans 8:39, Job 28:14). The prayer culminates in a longing to know the love of Christ that surpasses all knowledge, so that we may be filled with all the fullness of God (Ephesians 3:19), attributing glory in the church through Christ Jesus throughout all generations to God, who is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine (Ephesians 3:20-21, Philippians 3:21).

[1-4] The poem opens by identifying Solomon as the author of the supreme song among his thousand and five compositions (1 Kings 4:32). The Bride expresses a fervent longing for the kisses of the Beloved's mouth, acknowledging that his love is superior to wine, a symbol of earthly and temporary pleasures (Psalms 4:7, Psalms 104:15). The name of the Beloved is like ointment poured out because of the fragrance of his grace (Psalms 45:7, John 12:3), causing the virgins to love him. In the dispensational scheme, the virgins in the plural represent the Jewish saints preserved during the Great Tribulation (Matthew 25:1, Revelation 14:4), as distinct from the singular body of the Church conceived as the bride and chaste virgin (2 Corinthians 11:2, Ephesians 5:30-32). The attraction exerted by the Lord will prompt the believer's joyful response {{quote:Song of Solomon 1:4|Draw me after you, let us run}}, being ushered into the King's chambers to rejoice in divine communion and remember His love more than earthly wine.
[5, 6] The Bride describes her physical appearance to the daughters of Jerusalem {{quote:Song of Solomon 1:5|I am dark, O daughters of Jerusalem, but lovely}}. Doctrinally, the young woman's dark complexion indicates her Gentile and Hamitic origin—historically associated with Pharaoh's daughter (1 Kings 3:1)—functioning as a type of the Church composed primarily of Gentiles redeemed from sin (Ephesians 2:11-13, 1 Peter 2:9-10). The comparison to the booths of Kedar—son of Ishmael (Genesis 25:13)—evokes the outer tent of black goatskin (Exodus 26:7) that shelters the inner glory of Solomon's curtains. The sun caused her complexion to turn dark because she was forced by her mother's sons to tend other people's vineyards, neglecting her own. This condition portrays the danger of the believer who wears himself out on external works or human impositions while neglecting his own spiritual life and private communion with the Lord (Jeremiah 17:5, 1 Corinthians 3:12-15).
[7, 8] The Bride seeks the Beloved, addressing Him as the Shepherd of her soul, inquiring where He pastures His flock and where He makes them rest at midday so that they do not wander after the flocks of false companions (Psalm 23:1-2, John 10:1-5). The midday rest foreshadows the refuge in the Messianic presence from the heat of judgment and trials (Isaiah 4:6, Isaiah 32:2). The Beloved responds tenderly, calling her the most beautiful among women and guiding her to follow the tracks of the flock, tending her little goats beside the shepherds' tents. This instruction teaches that communion with the Lord is not found in mystical or sectarian isolation, but in walking alongside the congregation of the saints and in submission to the doctrine of the true shepherds of the flock (1 Peter 5:2-4, Hebrews 13:7).
[9-11] The Beloved compares the Bride to a mare in Pharaoh's chariots {{quote:Song of Solomon 1:9|I have compared you, my love, to a mare in Pharaoh's chariots}}. In ancient times, the Egyptian horses of Solomon's chariots (1 Kings 10:28) were distinguished by their strength, nobility, and royal adornments. Her cheeks look beautiful among the earrings, and her neck stands out among the necklaces, symbolizing the adornments of the Holy Spirit and the submission of the believer's yoke to the divine will (Proverbs 1:9, 1 Peter 3:3-4). The King and his court promise to make her gold earrings inlaid with silver. Doctrinally, gold represents God's divine nature and imputed righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30), while silver symbolizes redemption through the price of blood (Exodus 30:12-16, 1 Peter 1:18-19).
[12-14] As the King sits at his table on his prie-dieu, the Bride's spikenard releases its fragrance, foreshadowing genuine worship rising like a sweet aroma before the divine presence (John 12:3, 2 Corinthians 2:15). The Bride declares that her Beloved is to her a bundle of myrrh resting between her breasts {{quote:Song of Solomon 1:13|My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh}}, the myrrh alluding to the bitterness of Christ's passion, burial, and atoning sacrifice (John 19:39). The constant remembrance of the sacrifice of Calvary dwells near the heart of the believer in the night of this world (Galatians 2:20). Likewise, the Beloved is compared to a cluster of henna or copher in the vineyards of En Gedi, a lush oasis in the midst of the Judean desert (1 Samuel 23:29), representing the beauty of saving grace amid earthly aridity.
[15-17] The chapter culminates with a mutual declaration of admiration and the description of their shared dwelling place. The Beloved proclaims the Bride's beauty, highlighting her dove-like eyes (Song of Solomon 1:15, "Behold, you are beautiful, my love"), where the dove symbolizes simplicity, purity, and a spiritual vision focused exclusively on the Messiah through the Holy Spirit (Matthew 3:16, Matthew 10:16). The Bride responds by celebrating the King's beauty and sweetness, affirming that their shared bed is blossoming, alluding to the fruitfulness and rest of the regenerated soul (Hebrews 4:9-10). The structure of the spiritual dwelling is composed of cedar beams and cypress paneling (1 Kings 6:15), incorruptible and fragrant woods that symbolize the firmness, royal dignity, and eternal permanence of the dwellings prepared by Christ for his redeemed (John 14:2, 2 Corinthians 5:1).

[1, 2] The Lord Jesus Christ prophetically reveals Himself in the first person through the writings of Solomon, using the divine title that directly connects with the manifestation on Mount Horeb (Exodus 3:14, John 8:58) {{quote:Song of Solomon 2:1|I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys}}. In the dispensational scheme, the rose of Sharon evokes the restoration of the promised land during the millennial kingdom, a time when the desert will bloom abundantly before the Messianic presence (Isaiah 35:1-2). The identification as the lily of the valleys—in the plural—teaches that the Savior accompanies the believer through every valley of trial and affliction throughout their earthly pilgrimage (Psalm 23:4). Likewise, the comparison of the wife to a lily among thorns portrays the ontological and positional distinction of the Church (Ephesians 5:27). While the thorns represent unregenerate humanity (Genesis 3:17-18, Hebrews 6:7-8) or other groups of saints from various dispensations who do not possess the permanent indwelling of the Holy Spirit (Song of Solomon 6:8-9), the Church stands out as the spiritual body of Christ clothed in his imputed righteousness (1 Corinthians 12:13, Ephesians 5:30-32).
[3-7] The Bride responds by comparing the Beloved to a leafy apple tree among the trees of the forest {{quote:Song of Solomon 2:3|Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among my sons}}, affirming Christ's preeminence over all the children of Adam (Psalm 45:2, Colossians 1:18). The banqueting house and the jars of wine foreshadow the wedding feast of the Lamb in the heavenly mansions (Revelation 19:7-9) and hint at the pure wine of the kingdom (Matthew 26:29). The declaration of being lovesick expresses the fervent longing of the redeemed soul for intimate communion with its Savior (Psalm 63:1, Philippians 1:23). Finally, the admonition addressed to the daughters of Jerusalem constitutes a prophetic warning to the nation of Israel, requiring them not to rush or attempt to awaken the Messianic program before the time sovereignly appointed by God (Habakkuk 2:3, Acts 1:7).
[8-14] This passage contains a foreshadowing of the rapture of the Church prior to the Great Tribulation (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17, 1 Corinthians 15:51-52). The Bride joyfully recognizes the voice of the Beloved approaching, leaping over the mountains and appearing through the lattice of the heavenly mansions (2 Corinthians 11:2, 2 Corinthians 12:2). The temporal setting for this summons is springtime {{quote:Song of Solomon 2:11|For behold, the winter is past, the rain is turned and gone}}, a time when vegetation blossoms and the fig tree produces its first figs, a sign symbolizing the national resurgence of Israel on the eve of the end (Matthew 24:32, Luke 21:29-32). The Savior addresses to His betrothed the call to resurrection and bodily transformation {{quote:Song of Solomon 2:10|Arise, my love, my fair one, and come away}}, gathering her in the air (1 Thessalonians 4:17). The allusion to the dove sheltered in the clefts of the rock emphasizes the eternal security of the believer's life, which is hidden with Christ in God, the immovable Rock of ages (Exodus 33:22, Psalm 18:2, Colossians 3:3).
[15-17] The command to hunt the little foxes addresses the preservation of the testimony and spiritual fellowship {{quote:Song of Solomon 2:15|Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vineyards}}. In the Christian life, the little foxes represent subtle doctrinal deviations, compromises with the world, or unconfessed sins that undermine the fruit of the Spirit in the local congregation (1 Corinthians 5:6, Galatians 5:9, 2 Corinthians 2:17). The Bride reaffirms the covenant of mutual belonging {{quote:Song of Solomon 2:16|My beloved is mine, and I am his}}, guaranteeing the indissoluble union between the Redeemer and his chosen ones (1 Corinthians 6:19-20, Romans 8:38-39). The expectation of the passage contemplates the arrival of the Messianic dawn at the Second Coming, the moment when the shadows of this world's night and of tribulation judgment will definitively flee before the rising of the Sun of Righteousness (Malachi 4:2, 2 Peter 1:19). The reference to the mountains of Bether—whose translation denotes separation—concludes with fervent prayer for the soon return of Christ (Revelation 22:20).

[1-5] The Bride searches intensely for her Beloved throughout the night in his bed, but cannot find him. Therefore, she wanders the streets and squares of the city, questioning the watchmen, before finally finding him and bringing him into his mother's house. The initial mention of the nights prophetically places this passage within the period of the Great Tribulation, the time of moral darkness and uncertainty for Israel that follows the rapture of the Church (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17). In the pre-millennial structure of the poem, Song of Solomon 2 presents the spring rapture, Song of Solomon 3:1-5 portrays tribulation anguish, and Song of Solomon 3:6-11 culminates in the Second Coming. The search in the city reflects the anguish of the Jewish remnant crying out for the Messiah's presence amidst the judgments (Jeremiah 30:7, Hosea 5:15). The guards or sentinels patrolling the streets represent the prophets and watchmen commissioned during the Tribulation (Ezekiel 3:17, Isaiah 21:11-12). In this first stage, the guards do not attack the young woman, symbolizing the initial three-and-a-half-year phase of relative peace before the open persecution breaks out in the second half of the Tribulation (Song of Solomon 5:7). Upon finding her Beloved, the Bride leads him to her maternal chamber, concluding the section with the exhortation to the daughters of Jerusalem {{quote:Song of Solomon 3:5|do not show favor, nor make my love watchful, until he pleases}} so as not to alter the sovereign calendar set by God (Habakkuk 2:3, Acts 1:7).
[6-8] The scene shifts to the triumphal vision of the King's return, contemplating a procession ascending from the desert in columns of smoke {{quote:Song of Solomon 3:6|Who is this coming up from the wilderness like columns of smoke?}}. Just as the pillar of cloud and fire guided Israel out of Egypt in the Exodus (Exodus 13:21-22), the Savior returns, tracing the historical journey of the Second Coming from Mount Sinai, through Edom, Selah-Petra, Mount Paran, and across the Jordan to the Mount of Olives (Deuteronomy 33:2, Psalms 68:7-8, Habakkuk 3:3, Isaiah 63:1). The fragrances of myrrh and frankincense highlight the Messianic virtues of His atoning sacrifice and His eternal priesthood in the heavenly heights (Psalms 45:8, Hebrews 7:25). Solomon's processional litter evokes the majesty of the King leading His chosen ones to the wedding feast of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7-9). The sixty mighty men of Israel who guard the litter, each with his sword on his thigh (Song of Solomon 3:8), represent the armed escort and army of saints who accompany the Lord to execute judgment on the ungodly nations during the night of Tribulation (Joel 2:1-11, Zechariah 14:5, Revelation 19:14).
[9-11] King Solomon had a chariot built for himself, made of wood from Lebanon, with silver pillars, a gold back, a scarlet seat, and a pavement overlaid with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem. This chariot or litter is a type of the heavenly throne and the vehicle of victory in which the Lord manifests himself in his glory (Ezekiel 1:15-28, Psalm 68:17). The materials used have clear doctrinal significance: the incorruptible Lebanese wood symbolizes the sinless humanity of the Savior (Isaiah 11:1, 1 Kings 6:15); the silver pillars represent the redemption purchased at the price of blood (Exodus 30:12-16, 1 Peter 1:18-19); the gold backrest affirms the deity and divine immortality of the Son (Colossians 2:9); and the scarlet or purple seat proclaims his dignity and royal dominion (Matthew 27:28, Revelation 19:16). The lovingly adorned interior pavement reflects the foundation of grace upon which God restores his relationship with his people (Exodus 24:10, Esther 1:5-6). The passage concludes with the call to the daughters of Zion {{quote:Song of Solomon 3:11|Go forth, O daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon with his crown}}, prophesying the Messianic coronation of Jesus Christ when the Jewish nation recognizes its King after the final victory and the establishment of the millennial kingdom (Zechariah 12:10-14, Matthew 23:39, Revelation 19:12).

[1-5] The Bridegroom praises the Bride's beauty in detail {{quote:Song of Solomon 4:1|Behold, you are beautiful, my love}}, expressing Christ's delight in the spiritual organism of the Church (Ephesians 5:27). The young woman's gaze is like that of a dove behind her veils, symbolizing simplicity, purity, and a vision focused on heavenly things through the Holy Spirit (Matthew 10:16, Colossians 3:2). Her hair is compared to a flock of goats descending from Mount Gilead, evoking consecration and abundance; her teeth are likened to a flock of shorn sheep coming up from the washing place, all producing twins without any barren ones among them, reflecting purity, order, and fruitfulness in doctrine (Titus 2:7). Her temples, nestled among her braids, resemble a pomegranate seed, signifying modesty and inner integrity, while her neck stands out like the tower of David, built as an armory, from which hang a thousand shields and the shields of mighty men (2 Chronicles 11:11), representing doctrinal strength and the faith that quenches the darts of the evil one (Psalm 18:2, Ephesians 6:16). The Bride's two breasts are compared to twin fawns grazing among the lilies, portraying beauty and purity in spiritual affection.
[6, 7] The Bridegroom proclaims his determination to go to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense until the day dawns and the shadows of night flee from this world (Song of Solomon 2:17, 2 Peter 1:19). In the typology of Scripture, myrrh represents the bitterness of suffering, the physical death, and the atoning burial of the Savior (John 19:39), while frankincense alludes to His resurrection, ascension, and continued priestly intercession in the heavenly sanctuary (Hebrews 7:25). By virtue of this atoning work accomplished on the cross, the Lord pronounces the declaration of perfect sanctification upon His betrothed: {{quote:Song of Solomon 4:7|You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you}}. Doctrinally, this passage ratifies the position of the justified believer in the present age, who is presented before the holy Father, blameless and without spot or wrinkle through the imputation of divine righteousness (2 Corinthians 5:21, Ephesians 5:25-27, Colossians 1:22).
[8-11] The Savior addresses the Bride with the Messianic call {{quote:Song of Solomon 4:8|Come with me from Lebanon, my bride}}, an invitation that in the prophetic scheme foreshadows the rapture of the Church before the Great Tribulation (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17). The peaks of Amana, Senir, and Hermon in Lebanon (Deuteronomy 3:9) offer a geographical representation of the universe: the land of Palestine serves as a model of the cosmos, where the firmament separates the lower waters from the frozen celestial ocean above—the sea of ​​glass like crystal (Job 38:30, Revelation 4:6)—upon which rises the celestial Mount Zion in the northern regions (Psalms 48:1-2, Isaiah 14:13, Hebrews 12:22). The dens of lions and the mountains of leopards allude both to the dominion of the adversary who prowls like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8) and to the coming of the Lion of the tribe of Judah who will return with his saints (Revelation 5:5, Jude 14-15). The Bridegroom confesses that his heart has been captivated by one of the Bride's eyes and by a necklace around her neck, celebrating the exclusive devotion of her own (2 Corinthians 11:2). Likewise, under her tongue is honey and milk, a metaphor for the sweetness and edification of God's word proclaimed by the redeemed (Psalm 119:103, 1 Peter 2:2, 1 Peter 4:11), and the fragrance of her garments is likened to the scent of the cedar of Lebanon (Hosea 14:6-7).
[12-15] The Bride is defined by three figures of separation and sacred reserve {{quote:Song of Solomon 4:12|You are a garden locked, my sister, my bride; a spring shut up, a fountain sealed}}. In the practical sphere of marriage, this metaphor demands absolute fidelity and mutual exclusivity (Proverbs 5:15-18). On the dispensational and spiritual level, the enclosed garden prefigures Paradise and the New Jerusalem (Revelation 2:7, Revelation 21:9-12), containing within its boundaries twelve aromatic plants and spices (pomegranates, sweet fruits, henna, spikenard, saffron, calamus, cinnamon, frankincense trees, myrrh, aloes, and the principal spices). The spring of the gardens, the well of living water, and the streams flowing from Lebanon symbolize the Lord Himself as the inexhaustible source of divine grace (Jeremiah 2:13, Jeremiah 17:13, John 4:14, John 7:38). This spiritual provision satisfies the believer and anticipates the millennial river that will flow from the temple to heal the waters of the Dead Sea and impart life to creation (Ezekiel 47:1-12, Zechariah 14:8, Revelation 22:1).
[16] The poetic structure records a change of interlocutor, with the Bride taking the floor to raise her petition {{quote:Song of Solomon 4:16|Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind! Blow on my garden, that its spices may flow forth}}. The north wind (North Wind) and the south wind (South Wind) represent the sovereign action of the Holy Spirit, who works through afflictions or through consolations to cause the fragrance of Christ's virtues to blossom in the believer's testimony (John 3:8, 2 Corinthians 2:14-16). The chapter culminates with the bride's fervent invitation for her Beloved to come to her garden and eat of its sweet fruits, expressing the longing of the redeemed soul and the Church for the soon return of Jesus Christ in his glory (Song of Songs 8:14, Revelation 22:20).

[1] The Bridegroom enters his garden having previously prepared the food and invites his friends to partake of the banquet of spiritual communion (Song of Solomon 4:16, John 14:2-3). From a dispensational and practical perspective, Christ takes the initiative in divine communion, preparing the provision of the Gospel and inviting the believer to voluntarily feed on the truth of his word (Psalm 23:5, Revelation 3:20). The reference to wine, honey, and spices symbolizes the joy and complete satisfaction that the Lord finds in the life of the redeemed when they respond to the call of grace (Proverbs 9:5, Isaiah 55:1, Ephesians 5:18-20).
[2, 3] The Bride experiences an earthly lethargy manifested in the phrase {{quote:Song of Solomon 5:2|I slept, but my heart was awake}}, portraying the state of inner alertness of the redeemed soul amidst physical lethargy or spiritual lukewarmness (Matthew 25:5, Romans 13:11). Upon hearing the voice of the Beloved knocking at the door, the young woman offers carnal excuses after having removed her shoes and washed her feet {{quote:Song of Solomon 5:3|I have taken off my clothes; How shall I clothe her?}}, which in spiritual typology represents the believer who has stopped wearing the shoes of the Gospel of peace (Ephesians 6:15) and abstains from active witness in the world to withdraw into a false, sterile, and ineffective separation (1 Corinthians 5:9-10, 1 Thessalonians 5:6-8).
[4-7] When the Beloved puts his hand through the crack in the door and the Bride gets up to open it for him, she discovers that he has withdrawn, leaving her plunged into an anguished search (Song of Solomon 3:1-2). As she wanders through the city streets, the young woman is intercepted by the sentinels patrolling the walls, who, unlike in their first encounter, beat her, wound her, and strip her of her veil {{quote:Song of Solomon 5:7|They have wounded me, they have hurt me; The watchmen of the walls took my cloak from me. In the prophetic and dispensational structure, this violent aggression portrays the fierce persecution that the Jewish remnant will suffer during the second half of the Great Tribulation (Jeremiah 30:7, Daniel 7:25, Matthew 24:15-21, Revelation 12:13-17), when the apostate authorities and instruments of the false messiah will punish the saints who seek the true Redeemer with excessive force (Revelation 13:7).
[8, 9] The Bride solemnly charges the daughters of Jerusalem to convey to the Beloved that she is lovesick (Song of Solomon 2:5), prompting their inquiry into the superiority of their Beloved over any other suitor {{quote:Song of Solomon 5:9|What is your beloved more than another beloved?}}. This question from the daughters of Jerusalem provides an opportunity to proclaim the Messianic excellence of Christ in contrast to the false choices of human religion or the world system (Psalm 45:2, Colossians 1:18). Doctrinally, the distinction between the Bride and the daughters of Jerusalem preserves the preeminence of the Church as the unique body of Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2, Ephesians 5:31-32) in relation to other groups of the redeemed from various dispensations (Song of Solomon 6:8-9, Hebrews 12:22-24).
[10-16] The Bride responds with a detailed description of the personal glory of her Beloved {{quote:Song of Solomon 5:10|My beloved is white and ruddy, distinguished among ten thousand}}. While the unregenerate world sees in Jesus an ordinary man without outward appeal (Isaiah 53:2-3), the believer redeemed by the Holy Spirit sees his spotless and immaculate whiteness, without the stain of sin (2 Corinthians 5:21, 1 Peter 2:22, 1 John 3:5). The anatomical and symbolic description highlights his head of fine gold (Colossians 2:9), his hair as black as a raven's, his eyes like doves washed with milk that discern all things with purity (Song of Solomon 1:15, Matthew 3:16), his cheeks like beds of fragrant spices, his lips like lilies dripping with precious myrrh, evoking his atoning sacrifice on the cross (John 19:39), his hands like gold rings set with beryl, his legs like marble pillars on bases of fine gold, and his majestic appearance like Lebanon. The proclamation culminates by affirming that His mouth is sweet and He is altogether desirable {{quote:Song of Solomon 5:16|His mouth is most sweet, and He is altogether desirable}}, intoning the song of admiration of the soul that recognizes Christ as its Savior and inseparable Intercessor (Psalms 119:103, Hebrews 7:25, 1 Peter 2:7).

[1-4] James addresses his letter to the twelve tribes of Israel scattered among the nations (John 11:51-52, Acts 26:7), creating a general letter with primary doctrinal application for the Jewish remnant during the Great Tribulation (Matthew 24:13, Revelation 12:17). The apostle exhorts believers to consider facing various trials or temptations a great joy, knowing that the testing of faith produces the virtue of patience (Romans 5:3, 1 Peter 1:6-7). This patience must complete its work so that the believer may reach spiritual maturity and integrity, remaining blameless before the demands of divine service (Philippians 3:12-15, Hebrews 5:9). {{quote: James 1:4|But let patience have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking nothing}}.
[5-8] In the face of a lack of wisdom to endure the afflictions of the Christian life, we are instructed to ask for it directly from God, who grants it abundantly to all without reproaching human frailty (Proverbs 2:6, 1 Kings 3:9-12). However, the request must be made with unwavering faith, for whoever wavers in their trust is like a wave of the sea, tossed and driven by the wind (Mark 11:24, Ephesians 4:14). The double-minded man exhibits structural instability in all his ways, rendering himself incapable of receiving the blessings of the Most High {{quote:James 1:8|A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways}}.
[9-11] The brother of humble condition should glory in his spiritual exaltation upon being made heir of the kingdom (James 2:5, Romans 8:17), while the rich man should acknowledge his humiliation upon considering the perishable nature of earthly riches (Psalm 49:16-17, 1 Timothy 6:17). The brevity of human glory is illustrated by the flower of the grass: as soon as the sun rises with scorching heat, the grass withers, the flower falls, and its beautiful appearance perishes (Psalm 103:15-16, Isaiah 40:6-8, 1 Peter 1:24). Likewise, the rich man will wither away in the midst of his material endeavors, a prophetic warning that points to the judgment upon the powerful on the day of divine wrath (James 5:1-3, Revelation 6:15-17) {{quote:James 1:11|so also the rich man will wither away in his ways}}.
[12-16] The text proclaims the blessedness of the one who endures the trial with perseverance, for upon being approved he will receive the crown of life (Revelation 2:10), one of the five rewards promised to those who love the Lord and endure suffering for His sake (1 Corinthians 9:25, 1 Thessalonians 2:19, 2 Timothy 4:8, 1 Peter 5:4). In addressing the origin of moral temptation, it is established that God cannot be tempted by evil nor does He tempt anyone to sin (Job 1:12, Matthew 6:13). Transgression originates within the human being when they are attracted and seduced by their carnal desires {{quote: James 1:15|And desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death}}. Desire conceives wrongdoing in thought, which matures into action and culminates in physical or spiritual death (Genesis 3:6, Romans 6:23, Romans 7:23).
[17-21] Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights, who does not change like shifting shadows (Malachi 3:6, John 1:9). By his sovereign will, God spiritually begot his elect through the word of truth, to constitute them as a kind of firstfruits of his creatures (Jeremiah 2:3, Ephesians 1:13, 1 Peter 1:23). In light of this divine revelation, it is required that every person be quick to hear biblical instruction, slow to speak rashly, and slow to anger, for human anger does not accomplish God's justice (Proverbs 16:32, Ecclesiastes 5:2). Therefore, putting aside all impurity and the abundance of wickedness, the believer must meekly receive the word grafted into their soul, which has the power to preserve and liberate spiritual life (1 Peter 1:9, 1 Peter 1:25).
[22-27] The instruction culminates in demanding that we be doers of the word and not merely hearers who deceive themselves with an empty profession (Romans 2:13, Matthew 7:21). Anyone who hears the word without putting it into practice is like a man who looks at his natural face in a mirror; after looking at himself, he goes away and immediately forgets what he was like (James 1:23-24). The Mosaic Law and the Scriptures operate like a mirror that exposes the sinner's stains but does not cleanse them (Romans 3:20, Galatians 3:24). On the contrary, those who carefully examine the perfect law of liberty and persevere in it—being doers of the work and not forgetful hearers—will be blessed in their actions (James 2:12, Romans 8:2, Galatians 5:1). If someone boasts of religiosity but does not bridle their tongue, they deceive their own heart, and their worship is worthless (James 3:2-6, Psalm 39:1). Finally, pure and undefiled religion before God the Father consists in visiting orphans and widows in their affliction, and in keeping oneself unstained from the corruption of the world {{quote:James 1:27|Pure and undefiled religion before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world}} (1 John 2:15-17, 1 John 5:18).

[1-3] The prophetic commission given to Jonah, son of Amittai—whose origins are traced to Gath-hepher of the tribe of Zebulun in Galilee (Joshua 19:13, 2 Kings 14:25, John 7:52)—begins with the divine command to go to Nineveh, capital of the Assyrian Empire (2 Kings 17:3-6). {{quote: Jonah 1:2|Arise, and go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry out against it}}. From a historical and dispensational perspective, the call to a Gentile metropolis was an extremely severe command for a Jewish prophet, since Assyria represented the oppressive power destined to execute judgment on the Northern Kingdom (2 Kings 17:23). The repentance of the pagan city implied the postponement of divine punishment upon the enemy power and the subsequent ruin of Israel (2 Kings 14:24-25). Attempting to evade the Lord's presence and escape his Messianic responsibility toward the Gentile nations, Jonah flees to Tarshish in Spain, traveling in the opposite direction to the command he received. The passage describes the sequence of the believer's descent into rebellion: he goes down to Joppa, he goes down to the ship, he goes down into the interior of the vessel, and he incurs the expense of passage to distance himself from God's purpose (Psalm 139:7-10, Ecclesiastes 9:18, Hebrews 4:13).
[4-6] The Lord's response to his servant's disobedience is manifested by unleashing a great wind and a raging storm in the Mediterranean Sea, to the point of threatening the ship's structural integrity (Lamentations 3:39, Jonah 4:8). The impact of the storm terrifies the pagan sailors, who resort to the intercession of their personal idols and throw the cargo overboard to lighten the ship, demonstrating the powerlessness of human religiosity in the face of divine judgment (1 Kings 18:26, Psalm 107:23-27). In contrast to the crew's distress, the prophet lay slumped on the sides of the ship, deep in sleep, portraying the spiritual numbness that befalls the believer separated from divine communion (Proverbs 19:15, Acts 12:6, Ephesians 5:14). The ship's captain interrupts his slumber with a stern rebuke: "What's wrong, sleeper? Get up and call on your God!" It is paradoxical that a pagan sailor should have to awaken the messenger of the Most High to come to prayer.
[7-10] Faced with the persistence of the storm, the sailors agree to cast lots to identify the one responsible for the calamity that afflicts them, and the decision falls on Jonah through God's sovereign intervention over chance (Proverbs 16:33, Acts 1:26). The crew subjects the prophet to an interrogation about his profession, his origin, his nation, and his ethnic background. Jonah pronounces the profession of faith that defines his identity: {{quote: Jonah 1:9|I am a Hebrew, and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the land}}, acknowledging the majesty and dominion of the God of Israel over the created elements (Genesis 1:1, Psalms 95:5). Upon revealing that he was fleeing from the presence of the Lord, deep consternation comes over the men, who rebuke him for having acted so foolishly in defying the deity who controls the seas (Romans 2:23-24, Hebrews 10:31).
[11-14] Seeing that the sea was becoming increasingly rough, the crew inquires about the necessary measures to calm the waters. The prophet proposes his own surrender (Jonah 1:12: “Pick me up and throw me into the sea, and the sea will become calm”), acknowledging that the storm's violence stemmed solely from his rebellious behavior. Typologically, Jonah's willingness to be thrown into the waters to save the ship from death foreshadows the Messianic principle of substitution, where the righteous suffer for the unrighteous to save humanity (John 11:50, 1 Peter 3:18). However, the sailors strive to row with vigor toward dry land to avoid the prophet's sacrifice, illustrating the efforts of human endeavors to achieve salvation through their own means without submitting to the decree of the substitute's death (Romans 3:20, Galatians 2:16, Ephesians 2:8-9). When all human efforts proved futile against the sea's fury, the crew cried out to the Lord, imploring that the guilt of innocent blood not fall upon them (Deuteronomy 21:8, Acts 28:4).
[15-17] The sailors carried out the proposal and threw Jonah into the raging sea. Instantly, the ocean's fury ceased, and calm was restored to the surface (Psalm 89:9, Psalm 107:29, Matthew 8:26). The manifestation of this miracle impacted the sailors' consciences. They feared the Lord greatly, offered sacrifices, and made solemn vows, converting from paganism to the worship of the living God (Ruth 1:16, 2 Kings 5:17). The chapter concludes with divine provision for the prophet's preservation: {{quote: Jonah 1:17|Now the Lord had prepared a great fish to swallow Jonah; And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights. In Messianic theology, Jonah's three days and three nights in the belly of the fish constitutes the quintessential sign invoked by the Lord Jesus Christ to authenticate his own physical death, his descent into the earth, and his glorious resurrection on the third day (Matthew 12:39-40, Matthew 16:4, 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Likewise, in the dispensational prophetic dimension, Jonah's immersion and preservation portrays the testing and miraculous sustenance of the Jewish remnant during the Great Tribulation, as well as the future commission of the evangelists of Israel sent to proclaim the truth to the Gentiles in the nations (Acts 9:15, Revelation 7:4-8, Revelation 12:14-17).

[1, 2] Jonah raises his prayer to the Lord his God from the belly of the fish, declaring that he cried out in his anguish. In biblical theology, the passage establishes the reality of the prophet's physical death inside the great fish; while his body remained lodged in the marine organism, his soul descended to Sheol, or Hell, located in the heart of the earth {{quote: Jonah 2:2|from the belly of Hell I cried}} (Matthew 12:40, Acts 2:27, Psalms 18:4-5). This experience is not a mere allegory or a loss of consciousness, but the literal experience of death and descent into the lower regions (Luke 16:22-23, Ephesians 4:9). In the Messianic realm, the Lord Jesus Christ designated the sign of the prophet Jonah as the unique miraculous type granted to authenticate his own bodily death, burial, and glorious resurrection on the third day (Matthew 12:39-40, Matthew 16:4, 1 Corinthians 15:3-4).
[3-6] The prophet describes his immersion in the abyssal depths, surrounded by ocean currents and submerged until his soul fainted, while seaweed enveloped his head (Psalm 42:7, Psalm 69:1-2). The descent reaches the roots of the mountains and the locks of the earth in Hell (Job 38:30, Psalm 88:6). At this point a doctrinal distinction is drawn between Jonah and the Messiah: while the Savior's flesh did not see corruption in the grave (Psalms 16:10, Acts 2:31, Acts 13:35-37), Jonah's body began to experience the process of physical decomposition before God resurrected his life {{quote:Jonah 2:6|but you brought my life up from corruption}} (Job 17:14, Psalms 30:3).
