All those possessed by demons in the New Testament profess faith in the divinity of Christ and tremble before Him (Mark 5:7, Acts 16:17, Acts 19:15, James 2:19). The Lord forbids demons from bearing witness to his identity to avoid being unequally yoked with darkness (2 Corinthians 6:14-15). Later, Jesus enters Simon Peter's house and heals his mother-in-law, who was lying with a fever (Mark 1:29-30), an event that demonstrates that the apostle Simon Peter was a married man (1 Corinthians 9:5).

[1-4] Jesus returns to Capernaum, and the news spreads throughout the city, with a crowd gathering that fills the house to the door. Jesus is constantly engaged in preaching the word (Mark 1:14, Mark 1:38). Four men bring a paralytic on a stretcher, but unable to get close because of the crowd or the press, they uncover the roof and lower the stretcher. It is observed that the function of the press or media is to make it difficult for people to come to Jesus and the Bible in search of the truth.
[5-12] Jesus declares to the paralytic: {{quote:Mark 2:5|Son, your sins are forgiven}}. The term "son" identifies the paralytic as a son of Abraham in a Jewish context (James 5:15). The educated scribes reasoned in their hearts, considering the statement blasphemous, since only God could forgive sins (Psalm 130:4, Micah 7:18). Jesus, knowing and perceiving in his spirit their thoughts (1 Chronicles 29:17, Romans 2:16), demonstrated his divinity by physically healing the man, instructing him to take his mat and go home (John 2:25). Seeing the man rise and go, glorifying God, the crowd was astonished.
[13-17] Jesus taught by the sea and called Levi, son of Alphaeus, who adopted the name Matthew. Alphaeus could also be the father of James (Mark 3:18). Levi left his job as a tax collector for Rome, an occupation despised by his countrymen because of the extortion of money. Jesus dines at Levi's house with tax collectors and sinners, the latter understood in the Old Testament context as people of the worst moral standing (Genesis 13:13) and not in the general Pauline sense (Romans 3:23). Faced with the murmuring of the scribes and Pharisees, Jesus declares that the healthy do not need a doctor, but the sick, since he has not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.
[18-22] When asked why the disciples of John and the Pharisees fast frequently while Jesus' disciples do not, the Lord replies that children cannot fast while their husband is with them. In the text, the children of the marriage represent the Jewish disciples, while the Bride of Christ is the Church (Ephesians 5:25-32), a distinction that also encompasses the virgins in the prophetic framework (Psalm 45:14, Revelation 14:4). When the Bridegroom is taken away, they will fast, a practice observed in the Church Age for important decisions (Acts 13:2-3, 2 Corinthians 6:5). Jesus illustrates the impossibility of mending an old garment with new cloth or putting new wine into old wineskins. The new wine represents the grape juice pressed from the bunch (Genesis 40:11, Isaiah 65:8) and typifies the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), requiring a new wineskin generated by the regeneration and spiritual circumcision of the soul from the flesh (Colossians 2:11-13).
[23-28] While passing through the grainfields on the Sabbath, the disciples pick heads of grain to satisfy their hunger, an action permitted by Mosaic law without constituting theft (Deuteronomy 23:25). In response to the Pharisees' accusation, Jesus appeals to the Scriptures, asking if they haven't read what David did when he was hungry and in need, entering the house of God in the days of Abiathar the high priest and eating the consecrated bread (1 Samuel 21:1-6, Leviticus 24:6-9). Jesus presents himself as the Son of David in exile before assuming the royal throne (2 Samuel 20, Luke 1:32). Jesus concludes by stating that {{quote: Mark 2:27|the Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath}}, proclaiming that the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.

[1-6] In the synagogue, a man with a withered hand is present, and the Pharisees watch the Lord to see if He will heal him on the Sabbath so they can accuse Him. Jesus calls the man to the center and asks His detractors whether it is lawful to do good or evil on the Sabbath, to save life or to kill (Proverbs 3:28, Leviticus 19:18). Looking around at them with anger and saddened by the hardness of their hearts, the Lord commands him to stretch out his hand. The man obeys in faith in the face of a physically impossible command, and his hand is immediately restored. After the miracle, the Pharisees go out and consult with the Herodians to destroy him.
[7-12] The Lord withdraws to the sea with his disciples, and a large crowd follows him from Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, and Idumea, from beyond the Jordan, and from the regions of Tyre and Sidon (Jeremiah 49:13, Ezekiel 35:15). Idumea represents Edom in biblical geography. The unclean spirits, seeing him, prostrate themselves before him and cry out, acknowledging his divinity and declaring that he is the Son of God (Mark 1:23-24, James 2:19). However, the Lord strictly rebukes them not to make Him known, thus avoiding being yoked with darkness or receiving testimony from the demonic world (2 Corinthians 6:14-15).
[13-19] Jesus goes up the mountain and calls twelve apostles to be with Him, sending them out to preach and giving them authority to heal diseases and cast out demons (Luke 9:1, 2 Corinthians 12:12). The list includes Simon Peter, James and John (surnamed Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder), Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew the tax collector, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who is explicitly singled out as the traitor who betrayed him (John 6:70-71, 2 Thessalonians 2:3).
[20, 21] The crowd again gathers in such a way that they cannot even eat bread. Hearing of this ceaseless activity, his earthly friends and relatives go out to arrest him, claiming that he is out of his mind (John 7:5, Acts 26:24). The Lord's family, not yet understanding his divine mission, tried to distance themselves from him, considering him delusional because of his ministerial zeal.
[22-27] The scribes who came from Jerusalem claim that the Lord has Beelzebub and that he casts out demons by the prince of demons (Matthew 12:24). Jesus calls them and speaks to them in parables, questioning how Satan can cast out Satan. The Lord teaches that if a kingdom or a house is divided against itself, that kingdom or house cannot stand, and that no one can plunder the treasures of a strong man in his house without first binding him (Isaiah 49:24-25).
[28-30] This passage expounds the doctrine of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, or the unforgivable sin. This sin was committed verbally and in the present tense while Christ was walking on earth {{quote: Mark 3:30|For they said, “He has an unclean spirit”}}, by verbally attributing the manifestations and miracles of the Holy Spirit to a demon or unclean spirit (Matthew 12:31-32, Luke 12:10).
[31-35] Jesus’ mother and brothers arrive at the place, and remaining outside, send word to call him while the crowd sits around him. Upon receiving the message that his family is looking for him outside, the Lord asks who his mother and brothers are. Looking at the disciples seated around him, the Lord declares that whoever does the will of God is his brother, sister, and mother (Matthew 12:48-50, Luke 8:21), subordinating earthly blood ties to spiritual obedience.

[1, 2] Jesus teaches again by the Sea of ​​Galilee, and gets into a boat because of the large crowd gathered on the shore (Mark 3:9). The Lord instructs the crowd through parables in his teaching.
[3-9] The Lord tells the parable of the sower, where the seed falls on four types of soil: along the path, on rocky ground, among thorns, and on good soil. This parable focuses primarily on the person of the Lord as the Sower (Matthew 13:37) and on the reaction of different human hearts to the word.
[10-20] Jesus explains to his disciples the mystery of the kingdom of God, reserving the revelation for those who listen in faith while concealing it from outsiders through parables (Isaiah 6:9-10, Acts 28:26-27). This dispensation toward Israel responds to the nation's spiritual blindness in rejecting its Messiah (Romans 11:8). In interpreting the parable, the seed is identified as the word of God (Luke 8:11), differentiating it from the parables of the kingdom of heaven focused on the literal Jewish kingdom (Matthew 13:11, Matthew 13:19). The four types of soil represent the condition of the human heart: the soil along the path reflects the negligent listener whose hardened heart allows Satan to take away the word that was sown in their hearts, represented by the birds of the air (Luke 8:12); the rocky ground represents those who receive the word with joy but stumble in the face of persecution; the thorns choke the word through the cares and riches of this world; And the good soil yields thirty, sixty, and a hundredfold.
[21-25] A light is not put under a basket or a bed, but on a lampstand to give light. The Lord warns the listeners to pay attention to what they hear, promising that to those who have, more will be given, and from those who do not have, even what they have will be taken away (Luke 11:28, Romans 10:17).
[26-29] The parable of the seed and its growth is unique to the Gospel of Mark and to the kingdom of God. In this passage, the sower represents the earthly soul winner who sows the good seed in the world without understanding the biological and internal process of divine growth (Ecclesiastes 11:5, 1 Corinthians 3:6-7). The earth produces fruit by itself, first the stalk, then the head, then the full grain in the head, until the harvest.
[30-34] The kingdom of God is like a mustard seed, which is the smallest of all seeds on earth. Yet when it grows up, it becomes the largest of garden plants and puts out large branches. Doctrinally, the mustard seed represents faith (Matthew 17:20, Luke 17:6), which undergoes an unusual transformation, becoming a tree that serves as a dwelling place for the birds of the air. The birds represent unclean spirits and demons (Mark 4:4, Mark 4:15, Revelation 18:2), typifying an apostate religious structure in connection with end-time Babylon and the kingdom of the Antichrist (Daniel 4:20-22, Ezekiel 31:3-6).
[35-41] At sunset, Jesus commands his disciples to cross to the other side of the sea, guaranteeing from the beginning their arrival at their destination. During the crossing, a great windstorm arises and fills the boat. Jesus was asleep in the stern on a cushion, manifesting his perfect humanity (1 Timothy 2:5, Psalm 121:4). Faced with the disciples' panic, the Lord rises and rebukes the wind and the sea, commanding, "Peace! Be still!" (Mark 4:39). The wind ceased, and a great calm ensued (Psalm 93:4, Psalm 107:29). By demonstrating his authority over creation, the Lord manifests his divinity and rebukes the lack of faith of his disciples (Colossians 1:17).

[1-20] In the land of the Gadarenes, the Lord delivers the demon-possessed man who lived among the tombs (Mark 5:1-3). Critical editions corrupt the biblical text by altering geographical names to equate the accounts, destroying the accuracy of the Received Text. The man possessed by an unclean spirit exhibits the physical and spiritual characteristics of demonization: residence in tombs, uncontrollable violence capable of breaking chains and shackles, nakedness, cries, and self-mutilation with stones (1 Kings 18:28, Matthew 8:28). An unclean spirit in the singular is composed of a multitude of spirits, identified in this case as Legion (Mark 5:9, Mark 1:23-24). Demons seek to inhabit human bodies because they are warm and moist (Matthew 12:43); Upon being expelled, they ask to join a herd of two thousand pigs rushing into the sea. The inhabitants of the region beg Jesus to leave their area, prioritizing the economic loss of their livestock over the restoration of a human being. The freed man is found sitting, clothed, and in his right mind (2 Timothy 1:7, Isaiah 61:10), typifying the transformation of regeneration. Although he desires to accompany the Lord, Jesus sends him home to testify among his people about the great things God has done (Acts 1:8).
[21-34] Upon returning to the other side, Jairus, one of the synagogue leaders, kneels before Jesus, pleading for his twelve-year-old daughter who is near death (Mark 5:21-23). On the way, a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years and who had spent all her money on doctors without getting better, but rather growing worse, approached from behind in the crowd (Leviticus 15:19-27). The coincidence of the number twelve in the girl's age and in the years of the woman's illness prophetically points to the condition of the nation of Israel in its state of spiritual impurity and unbelief (Isaiah 64:6, Romans 11:15). The woman touched the hem of the Lord's garment, believing she would be healed; the text dismisses the pagan notion of the veneration of relics or the existence of magical power in garments, attributing healing to faith placed directly in the person of Christ. Immediately, her flow of blood stopped. Perceiving that power had gone out from Him, Jesus asked who had touched His garments (Mark 5:30), not out of a lack of omniscience, but to give the woman the opportunity to speak out and give public testimony. When she confessed everything, trembling, the Lord comforted her, declaring: {{quote:Mark 5:34|Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace}}.
[35-43] While Jesus was still speaking, people came from the house of the synagogue leader, saying that the girl had died and questioning the need to trouble the Teacher any further. Jesus said to the synagogue leader: {{quote:Mark 5:36|Do not be afraid; only believe}}. The apparent discrepancy with Matthew's concise account, where it is mentioned that the daughter had already died (Matthew 9:18), is clarified by the progressive detail in Mark and Luke, showing that Jairus continued to plead with the Lord after receiving the news. Jesus did not allow anyone to follow him except his inner circle consisting of Peter, James, and John (Mark 9:2, Matthew 17:1), along with the girl's parents. Upon entering the house and seeing the commotion of the mourners who were weeping and wailing loudly, the Lord questions their weeping, stating that the girl is not dead, but asleep. The professional mourners mock Him, a typical behavior of the pagan who lacks hope in the face of death (1 Thessalonians 4:13). After sending the mockers out, Jesus takes the girl by the hand and speaks to her in Aramaic, saying, “Talitha koum,” which translates as, “Little girl, I say to you, arise.” The twelve-year-old girl gets up and walks immediately, causing great astonishment. The Lord strictly commands that no one know about it and orders that she be given something to eat.

[1-6] In his hometown, Jesus teaches in the synagogue in Nazareth, and the listeners stumble over him by asking if he is not the carpenter, the son of Mary, and identifying his brothers James, Joseph, Judas, and Simon, and his sisters (Mark 6:3). The mention of brothers and sisters confirms that Mary had other children with Joseph after the virgin birth of Christ, refuting the dogma of her perpetual virginity (Psalm 69:8, Matthew 1:25). The claim that the Greek word adelphos refers to cousins ​​or distant relatives lacks linguistic and exegetical support, since Scripture uses syngenes for cousin (Luke 1:36). Jesus declares that a prophet is not without honor except in his own country, and lays his hands on a few sick people to heal them (Mark 6:5). This fact demonstrates that the manifestation of the apostolic power of healing did not depend on the faith of the sick person, the Lord marveling at their unbelief (Mark 6:6).
[7-13] The Lord calls the twelve and sends them out two by two, granting them authority over unclean spirits. The apostles preach repentance (Mark 6:12), a message proclaimed to Israel before the revelation of the gospel of grace entrusted to the apostle Paul (Acts 20:24). They also anoint many sick people with oil and heal them (Mark 6:13), constituting an apostolic sign directed to the Jewish people (1 Corinthians 1:22, James 5:14-15). If any place does not receive them or listen to them, they are told to shake the dust off their feet as a testimony against them, with the warning that on the day of judgment it will be more tolerable for Sodom and Gomorrah than for that city (Mark 6:11).
[14-29] King Herod Antipas hears about Jesus and claims that John the Baptist has risen from the dead, while others believe he is Elijah or one of the prophets. John had rebuked Herod for living in adultery with Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip (Leviticus 18:16, Mark 6:18). Although Herod feared John, knowing him to be a righteous and holy man, and tried to protect him while listening to him willingly (Mark 6:20), Herodias was lying in wait, seeking his death. On Herod's birthday, Herodias's daughter dances before the princes and leaders of Galilee. Herod swore an oath to give her whatever she asked for, up to half his kingdom. Urged on by her mother, the girl asked for the head of John the Baptist on a platter. Herod, because of his oath and those who were with him at the table, had John beheaded in prison (Ecclesiastes 5:6). John's disciples took his body and laid it in a tomb.
[30-44] The apostles gathered with Jesus and told him all they had done and taught. The Lord invited them to rest in a deserted place, but the crowd followed them on foot. Jesus had compassion on them because they were like sheep without a shepherd (Mark 6:34). At sunset, the disciples suggested sending the crowd away to buy bread, but the Lord commanded: {{quote:Mark 6:37|You give them something to eat}}. Faced with the human impossibility of buying two hundred denarii worth of bread, they find five loaves and two fish. Jesus tells the crowd to sit down in groups of hundreds and fifties on the green grass. Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looks up to heaven, blesses them, breaks the loaves, and gives them to the disciples. About five thousand men eat, and they collect twelve basketfuls of broken pieces (Mark 6:43). Doctrinally, the word of God and the servant must be broken to be a blessing (2 Corinthians 12:1-8), this miracle foreshadowing how God will feed the Jewish remnant in the wilderness during the Great Tribulation (Micah 7:14, Revelation 12:6).
[45-52] Jesus compels his disciples to get into the boat and go on ahead to Bethsaida, while he dismisses the crowd and goes up on the mountain to pray (Mark 6:46). In the fourth watch of the night, the boat is in the middle of the sea, buffeted by the contrary wind. Jesus comes to them, walking on the sea, and tries to pass them by (Mark 6:48). Prophetically, the Lord's position on the mountain praying while his disciples are on the water portrays Christ interceding in heaven as Israel goes through the Great Tribulation, returning in the fourth watch or Second Coming (Revelation 19:11). The disciples see him walking on the sea and cry out, thinking he is a ghost, but the Lord reassures them, saying, “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.” When they get into the boat, the wind dies down, and they are utterly amazed because their hearts were hardened and they had not understood the miracle of the loaves (Mark 6:52).
[53-56] Upon crossing to the other side, they reach the land of Gennesaret and anchor on the shore. The inhabitants immediately recognize him and travel throughout the province, bringing the sick on beds to wherever they heard he was. They placed the sick in the streets and begged him to let them touch even the fringe of his garment, and all who touched it were healed (Mark 6:56). Doctrinally, this recognition and widespread healing at Gennesaret foreshadows the Second Coming of Jesus Christ, when the nation of Israel will recognize its Messiah and be restored in a single day (Zechariah 12:10, Zechariah 13:1, Romans 11:26).

[1-13] The confrontation between the Lord Jesus and the scribes and Pharisees from Jerusalem arose from the ceremonial washing of hands. The tradition of the elders demanded ritual purifications that were not part of Mosaic Law, but rather precepts added by human religion (Colossians 2:8). By questioning the disciples' conduct for eating bread with uncommon or unwashed hands, the religious leaders were placing the commandments of men above the authority of the divine Word (Isaiah 29:13). This passage represents a powerful denunciation of the establishment of ecclesiastical traditions imposed as dogma over the Holy Scriptures (Mark 7:7). The Lord presents a concrete example with the practice of "Corban," by which a son was allowed to declare consecrated to God the portion of his property intended for the support of his elderly parents. Thus, rabbinic tradition nullified the divine commandment to honor one's father and mother (Exodus 20:12, Deuteronomy 5:16), which carried the death penalty for anyone who cursed their parents (Exodus 21:17, Leviticus 20:9). Religious leaders promoted greed and filial neglect under the guise of a religious vow (Proverbs 20:20, Proverbs 28:24), invalidating Scripture in favor of their own human standards.
[14-23] After confronting the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, the Lord summons the crowd to impart a teaching on the true nature of spiritual defilement. No external element that enters through the mouth can defile a person's soul, since it does not pass to the heart, but to the stomach, and is expelled in the latrine. What truly defiles a person is that which comes from within their fallen nature. From the human heart spring evil thoughts, adultery, fornication, murder, theft, greed, wickedness, deceit, lust, the evil eye, blasphemy, pride, and foolishness. This list demonstrates the inherent depravity of unregenerate humanity (Matthew 7:11) and confirms that external purification rites or ceremonial washings are ineffective in cleansing the conscience or transforming the spirit. True impurity lies in the ungodly heart's inclination toward sin, which requires divine grace and spiritual illumination rather than human rituals.
[24-30] In the region of Tyre and Sidon, the Lord enters a house seeking to remain unrecognized, but a Greek woman, Syrophoenician by birth and Canaanite by ethnicity (Genesis 10:15), comes upon learning of His presence and prostrates herself at His feet. The woman requests the expulsion of an unclean spirit that tormented her daughter. In response to this request, the Lord establishes the dispensational order of earthly ministry, stating that it is necessary to feed the children first and that it is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs (Mark 7:27). Far from being offended or reacting with pride, the woman demonstrates a profound understanding of her position before the Lord and acknowledges the truth of the divine Word, responding that even the little dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs. By humbling herself, accepting her condition, and clinging in faith to the Lord's grace, she obtains the immediate release of her daughter from afar, demonstrating that humble faith breaks down barriers and receives the divine blessing that the religious leaders of Israel rejected (Matthew 15:21-28, Acts 13:46).
[31-37] Leaving the confines of Tyre and Sidon, the Lord returns to the Sea of ​​Galilee, passing through the region of the Decapolis. There, a man who was deaf and mute was brought to him, and he was begged to lay his hand on him. The Lord took him aside from the crowd, put His fingers into the man's ears, spat, and touched his tongue. Looking up to heaven, He sighed and uttered the Aramaic word "Ephphatha," which means "be opened." At that moment, the man's ears were opened, his tongue was unbound, and he began to speak clearly. Although the Lord commanded them not to divulge the event, those present proclaimed the miracle with even greater fervor, marveling greatly to see that the Lord does all things well, making the deaf hear and the mute speak in fulfillment of the Messianic prophecies (Isaiah 35:5-6, Revelation 1:8).

[1-9] In the second multiplication of the loaves, the Lord shows His compassion for the multitude of four thousand men who had remained with Him for three days without food. Anticipating that they might faint on the return journey, fasting, the Lord takes the seven available loaves and a few small fish, gives thanks, breaks them, and distributes them through His disciples. The collection of seven large baskets filled with leftover fragments demonstrates God's omnipotence to supply physical need in the wilderness. Typologically, this miracle foreshadows the miraculous food that the Lord will provide for the Jewish remnant preserved in the wilderness for three and a half years during the Tribulation (Revelation 12:14). Unlike the first multiplication of the loaves, the crowd sits directly on the ground, and larger baskets are collected, demonstrating the Lord's sovereign care for those who seek His teaching.
[10-13] After moving to the region of Dalmanutha, the Pharisees approach to argue with the Lord and test Him, demanding a sign from heaven. The Lord sighs deeply in His spirit at the hardness of heart of the religious leaders and declares that no sign will be given to this generation. From a biblical hermeneutical perspective, this incomplete statement recorded in Mark must be interpreted in light of the full account in the Gospel of Matthew, where it is specified that the only sign granted is that of the prophet Jonah (Matthew 16:4). This sign typologically points to the Lord's death, burial, and resurrection on the third day (Matthew 12:39-40). Having witnessed numerous miracles, healings, and multiplications of food, the Pharisees' demand did not stem from a sincere desire for faith, but from a malicious unbelief that sought to tempt the Messiah.
[14-21] As they crossed to the other side of the Sea of ​​Galilee, the disciples realized they had forgotten to bring bread, having only a loaf of bread with them in the boat. The Lord took the opportunity to warn them to beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and the yeast of Herod, which symbolized false doctrine and hypocrisy. However, the disciples reasoned incorrectly among themselves, concluding that the warning was due to the lack of physical bread. The Lord rebuked them for the hardness of their hearts, questioning their lack of spiritual understanding after having witnessed the gathering of twelve baskets for the feeding of the five thousand and seven baskets for the feeding of the four thousand. The teaching emphasizes that concern for material things should not cloud trust in the Lord's provision.
[22-26] Upon arriving at Bethsaida, they bring a blind man before the Lord, begging Him to touch him. The Lord takes the man by the hand, leads him outside the village, spits on his eyes, and lays His hands on him. The act of spitting is a gesture of contempt and ignominy in Scripture (Numbers 12:14, Deuteronomy 25:9, Job 30:10, Isaiah 50:6), employed on this occasion as a test of humility and an examination of faith to verify whether the man was willing to submit to the process without taking offense. When questioned about his vision, the man says he sees people as walking trees, reflecting the biblical analogy where human beings are compared to trees (Matthew 3:10, Matthew 7:17). Through a second laying on of hands, the Lord fully restores his sight, teaching that divine healing can operate progressively according to His sovereign will, before commanding him not to enter the village or make it known.
[27-33] On the way to the villages of Caesarea Philippi, the Lord questions His disciples about the identity the crowd attributes to Him, receiving answers that equate Him with John the Baptist, Elijah, or one of the prophets. When questioned directly about Himself, Peter declares that He is the Christ. The Lord then begins to teach them openly the dispensational necessity of the Son of Man suffering greatly, being rejected by the elders, the chief priests, and the scribes, being killed, and rising again on the third day. At this announcement, Peter takes Him aside and begins to rebuke Him, considering the suffering an unacceptable destiny. The Lord severely rebukes Peter, identifying his stance with satanic influence, for his thoughts were not focused on the things of God, but on the things of men, as he opposed the redemptive plan of the cross.
[34-38] Summoning the crowd along with His disciples, the Lord establishes the fundamental requirements of true discipleship, declaring that whoever wants to follow Him must deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow Him. Seeking to preserve earthly life through the pleasures of the flesh and the rejection of suffering leads to the loss of the soul and spiritual ruin (Mark 8:35). No temporal gain or possession of the whole world can compensate for the loss of salvation or serve as a ransom for the human soul. Finally, the Lord warns that anyone who is ashamed of Him and His words in the midst of this adulterous and sinful generation will suffer the shame of the Son of man when He returns in the glory of His Father surrounded by the holy angels (Revelation 19:11-14).

[1-13] The statement about seeing the kingdom of God before experiencing death is chronologically connected to the Transfiguration that occurred six days later (Matthew 17:1, Mark 9:2), a number which, along with the allusion to eight days (Luke 9:28), points to the seventh day as a prophetic type of the Lord's glorious coming. The mountain of the Transfiguration typologically represents Mount Sinai (Exodus 3:1-4, 1 Kings 19:9-12), which constitutes the common geographical and spiritual point between Moses and Elijah (Malachi 4:4-5). In this event, the Transfiguration alters the Lord's physical appearance, manifesting the divine light of creation (Psalm 74:16) through garments as radiant and white as snow. The cloud of glory that covers them and the voice of the Father confirm the Son's supremacy over the law and the prophets, commanding them to listen to Him. Upon descending from the mountain, the Lord forbids Peter, James, and John to divulge the event until the Son of Man rises from the dead, a concept the disciples sought to understand among themselves, while also clarifying for them the fulfillment and prophetic restoration associated with Elijah.
[14-29] Upon meeting with the other disciples the next day (Luke 9:37), an astonished crowd observes the Lord (Mark 9:15), perceiving on His face a lingering radiance similar to that of Moses upon descending from the mountain (Exodus 34:30). A father presents his son possessed by a mute spirit that convulses him, makes him foam at the mouth, grind his teeth, and wither away, a condition described in the Gospels as lunacy and sadomasochistic demonic torment (Matthew 17:15). Faced with the disciples' inability to free the boy, the Lord rebukes the unbelief of that generation. The young man's father cries out in tears, expressing his faith and need: {{quote:Mark 9:24|Lord, I believe; help my unbelief}}. The Lord rebukes the unclean spirit, commanding it to come out and never enter him again. When the disciples privately inquire about their failure to cast it out, the Lord teaches them that this kind of unclean spirit, characterized by higher ranks of wickedness and authority (Ephesians 6:12), can only be cast out through prayer and fasting, which involves the voluntary deprivation of food to seek God's power.
[30-41] As they traveled through Galilee toward Capernaum, the Lord privately teaches His disciples about His surrender into the hands of men, His death, and His resurrection on the third day—a message they were unable to grasp for fear of questioning Him. Once at the house, the Lord questions them about the argument they had on the road regarding who was the greatest among them. Taking a child in His arms, the Lord establishes the principle of service, declaring that the first must be last and the servant of all, so that receiving a child in His name is equivalent to receiving Him and the Father who sent Him. Later, when John intervenes, mentioning that they had forbidden a man to cast out demons in His name because he did not follow the group of apostles, the Lord commands them not to hinder him, teaching that no one who performs miracles in His name can speak ill of Him and that whoever is not against us is for us.
[42-50] Recognizing the seriousness of spiritual stumbling is imperative, for causing one of the little ones who believe in the Lord to stumble carries such a severe judgment that it would be preferable to be thrown into the sea with a millstone tied around one's neck. The Lord demands a radical renunciation of sin, teaching that it is preferable to cut off a hand, a foot, or pluck out an eye rather than keep one's whole body and be cast into Hell (Mark 9:44, "Where their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched"). In the lake of fire and brimstone (Isaiah 66:24, Revelation 20:10), the ungodly soul suffers decay and loss of human form, becoming deformed into a vile creature that experiences eternal torment without being consumed. Every individual will be salted with fire, and every sacrifice salted with salt (Leviticus 2:13), demonstrating that divine judgment will inexorably purify or consume. Finally, the Lord exhorts us to have salt in ourselves and to maintain peace among our brothers and sisters.

[1-12] On the journey to the borders of Judea across the Jordan, which foreshadows the Lord's coming and the route of the ark from Sinai through Edom, the Pharisees approach to tempt him by questioning him about the lawfulness of divorce. The question recorded in Mark is incomplete compared to the parallel account in Matthew, where it is specified whether it is lawful to divorce a woman for any reason (Matthew 19:3), a hermeneutical principle that requires interpreting an incomplete statement in light of a complete one. Faced with the Mosaic concession of the precept of divorce due to the hardness of heart of the people (Deuteronomy 24:1-4), the Lord refers to the original institution of marriage at creation, where God constituted man and woman as one flesh (Genesis 1:27, Genesis 2:24). Marriage constitutes a union in which flesh is joined to flesh (1 Corinthians 6:15-16, Ephesians 5:30-31), transcending a mere ritual or human ceremony. Scripture establishes legitimate grounds for the dissolution of the marriage bond, such as death (Romans 7:1-3), fornication or adultery (Matthew 19:9, 1 Corinthians 6:16), and desertion by the unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:15). When a separation occurs due to these grounds for dissolution, the union is broken, and the aggrieved person does not commit adultery by remarrying, just as the Lord issued a certificate of divorce and intervened by separating himself from Israel because of its idolatrous anointing (Isaiah 50:1, Jeremiah 3:8, Hosea 2:2).
[13-16] When some children were brought before the Lord to be touched by him, the disciples rebuked those who brought them, provoking the Lord's indignation, who proclaimed the welcome of the little ones {{quote:Mark 10:14|Let the children come to me}}. The kingdom of God belongs to those who receive it with the disposition, simplicity, and innocence of a child. This teaching emphasizes that access to the divine kingdom is not obtained through ritual merits, human intellect, or self-righteousness, but through a humble and dependent faith that embraces the Lord's grace without religious pretensions.
[17-31] A wealthy and prominent man comes running and kneeling before the Lord to ask Him what he must do to inherit eternal life. Addressed as a good teacher, the Lord responds by questioning the attribution of goodness, declaring that there is no one good but one, who is God, stating that if He were not God, He would be a sinner like any other human being. The Lord quotes the commandments concerning love of neighbor (Exodus 20:12-16), intentionally omitting the commandments concerning God and the prohibition against covetousness. Although the young man claims to have kept those precepts since his youth, the Lord looks at him with love and points out His central failing: selling all his possessions, distributing them to the poor, taking up his cross, and following Him. This demand exposes the idol in the heart of the rich young man, who withdraws saddened, preferring earthly riches to the Lord (Matthew 6:24). The Lord then warns of the immense difficulty the rich face in entering the kingdom of God, employing the parable of the camel and the eye of the needle (Mark 10:25). To the astonishment of the disciples, who, according to the Old Testament perspective, assumed that material prosperity was an unequivocal sign of divine blessing and justice (Job 1:1-3, 1 Kings 3:11-13), the Lord clarifies that what is impossible for men is possible for God through the miracle of being born again. Finally, in response to Peter's question about the reward for having left everything, the Lord promises to receive a hundredfold in this life: houses, brothers, sisters, mothers, children, and lands, along with persecutions, and in the age to come, eternal life.
[32-45] On the ascent to Jerusalem, the Lord walks ahead of the disciples as they experience awe and fear. For the third time, the Lord reveals to them with prophetic accuracy the details of His suffering, declaring that the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes, condemned to death, handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, flogged, spat upon, killed, and raised on the third day (Mark 10:33-34). In the midst of this announcement, James and John, the sons of Zebedee, request to sit at His right and left in His glory. The Lord questions them about whether they can drink the cup He drinks and be baptized with the baptism He receives, announcing that they will indeed share in His suffering. Faced with the indignation of the other ten disciples, the Lord teaches the principle of leadership in the divine kingdom: while the rulers of the Gentiles exercise power and dominion over their subjects, in the church, whoever wants to be great must be a servant, and whoever wants to be first must be the servant of all, imitating the Son of Man, who did not come to be served, but to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many (Isaiah 53:10-11).
[46-52] As they left Jericho, blind Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus, sat by the roadside begging. Hearing that Jesus of Nazareth was approaching, he began to cry out in a loud voice, identifying Him as the Son of David and pleading for mercy. Although many rebuked him, telling him to be quiet, the man cried out with even greater fervor until the Lord stopped and commanded that he be called. Bartimaeus threw off his beggar's cloak, which represented the garment of his old nature and self-righteousness (Ephesians 4:22), got up, and went before the Lord. When questioned about his request, the blind man asked to regain his sight, receiving immediate healing through God's word in response to his faith. Unlike the rich young man who strayed from the truth, Bartimaeus regained his sight and followed the Lord on the path, becoming a testament to redeeming grace.

[1-10] In his triumphal entry into Jerusalem as the Jewish King, the Lord sends two disciples to bring a donkey, in fulfillment of Zechariah 9:9 and Genesis 49:11. Typologically, the donkey tied outside the gate, at a place where two roads meet, represents the lost sinner bound by Satan outside of Christ (who is the gate), at the crossroads between the wide road and the narrow road. When unbound by the Gospel, the sinner is led to the Lord for His service. The crowd pays homage by carpeting the road with their garments and palm branches, a gesture associated with the Lord's victory and glorious coming (Revelation 7:9, Leviticus 23:40, Zechariah 14:16-18). The cry of "Hosanna," derived from Psalm 118:25-26, acknowledges the messianic kingdom of David offered to the nation of Israel.
[11-14] On Sunday evening, the Lord enters the temple, observes everything, and leaves for Bethany with the twelve. The Gospel according to Mark provides the precise chronological sequence of Passion week. The next day, walking from Bethany, the Lord is hungry and sees a fig tree in the distance with leaves. The state of the fig tree represents the profession without possession or self-righteousness of human religion (Genesis 3:7). Since figs appear on fig trees before or along with the leaves, the presence of foliage presupposed fruit. Finding no fruit, the Lord curses the fig tree, declaring that no one will ever eat its fruit again—an act symbolizing judgment on the self-righteous and professing Israel that lacked the fruit of faith (Jeremiah 24:2, Luke 13:6-9).
[15-19] Upon arriving in Jerusalem, the Lord performs the second cleansing of the temple (the first having taken place at the beginning of His ministry in John 2:13-16), an event prophetically linked to His second coming and the purifying judgment (Malachi 3:2-4). By driving out the merchants and overturning the tables of the money changers, the Lord denounces that they have turned His house of prayer into a den of thieves (Isaiah 56:7, Jeremiah 7:11), placing greedy profit and the idolatry of money before divine worship (Colossians 3:5). In response, the scribes and chief priests sought to destroy Him out of fear of His authority, while the crowd listened attentively to His teaching. As night fell, the Lord again left the city.
[20-26] As they passed by the fig tree again on Tuesday morning, the disciples observed that it had withered from the roots. The withered fig tree represents the spiritual condition of the nation of Israel, which was judicially withered and unable to bear fruit after rejecting its Messiah (Ezekiel 17:9-10, Hosea 3:4), remaining in that state until its future restoration. To Peter's astonishment, the Lord exhorted them, saying, "Have faith in God." It also teaches about the power of faith to move mountains and the necessity of forgiving offenders in prayer, so that the heavenly Father may also forgive offenses.
[27-33] Back at the temple in Jerusalem, the chief priests, scribes, and elders approached the Lord to question the authority with which He performed these actions. In response, the Lord posed a conditional question to them about the baptism of John the Baptist, asking whether it was from heaven or from men. The religious leaders pondered among themselves in obvious hypocrisy: if they claimed it was from heaven, they risked being questioned for not having believed Him; and if they said it was from men, they feared the people, for everyone considered John a true prophet. By evasively answering that they did not know, the Lord refused to declare to them the authority with which He acted, exposing the dishonesty of those who rejected divine revelation in order to preserve their own religious position.

[1-12] In the parable of the wicked tenants, the Lord presents the story of salvation and humanity's rebellion against divine authority. The man who plants the vineyard, fences it, digs the winepress, and builds a tower represents God the Father, who entrusts His creation and the institution of Israel to the religious leaders. The owner's departure to a distant land symbolizes the Lord's heavenly dwelling place. The servants sent successively to receive the fruit represent the Old Testament prophets, who were beaten, stoned, and killed by the unrepentant nation (Amos 3:7, Jeremiah 38:6). Finally, the sending of His beloved Son shows the ultimate outpouring of divine grace; nevertheless, the tenants conspire to kill Him and seize the inheritance, foreshadowing the conspiracy of earthly rulers against the Messiah (Psalm 2:2-3, Acts 4:26-28). The destruction of the tenants and the handing over of the vineyard to others signifies divine judgment upon the apostate hierarchy. The quotation from Psalm 118:22 identifies the Lord Jesus as the stone rejected by the builders that has become the cornerstone, the cornerstone that will crush the kingdoms of the world at His glorious coming (Daniel 2:34-35, Acts 4:11).
[13-17] The alliance between the Pharisees, religious conservatives, and the Herodians, political liberals, seeks to trap the Lord in His words through a diplomatic snare (Proverbs 10:19). After employing flattery and hypocrisy regarding His impartiality, they pose the loaded question about whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar. If the Lord answered negatively, the Herodians would accuse Him of sedition before Rome; If he answered affirmatively, the Pharisees would alienate the Jewish people who abhorred the Roman yoke (Deuteronomy 17:14-15). Knowing their hypocrisy, the Lord asks for a denarius and inquires whose image and inscription it is. When they answer that it is Caesar's, the Lord dictates the transcendent principle: {{quote:Mark 12:17|Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's}}. This statement exposes the negligence of the religious leaders, who paid monetary taxes but withheld the devotion, justice, and love due to God (Matthew 23:23).
[18-27] The Sadducees, religious materialists who denied the resurrection, angels, and spirits (Acts 23:8), approach the Lord with a hypothetical case concerning the law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5-6). They present the dilemma of a woman who was successively married to seven brothers who died without leaving offspring, and they question which of them she will be married to in the resurrection. The Lord refutes their skepticism by pointing out two fundamental deficiencies: ignorance of the Scriptures and ignorance of God's power {{quote:Mark 12:27|He is not the God of the dead, but the God of the living}}. In the resurrection from the dead, human beings will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like the angels in heaven. To demonstrate the resurrection from the writings of Moses, which the Sadducees accepted, the Lord quotes Exodus 3:6, where God proclaims Himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Since God is the God of the living and not of the dead, the patriarchs remain conscious and await bodily restoration (Luke 16:22-31, 1 Corinthians 15:52).
[28-34] A scribe, impressed by the Lord's answer to the Sadducees, approaches to ask Him which is the most important commandment within the precepts of Mosaic Law. The Lord responds by quoting the fundamental teaching of Deuteronomy 6:4-5 and Leviticus 19:18. The first commandment requires loving the Lord with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength, while the second establishes loving your neighbor as yourself. These two commandments summarize the entirety of the Decalogue and the law of God: the first four govern our relationship with God, and the last six govern our relationship with our neighbor. The scribe discreetly and appropriately recognizes that loving God and neighbor surpasses all burnt offerings and ritual sacrifices, to which the Lord declares that he is not far from the kingdom of God, demonstrating the primacy of spiritual devotion over formal ritualism.
[35-37] Teaching in the temple, the Lord challenges the scribes' superficial interpretation of the Messiah's origin, which limited him to simply being the son of David. Citing Psalm 110:1 under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, the Lord explains how David himself calls the Messiah his Lord, declaring that the Lord told his Lord to sit at His right hand until He makes His enemies a footstool for His feet. If David in spirit calls Him Lord, biblical theology demonstrates that Christ is not merely a human descendant of David, but God incarnate and the eternal Son of God in the Scriptures (Romans 1:3-4). While the religious rulers rejected this revelation of His deity, the common people listened to Him with pleasure.
[38-40] The Lord publicly warns the crowd about the conduct of the scribes, who sought social recognition and religious exaltation. These leaders delighted in walking around in long robes, receiving greetings in the marketplaces, occupying the best seats in the synagogues, and the places of honor at banquets. Beneath a facade of piety characterized by lengthy prayers, these hypocrites devoured widows' houses by exploiting their resources and manipulating religious vows (Matthew 23:14, Luke 20:47). This warning denounces the greed and pride of institutionalized religion, declaring that such leaders will receive greater condemnation in divine judgment.
[41-44] Observing the offering box in the temple (2 Kings 12:9), the Lord sees how the crowd was putting money into the treasury and how many rich people were contributing large sums from their abundance. A poor widow approaches and puts in two small coins, equivalent to a quarter or half a cent in the economy of the time. Calling His disciples together, the Lord teaches that this poor widow gave more than all those who contributed to the treasury, since the rich gave from their surplus, while she, in the midst of her extreme poverty, gave all she had, all her livelihood. The teaching emphasizes that God's evaluation of offerings is not measured by the quantitative amount, but by the degree of sacrifice and devotion of the heart towards God.

[1-4] As the Lord left the temple, the disciples pondered the magnitude and beauty of the stones and buildings of the sanctuary. To their amazement, the Lord pronounced the ruin of the temple in Jerusalem, declaring that not one stone would be left upon another that would not be thrown down. While seated on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John, and Andrew privately asked Him when these things would occur and what sign there would be when they were all to be fulfilled. The revelation the Lord imparted to this close group of disciples did not concern the church age or the building up of the body of Christ, but rather the future destiny of the Jewish nation and the prophetic events that would precede His glorious coming (Matthew 24:1-3, Acts 1:6).
[5-13] The Lord began His discourse by warning that no one should deceive you, for many would come in His name claiming to be the Christ. The announcement of wars, rumors of wars, uprisings of nations and kingdoms, earthquakes in various places, and famines signify only the beginning of sorrows. The disciples and the Jewish remnant will suffer betrayals before councils, beatings in synagogues, and appearances before governors and kings for the sake of the Messiah, as a testimony to them. The gospel of the kingdom must first be preached to all nations before the end (Matthew 24:14). Upon being betrayed, the Holy Spirit will speak through them without the need for premeditated defense. The persecution will involve betrayal among brothers, parents, and children, culminating in widespread hatred against believers for the sake of the Lord's name. The doctrinal affirmation of salvation in this period states that {{quote: Mark 13:13|but he who endures to the end will be saved}}. This perseverance does not describe the eternal security of the believer in the church age—who is sealed by the Holy Spirit until the day of redemption (Ephesians 4:30) and confirmed blameless (1 Corinthians 1:7-8)—but rather the demand for faith and faithfulness that the Jewish remnant will face during the Great Tribulation.
[14-23] The turning point in the Great Tribulation occurs when the abomination of desolation, spoken of by the prophet Daniel, appears, set up where it should not be. At this time, the inhabitants of Judea must flee to the mountains immediately. No one on the housetop should go down to take anything from their house, and no one in the field should return to get their clothes. At the same time, they must cry out, “Woe to pregnant women and nursing mothers in those days!” The Lord urges us to pray that the exodus will not occur in winter, for those days will be marked by affliction so severe that it has never existed since the beginning of creation, nor will it ever exist again (Jeremiah 30:7, Daniel 12:1). If the Lord had not shortened those days, no one would be saved; but for the sake of the elect, whom He chose, He shortened the days. This shortening implies a cosmic alteration in the Earth's rotation that reduces the length of the day (Isaiah 24:20, Amos 8:9). The elect in this context represent the preserved Jewish remnant, not the believers of the body of Christ (Romans 11:25-28). During this time, false Christs and false prophets will perform signs and wonders to deceive, if possible, even the elect.
[24-27] Immediately after the affliction of those days, there will be astronomical disturbances in the heavens: the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken (Isaiah 13:10, Joel 2:31). Then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory (Revelation 1:7). At that time, the Lord will send His angels to gather His elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of the heavens. The gathering of the elect by angels constitutes the gathering of the Jewish remnant at the end of the Tribulation, in contrast to the rapture of the church where the Lord Himself descends to meet believers in the air (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17).
[28-31] Through the parable of the fig tree, the Lord imparts a prophetic lesson about the nearness of the kingdom. When the fig tree branch becomes tender and puts forth leaves, it is recognized that summer is near; likewise, by beholding the fulfillment of these signs, it is understood that the Lord's coming is at hand. The generation that witnesses the events of the Tribulation will not pass away until all these things occur first. The Lord emphasizes the absolute and unchanging authority of divine revelation by declaring that heaven and earth will pass away, but His words will not pass away (Psalm 119:89). This statement guarantees the faithfulness of God's promises both for the preservation of Israel and for the complete fulfillment of the redemptive plan.
[32-37] Regarding the day and hour of the glorious coming, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father (Matthew 24:36). This ignorance of the exact day concerns the times and seasons of the Lord's coming and does not eliminate the duty to discern prophetic times (1 Thessalonians 5:1-4). The instruction given exhorts us to watch, be alert, and pray, since the time is unknown. The Lord illustrates the believer's attitude by comparing himself to a man who, going on a journey, left his house, gave authority to his servants, assigned each one their task, and commanded the doorkeeper to keep watch. The imperative command demands constant vigilance, for no one knows when the master of the house will return: whether at nightfall, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning, referring to the four watches of the night. The Lord concludes by reaffirming the warning to all believers of all ages: be watchful.

[1-11] Two days before Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the chief priests and scribes sought to arrest the Lord by deception in order to kill Him, fearing a riot among the people. In Jewish chronology (6 p.m. to 6 p.m.), temporal references place the crucifixion on Wednesday, with the Lord remaining in the tomb for three days and three nights until His resurrection at the end of Saturday. In Bethany, at the house of Simon the leper, a woman broke an alabaster jar of very expensive perfume made of pure nard and poured it on the Lord's head. The objection regarding the supposed waste of three hundred denarii that could have been given to the poor comes from Judas Iscariot, whose downfall is linguistically linked to the word "waste" (Revelation 9:11). The Lord commended the woman's good deed, declaring that she had anointed His body in advance of His burial. Later, Judas makes a pact with the chief priests to betray the Lord in exchange for money.
[12-25] On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb was sacrificed, the disciples inquire about the preparation of the meal. The Lord sends two of them into the city, instructing them that a man carrying a jar of water will meet them and lead them to a large upper room already prepared. The celebration takes place before the people's usual time so that the Lord himself may act as the true Passover Lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7). During the meal, the Lord reveals that one of the twelve who dips the bread with him in the dish will betray him. In instituting the Lord's Supper, he takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it, saying, {{quote:Mark 14:22|Take, eat; This is my body, then offering the cup as His blood of the new testament shed for many, and affirming that he will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until the day he drinks it anew in the kingdom of God.
[26-31] After singing a hymn, they go to the Mount of Olives, where the Lord announces that everyone will be offended because of Him that very night, fulfilling the prophecy of striking the shepherd and scattering the sheep (Zechariah 13:7). Despite the promise to go before them to Galilee after His resurrection, Peter vehemently affirms that he will not be offended even if everyone else is. Faced with the precise prophecy that he will deny Him three times before the rooster crows twice, Peter passionately reiterates that he will not deny Him even if he must die with Him, a stance seconded by all the disciples.
[32-42] In the Garden of Gethsemane, whose name alludes to the olive press where the Lord experiences extreme anguish, He asks Peter, James, and John to keep watch while He kneels in prayer. The Lord begs the Father to take this cup from Him if possible, submitting Himself entirely to the divine will. Finding the disciples asleep three times, the Lord rebukes Peter for not having been able to stay awake for one hour, warning that the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak, until He announces that the hour has come and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.
[43-52] Judas appears leading a crowd armed with swords and clubs sent by the religious hierarchy, consummating the betrayal with a kiss. As they seized the Lord, Peter drew his sword and struck Malchus, the high priest's servant, cutting off his ear (John 18:10), an action the Lord stopped to fulfill the Scriptures. All the disciples deserted him and fled, fulfilling the prophetic scattering. Likewise, a young man covered with a sheet over his naked body followed him, but when seized by the servants, he threw off the sheet and fled naked.
[53-65] Brought before the high priest, an illegal night trial was held before the council, which sought false testimony to condemn the Lord to death, but found no agreement. When directly questioned about whether He is the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One, the Lord affirms His deity, saying, "I am," and prophesies the vision of the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, coming on the clouds of heaven at His second coming (Daniel 7:13-14). The high priest tears his garments, accusing Him of blasphemy, and the council condemns Him as worthy of death, subjecting Him to spitting, beatings, and insults.
[66-72] While Peter is down in the courtyard warming himself by the fire, a servant girl of the high priest and others present point him out as a follower of Jesus of Nazareth because of his Galilean accent. Peter denies knowing the Lord three times, accompanying his third denial with oaths and curses to distance his testimony. When the rooster crowed for the second time, Peter remembered the word spoken by the Lord, and noticing his fall, he went out and wept bitterly in repentance.

[1-15] At dawn, the chief priests held a council with the elders, the scribes, and the entire council to hand the Lord over bound to Pontius Pilate. Since the Jewish hierarchy lacked the authority under Roman rule to carry out capital punishment, they brought charges against Him; however, when the Roman governor questioned Him about His kingship, the Lord answered affirmatively and remained silent in the face of the false accusations. Following the custom of releasing a prisoner during the festival, Pilate attempted to free the Lord, but the crowd, incited by the religious leaders, demanded the release of the prisoner Barabbas and the crucifixion of the Messiah. Seeking to appease the people through a compromise, Pilate handed over Barabbas and ordered the Lord to be flogged before crucifying Him. Roman flogging, carried out with whips of multiple strands fitted with fragments of bone and metal, tore the victim's flesh without the limit of forty lashes of Mosaic law (Deuteronomy 25:2-3), prophetically fulfilling the disfigurement of the Suffering Servant (Isaiah 52:14).
[16-20] The soldiers lead the Lord into the courtyard of the Praetorium and summon the entire company. Dressed in a purple robe, they place a woven crown of thorns on His head and put a reed in His right hand as a false scepter (Matthew 27:29-30), striking His head with it to pierce the thorns without injuring their hands. This mockery by the Gentiles scorns the royal authority of the Messiah, who at His second coming will rule and inflict judgment on the nations with a rod of iron (Revelation 2:27, Revelation 19:15). After mocking Him, they strip Him of His purple robes, dress Him in His own garments, and lead Him out to be crucified.
[21-32] On the way, the soldiers force Simon of Cyrene to carry the Lord's cross. Upon arriving at the place called Golgotha, they offer Him wine mixed with myrrh to drink (Mark 15:23), a concoction that the Lord refuses to take, unlike the vinegar later offered to numb the pain (Matthew 27:34, John 19:29). Crucified at the third hour, nine in the morning, the soldiers divided His garments among themselves by casting lots (Psalm 22:18), placing above His head the title of His accusation: "THE KING OF THE JEWS." Likewise, they crucified two thieves, one on His right and one on His left, fulfilling the Scripture that foretold He would be numbered with the wicked (Isaiah 53:12). While passersby and religious instructors hurled insults at Him, sarcastically recalling His statement about the temple (John 2:19-21), the chief priests mocked His inability to save Himself.
[33-41] From the sixth hour until the ninth hour, from noon to three in the afternoon, darkness fell over the whole land. At the ninth hour, the Lord cried out in a loud voice, "Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?", which translates as, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" After uttering a loud cry, he gave up his spirit, at which moment the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom, accompanied by an earthquake (Matthew 27:51-53). Upon seeing the way the Lord expired, the Roman centurion in charge exclaimed: {{quote:Mark 15:39|Truly this man was the Son of God}}. Several women observe the event from afar, among them Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joseph, and Salome, who had followed and ministered to him from Galilee.
[42-47] On the evening of the eve of the Sabbath, the day of preparation for the great Passover feast (John 19:31), Joseph of Arimathea, a prominent member of the council awaiting the kingdom of God, boldly goes to Pilate to request the Lord's body. Surprised that he was already dead, Pilate verifies the death with the centurion of execution, refuting pagan theories about a mere fainting spell. Having obtained permission, Joseph buys a fine linen cloth, takes the body down from the cross, wraps it in the cloth, and places it in a tomb hewn out of the rock, rolling a stone across the entrance. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joseph attentively contemplate the place where the Lord is laid.

[1-8] After the weekly Sabbath and the Passover festival, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought aromatic spices to anoint the Lord's body, going very early to the tomb on the first day of the week. The mention of two different Sabbaths in the context of the Passion clarifies the chronology of the Lord's burial, refuting human traditions about the crucifixion occurring on a Friday. Upon arriving at dawn, the women observed that the large stone at the entrance had been rolled away by divine intervention. Inside the tomb, they saw a young man dressed in white, an angel sent from heaven, who announced to them the resurrection of the Lord Jesus of Nazareth, the crucified one, pointing to the empty place where they had laid him. The angel instructed them to go and tell his disciples and Peter that the Lord was going before them to Galilee, where they would see him according to his promise. The women fled from the tomb, terrified and astonished, saying nothing to anyone along the way because of their fear.
[9-20] The final section of the Gospel constitutes a legitimate and inspired portion of Holy Scripture, attested to by the oldest patristic testimonies and by the vast majority of biblical manuscripts, refuting the omissions of the corrupt Alexandrian manuscripts. Having risen on the morning of the first day of the week, the Lord first appeared to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. When she went to announce the news to those who had been with him, who were saddened and weeping, they did not believe her. Later, the Lord appeared in another form to two disciples walking toward the countryside, who went to tell the others, but they too were not believed. Finally, he appears to the eleven apostles as they are seated at the table, and rebukes their unbelief and hardness of heart for not having believed those who had seen him after his resurrection. In that context, the Lord gives them the Great Commission: “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature,” declaring that “whoever believes and is baptized will be saved,” while whoever does not believe will be condemned. The promised signs—such as casting out demons, speaking in new tongues, handling snakes, drinking deadly poison without harm, and laying hands on the sick for healing—constitute apostolic signs given to the Jewish apostles to confirm the word before the people of Israel (2 Corinthians 12:12, 1 Corinthians 1:22). After speaking to them, the Lord was taken up into heaven and sat at the right hand of God. The disciples went out and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming his word by the signs that accompanied it.

[1-5] After the death of Moses, God spoke to Joshua, son of Nun, Moses' servant, commanding him to cross the Jordan and enter the promised land (Joshua 1:1-2). Doctrinally, Moses represents the Law, while Joshua is a type of Jesus Christ (John 1:17). The Law cannot justify the sinner or bring him into the heavenly inheritance; the ministry of the new Joshua is necessary (Romans 3:20, Galatians 3:24, Acts 13:39). Joshua faithfully served Moses before being exalted to leadership, illustrating the principle of service and humility in the Christian life (Matthew 20:26-28, 1 Peter 5:6). The promise that no one will be able to stand against him all the days of his life {{quote:Joshua 1:5|As I was with Moses, so I will be with you}} is fully and prophetically fulfilled at the Second Coming of Christ, when the Lord will destroy his enemies without opposition (Malachi 3:2, Revelation 6:17).
[6-9] The Lord exhorts Joshua to be strong and courageous in dividing the land and keeping the Law (Joshua 1:6-7). Sources emphasize that this chapter records, for the first time in sacred history, a leader guided and placed directly under the authority of a written Book (Deuteronomy 31:26). Unlike the earlier patriarchs who received direct revelations, Joshua is the first ruler commanded to submit to the written Scriptures (Joshua 1:8). The command to meditate on the divine word day and night guarantees success and spiritual prosperity (Psalm 1:2-3), reminding him of God's constant presence with his servant (Joshua 1:9).
[10-15] Joshua gives orders to the officials to inform the people that they will cross the Jordan in three days, preparing provisions to possess the land (Joshua 1:10-11). The method of communication employed was to give instructions to the elders and officials so that they could distribute them to the multitude (Exodus 12:21, Exodus 19:7-8). Likewise, Joshua addresses the Reubenites, Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, reminding them of Moses' command to march armed at the head of their brethren to help them conquer the land before settling in their possessions east of the Jordan (Numbers 32:17-23, Joshua 1:12-15).
[16-18] The people respond to Joshua by promising absolute obedience to everything sent and commanded (Joshua 1:16). This declaration resembles the commitment expressed by the nation before Moses on Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:8). The Israelites stipulate that anyone who rebels against their orders will be put to death (Joshua 1:18), a sentence later applied in the execution of Achan for taking from the devoted things (Joshua 7:25). Finally, the people exhort Joshua himself to be strong and courageous, reflecting a mind aligned with the thoughts of the Lord (Philippians 2:5).

[1-7] Joshua secretly sends two spies from Shittim to reconnoiter Jericho (Joshua 2:1). Doctrinally, these two emissaries foreshadow the two witnesses sent to preach during the Great Tribulation before the Second Coming of Jesus Christ (Matthew 10:7, Mark 6:7, Revelation 11:3). Upon arriving in Jericho, the spies stay at the house of the prostitute Rahab (Joshua 2:1). Informed of the Israelites' presence, the king of Jericho demands that Rahab hand over the men (Joshua 2:2-3). Rahab hides the men on the roof under bundles of flax (Joshua 2:6) and lies to the royal messengers, claiming ignorance of their whereabouts to protect them and diverting the search toward the fords of the Jordan (Joshua 2:4-5, 7). Regarding Rahab's lie and the Egyptian midwives' lies (Exodus 1:15-20, Joshua 2:4-5), the sources clarify that this act does not validate the ethics of the situation or clarify values, but rather was a response to preserving life in a circumstance of oppression and persecution (James 2:25).
[8-13] Before the spies fall asleep, Rahab goes up to the roof and proclaims her faith, stating that she knows the Lord has given the land to Israel (Joshua 2:8-9). Rahab declares that fear has fallen upon the inhabitants of the city upon hearing how the Lord dried up the waters of the Red Sea and destroyed the Amorite kings Sihon and Og (Joshua 2:10-11). She solemnly confesses that the Lord God of Israel is God in heaven above and on the earth below (Joshua 2:11). This declaration of faith (Hebrews 11:31) was manifested in her actions by hiding and protecting the Israelite spies (James 2:25). Rahab requests an oath in the name of the Lord to preserve the lives of her father, her mother, her brothers, her sisters, and all that they possess, asking for the salvation of her household (Joshua 2:12-13, Acts 16:31). The spies accept Rahab's request and establish three strict conditions to guarantee their protection (Joshua 2:14, 18-20). First, they demand absolute secrecy regarding the mission (Joshua 2:14, 20). Second, they require that the scarlet cord or crimson thread used to lower them remain tied to the window of the house above the wall (Joshua 2:18, 21). This scarlet cord symbolizes the covering of the blood of Jesus Christ and the protection of the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:22-23, Matthew 21:31). Third, they require that the entire family remain gathered inside the house, with anyone who leaves the doors being held responsible for their own blood (Joshua 2:19, Exodus 12:22). Rahab lowers them through the window with a rope, since her house is built on the city wall (Joshua 2:15), and instructs the men to hide in the mountains for three days until the pursuers return (Joshua 2:16, 22).
[22-24] The spies remain hidden in the mountains for three days until the search ends (Joshua 2:22). Upon descending the mountain, they cross the Jordan River and report to Joshua that the Lord has delivered the entire land into the hands of Israel, since all the inhabitants of the land are fainthearted because of the people (Joshua 2:23-24). Prophetically, this report foreshadows the Lord's final victory and the faintheartedness of the inhabitants of the land at the Second Coming of Jesus Christ (Revelation 6:15-17).

[1, 2] The Israelites depart from Shittim, a site located in the plains of Moab (Numbers 25:1-3, Micah 6:5), where the river of life will flow during the Millennium (Joel 3:18), and camp for three days by the Jordan River before crossing (Joshua 3:1-2). This period of rest represents spiritual preparation through prayer and the study of Scripture before the battle, allowing them to consider the difficulties of a river swollen by the melting snows of Mount Hermon (Joshua 3:15).
[3, 4] The officers command the people to follow the ark of the covenant, maintaining a distance of two thousand cubits, equivalent to about three thousand feet (Joshua 3:3-4). Unlike the superior guidance previously provided by the pillar of cloud and fire (Exodus 13:21), divine guidance is now manifested on earth. Typologically, the separation of two thousand cubits portrays the two-thousand-year interval between the First and Second Coming of Jesus Christ (2 Peter 3:8), while the crossing of the Jordan represents entry into the heavenly inheritance and death to self.
[5-8] By commanding sanctification before the divine wonders (Joshua 3:5), Joshua, from the tribe of Ephraim (Numbers 13:8), gives commands to the Levitical priests. This authority exercised by a non-Levitical leader prefigures the Lord Jesus Christ, from the tribe of Judah (Hebrews 7:13-14), whose priesthood is superior to the Levitical order. The priests stop on the bank of the Jordan at Bethabara, the ford where the Lord was baptized by John (John 1:28, Acts 7:45), a type of baptism (1 Corinthians 10:1-2) and of the Second Coming. The ark's journey from Sinai, through Edom and Moab to the Jordan, traces the path of judgment that Christ will take in his glorious return to destroy his enemies (Revelation 18, Revelation 19).
[9-13] Joshua calls the congregation to listen to the words of the Lord (Joshua 3:9), a phrase that serves as the model for true biblical preaching in contrast to human psychology and positive thinking (2 Timothy 4:2, John 6:63). The passage proclaims the Lord as God of all the earth (Joshua 3:11), announcing the guaranteed victory over the seven Canaanite nations through the miraculous stopping of the river's flow (Joshua 3:10, Zechariah 14:9).
[14-17] When the priests stepped onto the overflowing riverbed, the flowing waters stopped and piled up in a heap near the city of Adam, by Zarethan, about thirty kilometers north of Jericho (Joshua 3:14-16). The people crossed over on dry ground opposite Jericho while the priests stood firm with the ark in the middle of the Jordan {{quote:Joshua 3:17|until all the people had finished crossing}}. On a spiritual level, this event teaches that victory over sin requires the believer's positional death to self and the stillness of faith before the power of God (Romans 6:3-4).

The people complete the crossing of the Jordan, and the Lord commands Joshua to select twelve men, one from each tribe, to take twelve stones from the riverbed where the priests' feet stood firm and carry them to the campsite (Joshua 4:1-3). Likewise, Joshua places twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan riverbed (Joshua 4:9). Doctrinally, these two monuments of twelve stones serve as a sign and memorial (1 Corinthians 1:22), typifying the death, burial, and resurrection of the believer in Christ (Romans 6:4). Being submerged in the waters represents death (Exodus 15:5, Revelation 18:21), while the retrieval of the stones to the promised land symbolizes resurrection to walk in newness of life. The cornerstone represents Jesus Christ as the stone rejected by the builders (1 Peter 2:7) who was raised by God as the living stone (1 Peter 2:4).
The priests carrying the ark of the covenant stood firm in the middle of the Jordan until everything God had commanded was fulfilled (Joshua 4:10). The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh crossed at the head with about 40,000 men, fulfilling their commitment to lead the march (Joshua 1:12-16, Joshua 4:12-13). On that day, the Lord magnified Joshua in the sight of all Israel, confirming his leadership as a type of the promised Prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:18, Acts 3:22-26). Once all the people had crossed, Joshua commanded the priests to come out of the Jordan; As they stepped onto dry land, the waters of the river returned to their place and overflowed its banks as before (Joshua 4:15-18).
The people came up from the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month and camped at Gilgal, on the eastern border of Jericho (Joshua 4:19). The term Gilgal means rolled away or removed, the place where God removed the reproach of Egypt from the nation through circumcision (Joshua 5:9). Joshua erected the twelve stones brought from the river at Gilgal to serve as a testimony to future generations in response to the question {{quote:Joshua 4:21|What do these stones mean?}}, reminding them that the Lord dried up the waters of the Jordan just as He did with the Red Sea (Joshua 4:23). The twelve stones represent the national unity of the twelve tribes redeemed by God (Exodus 28:17-21, 1 Kings 18:31-32, Revelation 21:19-20). Geographically, Gilgal is located west of the Jordan River, opposite the place where John the Baptist baptized centuries later, which gives meaning to his words about raising up children for Abraham from stones (Matthew 3:9). This miracle was intended to manifest the mighty hand of the Lord before all the peoples of the earth and to instill divine fear in Israel forever (Joshua 4:24).

The kings of the Amorites and Canaanites west of the Jordan were filled with sorrow when they heard how the Lord dried up the river before the Israelites. The Lord commanded Joshua to make sharp flint knives to circumcise the Israelites at Gilgal. The generation born in the desert during the forty years of wandering had not been circumcised, and the warriors who had left Egypt had died in the desert for disobeying the divine voice. After the entire nation was circumcised, they remained in the camp until they were healed. The Lord declared to Joshua, “Today I have rolled away from you the reproach of Egypt,” and that place was called Gilgal, a word that means rolled away or removed. Typologically, Gilgal represents the entrance into new life, preparation for spiritual warfare, and the mortification of the flesh. Likewise, the physical circumcision at Gilgal foreshadows the spiritual circumcision of the believer (Colossians 2:11-13), through which the soul is cut off and freed from the sinful flesh by the work of the Holy Spirit and the word of God. The children of Israel camped at Gilgal and celebrated Passover on the fourteenth day of the month at night in the plains of Jericho. The day after Passover, the people ate the fruit of the old grain of the land, unleavened bread, and roasted ears of grain. The manna ceased the day after they ate the fruit of the land of Canaan, the Israelites having no more manna. Doctrinally, the selection of the lamb on the tenth day of the month (Joshua 4:19, Exodus 12:3) is connected with the resurrection and presents Christ as the Passover of believers (1 Corinthians 5:7). The cessation of the manna marks the end of the miraculous wilderness sustenance, which is a prophetic type of how God will supernaturally feed the Jewish remnant fleeing into the wilderness during the Great Tribulation (Micah 7:14-15, Revelation 12:6, Revelation 12:14).
When Joshua was near Jericho, he looked up and saw a man standing before him with a drawn sword in his hand. Joshua approached him and asked if he was one of them or one of their enemies, to which the man replied: {{quote: Joshua 5:14|No; but as Commander of the army of the Lord I have now come}}. Joshua fell facedown to the ground, worshiping and asking what his Lord said to his servant. The Commander of the Lord’s army commanded Joshua to take off his sandals because the place where he was standing was holy (Exodus 3:5). Doctrinally, this Man is the theophany or pre-incarnate manifestation of the Lord Jesus Christ (Hebrews 2:10), the Commander-in-Chief and Unsurpassed Man of War (Exodus 15:3). The removal of the sandals connects this vision with the calling of Moses on Mount Sinai (Exodus 3:5), marking the beginning and end of the geographical route that Christ will travel at His Second Coming from Sinai to the Mount of Olives (Deuteronomy 33:2, Habakkuk 3:3-6, Zechariah 14:4).
